en: LiP 1.1: Homage to Rudra, to Hari, to Brahmā, to the Supreme Self,
the Lord of primordial matter and the individual soul, who brings about creation, preservation, and destruction.
Nārada, having worshipped Śaṅkara at Saṅgameśvara, at Hiraṇyagarbha, at Svarlīna, at Avimukta, and at Mahālaya— [all located] on the Lord of Mountains (the Himālayas).
Likewise in Raudra, Goprekṣaka, and the excellent Pāśupata;
in Vighneśvara, Kedāra, and Gomāyukeśvara.
Having visited Hiraṇyagarbha, Candreśa, Īśānya, Triviṣṭapa,
and Śukreśvara according to the prescribed rites, the sage proceeded to Naimiṣa.
Then the inhabitants of Naimiṣa, their minds filled with joy upon seeing Nārada,
honored him and prepared for him a seat worthy of his status.
Delighted, he occupied that seat offered by the best of sages;
being honored by the munis, he sat comfortably upon the excellent throne.
He recounted a discourse of manifold meanings based on the majesty of the *liṅga*;
at that very time, however, the Paurāṇika Sūta himself appeared.
The wise one went to Naimiṣa for the purpose of paying homage to the ascetics;
they then offered him both welcome and worship according to tradition.
The residents of Naimiṣa, however, were the disciples of Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana;
then, a desire to hear the Purāṇa arose within them.
Having seen that learned Romaharṣaṇa, who was extremely confident,
all those ascetics rich in austerity then questioned the Sūta, the sage.

The residents of Naimiṣa said: "O Sūta of great intelligence, you have [related] the meritorious Purāṇa-saṃhitā, which is endowed with the majesty of the Liṅga; [and so has] the sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana. (LiP 1.1.11)
Having served him for the sake of the ancient lore, we obtained the *Saṃhitā* from him;
therefore, O Sūta, best among the knowers of the Purāṇas, we question you.
Nārada [received] this divine Purāṇa-saṃhitā, which is endowed with the greatness of the Liṅga, concerning this very god Rudra, the Supreme Self.
Having visited the sacred fields and worshipped the lingas,
the illustrious Nārada, the son of Brahmā and a preeminent among sages, is present here.
Devoted to Bhava, you yourself, as well as we and Nārada,
ought to recount this meritorious Purāṇa in the presence of this sage.
"Everything has been accomplished with fruit; it must be known by you.
Thus addressed, that Sūta, the best of Paurāṇikas, was delighted in his heart.
Having first paid homage to Nārada, the son of Brahmā,
and to the meritorious souls of Naimiṣa, that wise one began to proclaim the Purāṇa.
Sūta said:
Having paid homage to Mahādeva, Brahmā, Janārdana, and likewise to Vyāsa, the lord of sages, I shall speak; I call upon the Liṅga to bear witness.
Sound is the very body of Brahman, the direct revealer of the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman);
it consists of the components of phonemes, is characterized by the unmanifest, and exists in manifold ways.
He consists of the syllables *a*, *u*, and *m*; he is gross, subtle, and higher than the highest;
his form is the syllable *oṃ*, his face is the *Ṛgveda*, and he is endowed with an even tongue.
He whose great neck is the Yajurveda and whose heart is the Atharvaveda,
the all-pervading one who transcends primordial matter (pradhāna) and the individual soul (puruṣa), and who is devoid of dissolution and origination.
Through *tamas* he is known as Kālarudra; through *rajas*, he is the one born from the golden egg;
through *sattva*, he is the all-pervading Viṣṇu; and in his state beyond qualities (*nirguṇatva*), he is Maheśvara.
Pervading the primary constituent and presiding over it in seven ways in succession,
the twenty-sixth principle, born from the Unborn, likewise exists in sixteen ways.

Having prostrated according to the proper rule before the one who has the form of the *liṅga* for the sake of the play of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal, I shall describe the auspicious origin of the *liṅga*.
Thus ends the first chapter in the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
Concerning the history of the Īśāna-kalpa, the great-souled Brahmā formerly composed this supreme Purāṇa known as the Laiṅga.
Indeed, [the scripture] consists of ten million verses, expanded into one billion;
it has been condensed into four hundred thousand [verses] by Vyāsa throughout all the intermediate versions.
In the ages beginning with the Dvāpara and following those of Brahmā and the others, the [cult of] Vyāsa was desired in ten ways;
the eleventh is declared to be the Liṅga, which I heard from Vyāsa.
O twice-born ones, the extent of this work here is eleven thousand verses;
therefore, I shall speak in brief that which was not heard by me in detail.
In the abridged version consisting of four hundred thousand verses composed by Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana,
the origin of the Liṅga is recounted here in eleven thousand verses.
First is the creation pertaining to Pradhāna, followed by that of Prakṛti and the Vaikṛta creations;
then the origin of this Egg and the eightfold covering of the Egg.
Śarva’s state of being born from an egg arises from his reliance upon the quality of rajas;
likewise, his state as Viṣṇu, his state as Kālarudra, and his reclining upon the waters are due to that same quality.
The creation of the Prajāpatis, as well as the lifting up of the earth, and furthermore,
the calculation of the day and night and the lifespan of Brahmā.
The hearing of the Brahman, as well as its yugas and kalpas, its divine and human years, and indeed its eternal nature— these belong to it.
The ancestral rite, the origin of the ancestors, as well as the dharma of those in the stages of life;
the non-increase of the world, and likewise the emergence of the Goddess’s power.
The state of female and male belongs to Viriñca; creation arises from the union of a couple.
Indeed, the eight names of Rudra were spoken during his weeping.
Furthermore, the dispute between Brahmā and Viṣṇu, the manifestation of the Liṅga, the penance of Śilāda, and likewise the vision of Vṛtrāri; LiP 1.2.12.
Then [the topics are] the prayer for a son born from a womb, the difficulty of obtaining such a son,
the dialogue between Śilāda and Śakra, and the state of being lotus-born.
The vision of Bhava, as well as that of the teacher and disciple during the Tiṣya ages,
the incarnations of Vyāsa, and likewise the Kalpas and Manvantaras.

And likewise, the nature of the Kalpas and their sequence according to the various names of the Kalpas; and within those Kalpas, specifically in the Vārāha Kalpa, the state of being Vārāha belonging to Hari.
The account of the Meghavāhana Kalpa, the majesty of Rudra,
and furthermore, the manifestation of the liṅga of the wielder of the Pināka bow in the midst of the sages.
The worship of the Liṅga, the procedure for bathing, the characteristics of purity, the majesty of Vārāṇasī, and the description of the greatness of the sacred field (kṣetra). LiP 1.2.17.
The number of Rudra-temples on earth and of the abodes of Viṣṇu,
as well as the description of the dwellings of the gods in the intermediate space and within this cosmic egg, [shall be told].
The fall of Dakṣa to the earth, his birth again during the Svārociṣa interval, the curse of Dakṣa, and likewise the release from that curse; LiP_1,2.19.
The description of Kailāsa, as well as the Pāśupata Yoga, the measurement of the four Yugas, and the extensive duties of the Yugas; LiP_1,2.20 //
The measure of the twilight periods and the conduct of Bhava during those twilights;
his dwelling in the cremation ground and his origin from the crescent moon.
Then there was the marriage of Śaṃkara and the procreation of sons;
through excessive indulgence in sexual union, there came the destruction of the worlds and fear.
The curse was made true by the gods, and Viṣṇu was protected in the past;
likewise, the emission of Rudra’s seed resulted in the birth of Gaṅgā’s son.
Likewise, at times such as eclipses and the like, bathing the *liṅga* yields fruit;
so too did the agitated mind of Dadhīca and the dispute between Upendra and him. 24.
The birth of the trident-bearing God of gods by the one named Nandin, the narrative of the devoted wife, and the investigation into the bonds of the individual soul (paśu-pāśa). LiP 1.2.25.
Knowledge characterized by worldly engagement, as well as that pertaining to liberation,
[is taught here], along with the birth of Vasiṣṭha’s sons and the lineage of the high-souled Vāsiṣṭhas.
The expansion of the lineage of the sages, the destruction of the power of the kings,
the wickedness of Kauśika, and likewise the binding of Surabhi.
The grief of Vasiṣṭha over his son, the lamentation of Arundhatī,
the dispatching of his daughter-in-law, and likewise the speech of the one still in the womb.
The incarnations of Parāśara, Vyāsa, and Śuka,
as well as the destruction of the Rākṣasas, were indeed accomplished by the son of Śakti.
Furthermore, by the command of his preceptor Pulastya, he attained the ultimate truth regarding the deities, as well as consciousness and the power to create the Purāṇas, through his grace.
The measurement of the worlds, the movement of the planets and luminaries,
the procedure for the Śrāddha for the living, those worthy of the Śrāddha, and the Śrāddha rite itself.
The ritual procedure for the Nāndī-śrāddha, as well as the characteristics of Vedic study, the power of the five sacrifices, and likewise the rules for the five sacrifices; LiP 1.2.32.

The conduct of women during their menses, the means of livelihood, the distinction of sons according to their mothers, and the rules for sexual intercourse, are set forth in sequence for each social class.
The rules regarding what may and may not be eaten for all social classes,
as well as the penances for every single transgression in full detail, [shall be explained].
The nature of the hells and the punishment corresponding to one's karma,
as well as the marks of men who have been gods or hell-beings in their future births.
Various kinds of gifts, as well as the city of the King of the Pretas, the Kalpa of the Five Syllables, and also the majesty of Rudra; LiP 1.2.36.
The great battle between Vṛtra and Indra, the crushing of Viśvarūpa,
the dialogue of Śveta with Death, and the destruction of Kāla for the sake of Śveta.
The entry of Śambhu, that is Śaṅkara, into the Devadāru forest;
the narrative of Sudarśana; and the characteristics of the gradual renunciation (kramasaṃnyāsa).
Then Rudra, who is to be accomplished through faith, was described by Brahmā at that time,
when the movement of the Lord had been seized by Madhu and Kaiṭabha in the past.
Hari assumed the form of a fish in order to receive the supreme knowledge from Brahmā;
and the birth of Viṣṇu in all his various states occurs solely through divine play (līlā).
The manifestation [of Viṣṇu] as Jīṣṇu arose through the grace of Rudra and Viṣṇu;
likewise, Hari assumed the form of a tortoise for the purpose of supporting the churning-stick.
The birth of Saṃkarṣaṇa, the rebirth of Kauśikī, the origin of the Yadus, and how Hari himself became a Yādava.
The wickedness of King Bhoja, the [story] of his maternal uncle, the lord Hari;
the childhood play of Hari, and the worship of Śaṅkara for the sake of a son. LiP 1.2.43.
And likewise, the birth of Nara from the Vaiṣṇava portion of Hari occurred within the skull;
furthermore, Hari performed the propitiation of Rudra for the purpose of removing the burden of the earth.
In ancient times, Vainya Pṛthu initiated the milking of the Earth,
and formerly Viṣṇu received a curse from Bhṛgu during the war between the gods and the asuras.
While Kṛṣṇa was in Dvārakā, Mādhava’s residence there was secured for his own benefit; however, a curse was received by Hari from the mouth of Durvāsas.
The curse upon the inhabitants of Piṇḍāraka for the destruction of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas,
as well as the origin of Eraka and the birth of Tomara.
Due to a dispute over the acquisition of land, there will be a conflict among the Vṛṣṇis;
and by Kṛṣṇa’s mere sport, his own lineage shall be destroyed.
By the power of the *erakā* weapon alone, one may travel according to one's own will;
furthermore, there is the very extensive knowledge of Brahmā and of liberation.
Of Purāṇ, Andhaka, Agni, Dakṣa, Śakra, the elephant, the deer, Madana, the primordial god, Brahmā, and the enemies of the gods.
The contempt shown by the wielder of the Pināka bow toward the Daitya Halāhala,
as well as the slaying of Jālandhara and the manifestation of the Sudarśana discus.
The acquisition of Viṣṇu’s excellent weapons, as well as the deeds of Rudra,
and likewise thousands of other exploits of Rudra.
Then follows the experience of the power of Hari, Pitāmaha, and the high-souled Śakra, as well as a description of the world of Śiva.
On earth, the world of Rudra; in the netherworld (pātāla), Hāṭakeśvara;
as well as the characteristics of austerities and the majesty of the twice-born.
The preeminence of all forms, and especially that of the linga form,
is proclaimed here in this linga in detail and in due order.
Having understood this summary of the Purāṇa, whoever recites it becomes liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Brahmā.
LiP 1.3: The Sūta said:
That which is without marks (aliṅga) has its root in the mark; the unmanifest (avyakta) is said to be the mark.
Śiva is said to be without marks (aliṅga), while the Śaiva [symbol] is traditionally known as the mark (liṅga).
That which they call Pradhāna and Prakṛti is the supreme subtle body (liṅga),
devoid of smell, color, and taste, and free from sound, touch, and the rest.
It is devoid of qualities, eternal, imperishable, and without marks;
it is characterized by auspiciousness, yet endowed with fragrance, color, and taste, as well as the characteristics of sound, touch, and the rest.
O best of the twice-born, the source of the world, the great being— both gross and subtle—
the body of all worlds, emerged spontaneously as the unmanifest mark from that which is without marks.
In seven ways, in eight ways, and likewise again in eleven ways,
the signs of the signless one have been spread out by Māyā.
From them, there arose a triad of principal deities whose essence was Śiva;
from one [of these] the universe came into being, and by one it was protected.
The entire universe has been seized and pervaded by Śiva alone;
he is both without mark (aliṅga) and with mark (liṅga), as well as the various forms consisting of both marked and unmarked manifestations.
And because he has described it exactly as it is, therefore Brahmā himself is the world;
that very Blessed One, the Supreme Lord, is without marks and is the seed.
The seed and the womb are seedless; the seedless is called the seed.
Here, however, the designation "Self" (ātman) applies to those for whom the seed and the womb are primary.
The supreme self, the sage, is Brahman by virtue of his eternally enlightened nature;
this same pure one is called Rudra, and in the Purāṇa he is called Śiva.
O twice-born ones, when Prakṛti was beheld by Śiva, she became Śaivī;
at the beginning of creation, she was endowed with the qualities (guṇas), though previously she was unmanifest by her very nature.
The entire universe, from the unmanifest (avyakta) up to the specific particulars (viśeṣa), has risen from her;
she is known as the "Unborn" (ajā), the sustainer of the universe, and is remembered as that primordial nature (prakṛti) belonging to Śiva.
He lay beside that unborn one— who was red, white, and black, single yet prolific,
the mother who possesses her own form— enjoying her.
But another goat abandons that very same goat after she has been enjoyed;
she is the unborn progenitor of the worlds, presided over by the Unborn.
At the time of creation, by the command of Brahmā, that great [ego] manifested from the primordial matter (pradhāna) presided over by the Supreme Person, through the three qualities (guṇas).
Impelled by the desire to create, the Great Principle (mahat), presided over by the Self, enters the unmanifest and imperishable and undergoes transformation for the sake of manifest creation.
The function of the Great One (mahat), however, consists of volition and determination;
from that Great One, which possesses the three qualities, arises the ego (ahaṃkāra), in which rajas predominates.
Enveloped by that very [tamas] and characterized by an excessive ego-sense (ahaṃkāra),
he indeed became the creator of the evolution of the gross elements from the subtle elements (tanmātra) of Mahat.
From the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) arises the subtle element of sound, from which the imperishable ether (ākāśa) is produced;
subsequently, that ether, which has sound as its cause, envelops the sound itself.
O twice-born ones, the creation of the elements from those subtle potentials has thus been proclaimed; likewise, O great sage, from space arises the subtle element of touch, and from that, the wind.
From that [sound] comes the subtle element of form (rūpamātra), from that fire, and from that taste;
from taste come the auspicious waters, and from those two [taste and water] comes the subtle element of smell (gandhamātra), and from that the earth.
O best of the twice-born, it enveloped space as mere touch;
then the wind, whose nature is action, blew, enveloping mere form.
The god Vibhāvasu himself indeed covered [the world] with the subtle element of taste alone;
the waters, whose essence consists of all tastes, covered it with the subtle element of smell alone.
The earth possesses those [qualities] plus five; from that, minus one, arise the qualities of taste.
The Lord Fire has three qualities; touch arises from two.
From that, O Lord, there arises the single, partless *avakāśa* (space);
and from those subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the creation of the gross elements (*bhūta*) is to be understood as occurring through mutual interaction.
The *vaikārika* [ego], which is indeed characterized by *sattva*, proceeds simultaneously;
thus, the creation from the *ahaṃkāra* is proclaimed here in this manner.
It has five sense organs and five organs of action;
and the mind, which is of a dual nature, exists for the purpose of attaining sound and the other objects of perception.
For the principles beginning with Mahat and ending with the Viśeṣas produce the cosmic egg;
from that, the Grandfather (Brahmā) emerged like a bubble upon the water.
That very Lord Rudra is Viṣṇu, the omnipresent Master;
within that egg are these worlds, and this entire universe exists therein.
The egg is surrounded on the outside by water ten times its size;
that water is likewise surrounded on the outside by fire ten times its size.
Fire, increased tenfold, is enveloped on the outside by wind;
wind, increased tenfold, is enveloped on the outside by space.
The wind, born of sound, is enveloped by space;
the cause of sound is indeed enveloped by the Great Principle (mahat), and that itself is enveloped by primordial matter (pradhāna).
They say that his self is the lotus-seated one (Brahmā), and that there are seven egg-enclosures;
indeed, it is said that within them there are millions upon millions of cosmic eggs.
In each of those places, four-faced Brahmās, Haras,
and Bhavas were then created by Pradhāna after they had obtained the presence of Śambhu.
Dissolution and likewise mutual [dissolution] are proclaimed as the beginning and the end; Maheśvara is the creator of creation, re-creation, and maintenance.
In the act of creation he is joined with *rajas*, in preservation he abides in *sattva*, and in dissolution he is dominated by *tamas*;
thus he is threefold according to the sequence.
He is the original creator of all beings, their destroyer, and their protector;
therefore, the god Maheśvara is Śiva, the sovereign lord of Brahmā.
Since Sadāśiva, Bhava, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā are the self of all, so too are these worlds within the single staff; he is the creator and the Grandfather.
O twice-born ones, this primordial creation, presided over by the Puruṣa, has been described by me; it was not preceded by conscious intent, and it was auspicious.
LiP 1.4, Sūta said:
Now, that which is the time of the first [creation] here is known as the day.
In brief, such is the night of the primary creation of the universe.
The omnipresent Lord brings about creation during the day and dissolution during the night;
yet this day and night of his is merely figurative, for no such [temporal] day and night truly exist for him.
During the day, all the divine manifestations, all the transformations, all the Viśvedevas,
all the Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis), and other great sages remain present.
At night all things dissolve, and at the end of the night they come into being;
day is its state of manifestation, while night is remembered as being of such a nature.
At the end of a thousand cycles of four yugas, there are fourteen Manus;
O twice-born ones, the Kṛta age consists of four thousand years.
The twilight period (saṃdhyā) of the Kṛta age is indeed three hundred years, as is its transitional period (saṃdhyāṃśa);
those of the Tretā and Dvāpara ages are respectively two hundred and one hundred years for both the twilight and the transitional periods.
From that [measurement], a six-hundredth part is the *saṃdhyāṃśaka*;
excluding this *saṃdhyāṃśaka*, the measurements are three thousand, two thousand, and one thousand [yojanas] respectively.
O you of virtuous vows, I shall describe to you the Tretā, Dvāpara, Kali, and Kṛta ages;
fifteen nimeṣas constitute one kāṣṭhā for one who is healthy.
O Brahmins, thirty of those *kalās* of a mortal’s eye are reckoned as one *muhūrta*. Thus is the *muhūrta* defined.
The night consists of fifteen muhūrtas, and the day is likewise;
a month constitutes the night and day of the ancestors (pitṛs), and their further division is as follows.
For them, the dark fortnight is the day and the night is for sleep;
thirty human months are traditionally reckoned as one month of the ancestors (pitrya).
Indeed, three hundred and sixty months constitute what is known as a year of the ancestors (pitrya) according to human reckoning.
That which constitutes one hundred years by human calculation is reckoned here as three years for the ancestors (pitṛs).
Indeed, ten months plus two more are remembered here as the number of months for the ancestors; this is according to the worldly measurement known as a human year.
"This is a divine day and night," so it is recited here in the *Laiṅga*;
a divine year consists of a divine day and night, and their division is as follows.
The northern course (udagayana) is their day, and the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) is their night;
these divine day and night are specifically reckoned in this manner.
Thirty human years, O Brahmins, are recorded as one divine month; three hundred human years, however, constitute three such divine months.
And likewise ten days; for this is remembered as the divine method.
As for those three hundred and sixty years, [they correspond to a single day in the divine reckoning].
For this divine year is proclaimed to be equal to three thousand human years in measure.
Thirty other years are considered a year of the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis);
that is nine thousand human years.
And there are ninety others; that is the Dhruva year, which consists of thirty-six thousand human years.
That hundred of years is to be known as the divine measure; indeed, this is recorded as the divine rule.
But they say that three million human years [constitute the lifespan of the gods].
Those who are experts in calculation state that sixty thousand [years] as reckoned by number constitute one thousand divine years.
The calculation of the number of yugas is determined by divine measure alone:
first is that which is called the Kṛta Yuga, and after that, the Tretā is ordained.
Dvāpara and Kali as well—these are the ages (yugas), O you of virtuous vows;
now the years have been observed according to human measurement.
O best of brahmins, it is proclaimed that the first Kṛta age measured by divine reckoning consisted of fourteen hundred thousand years in number.
Forty thousand years, as well as another [period], constitute the Kṛta Yuga;
likewise, ten thousand years multiplied by a hundred [constitute the Tretā].
The duration of the Tretā Yuga is said to be eighty thousand years,
and seven million human years as well.
The duration of the Dvāpara age is twenty thousand years,
and likewise three hundred thousand years by calculation.
The duration of the Kali Yuga is sixty thousand years;
thus the time of the four yugas is reckoned, excluding the transitional periods (saṃdhyāṃśaka).
Indeed, those [years] are thirty-six niyutas minus their fractional parts;
by calculation, they amount to forty-three niyutas here.
Twenty thousand years constitute the twilight period (saṃdhyāṃśa) of a cycle of four yugas;
thus, there are seventy-one such periods, plus a little more, that comprise what is called a cycle of four yugas.
The interval between Manus, comprising the Kṛta, Tretā, and other ages, is now described;
the duration of a Manvantara is proclaimed in terms of the total number of years.
O best of the twice-born, thirty-six million and sixty-seven hundred thousand years constitute a human lifespan.
O twice-born ones, this number of twenty thousand years, without any addition, is proclaimed in this *Laiṅga* as the measure of a *manvantara*.
Likewise, the number of years for a cycle of four yugas has been proclaimed;
indeed, O best of the twice-born, one thousand cycles of four yugas constitutes a single kalpa.
At the end of the night he creates the worlds, and at night living beings perish;
therein, however, there are twenty-eight crores of those who travel in celestial chariots (vaimānikas).
Indeed, the number of Manvantaras, along with the intermediate periods (Antaras),
is exactly three hundred and ninety-two crores.
O Brahmins, in a past eon, there were seventy thousand [kalpas], and likewise eight thousand more; in brief, this is the total for all of them.
When the dissolution has arrived, having abandoned those [beings] belonging to the end of the kalpa,
these people then depart from Maharloka for Janaloka.
Two thousand crores, eight hundred crores,
sixty-two crores, and seventy million.
Half a kalpa is indeed reckoned as one divine kalpa; in this manner, one should calculate a thousand such kalpas as a single year of the Unborn.
Eight thousand years constitute a single *yuga* of Brahmā;
indeed, a thousand such *yugas* form one day of the Creator, from whom all the gods originate.
A thousand such cycles of the three types of sacrifices, multiplied by three,
is declared to be the duration of the time of Brahmā, the Lord whose nature is time.
Bhavodbhava, Tapas, Bhavya, Rambha, Kratu,
Rtu, Vahni, Havyavāha, Sāvitra, and Śuddha.
Uśika, Kuśika, Gāndhāra, Ṛṣabha, Ṣaḍja, and Majjālīya—these are the Madhyamas, O best of sages. (LiP 1.4.46)
Vairāja, Niṣāda, Mukhya, Meghavāhana as the fifth, Citraka, Ākūti, and Jñāna.
Manas, Sudarśa, and likewise Bṛṃha, Śvetalohita,
Rakta, Pītavāsas, Asita, and Sarvarūpaka.
Thus, O best of sages, the kalpas of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest, are reckoned as thousands of millions upon millions of kalpas.
Furthermore, the remaining days and nights have indeed passed;
at the end of the cycle, all transformations everywhere undergo further transformation.
The withdrawal of the transformation occurs solely by the power of the command of Śiva;
and when the transformation has been withdrawn, the Pradhāna remains established in the Self.
Both Pradhāna and Puruṣa abide in a state of similarity; O Brahmins, it is traditionally held that creation occurs when there is a disparity among the guṇas.
The equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas) is the cause of those two [creation and dissolution], and Maheśvara is their cause;
by his divine play, such creations have been fashioned by the God of gods.
In brief, from the Pradhāna which is presided over by [the Lord], there are innumerable [emanations];
indeed, the eons called *kalpas* are innumerable, as are the Grandfathers (*pitāmaha*s).
Though the horses are innumerable, Maheśvara is indeed one alone;
yet the elemental manifestations, beginning with Pradhāna, proceed from him as if in sport.
And the activity of that deity, which consists of qualities, is indeed threefold;
for that Self, who is beyond material nature, there is no beginning, middle, or end.
Then, the period of the Grandfather (Brahmā) is twice a parārdha;
whatever has been created by him during the day perishes at night.
There, the worlds Bhūr, Bhuvas, Svar, and Mahas perish, as do those above them;
and at night, when all mobile and immobile beings have perished, Brahmā remains in the single ocean.
Because he slept upon the waters, he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa;
indeed, having awakened at the end of the night and seeing the world of moving and non-moving beings as empty, he [proceeded].
Then Brahmā, the best among the knowers of Brahman, the eternal one, resolved to create; taking up that earth which was submerged in waters, he set his mind upon it.
Assuming the form of a boar, the Lord established [the earth] as it was before;
he made the rivers, streams, and oceans just as they were previously.
Having diligently made the earth free from depressions and elevations,
he gathered all the mountains upon it that had previously been consumed by fire.
The Lord, the Creator, then again formed the resolve to create the four worlds beginning with Bhūr, just as before.
LiP 1.5: Sūta said:
When [Brahmā] set his mind upon creating, delusion arose within that Great Soul.
And the twice-born [were created] intentionally by Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest.
Tamas, moha, mahāmoha, tāmisra, and that which is called andhasaṃjñita—
this fivefold ignorance indeed manifested from the Self-Existent One.
The primary creation (mukhya-sarga) is remembered as being swallowed by the Sage through ignorance;
having realized that the primary creation was ineffective, Prajāpati [undertook another].
He indeed considered another; those known as the principal mountains arose from him.
As that sage was meditating, his throat indeed became threefold.
First, the horizontal stream (tiryaksrotas) was born from that great-souled one;
above that was the upward stream (ūrdhvasrotas), which is remembered as being of the nature of goodness (sāttvika).
Furthermore, there is the downward-flowing stream of grace, beginning with the primary elements;
of Brahmā and the Great Principle (mahat), the first is the primordial [stream] and the second is that of the material elements.
The third birth is that of the senses; the fourth is called the primary (mukhya);
the fifth is of animal origin, while the sixth is said to be divine.
O Brahmins, the seventh is the human, the eighth is remembered as the Anugraha, and the ninth is the Kaumāra; these are the natural (prākṛta) and the modified (vaikṛta) [ages].
In the beginning, the Lord created Sanandana, Sanaka, and Sanātana, O best of sages; through the state of actionlessness (naiṣkarmya), they have attained the Supreme.
By means of the science of yoga, he created Marīci, Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Dakṣa, Atri, and Vasiṣṭha.
These nine are the sons of Brahmā, knowers of Brahman, and the best of Brāhmaṇas;
they are indeed exponents of Brahman and are remembered as being equal to Brahmā himself.
Volition, Dharma, Adharma, and the Repository of Dharma—
these twelve are indeed the offspring of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest.
In the beginning, the Eternal One created Ṛbhu and Sanatkumāra;
they were both divine, celibate, the first-born, and exponents of the Veda.
The two youths were equal to Brahmā, omniscient, and destined for all things;
I shall now describe the families of their wives, those sages who were born from the first-born.
In brief, O best of sages, the Lord brought about the origin of progeny;
he created the queen Śatarūpā from Virāj.
From Svāyambhuva, however, the queen Śatarūpā— who was not born from a womb—
being virtuous, obtained two sons and likewise two daughters.
Uttānapāda was indeed the younger, while the wise Priyavrata was the elder;
Ākūti was known as the eldest and most excellent daughter, and Prasūti was remembered as the younger.
Then the lordly Prajāpati named Ruci married Upayeme— that is,
he wedded her— namely Dakṣa, the progenitor of the world, who was the blessed Yoginī Prasūti, the sustainer of the worlds.
Likewise, Ākūti gave birth to a sacrifice accompanied by sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā);
and Dakṣiṇā gave birth to twelve divine daughters.
Prasūti bore twenty-four daughters to Dakṣa:
Śraddhā, Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, Puṣṭi, Tuṣṭi, Medhā, and likewise Kriyā.
The one of great asceticism [bestowed] intellect, modesty, tranquility of body, accomplishment, fame,
renown, peace, prosperity, mindfulness, joy, and likewise forbearance.
He bestowed Saṃnati, Anasūyā, Ūrjā, Svāhā, Surāraṇi, and the highly fortunate Svadhā, each in their proper order.
And thirteen very beautiful daughters, Śraddhā and the others,
who were exceedingly difficult to obtain, went to their husband Dharmaprajāpati.
The wise Bhṛgu married that Khyāti, the daughter of Bhārgava; Marīci married Sambhūti, and the sage Aṅgiras married Smṛti.
The meritorious Pulastya [married] Prīti, the sage Pulaha [married] Kṣamā, the wise Kratu [married] Saṃnati, and Atri [married] Anasūyā.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha, the most excellent, [wedded] Ūrjā;
Vibhāvasu, the lotus-eyed one, [wedded] Svāhā; and likewise the Pitṛs [wedded] Svadhā.
She who was adopted as a daughter, born from the mind of Śiva and the sustainer of the worlds, remained with Rudra alone as her husband, even though she had been [given] by Dakṣa.
At the beginning of creation, upon seeing Ardhanārīśvara, the one born from the golden egg said,
"Divide yourself," and at that moment, when she was first born, she became so.
Likewise, all the women in the three worlds are born from her portions,
and the eleven types of Rudras are likewise born from his portions.
She indeed was the entire feminine gender, while Nīlalohita was the masculine gender;
seeing him, the Lord Brahmā looked toward Dakṣa and the lady of excellent vows.
Worship the Creator of the worlds, who is mine and yours as well;
for it is said here that she is called a "son" (putra) because she saves one from the hell named Put.
"This daughter of yours, O son of Kāntā, shall be praiseworthy and the mother of the universe;
therefore, she shall be known by the name Putrikā."
Thus addressed at that time, the sage Dakṣa, by the command of Brahmā,
having obtained his daughter, respectfully gave Satī herself to Rudra.
The thirteen wives of Dharma, beginning with Śraddhā, have indeed been proclaimed;
among them, I shall describe the offspring of Dharma in their proper order, unsurpassed in excellence.
Kāma, Darpa, Niyama, Saṃtoṣa, and Lobha;
Śruta, Daṇḍa, Samaya, and Bodha of great splendor.
O best of the twice-born, heedfulness, discipline, and perseverance,
as well as security, happiness, and fame, and indeed sons of righteousness, were born from them.
In the performance of dharma, indeed, there are both punishment and the agreement;
likewise, vigilance and awakening are the two sons of the intellect and of dharma.
Therefore, these fifteen were born from them; and here, Khyāti, the wife of Bhṛgu, gave birth to Śrī, the beloved of Viṣṇu, who is the daughter of Dharma.
Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ were the two sons born to Marīci’s wife named Prabhūti; they were the sons-in-law of Meru.
Then [he begot] Pūrṇamāsa and Mārīca, and from them four daughters:
Tuṣṭi, Jyeṣṭhā, Dṛṣṭi, and Kṛṣi, as well as Apaciti.
And Kṣamā bore to Pulaha four sons and one auspicious daughter, O best of sages: the most excellent Kardama, and Sahiṣṇu.
Likewise, Pulastya begot sons out of affection upon Prīti, who was golden-yellow, full-bodied, and equal to the earth.
The auspicious Saṃnatī gave birth to Dattorṇa, Vedabāhu, another daughter named Dṛṣadvatī,
and sixty thousand sons.
Kratu’s wives were all known as the Vālakhilyas;
[he also begat] Sinīvālī, Kuhū, Rākā, and Anumati.
And likewise, Smṛti, the wife of the sage Aṅgiras,
who was firm in her vows, gave birth to Agni, who had attained great power, and to Kīrtimat.
Anasūyā, the wife of Atri, indeed gave birth to six offspring;
among them was one daughter named Śruti, and five sons.
Satyanetra, Muni, Bhavya, Mūrti, Āpa, and Śanaiścara; and Soma is indeed the sixth—these are the five sons of Atri who are the Vedas.
The mother of sons, who was exceedingly fond of her children, obtained from Vasiṣṭha the power of vigor (ūrjā) and sons;
she, the one with beautiful eyes, was superior even to the lotus-eyed sons of Vasiṣṭha.
Rajas, Suhotra, Bāhu, Savana, Anagha, Sutapas, and Śukra— these were the seven sons of the sage.
And from that Lord Abhimānin, who is the self of Bhava and the vital breath of all creatures, the Fire born of Pitāmaha,
Svāhā gave birth to three sons for the welfare of the three worlds.
Sūta said:
Pavamāna, Pāvaka, and Śuci— these are remembered as the fires.
The Pavamāna fire is produced by friction, while the Vaidyuta is known as the Pāvaka.
Śuci is to be known as the son of Sūrya; they are his three sons, Svāhā’s progeny.
Here, the number of their sons and grandsons is recorded in brief.
Having first emitted the group of seven, and then forty-nine;
these are declared to be the fires that are brought forth in the sacrificial rites.
All these are known as ascetics, all are remembered as observers of vows;
all are lords of creatures, and all are remembered as being of the nature of Rudra.
The Pitṛs who have not performed sacrifices and those who have performed sacrifices are pleased in mind;
the Agniṣvātta Pitṛs are known as those who have performed sacrifices, while the remaining ones are remembered as the Barhiṣads.
Svadhā indeed gave birth to Menā, their mental daughter;
Menā was the mental daughter of Agniṣvātta, renowned throughout the world.
Menā gave birth to Maināka and to Krauñca, her younger sister Umā;
and from Himavat was born Gaṅgā Haimavatī, who purifies through her embrace with the body of Bhava.
Svadhā, whose face resembles a lotus, was the mind-born daughter of Merurāja; she performed sacrifices and became his wife.
The ancestors are declared to be the drinkers of nectar; listen now to their detailed account here, as well as the entire lineage of the sages, in its full extent.
I shall speak of that matter which is established in a separate chapter thereafter:
how Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, having become Pārvatī, went to the side of Rudra.
Afterwards, having censured Dakṣa, she obtained Bhava as her husband;
and meditating upon her, the blue-and-red Rudra emitted many Rudras.
O tigers among sages, when Brahmā requested that all beings equal to himself— who are honored by the entire world— be granted [as sons], he granted them in an instant with a smile.
By them, the entire fourteenfold world was completely covered;
having seen those various Rudras, stainless and blue-and-red in hue.
The Grandfather spoke of the Rudras as being liberated from old age and death:
"Homage be to you, O Great Gods, three-eyed and blue-and-red-hued! (LiP 1.6.14)
They are omniscient, all-pervading, long, short, dwarfish, and auspicious;
they have golden hair, destroy the gaze [of enemies], are eternal, awakened, and stainless.
Free from dualities, devoid of passion, and the souls of the universe,
these sons of Bhava are thus praised. Having then circumambulated Rudra, the auspicious Bhava, the Lord born from the golden egg spoke to the Rudras.
Homage be to you, O Mahādeva! O Śaṅkara, it does not behove you to create subjects who are free from death; O All-pervading Lord, O Sovereign, create them endowed with death.
Then the Blessed One said to him: "Indeed, my state is not such as yours;
therefore, O Lord, create at your will the subjects endowed with death."
Having received it from Śaṅkara, the four-faced one created this entire universe,
both moving and unmoving, subject to old age and death.
Then Śaṃkara, his self withdrawn by the Rudras and established in that state,
attained the condition of Sthāṇu, O brahmins, for that high-souled Śaṃkara.
Because Śambhu, the partless Self who assumes a body by his own will,
acts out of compassion to bring welfare (śam) to all beings, he is called Rudra.

And Śaṃkara, being of that very nature, effortlessly bestows through the science of yoga liberation upon the dispassionate one who abides in detachment; this is what is called "bestowing. ||| LiP_1,6.22 |||
In another system of philosophy, the abandonment of sense objects by a person arises gradually from fear of saṃsāra and leads to dispassion through the cultivation of detachment.
The primary means of liberation is the abandonment of defects through the non-discrimination of consciousness;
and the reconnection of that [consciousness] with this [body] occurs through the grace of the Supreme Lord.
Dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty—these originate here from Śaṅkara;
he alone is Śaṅkara himself, the wielder of the Pināka bow, Nīlalohita.
All those who have taken refuge in Śaṅkara are liberated without a doubt;
even the most wicked do not go to the terrible hell.
Therefore, those who have taken refuge in Śaṅkara attain the eternal state.
The sages said:
"The twenty-eight [deities], beginning with Ghora and ending with Māyā," LiP 1.6.27.
Tens of millions of sinners are cooked in those hells,
for they have not taken refuge in Śiva, Rudra, Śaṅkara, or Nīlalohita.
The support of all beings, the imperishable Lord of the worlds,
the Puruṣa, the Supreme Self, invoked by many and praised by many.
Through *tamas* he is known as Kālarudra; through *rajas*, he is born from the golden egg;
through *sattva*, he is the all-pervading Viṣṇu; and in his state beyond qualities (*nirguṇatva*), he is Maheśvara.
O Mahāmati, by what means do men go to hell—by action or even by non-action? We have a great curiosity to hear this.
LiP 1.7: Sūta said:
"I shall declare to you the secret concerning Bhava, who possesses immeasurable splendor."
The primordial power of Śaṅkara, the all-seeing one, [shall be told] in brief today.
The yogins, who know all principles, abide in supreme dispassion.
And they are accompanied by the eight means of practice, such as breath control (prāṇāyāma) and the rest.
Endowed with virtues such as compassion, even after performing various deeds,
they go indeed to hell or heaven according to their own karma.
From grace arises knowledge; from knowledge, yoga proceeds;
through yoga, liberation is born; therefore, everything [arises] from grace.
The sages said: "O best among those who know yoga, if you are pleased, you ought to explain the divine yoga of Maheśvara, as well as its essential nature and the means of realization."
How does the Lord Śiva, who is free from thought, bestow grace through the path of yoga? At what time does the All-pervading One grant this to human beings?
Romaharṣaṇa said:
"In former times, in the presence of the gods, the ṛṣis, and the ancestors, it was narrated by Śailādi; let them hear it from the son of Brahmā."
Likewise, O you of excellent vows, there are the incarnations of Vyāsa at the end of the Dvāpara age,
and similarly, during the Tiṣya age, there are the incarnations of the wielder of the trident as masters of Yoga.
In each of those places, the Lord had four disciples who were vessels of tranquility, and many were their own disciples; thus the Lord was truly pleased with them.
In this way, the knowledge that had come down through tradition was imparted by the Lord directly from his own mouth to men,
beginning with the Brāhmaṇas and ending with the Vaiśyas, out of compassion and according to their fitness.
The sages said:
"In every Dvāpara age, who indeed were the Vyāsas, and in which intermediate periods (antaras)? You ought to tell us here, in which Kalpa and in which specific instance they appeared."
Sūta said: "O twice-born ones, listen to [the account] regarding the Vārāha Kalpa within the Vaivasvata Manvantara,
as well as the Vyāsas and Rudras in all the intermediate periods."
I shall now duly proclaim, for all the current cycles, the Vedas, the Purāṇas, and likewise those that reveal knowledge.
Kratu, Satya, Bhārgava, Aṅgiras, Savitṛ, O twice-born ones, Mṛtyu, the wise Śatakratu, and Vasiṣṭha, the bull among sages; LiP_1,7.15 //
Sārasvata, Tridhāman, Trivṛta, the bull among sages Śatatejas, Svayandharma, and he who is known as Nārāyaṇa.
Tarakṣu, the wise Āruṇi, as well as the divine Kṛtañjaya, Ṛtañjaya, Bharadvāja, and Gautama, the best of poets; LiP_1,7.17 //
The sage Vācaśravas was manifest, as was the pure Śuṣmāyaṇi;
the sages Tṛṇabindu and Rūkṣa, as well as Śakti and his son Śākteya the elder.
Jātūkarṇya, Hari himself, the sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana Vyāsa, and these other Vyāsas— let them hear [this] in succession from the Lords of Yoga in the Kali age.
Indeed, throughout countless eons and all their intermediate periods, there have been,
due to the weight of [the world's need], innumerable incarnations of Rudra as Vyāsas during the Kali age, O Lord.
I shall further proclaim those incarnations which occurred during the Vaivasvata Manvantara in the Vārāha Kalpa, as well as all those that occurred in every other interval.
The sages said:
"You ought to tell us now of the Manvantaras in the Vārāha Kalpa, as well as of the Siddhas in the subsequent Kalpas within the Vaivasvata interval."
Romaharṣaṇa said:
O twice-born ones, Manu Svāyambhuva was the first; after him were Svārociṣa, Uttama, Tāmasa, Raivata, and likewise Cākṣuṣa.
Vaivasvata, Sāvarṇi, Dharma, Sāvarṇika, Piśaṅga, Apiśaṅgābha, Śabala, and likewise Varṇaka.
The Manus are proclaimed to end in the vowel *au* and begin with the vowel *a*;
they are Śveta, Pāṇḍu, Rakta, Tāmra, Pīta, and Kāpila.
O best of the twice-born, [the elephants] are Kṛṣṇa, Śyāma, Dhūmra, Sudhūmra,
Apiśaṅga, Piśaṅga, Trivarṇa, and likewise Śabala.
The Kālāndhurās are said to be auspicious men by their color;
they are described by name and color, and again by color alone.
In brief, those whose nature is the vowels are declared to be the intermediate lords (antareśas):
Vaivasvata is the vowel ṛ, while Manu Kṛṣṇa is Sureśvara.
I shall describe to you that seventh [chapter], concerning the yogins during the cycles of the ages (yugāvarta) throughout kalpas already passed as well as those yet to come.

The Vārāha [incarnation] is now to be known as occurring at the end of the seventh interval (manvantara) in due order; likewise, one should know the introduction of Yoga by the Lord, his disciples, and their lineage.
Having observed [the conduct] of yogins at all times and in such cycles,
[it is known that] in the first age Śveta was the Rudra, and likewise Madana was the Sutāra in the Kali age.
Suhotra, Kaṅkaṇa, Lokākṣi, Jaigīṣavya of great splendor, and the venerable Dadhivāhana, O best of sages.
And the wise sage Ṛṣabha, Ugra, Atri, Subālaka,
and the venerable Gautama, who is saluted by all the gods.
Vedaśīrṣa, Gokarṇa, Guhāvāsī, Śikhaṇḍabhṛt,
Jaṭāmālya, Aṭṭahāsa, Dāruka, and likewise Lāṅgalin.
Mahākāyamuni, Śūlin, Daṇḍin, Muṇḍīśvara himself, Sahiṣṇu, Somaśarman, and Nakulīśa, the teacher of the world; // LiP_1,7.35 //

Indeed, in the Vaivasvata interval, those who were the incarnations of the Yogācāryas— those of excellent vows who appeared throughout all the cycles— have been correctly proclaimed as manifestations of the Supreme Self.
And thus, O best of sages, in every Dvāpara age there are these Vyāsas;
each one has four imperishable disciples who are masters of yoga.
Śveta, Śvetaśikhaṇḍin, Śvetāśva, Śvetalohita,
Dundubhi, Śatarūpa, Ṛcīka, and likewise Ketumān.
Viśoka, Vikeśa, Vipāśa, Pāpanāśana,
Sumukha, Durmukha, Durdama, and Duratikrama.
Sanaka, Sananda, the lord Sanātana,
Ṛbhu, Sanatkumāra, Sudhāmā, and likewise Virajas.
Śaṅkhapāda, Vairaja, Megha, Sārasvata,
the best of sages Suvāhana, and the highly resplendent Meghavāha.
Kapila, Āsuri, as well as the sage Pañcaśikha,
and the great yogi Vālkala— all of whom were righteous-souled and possessed of great splendor.
Parāśara, Garga, Bhārgava, and likewise Aṅgiras;
Balabandhu, Nirāmitra, and Ketuśṛṅga, whose wealth is asceticism.
Lambodara, Lamba, Lambākṣa, Lambakeśaka,
Sarvajña, Samabuddhi, Sādhya, and likewise Sarva.
Sudhāmā Kāśyapa, Vāsiṣṭha Virajas, Atri Devasada, Śravaṇa, Śraviṣṭhaka,
Kuṇi, Kuṇibāhu, Kuśarīra, and Kunetraka.
Kaśyapa, Uśanas, Cyavana, Bṛhaspati,
Utathya, and Vāmadeva were also great yogis of immense power.
Vācaśravas, Sudhīka, Śyāvāśva, Yatīśvara,
Hiraṇyanābha of Kośala, Logākṣi, and likewise Kuthumi.
Sumantu, the learned Barbarī, Kabandha, Kuśikandhara,
Plakṣa, Dālbhyāyaṇi, Ketumān, and likewise Gopana.
Bhallāvin, Madhupiṅga, Śvetaketu, Taponidhi, Uśika, Bṛhadaśva, Devala, and Kavi; LiP_1,7.49.
Śālihotra, Agniveśa, Yuvanāśva, Śaradvasu,
Chagala, Kuṇḍakarṇa, Kumbha, and Pravāhaka.
Ulūka, Vidyuta, Maṇḍūka, Āśvalāyana, Akṣapāda, Kumāra, Ulūka, and Vatsa. (LiP 1.7.51)
Kuśika, Garbha, Mitra, and Kauruṣya—
these high-souled ones were the disciples of the yogins in all the āvartas.
Stainless, predominantly absorbed in Brahman, and devoted to the yoga of knowledge—
these are the perfected Pāśupatas, their bodies smeared with ashes.
Their disciples and grand-disciples, by the hundreds and thousands,
having attained the Pāśupata yoga, have established themselves in the world of Rudra.
Devas and others down to the Piśācas are proclaimed to be "bound souls" (paśus); because he is their lord, Bhava is known as Paśupati, the Lord of Bound Souls.
O twice-born ones, that Pāśupata yoga which was promulgated by Rudra, the Lord of Creatures, should be known for the sake of attaining both the higher and lower manifestations.
LiP 1.8: Sūta said:
I shall now describe the stations of yoga (yogasthāna) in brief.
O twice-born ones, these were fashioned by Śiva himself for the welfare of the worlds.
That which is one span below the throat and above the navel is the supreme station of yoga;
that below the navel is the lower, and that between the eyebrows is the middle.
The accomplishment of the knowledge of all objects is said to be the yoga of the self;
and through its grace, one-pointedness of mind shall indeed arise at all times.
O best of the twice-born, the true nature of serene faith (prasāda), which is to be personally realized, cannot be described even by Brahmā and the other gods; it arises in men gradually.
By the word "yoga," the state of Nirvāṇa, the station of Maheśvara, is expressed;
the cause of that is the sage's knowledge, and his knowledge [arises] through His grace.
One should burn away evil with wisdom, always restraining the sense objects;
for one whose sensory functions are restrained, the perfection of yoga will come to pass.
O best of the twice-born, yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind;
its eightfold means for accomplishment have been described here.
Yama is declared to be the first, and likewise Niyama is the second;
Āsana is declared to be the third, and after that comes Prāṇāyāma.
Withdrawal is indeed the fifth, and concentration follows after that;
meditation is said to be the seventh, while absorption is remembered as the eighth.
The cessation of ascetic toil is designated as *yama*;
non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), O best of self-restrainers, is the primary cause of *yama*.
Truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness—these are indeed the roots of restraint (niyama);
there is no doubt that they are rooted in self-restraint (yama) itself.
Acting solely for the benefit of all beings as one does for oneself—
this is declared to be non-violence (ahiṃsā), which bestows the accomplishment of self-knowledge.
Speaking of what is seen, heard, inferred, or personally experienced exactly as it is, while avoiding any harm to others, is called truth. (LiP 1.8.13)
"One should never utter anything vulgar regarding Brahmins; such is the Vedic revelation.
Furthermore, having recognized the faults of others, one should not speak of them. (LiP 1.8.14)
Not taking the property of others, even in times of distress, whether by thought, deed, or speech, when examined with discernment— this, in brief, is non-stealing (asteya).
The non-engagement in sexual intercourse through the actions of mind, speech,
and body is declared to be *brahmacarya* for ascetics and students of sacred knowledge.
In this regard, I shall describe to you specifically the household life of the Vaikhānasas and the Vidāras, including their wives.
Always engaging with one's own wife according to the prescribed rule and always abstaining from others in thought, deed, and speech— this is remembered as *brahmacarya*.
Having engaged in sexual union with his own wife, who is pure, he should perform a bath;
thus the householder whose mind is disciplined is undoubtedly a celibate student.
In the same way, even this non-violence (ahiṃsā) [is defined] by the ritual procedure for worshiping Brahmins, gurus, and fire;
for that very kind of violence which is performed according to the rule is traditionally known as non-violence.
Women should always be avoided and one should never form an attachment to them;
a wise man should regard them as he would a corpse.

Just as one directs the mind toward the external ground at the time of voiding feces and urine, so too should it be directed during sexual union with one's own wife; for what need is there for another?
A woman is like glowing coals, and a man is like a jar of clarified butter;
therefore, one should avoid association with women from afar.
Upon reflection, there is no satisfaction in the enjoyment of sense objects;
therefore, detachment must be cultivated through mind, deed, and speech.
Desire is never quenched by the enjoyment of desired objects;
rather, like a fire fed with clarified butter, it increases all the more.
Therefore, renunciation should always be practiced by the yogi for the sake of immortality;
for as long as one is not dispassionate, a mortal wanders through various wombs.

"O best among the knowers of the Śruti and Smṛti, O most excellent of the twice-born, immortality is attained through renunciation alone; it is not attained through ritual action, progeny, or material wealth."
Therefore, detachment should be practiced through the actions of mind, speech, and body;
the cessation [of sexual union] during every fertile period is traditionally known as *brahmacarya*.
The restraints (yamas) have been briefly declared; now I shall tell you the observances (niyamas):
purity, sacrifice, austerity, charity, study of the Vedas, and restraint of the generative organ. (LiP 1.8.29)
Vows, fasting, silence, and bathing—these are the ten observances (*niyamas*).
Furthermore, *niyama* consists of non-exertion, purity, contentment, and likewise austerity.
Recitation, meditation on Śiva, and likewise postures such as the lotus and others are prescribed;
purification is said to be both external and internal, but internal purification is superior.
Being endowed with external purification, one should likewise practice internal purification;
those who worship Śiva must perform the purifications pertaining to Agni, Varuṇa, and Brahmā.
Having performed the bath properly according to the prescribed rules, one should thereafter practice the internal [rite];
always, until the end of the body, one should smear oneself with clay while in the waters of sacred fords.
For even though they have plunged into it, the Śaivalas, Jhaṣakas, and Matsyas— beings who subsist on fish— remain inwardly impure and devoid of purity.
O best of the twice-born, since you are purified by always plunging into water,
you should therefore always practice internal purity according to the prescribed rule.
Having bathed in the waters of self-knowledge and having once smeared oneself with the clay of excellent dispassion through devotion, one becomes pure; this is proclaimed as true purification.
Accomplishments are seen for one who is pure, but never for one who is impure;
he who is firm in his vows is content with a livelihood obtained through righteous means.
He is constantly contented and does not dwell upon the past;
he is skilled in the Cāndrāyaṇa and other such fasts, as well as in auspicious ascetic practices.
The recitation of the sacred texts is declared to be *japa*, which is remembered as being of three kinds:
the vocal is the lowest, the primary [mental] is the intermediate, and the whispered (*upāṃśu*) is the highest of all.
The mental [practice] is taught in detail in the *Pañcākṣara-kalpa*;
likewise, there is the dedication to Śiva through the actions of mind, speech, and body.
Knowledge of Śiva, unwavering and firmly established devotion to the Guru,
and the swift restraint of the senses that have become attached to their objects.
The withdrawal of the senses from their objects is briefly proclaimed as *pratyāhāra*;
the binding of the mind to its location is briefly declared to be *dhāraṇā*.
Through her well-being, there arises meditation (dhyāna) and concentration (samādhi) by means of discernment.
In that state, meditation is one-pointedness of mind, free from other mental objects.
When the object of consciousness appears as if devoid of a body, that is samādhi;
it is also remembered as the cause of all and is called prāṇāyāma.
Prāṇa is the wind born from one's own body; yama is its restraint.
Yama is declared by the twice-born to be threefold: namely, low, middling, and superior.
The restraint of the prāṇa and apāna breaths is proclaimed as prāṇāyāma;
the measure of prāṇāyāma is traditionally held to be twelve mātrās.
The low [breath] consists of twelve mātrās, while the elevated is recorded as twelve;
the middle, however, has two elevations and consists of twenty-four mātrās.
The primary [breath], however, which consists of thirty-six mātrās and is called *triruddhāta*,
produces perspiration, trembling, and rising up, respectively.
For the sake of the yoga arising from bliss, there likewise occurs drowsiness and rolling about,
as well as horripilation, the awareness of sounds, the twisting of one's own limbs, and trembling.
When that consciousness, born of perspiration, becomes a state of whirling and fainting,
then that most excellent and beautiful breath-control (prāṇāyāma) is said to be the "highest of the high" (uttamottama).
That which is "with seed" (sagarbha) is said to be "with recitation" (sajapa), and that which is "without seed" (agarbha) is "without recitation" (vijapa), respectively;
it is like an elephant, or a śarabha, or even a lion, difficult to overcome.
Just as one who has been seized and subdued becomes healthy,
so too the vital breath (samīraṇa), when it is unsteady, is difficult for yogins to master.
But when served according to the proper method, he shall likewise attain composure,
just like the king of beasts, the elephant, or even the fierce śarabha.
Through practice over the course of time, one is disciplined with the utmost care;
likewise, through familiarity, one attains composure and equanimity.
For one who practices through yoga, no calamity whatsoever arises;
thus practiced, O Sage, his vital breath shall utterly consume [all impurities].
Just as one protects the body of the agent from the defects born of mind, speech, and body,
so too does the wise person who is properly engaged in breath control (prāṇāyāma) protect it.
Because of that defect, [the vital breaths] perish; therefore, they are digested by exhalation.
Through *prāṇāyāma*, the divine states such as tranquility (*śānti*) and the rest are gradually accomplished.

O twice-born ones, peace (śānti), tranquility (praśānti), radiance (dīpti), and clarity (prasāda) are declared here, in this sequence, as the fourfold [manifestations] at the beginning; among these, O brahmins, peace is described first.
The pacification of both innate and adventitious evils is taught;
it is traditionally remembered as tranquility, self-restraint, and the correct application of speech.
O twice-born ones, light is said to be radiance that is present everywhere and at all times;
it is the clarity of all the senses, as well as of the intellect and even of the vital winds.
In this context, "serenity" (prasāda) is said to reside within the mind and the fourfold group consisting of prāṇa,
apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna.
Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkala, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya—
the grace of these is traditionally remembered as that of the Maruts.
Because it initiates movement, it is known as *prāṇa*;
the *apāna*, however, carries away food and other substances in their proper sequence.
Vyāna causes the limbs to tremble and provokes diseases and other ailments;
this Udāna is proclaimed to agitate the vital points (marmans).
The Samāna wind equalizes the limbs; among the five winds, Nāga is said to be responsible for belching, while Kūrma is for the opening of the eyes.
Kṛkala is like the sound of sneezing; Devadatta is manifested in yawning; Dhanañjaya is a great roar; and Sarvaga indeed exists even when one has died.
Thus, for one who achieves mastery over the ten winds through breath control (prāṇāyāma), there arises a state of clarity; O Brahmins, this is the fourth designation among the fourfold group.
Viśvara, Mahān, Prajña, Manas, Brahmā, Citis, Smṛtis,
Khyātis, Saṃvits, and thereafter Īśvara and Mati.
O twice-born ones, these are proclaimed to be the designations for the intellect (buddhi) and the Great Principle (mahat).
The clarity of this intellect, however, is accomplished through breath control (prāṇāyāma).
O best of sages, he is the manifold and the state of manifoldness of all dualities;
he is the first-born of all principles and is great in extent.

O best among the knowers of Brahman, that which is the cave of the means of valid cognition is wisdom (prajñā), while the mind (manas) is so called because it cogitates; and because of its vastness and its capacity to nourish, it is Brahman.
That which accumulates all actions for the sake of experience is known as *citi*;
that which remembers everything is *smṛti*, because consciousness (*saṃvit*) indeed perceives it all.
That which is manifested is called "manifestation" (khyāti) in various ways through knowledge and other means;
for the Lord, the sovereign of all principles, knows everything. (LiP 1.8.73)
O best among the wise, because it thinks and reflects, it is called *mati*;
and because it causes the object to be understood and is itself understood, it is called *buddhi*.
The clarity of this intellect, however, is accomplished through breath control (prāṇāyāma);
by means of breath control, that self-restrained one burns away all defects. (LiP 1.8.75)

One should burn away sin through meditative concentrations (dhāraṇās) and withdraw the senses through withdrawal (pratyāhāra); one should contemplate sense-objects as poison and, through meditation (dhyāna), [burn away] those qualities that do not belong to the Lord.
Through meditative concentration, the best of ascetics should increase the growth of wisdom;
having indeed attained a stable state, they should practice the eight limbs of yoga in their proper sequence.
Having duly obtained seats for the sake of attaining yoga, the knower of the self [should practice],
for indeed there is no fixed rule regarding the place or time for yoga.
Near a fire, or even in water, as well as on a heap of dry leaves, in a cremation ground infested with creatures, in a dilapidated cow-pen, or at a crossroads; LiP 1.8.79.
In a place that is noisy or fearful, or where there is a heap of shrines and anthills;
in an inauspicious spot, one frequented by wicked people, or infested with mosquitoes and the like.
One should not practice when there is bodily affliction or when dejection and the like arise;
rather, one should do so in a well-concealed, auspicious, and delightful mountain cave.
Whether in a well-guarded field of existence, or in a grove within the garden of existence, or in a very beautiful house in a secluded place devoid of living beings; LiP_1,8.82 //
In a place that is utterly pure, well-smeared, and variegated, resembling the surface of a mirror and well-perfumed with black agallochum; LiP_1,8.83.
It was strewn with various flowers, beautified by a canopy above,
rich with fruits, sprouts, and roots, and provided with *kuśa* grass and blossoms.
Seated in a secluded place, he himself should joyfully practice the limbs of yoga,
after first prostrating before the Guru, Bhava, the Goddess, and Vināyaka.
The knower of yoga, having assumed the svastika, padma, or ardhāsana posture, should practice yoga together with the lords of yogis and their disciples.
Likewise, the wise one, having made his knees even— or even with one knee—
and having drawn together both feet, should remain with a steady and firm posture.
With his mouth covered, his eyes bound, and his chest pressed forward,
he should protect his testicles with his two heels and likewise his generative organ.
With his head slightly raised, he should not let his teeth touch one another;
he should gaze at the tip of his own nose without looking toward the directions.
Having veiled *tamas* with *rajas*, one should veil *rajas* with *sattva*;
then, established in *sattva*, one should practice the meditation on Śiva.
With a concentrated mind, one should meditate upon that which is denoted by the syllable *oṃ*— the supreme, pure [reality] in the form of a lamp flame— within the pericarp of the lotus.
Or else, the wise man, having meditated upon an excellent lotus below the navel—
either three finger-breadths [in size], or eight-cornered, or even five-cornered— LiP_1,8.92.
And likewise, the triangle belongs to Agni, Soma, and Sūrya along with their respective powers;
or alternatively, it follows the sequence of Sūrya, Soma, and Agni.
Then, according to the prescribed rule, one should likewise arrange the [mandalas] of Agni, Sūrya, and Soma below the fire; thus is the tetrad of Dharma and the others established.
One should visualize the three qualities (guṇas) in sequence upon the mandala;
one should contemplate Rudra, established in sattva and adorned by his own Śakti.
One should perform meditation according to the prescribed rule at the navel, or at the throat, or between the eyebrows, or on the forehead, or upon the crown of the head.
One should meditate upon Śiva within a two-petaled lotus, or a sixteen-spoked wheel, or sequentially in a twelve-spoked, ten-spoked, six-cornered, or four-cornered [mandala].
Whether it be golden-hued, resembling a temple, or very white;
whether it resembles twelve suns or the orb of the moon.
With a concentrated mind, one should contemplate the Supreme Lord in a place resembling ten million flashes of lightning,
or in a fiery color, or with the luster of a circle of lightning.
In a place possessing the luster of a diamond-peak, or resembling a ruby,
or having a blue-and-red form, the yogi should practice meditation.
One should meditate on Maheśvara in the heart, Sadāśiva in the navel-lotus,
the Moon-crested Lord on the forehead, and Śaṅkara himself between the eyebrows.
And in the divine, eternal abode, one should practice meditation on Śiva—
Brahman, which is stainless, partless, perfectly peaceful, and whose nature is knowledge.
It is without characteristics, indefinable, subtler than the subtle, and auspicious;
it is without support, beyond reasoning, and devoid of both destruction and origination.
It is indeed isolation (kaivalya), liberation (nirvāṇa), the unsurpassed supreme good (niḥśreyasa),
the immortal, the imperishable Brahman, the marvelous state beyond rebirth.
The auspicious one, who is great bliss, supreme bliss, the bliss of yoga, and free from ailment; who is devoid of anything to be rejected or accepted, and subtler than the subtlest.
That supreme Śiva, consisting of pure knowledge, is self-cognizable yet unknowable;
it is beyond the senses, devoid of appearance, the highest reality, higher than the highest.
Freed from all limiting adjuncts, attainable through meditation by means of inquiry,
non-dual, and situated beyond even darkness— that is the Supreme.
One should contemplate Mahādeva within the mind, or likewise in the lotus of the heart;
or one may contemplate the all-pervading Sadāśiva, the soul of all gods, in the navel.
One should [meditate upon] the pervasive Lord Śiva, who consists of pure knowledge, within the center of the body;
and one should likewise [worship] Śaṅkara by means of the "small" path and also through the upward thrust (udghāta).
The wise practitioner of excellent vows should practice the kumbhaka gradually, beginning with the lowest, then the middle, and finally the highest.
The wise one, composed in mind, should exhale thirty-two times at the heart and the navel;
O best of the twice-born, having abandoned both exhalation (recaka) and inhalation (pūraka), he should practice retention (kumbhaka).
One should meditate on Śiva within the center of the body through the very state of direct union;
having thus attained oneness, that which arises there from the essence [of that state]— LiP_1,8.112.
The knower of Brahman as bliss, established directly in the state of equal flavor,
[attains] twelve *prāṇāyāmas* as *dhāraṇā*, and twelve *dhāraṇās* as *dhyāna*.
Meditation up to twelve stages is designated as *samādhi*;
alternatively, O Brahmins, it arises simply from contact with those who possess knowledge.
O twice-born ones, through effort, those two may become equal either after a long time or quickly;
however, obstacles to yoga arise again for him as he practices.
Even those [obstacles] perish through practice, indeed, by means of the preceptor’s formal resolve.
LiP 1.9 Sūta said:
First comes indolence, and afterwards the affliction of disease arises.
Heedlessness is the mind's lack of stability here in a state of doubt.
From that arise lack of faith, false vision, delusion, and the three kinds of suffering,
as well as dejection regarding unsuitable objects and the notion of suitability regarding them.
Ten obstacles to the yoga of the sage arise:
laziness and lack of application, due to the heaviness of body and mind.

Diseases arise from an imbalance of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), as well as from karma and from the humors (*doṣa*); negligence, however, consists in the failure to cultivate the means for meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The consciousness that touches upon both "this" and "that" is doubt regarding the locus;
indeed, for a yogin, this lack of stability is the state of an unsettled mind.
And even when a stage has been attained, there is the mind's bondage to existence;
likewise, there is the state of being devoid of faith regarding the means of accomplishment.
Indeed, when there is a misconception regarding the object of attainment—the Guru, the practice of knowledge, Śiva, and so forth—it is called the vision of delusion (*bhrāntidarśana*). (LiP 1.9.7)
The perception of a self in that which is not-self arises from ignorance in its proximity;
this is declared to be internal suffering, as well as suffering caused by external beings.

That which is called *ādhidaivika* (caused by divine or supernatural agencies) has been described; furthermore, that which is innate (*sahaja*) is declared to be the agitation of the mind resulting from the frustration of one's desires.
Sorrow is to be suppressed by means of supreme dispassion;
for the mind is known as "depressed" when it is touched by both *tamas* and *rajas*.
Then, that which arises in the mind is known as *daurmanasya* (dejection),
occurring through the forceful acceptance [of objects] regardless of the discrimination between what is suitable and what is unsuitable.
For living beings, the greed for sense objects amidst the various sensory realms is known as an obstacle; indeed, these are the obstacles to yoga for practitioners of yoga.
For one endowed with extreme enthusiasm, obstacles perish without a doubt; O twice-born ones, once the obstacles have been destroyed, the yogin subsequently [attains his goal].
All such portents that arise are indicators of failure;
the first accomplishment is intuitive inspiration (*pratibhā*), and the second is said to be the hearing [of the mantra] (*śravaṇa*).
O best of Brahmins, the third is Vārttā, and the fourth here is Darśanā;
the fifth is declared to be Āsvādā, and the sixth is remembered as Vedanā.
By renouncing even the slightest of the six supernatural powers (ṣaṭsiddhi), the powers of the sage bestow true success;
such is the established rule regarding intuition (pratibhā), the veil of intuition (pratibhāvṛti), and the manifestation of intuition (pratibhāva).
Intellect is discernment; that by which the object of knowledge is understood is called intellect.
It perceives the subtle, the concealed, the past, the remote, and the future.
Through the sequential unfolding of intuitive insight, the yogi possesses knowledge of all things at all times,
hearing all sounds without effort.
Even from hearing the secret syllables such as the short, long, and protracted [vowels],
that which is the attainment of touch is indeed established as sensation (vedanā).
From the sight of those of divine form, there is the vision [of them] without effort;
in that divine essence of consciousness, there is indeed the savoring of it without effort.
And through the cognition of the intellect regarding those subtle elements of divine fragrances, O twice-born ones, yogins perceive [all things] up to the world of Brahmā. (LiP 1.9.21)
For in this world, O twice-born ones, that which resides within the body consists of sixty-four qualities; among these qualities, the secondary afflictions (aupasargika) are multiplied.

O twice-born ones, in the city of the Piśācas and also in the city of the Rākṣasas, one must by all means completely abandon everything pertaining to the self that is subject to affliction, as well as earthly and watery things.
In the Yakṣa [mantra], it is said to be of the nature of fire; in the Gāndharva, it consists of wind;
in the Aindra, it is entirely of the nature of space; and in the Saumya, it is indeed mental.
In the Prājāpatya [kalpa] there is egoity (ahaṅkāra), and in the Brāhma [kalpa] there is unsurpassed consciousness (bodha);
in the first [kalpa] there are eight [forms], and in the second likewise sixteen forms.
In the third [day] there are twenty-four, in the fourth thirty-two, and in the fifth forty; it is remembered as consisting of the elements and the subtle constituents (bhūtamātra).
Smell, taste, form, sound, and likewise touch—each of these five is established as eightfold; such is the case with the fifth, belonging to Śatakratu.
Likewise, O best of the twice-born, one obtains forty-eight, fifty-six, and sixty-fourfold merit pertaining to Brahmā.
The knower of yoga, having perceived through yoga the supreme bliss in the worlds, should abandon all adventitious afflictions throughout the realms up to the world of Brahmā.
Bigness, shortness, childhood, old age, as well as youth,
the forms of various species, and the maintenance of the body by means of the four [elements].
Constantly free from any earthly element, yet endowed with a fragrant scent—
this is declared to be the great eightfold sovereignty of the earth-lord.
Just as one dwelling in water might emerge upon the earth,
so a capable person, being unafflicted, would wish to drink even the ocean itself.
Wherever he desires in this world, there he sees water; whatever object he wishes to take up and enjoy according to his desire, [he obtains it].
The maintenance of the bodies of those three, endowed with their respective fluids,
is like holding a mass of water in the hand without a vessel.
The flawlessness of the body, endowed with the quality of earth—
this is declared to be the sixteenth, the supreme sovereignty pertaining to water.
One may emanate fire from one's body, free from the fear of its heat;
even if the world is burned here, another remains unburned through one's own power of creation.
Having placed fire in the midst of water for protection,
the suppression of that fire occurs in his hand, and he returns by the mere power of remembrance.
The manifestation of the body as ashes occurs according to one's will as it did before;
the accomplishment of form through two [means] occurs without those three for oneself.
O best of sages, this Taijasa principle consists of twenty-four constituents;
it is the movement of the mind and likewise the internal dwelling place of all beings.
Furthermore, carrying great burdens such as mountains upon one's shoulders, as well as both lightness and heaviness, and the supporting of the wind with the hands; LiP 1.9.40.
The shaking of the entire earth by the strike of a fingertip,
and the manifestation of a body by means of a single [breath]— this is known by the wise as mastery over the winds.
The manifestation of the sense organs without shadows, the vision of the senses, and constant movement through the sky while endowed with the objects of the senses; LiP 1.9.42.

The perception of sound at a distance, the comprehension of all sounds, the grasping of their subtle causal signs (*tanmātra*), and the manifestation of all living beings [occur through this]. 1.9.43.
It is said that Indra’s sovereignty consists of these things as declared by the ancients:
the attainment of whatever one desires and the departure at will.
Mastery everywhere, the manifestation of all secrets, the creation of emanations according to desire, sovereign power, and being pleasing to behold.
The vision of saṃsāra, the mental characteristics of the qualities (guṇas),
as well as cutting, striking, binding, and the revolving of saṃsāra.
It brings favor from all beings and likewise victory over the time of death;
this is declared to be the Prājāpatya rite, the supreme among those pertaining to the ego (āhaṅkārika).
The creation of the world without a cause, as well as its favoring, dissolution, the exercise of authority, and the setting in motion of the worldly course; LiP_1,9.48 //
This manifest creation is clearly distinct from that [previous] one;
this supreme state of Brahmā is the agency over the cycle of worldly existence.
"This much is the reality," it was said; the state of Viṣṇu is indeed preeminent.
That [reality] can be known through its qualities by Brahmā, but it cannot be known by others.
That supreme Śaiva state exists, which is not even comprehended by Viṣṇu;
who could know that pure essence of Śiva, possessed of innumerable qualities?
These perfections during the state of emergence are indeed proclaimed to be obstacles;
they must be restrained with effort by means of supreme dispassion.
Having understood that there is no excellence in sense objects and that they are sources of fear,
one who abandons everything through lack of faith is proclaimed as "dispassionate" (virakta).
The state of being free from thirst (vaitṛṣṇya) is well known in relation to the Person; it is called freedom from craving for the qualities (guṇavaitṛṣṇya).
By means of dispassion alone, even the supernatural powers (siddhis) that arise as obstacles must be renounced.
One should abandon all that is adventitious even up to the worlds of Brahmā;
by restraining everything and renouncing it, Maheśvara becomes propitious.
When he is pleased, liberation is stainless through supreme detachment;
or else, for the sake of bestowing grace or for the sake of divine play, the Sage [acts] at that time.
He who would exert himself without restraining [his senses] will likewise become happy;
having abandoned the earth in certain places, he indeed sports in the sky with splendor.
In some places he would utter the Vedas, and in brief, their subtle meanings; in other places, having heard them along with their meaning, he composed them in verse.
In some cases, one may perform the *daṇḍakabandha* or the *bandha* a thousand times;
thus, one attains knowledge of the cries of multitudes of beasts and birds.
