From Brahmā down to the stationary beings, everything becomes like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand; what need is there for much speaking here—there are thousands of such forms of higher knowledge.
The best of sages arise from that great-souled sage;
through practice alone, his knowledge becomes pure and firm.
The knower of yoga sees all forms of light and everything else:
numerous divine images and thousands of celestial mansions.
He beholds Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, Yama, Agni, Varuṇa, and the others,
as well as the planets, lunar mansions, and stars, and thousands of worlds.
And remaining in meditative absorption, he beholds those dwelling in the depths of Pātāla by means of the steady and immovable lamp of self-knowledge.
But by means of that which is filled with the nectar of serenity and contained within the vessel of the sattva-nature,
a person, having destroyed darkness, beholds the Lord within the self.
Through his grace, there is dharma, sovereignty, and knowledge, as well as dispassion and liberation; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
It is not possible to describe it in detail even in ten thousand years;
O lords of sages, one must remain steadfast in the perfection of the Pāśupata yoga.
Sūta said:
O best of the twice-born, [this is the teaching] of the virtuous, the self-conquered, the manifest twice-born.
And of the virtuous teachers who know the Dharma and whose nature is auspiciousness.
O best of the twice-born, [this applies] likewise to the compassionate, to ascetics,
to renunciants, to those free from passion, and to the wise who have brought their selves under control.
O twice-born ones, [this applies] to those who are self-controlled, disciplined, truthful, free from greed, devoted to yoga, and conversant with the Śruti and Smṛti.
Maheśvara is pleased with those who perform actions that do not contradict the Śrauta and Smārta injunctions;
moreover, at the end, they attain the word "Sat" (Being), which is Brahman.
Because of this, the virtuous declare that one attains union with Brahman regarding the object consisting of ten aspects and the means characterized by eight features.
Those who neither become angry nor rejoice, whether regarding common objects or extraordinary ones, are known as those who have conquered their own selves.
Because the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas are joined [to this discipline], they are therefore called the twice-born;
for one who is joined to the duties of the castes and stages of life, it brings about the happiness of heaven and other such rewards.
One is called a knower of dharma through knowledge of the dharma prescribed by the Śrutis and Smṛtis;
one is a virtuous student of sacred learning (brahmacārī) through the pursuit of knowledge and through being devoted to the welfare of the guru.
Because he accomplishes ritual actions, the householder is called a virtuous man;
because he practices austerity in the forest, the hermit is remembered as a virtuous man.

A *yati* who exerts himself is considered virtuous (*sādhu*) because of his practice of yoga; likewise, those who practice the duties of their respective stages of life (*āśrama-dharma*) are considered virtuous because of their practice.
The householder, the student, the forest-dweller, and likewise the ascetic—
these two words, "dharma" and "adharma," are declared here to be essentially composed of action.
"Wholesome and unwholesome karma are known as dharma and adharma;
for this word 'dharma' is proclaimed in its great sense as that which upholds. (LiP 1.10.12)
Non-retention and greatness are called *adharma*; herein, *dharma* is taught by the teachers as that which brings about what is desired.
For unrighteousness is taught by the teachers to have undesirable fruits;
[those who follow it] are neither aged nor free from greed, for they lack self-control and are hypocritical.
Those who are rightly disciplined and upright are declared to be teachers (ācāryas),
because they practice [the dharma] themselves and also establish others in right conduct.
And because he gathers the meanings of the scriptures, he is called an Ācārya;
that which is to be known from hearing is called Śrauta, and that which is known from remembering is called Smārta.

The Supreme Person, the Self of all, invoked by many and praised by many—
Vishnu, the infallible Lord, the source and origin of the universe.
"There is no fault of yours in this; rather, this was brought about by my *māyā*.

The Lord who is the creator, the leader, and the destroyer—there is no one equal to me;

Abounding with thousands of garlands of flames, resembling hundreds of fires of cosmic destruction,

"You ought to proceed upward with effort and speed";

"He who shall say, 'Haṃsa, haṃsa,' he shall become a haṃsa;

O gods, having become as swift as the wind, I went upwards;

Ten yojanas wide and a hundred yojanas long,

He has a luster equal to the sun at the end of time, a long nose, and a great voice;

Assuming the dark form of a boar, Viṣṇu went downwards;

The boar did not see even the slightest root of this sign;

Desiring to know its end with all effort and speed,

Beyond the fourth state, immortal, partless, free from affliction,

Failing to reach it, they turn back; yet he is to be expressed by the single syllable.

A lotus was created from his navel, a hundred yojanas in width, resembling the rising sun, with a vajra-stem and great height.
While Devamīḍhuṣa was thus sporting,

The four-faced one, with wide eyes, arrived by chance,

He rose from his cross-legged seat with eyes wide open in wonder, and he, who provides refuge in age after age, replied with this further answer:
Whatever is to be done, has been done, or is being done—
whether it be heaven, the intermediate space, or the earth— I am that supreme state of existence.
Having spoken thus to him, the Blessed Viṣṇu then spoke again:
"Who indeed have you come to be? And from where, O Blessed One, have you arrived?"
Where must you go further, and what is your place of rest?
Who are you, O you who possess the universal form, and what may be done for you by me?
To Vaikuṇṭha who was speaking thus, the Grandfather replied,
being deluded by the Māyā of Śambhu and failing to recognize Janārdana.
The Great-Souled One, deluded by Māyā, did not recognize the God;
for just as you are, so am I—the primordial creator and Lord of Creatures.
Having heard these words of wonder from Brahmā, the sustainer of the worlds,
O Lord, Vaikuṇṭha, the source of the universe, was granted permission by him.
Out of curiosity, the great yogi entered the mouth of Brahmā [and beheld] these eighteen islands, along with the oceans and the mountains.
Having entered the eternal seven worlds, which are filled with the four social orders and extend from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, he of great splendor [proceeded].
Seeing them all within the belly of Brahmā, the mighty-armed Viṣṇu said again and again, "Oh, how great is the power of his asceticism!"
Having wandered through various worlds of diverse kinds, Viṣṇu,

Then, emerging from his mouth, Nārāyaṇa, the sustainer of the world and abode of the lords of serpents, spoke to the Grandfather.
O Blessed One, O sinless one, though I am the beginning, the mark, the middle, time, the quarters, and the sky, I do not perceive the end of your belly.
Having spoken thus, Hari further said this to the Grandfather: "O Blessed One, it is exactly so; for my belly is indeed eternal."
"O best of gods, enter and behold these incomparable worlds.
Then, having heard his gladdening words and having rejoiced in them, [he entered].
The Grandfather, whose valor is truth, entered once more into the belly of the Lord of Śrī and beheld those very same worlds situated within the womb.
Having wandered about, he indeed did not see the end of the god Hari;
then Viṣṇu, the omnipresent Lord, knowing the course of the Grandfather (Brahmā), closed all the gates and desired to quickly make his mind turn away, thinking, "I am sleeping comfortably."
Then, having observed that all the doors were indeed closed,
he made his own form subtle and found an opening through his navel.
Following the lotus stalk, the Grandfather,
the four-faced one, beheld it and drew forth his own form from the lotus.
Seated upon a radiant lotus, possessing a splendor like the interior of a lotus,
he is Brahmā, the self-existent Lord, the source of the universe, and the Grandfather.

From somewhere [there appeared] the immeasurable self, the Lord and Master of all beings,
Mahādeva with the trident in his hand, clothed in golden heroic garments.
He went to where Hari, the lord of the serpent coils, was present as Ananta;
by his swift strides, the earth was trodden upon and oppressed by his two feet.
Large drops of water quickly rose up into the sky,
and thereupon a wind, both excessively hot and excessively cold, blew there again.
Seeing that great marvel, Brahmā spoke to Viṣṇu:
"These drops of water, both cold and hot, are violently shaking the lotus."
"Tell me this doubt of mine, or what else do you wish to do?
Such were these words that issued from the mouth of the Grandfather."
Having heard this, the Blessed One, whose deeds are incomparable and who is the destroyer of the asuras, thought:
"What indeed is this being that has made its abode here within my navel?"
"He speaks excessively kindly, yet I have caused him grief"—
having reflected thus in his mind, he replied with this answer.
Why is the Blessed One today so agitated at Puṣkara?
And what have I done, O Lord, that you show me such unsurpassed affection?
"O best of men, you speak; tell me the truth for what purpose [you do so]?
To the Lord of Gods who was speaking thus, he then replied in accordance with the ways of the world:
The Lord Brahmā, the storehouse of the Vedas, replied to the lotus-eyed one:
"I am he who previously entered your womb by your will."
O Lord, just as all the worlds were seen by you within my belly,
so too have all the worlds been seen by me in their entirety within yours.
Then, O sinless one, after I had returned from those thousand years,
you, desiring to bring me under your control through a spirit of envy, [acted as you did].
"O illustrious one, all the doors were quickly closed on every side; then, having reflected by my own power, I [acted]."
The emergence from the lotus-fiber has been obtained by the region of the navel;
let there not be even the slightest obstruction to your mind in any way whatsoever.
"O Viṣṇu, this is the sequence of your deeds that has followed me;
tell me what must be done by me next—what shall I do?"
Thereafter, the enemy of Hiraṇyakaśipu, whose self is immeasurable,
received from the Grandfather a faultless, beloved, cherished, and auspicious speech.
Having heard these words, Hari, free from envy, said to him:
"Indeed, such a deed as this was not at all intended by me for you."
Desiring to awaken you, and acting out of sport as if by chance,
I quickly bolted all the doors of my own house.
"You must not understand this otherwise; you are to be honored and worshipped by me.
O auspicious one, forgive everything that has been done wrong to you by me."
"O Lord, being carried by us, descend from the lotus;
I am not able to sustain you, who are heavy and full of splendor."
He said: "Choose a boon, O Lord; descend from the lotus. Become my son, O slayer of enemies; you shall obtain beautiful joy."
"Speak words of truth; descend from the lotus, O Lord! You are our great yogin, you are the one worthy of praise, whose essence is the Praṇava."
"From this day forward, O Lord of All, adorned with the white turban,
you shall indeed be renowned by the name 'Lotus-born' (Padmayoni)."
"O Brahman, O Lord, become my son, the sovereign of the seven worlds.
Then that blessed god, having granted this boon to the diadem-wearing one, [departed].
Having said, "So be it," with a joyful soul and free from envy,
he beheld a great-mouthed being approaching nearby, radiant like the rising sun.
Having seen that most wonderful being, Nārāyaṇa then spoke to him—
he who was immeasurable, possessed of a great mouth, fangs, and disheveled hair.
Ten-armed and marked with the trident, stationed everywhere with his eyes,
the Lord of the World himself appeared in person, transformed, wearing a girdle of muñja grass.
"O Viṣṇu, who indeed is this man, a mass of splendor and great radiance, bellowing most terrifyingly with his massive, upraised penis?"
"Pervading all directions and the heavens, he is advancing right here. Thus addressed, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu spoke to Brahmā.
As he strode across the ocean, by the forceful impact of his feet,
even the water-dwellers rose up into the sky with great speed.
O Lotus-born One, you are drenched on all sides by copious waters,
while trembling together with you in the wind arising from the nose.
The great lotus born from my navel trembles at will;
for Bhavānīśa, the beginningless Lord who brings an end to all, has arrived.
"Both you and I shall worship the one whose banner is a bull with this hymn.
Then the enraged Brahmā spoke to Keśava, whose eyes resemble lotus petals.
Surely you do not know yourself to be the Lord of the worlds, the all-pervading one;
you do not know me, the eternal Brahmā, the creator of the worlds.
"For who indeed is this so-called Śaṅkara, distinct from us?
Having heard those words born of his anger, Hari spoke.

Dharma is the fuel for the great lords of yoga, invincible and the bestower of boons."
Now, the ancient, imperishable Puruṣa is the cause of this world;
indeed, he is the sower of seeds, shining as the one light.
Lord Śaṅkara himself plays with children's toys;
he is the Pradhāna, the imperishable source, the unmanifest, primordial nature, and darkness.
And these names of mine, who am eternally subject to the nature of procreation,
are seen by ascetics afflicted by suffering as "Whoever he may be"— Śiva.
"You are the possessor of the seed, and I am the eternal womb.

Of him who knows the methods of illusion and who is impenetrable and profound,

That seed, united within my womb, by the course of time,

An egg, established in the waters, remained for ten hundred years;
at the end of a thousand years, it was split asunder by the wind.
One skull became the sky and the other skull became the earth;
the great elevation of that [egg] was the golden mountain which is Meru.

But the ascetics Priyadarśanas, who were the ancestors of your ascetics,

Resembling the fire at the end of an aeon, with eyes as broad as lotus petals,

Sanaka, Sanātana, and likewise Sanandana—

"May it be well with you; I shall depart. May your consciousness be restored, O observer of noble vows.

"Alas, fie upon my asceticism if its fruit is such that my offspring were born at the very outset as destroyers of the world!"

Plakṣa, Dārbhāyaṇi, and likewise Ketumān Gautama—

then he should be considered liberated, standing like a fully ripened fruit.
A man who correctly observes the Pāśupata vow for even a single day never attains that goal which is found in either Sāṃkhya or Pañcarātra.
Thus, indeed, have I declared these characteristics of the incarnations,
from Manu onwards to Kṛṣṇa, following the sequence of twenty-eight ages.
In that future kalpa, when Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana appears, there will be a classification of the collections of revealed scriptures (śruti) according to their characteristics.
Sūta said:
Having thus heard the manifestation of Rudra proclaimed by Mahādeva, the illustrious one of great splendor prostrated before Maheśvara.
He praised him with pleasing words and spoke again to Śaṅkara.
The Grandfather said:
"All the gods consist of Viṣṇu; all the hosts consist of Viṣṇu."
"Indeed, no other goal equal to Viṣṇu is ordained;
thus do the Vedas constantly sing—of this there is no doubt."
How did that Lord, the God of gods, come to be devoted to the worship of your *liṅga* and intent upon prostrating before you, O Sovereign?
Sūta said:
Having heard those words of Brahmā, the Supreme Lord,
he was delighted by the weight of his question and seemed to drink them in with his eyes.
Having observed him, Śaṅkara said to him in that section concerning worship:
And the sages, having always worshipped the *liṅga* according to the prescribed rites, attained their respective stations, O Lord; therefore, they continue to worship it.
Without the worship of the *liṅga*, there is no steadfastness; therefore, the Lord Janārdana, the sovereign master, constantly worships his own self with faith.
Having spoken thus to Brahmā and bestowed his grace upon him, Maheśvara,
looking once more at the Lord of the Gods, vanished right there.
Then, having paid homage to him with palms joined in reverence, the Lord Brahmā,
having received his inspiration from Śaṅkara, resolved to create the entire universe without exception.
The sages said:
How is Mahādeva, the Great Lord, to be worshipped in his form as the *liṅga*?
O Romaharṣaṇa, you ought to tell this to us now.
Sūta said:
Thus questioned by the goddess on Kailāsa, Mahādeva, the lord of gods, spoke in due order to that daughter of the mountain seated upon his lap regarding the procedure for the worship of the Liṅga.
Then, O observers of excellent vows, Nandin, the son of Śālaṅkāyanaka, who was standing by his side,
having heard everything previously, spoke to the son of Brahmā.
From him, Vyāsa of great splendor heard the supreme and auspicious rite for the worship of the Liṅga, which was equal to the Vedas, from Sanatkumāra.
Having heard from the mouth of Śailādin the procedure for the ritual service of bathing, I shall now proclaim that method of bathing and the subsequent rite of worship.
Śailādi said: Now I shall describe the procedure for bathing for the benefit of Brāhmaṇas;
it directly removes all sins and was taught by Śiva in the past.
Having bathed according to this rite, having worshipped Śaṅkara even once,
and having drunk the *brahmakūrca* mixture, one is liberated from all sins.
O best of the sons of the Four-faced One, the God of gods, Śambhu, has declared a threefold bath for the benefit of the Brahmins and the other castes.
Having first performed the Varuṇa bath and then the excellent Āgneya bath,
and having then performed the mantra-bath, one should worship the Supreme Lord.
One whose inner disposition is corrupt is not purified by bathing in water or by applying ashes;
one whose disposition is pure should practice purification, otherwise one should not perform it.
Even if a man bathes in all rivers, lakes, and ponds until the dissolution of the world, he is not purified if his inner disposition is corrupt; of this there is no doubt.
For when the lotus-heart of men, which had been dormant due to darkness, became awakened by the radiance of the sun of knowledge, it then became pure.
Having taken clay, sesame seeds, flowers, ash, and likewise kusha grass for the purpose of bathing, he should place them on the bank at the bathing site.
Having washed and sipped water, and having cleansed the impurities from his body,
he should then perform his bath using substances located on the bank.
One should purify the body again with the mantra "uddhṛtāsi";
then, having taken up earth and another garment, one should bathe in a way that is not ostentatious.
With the mantra "gandhadvārāṃ durādharṣām," the knower of mantras should smear [the area] with the dung of a tawny cow while it is still fresh from the sky.
Having bathed again and discarded that soiled garment,
one should perform the ritual bath after having put on white clothes.
For the sake of purifying all sins, one should likewise invoke Varuṇa and worship the god Bhava with a mental sacrifice through meditation.
Having sipped water three times at that sacred bathing place (tīrtha) and immersed himself while remembering Bhava,
he should sip water again according to the rules and consecrate the great water with mantras.
Having immersed oneself therein, one should indeed recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn;
then, the self-controlled practitioner should meditate upon the orbs of the Sun, Moon, and Fire within that water.
Having sipped water and emerged again from that water, the knower of mantras should enter into the middle of the sacred bathing place (tīrtha) once more for the further increase of merit.
One should perform the consecration with water alone, using a horn, or with washed leaf-cups made of *pālāśa* wood, accompanied by *kuśa* grass and flowers.
The knower of mantras [should perform the rite] with the Rudra, Pavamāna, and the hymns known as Tvarita,
beginning with the Taratsamandī section, as well as with the two Śānti hymns.
And with the single *śāntidharma* rite and the five *brahmapavitraka* rites,
while recollecting the specific forms of the presiding deities of those respective mantras and their *ṛṣis*.
O twice-born ones, having thus consecrated his own head with water,
he should then meditate in his heart upon the three-eyed Lord, the five-faced Īśvara.
Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should perform the formal rite of purification (ācamana) after consulting one's own Sūtra,
sitting comfortably with the sacred grass (pavitra) in hand in a clean place according to the prescribed rule.
Having sprinkled water along with kuśa grass with his right hand,
he should drink the water three times after casting it [into the mouth], having become a *cakrī* (wielder of the discus) and remaining unwearied.
Then one should perform a circumambulation for the pacification of the sin of violence.
Thus has the excellent ritual of bathing and sipping water been briefly described.
O best of the twice-born, this was for the benefit of all brāhmaṇas.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Bathing," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Nandin said:
Then one should invoke the goddess Gāyatrī, the mother of the Vedas, and likewise the Great Goddess with the mantra: "May the boon-granting goddess come. (LiP 1.26.1)
One should cause water for the feet, water for sipping, and the respectful offering (arghya) to be presented to her;
having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), one should remain either seated or standing.
One should perform one of these three types of recitation— one thousand, half of that, or one hundred and eight repetitions— of the Gāyatrī mantra together with the Praṇava.
Having offered the *arghya*, having worshipped her thoroughly, and having bowed with his own head,
he should dismiss the Mother by reciting, "O Goddess on the highest peak."
Having worshipped Īśa, who is to be beheld from the east, and Gāyatrī, the mother of the Vedas,
one should likewise pray to Bhāskara with palms joined in reverence.
Likewise, having recited the hymns dedicated to the Sun and those originating from the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas,
one should thereafter perform three circumambulations of the Fire.
Having saluted the self, the inner self, and the supreme self, as well as the Sun, Brahmā, and Agni; ||| LiP_1,26.8 |||
Then, one should invoke the sages and the ancestors according to the rule by their own names;
thereafter, having invoked the gods from all sides with the words, "I invoke you all."
Thereafter, facing either east or north, one should satisfy [the deities] according to the prescribed rite,
having meditated upon their respective essential natures (tattva) and having paid homage to them in due order.
One should offer to the gods with water and flowers, to the sages with water and kuśa grass,
and to the ancestors everywhere with water mixed with sesame seeds and fragrances.

Wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī), one should satisfy the gods; wearing it around the neck (nivītī), one should perform the libation for the sages; and wearing it over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), O best of Brahmins, one should satisfy the ancestors in their proper order.
The wise one should indeed satisfy the deities with the tip of the forefinger;
for the sake of all success, the learned scholar should satisfy the sages with the little finger.
The wise man should satisfy the ancestors with the thumb of his right hand;
likewise, O tiger among sages, the twice-born should perform the sacrifice to Brahman.

Pure in soul and devoted to the performance of sacrificial rites, he likewise performed the sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice to human beings, the sacrifice to the spirits, and the sacrifice to the ancestors.
O Brahmin, the study of one's own Vedic branch is remembered as the Brahma-sacrifice (brahmayajña);
and whatever food one offers into the fire is remembered as the Deva-sacrifice (devayajña).
The offering of oblations to all beings according to the prescribed rule is called the *bhūtayajña*; it bestows prosperity upon all embodied beings.
Having prostrated before Brahmins who are accompanied by their wives, who know all principles, and who have mastered the Vedas, the food that is given to them is called "human" (mānuṣa).
That which is given with the ancestors in view is called the Pitṛyajña;
in this way, one should perform the five great sacrifices for the accomplishment of all goals.
Listen: among all sacrifices, the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmayajña) is remembered as the supreme.
A mortal devoted to the sacrifice to Brahman is glorified in the world of Brahman.
By the Brahmayajña, all the gods together with Indra are satisfied,
as are the Lord Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śaṅkara Nīlalohita.
The Vedas and all the ancestors [are present]; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Having gone outside the village, a Brāhmaṇa who knows the Brahmayajña [should perform it].
As long as the roof of the huts was not seen by the man—whether in the east, in the north, or even in the northeast—so long [he remained there]. (LiP 1.26.23)
O Brahmins, for the sake of the Brahma-sacrifice and for the gratification of the Ṛg-verses, one should perform the meritorious sipping of water (ācamana),
drinking three times and rinsing the mouth after each sip.
Having thus wiped the Yajus formulas and washed them twice with water,
he should touch his head for the sake of pleasing the Sāma Vedas.
Having repeatedly washed them with water, he should touch the Atharva-veda and the Aṅgirasas to his eyes, and the Brāhmaṇa-aṅgas to his nostrils.
Likewise, he [should recite] the eighteen Purāṇas beginning with the Brahma-purāṇa,
as well as the Upapurāṇas beginning with the Saura-purāṇa, in their proper order.

One should touch the region of the heart for the sake of satisfaction after touching the ears with meritorious histories and likewise with the Śaiva and other scriptures; thereafter, one should touch the region of the heart.
O knower of the ritual, best among those who know the ritual, having thus sipped water and spread a blade of *darbha* grass for oneself at the beginning of all rituals; 29. LiP_1,26.29.
The wise man, having placed his right hand over his left palm,
adorned with golden rings or even bound with the sacred thread (brahmagranthi), [should perform the rite].
One who has received the sacred thread should perform the Brahma-yajña according to the rules with a concentrated mind;
for if he does not perform these five great sacrifices, O best of the twice-born, he is no longer a sage.
And having eaten [the meat] of pigs, a man is indeed born into the womb of a pig;
therefore, by every effort, those who desire auspiciousness should avoid them.
Then, having first performed the Brahma-sacrifice and a bath for himself in every respect,
the self-controlled king, having duly taken up the sacred water (tīrtha), should enter his palace.
Having washed his feet and hands with water outside the house,
he should then perform the ash-bath according to the prescribed rule for the purification of the body.
Having purified the ashes according to the rule with the *praṇava* produced from the *agnihotra*,
one should offer oblations in the morning with the mantra "jyotiḥ sūrya," since [the sun] has risen.
The fire is light; likewise, [an offering] made at evening is perfect, whereas that made before sunrise is false.
Therefore, the ash remaining from an offering made after sunrise is purifying and auspicious.
Since there is no sin equal to untruth, [he should protect it];
the region of the head is presided over by Īśāna, and the face by Tatpuruṣa.
O you of excellent vows, one should consecrate the chest region with the Aghora mantra, the private parts with the Vāma mantra,
the feet with the Sadyojāta mantra, and the entire body with the Praṇava.
Then, the best among the knowers of Brahman, having removed the ashes and taking some up while recollecting the God of gods, should wash his feet and hands.
Then one should perform the mantra-bath in due order with the *āpohiṣṭhā* verses and other meritorious mantras originating from the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
Thus, for the benefit of the twice-born, this bath has been described to you today in brief;
he who performs it even once attains the supreme state.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Five Sacrifices," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*. Śailādi said:
I shall describe the sequence of the ritual for the worship of the *liṅga* in brief; listen, for it cannot be fully told even in a hundred years through detailed exposition.
Having bathed in this manner according to the rule and entered the place of worship,
one should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and meditate upon the three-eyed God.
Five-faced and ten-armed, resembling pure crystal,
endowed with all ornaments and adorned with variegated garments.
Having assumed his form through burning, immersion, and other such rites,
and having established oneself in the body of Śiva, one should worship the Supreme Lord.
Having performed the purification of the body, one should install the root mantra in due order;
everywhere, one should likewise install the Brahmans with the *praṇava* (OM) in the proper sequence.
Because the Vedic meters and the mantras abide in a subtle form within the most auspicious "Namas Śivāya" in the Sūtra, [it is the source].
Just as a banyan tree exists within a banyan seed, so too does the Great Brahman abide within the beautiful thread; though it is vast, it itself remains subtle.
One should sprinkle the place of worship with water scented with sandalwood;
thereafter, one should purify the ritual materials by means of washing, sprinkling, and other such rites.
Washing and sprinkling are prescribed with the *praṇava* (the syllable Om);
and the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, the *arghya* vessel, and the *pādya* vessel follow in that order.
Likewise, the wise one should place the vessel prepared for the purpose of sipping water according to the rule, having veiled it according to the prescribed method.
One should cover [the area] with *darbha* grass and sprinkle it with pure water;
then, one should pour cool water upon each and every one of those [spots].
Having observed the materials, the wise man should cast them into those [vessels] with the syllable *praṇava*; he should prepare *uśīra* and sandalwood for the water for the feet (*pādya*).
Having ground nutmeg, clove, camphor, and plenty of tamāla root into a powder according to the prescribed rule, one should cast it into the water for rinsing the mouth.
In this manner, one should cause sandalwood, as well as camphor and various kinds of flowers, to be offered into all the vessels according to the prescribed rule.
Kusa grass tips, unbroken grains, barley, rice, sesame seeds,
clarified butter, white mustard seeds, flowers, and sacred ash should be placed in the arghya vessel.
One should cause kuśa grass, flowers, barley, rice, bahumūla, and tamālaka,
as well as ashes, to be placed in the prokṣaṇī vessel while reciting the *praṇava*.
One should likewise place the five-syllabled mantra and the Gāyatrī whose deity is Rudra,
or even the Praṇava alone, which is the unsurpassed essence of the Vedas.
Then, one should subsequently sprinkle the ritual materials with the *praṇava* (oṃ),
using the water contained in the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, and with the five [mantras] beginning with Īśāna.
At the side of the God of gods, one should worship Nandin,
who resembles ten thousand blazing fires, who has three eyes, and who is the lord of the thirty deities.
He has the crescent moon as his crown, a face like that of Hari, and four arms;
he wears a garland of flowers, is gentle, and is adorned with all ornaments.
And he saw his own auspicious wife, who was like a goddess among the Maruts,
the highly renowned Suyaśā of excellent vows, who was devoted to adorning his feet.
Having thus worshipped and entered the inner abode of the Supreme Lord,
he should devoutly offer a handful of flowers upon his five heads with the five [mantras].
Having worshipped Śaṅkara with perfumes, flowers, and various incenses,
one should perform the purification of the liṅga for Skanda, Vināyaka, and the Goddess.
Having recited all the mantras beginning with *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*,
one should thereafter fashion the seat called *padma* by means of the *praṇava*.
Its eastern petal is the manifest imperishable consisting of *aṇimā*;
likewise, the southern is *laghimā* and the western is *mahimā*.
Likewise, the attainment of the subsequent leaf is sovereignty over fire;
the southern leaf is lordship, and mastery is found in the domain of the wind.
Omniscience and likewise sovereignty are said to be the pericarp and Soma;
below Soma is Sūrya, and below that is Pāvaka himself.
These, beginning with Dharma, are in the intermediate directions; one should then arrange the infinite [deities] in sequence.
In the four cardinal directions starting from the Unmanifest (avyakta), at the end of Soma, are the three qualities (guṇatraya).
Above that are the three selves, and at its end is the pedestal of Śiva;
having invoked the Supreme Lord with the mantra "I take refuge in Sadyojāta," [one should proceed].
One should establish [the deity] upon the seat with the Vāmadeva mantra;
one should effect its presence with the Rudra-gāyatrī and then bind it with the Aghora mantra.

One should worship with the mantra "Īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām" and cause the water for the feet (pādya), the water for sipping (ācamanīya), and the respectful offering (arghya) to be presented to the Lord.
One should bathe Rudra according to the prescribed rite with water scented with sandalwood,
having taken the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) into a vessel and consecrated it with mantras.
One should bathe [the image] according to the prescribed rite with products of the cow while reciting the *praṇava*,
as well as with clarified butter, honey, and sugarcane juice.
One should consecrate Mahādeva with meritorious substances using the *praṇava*;
then, one should pour water from pure water-vessels while reciting the mantras.
Having performed purification according to the rule with a white cloth,
the practitioner [should worship] with kuśa grass, apāmārga, camphor, jasmine flowers, and campaka flowers.
Having filled that water with white karavīra flowers, as well as mallikā, kamala, and utpala, and with other very beautiful blossoms, sandalwood, and so forth; LiP_1,27.36.
Then, one should place the mantras beginning with Sadyojāta into that water,
using either a golden vessel or a silver one.
With a copper lotus leaf, or a palāśa leaf, or with a conch, or a purified and auspicious earthen vessel; LiP_1,27.38 //
One should perform the ritual bath with water and flowers while preceded by mantras;
I shall proclaim those mantras for you, so listen for the sake of accomplishing all goals. (LiP 1.27.39)
O knowers of mantras, by bathing the *liṅga* even once in this manner with the *pavamāna* and the *vāmīyaka* [hymns], a human being shall be liberated.
With the Rudra and Nīlarudra hymns, with the auspicious Śrīsūkta, with the Rajanīsūkta, and with the auspicious Camaka; LiP_1,27.41.
Then with the Hotṛ, the Śiras, the auspicious Atharva, with Śānti and again with Punarśānti, and with the Bhāruṇḍa and Aruṇa; // LiP_1.27.42 //
And with the Vāruṇa, the Jyeṣṭha, and likewise the Vedavrata;
and with the meritorious Antaryāma and the Puruṣa Sūkta.
By Rudra himself acting swiftly, by Kapardin,
and by Viṣṇu with his great moon, [he was addressed] with the Sāman chant beginning with "ā vosajema."
With the Virūpākṣa, Skanda, and Śatarcika hymns, as well as with the Śivas, the Pañcabrahma mantras, the Sūtra, and the solitary Praṇava; 27.45.
One should bathe the Lord of the God of Gods for the pacification of all sins,
[offering] a garment, a sacred thread for Śiva, and likewise water for sipping.
One should offer perfume, flowers, incense, a lamp, food in due order, fragrant water, and again water for sipping.
One should cause him to be given a beautiful, covered crown as well as ornaments,
and items such as mouth-perfumes, using the *praṇava* alone.
Then [he beheld] the God, resembling crystal, partless and imperishable,
the cause of all gods, consisting of all worlds, and supreme.
"He is beyond the reach of Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the other sages and gods;
indeed, the Śruti declares that he is beyond the reach even of the Vedāntas known by those who know the Vedas."
The medicine for those afflicted by the disease of worldly existence, devoid of beginning, middle, and end,
is known as the Śiva-principle (śivatattva), which is established within the Śivaliṅga.
One should worship at the top of the liṅga with the mantra consisting of the syllable *praṇava* alone;
and according to the prescribed rule, one should recite hymns, offer salutations, and perform circumambulation.
Having offered the *arghya* and scattered flowers at the feet,
and having prostrated before the Lord of Gods, one should then internalize Śiva within oneself.
Thus has the unsurpassed worship of the liṅga been described in brief;
now, today, I shall explain to you the internal worship of the liṅga here.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Worship of the Liṅga," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅgamahāpurāṇa*. Śailādi said:
Thereafter, one should meditate upon the solar disc, which is the immortal essence of fire, above that;
likewise, one should meditate in sequence upon the three qualities (guṇas) and the three selves (ātmanas) within the heart.
Above that, one should worship Mahādeva— who is partless yet possesses a manifest form,
and whose body is mounted upon half of his beloved— by means of the knowledge of meditation.

Therefore, it has been declared that there are many kinds of objects to be contemplated; for if there exists something to be contemplated therein, then the contemplation of the contemplator follows from that, otherwise it would not be possible.
Therefore, the sacrificer should meditate upon that which is to be meditated upon and the purpose [of the rite];
he must remember this, for otherwise a person never truly understands.
He lies within the city of the body; therefore he is called Puruṣa.
He who worships with sacrifice is remembered as the sacrificer (yajamāna).
Maheśvara is the object of meditation; meditation is reflection, and its fruit is liberation.
One attains the true nature of the Lord of Pradhāna and Puruṣa.
In this system, the twenty-sixth principle is to be meditated upon as the object of meditation, while the twenty-fifth is indeed the meditator;
the unmanifest (avyakta) is the twenty-fourth, and there are seven principles beginning with the Great One (mahat).
Likewise, the Great Principle (mahat), the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), and again the five subtle elements (tanmātra),
as well as the five organs of action and the five organs of perception.
The mind, the five elements, and Śiva as the twenty-sixth [tattva]—
He alone is the sustainer and the agent, the Great Lord even of the Creator.
Rudra, that Śaṅkara, brought forth Hiraṇyagarbha;
he is remembered as the one superior to the universe, the soul of the universe, and the universal form.
Just as sons are not born here without a father and a mother,
so too the three worlds do not exist without Soma.
Sanatkumāra said:
If Mahādeva, the Supreme Self, the Great Lord, is the doer, as well as the one who causes others to act, including those of small intellect who act for themselves; 12.
"You have described the Supreme Lord as eternal, pure, awakened, partless, and the bestower of liberation; yet if he is partless, what can he possibly do?"
Śailādi said: Time creates everything; it always measures time itself;
it considers the entire mind to be partless, and it too is partless.
By his very action, the entire world here is established;
what else is this world but the eightfold form of the God of gods?
The world does not exist without space, nor without earth, wind,
fire, or water, just as it does not exist without the sacrificer.
The world [consists of] the sun and the moon; these are the bodies of that Lord.
But upon reflection, this entire realm of moving and non-moving things is merely the gross form of Rudra.
O best of the twice-born, the seers speak of that which is subtle and inexpressible,
from which words turn back along with the mind, failing to reach it.
One who knows the bliss of Brahman fears nothing from any quarter;
likewise, having known the bliss of the wielder of the Pināka bow, one should not fear.
Having realized through their inner being that these are the manifestations of Rudra everywhere,
the sages who perceive reality declare, "All is Rudra."
By constantly offering salutations with reverence to the Supreme Lord, one realizes:
"All this, indeed, is Brahman; all is truly Rudra, the Sovereign."
The Supreme Person is indeed Mahādeva, the Great Lord, the highest Śiva;
thus is the All-pervading One designated, and meditation is precisely the contemplation upon Him.
O observer of noble vows, having investigated and observed by means of the fourfold path,
[one understands that] saṃsāra is the cause of saṃsāra, and nirvṛti is the cause of liberation.
The fourfold manifestation is declared here for the meditating yogin;
that meditation is said by the Supreme Lord to be of many kinds, yet it is unified in one.
In the mantra *suniṣṭhā*, Raudrī is said to reside in Rudra, without a doubt;
likewise, Aindrī resides in Indra, Saumyā in Soma, and Nārāyaṇī in Nārāyaṇa.
In the sun and in fire, for all [beings], one should thus contemplate everywhere;
having established it in two ways through devotion, thinking "She is I" and "I am He."
There is no one who is not devoted to him; therefore, there is no doubt that his meditation is of the nature of Brahman.
O Brahmin, in this way, one should first meditate upon the entire world of moving and non-moving beings as being composed of Brahman.
Remembering the beloved [Self], one should abandon the distinction between the moving and the unmoving,
as well as what is to be abandoned and what is to be grasped, what is unattainable, and indeed what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.
For one who is fully satisfied, the state of Brahman exists; it is not otherwise.
This is declared to be the internal [worship]; such is the sequence of worship.
The inner priests are likewise to be honored with prostrations and other such marks of respect;
even if they are deformed or disfigured, these exponents of Brahman must not be reviled.
All those who serve within [the temple] should not be scrutinized by one who possesses true knowledge;
for those of small intellect who revile [the deity] will surely become afflicted with suffering.
Just as in the past the sages censured Rudra in the forest of wood,
so too should those who know Brahman always be served and honored.
They are liberated from the system of castes and stages of life by those who are devoted to that very system of castes and stages of life.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Number and Principles of Śiva’s Worship," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sanatkumāra said:
O Lord, I now wish to hear what occurred in the past in the Dāruvana forest among those dwelling in the woods whose souls were purified by austerity.
How did the Lord Nīlalohita, having assumed a deformed form, arrive at the Dāruvana forest, with his vital energy drawn upward and clad only by the directions?
What took place in that forest of Rudra, the Supreme Self?
You ought to tell me truly of the deeds of the God of gods.
Sūta said:
Having heard those words of his, the blessed son of Śilāda, the best among those who know the essence of the Vedas, spoke something while smiling slightly.
Śailādi said: "O sages, in the Dāru forest they performed most rigorous austerities."
For the sake of pleasing the God of gods, [he gave] his wife, his sons, and the sacred fires.
Rudra, the Lord of the World, Cekitāna, the bull-bannered one, Dhūrjaṭi, the Supreme Lord, the Blessed One Nīlalohita, was pleased.
In order to test the knowledge of those dwelling in the forest of wood regarding the nature of worldly activity,
that Lord of the World, out of both faith and sport, [approached them].
And for the sake of establishing the knowledge characterized by cessation among those dwelling in the Devadāru forest whose minds were intent on the knowledge of worldly activity, Śaṅkara [acted].
Assuming a deformed appearance, naked, with uneven eyes,
appearing bewildered, two-armed, and dark-limbed, he went to the divine forest of Dāruvana.
And the Blessed One, exceedingly beautiful, manifested a gentle smile born of the god of love toward the women, as well as playful movements of his eyebrows and song.
Having sprinkled the group of women again and again, he who was the destroyer of the bodiless god (Kāma) and possessed an exceedingly sweet form caused the bodiless god to increase even further.
Seeing that man in the forest, deformed and blue-and-red in hue,
even the women devoted to their husbands followed him with great reverence.
And the women standing at the doorways of the forest huts, their garments and ornaments disheveled and their movements agitated,
having obtained a smile from his lotus-like face, followed him as he stayed in his tree-dwelling.
Seeing you, some women, their eyes rolling with intoxication, even though they were devoid of grace,
performed playful movements of their eyebrows.
Then, seeing him, other women, their faces slightly smiling,
their garments somewhat disheveled and the strings of their girdles slipping, sang:
Then, seeing him in the forest with his new garment slipping off, some of the brahmin women,
filled with passion, cast aside their various bracelets and went to their kinsmen.
At that time, some woman, having seen him, did not recognize him because she was in exile and her great silken garments were disheveled;
while others, intoxicated with passion, [recognized] the well-known branches and twigs variegated by foliage, as well as their kinsmen.
O best of the twice-born, some spoke to him, others danced, some fell upon the surface of the earth, and others sat down like elephants. Thus he spoke.
Looking at one another with smiles, they embraced him from all sides;
blocking Rudra’s path, they displayed their various skills.
Others asked him, "Who are you? while still others said, "Please be seated. Then, with joyful minds, they cried out, "Where [are you from]? and "Be gracious! LiP 1.29.20.
By the power of Bhava, the devoted wives fell down in a state of reversal, their garments and hair disheveled, even in the presence of their husbands.
Having seen and heard their actions and words— whether auspicious or inauspicious— the immutable Supreme Lord did not speak a word.
Having seen the assembly of women and Śaṅkara in such a state, those lords of sages, the brahmins, uttered exceedingly harsh words.
The ascetic powers of all those were struck down by Śaṅkara,
just as the stars situated in the sky are eclipsed by the light of the sun.
It is heard that, due to the curse of the great-souled seer Brahmā,
the sacrifices— which are indeed the source of all abundant blessings— have met with destruction.
Moreover, by the curse of Bhṛgu, Viṣṇu, though possessed of supreme heroism,
underwent ten incarnations and was rendered perpetually distressed.
O knower of dharma, even Indra’s [penis] was once severed on earth and cast down by the enraged sage Gautama, along with his testicles.
Likewise, the dwelling in a womb was ordained for the Vasus by a curse;
and by the curse of the sages, Nahuṣa became a serpent.
And this ocean of milk is the eternal abode of Hari;
it is the second reservoir of nectar, which was rendered undrinkable by the Brahmins.
Having reached Avimukteśvara in Vārāṇasī, Janārdana bathed the Lord,
the God of gods, the Three-eyed One, with milk.
Endowed with supreme faith,
the Lord Madhusūdana himself was indeed sprinkled with the nectar of the embrace of the body, as if with milk.
Then, having been sprinkled by Brahmā together with the sages, the Lord, the Blessed One,
made Kṣīroda his abode once again as before.
Likewise, Dharma was cursed by the high-souled Māṇḍavya,
and the Vṛṣṇis were cursed by Kṛṣṇa and other great-souled ones such as Durvāsas.
And Rāghava, along with his younger brother, [received blessings] from the high-souled Durvāsas;
and Śrīvatsa [did so] by prostrating at the feet of that wise sage.
These and many others have fallen under the power of the brahmins,
with the exception of Virūpākṣa, the god of gods and lord of Umā.
Thus deluded by him, they did not recognize Śaṅkara;
they spoke words of extreme severity, and though he was fierce, he vanished from their sight.
Then, in the morning, with their minds filled with agitation, they departed from that forest of trees and approached the high-souled Grandfather seated upon his supreme throne.
Having gone there, the sages, their hearts distressed, informed the Lord of everything that had occurred in that auspicious Dāruvana forest.
The Grandfather, having reflected in his mind for a moment,
[recounted] to them everything that had occurred in the past in the sacred Dāruvana forest.
Having risen, joined his palms in reverence, and prostrated before Bhava,
Brahmā quickly spoke to the lords of sages dwelling in the Dāruvana forest.
"Fie on you, O Brahmins, who have met your end after failing to obtain the unsurpassed great treasure, since it was rendered futile by you who were devoid of fortune!"
But he who was seen by you in that forest of wood as a bearer of sectarian marks (liṅgin) with a deformed appearance, though you yourselves were without such marks— he is indeed the Supreme Lord.
Householders must never despise guest Brahmins,
whether they be deformed or handsome, soiled or unlearned.
In former times, the sage Sudarśana, the foremost of the twice-born, conquered even Time and Death itself on earth through his worship of guests. (LiP 1.29.44)
Otherwise, there is no way for the best of the twice-born to cross over [to the higher realms] with householders, except by performing that purification for oneself on earth: the honoring of guests.

Long ago, even while he was a householder, the one known as Sudarśana made a vow; he spoke thus to his wife, who was devoted to her husband: ||| 46 ||In this way, O best of Brahmins, the king performed various sacrifices and gave many gifts to the twice-born. ||| 50 || Then, having attained the supreme state, that king went to heaven. Having heard this account of the great-souled Sudarśana, ||| 51 || one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice and goes to the world of Viṣṇu. ||| 52 || Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Story of Sudarśana," in the first part of the *Liṅgapurāṇa*. ||| 53 || O sage, I shall now tell you the story of the great-souled Vīrabhadra, which destroys all sins. ||| 1 || Formerly, there was a king named Śaṅkara, who was a devotee of Śiva and a performer of sacrifices. He had a son named Vīrabhadra, who was very powerful and a devotee of Śiva. ||| 2-3 || Once, the king went to the forest for hunting. There, he saw a deer and pursued it with great speed. ||| 4 || While running, the king fell into a great pit. Having fallen, he lamented greatly and called out to his son. ||| 5 || "O Vīrabhadra, come quickly! Save me from this great danger! Hearing his father's words, Vīrabhadra arrived at that place. ||| 6 || Seeing his father fallen in the pit, he lifted him up with effort. Then, taking his father by the hand, he brought him back to his own city. ||| 7 || Having reached his home, the king was honored by his ministers and subjects. O lady of virtuous vows, beautiful brows, and good fortune, listen attentively to everything:
guests must never be disregarded by you while they are in the house.
Since the wielder of the Pināka bow is himself directly present as every guest,
therefore, by giving even yourself to the guest, worship him.
Having spoken thus, that devoted wife, tormented and helpless, said to her husband while weeping: "O Lord, what has been said by you?"
Having heard those words of hers, Sudarśana spoke again:
"Noble lady, everything is to be given for the sake of Śiva; indeed, Śiva himself is the guest."
"Therefore, all are always to be honored, and all are guests.
When her husband had spoken thus, his devoted wife then [replied].
Then, O best of the twice-born, she proceeded after receiving his command upon her head as if it were a final decree, in order to directly test their faith.
Dharma, having become a most excellent twice-born, then went to the hermitage of the sage;
seeing him, the sinless woman honored the brahmin with offerings of arghya and other gifts.
Having been worshipped by her, Dharma himself, appearing as a twice-born brahmin, said to her:
"O blessed lady, where is your wise husband Sudarśana?"
"Noble lady, enough with food and drink; you ought to give me your own self here.
And that woman, covered in shame, recalled what had been said previously.
Her husband closed his eyes, and the devoted wife moved away; she spoke to him again, saying "What is this?", and set her mind upon dharma.
In the meantime, it was said that she had come there by her husband's command to present herself to him;
meanwhile, Sudarśana, the husband of that woman, arrived.
Having gone to the door of the house, the wise great sage said to her, "Come, come! Where have you gone, O blessed lady? To him, the guest himself replied.
"O illustrious Sudarśana, today I am indeed engaged in sexual union with this wife of mine; tell me, what should be done here?"
"O best of Brahmins, O foremost of the twice-born, I am well-pleased by the end of this conversation.
Then Sudarśana, the most excellent of the twice-born, spoke with great joy.
"Enjoy her as you desire, O best of the twice-born; I shall depart.
Then the King of Dharma himself, being pleased, revealed his own form.
The one of great splendor granted him everything he desired and said to him:
"O best of Brahmins, this most beautiful woman has not been enjoyed even by thought."
And he has come here, without a doubt, to test my faith;
for you, O observer of noble vows, have indeed conquered Death by means of Dharma alone.
"Ah, the power of his asceticism! Having said this, he departed;
therefore, all guests must always be honored in such a manner.
What is the use of saying more here, O best of the twice-born? You who are bereft of fortune ought to go quickly for refuge to that very Śaṅkara.
Having heard those words of Brahmā, O bulls among Brahmins,
those distressed beings, with eyes agitated by fear, paid homage to Brahmā and spoke.
The Brāhmaṇas said:
"O highly fortunate one, we have no regard for our lives, for we are women who have been transformed;
we have beheld Mahādeva, who, though blameless, was reviled by us."
And Śarva—the all-pervading, trident-bearing, wielder of the Pināka, and blue-and-red-hued—was cursed;
due to ignorance, the power born of the curse became blunted at its tip from the mere sight [of him].
O Lord of Gods, you should indeed explain renunciation in its proper sequence,
so that we may behold the God of gods, the fierce, formidable one with matted hair.
The Grandfather said:
"O best of the twice-born, having first studied the Vedas with constant faith from a guru, and having reflected upon the meanings and the duties of the sages, you must take a solemn vow."
Or else, the learned man may perform the twelve-year penance until the end of his formal study;
having bathed and taken a wife, he should procreate sons who are firm in their vows.
Having divided those sons according to their respective vocations, the sage performed sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma for the sake of the all-pervading Lord of Sacrifice.
Having reached a forest, the sage should worship the Supreme Self in the sacrificial fire for either twelve years or even for just one year.
For either twelve fortnights or twelve days,
subsisting on milk, self-restrained and tranquil, he should worship all the gods.
Having performed the sacrifice in this manner, one should offer the sacrificial vessels into the fire with the appropriate mantras;
having placed the earthen ones in water, one should give the metallic ones to the preceptor.
Having prostrated on the ground before his guru, the ascetic, being dispassionate, should renounce all of his own wealth to the Brahmins without hesitation.
Having shaved off his hair along with the top-knot and having discarded the sacred thread, the wise man should offer oblations into the water five times, saying: "bhūḥ svāhā" and so forth.
Thereafter, for the sake of liberation through Śiva, the ascetic should indeed proceed in this manner,
either by means of a vow, fasting, or even by subsisting on water alone.
A renunciant may subsist on leaves, on milk, or even on fruits;
otherwise, he is as good as dead while still alive within six months or a year.
Even by performing such exertion as setting out on a journey and so forth for the sake of his own body,
an ascetic who acts in this manner attains union with Śiva through that very action.
Even immediately, those of firm vows who are endowed with devotion obtain liberation.
What need is there for renunciation, or even for this ritual procedure, for one devoted to Rudra through auspicious vows,
sacrifices, various gifts, burnt offerings, acquired scriptures, and the various Vedas?
Thus was Death conquered by the high-souled Śveta through devotion to Bhava;
may you likewise possess devotion toward Mahādeva Śaṅkara, the Supreme Self.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*. Śailādi said:
Having been addressed thus by Brahmā, those supreme sages, the bulls among brāhmaṇas, then asked about the meritorious story of Śveta.
The Grandfather said:
There was a glorious sage named Śveta whose life had reached its end; dwelling in a mountain cave, he remained devoted and, having worshipped him with devotion, praised Maheśvara.
Then, O twice-born ones, with the meritorious Rudrādhyāya beginning with "namaste," the highly effulgent Kāla approached the best of the twice-born who had reached his end.
O best of Brahmins, having resolved to lead [him] away, he brought about the presence of the Sage;
and Śveta, seeing that time had arrived, though he himself was already subject to death, beheld Śaṅkara.
The meritorious soul performed worship while recollecting Tryambaka;
he should thus worship the god Tryambaka, who is fragrant and the increaser of prosperity.
"What will death do to me, since I am the death of death?
Seeing him, the one who causes fear to the worlds spoke with a smile to Śveta.
"Come, come, O Śveta! What fruit do you seek by this rite?
Are you Rudra, or the Lord Viṣṇu, or Brahmā, the Sovereign of the World?"
"O best of the twice-born, who is capable of rescuing one seized by me? O Brahmin, what use have I for this terrible decree of my lord? (LiP 1.30.8)
"I have indeed risen to lead you to the realm of Yama in an instant;
since your life has departed, O sage, I am therefore prepared to take you there."
Having heard those words of his, which were both terrifying and infused with dharma, the bull among sages lamented: "Alas, Rudra! Rudra! Rudra!"
Beholding Kāla with a gaze mixed with tears, he, agitated and overwhelmed, spoke to that Mahādeva.
Śveta said: "O Lord, what is the purpose of our time here, if indeed Śaṅkara Rudra, the source of the birth of all gods, resides in this linga, O bull-bannered one?"
O mighty-armed one, what can be done by fate for great-souled ones like me who are so intensely devoted to worldly existence? Go, go as you came.
Then, having heard those words of Śveta, the terrifying Tīkṣṇadaṃṣṭra became enraged; holding a noose in his hand, he appeared formidable.
Having let out a great lion’s roar and lashing his tail again and again,
Kāla bound the Sage and spoke to him, who had reached his appointed time.
"O brahmin-sage, you have been bound by me to lead Śveta to the abode of Yama;
what indeed has been done for you today by Rudra, the god of gods?"
Where is Śarva, and where is your devotion? Where is the worship, and what is the fruit of that worship?
Where am I, and where is my fear? O Śveta, you are indeed bound by me.
O Śveta, Rudra Maheśvara is established within this liṅga;
since that Mahādeva is motionless, how is Maheśvara to be worshipped?
Then Sadāśiva himself, Hara— the enemy of Smara and destroyer of the sacrifice— smiling, prepared to slay Antaka, who had come to kill the twice-born.
The supreme Śiva himself, the three-eyed Tryambaka, quickly emerged together with Ambā, Nandin, and the lords of the Gaṇas.
Beholding Bhava out of fear, he indeed cast off his life in an instant;
O twice-born ones, the powerful one quickly fell into the presence of the sage.
O best of brahmins, having gazed upon the destroyer of Death himself, he of exalted intellect roared aloud; for by that very glance, Bhava was indeed rendered dead.
The lords of the gods cried out loudly to Maheśvara,
while the lords of the sages, filled with joy, bowed down to Ambikā Umā.
The sky-dwellers indeed showered from the heavens a most beautiful, cool, and excellent rain of flowers upon the head of that sage Bhava.
Then, having beheld Antaka dead, he was greatly amazed;
the son of Śilāśana bowed down to the imperishable Śiva, the auspicious Śaṅkara.
The young-minded one said to the sage, "Be gracious to the deceased," while Maheśvara’s follower, Gaṇeśvara, [spoke] to Maheśvara.
Then the Blessed One, having shown favor to that best of the twice-born, entered [the city];
for in an instant he saw Antaka destroyed, his body vanished in a moment.
Therefore, O twice-born ones, one should worship Mṛtyuñjaya with devotion;
he is Śaṅkara, the bestower of both liberation and worldly enjoyment upon all.
What is the use of much talk? Having renounced [all else] and worshipped Bhava with supreme devotion, you shall indeed become free from sorrow.
Śailādi said: Having been addressed thus by that Brahmā, the speakers of Brahman [requested]:
"Be gracious; let there be devotion toward Rudra, the wielder of the Pināka bow, the Lord of Gods."
O Lord, by what austerity, or by what sacrifice,
or even by what vows shall the twice-born become devotees of the Blessed One?
The Grandfather said:
"O best of sages, it is not by giving, nor by austerity, nor by knowledge; not by sacrifices, oblations, vows, the Vedas, the treatises on yoga, or by restraints."
"That devotion toward Śiva, the supreme cause, does not exist at all within him.
Then, having heard those words, all those great sages—
Accompanied by their wives and sons, they were weary, yet they prostrated before the Grandfather;
therefore, devotion to Pāśupati bestows the attainment of dharma, kāma, and artha.
She is the victory of the Sage and the bestower of triumph over all death;
for in ancient times, Dadhīca, having conquered the omnipresent Lord Hari through devotion, [conquered] the immortals.
He struck Kṣaya with his foot and attained the state of having bones as hard as a thunderbolt;
even death was conquered by me through the chanting of Mahādeva’s names.
But by that best of sages, Śveta,
having gone [to the abode of Śiva], death was conquered through the grace of Mahādeva, just as death has been conquered by me.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter in the first part of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
O Lord, you should explain to me how the inhabitants of the Devadāru forest, through their devotion to Bhava, sought refuge in the God.
Śailādi said: The Blessed One, the Self-born himself, spoke to those illustrious ones who were staying in the Devadāru forest, shining with the brilliance of fire due to their ascetic penance.
The Grandfather said:
This god is to be known as Mahādeva, the Great Lord;
no state superior to him can ever be attained.
He is the Lord of the gods, the sages, and the ancestors;
at the end of a thousand yugas, during the dissolution, he [withdraws] all embodied beings.
Becoming Time, this Lord Maheśvara withdraws all things;
and he alone, by his own splendor, creates all creatures.
He is the wielder of the discus and the wielder of the thunderbolt, marked with the Śrīvatsa;
he is the yogin in the Kṛta age, and in the Tretā age he is called Kratu.
In the Dvāpara age he is Kālāgni, and in the Kali age he is remembered as Dharmaketu;
these are the forms of Rudra which the wise meditate upon.

One should worship the *liṅga* thus: it should be quadrangular on the outside and octagonal within, resting upon a pedestal (*piṇḍikā*), and the *sudarśana* [portion] should be circular; such is the fit form.
For Tamas is Agni, Rajas is Brahmā, and Sattva is Viṣṇu, the illuminator;
his single form stands established, and [these] are proclaimed as his forms.
Wherever that Brahman, endowed with yoga, abides,
[there one should worship] the Lord of the gods, Īśāna, the immutable Master.
The best of Brahmins, having conquered anger and subdued their senses,
propitiate [the deity] by fashioning a linga according to the rules and endowed with all the required characteristics.
It should be the size of a thumb, very beautiful, well-rounded, and approved by all;
it may likewise be circular, octagonal, or even sixteen-sided.
It should be well-rounded, circular, divine, and bestowing the fruits of all desires;
its altar (vedikā) should be twice its size, or equal to it, as is approved by all.

O best of the twice-born, the altar (vedi) should be one-third of that [height] and endowed with the proper characteristics; and the fillet (paṭṭikā) should indeed be one barley-corn (yava) wide all around.
Having made [the pedestal] of gold, silver, stone, or likewise of copper,
its width on all sides should indeed be three times that of the altar.
It may be circular, square, hexagonal, or triangular;
it should be flawless on all sides, bright, and well-characterized by auspicious marks.
O twice-born ones, having established [the image] according to rule and accompanied by the characteristics of worship, one should likewise place a water-pot (kalaśa) in the center of its altar.
Then one should sprinkle the liṅga with auspicious, pure water containing gold and seeds, consecrated by the Brahmā-mantras, using the five purifying substances.
And you shall worship according to what you obtain; then you will attain success.
With concentrated minds, perform the worship together with your sons and kinsmen.
All of you, with palms joined in reverence, take refuge in the wielder of the trident;
then you shall behold the Lord of Gods, who is difficult to be seen by those who have not disciplined themselves.
Having seen him, all ignorance and unrighteousness perish; then, one should circumambulate Brahmā, who possesses immeasurable splendor.
Then those forest-dwellers set out for the Devadāru forest and began to propitiate [the deity] exactly as it had been described by Brahmā.
On various sacrificial altars, in mountain caves,
and on the secluded, auspicious sandbanks of rivers.
Some were adorned with *śaivāla* moss, some lay within the water,
and some stood upon the tips of their big toes amidst the blades of *darbha* grass.
Others, however, used their teeth as a mortar; likewise, others were grinders with stones.
Some remained in fixed postures, while others delighted in the lifestyle of wild animals.
Those of great intelligence pass their time through austerity and worship;
thus, when a full year has elapsed and spring has arrived— LiP_1,31.26.
Then, out of compassion for those devotees, the Lord, for the sake of their grace,
[appeared] on that auspicious mountain of Himavat during that Kṛta Yuga.
Having reached the Devadāru forest, the Supreme Lord appeared serene,
his limbs smeared with ashes and dust, naked, and possessing deformed characteristics.
With a firebrand held in his hand and eyes reddish-brown,
he sometimes laughs fiercely and sometimes sings in wonder.
In one place he dances with amorous passion; in another he cries out again and again;
in the hermitage he wanders about for alms and begs repeatedly.
Having assumed such an illusory form, the god came to that forest;
then all those sages, with concentrated minds, offered him praise.
With water, various garlands, incense, and likewise with perfumes,
those highly fortunate ones, together with their wives, sons, and retinues, [should perform the rites].
Then those sages spoke thus to the Lord with these words:
"O Lord of the gods, whatever has been performed by us was done out of ignorance."
You ought to forgive all that— whether by deed, thought, or word—
including their various, secret, and profound conduct.
O Hara, these [powers] of yours are difficult for even the gods, beginning with Brahmā, to comprehend;
we know neither your coming nor indeed your going.
O Viśveśvara, O Mahādeva, you who are what you are—salutations be to you!
The great-souled ones praise you, the God of gods, the Great Lord (Maheśvara).
Homage to Bhava, to Bhavya, to Bhāvanā, and to Udbhava;
homage to the Lord of beings, who possesses infinite strength and vigor.
Salutations to the destroyer, to the tawny one, to the imperishable and to the perishable,
to the stream of the Gaṅgā’s waters, to the support, and to the one whose essence is the qualities.
Salutation be to the three-eyed Tryambaka, who bears the trident and the boon-granting gesture;
salutation to Kandarpa, to Hutāśa, and to the Supreme Self.
Salutation to Śaṅkara, who is marked by the bull, the lord of the Gaṇas;
salutation indeed to Kāla, who holds a staff in his hand and holds a noose in his hand.
Salutations indeed to the one whose primary essence is the Vedic mantras, who possesses a hundred tongues;
to that which is past, present, and future, and all that is stationary and moving.
O Lord, this entire universe has arisen from your body;
you protect it and you destroy it—blessings be upon you! Therefore, O Blessed One, be gracious.
Whatever a person does, whether out of ignorance or through true knowledge, all that is done by the Blessed Lord alone through his yogic power (yogamāyā).
Having thus praised him, the sages, endowed with ascetic power and with their inner selves filled with joy, entreated: "May we behold you as before."
Then the Lord Śaṅkara, with a gracious soul, assuming his own form, the three-eyed one, the Lord granted him divine vision so that he might behold it.
Having obtained that vision and beheld the three-eyed God of gods,
the inhabitants of the Devadāru forest praised Īśāna once again.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
The sages said:
Homage always to the sky-clad one, to Kṛtānta, to the wielder of the trident,
to the formidable, to the terrifying, and to the one with a gaping mouth.
Salutation to you who are formless, beautifully formed, and the universal form;
salutation indeed to Kaṭaṅkaṭa, to Rudra, and to Svāhākāra.
Salutations again and again to Śrīkaṇṭha, whose body is bowed by all, who himself bows to his own self, and who eternally possesses a blue crest-lock.
To the blue-throated god who wears the ashes of the funeral pyre upon his limbs:
you are Brahmā among all the gods, and Nīlalohita among the Rudras.
The Sāṃkhyas call the Self the Puruṣa of all beings;
as Mahāmeru is among mountains, so is the Moon among the stars.
Among the sages you are Vasiṣṭha, and likewise among the gods you are Vāsava;
you are the syllable Oṃ among all the Vedas, and the Sāman among the Sāmans is the most excellent.
Among wild animals, you are the lion, the supreme lord;
among domestic animals, you are the bull, the Blessed One worshipped by the world.
"Whatever entity may exist in every way throughout the future, we perceive you alone therein; so it was declared by Brahmā."
Lust, anger, greed, despondency, and even arrogance—
O Supreme Lord, be gracious and grant us the means to understand these.
O God, when the time for the great dissolution arrived, you, whose self is perfected,
pressed your hand against your forehead and produced fire.
At that time, the worlds were enveloped on all sides by the flames of that fire;
therefore, these many transformed fires are indeed equal to that [primordial] fire.
Lust, anger, greed, delusion, hypocrisy, and affliction—
whatever other beings there are, whether stationary or moving.
Those living beings are being consumed by the fire arising from you;
O Lord of the Gods, become the protector of us who are being burned.
And you, O Maheśvara, illustrious lord and auspicious observer, sprinkle living beings for the sake of the welfare of the world.
"Command us, O Lord; we shall carry out your word throughout thousands of millions of spirits and hundreds of millions of forms."
We were unable to reach the end; O God of gods, salutations be unto you!
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter in the first part of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Nandin said:
Then, having heard their hymn of praise, the Blessed One Maheśvara was pleased; bestowing his grace upon them after being lauded, he spoke these words.
The Brahmin who recites, or even listens to, this hymn proclaimed by you,
or causes the twice-born to hear it, shall attain the status of a leader of the Gaṇas.
O best of sages, I shall declare for your benefit and for the sake of my devotees that which is meritorious:
the entire female gender is the Goddess, Prakṛti, born from my own body. (The advantages of the Pāśupata conduct)
The male gender, O Brahmins, is Puruṣa, who has arisen from my body;
indeed, O Brahmins, the creation proceeds from both of us, of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, one should not revile an ascetic who is clad only in the directions (naked),
who acts like a child or a madman, who is devoted to Me, and who speaks of Brahman.

For those brahmins who are devoted to the sacred ash, whose sins have been burnt away by the ash, who act according to what has been taught, who are self-controlled, and who are intent upon meditation; LiP_1,33.6 //
Constantly devoted to Mahādeva, practicing the vow of perpetual celibacy (ūrdhvaretas), and restrained in speech, mind, and body, they worship Mahādeva.
Having reached the world of Rudra, they do not return again;
therefore, this divine vow is unmanifest, even for those who possess manifest emblems.

A wise man should not speak ill of those who observe the ash-vow, those who are shaven-headed, those under religious observances, or those of manifold forms; nor should he ever transgress against them.
One who seeks his own welfare in this world and the next should not laugh excessively nor speak what is unpleasant;
for that deluded soul who reviles them reviles Mahādeva himself.
But whoever should constantly worship these, he worships Śaṅkara;
thus does this Mahādeva act out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
In age after age, the great yogi sports, covered in ashes;
practice in this manner, O blessed ones, and you shall thereby attain perfection.
Having realized here that supreme state taught by Śiva— the cause of destroying incomparable and great fear—
those whose minds were free from the greed and delusion of worldly existence suddenly prostrated with their heads before the Fierce One.
Then, having heard what was thus related, the brahmins were delighted;
with very pure water mixed with perfumes, *kuśa* grass, and flowers, they [proceeded].
They bathe Maheśvara with water from great jars,
and they sing various secret hymns as well as beautiful-sounding *huṃ* syllables.
Homage to the God of gods, to Mahādeva;
homage indeed to him whose body is half-female, the promulgator of Sāṃkhya and Yoga.

To the one whose vehicle is the cloud, who is dark-hued, who dwells in an elephant hide, who has a black antelope skin as his upper garment, and who wears a serpent as his sacred thread; LiP_1,33.17 //

Salutations be to Śaṅkara, who is renowned for his fame, who wears well-fashioned and most variegated earrings, who is adorned with exquisitely crafted garlands and ornaments, and who is clothed in the skin of the best of beasts.
Then Maheśvara, pleased, replied to those sages:
"I am gratified by your asceticism; choose a boon, O you of noble vows."
Then all those sages— Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Vasiṣṭha, and likewise Viśvāmitra— having prostrated before Maheśvara, [spoke].
Gautama, Atri, Sukeśa, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Marīci, Kaśyapa, Kaṇva, and Saṃvarta of great asceticism; LiP_1,33.21.
Having prostrated before Mahādeva, they spoke these words:
"The bathing in ashes, nakedness, left-handedness, and contrariety."
"And thus we wish to know that which is to be served and that which is not to be served.
Then, having heard their words, the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Sovereign, [spoke].
Then, looking at all those excellent sages, he spoke with a smile.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Words of the Sages," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Then the Blessed Lord said:
Today I shall indeed proclaim to you this narrative, the very essence of all things:
for I am Agni, the creator of Soma, and Soma is dependent upon Agni.
Fire carries away this world again because it is the refuge of all beings;
for the entire world, both mobile and immobile, has been repeatedly consumed by fire.
All this has been rendered into ashes; this is the supreme purifier.
Having established its power through the ash, one sprinkles it upon all beings.
And whoever, having performed the fire-ritual, shall perform the *triyāyuṣa* rite with my ashes through my power, is liberated from all sins.
That which shines, that which is auspicious, and that which one contemplates—because of its consumption, it destroys all sins; thus it is proclaimed as "Bhasma" (ashes).
The ancestors are to be known as those who drink the warm [steam], while the gods indeed originate from Soma;
the entire world, both stationary and moving, consists of the nature of Agni and Soma.
I am Agni of great splendor, and this Great Ambika is Soma;
I am both Agni and Soma, being by nature the Puruṣa himself.
Therefore, O highly fortunate ones, ash is said to be my own virility;
it is my established nature that I sustain this as my own virility through my very body.
From that time forward, for the sake of protection against inauspicious things in the worlds,
protection with ashes is performed in the houses of women who have recently given birth.
One whose self is purified by the ash-bath, who has conquered anger and subdued the senses,
having come into my presence, does not return again.
The Pāśupata vow and the Yoga system were fashioned by Kapila;
indeed, this Pāśupata was fashioned first, and it is unsurpassed.
And all the other stages of life were created later by the Self-born One;
this creation was fashioned by me as consisting of shame, delusion, and fear.
For indeed, the deities and likewise the sages are born naked;
and all other human beings in the world are born without clothing.
One whose senses are unsubdued is naked even if clothed in fine silk; one whose senses are restrained is truly protected. It is taught that clothing is not the cause of modesty.
