Forgiveness, fortitude, non-violence, and complete dispassion,
as well as equanimity toward honor and dishonor— these constitute the supreme means of its obscuration.
One whose limbs are smeared with the ash-bath meditates upon Bhava with the mind;
even if one has committed thousands of improper acts, he who bathes with the ash [is purified].
Just as fire consumes a forest with its brilliance, reducing it all to ashes,
so too does he who is always devoted to effort [burn away his sins] even three times a day.
He who performs his bath with ashes attains the state of a leader of the Gaṇas;
having gathered all the sacrifices and undertaken the supreme vow.
Those who meditate upon Mahādeva, being permeated by the true nature of his divine play,
shall attain immortality by means of the northern path of the noble ones.
And on the southern path are those who have resorted to the cremation grounds:
Aṇimā, Garimā, Laghimā, and Prāpti.

Desire, the power of fulfilling desires at will, as well as irresistible will; and those who, by means of their vision, frequented the cremation grounds [attained] atomization, heaviness, lightness, and extension.
Likewise, Indra and the other gods, having undertaken the Kāmika vow,
all attained supreme sovereignty and became renowned for their splendor.

Having understood this supreme state of transcendence, one whose nature is free from the defects of darkness and passion, and who is liberated from attachment and freed from pride and delusion, should always be devoted to the yoga of Paśupati.
Meditating upon this *pāśupata* [mantra], which destroys all sins,
whoever shall recite it— having become pure, full of faith, and with senses subdued— [attains the supreme goal].
With his soul purified of all sins, he goes to the world of Rudra;
having heard this, all those sages, the best of the twice-born, beginning with Vasiṣṭha, [were filled with wonder].
With their limbs smeared white with ashes and free from all worldly desire,
they remained established for the sake of the world of Rudra at the end of the aeon through the splendor of Śiva.
Therefore, the best of Brahmins— whether deformed or filthy, or even endowed with beauty— are never to be despised but are to be honored, always out of suspicion that they may be lords of yogis.
What is the use of much talk? O best of the twice-born, those devoted to Bhava should be honored with every effort as if they were Śiva himself; there is no doubt in this matter.
And the lords of brahmins, though they were devoted to Bhava and firm in their vows, became defiled;
yet Dadhīca remained steadfast after having conquered the God of gods.
Likewise, there is no doubt that one attains Nārāyaṇa in this world through devotion to Rudra;
therefore, with every effort, let the hairs of your body be smeared with ashes.
Those with matted hair, those with shaven heads, the naked, and those of various other kinds,
should always be honored like Śiva through thought, deed, and speech.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Praise of Yogis," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sanatkumāra said:
O observer of noble vows, how did Dadhīca, having conquered Janārdana, the God of gods, strike King Kṣupa with his foot in battle?
O Śailādi, you of great asceticism, you ought to tell me how you obtained the state of being a Vajra-body from Mahādeva, and how death was conquered by you.
Śailādi said: O lord of men, there was a king of great splendor known as Kṣupa, the son of Brahmā,
who was a friend of Dadhīci, the lord of sages.
After a long time, due to their mutual encounter, a dispute arose between Kṣupa and Dadhīca, which became renowned as to whether the best of Kṣatriyas or the Brahmin was superior.
The king assumes the forms of the eight world-protectors;
therefore, he is indeed Indra, Agni, Yama, and likewise Nirṛti.
Varuṇa, Vāyu, Soma, and Dhanada as well—I am Īśvara, there is no doubt; I must certainly not be disregarded.
O observer of noble vows, she who is the Great Deity is also the Great One;
therefore, O highly fortunate son of Cyavana, I am always [to be honored] by you.
Having heard that opinion of Kṣupa, the best of sages [replied]: "In this world, he is certainly not to be despised, but must be honored in every way. LiP_1,35.8.
The fierce twice-born Dadhīca and Cyāvani, out of pride in their own status,
struck Kṣupa on the head with their left fists;
then the powerful Kṣupa cut Dadhīca down with his thunderbolt.
Formerly, in the world of Brahmā, that thunderbolt was indeed produced from the hunger of Brahmā; and the Lord, being urged by the Wielder of the Thunderbolt for the sake of his purpose, obtained it.
Having become a man by his own will, he became a protector of men;
therefore, that mighty king indeed conquered the best of Brahmins.
Just as the glorious and powerful Vajradhara, overcome by darkness,
fell to the ground when struck by the thunderbolt, so did that bull among the twice-born fall.
And then, in that place, he remembered the sage Bhārgava out of his distress;
Śukra also restored him who had been struck by the thunderbolt.
Having returned from the yoga [of absorption] to the body of Dadhīca, that best among embodied beings,
Bhārgava, restored Dadhīca’s body as it was before and spoke to him.
O illustrious Dadhīca, having worshipped the God of gods, the Lord of Umā, who is worthy of worship by Brahmā and the other deities, and who is the stainless God of gods; LiP_1,35.15.
"O brahmin-sage, by the grace of Tryambaka, you shall be invulnerable;
for I have obtained this power of reviving the dead from him, O twice-born one."
For the devotees of Śambhu, there is no fear of death here from any quarter;
today I shall also declare to you the Śaiva "Revival of the Dead" (Mṛtasaṃjīvana).
We worship Tryambaka, the Lord who is the father of the three worlds,
the father of the triple sphere, the Great Lord of the three qualities.

To Mahādeva— the essence of the three principles, the triple fire, manifested in three ways everywhere, the possessor of the three Vedas, fragrant, and the increaser of nourishment— [I offer salutation].
In all beings everywhere, in the three qualities (guṇas) and likewise in primordial nature (prakṛti), as well as in the sense organs, and in other deities and their hosts; ||| 1,35.20 |||

O best of the twice-born, just as fragrance is subtle within flowers, so is the Supreme Lord a subtle fragrance; and from Him comes the nourishment that is the primordial nature (prakṛti) of the Puruṣa.

O observer of noble vows, O great sage, even for Viṣṇu, Pitāmaha (Brahmā), and the sages, there exists the conceptual differentiation of everything from the Great Principle (mahat) down to the specific elements (viśeṣa).
Therefore, he is indeed the nourisher of Indra and of the gods;
one should worship that immortal god Rudra through ritual action as well as through austerity.
Through the study of sacred texts, through yoga, and through meditation, we offer our worship;
by this truth, may Bhava himself release me from the noose of death.
Since it brings about both bondage and liberation, like the urvāruka fruit,
this mantra— the reviver of the dead— has been obtained by me from Śaṅkara.

O twice-born one, by reciting [the mantra], offering oblations, consecrating water in this manner, drinking that water day and night, and meditating in the presence of the Liṅga, there is no fear of death.
Having heard those words of his, he propitiated Śaṅkara through ascetic penance and obtained the state of having a vajra-like bone, invincibility, and freedom from dejection.
Having thus propitiated the Lord of Gods, Dadhīca, the best of sages,
diligently obtained invulnerability from others as well as the state of having adamantine bones.
And he struck the lord of kings on the head with his foot;
the powerful Kṣupa then struck Dadhīca on the chest with his thunderbolt.
That thunderbolt did not bring about the destruction of the high-souled Dadhīca,
due to the power of the Supreme Lord, whose body was bound by the thunderbolt.
Having witnessed the invincibility and the lack of dejection of Dadhīca, as well as his power,
Kṣupa then propitiated Hari Mukunda, the lotus-eyed younger brother of Indra, upon seeing him.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Defeat of King Kṣupa," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Nandin said:
Satisfied by his worship, the Blessed One, the Supreme Person—
glorious, accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi, and bearing the conch, discus, and mace— appeared.
Wearing a crown and holding a lotus in his hand, adorned with all ornaments,
the Blessed One was clad in yellow garments and surrounded by gods and daityas.
The one whose banner is Garuḍa indeed granted him a divine vision;
having seen the god Janārdana through that very divine vision, [he was filled with joy].
Having prostrated before the one whose banner is Garuḍa, he praised him with pleasing words:
"You are the beginning, you are without beginning; you are Prakṛti, O Janārdana."
"You are the Puruṣa, the Lord of the World; you are Viṣṇu, the Sovereign of the Universe.
You who are this Brahmā, the Puruṣa, the Grandfather whose form is the universe."
O Janārdana, you alone are the primordial reality, the supreme light;
O Lord of Śrī, O Lord of the earth, O Master, you are the Supreme Self and the highest abode.
Rudra, born from your anger and enveloped by darkness (tamas), became the destroyer of the world;
and through your grace, the Grandfather (Brahmā) became the creator of the world through passion (rajas).
Through your grace, Viṣṇu himself, the Supreme Person, exists by means of his essence; O Hara, O Hari, O Viṣṇu, O Nārāyaṇa, you who are identical with the universe! LiP_1,36.8.
Likewise, O Maheśvara, whose form is the universe, Mahat, as well as the source of the elements (bhūtādi), the subtle elements (tanmātrāṇi), and the sense organs, are presided over by you alone.
O Mahādeva, Lord of the World, Grandfather, Teacher of the Universe!
Be gracious, O Lord of the Gods; be gracious, O Supreme Lord!
Be gracious, O Lord of the World! I have come to you for refuge, O Vaikuṇṭha, Śauri, Omniscient One, Vāsudeva of mighty arms!
O Saṃkarṣaṇa, O highly fortunate one; O Pradyumna, O Supreme Person;
O Aniruddha, O Great Viṣṇu; O Eternal Viṣṇu, let there be salutation unto you!
O Viṣṇu, your divine seat is unmanifest and pervasive in the center;
it is the bearer of the earth, possessing a form of darkness and endowed with a thousand hoods.
Furthermore, O Lord of Gods, dharma, knowledge, dispassion,
and sovereignty constitute the feet of this throne, O observer of noble vows.
The seven netherworlds are your feet, and the earth is your hips;
the seven oceans are your garments, and the quarters of space are your great arms.
O All-pervading One, heaven is your head, space is your navel, and the wind has entered your nostrils;
the moon and the sun are your eyes, and the lotuses and other such plants are indeed your hair.
With the constellations, stars, and the heavens as my neck-ornaments,
how shall I praise the Lord of Gods, the Supreme Person who is worthy of worship?
Whatever has been performed with faith, whatever has been heard, and whatever has been proclaimed—O Lord Nārāyaṇa, forgive all that which was desired; salutations be unto you!
Śailādi said: This Vaiṣṇava hymn, which destroys all sins, was proclaimed by Kṣupa; whoever recites it or even hears it [shall be purified].
Or if he causes the twice-born to hear it with devotion, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Having thus worshipped and praised the unconquerable Lord, who is himself praised by the lords of the thirty gods and others,
he gazed upon Janārdana with devotion, prostrated with his head, and made this request.
The king said:
"O Blessed One, there was once a certain Brāhmaṇa renowned as Dadhīca;
he was a knower of dharma and a humble soul, who was my friend in the past."
"Though he is forever invulnerable to all, being solely intent on the worship of Śaṅkara,
he then placed his left foot contemptuously upon my head in the midst of the assembly."
He struck Viṣṇu, the lord of gods and master of the entire world;
and, possessed by intoxication, he said, "I am not afraid of anything."
"O Lord of the World, O Janārdana, I wish to conquer that brahmin Dadhīca; you ought to act in such a way as will be for our benefit."
Śailādi said: Having realized that the high-souled Dadhīca was indeed incapable of being slain,
Hari called to mind the incomparable power of Maheśa.
Having remembered this, Hari spoke to Brahmā regarding the origin of hunger;
O king of kings, having approached Maheśvara, there is no fear for the Brahmins.
O King, there is always fearlessness for those especially devoted to Rudra everywhere;
how much more so for this Dadhīca, even though he was of low birth?
Therefore, O illustrious lord of the earth, there shall be no victory for you;
I cause this suffering for the sake of the brahmin’s curse upon me and the gods.
O King of kings, by his curse at the sacrifice of Dakṣa, my destruction along with the gods shall come to pass, as well as my subsequent restoration.
Therefore, O lord of the earth, having approached that best of Brahmins with every effort,
O Indra among kings, I shall make an endeavor for your victory over Dadhīca.
Śailādi said: Having heard these words, Kṣupa said to Janārdana, "So be it," and the Blessed One then went to the hermitage of the brahmin Dadhīca.
Assuming the form of a Brahmin, the Blessed One, the teacher of the world who is compassionate toward his devotees, saluted the brahminical seer Dadhīca and spoke to him.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O Dadhīca, O Brahman-sage, O imperishable one devoted to the worship of Śiva!
I choose a single boon from you; you ought to grant it."
Requested by Viṣṇu, the god of gods, Dadhīca said:
"I know all that you desire; I do not fear even you."
O Janārdana, you have come in the form of a brahmin;
O Lord of Gods, O Janārdana, you are the past, the future, and the present.
"O you of noble vows, abandon your status as a twice-born through the grace of Rudra;
O Madhusūdana, you have been propitiated by Kṣupa, O Lord of Gods."
O Lord Hari, I know this affection you have for your devotees;
O Lord Hari, this devotion-loving kindness of yours is indeed fitting.
"O Blessed One, if there is fear for me who am devoted to the worship of Bhava,
you ought to explain it with effort, O lotus-eyed giver of boons."
Therefore, O Janārdana, I speak no falsehood;
for that reason, I have no fear even of gods, daityas, or brahmins in this world.
Nandi said:
Having heard the words of Dadhīci, Janārdana then abandoned his form as a twice-born in an instant and, assuming his own form with a smile, spoke.
The Blessed One said: "O Dadhīca of noble vows, there is no fear for you anywhere,
because you are devoted to the worship of Bhava and you are indeed all-knowing."
"O best of Brahmins, you ought to say 'I am afraid' just once; by my command, O lord of sages, go now toward Kṣupa in the assembly."
Even after hearing those conciliatory words of Viṣṇu, the great sage Dadhīca said to that best of gods, "I am not afraid."
By the power of Śambhu, the god of gods, the wielder of the Pināka bow,
of this Śarva, the benefactor, the omniscient one, the great sage [attained his state].
Then, having heard the words of that sage, the Lord Hari became enraged;
raising his discus, he desired to incinerate that best of sages.
Indeed, Viṣṇu’s Sudarśana discus had its edge blunted by the power of Dadhīca,
in the very presence of Kṣupa.
Seeing that the edge of his discus had been blunted, Dadhīca spoke with a smile to the wielder of the discus, who is the manifest cause of both the existent and the non-existent.
O Blessed One, you obtained in the past a most formidable discus,
known as Sudarśana, through great effort, O Viṣṇu.
"This auspicious wheel of existence does not wish to strike me down here;
therefore, you ought to make an effort with the Brahmā-weapon and other such means."
Śailādi said: Having heard those words of his and seeing that his weapon was devoid of power,
he discharged all his missiles toward him from every side once again.
Then the imperishable gods, possessed of great strength, rendered assistance to Viṣṇu as he set out to fight with that single twice-born one.
Then, taking a handful of kusha grass and remembering Bhava,
the self-controlled Dadhīca emitted adamantine bones for all the gods from every part of his body.
A divine trident appeared, possessing a radiance like the fire of cosmic destruction;
it resolved to burn the gods, like another conflagration at the end of an eon.
O Sage, all the weapons that had been abandoned by the gods, beginning with Indra and Nārāyaṇa, bowed down before the trident.
And all the gods fled, their vigor destroyed, O best of the twice-born;
then the Blessed Viṣṇu, the Supreme Person, emitted [a being] from his own body.
The best of sages suddenly incinerated all those divine hosts, numbering tens of millions, which were equal to himself.
Then, for the sake of causing wonder, Hari became the universal form;
the best of the twice-born beheld within the body of that Hari all things manifest.
The venerable brahmin Dadhīca [addressed] the various hosts of deities:
the crores of Rudras and the crores of their attendants at that time.
Then, having seen all this— including tens of millions of eggs upon the body of the Universal Form— Cyavana was struck with wonder.
Having sprinkled Viṣṇu with water, the great sage addressed that Viṣṇu— the Lord of the World, who consists of the world, the unborn, and the all-pervading one— who possesses a universal form.
Abandon illusion, O mighty-armed one; appearances vanish upon investigation.
Thousands of consciousnesses are difficult to comprehend, O Mādhava.
"O blameless one, behold within me the entire universe together with you, as well as Brahmā and Rudra; I grant you divine vision."
Having said this, the sage displayed everything within his own body and spoke to that god Hari, who is the source of the birth of all the gods.
O Lord Viṣṇu, was this accomplished through illusion, or perhaps through the power of mantras, or through the power of the object itself, or again, through the power of meditation?
"Therefore, having abandoned this illusion, you ought to strive to fight.
Having heard these words of his and beheld that wonderful majesty, [he did so].
The gods fled further toward that god Nārāyaṇa;
then the lotus-born one, the teacher of the world, restrained him while he remained motionless.
Having heard those words of Brahmā,
the Blessed Viṣṇu, defeated by him, bowed down to the great sage and departed.
Kṣupa, becoming afflicted by grief, honored the lord of sages;
having quickly saluted Dadhīca, he, being distraught, made this request.
"O Lord, O friend Dadhīca, please forgive what has been done by me out of ignorance;
for what does it matter to you, a devotee of Rudra, whether it was done by Viṣṇu or even by the gods?"
Be gracious, O Supreme Lord! Devotion, O best among the devoted, is difficult for the wicked to attain, O twice-born one; it is even more so for those like me, the lowest of kṣatriyas.
Having heard this and shown him favor, the brahmin Dadhīca,
the best of ascetics and a tiger among sages, cursed the king and the foremost of the gods.
May the gods, together with Indra and accompanied by Viṣṇu, be destroyed by the god along with the lords of sages through the fire of Rudra’s wrath.
At the sacred sacrifice of the high-souled Prajāpati Dakṣa,
having thus cursed Kṣupa and looking at him, the best of the twice-born spoke again.
O Indra among kings, they are worshipped by the gods, by various kings, and by diverse hosts;
indeed, O Indra among kings, the Brāhmaṇas alone are powerful and sovereign.
Having spoken thus, the brahmin of great luster entered his own hut;
and having paid homage to Dadhīca, the king departed for his own abode.
That very place became a sacred ford (tīrtha) known as Sthāneśvara;
having reached Sthāneśvara, one attains union with Śiva (śivasāyujya).
O great sage, I have related to you in brief the dispute between those two of agitated minds,
as well as the supernatural power of Dadhīca and of Bhava.
He who recites this divine account of the dispute between the two of agitated intellects,
having conquered untimely death, goes to the world of Brahmā at the end of his body's life.
Whoever enters battle after reciting this shall never have fear of death and shall be victorious.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Kṣupa and Dadhīci," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sanatkumāra said:
"How did you come to encounter Mahādeva, the lord of Umā?
O Lord, I wish to hear all of that; you should tell it to me."
Śailādi said: O great sage, my father was Śilāda, who desired offspring;
he was blind and for a very long time performed most difficult penance.
As he was performing penance, the Lord who wields the thunderbolt became gratified by his asceticism;
pleased, he said to Śilāda, "I am satisfied; choose boons."
Then, O tiger among sages, having prostrated before the Lord of Gods, the thousand-eyed Hari, together with the immortals, he spoke with palms joined in reverence.
Śilāda said:
"O Blessed One, slayer of the enemies of the gods, thousand-eyed one, bestower of boons,
O you of noble vows, I desire a son who is not born from a womb and is free from death."
Śakra said:
"O brahmin-sage, I shall give you a son born from a womb who is subject to death;
otherwise, I will not grant one, for indeed there are none who are free from death."
"Even the blessed Grandfather will not grant you a son here who is free from death and not born of a womb; how much less so others, O great sage? (LiP 1.37.7)
Even that god Brahmā himself is not free from death, nor is he the Supreme Lord;
for though he possesses great splendor, he was born from a womb, born from an egg, and originated from a lotus.
The son of Maheśvara and the lordly offspring of Bhavānī—
his lifespan is likewise declared to be equal to two parārdhas.
Indeed, thousands of millions upon millions of days have already passed in the three remaining eons.
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, abandon all hope for a son born of no womb who is free from death; instead, accept a son who is equal to yourself.
Śailādi said: Having heard those words of his, my father, the world-renowned and meritorious Śilāda, spoke again to the Lord of Śacī.
Śilāda said:
"O Blessed One, I have indeed heard that Brahmā has his origin in the cosmic egg (aṇḍayoni), his origin in the lotus (padmayoni), and his origin from the body of Maheśvara."
O mighty-armed one, tell us quickly how this occurred long ago from Nārada, the elder brother of the son of Mahendra, as he was speaking. LiP_1,37.14.
She was the daughter of Dakṣa, and Dakṣa himself was the son of the lotus-born Brahmā; how then could that powerful lord be the son of her granddaughter, Kanakagarbha?
Śakra said:
"O Brahmin, it is fitting that you should have had this doubt; I shall tell you the reason for it, which occurred during the Kalpa of Parameṣṭhin Brahmā, known as Tatpuruṣa."
At the beginning of the Meghavāhana kalpa, Janārdana, the Supreme Lord and Master of the World, meditated upon Brahmā and created him in his entirety.
Having become a cloud, Nārāyaṇa bore Mahādeva for a thousand divine years with great honor and reverence.
Having perceived within his own self the nature of Hari, the great god Śaṅkara bestowed everything upon him, together with Brahmā, for the purpose of creation.
Then they indeed called that eon by the name Meghavāhana;
having seen him, Hiraṇyagarbha then arose from his body.
The son of Janārdana, having attained Śaṅkara through ascetic penance, said:
"Viṣṇu was born from your left side, and I am indeed born from your right side."
Nevertheless, Acyuta, who is identical with the universe, created the entire world together with me;
for he bore us day and night, having become a cloud.
Viṣṇu carried you, the God of gods and the Teacher of the world;
O Lord Śaṅkara, I am a devotee of you even more than of Nārāyaṇa.
"Be gracious, O Lord; grant me all, for you are the self of all.
Then, having obtained from Bhava the state of being the self of all in an instant, the Blessed One—
Then, hastening forward, he encountered and beheld the Supreme Person within the white abode of the single ocean, amidst a most dreadful darkness.
It was divine, studded with gold and jewels, fashioned by the mind alone;
difficult for the wicked to attain, it was beyond the reach even of Sanaka and the other sages through their merits.
The Unborn One beheld the Person, the heart of the world’s dwelling,
lying upon a bed of infinite coils, with eyes like lotuses.
Holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus, four-armed,
adorned with all ornaments, and resembling the orb of the moon.
[He beheld] the god Janārdana, who bears the Śrīvatsa mark, whose face is serene,
and whose lotus-feet are reddened by the touch of the soft lotus-hands of Ramā.
The Supreme Self, the Lord, who in the form of darkness is Time itself,
and through passion (rajas) is the one who sets in motion the play of creation for all the worlds.
The Supreme Lord, the establisher of all beings through his essence,
the self of all, the Great Self, the Supreme Self, the Sovereign.
Having seen the Blessed Janārdana reclining upon the ocean of milk filled with nectar in the sleep of yoga, Brahmā spoke to him.
"I embrace you with favor, so that you shall be as I was before";
thus the Blessed One, smiling, awoke the Grandfather.
The mighty-armed one looked up and gave a slight smile;
he then entered that egg-born being, having been swallowed by that great-souled one.
Then Brahmā created that Acyuta from between his eyebrows;
having been created by him, Hari looked upon him and then stood in his presence.
In the meantime, Rudra, the source of the existence of all the gods,
having assumed a transformed form in the past, had granted them a boon.
The Supreme Lord Viṣṇu, the soul of the universe, arrived at that place where the Lord was to bestow incomparable grace upon Brahmā and Hari.
Then, having come together, those two gods beheld the god Bhava, the source of the existence of all gods, the Lord who resembled the fire of cosmic destruction.
They both praised Śarva, the fierce one with matted hair,
and bowed from afar with great reverence to the granter of boons.
The Blessed Lord Bhava, the Lord of the World, having shown favor to the god Pitāmaha and Janārdana, vanished right there.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Bestowing of Boons upon Brahmā," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*. Śailādi said:
When the god Maheśvara had departed, Janārdana,
the Blessed One born from the lotus, bowed down toward him and spoke to the lotus-born Brahmā.
The illustrious Viṣṇu said: "This Śaṅkara is the Supreme Lord, the Master of the World, and the All-pervading One;
Maheśvara is the Lord of us both and of the entire universe, and our refuge."
"O Brahmin, I am born from the left limb of the high-souled Śaṅkara;
you yourself are born from the right limb of the god Bhava."
Having beheld me, the sages call me Pradhāna, as well as Prakṛti, the Unmanifest, and the Unborn; they likewise call you, O Lord, Puruṣa.
Thus they spoke to Mahādeva, saying: "He is the cause of even us two—the Lord of the entire world, the immutable Sovereign."
At the word of that Lord of the Immortals, the Lotus-born one also praised and bowed down to Rudra, the most excellent giver of boons.
Then Janārdana, having leveled the earth submerged by the waters,
established it as before while remaining in his form as a boar.
The Lord also created the rivers, streams, and oceans as before;
and having diligently made the earth free from depressions and elevations, he established it.
Having the form of a mountain, he gathered all the mountains upon the earth and fashioned the four worlds,
beginning with Bhūr, as before.
And the Blessed One, the best among the wise, set his mind upon creating the primary [creation],
as well as that of animals, the divine, and likewise the human.
And there, the omnipresent Lord, whose intellect is undepressed, first created the Kaumāra grace, namely Sananda and likewise Sanaka.
Having attained the supreme state through the cessation of ritual action (naiṣkarmya), they reached the eternal one, the best among the virtuous—
Marīci, Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu.
By means of the science of yoga, that blessed Lord created Dakṣa, Atri, and Vasiṣṭha,
as well as Saṃkalpa, Dharma, and Adharma.
These twelve indeed are the progeny of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest;
at the beginning, the Eternal One created Ṛbhu and Sanatkumāra.
And those two were of sublimated vital energy (ūrdhvaretas), divine, the first-born, exponents of the Veda (brahmavādin),
equal to Brahmā, omniscient, and all-pervasive.
Having thus created the principal [beings] and others, the lotus-born Śilāśana,
the creator of the universe, ordained all the dharmas of the ages (yugas).
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Discourse on the Vaiṣṇavas," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*. Śailādi said:
Having heard what was said by Śakra, my father, the great sage,
bowed to the Lord of the Gods and, with palms joined in reverence, questioned him again.
Śilāda said: O Blessed One, Śakra, omniscient one, saluted by the gods of gods;
O Lord of Śacī, Lord of the World, thousand-eyed one, Great Lord!
How did the Blessed One, born from the lotus, establish the duties of the ages?
You ought to tell all of this to me, who am now bowed before you.
Śailādi said: Having heard those words of the high-souled Śilāda,
he spoke at length about the dharma of the age exactly as it had been seen.
Śakra said:
"O Sage, know that the first is the Kṛta Yuga, and after that comes the Tretā Yuga."
Dvāpara and Tiṣya—these four, in brief, [are the ages].
Sattva is established in the Kṛta age, Rajas in the Tretā, and both Rajas and Tamas in the Dvāpara; Tamas alone is to be known as the Kali age—such is the conduct of the ages within the Yugas.
In the Kṛta age, meditation is supreme; in the Tretā age, sacrifice is said to be so;
in the Dvāpara age, pure devotion; and in the Kali age, only charity.
Four thousand years constitute that Kṛta Yuga; its dawn (saṃdhyā) lasts for as many hundreds of years, and its twilight (saṃdhyāṃśa) is of the same duration.
O Śilāśana of noble vows, know that the lifespan of human beings here in this Kṛta Yuga is four thousand years. LiP_1,39.9.
Then, when that Kṛta Yuga has passed along with its transitional period (saṃdhyāṃśa), the dharma of the Yuga remains in every respect as a mere quarter-remnant.
Know that the unsurpassed Tretā Yuga is one-quarter less than that;
Dvāpara is half of Kṛta, and Tiṣya is said to be half of that.
O Sage, there are three hundred, two hundred, and likewise one hundred years for the twilight (saṃdhyā);
the twilight portion (saṃdhyāṃśaka) is exactly the same, and thus it is in each kalpa and in each yuga.
In the first Kṛta Yuga, the eternal Dharma stands on four feet;
in the Tretā Yuga, it has three feet, and in the Dvāpara, it remains with two feet.
In the Kali age, however, it exists as a mere presence, deprived of three-quarters;
but in the Kṛta age, there is the birth of couples, and their livelihood consists directly of the overflowing of aesthetic essence (*rasa*).
All subjects were always satisfied, possessing every joy and enjoyment;
among those auspicious subjects, there was no distinction of high or low status.
In that Kṛta Yuga, their lifespan, happiness, and form were equal;
they possessed no sexual passion, no hatred, and no fatigue.
Dwelling upon mountains and in the ocean, they indeed have no fixed abode;
they are free from sorrow, full of goodness, and likewise devoted to solitude.
They indeed moved about free from desire, their minds always joyful;
in the Kṛta age, there was no engagement in actions that are either auspicious or sinful.

O twice-born one, at that time there was the established order of castes and stages of life, and no intermixture; however, through the influence of time, the manifestation of the [highest] rasa perishes in the age known as Tretā.
When that accomplishment has perished, another accomplishment arises;
for when the subtlety of the waters has been attained, they then indeed exist in the form of clouds.
When the release of rain proceeds from the clouds and thunderbolts, and the surface of the earth is thus once joined with that rain; LiP_1,39.21.
Then those trees, designated as houses, appeared for them;
from them, all means of subsistence and enjoyment were produced for them.
At the beginning of the Tretā Yuga, those beings sustained themselves by means of them;
then, after a long time, due to their very reversal, [the world became as it is].
At that time, their state of being, characterized by passion and greed, became sudden;
for they were affected by that which arose at that very moment through a reversal of their usual nature.
Then all those trees known as houses perished;
when they had perished, those born of sexual union became bewildered.
Then those who meditated with truthful intent upon that perfection saw those trees, known as houses, appear before them.
Their garments produce fruits as well as ornaments;
within those very fruits, there arises for them that which is endowed with fragrance, color, and flavor.
In every leaf-cup there was honey, earthy in potency and free from bees;
with that they prepared their pills, for it indeed always ensured a happy life.
By that success, the subjects indeed became joyful, well-nourished, and free from affliction;
yet, after a short time, they were once again enveloped by greed.
They forcibly seized those trees and the honey of the bees;
indeed, by that conduct of theirs, which was once again driven by greed, [the world was afflicted].
Then, due to the power of time, when that very accomplishment had only slightly remained, the wish-fulfilling trees perished here and there along with the honey.
But at the turning point toward the Tretā age, pairs of opposites indeed arose;
because of intense cold, rain, and heat, they were then greatly afflicted by suffering.
Afflicted by the pairs of opposites, they then constructed shelters on the mountain; having warded off those dualities, they established their dwellings there.
Formerly, they lived without fixed dwellings, wandering at will; then, however, they came to live in houses according to their suitability and their pleasure.
Having suffered those mutual afflictions and no longer considering any means of subsistence,
the kalpavṛkṣa trees indeed perished along with the honey at that time.
Those creatures, indeed, were agitated by disputes and afflicted by thirst and hunger;
then, in the Tretā Yuga, their success (siddhi) appeared once again.
There was also another rain that fully supported their livelihood;
indeed, from that rain came water and other resources that became rivers for them.
By the continuous flow of rain, the rivers became established as streams;
thus did the rivers come into being during the second creation of rain.
Furthermore, those drops of water that fell upon the surface of the earth became medicinal herbs through the union of water and earth.
Then, fourteen kinds of cultivated and wild plants— both those that require little tilling and those that do not,
as well as trees and shrubs that flower and bear fruit according to the seasons— were produced.
These species of trees and medicinal herbs appeared;
at that time, in the Tretā Yuga, living beings subsisted on those herbs.
Then, once again, passion and greed arose among them in every respect,
due to the inevitable course of events and the influence of the Tretā Yuga.
Then they seized the rivers, the fields, and the mountains,
as well as the trees, shrubs, and medicinal herbs, by force according to their strength.
Due to this reversal, those fourteen medicinal herbs were lost;
thinking that they had entered the earth, the Grandfather [Brahmā] considered them to be "auṣadhyas" (those who have gone into the earth).
He milked the earth with great effort, indeed for the welfare of all living beings;
and from that time forward, medicinal herbs were produced here and there by means of the plow.
Those who have come together with the desire to practice agriculture diligently are called "vārtā";
thus, vārtā is declared to be the livelihood resulting from diligent effort in farming.
Otherwise, their very existence would not endure at the end of the Tretā Yuga;
for at that time, waters arise abundantly from the hands [of the sages].
There too, all of them, overcome with mutual rage, seized one another’s sons, wives, wealth, and so forth by force, through the power of their arms.
Having understood all that, the omnipresent Lord born from the lotus created the Kṣatriyas for the sake of establishing the boundaries of conduct and for protecting [the world] from injury.
And by his own splendor, he established the system of castes and stages of life;
the Soul of the Universe himself fashioned the conduct of the world through his own conduct.
And the performance of sacrifice occurred in due order during the Tretā age;
yet even then, some of excellent vows did not practice animal sacrifice.
Then Viṣṇu, the all-seeing one, performed the sacrifice by force in due order;
at that time, O sage, the twice-born praised him as being non-violent.
Even during the Dvāpara ages, there arise divergences of opinion among men;
through mind, deed, and speech, their livelihood is accomplished only with great difficulty.
At that time, however, due to the gradual exhaustion of the bodies of all beings,
there will arise greed, wage-earning, trade, war, and a lack of certainty regarding the true principles.
The promulgation of Vedic branches, the confusion of religious duties, the subversion of the castes and stages of life, as well as desire and hatred; LiP_1,39.55 //
In the Dvāpara age, however, passion, greed, and pride prevail;
at the beginning of the Dvāpara, the Veda is divided into four parts by Vyāsas.
In the Tretā ages, this single Veda with four quarters is prescribed here;
however, due to the decline of the lifespan, it is divided during the Dvāpara ages.
Furthermore, the sons of the sages divide the distinctions through delusions of view,
by means of the arrangement of mantras and brāhmaṇas, and through the inversion of vowels and consonants.
The *saṃhitās* of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman [Vedas] were compiled separately by those wise seers,
both in their general and modified forms.
The Brāhmaṇas, the Kalpasūtras, and the Mantrapravacanās—
some indeed have set out toward them, while others stand opposed to them.
The Itihāsas and Purāṇas are divided according to the weight of time:
the Brāhma, Pādma, Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, and likewise the Bhāgavata.
The Bhaviṣya, the Nāradīya, and after that the Mārkaṇḍeya; the Āgneya, the Brahmavaivarta, the Laiṅga, and the Vārāha as well.
Then there is the one called Vāmana, as well as Kūrma, Mātsya, Gāruḍa, Skānda, and Brahmāṇḍa; their divisions are now being proclaimed.
Yama, Āpastamba, Saṃvarta, Kātyāyana, Bṛhaspati, Parāśara, Vyāsa, Śaṅkha, Likhita, Dakṣa, and Gautama; (LiP 1.39.65)
Śātātapa, Vasiṣṭha, and thousands of others such as these [have declared that] drought, death, as well as afflictions such as disease and the like [will occur].
From the sufferings born of the actions of speech and mind, disenchantment arises;
from that disenchantment, there arises for them a contemplation on liberation from suffering.
From reflection comes detachment; from detachment, the perception of defects;
and from the perception of defects, the arising of knowledge occurs in the Dvāpara age.
This state of being joined with rajas and tamas is indeed recorded as the condition in the Dvāpara age;
in the first age, Kṛta, dharma exists in its entirety, and it proceeds [in diminished form] during Tretā.
In the Dvāpara age it becomes disordered, and in the Kali age it perishes.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Śakra said:
During the Tiṣya age, men whose senses are agitated by darkness will practice deceit, malice, and even the slaughter of ascetics.
In the Kali age, there will be the disease of negligence, constant fears of hunger,
the terrible fear of drought, and the upheaval of countries.
The Veda possesses no authority, and men practice unrighteousness;
they are unrighteous and ill-behaved, full of great wrath and small intelligence.
Those born in the Kali age (Tiṣya) are greedy and speak untruths; they are of wicked progeny due to ill-performed sacrifices, poorly studied texts, improper conduct, and false traditions.
Through the fault of the actions of the Brahmins, fear arises among the subjects;
at that time, the twice-born do not study the Vedas nor perform sacrifices.
Men, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas will gradually perish,
as will the association of Śūdras with Brāhmaṇas through the practice of mantras.
In that Kali age, kings— being for the most part of the Śūdra caste— oppress the Brāhmaṇas here with [their control over] beds, seats, and food.
The killing of embryos and the killing of heroes are indeed born among the progeny;
Śūdras adopt the conduct of Brāhmaṇas, and Brāhmaṇas adopt the conduct of Śūdras.

Thieves will abide by the conduct of kings, and kings will adopt the behavior of thieves; women faithful to a single husband will no longer remain, while women who go to meet their lovers will increase in number.
Established in the system of castes and stages of life, he is born among men everywhere;
at that time, the earth yields little fruit, though in some places it yields great fruit.
O eater of stones, kings will be non-protectors and plunderers;
indeed, all Śūdras will be considered wise and will be saluted by Brāhmaṇas.
Kṣatriya kings who were not true warriors, and Brahmins who lived like Śūdras—
these small-minded men, seeing twice-born ones seated on thrones, did not rise to greet them.
Indeed, Śūdras of very limited intellect strike the foremost of the twice-born;
and the twice-born place their hand upon the mouth or the ear of a Śūdra.
O bull among the twice-born, at that time they spoke with humility to those Śūdras seated on high thrones in the midst of the twice-born, as if to one of low birth.
Having understood this, the king does not cause harm in the Kali age due to the power of time;
rather, he honors him with perfumed flowers and other auspicious, propitious items.
O twice-born one, those Śūdras who possess little learning, fortune, and strength worship [only] Śūdras;
being arrogant, they do not even look upon the best of the twice-born.
Observing the opportunity for service, the twice-born stand at the gate,
while the Śūdras and those who live off Śūdras surround those mounted on vehicles.
In the Kali age, the brahmins there serve [others] and praise them with hymns;
these best of the twice-born are sellers of the fruits of austerity and sacrifice.
And there will be many ascetics in this Kali age;
when the end of the age has arrived, men will be few and women will be many.
In the Kali age, the twice-born indeed censure the Vedic sciences and ritual acts;
in the Kali age, the god is Mahādeva, Śaṅkara, Nīlalohita.
He manifests in a transformed form for the sake of establishing the Dharma;
those Brahmins who serve that Śaṅkara by whatever means possible [attain their goal].
Having completely conquered the defects of the Kali age, they proceed to the supreme state;
[otherwise, there will be] the increase of wild beasts and the total destruction of cows.
And the withdrawal of the virtuous should be known to occur at that end of the yuga;
then, the subtle, great fruit, rooted in charity, becomes difficult to attain.
When the four stages of life become lax, righteousness will decline;
kings will fail to protect and will instead seize the share of the tribute.
At the ends of the ages, people will be intent solely on their own protection;
the countryside will have its watchtowers as its main concern, and crossroads will have their shrines to Śiva as their main concern.
In the Kali age, women will have disheveled hair;
at that time, when they say the end of the age has arrived, the god will rain down in various ways.
Moreover, in that degenerate age, all merchant folk will become practitioners of immoral conduct, shrouded by heretics of false appearance.
The world will become full of mutual sacrifices;
there will be no one who does not utter cruel speech, nor anyone who is upright or free from envy.
In the waning age, there will be no one to repay what has been done;
revilers and outcasts shall be the characteristics of the end of the Yuga.
The earth will be devoid of kings and not covered with grain or wealth;
there will be [only] districts in the provinces and cities.
The earth will have little water and yield few fruits; and those who should be protectors will become non-protectors, lacking any sense of discipline.
Those who seize the wealth of others, those who violate the wives of others, who are possessed by lust, evil-minded, base, and fond of reckless violence; LiP_1,40.32 //
At the end of the Yuga, people lose all physical activity; they have disheveled hair, suffer from piercing pains, and men are born at the age of sixteen.
When the end of the Yuga has arrived, Śūdras will practice the Dharma, wearing white teeth-sticks, deer skins, and rosaries, shaven-headed and clad in saffron robes.
There will be thieves of grain who long for fine garments;
there will be thieves who steal the property of other thieves, and yet another who steals from that thief.
When the world has ceased from its proper duties and has fallen into inactivity,
insects, mice, and snakes will harass human beings.
At that time, abundance, security, health, and capability will be difficult to find;
oppressed by the fear of famine, people will flee to the lands of Kauśikī.
And for those overwhelmed by suffering, the maximum lifespan at that time will be one hundred years;
furthermore, in the Kali Yuga, the Vedas are seen in their entirety and yet are not seen.
Then sacrifices will perish, oppressed solely by unrighteousness;
even those wearing saffron robes will not be true renunciants, for there will be many here who follow the Kāpālika path.
Others are sellers of the Vedas, and still others are sellers of sacred fords;
there are also other heretics who act as adversaries to the castes and stages of life.
When the Kali age has arrived, those who are experts in the matters of dharma and worldly affairs will indeed arise; at that time, even Śūdras will study the Vedas.
Kings born of the Śūdra womb perform the horse sacrifice after having committed the slaughter of women, children, and cows, and after having killed one another.
At that time, the people will afflict one another with calamities;
there will be an abundance of suffering, short lifespans, the wasting away of the body, and the presence of disease.
Because of their attachment to unrighteousness, the Kali age is known to be characterized by darkness;
at that time, acts such as the killing of a Brahmin indeed prevail among the people.
Therefore, when the Kali age is reached, lifespan, strength, and beauty decline;
yet at that time, human beings attain perfection in a very short period of time.
Blessed are those best of the twice-born who will practice the Dharma at the end of the age—
those who, free from malice, follow the Dharma proclaimed in the Śruti and Smṛti.
The dharma that lasts for a year in the Tretā age and for a month in the Dvāpara age,
a wise man practicing according to his capacity attains in a single day during the Kali age.
(This is the state of the Kali Yuga. Now learn from me regarding the transitional period (saṃdhyāṃśa):
in each successive age, the spiritual accomplishments (siddhis) diminish by three-quarters.

The transitional periods (saṃdhyā), which possess the nature of the yugas, remain here for one quarter; those transitional periods, possessing their own natures, are established for one quarter each within their respective portions.
Thus, when the time of the twilight period has arrived at the end of the age,
he who rose from the destruction of beings becomes the teacher of those wicked creatures.
In this lineage, he who was formerly known as Pramiti by name during the Svāyaṃbhuva interval was indeed a partial incarnation of Candra.
For twenty full years he wandered the earth,
leading an army consisting of horses, chariots, and elephants.
Then, surrounded by hundreds and thousands of Brahmins with uplifted weapons,
he slaughtered the Mlecchas by the thousands.
Having slain all those kings born of Śūdra lineage,
the Lord then completely exterminated all the heretics without exception.
He slays in every way all those who are excessively righteous,
as well as those born from the confusion of castes and those who subsist upon such mixed births.
Having set his wheel in motion, powerful, and the destroyer of the Mlecchas,
he— who was unassailable by all beings— then traversed the earth.
In a previous birth, that powerful one, known as Pramiti, was born here on earth as a partial incarnation of the divine Viṣṇu in the lineage of Manu.
Indeed, from the lineage of the Moon, when the Kali Yuga was complete,
the Lord appeared in his thirty-second year and proceeded for twenty years.
Then, slaughtering all beings by the hundreds and thousands,
that man of cruel deeds left the earth with nothing remaining but seeds.
Driven by mutual provocations and sudden outbursts of anger,
he brought about the downfall of those commoners, who for the most part were unrighteous.
Accompanied by his followers, he reached a place situated between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā;
then, after some time had passed, he was together with his ministers and his army.
Having exterminated all the kings and thousands of Mlecchas,
when the twilight period at the end of the Yuga had arrived, [he did so].
When only a few subjects remain here in various places,
they will indeed be entirely devoid of restraint and overwhelmed by greed.
And they will harm one another, bowing down to each other in turn, when,
due to the power of the age, a state of anarchy has arisen and uncertainty has set in.
Then all those subjects, afflicted by fear of one another,
became distraught and wandered about, abandoning their wives and homes.
Disregarding their own lives, devoid of compassion, and deeply distressed,
they then slaughtered one another when the Vedic and Smṛti-based dharma had perished.
Transgressing all bounds, devoid of compassion, shameless,
and hostile toward the lost Dharma, they will be short-lived, reaching only twenty-five years.
Having abandoned their sons and wives, their senses agitated by disputes, and having cast agriculture far aside like those struck by drought, they departed.
Abandoning their own countries, they frequent the borderlands;
they resort to rivers, oceans, wells, and likewise to mountains.
Extremely distressed, they subsist on honey, meat, roots, and fruits;
wearing bark, leaves, and skins, they are inactive and possess nothing.
Then the subjects, having fallen away from their castes and stages of life, were beset by terrible distress; thus having encountered such hardship, they remained with but a small remnant.
Those afflicted by old age, disease, and hunger, with minds weary from suffering, engage in reflection; from that weariness comes reflection upon the state of equanimity.
Awakening consists of the state of equilibrium; from perfect enlightenment comes the nature of righteousness.
Those remaining in the Kali age are indeed themselves devoid of form and joined with tranquility.
Then, after a day and night, their age-cycle (yuga) revolves;
having caused the delusion of their minds, they indeed become like those who are asleep or intoxicated.
And by the power of the destiny that was to be, the Kṛta age proceeded from that;
once it had begun, indeed, the Kṛta Yuga continued once more.
Then the subjects born in the Kali age will become like those of the Kṛta age;
and those Siddhas who remain here move about unseen.
And there, those seven who were established as the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis) remained;
they are remembered here as the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras for the sake of the seed.
At that time, they all became indistinguishable from the Kali-yugas;
the seven sages and the others likewise discoursed on dharma for them.

In the Kṛta age, the twice-born flourish among those who perform ritual actions, following the two-fold path of conduct consisting of the Vedic (śrauta) and the traditional (smārta), which is endowed with the duties of the social classes (varṇa) and stages of life (āśrama).
And at the end of the age, some remain here for the sake of establishing the dharma shown by the seven seers, consisting of the rites prescribed by the Śruti and the Smṛti.
Indeed, the sages remain during the periods of the Manvantaras,
just as grass here on earth remains even after it has been consumed by a forest fire.
Just as the first growth of forests occurs at their roots through rain,
so too does the appearance of those belonging to the Kṛta Age occur here among those of the Kali Age.
In this manner, the succession of one age from another proceeds here without interruption until the end of the manvantara.
Happiness, longevity, strength, beauty, dharma, artha, and even kāma—
these all diminish by three-quarters each in successive ages.
"In each successive *saṃdhyāṃśa* of the ages, the accomplishments of dharma decline;
thus has this prohibition indeed been proclaimed in due order."
By this very means, indeed, is the accomplishment of all the four yugas;
this cycle of the four yugas is multiplied up to a thousand times.
That is declared to be the day of Brahmā, and his night is remembered to be of equal duration;
it is a period of crookedness and dullness among living beings until the end of the Yuga.
This indeed is recorded as the defining characteristic of all the ages;
and seventy-one cycles of these four ages multiplied together [constitute a Manvantara].
When, however, [the cycle] has gradually revolved, it is called the interval of Manu (manvantara);
for whatever occurs here in one four-age cycle (caturyuga) likewise occurs in each.
And likewise, it occurs again in other [ages] in that same sequence;
for in each creation, the various distinctions arise in exactly that manner.
The kalpas, together with the yugas and the marks, are exactly twenty-five in number, neither fewer nor more.
This indeed is the characteristic of all the Manvantaras.
Just as the revolutions of the ages have proceeded for a long time according to the inherent nature of the ages,
so does the world of living beings remain, revolving through decline and rise.
Thus has the characteristic of the ages been declared in brief,
regarding all those of the past and the future throughout all the Manvantaras.
By means of a single Manvantara, all intermediate periods (Antaras) are explained, without a doubt; indeed, a Kalpa is explained by means of a Kalpa.
Likewise, a wise person should apply such reasoning regarding all past and future Manvantaras here in this world.
All those who possess equal pride arise indeed through names and forms—
the eightfold classes of gods and those who are the lords of the manvantaras.
The sages and the Manus alike all have the same purpose;
thus, in every age, there is this division of the social classes and stages of life.
And then the Lord indeed ordains the inherent nature of the yugas,
as well as the divisions of the castes and stages of life, the yugas themselves, and the accomplishments specific to each yuga.
The measurement of the Yugas has indeed been told to you in this context;
now I shall briefly describe the sonship of the Lotus-born One to the Goddess.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Measurement of the Four Yugas," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Indra said:
Furthermore, at the dawn at the end of a thousand yugas, the Lord Grandfather created beings who had fallen away, just as before.
O best of Brahmins, when a second half-parārdha has likewise passed in this manner,
then the earth is pervaded by water, and the waters by fire, and the fire by wind.
Fire and wind, joined with their respective subtle elements (tanmātra) in space,
as well as the ten senses and the one [internal organ], and the subtle elements themselves, O best of the twice-born.
Alas! Having reached the ego (ahaṅkāra), they dissolved into it in that very instant;
then, at that moment, the conceit (abhimāna) indeed pervaded the Great One (mahat).
O twice-born one, even the Great One (Mahat), having reached the Unmanifest (Avyakta), clearly became dissolved;
together with its own qualities, it was absorbed into the Source (Bhava).
Then, from that Puruṣa Śiva, creation occurred as before;
then, by means of his mind, those who were mind-born (mānasa) were created by him.
The progeny did not increase in this world despite the lotus-born Brahmā;
therefore, for the sake of their growth, the Blessed Lord Brahmā, together with his mind-born sons, [acted].
He himself performed difficult austerities directed toward the Lord;
and Bhava, being pleased by his penance, understood his desire.
Having pierced the center of the forehead of that Puruṣa, Brahmā,
and having uttered the words "affection for a son," he then assumed the form of both male and female.
His son was Mahādeva, who indeed became Ardhanārīśvara;
the Blessed One consumed everything, including Brahmā, the teacher of the world.
Then, for the sake of the prosperity of the worlds, Śiva enjoyed the auspicious half-measure of his own Supreme Goddess by means of the path of yoga.
In that [egg], the Supreme Lord, the Sovereign of the Universe and the Soul of the Universe, created Hari and Brahmā,
as well as the Pāśupata weapon.
Therefore, Brahmā, as well as Hari, was born from a portion of the Great Goddess;
he was born from the cosmic egg, born from the lotus, and indeed born from the body of Bhava.
Thus has this entire ancient history been told to you in brief,
concerning the prosperity that lasted for as long as half a parārdha of Brahmā’s lifespan.
I shall briefly describe the dispassion of Brahmā, which arose from him;
even the Blessed Nārāyaṇa, having divided his own body into two parts...
From his own body alone, he emitted the entire universe of moving and non-moving beings;
then the Grandfather Brahmā created Brahmā, and [from him] Rudra.
O sage, in another kalpa, Rudra created Hari, Brahmā, and Īśvara;
then, O sage, in another kalpa, Hari created Brahmā.
Then Brahmā reflected upon Nārāyaṇa, and Bhava in turn reflected upon Brahmā; indeed, the unborn Brahmā then considered that cyclic existence is suffering.
Having cast off the creative impulse and having yoked himself solely within the Self,
he withdrew the movement of the vital breaths and remained as motionless as a stone.
For ten thousand years the Lord remained absorbed in samādhi;
he gazed upon that most beautiful lotus situated in his heart, which was turned downwards.
Filled by means of inhalation (pūraka), it then became awakened;
by means of retention (kumbhaka), its upward-facing aspect became restrained.
He established Īśvara in the center of the pericarp of that lotus—
that god Śiva, who is "Om," beyond the half-mora, and supreme.
Having thus restrained the Lord within her heart, Yamī, whose soul was purified by self-restraint, perceived him as residing in a single hundredth part of a hundredth part of a lotus fiber.
Having worshipped with *yamapuṣpa* and other offerings, he indeed sacrificed to the Imperishable;
and by the command of that [Lord] who resides in the lotus of his heart, the omnipresent one was born as a partial incarnation (*aṃśaja*).
Having pierced his forehead, he emerged from Pitāmaha;
he himself became red, while the one born from the heart of Śiva was blue.
And from the union with fire, the Lord Puruṣa arises by nature;
he is both blue and red, since the Person has the form of Time.
Thus addressed as "Nīlalohita" by that lord Brahmā, the powerful and all-pervading Lord Kāla became pleased in his heart.
O great sage, the Grandfather, the soul of the universe, praised the God, whose mind was well-pleased, by means of his eight names, he being the soul of the universe himself.
The Grandfather said:
Salutations to you, O Blessed One, Rudra, whose splendor is immeasurable like that of the sun;
salutations to the god Bhava, who is the essence and who consists of water.
Salutations always to Śarva, who has the form of the earth and is ever fragrant;
salutations again and again to you, Īśa, the wind, and the sense of touch.
Salutations to you, the Lord of Animals, to Pāvaka of exceeding brilliance, to Bhīma whose form is the ether and who consists of the subtle element of sound.
Salutations be to you, the Great God, to Soma, to the Immortal;
salutations to you, the Fierce One, the Sacrificer, the master of the yoga of action.
"One shall attain union with the Eight-formed Lord after one year;
having thus praised Mahādeva, the Grandfather (Brahmā) gazed upon him."
Then Mahādeva established himself in eight forms on all sides;
at that time, the sun, the fire, and the moon shone forth.
"Earth, wind, the male principle, water, and likewise the all-pervading void—
from that time forth, they called that Lord 'the Eight-formed One' (Aṣṭamūrti)."
By the grace of the Eight-formed Lord (Aṣṭamūrti), the Lord Brahmā created once again; having created this entire universe, the Master [re-creates it] in another kalpa.
When all moving and non-moving beings were fast asleep at the end of a thousand yugas, he,
desiring to create progeny, performed great and fierce austerity.
As he was thus performing austerities, nothing at all came to pass for him;
then, after a long time, anger was born from his suffering.
From the eyes of him who was possessed by anger, drops of tears fell;
from those drops of tears, spirits and hungry ghosts (pretas) then came into being.
Seeing all those elder-born beings— the bhūtas, pretas, and niśācaras—
the unborn and omnipresent Lord Brahmā then censured himself.
When the Lord Prajāpati, overcome by anger, abandoned his vital breaths,
Rudra, consisting of those very breaths, emerged from the mouth of the Lord.
Having become Ardhanārīśvara, with a splendor like that of the rising sun,
he then established himself by dividing his self into eleven parts.
With half of his portion, that Soul of All created Śiva-Umā;
and she, in turn, then created Lakṣmī, Durgā, and the excellent Sarasvatī.
Vāmā, Raudrī, Mahāmāyā, Vaiṣṇavī, the lotus-eyed one, Kalā, Vikiraṇī, Kālī, and Kamalavāsinī.
He created the goddess Balavikariṇī, as well as Balapramathinī,
Sarvabhūtadamanī, and Manonmanī.
In that same way, many other women were created by her in their thousands;
and with them, Mahādeva, the lord of the three worlds, was united with the Rudras.
And the Supreme Lord stood before that very self of all;
indeed, he stood before that deceased god Brahmā, the Parameṣṭhin.
Then the compassionate Maheśvara, the son of Brahmā, restored life;
the Lord then returned the vital breaths that resided within himself to Brahmā.
Then Rudra, the Lord of Gods, being greatly delighted as Brahmā had somewhat regained his life-breath, addressed him with these supreme words.
"Do not fear, O illustrious god, Viriñca, teacher of the worlds!
My vital breaths have been established here by me; therefore, arise indeed, O Lord!"
Then, having heard those words which were in his mind as if they were a dream,
the Grandfather, with a serene soul, [looked] with eyes possessing the luster of blooming lotuses.
Then, having regained his life-breath, he gazed upon Maheśvara;
and looking up for a long time, [the Lord addressed him] with a voice that was affectionate and deep.
The blessed Brahmā, having risen with palms joined in reverence, said:
"O, O highly fortunate one, speak! You gladden my mind."
"Who are you, who stand here as the eight-formed one yet possessing an eleven-fold nature?
Having heard those words of his, Indra spoke, and Maheśvara replied: [LiP 1.41.55]
Touching Brahmā with his two pleasant hands,
Śrī Śaṅkara, the slayer of the enemies of the gods, said: "Know me to be the Supreme Self (paramātman), and know this to be the unborn Māyā."
"These Rudras have indeed arrived here to protect you.
Then Brahmā, having bowed down to that God of gods, spoke.
With palms joined in reverence, he spoke with a voice faltering with joy:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, I am indeed overwhelmed by sorrows."
"O Śaṅkara, O Lord, you ought to liberate me from this saṃsāra.
Then the Blessed One, the Grandfather and Lord of Umā, laughed.
Then the Lord of the World, the omnipresent one, vanished along with the Rudras and her.
Indra said:
"Therefore, O Śilāda, one who is not born from a womb is indeed difficult to find in the worlds."
"Know that a man is free from death, even if he be the lotus-born Brahmā himself, who is subject to death;
however, if the Lord Rudra, the sovereign of gods, is pleased."
Indeed, a son who is free from death and not born from a womb is not difficult for you to obtain,
for he has been granted by me, by Viṣṇu, and by the high-souled Brahmā.
"Born not from a womb, free from death, and incapable of being described," Śailādi said,
having thus addressed the best of Brahmins and having shown him favor out of compassion.
Surrounded by the gods, the Lord, the deity, departed indeed upon his white elephant.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Speech of Indra," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
When Puṇya and Varada had departed, Sahasrākṣa, subsisting on stone,
propitiated Mahādeva and satisfied Bhava through his ascetic penance.
Then, for that twice-born man who was thus constantly devoted to it,
a thousand divine years passed by as wondrously as a single moment.
The sage was covered by an anthill on his limbs and visible to swarms of insects,
as well as to other red insects with mouths like diamond needles from all sides.
Devoid of flesh, blood, and skin, entirely free from any coating, he stood like a wall;
afterwards, he became nothing but a skeleton, and Śaṅkara regarded him as such.
When the sage was touched by that hand of the enemy of Smara,
at that very moment the tiger among sages, the twice-born one, cast off his exhaustion.
Then, as he was performing penance, Śaṅkara became pleased by his austerity;
together with Umā and his attendants, he said, "I am pleased with your hymn."
"O high-minded one, what need have you for this asceticism?
I shall grant you a son who is omniscient and has mastered the meaning of all the scriptures."
Then, having prostrated before the Lord of Gods and praised him, Śilāśana spoke with a voice faltering with joy to Soma, who is adorned by the moon: LiP_1,42.8 //
Śilāda said: "O Blessed One, Lord of the gods, Śaṅkara, destroyer of Tripura,
O most excellent one, I desire a son who is not born from a womb and is free from death."
Sūta said:
Having been previously propitiated by his ascetic penance, the Supreme Lord Rudra spoke again to Śilāda with the greatest affection, even as Brahmā looked on.
The illustrious God of gods said: "O Brahmin, rich in asceticism, I was previously propitiated by Brahmā through penance,
as well as by the sages and the highest of gods for the sake of an incarnation."
"I shall become your son, born not from a womb, by the name of Nandin;
O Sage of the worlds, you shall indeed be the father of my father."
Having spoken thus, the compassionate Soma, who resembles the moon, looked at the sage, bowed down, and while he stood there, he vanished on the spot.

O great sage, having obtained a son from Rudra, my father, the best of those who know the sacrifice, was filled with joy; he reached a vast sacrificial ground for the purpose of performing a sacrifice.
Then, by the command of Śambhu, I was born from his courtyard as his very son,
appearing even before [the birth of the others] with a radiance equal to the fire at the end of an eon.

Then the Puṣkarāvartaka and other clouds rained down, while the sky-dwelling Kinnaras, Siddhas, and Sādhyas sang; once I had attained the state of being Śilā’s son, Upendra then released a rain mixed with a profusion of beautiful flowers.
Having seen me, who resemble the sun at the end of time, wearing a crown of matted locks, three-eyed, four-armed, youthful, and bearing a trident, an axe, and a mace; LiP_1,42.17 //
To Vajrin, Vajradaṃṣṭra, and the youth propitiated by Vajrin;
to the terrible Vajrakuṇḍalin, whose voice is like the sound of a rain cloud.
Brahmā and all the others—Indra, the lord of the gods, and the lords of the sages—all offered hymns of praise;
they all sounded forth from every side, and the hosts of apsarases danced.
O tiger among sages, the ṛṣis, having praised him with Maheśvara-mantras originating from the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, bowed down to him filled with joy.
Brahmā, Hari, Rudra, Śakra, Śivā and Ambikā in person, Jīva, the Moon, the highly effulgent Bhāskara, Pavana, and Anala; LiP_1,42.21 //
Īśāna, Nirṛti, Yakṣa, Yama, and Varuṇa,
as well as the Viśvedevas, the Rudras, and the mighty Vasus.
Lakṣmī herself, Śacī, the elder goddess Sarasvatī, Aditi, Diti, as well as Śraddhā, Lajjā, and Dhṛti; LiP_1,42.23.
Nandā, Bhadrā, Surabhī, Suśīlā, and likewise Sumanā; and the bull-king of great splendor, as well as Dharma and Dharmātmaja.
Having thus covered me and embraced me, they offered praise, O best of sages;
and my father, the sage Śilāda, having then seen me in such a state, [was filled with joy].
Having bowed down with affection, the virtuous Śilāda praised his son, the bestower of desired boons;
Śilāda said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, O Tryambaka, O Imperishable One, [be gracious] unto me! (LiP 1.42.26)
Since you are the son of the worlds, why indeed would you not be their protector from suffering? O omnipresent son, since you are the guardian of the worlds, you are my father.
O you who are not born from a womb, salutations to you, O Grandfather, the source of the universe!
O Great Lord, Father and Son, O Teacher of the worlds!
"O child, O child, O highly fortunate one, protect me, O Supreme Lord!
Since I have been gladdened by you, O Lord of the Gods, I am Nandin by name."
Therefore, O Nandin, gladden me; I bow to the Lord of the World. Be gracious, O All-pervading One, for my parents have today gone to the world of Rudra.
And the Grandfather said, "O Nandin, now that Maheśvara has descended,
my very birth in this world has become fruitful, O Lord of the worlds."
O Lord, when my son Nandin has descended for the sake of my protection—salutations to you, O Sovereign of the Gods; salutations be to you, O Nandīśvara!
"O son, protect me, O mighty-armed one, O God of gods, O Teacher of the World!
Since you have been addressed by me as 'son,' considering that very fact, O Lord Nandin. (LiP 1.42.33)
O child, you who are worthy of praise by gods and asuras alike, may this be forgiven by you;
whoever shall read or even hear that which was spoken by my son, [may they attain success].
Or, by reciting it with devotion to the twice-born along with me, he rejoices;
having thus praised the young son and bowed down with great reverence.
Beholding the lords of sages, Śilāda, firm in his vows, said:
"O all you sages, behold my imperishable great fortune."
Since the Lord, the God, has descended here at the sacrificial ground of Nandi,
what man in the world is equal to me— be he a god or even a dānava?
This Nandin was born upon the sacrificial ground for my benefit.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Origin of Nandikeśvara," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Nandikeśvara said:
Delighted, my father prostrated before Maheśvara along with me and quickly returned to his own hermitage, like a pauper who has found a treasure.
When I arrived at the hermitage of the great sage Śilāda,
I indeed cast off my divine form and assumed a human one.
And my divine memory was lost due to some cause or other,
when my father, who is honored by the world, saw me having assumed a human form.
Afflicted by extreme grief and surrounded by his kinsmen, he lamented;
and the omniscient one performed for me all the rites, beginning with the birth-ceremony (jātakarman).
Śilāda, the son of Śālaṅkāyana, was indeed devoted to his sons;
by him alone were the Ṛgveda and Yajurveda branches taught.
O great sage, [he taught] a thousand branches of the Sāma Veda along with their auxiliary and secondary limbs,
as well as Ayurveda, Dhanurveda, Gāndharvaveda, and the characteristics of horses.
The behavior of elephants and the characteristics of men;
then, when the seventh year was complete, those two best of sages—
The two divine ones named Mitra and Varuṇa, endowed with the power of asceticism and yoga,
went to his hermitage at the command of the Lord in order to see me.
And those two great-souled ones, looking at me again and again, said:
"Father, this Nandi, though short-lived, has mastered the meaning of all the scriptures."
"Such a wonder has never been seen before; there is no lifespan beyond this number of years," said Śilāda, the lord of sages, who was deeply affectionate toward his son.
Embracing him, afflicted by grief, he wept most piteously;
crying out, "O son, son, son!", he fell down on all sides.
"Alas! What power does the ordainer of destiny possess! Thus he lamented in distress; and hearing his cry of anguish, the inhabitants of that hermitage [gathered].
The Rākṣasas fell down utterly overwhelmed and cried out for auspiciousness;
they praised Mahādeva, the three-eyed Lord of Umā.
Having offered oblations with the *tryambaka* mantra and with honey,
one should offer ten thousand blades of *dūrvā* grass, accompanied by all the ritual substances.
His father lost consciousness, and likewise his grandfather;
he writhed, uttered incoherent cries, and fell down as if dead.
Fearing death, I soon bowed my head in salutation to him,
who was my father and grandfather in person, fallen down like one dead.
Having circumambulated him, I became devoted to the recitation of the Rudra-hymns,
meditating upon the three-eyed God within the hollow lotus of my heart.
The Supreme Lord [beheld] me— the three-eyed, ten-armed, peaceful, five-faced Sadāśiva—
dwelling within the sacred confluence of rivers.
Delighted, Mahādeva—Soma, whose ornament is the half-moon of Soma—said:
"O child Nandin, O mighty-armed one, whence comes this fear of death in you?"
"The two brahmins were sent by me alone; you are equal to me, of this there is no doubt. O child, both this body of yours and the world are, in the ultimate sense, [identical to] me."
In former times, Śilāda beheld that no divine [power] exists for you,
even by the gods, sages, Siddhas, Gandharvas, and the foremost of the Dānavas.
O child Nandikeśvara, that which was honored by you in the past was divine;
such is the nature of saṃsāra: happiness and suffering again and again.
"For discerning men, the abandonment of the womb is by all means necessary.
Having spoken thus to me directly, the Great Lord of all the gods—
With both of his most beautiful hands,
the Blessed Lord Rudra, Hara, the Supreme Sovereign who removes the greatest suffering, touched him.
And Mahādeva, whose banner is the bull, being pleased in spirit,
spoke while looking at the leaders of his hosts and the goddess, the daughter of Himavat.
And having beheld him, Mahādeva, the lord of the gods, was pleased in soul;
he is ageless, abandoned by old age, and eternally free from suffering.
He is indeed inexhaustible and immutable, together with his father and his circle of friends;
he is my beloved leader of the hosts, possessing my own vigor and my own prowess.
"He shall always be dear to me and ever remain by my side;
he shall possess my own power, endowed with the strength of great yoga."
Having spoken thus to me, the Lord, the Blessed One, together with his retinue,
then untied from himself a garland made of lotuses.
The god whose banner is the bull, possessed of great splendor, bound it for me;
by that auspicious garland, once fastened around my neck, I became [transformed].
Three-eyed and ten-armed, like a second Śaṅkara,
the Supreme Lord then took [the weapon] with his hand.
He said, "Tell me, what supreme boon shall I grant you today? Then, taking the exceedingly pure water resting within his matted locks, he spoke.
"Be a river," said the bull-bannered god, and he released her;
thereafter she became auspicious, filled with divine water and dark waters.
A great river, endowed with groves of lotuses and water-lilies, began to flow;
and Mahādeva spoke to that most beautiful river.
"Since you, O great river, have issued forth from the very waters of Jaṭodaka,
therefore you shall become the meritorious Jaṭodakā, the best of streams."
"Having bathed in you, a certain man is liberated from all sins.
Then the Lord Mahādeva [spoke] to the son of Śilāda regarding the Goddess.
Saying, "This is your son," she made me prostrate at her feet;
she then smelled my head and stroked me with both her hands.
Beholding the God of gods, she consecrated him with the three streams of her sons out of love for her children, using water as white as a conch shell.
Then those three streams of hers became rivers;
the divine Lord Bhava called that river Trisrotas.
Seeing the river with its three streams, Vṛṣa was exceedingly delighted;
he let out a roar, and from that sound another river came into being.
That river is known as Vṛṣadhvani by the God of gods;
it is wonderful, composed of Jāmbūnada gold, consisting of all kinds of jewels, and auspicious.
And the Lord whose banner is the bull bound upon my head his own wonderful, divine crown, fashioned by Viśvakarman.
And Mahādeva Maheśvara himself fastened upon him two auspicious, divine earrings, adorned with diamonds and lapis lazuli.
O Sage, seeing me thus honored in the sky by the clouds, the Sun-god then sprinkled Śilādana with the water of the clouds.
At that time, as he was consecrated, this river began to flow strongly from the stream;
for having issued forth from Suvarṇa, it flows forth in this manner.
The three-eyed God of gods called that auspicious second [river] "Svarṇodakā" because it consists of gold (jāmbūnada) flowing from his crown.
A sacred river began to flow, which they called the Jambūnadī;
this is the place known as Pañcanada, situated near Japyeśvara.
He who, having reached Pañcanada and bathed, worships Japyeśvareśvara, attains union with Śiva; of this there is no doubt.
Then the god Mahādeva, Bhava, the lord of all beings,
spoke to the goddess Śarvāṇī, Umā, the daughter of the mountain, the unborn one.
"O Goddess, I shall consecrate the god Nandīśvara as the lord of beings;
I shall proclaim him the chief of the Gaṇas—or what do you think, O Imperishable One?"
Having heard those words of his, Bhavānī, her face beaming with joy,
smilingly spoke to her husband Bhava, the Lord of Beings and the giver of boons.
O Lord of Gods, you ought to grant me sovereignty over all the worlds as well as the status of Gaṇeśa; let Śailādi be my son.
Then the Blessed Lord Śarva, the God of gods whose banner is the bull and the sovereign of all lords of the worlds, called to mind his divine attendants, the leaders of the Gaṇas.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Nandikeśvara and the Mantra for the Consecration of Nandikeśvara," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*. Śailādi said:
