By the mere remembrance of Rudra, the lords of the Gaṇas arrived;
they were all possessed of a thousand hands and held a thousand weapons in their grasp.
And those great-souled ones were three-eyed, honored even by the gods;
they resembled ten million fires of cosmic destruction and wore crowns of matted hair.
With faces formidable with fangs, the Buddhas were eternally stainless;
accompanied by themselves and by hosts of equal lords of the Gaṇas numbering in the tens of millions,
those immeasurable great-souled ones arrived there filled with joy.
Singing, running, and dancing, those of great strength likewise played upon their mouth-organs and cymbals.
On chariots, elephants, and horses, as well as on vehicles borne by lions and monkeys,
the Gaṇas were indeed mounted upon celestial palaces variegated with gold.
With kettledrums, clay drums, and the like, with cymbals, gongs, and cow-horns, and with various other musical instruments such as paṭahas and single-headed drums; ||| LiP_1,44.6 |||
With the resounding blasts of kettledrums and clay drums, with ḍamarus and ḍiṇḍimas, with mṛdaṅgas, flutes, and lutes, and with various sounds of cymbals; LiP_1,44.7 //
To the assembly of the gods came the great yogis, accompanied by the sounding of drums, cymbals, tortoise-shaped drums, and small kettledrums.
Those lords of the Gaṇas, beings of great power and sovereigns over all the lords of the gods, bowed down to the God and the Goddess and spoke these words: LiP_1,44.9 //
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods, Three-eyed One, Bull-bannered One!
For what purpose have we been remembered, O God? Command us, O You of great splendor!"
"Shall we dry up the oceans, or Yama along with his servants?
Shall we slay the sons of Death, or Death himself, or shall we strike down the Lotus-born like a sacrificial beast?"
"Having bound Indra together with the gods, and Viṣṇu along with Vāyu, we shall bring them here in great wrath; or else, we shall bring the Daityas along with the Dānavas."
"Whose terrible calamity shall we bring about today by your command? Or whose festival shall we hold today, O Lord, for the fulfillment of all desires? (LiP 1.44.13)
Having honored those hundreds of millions upon millions of lords of the Gaṇas, all of whom were speaking thus and were esteemed by everyone, the Lord, the Sovereign, addressed them.
Listen to that for which you, who are intent on the welfare of the world, have been summoned here;
having heard it, being self-restrained, perform it without hesitation.
"This Nandīśvara is our son, the Lord of all lords;
he is a brahmin, a leader, and your prosperous commander-in-chief."
"In accordance with my message, all of you together shall consecrate this Mahāyogapati as your general and your lord."
Thus addressed by the Blessed One, all those leaders of the hosts deliberated, saying "So be it," and then brought forth the necessary materials.
They brought for him a beautiful, divine throne made of Jāmbūnada gold, which was the support of all, resembling Mount Meru and captivating the mind.
It was composed of a single pillar, possessed the excellent luster of refined gold,
hung with strings of pearls, and illuminated by precious gems and jewels.
And there was a pavilion facing all directions, with pillars made of lapis lazuli, covered with networks of tinkling bells, and adorned with beautiful jewels.
Having fashioned and placed that excellent, auspicious seat in the center,
one should place a footstool before it, illuminated by blue vajras.
For the purpose of providing a firm footing, they placed two jars at his sides,
filled with the finest water and their openings covered with lotuses.
A thousand jars— made of gold, silver,
copper, and even clay— should be filled with the waters of all the sacred fords (tīrthas).
Likewise, a pair of divine garments, divine fragrance,
as well as armlets, earrings, a crown, and a necklace.
A parasol with a hundred ribs and a fly-whisk were also given by that high-souled Brahmā, the Supreme Lord.
It was further adorned by a back as white as a conch shell,
a moon-bright fan, and a beautiful chowrie with a golden handle.
These two elephants, Airāvata and Supratīka, were highly honored;
likewise, a golden crown was fashioned for them by Viśvakarman.
The two divine and stainless earrings, the thunderbolt as a supreme weapon,
a necklace made of Jāmbūnada gold, and likewise a pair of armlets.
Likewise, the leaders of the hosts, esteemed by the gods, remained unperturbed and brought various other many kinds of requisites from all sides.
Then the gods, together with Indra, those whose mouth is Nārāyaṇa,
as well as the sages, the Lord Brahmā, and the nine Brahmas, [approached].
Then all those worlds, filled with joy, departed along with the gods;
and when they had all arrived, the Blessed Lord Parameśvara [spoke].
He commanded the Grandfather (Brahmā) to carry out the ritual for all the tasks;
and the venerable Grandfather, indeed by his very command, [did so].
The Blessed One, being composed in meditation, performed the entire consecration;
then Brahmā, having worshipped him, consecrated him himself.
Then, by the command of Śiva, Viṣṇu, Śakra, and likewise the world-protectors, consecrated the lord of the Gaṇas according to the prescribed rite.
The sages, led by Brahmā, offered praises;
and when they had finished their hymns, Viṣṇu, the Lord of the entire universe, [spoke].
Placing his joined palms to his head, he praised him with a concentrated mind;
bowing down with palms joined in reverence, he uttered the cry of "Victory! (Jaya).
Then all the lords of the Gaṇas, followed by the gods and the asuras, praised him; thus was he then consecrated by the gods together with Brahmā.
And there, by the command of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), the marriage was performed;
the goddess who was named Suyaśas became the daughter of the Maruts.
There she obtained a moon-bright parasol as her adornment,
accompanied by groups of women with yak-tail whisks held in their fingertips.
And that supreme lion-throne was presided over by her, as well as by me;
she was adorned with great fortune and beautiful ornaments such as a crown and other finery.
Furthermore, the supreme necklace was obtained and placed upon the Queen's neck;
likewise, the lordly white bull, the elephant, the lion, and the lion-banner were acquired.
The chariot and the golden parasol, radiant as the orb of the moon—
until this day, there has been no lord anywhere equal to me.
Having accepted him along with his lineage, as well as his kinsmen and relatives,
the Lord Śiva, the Sovereign, mounted his bull and departed together with me and the Goddess.
Then, O twice-born ones, having seen Bhava and the Goddess, I, along with the Gaṇas, the sages, the celestial seers, and the Siddhas, requested the Pāśupata command.
Then, by the command of the Lord, Nandika gave those Arhats the auspicious Pāśupata initiation of the Lord of the Mountain-born Goddess.
Therefore, having received that command from the bull among sages, the sages then became devoted to Bhava; for this reason, one should worship him in this manner.
If one utters the name [of the deity] in this world without performing a salutation,
his sin is most grave, equal to that of ten killers of Brahmins.
Therefore, one should utter salutations and so forth in every way;
one should perform salutation at the beginning and attain the state of Śiva at its end.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Consecration of Nandikeśvara," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
The sages said:
O Sūta, you have indeed explained everything concerning Śaṅkara very clearly;
now you ought to describe the true nature of Rudra, who is the self of all beings.
Sūta said:
Bhūr, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ, mahaḥ, as well as janaḥ and tapas manifestly,
satyaloka, pātāla, and tens of millions of hells and oceans.
The stars, the planets, the moon, and the sun, as well as Dhruva, the seven seers,
and others who travel in celestial chariots, all abide by his grace.
By this [power], those bulls among the twice-born were likewise emanated as his own selves;
Śiva, the soul of all, remains forever established as the universal totality.
The utterly deluded, bewildered by his *māyā*, do not recognize the Great Self, the Great God, the Supreme Lord, who is the soul of all.
The body of that god Rudra is indeed the three worlds;
therefore, having bowed to him, I shall declare the auspicious determination of the worlds.
Previously, I have told you everything regarding the formation of the cosmic egg (aṇḍa) and the nature of the worlds;
now I shall describe [them] within the Brahmāṇḍa.
The earth, the intermediate space, heaven, the mahas-world,
the janah-world, as well as tapas and satya— these seven auspicious worlds were born from the cosmic egg.
O twice-born ones, beneath these there are seven subterranean levels beginning with Mahātala; below those, the hells are situated in succession.
Mahātala has a golden surface and is adorned with all kinds of jewels,
as well as with various palaces and the abodes of Bhava.
And it was joined by Ananta, by the wise Mucukunda,
and by the powerful King who dwells in both Pātāla and heaven.
O Brahmins, Śaila is Rasātala, while Śārkara is indeed Talātala;
Sutala is said to be yellow, and Vitala has the luster of coral.
For that which is white is Atala, and that which is other than white is Tala;
and their extent beneath the earth, O you of good vows, is equal to the breadth of the earth itself.
The number of all those lakes is established as being equal to that;
the sky extends for a thousand yojanas and indeed ten thousand.
The measurement of the solid sky is indeed one hundred and seven thousand *talas*,
while its base is thirty thousand.
O best of sages, that auspicious realm known as Rasātala was likewise inhabited by Suvarṇa, Vāsuki, and others.
Served by Virocana, Hiraṇyākṣa, Naraka, and others,
it is renowned as Talātala and is endowed with every splendor.
And likewise, Sutala was crowded with the ancient gods, such as Vaināyaka and others led by Kālanemi, as well as other [beings].
And Vitala was [attacked] by the Dānavas and others, such as Tāraka and Agnimukha,
as well as by the Nāgas beginning with Mahāntaka, and by the Asura Prahlāda.
And here is the famous Vitala, frequented by Kambala and Aśva,
as well as by the heroic Mahākumbha and the wise Hayagrīva.
It was crowded with Śaṅkukarṇa and likewise with those headed by Namuci, as well as various other heroes; thus the ground itself was most beautifully adorned.
In all those various places, the Supreme Lord was accompanied by Ambā, Skanda, and Nandin, and was surrounded on all sides by the lords of the Gaṇas.
And above all the netherworlds (tala), there are seven times seven;
I shall describe to you the terrestrial surfaces and the earth as well, in their sevenfold division.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of Pātāla," in the first part of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said:
Likewise, the earth with its seven continents, crowded with rivers and mountains,
is adorned on all sides by the seven oceans.
Jambū, Plakṣa, Śālmali, Kuśa, Krauñca,
as well as Śāka and the one named Puṣkara— these are the continents in order, starting from the innermost.
In all seven continents, Hara, accompanied by Sāmba and surrounded by all his attendants,
manifests his presence while assuming various guises.
The Salt Ocean, the Sugarcane Juice Ocean, the Wine Ocean, the Clarified Butter Ocean,
the Curd Ocean, the Milk Ocean, and the Sweet Water Ocean follow in succession.
In all these oceans here, the glorious Śiva, accompanied by his attendants, always sports in the form of water with the waves as his arms.
Like the nectar of the milk-ocean, Hari always lies within the milk-ocean,
truly in the direct embrace of yogic sleep through his intellect focused on the knowledge of Śiva.
When the Blessed One is awakened, the entire world is awakened;
when he is asleep, then the moving and unmoving universe, being composed of him, is asleep.
By him alone was everything created, sustained, and protected;
and by the grace of the Supreme Lord, the God of gods, it was likewise withdrawn.
O best of sages, those renowned as the Suṣeṇās worship Aniruddha, the bull among men, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace.
And those foremost among the knowers of the Self who meditate upon the unceased Puruṣa are all equal to Nārāyaṇa and endowed with every perfection.
And the venerable Sanandana, Sanaka, and Sanātana,
as well as the Vālakhilyas, the Siddhas, and Mitrāvaruṇa.
There they constantly worship Hari, the source of the universe;
standing upon the seven islands, those mountains of great splendor possess various peaks.
Some mountains, extending as far as the ocean, were likewise filled with caves;
and many lords of the earth arose due to the gravity of the time.
By virtue of their power, they are supreme lords, born from the Lord Janaka, the enemy of Krauñca,
throughout all the past and future manvantaras here.
O lords of the earth, I shall proclaim for you those who presided over the Svāyaṃbhuva Manvantara, as well as those who have presided and will preside over all past and future Manvantaras.
Possessing equal pride and equal purposes,
they were all the mighty grandsons of Svāyambhuva Manu.
The heroic sons of Priyavrata are proclaimed here to be ten:
Āgnīdhra, Agnibāhu, Medhā, Medhātithi, and Vasu; [and further,] Prācīnabarhis, Śukra, Gaya, Ūru, and Aṅga.
Jyotiṣmat, Dyutimat, Havya, Savana, and Putra,
as well as Priyavrata— these seven he consecrated as kings over the seven continents.
He made the very powerful Āgnīdhra the lord of Jambūdvīpa,
and Medhātithi was likewise made the lord of Plakṣadvīpa by him.
And he consecrated Vapuṣmat as the king of Śālmala,
while the monarch made Jyotiṣmat the king of Kuśadvīpa.
Priyavrata appointed Dyutimat as the king in Krauñcadvīpa, and he also made Havya the lord of Śākadvīpa.
O you of excellent vows, he made Puṣkara the lord of the sacrifice and performed the Savana sacrifice at Puṣkara; Mahāvīta was the son of that Savana as well.
Dhātakī—these two were the sons of that great-souled one, the best among those who possess sons;
the region was known by the name of that high-minded one as Mahāvīta.
Because of the name Dhātaki, it is called Dhātakīkhaṇḍa;
moreover, the lord Havya, the sovereign of Śākadvīpa, begot sons.
Jalada, Kumāra, Sukumāra, Maṇicaka,
Kusumottara, Modākī, and the seventh is Mahādruma.
First, the rain of the cloud is said to be *alada*;
the second is proclaimed as the *kaumāra* rain of Kumāra.
The third is called Sukumāra, which is proclaimed as belonging to Sukumāra; the fourth is Maṇīcaka, which is here called Māṇīcaka.
The fifth region of Kusumottara is indeed Kusumottara;
and Modaka is proclaimed as the sixth region of Modākī.
The seventh among them is Mahādruma by name;
indeed, those seven regions there are named after their respective names.
The sons of Dyutimat, the lord of Krauñcadvīpa,
were indeed Kuśala, Manuṣya, Uṣṇa, Pīvara, and Andhakāraka.
Muni and Dundubhi were indeed the two sons of Dyutimat;
after them, the auspicious regions situated within Krauñcadvīpa were named according to their own names.
A favorable place is conducive to the welfare of one who follows what is wholesome;
a warm place is known to be beneficial for one who is cold, and a nourishing place for one who is emaciated.
The region of Andhaka is called Andhākāraka;
the region of Muni is declared to be Muni; and that of Dundubhi is remembered as Dundubhi.
These seven resplendent provinces exist in the Krauñca islands;
and in Kuśadvīpa, there were seven luminous regions of great power.
Udbhid, Veṇumān, Dvairatha, Lavaṇa, Dhṛti,
the sixth being Prabhākara, and Kapila is remembered as the seventh.
The first region is known as Udbhida, the second as Veṇumaṇḍala,
the third as Dvairatha, and the fourth is remembered as Lavaṇa.
The fifth was Dhṛtimat; the sixth was the unsurpassed Prabhākara;
the seventh was named Kapila, who is celebrated as the son of Kapila.
The seven sons of Śālmalī were indeed handsome lords;
they were Śveta, Harita, Jīmūta, and likewise Rohita.
Vaidyuta, Mānasa, and Suprabha as the seventh;
likewise, the region of Śveta is called Śveta, and that of Harita is Hārita.
Jīmūta was the son of Jīmūta, Rohita was the son of Rohita,
Vaidyuta was the son of Vaidyuta, and Mānasa was the son of Mānasa.
Suprabha was the son of Suprabha, and he indeed had seven regional marks;
I shall now describe them in Plakṣadvīpa immediately after Jambūdvīpa.
Medhātithi had seven sons who were kings and lords of Plakṣadvīpa;
Śāntabhaya was the eldest among them, and those seven regions indeed corresponded to their names.
Therefore, from that very Śāntabhaya, Śiśira— who brings about the arising of happiness—
was born, as well as Ānanda, Śiva, Kṣemaka, and Dhruva.
Those names of theirs were assigned by them, respectively, to those seven regions during the previous Svāyambhuva interval.
By those sons of Medhātithi who resided in Plakṣadvīpa,
the subjects there were settled, endowed with the conduct appropriate for the castes and stages of life.

In the five regions beginning with Plakṣadvīpa and ending with Śākadvīpa, the Dharma should indeed be known to exist according to the divisions of the social classes (varṇas) and stages of life (āśramas).
O best of the twice-born, happiness, lifespan, essential nature, strength,
and dharma are recorded as being common to all in these five continents.
Constantly devoted to the worship of Rudra and dedicated to Maheśvara,
others were also born on Puṣkaradvīpa as lords of creatures.
And those of Prajāpati and Rudra are intensely filled with the bliss of the nectar of existence.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Islands and the Lords of the Islands," in the Bhuvanakośa section of the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
King Priyavrata consecrated Āgnīdhra— the eldest heir, the beloved son, and one of great strength— as the sovereign of Jambūdvīpa.
O bulls among the twice-born, he was exceedingly devoted to Bhava, an ascetic who remained eternally youthful, dedicated to the worship of Bhava, illustrious, possessed of cattle, and wise.
He had nine sons who were equal to Prajāpatis;
they were all devotees of Maheśvara and dedicated solely to Mahādeva.
The eldest was known as Nābhi; his younger brother was Kiṃpuruṣa;
Harivarṣa was the third, and Ilāvṛta was indeed the fourth.
The fifth among them is Ramya, the sixth is said to be Hiraṇmaya,
Kurus is the seventh of them, and Bhadrāśva is recorded as the eighth.
Now learn of their regions: the ninth is Ketumāla;
the father gave the region to the south of Nābhi, which is called Hema.
He gave the region of Hemakūṭa to Kiṃpuruṣa,
and his father gave the region known as Naiṣadha to Hari.
He gave Ilāvṛta to Meru, where it is situated;
and the father gave the region resting against the Nīla mountain to Ramya.
O Hiraṇmata, that which was the northern region, Śveta, was given by his father;
and that which was the northern peak-varṣa, his father gave that to Kurus.
He assigned the region of Mālyavat to Bhadrāśva,
and he gave the region of Gandhamādana to Ketumāla.
Thus, these nine great regions here are divided by portions;
having consecrated his sons over those regions, Āgnīdhra indeed [departed].
Then, remaining steadfast in austerity according to the prescribed order, that righteous-souled one,
purified by asceticism, became devoted to the private recitation of the Vedas.
Thereafter, he became devoted to the private recitation of sacred texts and then devoted to the meditation on Śiva;
[he traversed] those eight auspicious regions, beginning with Kiṃpuruṣa.
For them, the accomplishment of their own nature is indeed easy and effortless;
there is no reversal for them, nor is there any fear of old age or death.
In those eight fields, virtue and vice do not exist, nor are there high, low, or middling [qualities]; nor does the state of the Yugas exist in any respect within them.
Those who die in the field of Rudra— whether mobile beings or immobile things, whether they are devotees or even those encountered incidentally— they all go to those sacred fields.
For their benefit, Rudra created the Aṣṭakṣetra;
there, Mahādeva always maintains his presence.
Having beheld Mahādeva in their hearts, those who dwell in the eight sacred fields are always happy; for them, he alone is the supreme goal in this world.
I shall describe the lineage from Nābhi; listen to this on this snowy peak.
The high-minded Nābhi begot a son upon Merudevī.
To Ṛṣabha, the best of kings and honored by all the kṣatriyas,
was born Bharata, a hero who was the eldest of a hundred sons.
Then, having consecrated Bharata, Ṛṣabha— who was devoted to his son—
resorted to knowledge and dispassion, thereby conquering the great serpents that are the senses.
Having established the Supreme Lord, the Self of all, within his own self by means of his entire being,
he remains naked, with matted hair, abstaining from food, clothed in rags, and dwelling in the darkness.
Free from desire and having abandoned all doubt, he attained the supreme state of Śiva;
he then offered the southern region of the Himālayas to Bharata.
Therefore, the wise know that this region of Bhārata is named after him;
Bharata’s son was the learned and righteous Sumati.
Bharata established that kingdom under his own rule;
having transferred the royal glory to his son, the king entered the forest.
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Bharatavarṣa," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Suta said:
In the center of this continent stands the great mountain named Meru,
the best among those who endure, situated with peaks composed of various jewels.
It is proclaimed to be eighty-four thousand [yojanas] in height;
it enters sixteen thousand [yojanas] below and is likewise sixteen thousand [yojanas] in width.
Because it is shaped like a shallow bowl, it is thirty-two [yojanas] wide across the top;
its circumference, measured along the circular perimeter, is three times that width.
And by the touch of Maheśa’s auspicious body, he was turned into gold;
resembling a dhattūra flower, he became the abode of all the gods.
And the sporting ground of the gods, endowed with many wonders,
is likewise one hundred thousand yojanas in length for that great mountain.
O best of Brahmins, sixteen thousand yojanas of that horned [mountain] are below the earth, and the remainder is above the earth.
Regarding the measurement of the length of the base,
they said that its width at the base of the mountain is twice the width of the mountain itself.
In the east it has the luster of a ruby; in the south, it resembles gold;
in the west, it appears blue; and in the north, it has the brilliance of coral.
(Amarāvatī) In the eastern part of Amarāvatī, it is crowded with various palaces,
filled with diverse hosts of gods, and covered with networks of jewels.
With gate-towers of various forms adorned with gold and jewels, and with archways variegated with gold and fashioned with gems standing along the path; LiP_1,48.10 //
They were skilled in conversation and discourse, adorned with every ornament,
bowed by the weight of their breasts, and their eyes rolled with intoxication.
It was crowded on all sides with thousands of women and celestial nymphs (apsaras),
and adorned with various long ponds filled with blooming lotuses.
With golden stairways, with heaps of golden sand, and with fragrant blue lotuses, white lotuses, and even golden lotuses; LiP_1,48.13 //
Endowed with such ponds, rivers, and streams,
that bright city shines forth, and by it, this auspicious mountain is made beautiful.
In the southeast of the Fire-god is a city named Tejasvinī;
it is divine, equal to Amarāvatī, and endowed with every enjoyment.
To the south, O best of those who practice self-restraint, is the realm of Vaivasvata Yama,
surrounded by divine and auspicious palaces made of gold from the Jambū river.
In the southwest is the auspicious Kṛṣṇavarṇā, and likewise the beautiful Śuddhavatī;
and in the direction of the wind (the northwest) is the splendid Gandhavantī, who is just like her.
Mahodayā is in the north, and Yaśovatī is in the northeast;
they always grace the mountain at its cardinal points as if in heaven.
The abode of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and others was likewise situated there—
a meritorious mountain endowed with all enjoyments and adorned with large ponds.
It was filled with Siddhas and Yakṣas, with Gandharvas and the foremost of sages,
as well as with various other multitudes of the four kinds of beings.
O best of brahmins, upon the mountain stands to the left a vast celestial chariot, possessing a thousand floors and resembling pure crystal.
On that throne made of jewels sat the mighty-armed Śarva, whose eyes are the moon, the sun, and fire, together with the Goddess and the six-faced one.
Half as wide as that of Hari,
there is also a divine celestial chariot made of rubies for the Lotus-born one, situated to his right.
In that [place] were the vast and beautiful cities of Śakra, Yama,
Soma, Varuṇa, Nirṛti, and Pāvaka.
And likewise, on all sides of the abode of Śarva, that of Vāyu and Rudra,
they dwell in various divine celestial chariots.
In the northeast, in the field of Īśvara, the daily worship is established;
and the Blessed One Śailādi, honored by his disciples, is present there along with the Siddheśvaras.
Sanatkumāra, the lord of the gods, sat comfortably together with the Siddhas,
as did Sanaka, Sananda, and thousands of others like them.
In some parts of it is the ground of yoga, and in various other places the ground of enjoyment;
there, a beautiful celestial chariot shines, resembling the rising sun.
There is auspiciousness for the followers of Śailādi; there dwells the Lord of Gaṇas, the six-faced Gaṇeśa, along with thousands of his attendants.
The river named Jambūnadī stands encircling the base of that [mountain], which belongs to Suyaśas, Sunetrā, the Mothers, and Madana.
On its right side, however, stands a most beautiful Jambū tree,
exceedingly tall and very wide, which yields fruit in all seasons.
Surrounding Mount Meru lies the auspicious region of Ilāvṛta, which is extensive;
there, some inhabitants subsist on the fruit of the Jambū tree, while others feed upon nectar.
O brahmins, this auspicious middle island is frequented by serpents of various colors, resembling pure gold, who dwell at the foot of Mount Meru.
It is endowed with nine regions and possesses rivers, streams, and lords of mountains;
I shall now describe Jambūdvīpa with its nine regions exactly as they are.
Understand now its extent and its mandala in terms of yojanas.
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter in the first part of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said:
That [central continent] is recorded as being one hundred thousand yojanas;
each subsequent island is twice the size of the preceding one, increasing twofold.
The earth is recorded as being fifty crores in extent, including the oceans;
it is endowed with seven islands and is auspiciously encircled by the Lokāloka mountain.
O brahmins, Nīla is likewise to the north of Meru, Śveta is further to its north, and Śṛṅgin is to the north of that; these three are the mountain ranges of the regions.
Jaṭhara and Devakūṭa are the two mountains in the eastern direction;
Niṣadha is to the south of Meru, and to the south of that is the mountain known as Hemakūṭa,
and to the south of that is Himavat.
To the west of Meru, there are two mountain ranges that support the earth;
Mālyavat and Gandhamādana—these two extend toward the north.
These are the kings of mountains, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas;
the distance between each of them is nine thousand [yojanas].
This region of the Himavat is renowned by the name Bhārata;
beyond that is Hemakūṭa, which is known by the name Kiṃpuruṣa.
To the east of Hemakūṭa lies the region called Harivarṣa;
beyond Harivarṣa, on the other side of Meru, is the auspicious Ilāvṛta.
Beyond Ilāvṛta is Nīla, renowned by the name Ramyaka;
further beyond Ramyaka is Śveta, which is celebrated as Hiraṇmaya.
Beyond the Hiraṇmaya region, Śṛṅgin and Kuru are also recorded;
these two regions, Dhanuḥ and Saṃsthita, are to be known as situated to the south and north respectively.
Among them, four are long, and in their center lies Ilāvṛta;
two, however, are recorded as being long in the other direction, situated to the west and east of Meru.
Now, that which is to the west of Niṣadha is known as the northern half of the altar;
on the southern half of the altar are three regions, and likewise three on the north.
And between those two, one should know that Ilāvṛta is situated in the middle of Meru;
it lies to the south of Nīla and to the north of Niṣadha.
To the north lies the great mountain named Mālyavat;
it extends for two thousand yojanas across its upper surface.
Its length is proclaimed to be thirty-four thousand [yojanas];
to its west, the mountain Gandhamādana is to be known.
In length it should be known as being like Mālyavat in its extent; it is equal on all sides to the width of Jambūdvīpa.
These six mountain ranges, well-jointed and extending eastward, are the boundary mountains;
they are immersed on both sides in the eastern and western oceans.
The Himavat is mostly composed of snow, while Hemakūṭa abounds in gold;
Niṣadha is said to be made of gold, resembling the rising sun.
Meru is known to be four-colored and golden, extending upwards;
it is circular in its circumference and rises up as a square.
The western mountain is blue and made of lapis lazuli; the white one is bright and golden;
and the eastern one, possessing three peaks, is made of gold and has the color of a peacock’s tail.
Thus have they been briefly described; now listen again to the lords of the mountains:
Mandara and Devakūṭa are the two mountains in the eastern direction.
Kailāsa and Gandhamādana, as well as the Hemavān mountain—
these two extend toward the east and are situated within the ocean.
Niṣadha and Pāriyātra—these two are excellent mountain ranges;
just as the first two [are situated], so these two are located to the south and the west.
Triśṛṅga and Jāruci are the two excellent mountains to the north;
both extend toward the east and are situated within the ocean.
O best of the twice-born, the wise call these eight the boundary-mountains;
and that Meru, O excellent brahmins, is the lofty golden mountain.
Its four feet are the four supreme mountains in the four directions,
by which the earth, consisting of seven continents, is supported and does not waver.
Their length is taught to be ten thousand yojanas;
Mandara is in the east, while Gandhamādana is in the south.
Vipula is known to be on the western side, and Supārśva on the north;
these four great trees have arisen as the banners of the continents.
On the peak of Mount Mandara stands a great tree, the king of banners,
a Kadamba tree with drooping branches and tips, serving as a sacred shrine-tree (caityapādapa).
On the peak of the southern mountain as well, there is a Jambū tree frequented by the gods,
which always bears meritorious fruit and is eternally adorned with garlands.
Saketu is renowned throughout the Jambū worlds in the southern continent,
as well as on the western side of the great mountain Vipula.
That great *aśvattha* tree, a sacred *caitya*, grew upon the peak;
that great tree also grew on the northern summit of Supārśva.
The nyagrodha tree has a vast trunk and a circumference of many yojanas;
I shall describe those four lords of mountains to you in their proper order.
There were four divine pleasure-grounds, non-human and delightful, possessing the seasons of every time, and enchanting to the mind.
Understand now the names of the forests in the four directions:
in the east is the one named Caitraratha, and in the south is Gandhamādana.
One should know Vaibhrāja to be in the west, the forest of Savitṛ in the north,
Mitreśvara in the east, and Ṣaṣṭheśvara beyond that.
Varyeśvara is in the west, while Āmrakeśvara is in the north;
likewise, O best of sages, there are four great lakes.
Where the sages sport upon the mountains and in the forests,
there is the lake Aruṇoda to the east, and Mānasa is remembered as being to the south.
Sitoda is the western lake, and likewise Mahābhadra is the northern;
the field of Śākha is to the south, and that of Viśākha is to the west.
To the north of Naigameya and to the east of Kumāra,
and to the east of Aruṇoda, the lords of mountains are known by their names.
I shall describe them briefly, for it is not possible to do so in detail:
Sitānta, Kuraṇḍa, Kurara, and Acalottama.
Vikara, Maṇiśaila, and Vṛkṣavān, the best of mountains;
then Mahānīla, Rucaka, Sabindu, and likewise Dardura.
Veṇumān, Samegha, Niṣadha, and Devaparvata—
these are indeed the best of mountains, as are other mountains likewise.
To the east of Mount Mandara, these abodes of the Siddhas are proclaimed;
they are located upon those various lords of mountains, in their caves, and in their forests.
The divine Rudra-fields and those of Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa are located here to the south of Lake Mānasa, amidst great mountains.
I shall now briefly recount all those who have been mentioned:
Śaila, Viśiras, and Śikhara, the best of mountains.
Ekaśṛṅga, Mahāśūla, Gajaśaila, Piśācaka,
Pañcaśaila, Kailāsa, and Himavat, the best of mountains.
Thus, these are the excellent mountains frequented by the gods;
and upon all those various mountains and in their forests, [the gods dwell].
Divine Rudrakṣetra sites have been established by the supreme gods;
those in the southern quarter have been described, and now I shall speak to you of those in the western quarter.
Furthermore, Sitoda and Surapa of great strength,
as well as Kumuda, Madhumat, Añjana, and Mukuṭa.
Kṛṣṇa, Pāṇḍura, and Sahasraśikhara;
Pārijāta, the lord of mountains, and Śrīśṛṅga, the best of peaks.
Thus, these excellent mountains, frequented by the gods and abounding in wild beasts,
all lie in the western quarter and are endowed with the fields of Rudra.
And to the north of the Mahābhadra lake dwell those of great strength;
listen now as I briefly describe them as they are being proclaimed.
The great mountain Śaṅkhakūṭa, Vṛṣabha, Haṃsaparvata, Nāga, Kapila, and the peaked Indraśaila; LiP_1,49.54 //
Nīla, Kaṇṭakaśṛṅga, and the mountain Śataśṛṅga;
Puṣpakośa, Praśaila, and Viraja, the best of mountains.
Varāhaparvata, Mayūra—the best of mountains—and Jārudhi, the lord of mountains; these are situated in the north.
Upon those divine mountains, there are thousands of countless celestial palaces belonging to the trident-bearing God of gods.
Between these principal mountains, in their respective order,
there are intermediate valleys, as well as lakes and groves.
Gods, sages, and perfected beings, imbued with the spirit of Śiva, dwell there together with their wives, having taken up residence through the grace of the Supreme Lord.
Kaśyapa and others [attain success] in a grove of bilva trees for Lakṣmī and the rest;
likewise, it is taught that Indra, Upendra, and those of serpent-nature [attain it] in a grove of palmyra trees.
Likewise, at the Udumbara tree of Kardama and at those of other great-souled ones—
Vidyādharas and Siddhas— in that auspicious and holy mango grove.
The Nāgas and the hosts of Siddhas likewise reside in the Nimba forest; the Sun and the retinue of Rudra reside in the Kiṃśuka forest.
In the meritorious Bījapūra forest, the preceptor of the gods resided;
and in the Kaumuda forest, he stayed with the high-souled ones headed by Viṣṇu.
Within a banyan tree situated in the midst of a forest of land-lotuses,
Śeṣa, the lord of all worlds, dwells exceedingly proud, while all other serpents remain there.
He alone is Time for the worlds, established in Pātāla;
he is the divine form of Viṣṇu, the teacher of the universe, manifest as Halāyudha.
The bed of Hari, the god of gods, the bracelet of the omnipresent Lord,
the jackfruit trees in the forest, and the Dānavas led by Śukra— [all these were seen].
Kinnaras and uragas likewise reside in the Viśākhaka forest;
and in the Manohara forest, there are trees endowed with all ten million [divine qualities].
Nandīśvara stood there being praised by the foremost of the Gaṇas,
while in the midst of the Saṃtānaka grove was the goddess Sarasvatī herself.
Thus have the forest-dwellers in the groves been described in brief;
they are so numerous that even I cannot describe them here in detail.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
On the peak of Śitānta, in the auspicious Pārijāta grove,
to its east lies that vast mountain-peak of Kumuda.
O best of the twice-born, there were formerly eight exalted cities of the Dānavas in the auspicious Suvarṇakoṭara, as well as those of the high-souled Rākṣasas.
O best of the twice-born, they say there are sixty-eight cities of the Nīlas,
and fifteen cities on Mahānīla, the lord of mountains.
O you of excellent vows, on the great mountain Veṇusaudha are the three cities of the Vidyādharas, belonging to the Hayānanas, the Mukhyas, and the Kinnaras.
In Vaikuṇṭha dwells the glorious Garuḍa, and in Karañja is Nīlalohita;
in Vasudhārā, however, the abode of the Vasus is proclaimed to be.
O Ratnadhārā, on that best of mountains, there are seven meritorious sites belonging to the high-souled Seven Sages, which are inhabited by perfected beings.
The great abode of Prajāpati is on Ekaśṛṅga, the best of mountains; on Gajaśaila dwell Durgā and others, as well as the Vasus, O Sumedhas.
Likewise, the Ādityas, the Rudras, and the two Aśvins have made their dwellings there;
indeed, eighty cities of the gods are situated on Hemakakṣa, the best of mountains.
In Sunīla, the abode of the Rākṣasas, there were five hundred crores of cities on Pañcakūṭa, measuring five crores in extent.
On Śataśṛṅga is the city of a hundred Yakṣas of immeasurable splendor;
on Tāmrābha is the city of the sons of Kadrū, and on Viśākha is indeed that of Guha.
O best of sages, the abode of the high-souled Suparṇa is on Śvetodara;
that of Kubera is on Piśācaka; and the residence of Hari is on Harikūṭa.
In Kumuda is the abode of the Kinnaras; in Añjana is the dwelling of the Cāraṇas;
in Kṛṣṇa is the residence of the Gandharvas; and in Pāṇḍura are seven cities.
O best of Brahmins, on the mountain with a thousand peaks, there was a city endowed with all enjoyments belonging to the Vidyādharas and to the Daityas of fierce deeds.
O twice-born ones, O lords of sages, there are seven thousand ancient crowns belonging to the enemies of Śakra; on these flower-bannered crowns dwell the serpents.
There are four shrines: those of Vaivasvata, Soma, Vāyu, and the Lord of Nagas, Takṣaka, as well as that on Śailendra.
Of Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, as well as of the high-souled Guha,
Kubera, Soma, and likewise other great-souled beings.
There are also principal sacred sites on the boundary mountains;
there dwells the Abode of All, together with Umā, in the cave of the Śrīkaṇṭha mountain.
Indeed, Śrīkaṇṭha is the sovereign lord of all the lords of the gods;
there is no doubt that the activity of this cosmic egg is directed by Śrīkaṇṭha.
Ananteśa and the others are likewise the guardians of each cosmic egg (cāṇḍapālaka);
they are called universal emperors (cakravartin), and from them, the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvara) arise here.
Today, listen as I speak briefly of the places presided over by Śrīkaṇṭha on the boundary mountains; I shall describe them now.
How shall I describe in detail this entire world of moving and non-moving beings, presided over by Śrīkaṇṭha, extending as far as Kālāgniśiva?
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "Description of the Locations and Arrangement of the World," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
In the center of the Devakūṭa mountain, upon the most beautiful Mahākūṭa peak,
[it shone] with the lusters of gold, beryl, ruby, sapphire, and emerald.
Likewise, it was fashioned by others out of choice jewels, stainless and auspicious,
enriched with hundreds of thousands of branches and adorned with every kind of tree.
Adorned with *campaka*, *aśoka*, *puṃnāga*, *vakula*, and *āsana* trees,
it was filled with *pārijātaka* trees and frequented by flocks of various birds.
It was variegated with hundreds of different realms, filled with diverse flowers,
possessed of mountain slopes adorned with blossoming *sāla* trees, and inhabited by hosts of many beings.
It was endowed with many single-springs of pure and sweet water,
and adorned with numerous waterfalls strewn with flowers.
It was adorned with flowing streams carrying rafts of flowers,
and it possessed trees of many trunks with glossy colors and massive roots.
For there is a delightful forest named Bhūtavana, ten yojanas in circumference, with dense shade, which is the abode of various hosts of spirits.
There was the radiant abode of the great-souled god Mahādeva Śaṅkara, adorned with magnificent jewels.
It was enclosed by a golden wall, adorned with jeweled archways,
and provided with various gate-towers made of crystal.
There were auspicious lion-thrones made of jewels, provided with beautiful coverings,
which had been properly established here and there upon the earth by Śarva.
With excellent houses of various colors covered with garlands of unfading flowers, and with most wonderful pavilions supported by pillars of crystal; LiP_1,51.11 //
He was joined by the lords of all beings, who were worshipped by Brahmā, Indra, and Upendra,
and who had the faces of boars, elephants, lions, bears, tigers, and young camels.

There were also other Pramathas with faces like vultures and owls, as well as those with faces like deer, camels, and goats; they were of various forms, some massive like mountain peaks, and others auspicious.
With formidable, tawny, and hairy arms,
they bore various colors and forms and were situated in various postures.

With radiant faces and radiant conduct, headed by Nandīśvara, auspicious, resembling Brahmā, Indra, and Viṣṇu, and endowed with the powers of *aṇiman* and the other supernatural qualities; // LiP_1,51.15 //
It is eternally not empty of immortals and likewise of great assemblies;
there, the gods constantly perform worship to the Lord of Beings.
With the clanging of conchs and kettledrums, with bherīs, ḍiṇḍimas, and gomukhas,
accompanied by the soft, lingering songs and the rhythmic, leaping roars.
Mahādeva, the lord of the Pramathas, was indeed worshipped by the Pramathas,
by the Siddhas, Rishis, gods, and Gandharvas, and by the high-souled Brahmā.
There Śaṅkara was worshipped by Upendra and others;
it was there that [the mountain] with its beautifully divided peaks possessed the luster of a conch shell.
(Kailāsa) Kailāsa is the residence of the high-souled Kubera, king of the Yakṣas, as well as that of ten million Yakṣas and other great-souled beings.
Therein also is the great abode of Bhava, the god of gods;
in that abode, Hara, together with Soma and his attendants, dwells eternally.
There, on the auspicious peak of Kubera, is a lotus-lake named Mandākinī with vast waters, featuring stairways made of gold and jewels.
With lotuses made of Jāmbūnada gold, endowed with the qualities of fragrance and touch,
and with great blue utpala lilies having petals of blue vaidūrya and filled with scent.
Likewise, it is adorned with clusters of night-lotuses and great lotuses,
and frequented by female yakṣas, gandharvas, and apsarases.
The auspicious and meritorious river Mandākinī has its waters touched by gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and kinnaras.
And on its northern side is the auspicious abode of Bhava, endowed with lapis lazuli gems; there dwells the imperishable Śaṅkara.
On the eastern bank of the Kanakanandā, toward the south,
there was a forest abounding with thousands of birds and filled with deer and fowl.
There too, accompanied by his attendants and Ambā, he sports in a house like unto a mountain,
on the western bank of the Nandā, slightly toward the south.
There was a city named Rudrapurī, crowded with various palaces;
there too, having divided himself into a hundred forms along with Ambā, he dwelt.
He sports there with his attendants and Ambā; that is called the abode of Śiva.
In this way, there are hundreds of thousands of shrines of Śarva.
O best of sages, on every continent, upon the mountains and in the forests,
on the banks of rivers, streams, and lakes, and at the shores of the oceans—
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter in the first part of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said:
O best of the twice-born, many auspicious rivers, always full of abundant water, have been described as originating from lakes; they are indeed innumerable.
Those facing east, those facing south, and those originating from the north are auspicious;
likewise, those with their tips pointing west are proclaimed to be pure in every year.
That which is the ocean of space is called Soma;
it is the support of all beings and the source of nectar for the gods.
From this [lake] flows forth the river Puṇyodā, which travels through the sky;
having entered the path of the wind on its seventh course, it becomes the Amṛtodakā.
Following after the luminaries and attended by hosts of lights, she was joined with the sky and thousands of millions of stars.
Just as the moon revolves day by day, so too does she;
and likewise, he rises up eighty-four thousand [yojanas] high.
Mahāmeru, which is as soft as the playground of Śrīkaṇṭha, measures many yojanas;
for it is there that Śarva sits together with Ambā and the lords of the Gaṇas.
Having played for a very long time, that auspicious and merit-bestowing river then proceeds clockwise around Mount Meru.
Dividing its waters by the force of the wind, it fell with speed upon all four of the intermediate peaks of Mount Meru.
Having completely bypassed all the mountains in their respective divisions,
she entered the great ocean by the command of the God of Gods.
From this [ocean] flow forth rivers by the hundreds and thousands;
many are proclaimed to exist throughout all the continents, mountains, and regions.
There are innumerable small rivers that flow from the sky into the Gaṅgā;
the people in Ketumāla are all long-lived and subsist on the fruit of the panasa tree.
The women have the luster of blue lotuses, and their lifespan is said to be ten thousand years;
in Bhadrāśva, the women are white in color and resemble the rays of the moon.
All of them, eating the black mangoes, free from disease and fond of pleasure,
live for ten thousand years, being permeated by Śiva.
Just as those whose minds are entirely dedicated to the Lord appear as if made of gold,
so too do the living beings in Ramaṇaka subsist on the fruit of the banyan tree.
For ten thousand years and fifteen hundred years,
all those who are pure live, being entirely devoted to the meditation on Śiva.
The highly fortunate ones made of gold, who dwell in the golden forests,
number eleven thousand one hundred and fifty.
There they live for many years, subsisting on the leaves of the *aśvattha* tree;
with their minds entirely surrendered to the Lord, they appear as if made of gold.
In Kuru-varṣa, however, the Kurus have descended from the heavenly world;
they are all born of sexual union, possess milk-yielding trees, and subsist on milk.
Mutually devoted like ruddy geese,
they were indeed free from disease and sorrow, constantly enjoying happiness.
Thirteen thousand five hundred [years] do those of great heroism live, and they do not consort with any other woman.
The death of those Kurus, who dwell in heaven, who are joyful, highly prosperous, and all of whom consume the nectar of immortality, occurs simultaneously.
But [he saw] those who were always as lovely as the moon, always endowed with youth, dark-limbed, and whose bodies were the locus for all ornaments.
In Jambudvīpa, moreover, the region of Kuru is most beautiful;
there stands the moon-bright celestial chariot of Śambhu, the moon-crested Lord.
In the land of Bhārata, mortals are meritorious, their lifespans determined by the power of their karma;
they are declared to have a hundred-year lifespan, possessing various complexions and small bodies.
Engaged in the worship of various deities, they consume the fruits of various actions;
though endowed with various forms of knowledge and wealth, they are weak and possess meager enjoyments.
Likewise, some went to Indradvīpa, and similarly to Kaseruka; some went to Tāmradvīpa, and others to the land of Gabhastimat.
They went to Nāgadvīpa, as well as Saumya, Gāndharva, and Vāruṇa;
there were some Mlecchas and Pulindas, born of various castes.
In its eastern extremity the Kirātas are known to dwell, and in the west the Yavanas;
in the center reside Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, while Śūdras are found everywhere.
Engaged in sacrificing, fighting, and trading, they remain established there;
thus does their mutual interaction proceed among them.

The resolve and the sense of self-importance regarding one's own duties among the social classes, as well as those pertaining to the stages of life according to the rules, are joined with virtue, wealth, and pleasure.
O bulls among sages, it is here that human activity proceeds for the sake of heaven and liberation, and it is here, and not elsewhere, that the activities of the Yugas take place.
The lifespan of humans in Kiṃpuruṣa is ten thousand years;
the men are golden-colored, and the women are like apsarases.
For they are all free from disease and sorrow, permeated by auspiciousness;
being pure in essence and golden-hued, they dwell with their wives and subsist on the fruit of the *plakṣa* tree.
In Harivarṣa as well, the humans resemble great silver;
they have all descended from the world of the gods and possess entirely divine forms.
They worship Hara, the Lord of All, and drink the auspicious sugarcane juice;
therefore, old age does not afflict them, nor do those men ever grow decrepit.
Human beings live there for ten thousand years;
that which I have described as the middle region is named Ilāvṛta-varṣa.
There the sun does not scorch, nor do those men grow old;
neither the moon nor the sun, nor the stars, nor any light exists in Ilāvṛta.
Those who have cultivated existence are born with the radiance of lotuses, faces like lotuses, eyes resembling lotus petals, and the sweet fragrance of lotus petals.
Subsisting on the juice of jambu fruits, motionless and fragrant,
those who have come from the world of the gods are born there indeed free from old age and death.
Those best of men live for a lifespan of thirteen thousand divine years in Ilāvṛta.
Having drunk the juice of the jambu fruit, old age does not afflict them;
nor do hunger, fatigue, or even death affect these people.
There, a gold known as Jāmbūnada, which serves as an ornament for the gods, is produced; it resembles an Indragopa insect and is intensely radiant.
Thus have I fully described, in brief and not at length, the castes, lifespans, foods, and other characteristics of those who dwell in the nine regions.
On Hemakūṭa, the Gandharvas and hosts of Apsarases are to be known;
and on Niṣadha, all the Nāgas, including Śeṣa, Vāsuki, and Takṣaka, reside.
The thirty-three gods, performers of sacrifice and possessed of great strength, take their delight there;
and on Nīla, which is made of lapis lazuli, dwell the pure Siddhas and Brahman-sages.
The mountain Śveta is said to belong to the Daityas and Dānavas,
while the mountain Śṛṅgavān is the eternal abode of the Pitṛs.
On all mountains, Mahādeva [was worshipped] by Hari, Brahmā, Ambā, the chief Yakṣas, and the Lord of Beings.
And with Nandin and the Gaṇas, in the rainforests and the groves,
as well as on the Blue, White, and Triple-peaked mountains, the Blessed One Nīlalohita [resides].
It is constantly beheld, especially by the Siddhas, gods, and ancestors;
it is blue and made of lapis lazuli, white and made of silver, and golden.
The golden mountain Śātakuṃbha has three peaks and the color of a peacock’s plumage;
these are the kings of mountains situated in Jambūdvīpa.
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Nature of the Cosmic Egg," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
In each of the seven islands, beginning with Plakṣadvīpa, there are seven mountains;
these mountain ranges, which demarcate the regions, are situated straight and extended in every direction.
I shall now describe the seven divine great mountains in Plakṣadvīpa:
Gomedaka is the first here, and the second is called Candra.
The third is named Nārada, the fourth is remembered as Dundubhi,
the fifth is named Somaka, and the sixth is called Sumanas.
That very one is declared to be Vaibhava; the seventh is remembered as Vaibhrāja.
These seven mountains are specifically said to exist in Plakṣadvīpa.
In Śālmalidvīpa there are indeed seven [mountains]; I shall describe them to you in order:
Kumuda, Uttama, Parvata, and Balāhaka.
Droṇa, Kaṅka, Mahiṣa, and Kakudman is remembered as the seventh;
in Kuśadvīpa, there are likewise seven islands and seven principal mountain ranges.
I shall describe them briefly, merely by name, in their proper order:
the first is said to be Vidruma, and the second is Hemaparvata.
The third is named Dyutimat, the fourth is remembered as Puṣpita;
the fifth is Kuśeśaya, while the sixth is remembered as Harigiri.
The seventh is the glorious Mandara, the abode of Mahādeva;
for "manda" is a name for waters, and Mandara is so called because it supports the waters.
There, in that supreme golden palace, the Lord Viśveśa, the stainless Śiva, marked with the bull, dwells together with Soma and Sanandin.
Formerly, Maheśvara, gratified by the asceticism of Mandara,
obtained a supreme boon in the great field of Avimukta.
And having been entreated by his mother for the sake of a dwelling, Mahādeva came from Avimukta and made his residence on Mount Mandara.
Accompanied by his attendants and accompanied by Soma, he does not abandon that place;
moreover, in Krauñcadvīpa, there are the Kulaparvatas beginning with Krauñca.
To the west is Krauñca, then Vāmanaka, and the third is Andhakāraka;
beyond Andhakāra is the mountain named Divāvṛt.
Beyond Divāvṛta, moreover, the mountain Vivinda is said to be;
and beyond Vivinda, furthermore, is the great mountain Puṇḍarīka.
And beyond Puṇḍarīka is proclaimed Dundubhisvana;
these seven mountains of Krauñcadvīpa are composed of jewels.
And in Śākadvīpa there are seven mountains; learn of them, O best of sages: Udaya, Raivata, and Śyāmaka.
And from Rājata comes the glorious and most beautiful mountain Āmbikeya;
beyond Āmbikeya is the delightful Sarvauṣadhi, endowed with all medicinal herbs.
In that very place is the one called Kesarī, from which the wind is produced;
and on Puṣkara is the glorious mountain, a single massive rock.
On the eastern half of that island stands a great mountain with variegated peaks made of jewels and lofty networks of rock, situated upon a multicolored ridge.
That great mountain rises fifty thousand yojanas upwards and extends thirty-four thousand yojanas downwards.
On half of the continent stands the Mānasottara mountain, encircling it;
situated near the shore, it is like the newly risen moon.
It rises fifty thousand yojanas in height,
and it is likewise broad in extent, being perfectly circular on all sides.
That very mountain Mānasa, the support of the earth, exists in the western half of the continent;
though it has but a single great peak, it is divided into two by its configuration.
On that island, two meritorious and auspicious regions are remembered;
they are silver and lie along the circular slopes of Mount Mānasa.
The region called Mahāvīta is that which lies outside of Mānasa;
that which is inside of it is called Dhātakīkhaṇḍa.
Puṣkara is surrounded on all sides by the ocean of sweet water;
it is as extensive as the breadth of Puṣkaradvīpa itself.
In extent and in circumference, they are equal to Puṣkara;
thus the continents are surrounded by seven oceans, each being sevenfold [in size].
The ocean that lies immediately adjacent to a continent is indeed the seventh;
in this manner, the increase of the continents and oceans should be understood as occurring progressively one after another.
Then, following after Puṣkara,
the great ocean of sweet water (Svādūdaka) stood surrounding it on all sides.
Beyond that, the vast arrangement of the world is seen:
a golden ground, double in extent, which is entirely like a single solid rock.
Beyond that is the mountain which forms the boundary of the outer circle;
being both illuminated and unilluminated, it is called Lokāloka.
O twice-born ones, this earth extends as far as the visible and invisible mountains;
its height is recorded as ten thousand yojanas.
Such is the extent of that great mountain Lokāloka;
however, the rays of the sun move only across its nearer half.
On the other side, however, there is eternal darkness; therefore, it is known as Lokāloka.
Thus has the detailed extent of Bhūrloka been briefly described.
O best of sages, from the sun down to the earth, and from the earth down to the pole star (dhruva),
there are seven rims beginning with Āvaha, which are established within the wind.
Āvaha and Pravaha, then Anuvaha as well, Saṃvaha and Vivaha, and above those, Parāvaha.
The seven rims of the wind are Dvija and Parivaha;
likewise, there are the clouds, the sun, the moon, and the constellations.
The seven sages, the planets, and the Pole Star (Dhruva), O wise ones, are situated here in succession fifteen yojanas above the surface of the earth, up to the Pole Star.
One hundred thousand yojanas from the surface of the earth is the solar disc;
the chariot of the Sun-god is likewise sixteen thousand yojanas above that.
Mount Meru rises eighty-four thousand yojanas above the surface of the earth;
having ascended ten million yojanas from there, one reaches Maharloka, which is as eternal as the Pole Star itself.
O twice-born ones, Janaloka is likewise two crores from Maharloka;
Tapoloka is considered to be four crores from Janaloka.

O twice-born ones, it has been declared that from the world of Prajāpati, the world of Brahmā extends by emitting six crores [of yojanas]; these seven meritorious worlds are indeed situated within this cosmic egg.
Beneath the seven netherworlds (talas), there are indeed ten million hells;
starting with Ghorā and ending with Māyā, they are exactly twenty-eight in number.
In those hells, beginning with Raurava and ending with Avīci, all sinners are cooked according to their respective karmas.
They say that there are specifically five distinct hells for each [of these];
first, I have described the cosmic egg (aṇḍa) and the coverings of the egg.
And the creation of Hiraṇyagarbha has been described at great length as a digression;
it should be understood that there are thousands of millions of such cosmic eggs.
Because Pradhāna is all-pervading, likewise horizontally, upwards, and downwards,
within all these cosmic eggs there are the fourteen worlds.
O tigers among the twice-born, for every individual egg, Maheśvara is the cause;
likewise, he is the cause of the eggs, of those outside the eggs, and of the enclosures of the eggs.
At the end of darkness and beyond darkness, the eight-formed one is established;
he is the self of the wise Maheśvara, the Great God.
Ah, how wonderful! This entire body belongs to the Supreme Self, to Śarva, to Śiva, the householder who possesses eight forms.
The divine Prakṛti is his wife, and the principles beginning with Mahat are his offspring;
all those who identify with their bodies are his cattle and servants.
The Blessed One is devoid of beginning and end, the infinite Person; and there are seven [principles] headed by Pradhāna.
Furthermore, he is the form of Pradhāna, the sixteen-limbed one, and Maheśvara himself is the eight-bodied one.
By the power of his command, the earth, the mountains, the clouds, the oceans,
the host of luminaries, the gods headed by Śakra, the celestial beings in their mansions, and all things mobile and immobile remain established here.
Having seen the Yakṣa devoid of [divine] marks, and having seen the Lord together with Indra, they asked, "What is this here?
Having approached the Yakṣa for a definitive conclusion, Agni and the others found their power exhausted even by that.
O brahmins, even the fire was unable to burn a blade of grass in the presence of this yakṣa;
likewise, the wind could not move a blade of grass, and all the other lords of the immortals were unable to exercise their respective powers.
Then the Lord of the Gods, the enemy of Vṛtra himself—the cause of all prosperity—being filled with curiosity, spoke thus to the Yakṣa Sureśvara: "Who are you? LiP 1.53.57.

For at that moment, the yakṣa had indeed become invisible; then Ambikā, the daughter of Himavat, with her auspicious face, Umā, shining brilliantly with many beautiful ornaments, appeared right after him.
Śakra and the other gods asked Umā, the unborn daughter of Himavat, who was exceedingly beautiful:
"O Īśā, O Ambikā, what is this that shines so brightly, appearing like the form of a yakṣa?
Having heard that, Umā said to the gods, including Śakra: "This yakṣa is beyond my perception."
They bowed down to her, who moves like the king of beasts, Umā, the Unborn, who is red, white, and black.
Honored by all the lords of the immortals, she—the source of all activity among gods and asuras—then said:
"In the past, I was the primordial nature (prakṛti) of the Yakṣa Puruṣa, and I remain subject to his command."
Therefore, O twice-born ones, by the command of that Unborn One, the egg indeed arose from the Unborn;
and from the egg, the Unborn and the entire universe emerged—thus that world, consisting of the Unborn, was filled with hosts of luminaries.
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Determination of the Arrangement of the Cosmic Egg," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
Having surveyed the celestial fields for the purpose of establishing the movements of the planets, I shall indeed describe, in brief, the course of the hosts of luminaries within the cosmic egg.
Above Mānasa stands the city of Mahendra; to the east of Meru is the city of Bhānuputra, and to the south is the city of Varuṇa, Vāruṇī.
In the north, belonging to Soma, are the vast [cities] where the deities of the directions reside:
Amarāvatī, Saṃyamanī, Sukhā, and Vibhā, respectively.
Now, understand that course which the sun takes when it has reached its limit in the southern solstice, above the Lokapālas and on all sides.
In its southern course, the sun runs like an arrow shot;
taking up the circle of luminaries, it revolves incessantly.
O twice-born ones, when the sun, the lord of Śakra, reaches the end of the city [of the setting mountain], the rising of the solar orb is indeed seen with all its evening rays.
That very same one, the all-seeing and omnipresent Lord, is seen dwelling in his palace in Sukhāvatī; yet the sun sets again in the night, for he is the light of the universe.
Just as I had described him in Amarāvatī as one who restrains thieves,
so too did that bird reach Saṃyamanī, which is both blissful and radiant.
O twice-born ones, when it is afternoon in the southeast, it is forenoon in the southwest;
and at that time, it is the dreadful dead of night in the northwest.
In the northeast, during the first watch of the night, this is the movement [of the moon] in every respect;
thus, when the lord of waters glides through the middle of Puṣkara.
In one muhūrta, it traverses a thirtieth part of the earth;
learn now this calculation of yojanas for a single muhūrta.
That [number] is recorded as one hundred and thirty-one thousand,
plus another fifty thousand in addition.
For this is the momentary course of the high-souled Sun;
by means of this movement, when he reaches the southern quarter, [he proceeds].
The sun also inquired about the northern quarter on the following day;
however, during the southern course, it revolves in the middle of Puṣkara.
On the Mānasottara mountain, the all-pervading Lord Vibhāvasu, possessed of great splendor,
[traversed] a full one hundred and eighty mandalas.
The external and the internal [paths] are declared to be the northern and southern courses;
indeed, the sun moves through those solar orbs every day.
Just as the rim of a potter’s wheel revolves rapidly,
so does the god move swiftly during his southern course.
Therefore, during the southern course, the sun traverses a great distance in a short time,
swiftly covering it in twelve muhūrtas.
During the day, the sun traverses thirteen and a half constellations;
during the night, it traverses as many constellations in eighteen muhūrtas.
Just as the center of a potter’s wheel moves slowly,
so the sun moves with slow progress during its northern course (udagayana).
Therefore, over a long period of time,
that chariot of the Sun, presided over by the Ādityas and likewise by the sages, traverses but a small portion of the earth.
The thousand-rayed sun blazed before him, behind him, and below him, along with the Gandharvas, Apsarases, Grāmaṇīs, Sarpas, and Rākṣasas.
Having cast his hand upward toward the unsurpassed assembly of Brahmā,
he [struck] the night-stalkers with the waters released by the sages during the twilight.
Having repeatedly struck down those who have arrived, the Sun moves among the Brāhmaṇas for eighteen muhūrtas during the latter part of the northern course (uttarāyaṇa).
During the day it becomes light,
and the sun of slow course traverses thirteen constellations; at night it traverses twelve constellations with twelve muhūrtas, while during the day it moves through eighteen constellations.
Then, just as a wheel rotates more slowly at the hub,
so too does Dhruva rotate while situated in the center, like a lump of clay.
Those who know the ancient lore say that a day and night consists of exactly thirty muhūrtas,
during which [the sun] revolves through the circles between the two solstitial points (kāṣṭhā).
Just as the hub of a potter’s wheel remains fixed in that very place,
so does the son of Uttānapāda, the foremost of planets, revolve together with the other planets.
The host of the sages' luminaries moves through his mind,
yet the sun, presided over by him, remains having taken [the light] upon itself.
By means of its rays, the Lord, together with the wind, draws up water from all sides;
this perpetual state of Dhruva, the son of Uttānapāda, exists indeed through his grace.
Viṣṇu obtained [his power] through Auttānapāda for the sake of his father;
the waters were drunk by Sūrya, and they proceed in the sequence of the Moon.
From the moon, the waters flow forth in succession toward the clouds;
and the mass of water-bearing clouds is indeed struck by the wind.
By that [light], the Sun emits and illuminates creation upon the earth;
yet there is indeed no destruction of the water, for it merely undergoes transformation at that very time.
For the welfare of all living beings, Śarva fashioned the worlds:
Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, as well as the waters, food, and even immortality itself.
The vital breaths, indeed, are the waters of the worlds, as well as the beings and the worlds themselves;
what need is there for much speaking here? This entire world, both moving and unmoving, is [composed of them].
The Blessed One is established in the lordship over the auspicious waters;
the god who is the sovereign of the waters is thus celebrated as Bhava.
What wonder is there in this world that the entire universe is of the nature of existence?
The lordship of Nārāyaṇa over the god Hari was established by the waters, O All-pervading One; Viṣṇu is the abode of the worlds, yet the waters are his own abodes.
While all moving and non-moving beings are being scorched, those that have become wheat emerge from the earth;
and whichever clouds are driven upward by the wind, they too are consumed by fire and wind.
Therefore, the conjunction of smoke, fire, and wind is called a cloud (*abhra*);
it is called a cloud because it rains water, and the thousand-eyed one is the lord of the cloud.
The cloud arising from the smoke of sacrifice always brings benefit to the twice-born;
the cloud produced from the smoke of a forest fire is known to be beneficial to the forest.
A cloud arising from the smoke of a corpse will bring misfortune;
O twice-born ones, one arising from the smoke of a fire used for malevolent magic (abhicāra) indeed leads to the destruction of living beings.
Thus, by means of specific smoke, one determines the welfare or misfortune of the worlds;
therefore, a person should conceal the smoke produced for malevolent rites.
If a twice-born man performs a smoke-offering without having clothed himself, or performs one intended for malevolent magic,
he will likewise bring about the destruction of the world by aiming it against it.
O you of good vows, the clouds— the repositories of water— rain down here for six months at the command of the Wind-god, solely for the welfare of the worlds.
O bulls among sages, the origin of clouds here is threefold: that produced by wind, that produced by lightning, and that produced by fire.
Because the clouds do not fall away from it, it is called *mehana*;
likewise, there are the wooden beams of Brahmā and various kinds of wings.
From the contact of wood with clarified butter, the smoke of fire is produced;
and the origin of the second [kind of fire] is from the wind of Viriñca’s exhalation.
Then, by the wings of the mountains shattered by Maghavan,
auspicious clouds born of fire arose, stationed in the region of Āvaha.
All [the clouds] born from the breath of Viriñca arise from the trunk of the Pravaha wind;
then those born from its wings, such as Puṣkara and the others, pour down water.
The Mūka, Śabdaduṣṭa, and Āśā [planets] perform their respective functions in due order:
they grant scanty rain for a long time and bring cold winds.
And likewise, the living beings, devoid of the sound of lightning,
remain on the surface of the earth, crying out here and there.
Indeed, all the clouds dwelling on the mountain within half a krośa are givers of abundant water,
for they are capable of covering an area of one yojana.
O twice-born ones, from the surface of the earth upon the ground, they are endowed with the quality of lightning;
their emission of rain is here described as being threefold.
All those greatest of mountains, born of the wings and born of the eons,
rain down at the end of the eon during the night for destruction, like autumnal clouds.
And when the clouds born of the wings, beginning with Puṣkara, pour down water, then everything becomes an ocean; therein the Lord Śiva lies at night.
O bulls among the twice-born, for the clouds born of fire, born of breath, and born of wings,
smoke is always known as their nourishment.
All the showers of rain from the Pauṇḍra clouds, which are electric and bestow cool crops,
fall as cold, frost-like droplets upon the elephants in the Puṇḍra regions.
The Gaṅgā was born from the waters of the Gaṅgā by means of the rain-clouds and their outpourings;
it was crowded with mountains, rivers, and the elephants of the quarters.
And the water, having become separate from the clouds, went forth and returned;
and the wind Parāvaha brought the preceptor of Ambikā.
O twice-born ones, having crossed beyond the region of Menāpati,
the remainder of the rain proceeds to the land of Bhārata for the sake of increasing the western regions.
Indeed, rains have been described today as being of two kinds for the increase of things;
I shall briefly explain them according to my understanding regarding the two types of crops.
The creator, the sun of great splendor, the all-seeing and omnipresent lord of rains—
he too, O best of the twice-born, is manifestly the supreme Śiva, the Lord.
He alone is splendor, vigor, strength, O brahmins, fame itself,
sight, hearing, mind, death, the self, wrath, the intermediate directions, and the cardinal directions.
He is truth and cosmic order, as well as wind, the sky, and that which moves through space;
he is the world-protector, Hari, Brahmā, Rudra, and Maheśvara himself.
The glorious thousand-rayed one, with eight arms and most auspicious,
is the lord of the thirty gods, manifest as the three-eyed one whose body is half-female.
O twice-born ones, it is by his grace alone that rain occurs here in various ways;
he takes up water with his rays and releases it a thousandfold.
Upon investigation, there is neither destruction nor increase of water;
rather, the wind, presided over by Dhruva, withdraws the rain once again.
Having emerged from the sun along with the planets throughout the entire circle of constellations,
they enter the sun at the end of their course, presided over by Dhruva.
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Motion of the Sun and Other Planets in the Jyotiścakra," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
I shall briefly describe the chariot of the Sun, as well as that of the Moon,
and how the other planets and the Lord of Waters (Varuṇa) move along.
O best of the twice-born, that solar chariot was created by Brahmā for a specific purpose, and it is fashioned from the constituent parts of the year.
Equipped with a golden wheel having three naves and five spokes, it is the abode of all the gods for the Sun-god.
Its width and length are recorded as nine thousand yojanas;
furthermore, the pole of the chariot is twice the measurement of the seat.
Yoked with unattached horses that stand wherever the wheel is directed,
his seven steeds were indeed fashioned from the Vedic meters.
Fixed to the wheel-assembly, the axle is joined to the *dhruva*;
together with the horses and the wheel it revolves, and together with the axle the *dhruva* revolves.
Driven by Dhruva, that axle revolves together with the single wheel;
the wise Dhruva is indeed the impeller of the luminaries by means of the rays of wind.
The two reins of the chariot are attached to the ends of the axle-pole;
bound by those reins at the two ends of the axle-pole, it revolves around Dhruva.
As the chariot of the sky-traveler revolves in its circles,
its two poles and axle-ends are indeed situated on the right side of that vehicle.
When the two horses are indeed held fast by Dhruva with ropes,
they both follow Dhruva and the reins as he revolves.
The yoke-pole of this chariot driven by the wind is attached to the axle-pin like a rope, and thus it revolves in all directions.
As it revolves through the circles during the northern course, its rays increase;
likewise, as it revolves through the circles during the southern course, they increase.
When those two are indeed drawn by Dhruva,
then the sun, situated within, revolves through its orbits.
Furthermore, the interval between the two poles is one hundred and eighty circles,
as they are released by the two rays from the Pole Star (Dhruva).
In the same way, the sun revolves externally through its orbits;
unwinding with great speed, it traverses those circular paths.
The gods as well as the sages constantly worship the god Bhāskara, the Lord Bhava, day and night, perpetually.
The charioteer was presided over by the gods, the Ādityas, and likewise by sages,
Gandharvas, Apsarases, as well as by the Grāmaṇīs, Sarpas, and Rākṣasas.
These indeed dwell in the sun for two months each in succession;
they nourish the auspicious Āditya, the maker of light, with their splendors.
The sages praise the Sun with their own composed verses,
while the Gandharvas and Apsarases attend upon him with dance and song.
The Yakṣas and Bhūtas act as village leaders and hold the reins;
the serpents indeed draw the chariot of the Sun, and the Yātudhānas follow behind.
"The Vālakhilyas lead the sun, surrounding him, as he sets on the mountain of sunrise.
Thus, these indeed dwell here for two months each while the sun is in the sky.
Madhu and Mādhava, Śukra and Śuci,
Nabhas and Nabhasya, O best of Brahmins, as well as Iṣa and Ūrja.
Saha and Sahasya, as well as Tapasya and Tapas—
these, O twice-born ones, are the twelve months that constitute a human year.
The seasons are traditionally reckoned as the spring (vāsantika), the summer (graiṣma), the auspicious rainy season (vārṣika), the autumn (śārada), the winter (himaka), and the cool season (śaiśira).
Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, and Indra;
Vivasvat, Pūṣan, Parjanya, Aṃśu, and Bhaga as well.
Tvaṣṭṛ, Viṣṇu, Pulastya, Pulaha, Atri,
Vasiṣṭha, Aṅgiras, and Bhṛgu, the best among the wise.
Bhāradvāja, Gautama, Kaśyapa, Kratu,
Jamadagni, Kauśika, Vāsuki, and Kaṅkaṇīkara;
And likewise, O twice-born ones, there were the nāgas Takṣaka and Elāpatra,
as well as another known as Śaṅkhapāla and Airāvata.
Dhanañjaya, Mahāpadma, and Karkoṭaka are likewise remembered;
as are Kambala, Aśvatara, Tumburu, and Nārada.
Hāhā, Hūhū, O best of sages, Viśvāvasu the unsurpassed,
Ugrasena, Suruci, and another named Parāvasu.
Citrasena of great splendor, Corṇāyu, Suvrata,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Sūryavarcas, and the goddess Sākṣāt-kṛtasthalā.
Śubhānanā, Śubhaśroṇi, the divine Puñjikasthalā,
Menakā, Sahajanyā, Pramlocā, and Śucismitā.
Anumlocā, Ghṛtācī, Viśvācī, Urvaśī, and the goddess known as Pūrvacitti, as well as Tilottamā herself— LiP_1,55.33.
Raṃbhā, Ambhojavadanā, Rathakṛt, the auspicious Grāmaṇī,
Rathaujas, Rathacitra, Subāhu, and Rathasvana.
Varuṇa and likewise another, Suṣeṇa, the auspicious Senajit, Tārkṣya, Ariṣṭanemi, Kṣatajit, and Satyajit.
The weapon of the Rakshasas, the Praheti, the slaughter by human agency,
as well as the serpent, the tiger, water, wind, lightning, and the sun.
The Lord of the Rākṣasas accompanied by Brahmā, and likewise he accompanied by Yajña—
all these gods and others dwell in the Sun in succession.
For these twelve groups of seven are indeed proud of their respective stations;
they are proclaimed as the twelve gods beginning with Dhātṛ and ending with Viṣṇu.
The sages, the best among ascetics, beginning with Pulastya and ending with Kauśika, cause that supreme sun, the radiant one, to swell with their own splendors.
And the auspicious Nāgas, headed by Vāsuki and ending with Aśvatara, praise the Sun with twelve hymns in due order.
In this manner, twelve [gandharvas], beginning with Tumburu and ending with Sūryavarcas, carry Mahādeva in due order, like water.
The twelve supreme Gandharvas,
beginning with Kṛtasthala and ending with Rambhā, as well as the divine Apsarases, worship this Sun with songs.
All the divine *grāmaṇīs*, beginning with Satyajit and ending with Rathakṛt, attend upon him in due order with passionate *tāṇḍava* dances.
Twelve [beings] take turns holding his reins;
accompanied by those who possess sacrificial rites, they proceed together with the foremost of the weapons of the Rākṣasas.
These twelve Rākṣasas, equipped with weapons, are as follows in order:
Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Pulastya, and Pulaha, the progenitor.
The serpent Vāsuki and Kaṅkaṇīka— both of them—
as well as Tumburu and Nārada, the two best of Gandharvas who sing, [were there].
Kṛtasthalā and Apsaras, as well as Puñjikasthalā,
Grāmaṇī, Rathakṛt, and both of those known as Rathaujas.
Rakṣoheti and Praheti are declared to be Yātudhānas;
this group dwells in the sun during the months of Madhu and Mādhava.
The two months of the summer season are presided over by Mitra and Varuṇa,
as well as the sages Atri and Vasiṣṭha, and the Nāga Takṣaka.
Menakā and Sahajanyā, the two Gandharvas Hāhā and Hūhū,
and the two leaders named Subāhu and Rathacitra— these were all there.
Human slaughter and the Yātudhānas are likewise declared;
these indeed dwell in the sun during the months of Śuci and Śukra.
