Then, when the sun [returns], other deities dwell here once more:
Indra, Vivasvat, Aṅgiras, and Bhṛgu.
The serpent Elāpatra, as well as both Śaṅkhapāla,
Viśvāvasu, Ugrasena, Varuṇa, and Rathasvana.
Pramlocā and the renowned Anumlocā—both of these were [his daughters];
likewise, Yātudhāna and Sarpa were both his sons, as was Vyāghra.
This group dwells in the sun during the months of Nabhas and Nabhasya:
Parjanya, Pūṣan, Bharadvāja, and Gautama.
Dhanañjaya and Irāvān, Suruci along with Parāvasu,
as well as Ghṛtācī, the most excellent of Apsarases, and the exceedingly beautiful Viśvācī.
Senajit and Suṣeṇa are the commander-in-chief and the village leader;
these two are both remembered as Yātudhānas, namely Water and Wind.
These indeed dwell in the sun during the months of Ūrja and Iṣa;
and they dwell in the sun during the two winter months as well.
Aṃśu and Bhaga— these two— together with Kaśyapa and Kratu,
as well as Bhujaṅga, Mahāpadma, and the serpent Karkoṭaka.
The Gandharva Citrasena and Ūrṇāyu— both of them—
and likewise the two Apsarases, Urvaśī and Pūrvacitti.
Tārkṣya and Ariṣṭanemi are both designated as the general and the village-leader,
while Vidyut and Divākara are both declared to be Yātudhānas.
These dwell during the months of Sahas and Sahasya while the sun is present;
thereafter, they indeed reside during the two months of the dewy season (śiśira).
Tvaṣṭṛ, Viṣṇu, Jamadagni, and likewise Viśvāmitra;
as well as both Kambala and Aśvatara, the two Nāgas who are the sons of Kadrū.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra along with the Gandharva Sūryavarcas,
as well as the Apsaras Tilottamā, and the goddesses Rambhā and Manoharā.
Rathajit and Satyajit were world-renowned leaders,
as were the Rakshasa Brahmopeta and he who is remembered as Yajñopeta.
These gods dwell in the sun for two months at a time in succession;
indeed, these twelve groups of seven are the presiding deities of the [solar] stations.
These sages nourish the sun, that supreme radiance, with their own radiant energy;
indeed, they praise the Sun-god with their composed words.
The Gandharvas and Apsarases attend upon him with dance and song, while the Grāmaṇīs, Yakṣas, and Bhūtas hold the reins.
The serpents indeed carry the sun; the sorcerers (yātudhānas) follow after him;
and the Vālakhilyas, surrounding the sun, lead him to his setting on the mountain of sunrise.
Of these very gods, according to their splendor, according to their austerity,
according to their application, according to their mantra, according to their dharma, and according to their strength—
Thus that sun shines, kindled by their splendor;
indeed, these [deities] dwell here in the sun for two months each.
The sages, the hosts of gods, gandharvas, serpents, and apsarases,
as well as the village chiefs, yakṣas, and preeminent yātudhānas.
These [suns] scorch, rain, shine, blow, and create;
they are celebrated here as those which dispel the inauspicious karma of living beings.
For these [deities] take away the merit of wicked men,
and they occasionally dispel the evil deeds of those who act rightly.
And stationed in divine celestial chariots that move at will and possess the speed of the wind,
they revolve together with the sun, following its daily course.
Raining, heating, and indeed gladdening, O twice-born ones,
they protect all beings here until the end of the celestial age.
This is indeed the station of those who possess pride regarding their status throughout the past,
future, and present Manvantaras.
These fourteen groups of seven indeed dwell in the sun;
they are all present here throughout the fourteen Manvantaras.
In brief and in detail, exactly as it occurred and as it was heard,
this has been narrated, O tigers among sages, concerning the wise God of gods.
These gods dwell in the sun for two months each in succession; these twelve groups of seven are indeed the deities who preside over the various stations.
Thus, with his single-wheeled chariot drawn by green horses whose speed is as constant as syllables, this maker of day, the Sun, swiftly traverses [the sky].
Traversing the sky on his single-wheeled chariot, he revolves day and night,
moving through the seven continents, oceans, and mountains by means of his seven horses.
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Sun’s Chariot," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
The Moon moves through the constellations that rest upon the celestial paths;
his chariot is indeed to be known as having three wheels and horses on both sides.
It was equipped with three wheels, each having a hundred spokes, and yoked to ten excellent, white horses— divine, unemaciated, unimpeded, and swift as thought.
Indeed, Soma, possessing white rays, travels in this chariot together with the gods and the ancestors, drawn by white, water-born cows.
Established in the supreme state, the sun begins its course at the start of the bright fortnight;
it is continuously filled within the other [fortnight] by the progression of the days.
The Sun, by means of a single ray, constantly replenishes the Soma that has been drunk by the gods during its waning for fifteen days.
Filling each portion in succession by means of the *suṣumṇā* [channel],
thus the body of the moon is nourished by the vital energy of the sun.
On the full moon day, he is seen bright with a perfectly full orb;
thus is Soma replenished during the bright fortnight through the succession of days.
Then, from the second day until the fourteenth of the bright fortnight,
the gods drink the honey-like, gentle nectar consisting of water.
Indeed, the nectar is accumulated for half a month by the solar radiance;
on the full moon day, they approach the Soma, the nectar, for the purpose of drinking it.
For one night, all the gods together with the ancestors and the sages [remain] at the beginning of the dark fortnight of the moon, facing the sun.
The digits (kalās) of the other [the moon] are gradually consumed; three hundred and thirty-three, and likewise thirty-three more, perish in succession.
Thirty-three thousand gods indeed drink the Soma;
thus, as the moon is drunk by the deities in the course of the days.
Having drunk [the nectar] for half a month, the best of gods go to the new moon;
and the ancestors likewise attend upon the moon on the day of the new moon.
Then, when fifteen parts remain, consisting of a mere fraction of a *kalā*,
during the afternoon, the hosts of ancestors wait upon him at the very end.
The remaining portion of that time, which consists of two units (kalās), is the new moon; from its rays, the nectar of *svadhā* flows forth.
Having attained supreme satisfaction for a month by drinking it, they go to the nectar; that which is the fifteenth digit of the moon being drunk by the ancestors—*LiP_1,56.16*.
However, that fifteenth part of it which is waning is filled again during the interval of the new moon (amāvāsyā).
The waxing and waning of the moon are indeed traditionally held to occur at the beginning of the fortnights on the sixteenth day;
thus, this increase of the lunar fortnight is caused by the sun acting upon the moon.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Soma," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
The chariot of the son of Soma (Mercury), moreover, is yoked with eight horses;
it consists of the essence of water and is adorned with beautiful, tawny-colored steeds.
The chariot of the wise preceptor of the Daityas, Śukra, is said to be yoked with ten sturdy horses of various colors made of earth.
Furthermore, the chariot of Bhauma is made of gold, beautiful and drawn by eight horses;
that of Jīva is also golden with eight horses, while that of Mandi is fashioned of iron.
The chariot of Svarbhānu, the enemy of the Sun, is known to have ten horses that are not white,
as well as eight horses.
All those planets are indeed bound to Dhruva by cords of wind;
being whirled around by this, they move according to their respective courses.
As many as there are stars, so many are the rays;
all of them, fixed to Dhruva, as they revolve, cause him to revolve.
Because they move like a whirling firebrand, driven by the wind-wheel,
and because he carries the luminaries, he is therefore known as Pravaha.
The constellations and the sun, together with the hosts of planets and stars, all turned their faces upward and toward him, forming a circle as they took their place in the sky.
Presided over by Dhruva, they indeed move clockwise around Dhruva alone,
who stands as the central pivot in the sky, in order to behold the Lord.
The diameter of the sun is recorded as nine thousand yojanas;
its circumference, according to measurement, is three times that.
The diameter of the moon is recorded as being twice that of the sun;
Svarbhānu, however, moves below them, having become equal in size to those two.
Having cast off the shadow of the earth fashioned in the form of a mandala,
Svarbhānu attained his vast third abode, which consists of darkness.
The portion of Bhārgava is ordained to be one-sixteenth that of the Moon,
both in terms of its diameter, its orb, and its measurement in yojanas.
Bṛhaspati is to be known as one-quarter shorter than Bhārgava;
likewise, Venus and Saturn are each one-quarter shorter in their measurement of height.
The wise one should know that both in width and in circumference, these are each one-quarter less than those two;
for those forms of stars and constellations which indeed possess bodies here in this world.
One who knows the truth should know that those lunar mansions are generally equal in extent and in their circularity to Mercury, and they are conjoined with the Moon.
The forms of the stars and constellations (tārā-nakṣatra) are smaller than one another,
measuring five hundred, four hundred, three hundred, and two hundred yojanas respectively.
But the circles of stars at the very top are the most minute, measuring only two yojanas; nothing smaller than they exists.
Above them are those three planets which travel at a great distance;
they are known as Saura, Aṅgiras, and Vakra, and they move slowly.
Below them, moreover, are four other great planets:
Sūrya, Soma, Budha, and Bhārgava, who move with great speed.
There are as many millions of stars as there are constellations in every respect;
however, by the fixed law of Dhruva, their position is established within the path of the constellations.
When the moon, situated on the path of the northern solstice, is at its conjunctions with the sun— the possessor of seven horses— in successive order, it reaches its lowest and highest positions.
Because of its height, it is seen quickly with rays that are not very distinct;
at that time, it is situated on the southern path, having resorted to a low orbit.
Then, on the days of the full moon and the new moon, the sun was seen enveloped by lines of earth; at the appropriate time, it would quickly set.
Therefore, while situated on the northern path, the Moon was seen on the new moon day;
by necessity, he is not seen when on the southern path.
Due to the movement and conjunction of the luminaries, the sun is enveloped by darkness;
at the equinoxes, its setting and rising occur simultaneously.
In the northern paths, the rising and setting of the Vyantara gods should be known as following the movement of the circle of luminaries on the full moon and new moon days.
When the sun, possessing rays, moves along the path of the southern solstice,
it glides beneath all the planets.
Having formed a vast mandala, the moon moves above it;
the entire circle of constellations glides above the moon.
Above the constellations is Mercury; above Mercury is Venus;
above Venus is Mars; and above Mars is Jupiter.
Above that is Saturn, and above that is the circle of the Seven Sages;
and the station of the Seven Sages is situated above Dhruva.
Knowing that supreme realm of Viṣṇu, one is liberated from sin;
it extends for two thousand and one hundred yojanas.
Above the planets, lunar mansions, and stars, they stand in their respective order;
the planets, as well as the moon and the sun, are endowed with divine splendor.
Moving day and night in succession through the constellations,
those planets, lunar mansions, and suns are situated in their respective positions of depression, exaltation, and rectitude.
In both conjunction and division, all beings perceive them simultaneously;
though the six seasons are traditionally enumerated, they all come together in five ways.
For these exist in mutual dependence and are joined with one another; their conjunction, however, should be understood by the wise as being without confusion.
Thus, O twice-born ones, the movement of the planets, headed by the Sun, has been described in brief, exactly as it was seen and heard.
The Blessed One, the thousand-rayed one, was consecrated by Brahmā, the lotus-born, into the lordship of the planets, just as Guha was consecrated by Rudra.
Therefore, when afflicted by the planet Āditya, the virtuous should perform the worship of the planets in the fire according to the prescribed rite for the sake of accomplishing their goals.
Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Movement of the Planets in the Sphere of Light," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
The sages said:
Tell me now, O Soul of All, how Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures, consecrated all the gods, Daityas, and others in their sovereignty.
Sūta said:
Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures, consecrated the divine Sun as the sovereign of the planets and Soma as the lord of the lunar mansions and the medicinal herbs.
And [he saw] Varuṇa, the god of the waters; Yakṣapuṅgava, the lord of riches;
Viṣṇu among the Ādityas; and likewise Pāvaka among the Vasus.
And among the Prajāpatis, Dakṣa; among the Maruts, Śakra himself;
and among the Daityas and Dānavas, Prahlāda, the preeminent among the Daityas.
Dharma, the lord of the ancestors; Nirṛti, of the flesh-eaters;
Rudra, of the cattle; and Nandin, the leader of the hosts of spirits.
Vīrabhadra among heroes, the terrifier of the Piśācas,
and Cāmuṇḍā among the Mothers, who is saluted by all the gods.
[He worshipped] Nīlalohita, the Lord of the Rudras and Sovereign of the gods;
and Vināyaka, the elephant-faced god born from space, who is the lord of obstacles.
Among women, he is the goddess Umā; among goddesses, Sarasvatī;
among those possessing illusory power, Viṣṇu; and likewise, among the worlds, his own self.
He is the Himavat among mountains, the Jāhnavī among rivers,
and the lord of all oceans, the repository of waters.
And among trees, the great-grandfather [Brahmā] is the Aśvattha and the Plakṣa.
Furthermore, he made Citraratha the lord of the Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, and Kinnaras;
Vāsuki of fierce valor the lord of the Nāgas; and Takṣaka of fierce valor the lord of the serpents.
He made Airāvata, the lordly elephant of fierce valor, the sovereign of the elephants of the quarters;
he made Suparṇa the lord of winged creatures, and Uccaiḥśravas the king of horses.
He made the lion the king of beasts, the bull the king of cattle, and the Śarabha the lord of wild animals.
He is Guha, the immeasurable lord of the commanders of the armies, and Lakulīśa, the lord of the Śruti and Smṛti scriptures.
He consecrated Sudharmāṇa, as well as Śaṅkhapada of the quarters,
Ketumān, and Hemaroman, in due order.
On earth, he is the broad lord, the great sovereign of all;
among the four forms, he is the omniscient Śaṅkara, whose banner bears the bull.
Out of grace, the Blessed Śambhu consecrated him in due order;
having been consecrated in the past, that meritorious soul, the lord of the world, shone resplendent.
This has been told to you in detail, O best of sages;
thereafter, these distinguished ones were consecrated by the Source of the Universe.
Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Consecration of Sūrya and Others," in the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
Having heard this, the sages, filled once again with doubt,
then questioned Romaharṣaṇa further for an answer.
The sages said:
"O Sūta, best among speakers, regarding that which has been mentioned by you here,
explain this in detail, as well as the definitive determination of the luminaries."
Having heard their words, the charioteer, composed in mind, then spoke these supreme words for the sake of resolving their doubt: LiP_1,59.3 //
In this matter, I shall declare to you that which has been spoken by those of great wisdom and tranquil intellect regarding the course of the sun and the moon.
(Fire-Water-Circle) Just as the sun, the moon, and other planets are here in the celestial abodes,
beyond this I shall describe the threefold origin of fire. (LiP 1.59.5)
Of the divine fire, of the elemental fire, and also of the terrestrial fire,
as well as of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest, when the night has dawned—
This world was then indistinct, shrouded in nocturnal darkness,
when only a fourth part remained of this universe that had been utterly destroyed.
There, the self-existent Lord, the accomplisher of all the world's aims,
moved about like a firefly, desiring to manifest himself.
Having created fire at the beginning of the world, that Lord, resting upon earth and water,
withdrew it for the sake of illumination and divided it threefold.
That which is called the earthly fire in this world is the wind;
and that which exists at the beginning of the world within the sun is known as the pure fire.
The fire born of water is to be known as the lightning-fire; I shall now describe their characteristics:
the lightning-fire, the digestive fire, and the solar fire—these are the three fires containing the essence of water.
Therefore, while drinking the waters, that all-pervading Sun shines with rays;
and the lotus is immersed in the water, yet the fire within it is not extinguished by the waters.
The fire that dwells within the bellies of human beings does not become extinguished;
though it is the radiant wind, that fire is known as the digestive fire (jāṭhara), which is devoid of visible flame.
And this white halo that arises, devoid of heat,
is the solar radiance when the sun has set by one quarter.
Fire enters the night, and therefore it shines from afar;
furthermore, as the sun rises, its heat enters the fire.
Because he touched the terrestrial fire with his foot, that fire burns there above;
thus, light and heat constitute the two forms of splendor belonging to the sun and the fire.
Through their mutual interpenetration, they nourish one another;
for the northern half of the earth is thus [sustained] by Soma, and the southern by Agni.
The sun rises again and indeed enters the waters once more;
therefore, the waters become copper-colored due to his entry during the day and night.
The sun sets and enters the waters during the day;
therefore, at night, the waters are seen again as bright and radiant white.
By this sequential process, on the southern and northern halves of the earth,
it constantly enters the waters during day and night at its rising and setting.
And that sun which blazes, drinking the water with its rays,
is known as the divine and pure fire, mixed with the earthly fire.
That fire is said to have a thousand feet and resembles a round jar;
it draws [the elements] from all sides through its thousand channels.
The waters of rivers and of the ocean, as well as those from wells and clouds,
whether stationary or moving, such as those in ponds and channels— [all these he should offer].
His thousand rays emit cold, rain,
and heat; four hundred of those channels, possessing diverse forms, pour forth rain.
The rays named Amṛtas— Bhajas, Mālyas, Ketanas, and likewise Patanas— all of them bestow rain.
And those channels carrying snow are the three hundred rays;
they are the Reśas, the Meghas, the Vātsyas, the Hlādinyas, which produce snow.
All of them are named Candrabhā; their rays are yellowish, as well as white, Kakubha, and Viśvabhṛt.
All those three hundred [streams] are white by name and are the creators of heat;
through them, Soma sustains human beings, ancestors, and deities.
In this world, he gratifies human beings with herbs, the ancestors with the ancestral offering (svadhā),
and all the gods with nectar— thus he satisfies them by means of these three.
In both spring and summer, he heats [the world] with three hundred rays;
then, during the rainy season and autumn, he pours down rain with four hundred.
In the late autumn and the winter, he emits frost by means of three [deities]:
Indra, Dhātṛ, Bhaga, Pūṣan, Mitra, Varuṇa, and Aryaman. (The Gods in the Sun) LiP 1.59.31.
Aṃśu, Vivasvat, Tvaṣṭṛ, Parjanya, and Viṣṇu [are the presiding deities];
Varuṇa is in the month of Māgha, while Sūrya himself is in Phālguna.
In the month of Caitra, the Sun shall be Aṃśu; in Vaiśākha, he is indeed Dhātṛ;
in the month of Jyeṣṭha, he is Indra; and in Āṣāḍha, the Sun is Aryaman.
Vivasvat is remembered as the sun in the month of Śrāvaṇa, Bhaga in Prauṣṭhapada;
Parjanya in the month of Āśvayuja, and Tvaṣṭṛ indeed in Kārttika.
In Mārgaśīrṣa he becomes Mitra, and in Pauṣa he is the eternal Viṣṇu;
Varuṇa possesses five thousand rays during his solar activity.
The god Pūṣan [is borne] by six thousand, and likewise Aṃśu by seven;
Dhātṛ by eight thousand, and Śatakratu by nine.
Vivasvat travels with ten [horses], Bhaga travels with eleven;
Mitra heats with seven, and Tvaṣṭṛ is recorded as having eight.
Aryaman moves with ten [rays], and likewise Parjanya with nine;
Viṣṇu, however, heats the earth with six thousand rays.
In spring the sun is tawny; in summer it has the brilliance of gold;
in the rainy season it is white in color; and in autumn the maker of light is pale.
In the winter season the sun is copper-colored, and in the cool season it is red;
thus have the colors originating from the Sun been fully described by me.
The Sun bestows strength upon the herbs, nourishment upon the ancestors through their own inherent power, and immortality upon the gods; thus he ordains this triad among these three.
In this way, that thousandfold solar ray, which accomplishes the welfare of the world,
becomes divided upon reaching the world, discharging water, cold, and heat.
This white and radiant maṇḍala, known as the Sun,
is indeed the foundation and source of the lunar mansions, the planets, and the Moon.
The moon, the constellations, and all the planets are to be known as originating from the Sun;
Soma is the lord of the constellations and the left eye of the Lord.
And the Sun himself is the right eye of the Lord,
because he leads those people in this world.
Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of the Sun’s Rays," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
The remaining five planets are to be known as lords who move according to their will;
moreover, it is recited that fire is Āditya and water is remembered as Candra.
Learn now correctly the nature of the remaining [deities] as it shall be explained:
Skanda, the commander of the divine army, is recited as the planet Aṅgāraka.
Those who know the truth call the wise Nārāyaṇa a god;
he is the manifest lord of all worlds, Yama himself, the lord of the world.
O best of the twice-born, the slow-moving Śanaiścara is a great planet;
likewise, the two preceptors of the gods and asuras are radiant and great planets.
Then Śukra and Bṛhaspati were said to be the sons of Prajāpati;
the entire three worlds have the Sun as their root—of this there is no doubt.
From this arises the entire world, including gods, asuras, and humans—
[the world] of Rudra, Indra, Upendra, and Candra, as well as the foremost of Brahmins, Agni, and the celestial dwellers.
He is the splendor of all splendid things, the entire mundane energy of all worlds,
the soul of all, the lord of all worlds, Mahādeva, the Lord of Creatures.
The Sun alone is the Lord of the three worlds, the root, and the supreme deity;
from him everything is born, and into him alone it dissolves.
For in ancient times, existence and non-existence for all worlds issued forth from the Sun;
O Brahmins, the Sun is a radiant and glorious planet that is difficult to comprehend.
Here they go to their destruction and are born again and again—
moments, hours, days, nights, and entire fortnights.
The months, the year, the seasons, and the yugas— indeed,
this reckoning of time does not exist without that Āditya.
Apart from time, there is no restriction, no initiation, no sequence of daily rites,
no division of seasons, and how could there be flowers, roots, or fruits?
Whence would there be the production of grain, nor even the multitude of grasses and herbs? There would be an absence of all worldly transactions for living beings, both in heaven and here on earth.
Except for the Sun, who torments the world and possesses the form of Rudra,
he is indeed Time, Fire, the twelvefold Soul, and Prajāpati.
O best of the twice-born, he shines upon the three worlds with all their mobile and immobile beings;
he is this entire mass of splendors, common to all the worlds.
Having established himself upon the supreme path, he heats this entire world on all sides— on its flanks, above, and below— for days and nights.
Just as a lamp that illuminates, when suspended in the middle of a house,
equally destroys the darkness on all sides, above, and below.
In the same way, the thousand-rayed Sūrya, the king of planets and lord of the world,
illuminates the entire universe from every side with his rays.
Regarding the thousand rays of the Sun that were previously described by me,
seven of them are preeminent; they are the rays that have the planets as their source.
Suṣumna, Harikeśa, and likewise Viśvakarman;
then Viśvavyacas, and again Ādya, and after that Saṃnaddha.
Furthermore, another is proclaimed as Sarvāvasu, and another as Svarāṭ;
Suṣumna, who possesses solar rays, increased the southern constellation.
Its movement upward and downward is celebrated as Suṣumṇā;
that which is proclaimed as Harikeśa is said to have its origin in the stars (Ṛkṣa) in the east.
In the south is Viśvakarman, and the ray Vardhana nourishes Budha;
while he who is behind is Viśvavyacas, known by the wise as the source of Śukra.
The ray named Saṃnaddha is the source of blood;
the sixth ray, Sarvāvasu, is the source of Bṛhaspati.
Furthermore, the self-ruling ray nourishes Śanaiścara as well;
thus, by the power of the Sun, the lunar mansions, planets, and stars [are sustained].
All those [stars] are seen in the sky, as is this entire world;
because they do not perish, they are known as *nakṣatra* (the stars).
Thus ends the sixtieth chapter in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
All these fields shine with their rays;
yet the sun takes away those fields from the lunar mansions and the stars.
By virtue of the good deeds performed here in this world, at the conclusion of those merits, they become the abodes of the planets;
for they are called *tārakā* because they deliver (*tāraṇa*) beings, and they are also called *tārakā* because of their whiteness (*śuklatva*).
The sun is the eternal taker of all divine, terrestrial, and nocturnal splendors, as well as of all forms of darkness.
This verbal root is explained as having the senses of "flowing" and "impelling";
because he causes the flow of splendor and of the waters, he is therefore considered Savitṛ.
The word *bahula* refers to the moon; this verbal root is said to denote "refreshing," and it is understood to signify whiteness, immortality, and coolness.
In the divine, radiant orbs of the sun and moon, moving through the sky, composed of water and fire, white, shaped like rounded jars, and auspicious; LiP_1,61.6 //
In that regard, the mandala of the moon is known to consist of condensed water,
while the white mandala of the sun consists of condensed light.
All the gods dwell in all these places throughout all the Manvantaras, taking refuge in the constellations, the sun, and the planets.
Therefore, the planets (graha) are indeed houses (gṛha), and they receive those names;
Sūrya entered his own place, and likewise Soma entered his own.
The powerful Śukra, possessing sixteen rays, entered the abode of Śaukra;
Bṛhaspati likewise entered the great [abode], and Lohita entered the red one.
Likewise, Śanaiścara occupies the station of Śanaiścara;
Budha occupies the station of Budha; and Svarbhānu has taken refuge in the station of Svarbhānu.
All the lunar mansions enter into the lunar mansions;
all these houses are the luminaries of those whose souls are virtuous.
These places, created by the Self-Existent One at the beginning of the eon, endure until the dissolution of all beings.
In all the Manvantaras, those very stations of the gods are occupied by the presiding deities again and again.
These [ages] exist together with the past deities, both those who have attained their state and those who have not,
as well as with the present deities who occupy those positions.
In this very Manvantara, the planets are known to be celestial beings;
Vivasvat, the son of Aditi, is the Sun in the Vaivasvata interval.
The son of the Ṛṣi Dyutimān is known as the Vasu Soma;
Śukra, the son of Bhṛgu, is to be understood as the deity who officiates for the Asuras.
The deity Bṛhattejā is remembered as the preceptor of the gods and the son of Aṅgiras;
he is also known as Budha, Manohara, and the son of a ṛṣi.
Śanaiścara, who was deformed, was the son of Vivasvat born of Saṃjñā;
moreover, that youth Agni, with his red flames, was born of Vikeśī.
They are known as the daughters of Dakṣa, bearing the names of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras) and constellations (ṛkṣas).
Svarbhānu, the son of Siṃhikā, is an Asura who causes torment to all beings.
The presiding deities (abhimānin) are proclaimed to reside in the moon, the constellations, the planets, and the sun;
these have been declared as the locations, and the deities themselves are the inhabitants of those locations.
The station of Sūrya, Vivasvat, the thousand-rayed one, consists of fire;
whereas the station of Himāṃśu is remembered as consisting of water and being white.
The lunar mansion Āpya is dark, charming, and is known as the abode of the rays of Mercury;
the mansion belonging to Venus is watery, white, and possesses sixteen rays.
The excellent abode of Mars has nine rays and is red;
that of Jupiter is large, yellow like turmeric, and possesses sixteen rays.
The house of eight rays is also declared to be black in Śanaiścara;
it is the dark abode of Svarbhānu, a dwelling that causes torment to all beings.
All the stars should be known as having many rays, whereas the sages have but a single ray;
they are the abodes of those of meritorious fame and are white by their own color.
They should be known as consisting of dense water, created at the very beginning of the kalpa;
through contact with the rays of the sun, they are traditionally held to be of the nature of light.
The diameter of the sun is recorded as nine thousand yojanas;
its circumference, according to measurement, is three times that.
The diameter of the moon is recorded as being twice that of the sun;
Svarbhānu, however, moves below them, having become equal in size to both.
Having removed the shadow of the earth fashioned in the form of a mandala,
there is the great third station of Svarbhānu, which consists of darkness.
Emerging from the sun, it moves evenly during the lunar nodes;
it returns to the sun from the moon during the solar nodes.
Because he drives away Svarbhānu, he is therefore called Svarbhānu;
the sixteenth part of the moon is ordained as belonging to Bhārgava.
In terms of its diameter, its orb, and its measurement in yojanas,
Bṛhaspati is to be known as being one-quarter smaller than Bhārgava.
Both Venus and Saturn are recorded as being one-quarter less than Bṛhaspati;
Mercury is one-quarter less than both of them in terms of both width and orb.
Those forms of the stars and constellations that indeed possess bodies here are equal to Budha in both their extent and their orb.

O Yoginī of the Moon, the knower of reality [should know] that the lunar mansions (vidyādṛkṣāṇi) generally take the form of stars and constellations (tārānakṣatra), yet they vary in their relative positions.
The circles of stars, however, extend from five hundred yojanas down to four, three, two, and even one, being the most inferior of all.
They are half a *yojana* each; there is nothing smaller than these.
Above them are three planets, which travel at a great distance.
Saura, Aṅgiras, and Vakra are to be known as those who move slowly;
their courses have already been described in due order.
O best of sages, all these planets have arisen within these very lunar mansions; Vivasvat, the son of Aditi, is indeed Sūrya.
Born under the asterism Viśākhā, he was the first among the planets;
the radiant Soma, son of Dharma, is indeed the Vasu deity.
The cool-rayed maker of night was born under the Kṛttikās;
the son of Bhṛgu, Śukra, possessed sixteen rays and appeared immediately after the Sun.
The most excellent among the lunar mansions and planets arose in the Tiṣya field;
he is the planet Bṛhaspati, the son of Aṅgiras, who possesses twelve rays.
The preceptor of the world, the planet Mars— the son of Prajāpati, whose body is red and whose light is new— was born under the constellations known as the Pūrvas during the month of Phālguna.
It is recorded that here, during the Pūrvāṣāḍhās, the Sun was born;
and during the Revatīs, Saturn (Śanaiścara) appeared in the station of Saptārcis.
The gentle Mercury rose in Dhaniṣṭhā; the five-rayed planet was the son of Death, composed of darkness, a comet that caused the destruction of living beings.
A great planet, the destroyer of all, was born under Āśleṣā;
likewise, the daughters of Dakṣa were born under the asterisms bearing their own names.
Rāhu, consisting of the quality of darkness (tamas) and vigor, is by nature a black orb;
born under the asterism Bharaṇī, he is the planet who eclipses the moon and the sun.
These stars and planets, such as Bhārgava and the others, must also be understood [in this context],
because they fall into a state of dysfunction during afflictions of one's birth asterism.
One is liberated from that fault by devotion to that particular planet;
among all these planets, the Sun is said to be the first.
Among the luminous planets, Śukra is the foremost; among the comets, it is Dhūmavān;
and Dhruva is indeed the chief of the planets distributed throughout the four quarters.
Among the lunar mansions, Śraviṣṭhā is [the first]; likewise, among the solstices, it is the northern;
and among the five-year cycles, the first year is traditionally known as Saṃvatsara.
Among the seasons, it is the cool season (śiśira), and among the months, it is said to be Māgha;
among fortnights, it is the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa), and likewise, among lunar days, it is the first day (pratipad).
Of the divisions of day and night, the day is proclaimed as the beginning;
likewise, among the muhūrtas, the muhūrta presided over by Rudra is the beginning.
O best among those who know time, a moment (kṣaṇa) consists of a blink of an eye and so forth;
a five-year cycle (yuga), beginning with the asterism Śravaṇa and ending with Dhaniṣṭhā, constitutes a period of time.
Due to the specific motion of the sun, it revolves like a wheel;
therefore, the Lord Īśvara, the maker of time, is known as Divākara (the Maker of Day).
The Blessed Lord Rudra is the god who directly impels that [unmanifest principle] as well, which in turn causes the four kinds of beings to proceed and withdraw.
Thus, this arrangement of the luminaries and the determination of their meanings was fashioned by Mahādeva for the sake of worldly convention.
At the beginning of the eon, the Blessed One intentionally set this in motion;
it is the substratum and the possessor of self-conceit for all, consisting of the nature of light.
This wondrous transformation of that which is primarily of a single form cannot be calculated in its true nature by anyone.
The coming and going of the luminaries by a human being with the eye of flesh is established through scripture,
inference, direct perception, and logical reasoning.
O best of sages, after examining them thoroughly with the intellect, a wise person should place their trust in these:
the eye, scripture, water, writing, and calculation.
These five causes are to be known in the determination of the measurement of the luminaries.
Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Number of Planets," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
The sages said:
How did Dhruva, the best among the wise, indeed become the central pillar for all the planets through the grace of Viṣṇu? You should tell me this now.
Sūta said: O twice-born ones, in former times, Mārkaṇḍeya— who was an expert in various scriptures— spoke of this matter to me when I questioned him, as I was desirous of hearing it.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: The immensely radiant King Uttānapāda, a sovereign ruler and the best among all wielders of weapons, indeed protected the earth.
He had two wives, Sunīti and Suruci;
by the elder wife, Sunīti, he had a son of great renown.
The highly wise and great-minded Dhruva, a lamp of his lineage,
once sat upon his father’s lap even at the age of seven years.
O best of Brahmins, Suruci, her mind filled with joy and proud of his beauty, cast her own son aside and seated him upon her lap.
Not having obtained his father's lap, the wise one, with a grieving mind,
approached his mother and wept again and again.
As her son was weeping, his mother, overwhelmed with grief, said this to him:
"Suruci was the beloved wife of my husband; even her son was just like him."
"Even though you were born as a son to me, an unfortunate woman, you too are ill-fated;
why do you grieve, and for what reason do you weep again and again?"
Having a tormented heart, you will grieve for me;
but, my son, may you surely attain your own stable station by your own power.
Thus addressed by his mother, he then departed for the forest;
thereupon, seeing Viśvāmitra, he prostrated before him according to the prescribed rite.
Having joined his palms in reverence, he said: "O Blessed One, O best of beings, you ought to tell me by what means I shall attain the station that stands above all."
O sage, while I was seated on my father’s lap, my mother Suruci shook me;
yet that king, my father, did not say anything at all.
For this reason, O Brahmin, I went to my mother in fear;
my mother Sunīti said to me, "Do not give way to excessive grief."
"O dear son, you ought to attain the supreme state through your own actions;
for, having heard her words, O great sage, that state shall be yours."
"O Brahman, O Lord, having reached this forest today, I have seen you;
through your grace, I shall attain a wonderful and supreme station."
Thus addressed, that illustrious sage smiled and said this:
"O prince, listen to this; you shall attain the highest station."
Having propitiated Keśava, the Lord of the worlds and the destroyer of afflictions—
who was born from the right side of the wise Mahādeva Śambhu— [he attained his goal].
O highly wise one, chant daily that which destroys all sins,
which grants desired objects, and is supremely pure, holy, stainless, and supreme.
"Recite this divine mantra, joined with the *praṇava* (OM),
saying 'Salutation to Vāsudeva,' while keeping your senses restrained."
"Meditating upon the eternal Viṣṇu and devoted to the practice of recitation and burnt offerings"—
having been addressed thus, the highly illustrious one prostrated before Viśvāmitra.
Facing the east, self-restrained and with a joyful mind,
he chanted for a year without weariness, subsisting on a diet of vegetables, roots, and fruits.
He recited the mantra incessantly and continuously, again and again;
[fearing] the terrible Vetālas and Rākṣasas, as well as lions and other great beasts.
Terrifying beings approached that great-souled one to delude his intellect;
yet, chanting "Vāsudeva," he did not perceive anything at all.
Disguised in the form of Sunīti, his mother,
the Piśācī approached him and wept, overcome with intense grief.
"You are my only son; why do you afflict yourself? Having abandoned me, who am left without a protector, you have taken up asceticism."
While she was speaking such words as these, that one of great asceticism,
with a joyful heart, chanted the name of Hari without even looking at her.
Then, indeed, all forms of obstacles were pacified everywhere there;
thereafter, he mounted Garuḍa, possessing a luster like that of a dark cloud.
Surrounded by all the gods and praised by the great seers,
the Blessed Viṣṇu, the slayer of enemies, approached the presence of Dhruva.
Then, beholding him who had arrived and wondering "Who is this?",
he gazed with both eyes at Hṛṣīkeśa, the Lord of the World, as if drinking him in.
"O Japan! O Vāsudeva! Thus the immensely radiant Dhruva stood firm;
then Govinda indeed touched his face with the edge of his conch shell.
Then, having attained supreme knowledge regarding the Supreme Person, he,
with palms joined in reverence, praised Hari, the Lord of all worlds.
Be gracious, O Lord of the gods of gods, wielder of the conch, the discus, and the mace;
O Soul of the world, O Soul of the secret of the Vedas, I have taken refuge in you, Keśava.
Even the great sages, Sanaka and the others, do not know you, the Great-Souled One; how then could I know you? Salutations to you, O Lord of the World!
Smiling, Viṣṇu said to him: "Come, child; you shall be Dhruva.
Having attained the station of Dhruva, become the foremost among the luminaries."
Accompanied by Mātrā, you shall attain there the station of the luminaries;
this is my supreme, eternal, constant, and most beautiful abode.
In ancient times, having propitiated the Lord of Gods through austerity, he indeed obtained from Śaṅkara that [name] "Vāsudeva," which is always accompanied by the *praṇava*.
The wise person who thus recites [the mantra] joined with the word "namas" and conjoined with the word "bhagavat" certainly attains the eternal abode.
Then all the gods, along with the gandharvas, siddhas, and supreme ṛṣis, together with his mother, established Dhruva in that place.
Placing the command of Viṣṇu before him,
the immensely radiant Dhruva attained the station of the luminaries by means of the twelve-syllable vidyā.
He attained great perfection; this has been told to you by me.
Sūta said:
Therefore, the man who offers salutation to Vāsudeva goes to the same world as Dhruva; for him, that state of being like Dhruva is indeed so.

Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Constellation of Dhruva," in the section on the Cosmography (*bhuvanakośa*) within the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
The sages said:
O Sūta, tell us today in due order the unsurpassed account of the origin of the gods, the Dānavas, the Gandharvas, the Uragas, and the Rākṣasas.
Sūta said:
It is said that the creation of the ancestors occurred through mere intention, sight, and touch;
from Dakṣa Prācetasa onwards, however, creation arose from sexual union.
But when the world did not increase as he was creating the hosts of gods, sages, and serpents through the practice of sexual union, then—
Dakṣa begot five thousand sons from Sūti;
seeing those illustrious ones, he desired to create various progeny.
Nārada spoke to the Haryaśvas, the sons of Dakṣa, who had assembled there after they had learned the entire extent of the earth, both above and below.
"Therefore, O best of sages, perform the creation in detail.
Having heard those words, they departed in all directions.
Even now they do not cease, like rivers flowing from the ocean;
and when the Haryaśvas had perished, Dakṣa, the Lord of Progeny, [created them again].
And at the very time of the extraction of the Soma juice, the Lord produced a thousand sons;
those brahmins, known as the Śabalas, were assembled together for the purpose of creation.
Nārada spoke again to those brothers of solar radiance who followed him, after he had repeatedly ascertained the entire measurement of the earth.
"Or else, having arrived, you shall indeed bring about creation in particular.
They too went by that very same path to the destination of their brother.
Then, when those [sons] had also perished, Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, begot sixty daughters upon Vairiṇī at that time.
He gave ten daughters to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa,
twenty-seven to Soma, and four to Ariṣṭanemi.
Two were given to the son of Bhṛgu, two to the wise Kṛśāśva, and likewise two to Aṅgiras; their names are as follows in detail.
Listen to the expansion of the progeny of the divine mothers from the beginning:
Marutvatī, Vasū, Yāmī, Lambā, Bhānu, and Arundhatī.
Saṃkalpā, Muhūrtā, Sādhyā, and Viśvā—the beautiful one—were proclaimed as the lawful wives; I shall now tell you of their sons.
The Viśvedevas were born of Viśvā; Sādhyā gave birth to the Sādhyas;
the Marutvats were born of Marutvatī; and likewise, the Vasus were born of Vasu.
The rays of Bhānu are said to be the Muhūrtas; the Muhūrtakas belong to Muhūrtā;
those named Ghoṣa belong to Lambā; and Nāgavīthi is born of Yāmī.
From Saṃkalpā came Saṃkalpa; I shall now describe to you the creation of the Vasus, those luminous gods who pervade all directions.
These Vasus have been fully described to you; they are seekers of the welfare of all beings:
Āpa, Dhruva, Soma, Dhara, Anila, and Anala.
Pratyūṣa and Prabhāsa are proclaimed as the eight Vasus;
[the Rudras are] Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Virūpākṣa, and Bhairava.
Hara, Bahurūpa, Tryambaka, Sureśvara,
Sāvitra, Jayanta, Pinākin, and Aparājita.
These are declared to be the eleven Rudras, the lords of the hosts;
now I shall proclaim the sons and grandsons born from the wives of Kaśyapa.
Aditi, Diti, Ariṣṭā, Surasā, Muni,
Surabhi, Vinatā, Tāmrā, as well as Krodhavaśā and Ilā.
Kadrū and Danu were likewise; I shall now tell you of their sons, those gods known as the Tuṣitas who existed during the interval of Cākṣuṣa Manu.
In the Vaivasvata interval, those twelve Ādityas are recorded as being Indra,
Dhātṛ, Bhaga, Tvaṣṭṛ, Mitra, Varuṇa, and Aryaman.
Vivasvat, Savitṛ, Pūṣan, Aṃśumat, and Viṣṇu—
these are remembered as the twelve Ādityas, each possessing a thousand rays.
We have heard that Diti obtained two sons from Kaśyapa:
Hiraṇyakaśipu and likewise Hiraṇyākṣa.
Danu obtained from Kaśyapa a hundred sons who were arrogant in their strength;
among them, O best of the twice-born, Vipracitti was the preeminent one.
And Tāmrā gave birth to six daughters, O best of the twice-born:
Śukī, Śyenī, Bhāsī, Sugrīvī, Gṛdhrikā, and Śuci.
Śukī gave birth to parrots and owls according to dharma;
likewise, Śyenī produced hawks, and Bhāsī gave birth to kuraṅga birds.
The female vulture gave birth to vultures and pigeons; the female dove gave birth to birds such as swans, cranes, kāraṇḍava ducks, and water-fowl.
Sugrīvī gave birth to goats, horses, sheep, camels, and donkeys;
and the auspicious Vinatā gave birth to Garuḍa and Aruṇa.
Likewise, there was the maiden Saudāminī, who causes terror to all the worlds;
and formerly, a thousand serpents were born from Surasā.
Kadrū, being firm in her vows, obtained a thousand sons with a thousand heads;
among them, twenty-six were renowned as the foremost and unsurpassed.
Śeṣa, Vāsuki, Karkoṭaka, Śaṅkha, Airāvata, Kambala,
Dhanañjaya, Mahānīla, Padma, Aśvatara, and Takṣaka.
Elāpatra, Mahāpadma, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Balāhaka,
Śaṅkhapāla, Mahāśaṅkha, Puṣpadaṃṣṭra, and Śubhānana.
Śaṅkhaloman, Nahuṣa, Vāmana, Phaṇita, Kapila, Durmukha, and he who is remembered as Patañjali; // LiP_1,63.37 //
Krodhavaśā gave birth to a host of Rākṣasas and Mahāmāyā;
likewise, Varāṅganā gave birth to a host of Rudras, as well as a cow and a buffalo.
We have heard that Surabhi gave birth to the host of sages from Kaśyapa,
as well as the host of apsarases.
Likewise, Ariṣṭā gave birth to many Kinnaras and Gandharvas;
and Ilā produced everything consisting of grasses, trees, creepers, and shrubs.
From Tviṣā, however, he produced Yakṣas and Rākṣasas by the millions;
these descendants of Kaśyapa have thus been described in brief.
The lineages of their sons, grandsons, and so forth are recorded as being many;
thus were the progeny created by the high-souled Kaśyapa.
When all mobile and immobile beings were established,
Prajāpati consecrated their leaders in positions of sovereignty.
Then, at the beginning of the Svāyaṃbhuva interval, Brahmā consecrated Vaivasvata Manu as the lord of men, along with those others who had been previously consecrated by him.
By them, this entire earth— with its seven continents and its mountains—
is even today protected according to the teaching and in accordance with dharma.
Those who were previously consecrated by Brahmā during the first Svāyambhuva interval—
these very ones are now being consecrated, and they become Manus.
Indeed, when the past Manvantaras have passed away, these kings have gone;
likewise, others are consecrated when a new Manvantara arrives thereafter.
All the kings of the past and future who are recorded in the Manvantaras have been produced from these sons for the sake of the continuity of progeny.
Kaśyapa, however, desiring a lineage, performed ascetic penance once more,
thinking, "May there be a son for me who will establish my lineage."
As that high-souled Kaśyapa was thus meditating,
two sons of great splendor subsequently appeared through the power of Brahman-yoga.
Vatsara and Asita were both exponents of the Veda;
from Vatsara was born Naidhruva, and the highly illustrious Raibhya.
The daughters of Raibhya are to be known as the Raibhyas; now I shall tell you of those of Naidhruva. Sumedhas was born of the daughter of Cyavana.
The wife of Naidhruva was indeed the mother of the Kuṇḍapāyins;
from her, Asita begot Brahmiṣṭha upon Ekaparṇā.
The illustrious Devala, of great ascetic power, was the best among the Śāṇḍilyas;
the Śāṇḍilyas, Naidhruvas, and Raibhyas were the three branches of the Kāśyapas.
I shall tell you of the nine classes of gods belonging to Pulastya;
this occurred when the four ages of the eleventh Manu had passed, O Lord.
When that Dvāpara age had proceeded until half remained,
there was indeed a son of Mānava Nariṣyanta named Dama.
The heir of that Dama was known as Tṛṇabindu;
he became king at the beginning of the third age, the Tretā Yuga.
His daughter was Ilavilā, who was peerless in beauty;
that royal sage bestowed that maiden upon Pulastya.
The sage Airāvila begot Viśravas upon her;
he had four wives who increased the lineage of Paulastya.
The auspicious daughter of Bṛhaspati was named Devavarṇinī;
Puṣpotkaṭā and Balākā are remembered as the two daughters of Mālyavat.
Kaikasī was the daughter of Mālin; hear now of their offspring. That woman of divine complexion gave birth to Vaiśravaṇa as her eldest son.
Kaikasī also gave birth to Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas,
as well as Kumbhakarṇa, Śūrpaṇakhā, and the wise Vibhīṣaṇa.
O best of the twice-born, Puṣpotkaṭā indeed gave birth to sons from him:
Mahodara, Prahasta, Mahāpārśva, and Khara.
Hear now, O subjects, of the daughter of Balā, Kumbhīnasī,
as well as Triśiras, Dūṣaṇa, and the Rākṣasa Vidyujjihva.
Kanyā and Mālikā are also known as the offspring of Balā;
these nine Rākṣasas of the Paulastya lineage are performers of cruel deeds.
Vibhīṣaṇa is proclaimed to be of exceedingly pure soul and a knower of dharma.
The sons of Pulastya were all deer, tigers, and fanged beasts.
Elemental spirits, piśācas, serpents, as well as boars, elephants, monkeys, kinnaras, and those who are kimpuruṣas; ||| 67 ||
In that Vaivasvata interval, Kratu was remembered as being childless;
Atri had ten wives who were beautiful and devoted to their husbands.
Bhadrāśva had ten Apsaras as his wives, and they bore him ten sons:
Bhadrā, Bhadrā, Jaladā, Mandā, and likewise Nandā; [and further] Ghṛtācī.
O best of Brahmins, Balābalā, she who is remembered as Gopābalā,
as well as Tāmarasā and Varakrīḍā— these indeed are the ten.
Their husband was Prabhākara, born of the lineage of Atri;
when the sun was eclipsed by Rāhu and had fallen from heaven to earth, he [acted].
"When it was said, 'May it be well with you,' the Sun himself fell here, for he by whom light was set in motion while this world was overwhelmed by darkness."
At the word of that Brahman-sage, the Lord did not fall from heaven;
thereafter, the Lord Atri was addressed as "Prabhākara" by the great rishis.
Upon Bhadrā he begot a glorious son, Soma;
that ascetic then again begot sons upon those [other wives].
There were sages known as the Svastyātreyas, who had mastered the Vedas;
among them were two of renowned fame, most devoted to Brahman, and possessed of great splendor.
Datta was indeed the eldest, having received three boons; Durvāsas was his younger brother; and their youngest sister was Amalā, a speaker of Brahman.
From his two lineages were born four sons renowned on earth:
Śyāva, Pratīpa, Vavalgu, and Gahvara.
And four lineages of the high-souled Ātreyas are recorded:
Kāśyapa, Nārada, Parvata, and Anuddhata.
Indeed, these were born as the mind-born sons of Arundhatī; learn of them now.
Nārada then bestowed Arundhatī upon Vasiṣṭha.

In former times, during the terrible war between the gods and asuras concerning Tāraka, Nārada, who possessed great luster and had his vital energy drawn upward, was [afflicted] by the curse of Dakṣa.
When the world was struck by drought,
the wise Vasiṣṭha, together with the lords of the world, sustained all creatures through his ascetic power.
Providing food, water, roots, fruits, and medicinal herbs,
he sustained these very beings out of compassion by means of medicine.
Vasiṣṭha begot a hundred sons upon Arundhatī;
moreover, Adṛśyantī bore Parāśara to Śakti, his eldest son.
When the two Śaktis had been devoured by the Rākṣasa,
Kālī then gave birth to the lord Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana from Parāśara.
Dvaipāyana indeed begot Śuka as a son upon Araṇī, and Upamanyu upon Pīvarī; know these to be the sons of Śuka.
Bhūriśravas, Prabhu, Śambhu, Kṛṣṇa, and Gaura as the fifth;
and the daughter Kīrtimatī, who was firm in her vows and the mother of Yoga.
She was the mother of Brahmadatta and the wife of Anuhas;
[her sons were] Śveta, Kṛṣṇa, Gaura, Śyāma, Dhūmra, and likewise Aruṇa.
Nīla and Bādarika—all these are Parāśaras;
these eight branches of the high-souled Parāśaras have been declared.
Henceforth, learn of the origin of Indrapramiti:
Kapiñjalī was born to Vasiṣṭha by Ghṛtācī.
He who is celebrated as Trimūrti is called Indrapramiti;
Bhadra was born to him from the daughter of Pṛthu, and his son was Vasu.
Upamanyu was his son, and from him indeed came many Aupamanyavas;
and those Kauṇḍinyas who are renowned as the offspring of Mitra and Varuṇa likewise descended from him.
Likewise, there are others known as the Vāsiṣṭhas who have a single ṛṣi-ancestry;
these are remembered as the ten branches of the high-souled Vasiṣṭhas.
Thus these sons of Brahmā, born of his mind, are renowned on earth;
they are highly fortunate lords, and their lineages have been proclaimed.
Capable of supporting the three worlds, they were born from the lineage of divine sages;
their sons and grandsons numbered in the hundreds and thousands.
By whom the three worlds are pervaded, just as by the rays of the sun.
Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, titled "The Narration of the Creation of the Gods and Others," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
The sages said:
O Sūta, best among speakers, you ought to tell us here how that descendant of Vasiṣṭha was devoured by the Rākṣasa along with his younger brothers.
Sūta said:
Formerly, a Rākṣasa named Rudhira [killed] the son of Vasiṣṭha.
He consumed Śakti, along with his younger brothers, due to the curse of Śakti.
Then, having instructed King Kalmāṣapāda— who was being officiated by Vasiṣṭha— the lord of the twice-born Rudhira, urged on by Viśvāmitra, [acted].
Hearing that he had been devoured by that Rākṣasa, Vasiṣṭha—
the best among the powerful and a knower of dharma— along with his brothers, [was overcome].
Crying out "O son, son, son!
again and again, the sage, together with Arundhatī, fell to the ground in deep distress.
Hearing that his lineage was destroyed, the powerful Vasiṣṭha then resolved to die,
remembering his hundred sons, of whom Śakti was the eldest.
Having resolved, "I shall not live without him," he was overcome with grief.
Having ascended to the summit, that self-possessed son of Aja, who was all-knowing and a knower of the Self,
then fell from the mountain to the earth along with his wife, his gaze filled with tears.
Then the Earth, whose neck was variegated with jewels, received him as he fell from the mountain;
moving with the playful gait of an elephant, she took up the weeping child with her lotus-like hands and wept herself.
Then his daughter-in-law, the wife of Śakti, weeping and overwhelmed by fear, spoke to the great sage Vasiṣṭha, the best among speakers.
O Blessed One, best of brahmins, O Lord, protect this auspicious body of yours so that I may see your grandson, my own son.
"O best of Brahmins, you must not abandon this most beautiful body of yours,
for while remaining in my womb, you shall accomplish all my purposes, as you are born of my power."
Having spoken thus, the lotus-eyed woman, who knew the Dharma, raised her father-in-law with both hands, bowed to him, and wiped his eyes with water.
Then, though she herself was suffering, she sought to protect her suffering father-in-law and entreated the virtuous Arundhatī, who was also in distress.
Then, having heard the words of his daughter-in-law, Vasiṣṭha rose from the ground; regaining consciousness, he embraced her, and she fell down, deeply distressed.
Touching her, whose eyes were clouded with tears, with both hands, Arundhatī wept along with her; that tiger among sages was deeply devoted to his wife and son.
Then, just as the four-faced Brahmā was seated upon the lotus at Viṣṇu’s navel,
so too did that youth, while lying on the bed of the womb, utter a Vedic verse.
Then, having heard that verse with reverence, the venerable Vasiṣṭha reflected, "By whom was this spoken? and remained there with a concentrated mind.
Then Hari, whose eyes resemble white lotuses, the soul of the universe and a treasury of compassion, standing in the courtyard of the sky,
spoke with pity to Vasiṣṭha.
O child, O child, O best of Brahmins, O Vasiṣṭha who is so affectionate toward your son,
this Ṛg-verse has today issued forth from the lotus-like face of your grandson.
"O Sage, this grandson of yours, born of Śakti, is equal to me in power;
therefore, O best of the sons of Brahmā, cast off your grief and arise."
Devoted to Rudra even while in the womb and intent upon the worship of Rudra,
your lineage shall cross over [the ocean of existence] through the power of the god Rudra.
Having spoken thus to the compassionate brahmin Vasiṣṭha, that tiger among sages, the Blessed One, Puruṣottama, vanished right there.
Then, having bowed his head to the lotus-eyed one, the immensely radiant Vasiṣṭha respectfully touched the womb of Adṛśyantī.
"Alas, son! Son! Son! he cried, falling down in extreme distress;
O twice-born ones, seeing Arundhatī weeping at that time, he lamented.
Remembering his own son out of grief, he cried out again: "Come back, come back, my little son!
O Śakti, look upon this son of yours who upholds the lineage!"
"I shall go to your presence with your mother; of this there is no doubt.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus, the brahmin, weeping, then embraced Arundhatī.
Striking her own belly with her hand as if in pain,
Adṛśyantī then struck the auspicious abode of Śaktija.
Distressed, she beat her breast upon the ground, lamented, and fell down;
at that time, Arundhatī was terrified, as was the high-minded Vasiṣṭha.
Having raised up their young daughter-in-law, the two of them, overwhelmed by fear, said:

O deluded woman, tell me, why have you, O noble lady, raised your lotus-like hands against your womb—the source of the entire Vasiṣṭha lineage which is so difficult to attain—and set yourself to destroy it? 64.31.

Having seen your son and the son of Śakti, and having tasted the nectar from the mouth of the noble son, the Lord of Sages is now firmly resolved to protect this body; therefore, protect your own body.
Sūta said:
Having thus reproached her daughter-in-law and the sage, Arundhatī, the wife of Vasiṣṭha, stood there; distressed and overwhelmed by grief, she spoke.
O lady of virtuous vows, my life and that of this sage depend on you alone; protect his life and act as a nurse for his body, doing whatever is for his benefit.
Adṛśyantī said:
"O best of sages, if I have indeed resolved to protect myself,
how can I somehow preserve this body of mine, which is both auspicious and inauspicious?"
"I have indeed attained the great sorrow of being separated from my beloved; I am unchaste, there is no doubt of this.
O Sage, I am consumed by grief because I am your daughter, O Sage."
"Oh, what a marvel I have seen! For I am indeed a vessel of suffering, O Lord.
Be my protector from suffering, O Brahman, Son of Brahmā, Teacher of the World!"
Nevertheless, a woman here who is bereft of her husband becomes wretched;
therefore, O noble Indra, protect me, for I shall be humiliated.
Father, mother, sons, grandsons, and even the father-in-law—these are not the true kinsmen of women; the husband is their relative and their supreme refuge.
For even that which was called "half" of myself by the wise was indeed false in this case; Śakti has departed and I remain.
"O bull among sages, alas, how great is the hardness of my mind here, since I remain for even a moment in this place after abandoning my husband, who was as dear to me as my own life!"
Just as the immortal creeper clings to the *aśvattha* tree of Vasiṣṭha, so too do I remain, though wretched and uprooted by my husband, clinging to him like the immortal vine.
Upon hearing the words of his daughter-in-law, the wise Vasiṣṭha, together with his wife,
then resolved to go to his own hermitage.
With great difficulty, the holy and virtuous Vasiṣṭha, together with his wife and Adṛśyantī, returned to his own hermitage in an instant and entered it while reflecting deeply.
O best of sages, Śakti’s devoted wife protected her embryo with great difficulty for the sake of sustaining the lineage.
Then, in the tenth month, she gave birth to a radiant son,
just as Śakti’s wife gave birth to Śakti and Arundhatī to Śaktimat.
Diti gave birth to Viṣṇu, just as Svāhā gave birth to her son Guha,
as the fire-drill produces Agni, and as the wife of Śakti [gave birth] directly to Parāśara.
Whenever Śakti’s son descended to the surface of the earth,
Śakti would then abandon his sorrow and attain equality with the ancestors.
O bulls among sages, that meritorious soul, the descendant of Vasiṣṭha, dwelling in the world of the ancestors with his brothers, shone like the sun with the Ādityas.
O best of Brahmins, when Parāśara had descended, the ancestors sang, and the grandfathers and great-grandfathers danced.
Those who discourse on Brahman danced upon the earth, while the deities in heaven and the sky-dwellers,
beginning with Puṣkara, released a rain of flowers.
O twice-born ones, while the Rakshasas raised a tumultuous cry amidst the pure [atmosphere],
the sages dwelling in the hermitage experienced a continuous flow of joy.
For just as the sun emerges from its egg, so too did that Parāśara emerge from the womb of Adṛśyantī like the sun from a mass of clouds, appearing with four faces.
O twice-born ones, happiness and sorrow arose for Adṛśyantī upon seeing her son and remembering her husband, as well as Arundhatī and the sage.
And seeing her son Parāśara of exceeding splendor,
the young woman, overwhelmed and with a faltering voice, lamented and fell down.
As soon as that sinless one of great intelligence was born, who is worshipped by the hosts of gods and dānavas, she of the pure smile, perceiving him, spoke with tears in her eyes: LiP_1,64.56.

"Alas, son of Vasiṣṭha! Where have you gone? Look for your sinless son, your own child, O Lord, who has abandoned this woman with her dejected face as she gazes for the sight of her son in the depths of the forest!"
O Śakti, behold your son Ṣaṇmukha together with his brothers,
just as Maheśvara beheld him with his attendants, his face beaming with joy.
Then, having heard those words of hers, Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages, spoke thus to his daughter-in-law in distress: "Do not weep."
By his command, that young woman of Vasiṣṭha’s family, her eyes like those of a young doe, cast aside her grief and protected the boy. (Parāśara: Childhood and Youth) 1.64.60.
Seeing that virtuous woman seated there, distressed and her eyes clouded with tears, devoid of her auspicious ornaments, he spoke to her.
The son of Śakti said:
"O Mother, O sinless one, this body of yours does not shine without its auspicious ornaments.
You ought to tell me the reason for this today, like a night deprived of the moon's orb."
"O mother, mother! Having indeed cast off your auspicious ornaments, you sit like one bereft of her husband; O beautiful lady, you ought to tell me why."
Then, having heard those words of her son, Adṛśyantī said nothing at all to her son, whether it was something auspicious or otherwise.
The venerable son of Śakti spoke again to Adṛśyantī: "O mother, tell me, where is my father of great splendor? Tell me, tell me! (LiP 1.64.65).
Upon hearing these words from her son, she wept, being utterly overwhelmed; "Your father has been devoured by a *rakṣasa*," she cried, and she fell down.
Upon hearing the words of his grandson, the compassionate Vasiṣṭha fell to the ground weeping;
so too did Arundhatī, the residents of the hermitage, and the lords of sages at that time.
Having heard from your mother’s mouth that your father had been devoured by a *rākṣasa*, the wise Parāśara spoke with his eyes clouded by tears.
(Parāśara will take vengeance upon his father) Parāśara said:
Having worshipped the Lord of the gods of the gods, [he beheld] the three worlds with all that is moving and unmoving.
"O Mother, it is my thought that I shall show my father to you in an instant."
Having heard those auspicious words, she, smiling yet amazed, spoke to her son:
"This is indeed the truth," she said, looking at him; "O son, O son, worship Bhava."
Having understood this resolve of the son of Śakti, the venerable Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages, wise and a treasury of compassion, spoke to his grandson.
"It is fitting, O grandson, O best of sages, that such is your resolve, O observer of noble vows;
nevertheless, listen: you ought not to bring about the destruction of the world."
"Perform worship of the Lord of All for the destruction of the Rākṣasas!
Listen, O Śākteya, does the three worlds offend you?"
Then, at the command of Vasiṣṭha, the high-minded son of Śakti resolved to bring about the destruction of the Rākṣasas.
Then, having bowed to Vasiṣṭha and Arundhatī while they were invisible,
he fashioned a temporary single-liṅga out of dust in the presence of the sage.
Having worshipped with the Śivasūkta and the auspicious Tryambaka mantra, and having recited the Tvaritarudra as well as the Śivasaṃkalpa; LiP_1,64.76.
The Śākta recites the Nīlarudra and likewise the beautiful Rudra;
the Vāmīya, the Pavamāna, and similarly the Pañcabrahma.
Having offered the eightfold arghya to Rudra and having worshipped according to the rules the Hotṛ, the Liṅgasūkta, and the Atharvaśiras; LiP 1.64.78.
Parāśara said: "O Lord Rudra, O Śaṅkara, my father of great splendor has indeed been devoured by the Rākṣasa Rudhira, along with his brothers."
"O Blessed One, I wish to see my father together with his brothers. Thus he made his request, prostrating himself again and again before the Linga.
"Alas, Rudra! Rudra! Rudra! she cried out, and fell down.
Seeing him, the Blessed Lord Rudra, Śaṅkara, spoke to the Goddess:
Behold this child, O illustrious lady, his eyes clouded with tears,
intent on remembering me and devoted to my worship.
And having seen Parāśara, the blameless Mahādevī, with all his limbs drenched in grief and his eyes clouded with tears; LiP_1,64.83.
To her husband, the Lord Īśāna, the benefactor of the worlds, Umā spoke as he was intent on the rite of worshipping the *liṅga* and uttering "Hara, Rudra."
"Grant all that is desired; be gracious, O Supreme Lord.
Having heard her words, Śaṅkara, the Supreme Lord, [responded].
Then the consumer of Hālāhala spoke to his noble wife Umā:
"I shall protect this young brahmin, whose eyes are like blooming blue lotuses."
"I grant you vision, for he is indeed capable of beholding my form.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Nīlalohita, together with his divine attendants, [bestowed it].
Surrounded by Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the other gods,
the Supreme Lord granted a vision of himself to that wise son of a sage.
Having seen Mahādeva, his eyes overflowing with tears of joy, he too,
with a thrilled heart, fell respectfully at his feet.
"Today my life has become fruitful, having seen the feet of Punarbhavānī and of the high-souled Nandin," he then said to Brahmā and the others.
"O you who are adorned by the crescent moon, you have come today for the sake of my protection;
who else in this world is equal to me, whether a god or even a dānava?"
Then, at that very moment, Parāśara, the son of Śakti, beheld his father stationed in the sky together with his brothers.
Seeing him together with his brothers in a celestial chariot that resembled the solar disc and was facing in every direction, he bowed down and rejoiced.

Then the bull-bannered god, together with his wife and the lord of his attendants, spoke thus to the son of Vasiṣṭha, who was intent on seeing his own son: LiP_1,64.94: "Then the bull-bannered god, together with his wife and the lord of his attendants, spoke thus to the son of Vasiṣṭha, who was intent on seeing his own son."
Śrīdeva said:
"O Śakti, behold your young son, his eyes overflowing with tears of joy,
and Adṛśyantī, O best of Brahmins, and your father Vasiṣṭha."
O high-minded one, pay homage to both your mother and father— the highly fortunate Arundhatī, who is auspicious and like unto a deity.
Then, by the command of Śaṅkara, Śakti quickly bowed down to Hara, the god of gods, as well as Umā and the most excellent Vasiṣṭha.
And by the command of the Lord of the World, the powerful one spoke to his illustrious mother, the virtuous Arundhatī, who was devoted to her husband as a deity.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O child, O child, O best of brahmins, O Parāśara of great luster!
I have been protected by you, my noble-souled one, while you were still in the womb."
"O child Parāśara, by my command, you have today obtained the sovereign power of the qualities such as *aṇimā* and you have beheld my face, O boy."
"O high-minded child, always protect the illustrious Adṛśyantī,
as well as Arundhatī and my father Vasiṣṭha."
"My entire lineage, my child, has been saved by you;
for it has always been said by the virtuous that one conquers the worlds through a son. (LiP 1.64.102)
I choose as my desired boon the Lord Īśāna, the source and sovereign of the worlds;
having paid homage to the Lord Śaṅkara, I shall depart together with my brothers.
Having thus addressed his son and bowed to Maheśvara,
the self-controlled one looked at his wife in the assembly and went to his father.
Then, seeing that his father had departed, the son of Śakti worshipped Śaṅkara and praised the moon-adorned Lord with pleasing words.
Then Mahādeva, the crusher of Manmatha and Andhaka, being pleased,
bestowed his grace upon the son of Śakti and vanished right there.
When Maheśvara, accompanied by Ambā, had departed, the knower of mantras, having prostrated before Maheśvara,
burned the clan of the Rākṣasas with a mantra.
Then Vasiṣṭha, the knower of dharma, surrounded by sages, said to his grandson:
"Enough with this excessive anger, my son; abandon this wrath."
The Rākṣasas have not offended you; rather, it was ordained by your father. Anger belongs only to the foolish, for it does not belong to the wise.
Who is slain by whom, my dear, since a person experiences the fruits of his own actions,
O child, after having accumulated such immense suffering through human efforts?
Anger is considered the destroyer of both fame and ascetic merit;
enough indeed with these wretched, innocent Rākṣasas who have already been consumed by fire.
"Let this sacrifice of yours cease; for the virtuous have forbearance as their essence.
By these words of Vasiṣṭha, the son of Śakti, that bull among sages, [was restrained].
Out of respect for those words, he immediately brought the sacrificial session to a close;
thereupon, the venerable Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages, was pleased.
Then Pulastya, the son of Brahmā, arrived at that sacrificial session;
having been offered the guest-offering by Vasiṣṭha, he took his seat.
The sage, having prostrated, spoke this to Parāśara as he stood before him: "Because of your word, I have today resorted to forgiveness despite our great enmity."
Therefore, you shall know all the scriptures;
for even when I was enraged, no interruption was made to my lineage.
Therefore, O highly fortunate one, I grant you another great boon:
my child, you shall become the author of a Purāṇa compendium.
And you shall understand the supreme reality of the deities as it truly is;
whether in the engagement with or the withdrawal from action, your intellect shall be stainless.
"O child, through my grace, it shall become free from doubt for you.
Then the blessed Vasiṣṭha, the best among speakers, said:
"Everything that was told to you by Pulastya shall come to pass. Then, [the sage] Parāśara [became the author of the Viṣṇupurāṇa] for that Pulastya and the wise Vasiṣṭha.
Out of grace, Parāśara indeed composed the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa,
which consists of six parts, accomplishes all goals, and is a treasury of knowledge.
Measuring six thousand [verses] and entirely endowed with the meaning of the Vedas,
this fourth [section] among the Purāṇic compendiums is indeed most beautiful.
O bulls among sages, this entire origin of the Vāsiṣṭhas and the power of the son of Śakti has been recounted to you in brief.
Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Narration of Vasiṣṭha," in the first part of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said:
O best among those who know the lineages, O Romaharṣaṇa, you ought to recount to us in brief the lineage of the Ādityas and the lineage of Soma.
Sūta said:
O twice-born ones, Aditi gave birth to Āditya as her son from Kaśyapa;
and that Āditya had three other wives.
Saṃjñā was the queen, Prabhā and Chāyā were her daughters; I shall tell you of their sons.
Saṃjñā, the daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ, gave birth to Sūrya and to Manu, the most excellent.
From the Sun, Saṃjñā fashioned Yama and Yamunā, as well as the queen Revatī; she also fashioned Prabhā from the dawn and Chāyā from herself.
And from him, O twice-born ones, Chāyā gave birth to Sāvarṇi from the Sun-god,
and then, in due order, to Śani, Tapatī, and Viṣṭi.
At that time, Chāyā showed greater affection for Manu than for her own sons;
the former Manu did not take offense, but Yama was overcome with rage.
Raising his right foot, he struck her in anger;
thus struck by Yama, that shadow indeed became distressed.
Due to the curse of Chāyā, one of Yama’s feet became afflicted;
it was filled with pus and blood and covered with swarms of worms.
He too, subsisting on air alone, took refuge at Gokarṇa with a wooden plank and worshipped Mahādeva for ten billion years.
Through his grace, having attained the supreme status of a world-protector,
he likewise obtained lordship over the ancestors and liberation from the curse.
In former times, that blameless woman, unable to endure the fiery splendor of the Sun, obtained [this power] through the majesty of the trident-bearing God of gods.
Tvāṣṭrī, however, fashioned from her own body a form called Chāyā;
assuming the form of a mare, she, firm in her vows, performed austerities.
Having understood through time and effort that she was his shadow, the Lord,
the Sun, the master of his shadow, assumed the form of a horse and approached Saṃjñā, who was in the form of a mare.
And then Saṃjñā, the daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ, in the form of a mare, bore from that Sun two divine Aśvins, the foremost physicians among the gods.
Afterwards, Bhāskara was written by the high-souled father of Saṃjñā;
indeed, it is from the orb of the Sun that Viṣṇu’s terrible discus [arises].
By the grace of Rudra, the Lord Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned a supreme, divine weapon, auspicious and known as the Sudarśana.
The Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa obtained a discus resembling the fire of cosmic destruction;
and Manu, the first, had nine sons who were equal to him.
Ikṣvāku, Nabhaga, Dhṛṣṇu, Śaryāti, the wise Nariṣyanta, Nābhāga, and Ariṣṭa.
Karūṣa and Pṛṣadhra—these nine are remembered as the Mānavas;
Ilā was the eldest and most excellent, she who formerly attained manhood.
O eminent sages, in ancient times, Ilā, who was renowned as Sudyumna, attained masculinity through the grace of Mitra and Varuṇa.
Furthermore, having reached Śaravaṇa by your command, the illustrious Sudyumna, a descendant of Manu, attained womanhood for the sake of increasing the Lunar dynasty.
Through Ikṣvāku’s horse sacrifice, Ilā became Kiṃpuruṣa;
and in her state as Kiṃpuruṣa, she is also called Sudyumna.
For one month the hero Ilā was male, and for another month he became female again;
he then took refuge in the abode of Budha, the son of Soma.
Having approached Budha, she engaged in sexual union;
and from Budha, the son of Soma, Aila Purūravas was born.
O you whose wealth is asceticism, I shall later describe the expansion of Ikṣvāku’s lineage— the wise, powerful, and devoted-to-Śiva elder brother of Soma.
O best of the twice-born, Sudyumna had three sons:
Utkala, Gaya, and Vinatāśva.
The kingdom of Utkala belongs to Utkala; the western region belongs to Vinatāśva;
and the city of Gayā is said to belong to Gaya—it is most magnificent.
In that [region], where the gods always abide and the ancestors likewise reside,
Ikṣvāku’s eldest heir obtained the Middle Country.
And because he was in the state of a maiden, Sudyumna did not obtain a share at all;
however, by the word of Vasiṣṭha, that one of great splendor came to reside in Pratiṣṭhāna.
Having attained the kingship, the highly illustrious one established the rule of the great-souled Sudyumna, the King of Dharma; he then bestowed that kingdom upon Purūravas.
The illustrious Mānaveya, endowed with the auspicious marks of both male and female,
was born as the heroic Vikukṣi, the best among those who know the dharma, from Ikṣvāku.
He had one hundred and fifteen sons, of whom the eldest was Kakutstha; from Kakutstha was born Suyodhana.
Then, O best of sages, Pṛthu was born; likewise, Viśvaka was the son of Pṛthu.
The wise Ārdraka was the son of Viśvaka, and Yuvanāśva was his son.
And Śābasti was of great luster; from him Vaṃśaka was born, O best of the twice-born, by whom Śābastī was founded in the Gauḍa country.
From Vaṃśa was born Bṛhadaśva, and his son was Kuvalāśva;
having slain the mighty Dhundhu, he attained the status of Dhundhumāra.
Dhundhumāra had three sons, renowned throughout the three worlds;
they are remembered as Dṛḍhāśva, Caṇḍāśva, and Kapilāśva.
The son of Dṛḍhāśva was Pramoda, and his son was indeed Haryaśva;
the son of Haryaśva was Nikumbha, and Saṃhatāśva was his son.
Then Kṛśāśva and Raṇāśva were both the sons of Saṃhatāśva; Yuvanāśva was the son of Raṇāśva, and Māndhātṛ was indeed his son.
From Māndhātṛ were born Purukutsa and the heroic Ambarīṣa, as well as the meritorious Mucukunda; these three were renowned throughout the three worlds.
