The heir of Ambarīṣa is remembered as the other Yuvanāśva; Harita was the son of Yuvanāśva, and from him the Haritas are said to have descended.
For these twice-born ones on the side of the Aṅgirasas were endowed with the status of Kṣatriyas;
the heir of Purukutsa was the highly illustrious Trasaddasyu.
Sambhūti was born from the Narmadā, and his son was Viṣṇuvṛddha; from him the Viṣṇuvṛddhas are said to have descended.
For these [sages] took refuge on the side of the Aṅgirasas, joined with the Kṣatriya order;

O twice-born ones, he who was slain by Rāvaṇa during the conquest of the three worlds was Bṛhadaśva; Haryaśva was his son.
From Haryaśva, by Dṛṣadvatī, was born King Vasumanas;
his son was King Tridhanvan, who was devoted to the Lord Śiva.

The best of the twice-born, whose origin is Brahman, obtained the status of a lord of the Gaṇas;

"Having recited the thousand names, he indeed attained the status of a leader of the Gaṇas.
The sages said:
"The thousand names of Rudra [were proclaimed] by Tāṇḍin, who was born from Brahmā."
O Sūta of noble vows, you have narrated the compendium of the meaning of all the Vedas; now you ought to recite the auspicious thousand names of the Brahmins.
Sūta said: Of Hara, who is the self of all beings and possesses immeasurable splendor—
Listen, O you of excellent vows, to the one thousand and eight names.
O best of sages, by reciting which one attained the status of a leader of the Gaṇas:
"Oṃ! Thou art firm, thou art the immovable pillar, the lord, the radiant one, the most excellent, the giver of boons, the boon-granting one."
The soul of all, renowned as all, the All, the creator of all, Bhava;
he who has matted hair, who carries a staff, and who wears a topknot; he who goes everywhere and brings all beings into existence.

The Blessed One dwells in the cremation ground; he moves through the sky, he is the one who destroys [suffering], he is to be saluted, he performs great deeds, he is an ascetic, and he is the sustainer of all beings.

Rājā, Rājyodaya, Kartṛ, Mṛgabāṇārpaṇa,

the creator of the hosts, the lord of the hosts, the sky-clad, and indeed the desirable one.
The supreme knower of mantras is the Mantra, the creator of all beings and the destroyer;

He who assumes the forms of lions and tigers, who wears garments of moist hide,

he who holds a bow, the mighty-armed, the most terrible, and the one of great asceticism.

Amarṣaṇa, Marṣaṇātman, Yajñaha, Kāmanāśana,

Samīra, Damanākāra, Artha, Arthakara, Vaśa,

he is the lord of the forest, the winner of booty, and is eternally honored in the hermitages.
He is the observer of the sacred vow (brahmacārī), the wanderer through the world, the all-pervading one, and the one who causes all to move rightly;

He who abides in signs and the sign itself; he who is delight, the creator of delight, and the destroyer;
the lord of delight, the one of beautiful delight, the progenitor, and the crusher of adversity.
The distributor of fortune, the restrainer, Time, the grandfather of the worlds,
the four-faced one, the great liṅga, and likewise the beautiful liṅga.
The overseer of signs, the overseer of the gods, the overseer of time, the bringer of the ages;

Itihāsa, Kalpa, Damana, Jagadīśvara,
Dambha, Dambhakara, Dātā, Vaṃśa, Vaṃśakara, and Kali.
The creator of the world, Paśupati, the great creator, indeed Adhokṣaja,

Nitya, Anīśa, Śuddhātman, Śuddha, Māna, Gati, Havis, Prāsāda, Bala, Darpa, Darpaṇa, Havya, and Indrajit.
The author of the Vedas, the author of the Sūtras, the learned one, the destroyer of enemies,
the dweller in the great cloud, the most terrible, and the subduer.
Agni-jvāla, Mahājvāla, Paridhūmrāvṛta, Ravi,
Dhiṣaṇa, Śaṅkara, Nitya, Varcasvin, and Dhūmralocana.

Utsaṅga, Mahāṅga, the majestic Mahāgarbha,
Kṛṣṇavarṇa, Suvarṇa, Indriya, and Sarvavarṇika.
He has great feet, great hands, a great body, and great fame;
he has a great head, is of great measure, is a great friend, and dwells in the mountains.
He has massive shoulders, massive ears, massive lips, and a massive jaw;
he has a massive nose, a massive throat, and a massive neck, and he dwells in the cremation ground.
He is of great strength and great splendor, the inner self, the abode of wild beasts;
he has hanging lips, is established in the ultimate, possesses great illusion, and is the ocean of milk.
He has great teeth, great fangs, a great tongue, and a great mouth;
he has great nails, great body hair, great hair, and great matted locks.
Asapatna, Prasāda, Pratyaya, Gītasādhaka,
Prasvedana, Asvedana, Ādika, and Mahāmuni.

The Atharvaśīrṣa is his head, the Sāman is his mouth, the Ṛk is his thousandfold powerful eyes,
the Yajus is his feet and arms, and he is likewise the secret one whose energy is manifest.
Amoghārthaprasāda, Antarbhāvya, Sudarśana, Upahāra, Priya, Sarva, Kanaka, and Kāñcanasthita are to be included.
Nābhi, Nandikara, Harmya, Puṣkara, Sthapati, Sthita,
Sarvaśāstra, Dhana, Ādya, Yajña, Yajvā, and Samāhita.
The mountain, the blue one, the poet, the dark one, the crocodile, the one worshipped by Time,
the one with his retinue, the creator of the Gaṇas, and the charioteer of the source of all beings.
He who reclines on ashes, whose protector is ashes, whose body and qualities have become ashes;
he is both the scripture and its dissolution, the Great Soul honored by all.
White, endowed with a female form, pure, frequented by spirits,
dwelling in hermitages, abiding in pigeons, he is the architect of the universe, the sovereign lord.
Viśālaśākha, Tāmroṣṭha, Ambujāla, Suniścita, Kapila, Kalaśa, Sthūla, and Āyudha are indeed hairy.
He is indeed the Gandharva, Aditi, Tārkṣya, the unknowable, and the one who is highly proficient;
he is the god armed with the battle-axe, the benefactor, and the true kinsman.
He who holds a lute made of a gourd, the one of great wrath, whose vital energy flows upwards, who reclines upon the waters;
the fierce one, the founder of the lineage, the lineage itself, the player of the flute, indeed the blameless one.
The illusory one who embodies all forms, the friend, the wind, and the strength;
the binder, the maker of bonds, and the liberator from strong bonds.
The slayer of Rākṣasas, the enemy of Kāma, the one with great tusks, the one with great weapons,
the one who hangs down, the one with hanging lips, the one with hanging hands, and the bestower of boons.
Bāhu, Tvanindita, Sarva, Śaṅkara, Akopana,
Amareśa, Mahāghora, Viśvadeva, and Surārihā.
Ahirbudhnya, Nirṛti, Cekitāna, and likewise Halin;
Ajaikapād, Kāpālin, Śaṅkukarṇa, Kumāra, and Mahāgiri.
Dhanvantari, Dhūmaketu, Sūrya, Vaiśravaṇa,
as well as Dhātṛ, Viṣṇu, Śakra, Mitra, Tvaṣṭṛ, Dharas, and Dhruva.
Prabhāsa, Parvata, Vāyu, Aryaman, Savitṛ, Ravi,
Dhṛti, Vidhātṛ, Māndhātṛ, and Bhūtabhāvana.
Nīrastīrtha, Bhīma, Sarvakarman, Guṇodvaha,
Padmagarbha, Mahāgarbha, Candravaktra, Nabhas, and Anagha.
Powerful and tranquil, ancient and the greatest of merit-makers,
the doer of cruel deeds and dweller in the cruel, the subtle self is the great medicine.
He whose intention is all-encompassing, who moves everywhere, the lord of life, the master of living beings,
the god of gods, overflowing with bliss, he knows all jewels, both existent and non-existent.
Dwelling on Kailāsa, residing in caves, and taking refuge on the Himavat mountain; the destroyer of lineages and the founder of lineages; possessing great wealth and many offspring.
Prāṇeśa, Bandhakī, Vṛkṣa, Nakula, and likewise Ādrika; Hrasvagrīva, Mahājānu, Alola, and Mahauṣadhi.
The author of the Siddhānta, the one whose purpose is accomplished, born from prosody and grammar;
he who has the lion’s roar, the lion’s fangs, the lion’s face, and the lion as his vehicle.
He is the essence of power, the time of the universe, Time itself, the trembling one, the tree, the subtle body;
he is the deer-marked one, marked by the wheel of beings, the one with a garland of banners, and the excellent piercer.
The abode of beings, the lord of beings, day and night, the impure and the pure,
the sustainer of the Vasus, the self of all beings, immovable, the well-knowing, the wise one.
He is unfriendly toward all beings, yet he is immovable; he is wise among those of fickle intellect.
His self-restraint is never in vain; he is joyful, a consumer of food, and the sustainer of life.
He is steadfast, wise, three-eyed, and the performer of good deeds; he is the lord of warriors, the protector of the earth, the master of the village, the one clothed in a cowhide, and Hara.
Hiraṇyabāhu, Guhāvāsa, Praveśana,
Mahāmanas, Mahākāma, Cittakāma, and Jitendriya.
Gāndhāra is fond of wine, devoted to the work of heating, and beneficial;
he is a great being surrounded by spirits and served by hosts of Apsarases.
He is the great banner, the supporter of the earth, delighting in non-duality, the primordial sound;
he is beyond sensation yet is to be known, all-pervading, and the bringer of bliss.
The Savior, the Foot, the Sustainer, the One Encompassed, the Fully Worshipped, the Uniter, the Increaser, the Aged, the Leader of the Host, and the Lord of the Host.
The eternal one, the sustainer, the companion, the lord of gods and asuras, the master, the one joined with yoga, the one with joined arms, the auspicious god, and the one with beautiful joints.
Āṣāḍha, Suṣāḍha, Skandhada, Harita, Hara,
Vapurāvartamāna, another named Vapuḥśreṣṭha, and Mahāvapuḥ.
Śirovimarśana, adorned with all marks and characteristics, Akṣaya, Rathagīta, Sarvabhogin, and Mahābala.
He is the sacred tradition and the great tradition, the deity of the holy ford, and the one of great renown;
he is the mantra that is lifeless yet gives life, the fortunate one, and the very firm.
He is the embodiment of jewels, whose limbs are jewels, and who knows how to plunge into the great ocean;
he is the root, the vast expanse, the nectar of immortality, both manifest and unmanifest, and a treasury of ascetic power.
Ārohaṇa, Adhiroha, Śīladhārī, Mahātapas,
Mahākaṇṭha, Mahāyogin, Yuga, Yugakara, and Hari.
He is the form of the ages, the great form, the vehicle, the impenetrable, the serpent; he is logic, the one who extinguishes [suffering], the footless, the wise one who is indeed like a mountain.
Bahumāla, Mahāmāla, Śipiviṣṭa, Sulocana,
Vistāra, Lavaṇa, Kūpa, Kusumāṅga, and Phalodaya.
Ṛṣabha, Vṛṣabha, Bhaṅga, Maṇibimbajaṭādhara,
Indu, Visarga, Sumukha, Śūra, Sarvāyudha, and Saha.
Nivedana, Sudhājāta, Svargadvāra, Mahādhanu, Girāvāsa, Visarga, and Sarvalakṣaṇalakṣavin; ||| 151 ||
The Blessed One is fragrant with garlands, infinite, and possessed of all auspicious marks; he is a vast continuum, mighty-armed, complete, and the purifier of all.
He holds a vessel in his hand and carries a skull; he is youthful with an erect body, well-renowned for his mastery of mechanical devices and rituals, the refuge of all worlds, and gentle.
Shaven-headed, deformed, and distorted, bearing a staff and a water-pot, he is a performer of miracles;
he is the protector of the waters, the one of the quarters, the wielder of the thunderbolt, possessed of blazing splendor, and having a thousand feet.
The Lord of Gods has a thousand heads; he is composed of all the gods and is the Guru.
He has a thousand arms, possesses all limbs, is the refuge of all, and the creator of all worlds.
The Purifier, the mantra of the three sweets, the youngest, dark-brown in hue,
the fashioner of Brahmā’s staff, the slayer of hundreds, and the wielder of a hundred nooses.
Kala, kaṣṭhā, lava, mātrā, muhūrta, day, night, and kṣaṇa;
he is the bestower of the field of the universe, the seed, the primordial linga, and the one without face.
He is both existent and non-existent, manifest and unmanifest; he is the father, the mother, and the grandfather;
he is the gate to heaven, the gate to liberation, the gate to progeny, and the triple heaven.
He is Nirvāṇa and the heart itself; he is the world of Brahmā and the supreme goal.
He is the creator of gods and asuras, and the ultimate refuge for both gods and asuras.
The god who is the preceptor of the gods and asuras, who is saluted by the gods and asuras,
who is the great minister of the gods and asuras, and the refuge of the hosts of gods and asuras.
The presiding lord of the hosts of gods and asuras, the leader of the hosts of gods and asuras,
the god of gods, the divine sage, the bestower of boons upon gods and asuras.
Viṣṇu is the lord of the gods and asuras, the great sovereign of gods and asuras;
he consists of all the gods, is inconceivable, the self of the deities, and is self-existent.
Udgata, Trikrama, Vaidya, Varada, Avaraja,
Ambara, Ijya, Hastin, Vyāghra, Devasiṃha, and Maharṣabha.
The foremost among the wise, the best of gods, the supreme deity of heaven;
he is endowed with excellence, a beautiful speaker, the source of all hopes, and the imperishable one.
The Guru, the beloved, the innate creation, the pure one who carries all;
the horned one, the lover of horns, the tawny-hued, the king of kings, the one free from disease.
He is delightful, a good refuge, free from disease, and the means for accomplishing all things;
he has an eye on his forehead, a universal body, is golden-hued, and possesses the splendor of Brahman.
He is the lord of the stationary beings, one whose senses are restrained;
he is the one who has accomplished his purpose, the benefactor of all creatures, inconceivable, truthful, and pure in his vows.
The Lord of Vows is the Supreme Brahman, the ultimate goal of those who are liberated;
he is the liberated one with disheveled hair, the glorious one, the increaser of prosperity for the world.
Thus have I praised the Blessed One with devotion according to his preeminence;
having thus placed devotion foremost, I have [praised] the all-pervading Lord of Sacrifice.
Then, having received permission, Śambhu—the goal of those possessed of devotion—was thus praised; and having received that hymn from him, the king became renowned throughout the three worlds.
Having obtained the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices,
the highly illustrious one attained the leadership of the Gaṇas through the splendor of his lord, O Ṭaṇḍi.
O twice-born ones, he who recites this, or hears it, or even causes Brāhmaṇas to hear it,
indeed obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices.
A slayer of a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, a thief, one who violates the teacher’s bed, a murderer of one who has sought refuge, and a betrayer of a friend's trust; LiP_1,65.173 //
A killer of a mother, a killer of a father, a killer of a hero, and likewise a killer of an embryo—
by reciting [the mantra] for one year at the hermitage of Śaṅkara during the three junctions of the day, in due order, they are purified.
By worshipping the god at the three junctions of the day, one is liberated from all sins.
Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Thousand Names of Rudra," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
By the grace of the god of gods, as well as that of Taṇḍin, Tridhanvan diligently obtained the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices.
Having attained firm leadership over the Gaṇas and being honored by all the gods,
there was also a learned king named Trayyāruṇa, the son of Tridhanvan.
He had a son, a prince named Satyavrata, who was possessed of great strength;
by him, having slain one of immeasurable luster, the wife of the King of Vidarbha was carried off.
While the mantras for taking the hand were not yet completed here,
King Trayyāruṇa abandoned him because of his connection with that unrighteousness.
"O twice-born ones, he said to his father, 'Having been cast out, where shall I go?
Then his father replied to him, 'Live together with the dog-cookers.'"
Thus addressed, the wise Satyavrata departed from the city at his father’s word and took up residence near the dwelling of a dog-cooker (śvapāka).
Abandoned by his father, the hero lived on; and his father went to the forest.
That valiant man became renowned throughout all the worlds as Triśaṅku.
In ancient times, due to the wrath of Vasiṣṭha, the meritorious King Satyavrata became Viśvāmitra of great splendor after [Vasiṣṭha] had granted a boon to Triśaṅku.
Having consecrated him in his father's kingdom, the sage Kauśika caused him to perform a sacrifice while the gods and Vasiṣṭha looked on.
Then the Lord indeed caused him to ascend to heaven in his physical body;
his wife, born of the Kaikeya lineage, was named Satyavratā.
She gave birth to a son, the stainless Hariścandra;
and the son of Hariścandra was the powerful one named Rohita.
Harita was the son of Rohita, and Dhundhu is said to be the son of Harita;
Vijaya and Sutejas were the two sons of Dhundhu.
Because he was victorious everywhere over the kṣatriyas, he is remembered as Jetṛ;
his son was King Rucaka, who was supremely righteous.
Vṛka was the son of Rucaka, and from him Bāhu was born;
Sagara was his son, a king who was supremely righteous.
Sagara had two wives, Prabhā and Bhānumatī;
desiring sons, he formerly propitiated the Aurva fire with them.
Aurva, being pleased with them both, granted an excellent boon as they desired:
one [of them] sixty thousand sons, and the other likewise a single son.
Prabhā took a son who was the founder of a lineage and many other sons;
Bhānumatī took one son, Asamañjasa.
Then that Prabhā indeed gave birth to sixty thousand [demons],
who were burning as they dug into the earth, struck by Viṣṇu’s arrows released with the *huṃkāra* sound.
The son of Asamañja was the renowned one named Aṃśumat;
his son was Dilīpa, and from Dilīpa came Bhagīratha.
By whom the Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā was brought down after performing austerities,
and who indeed became known by the name Bhagīratha-suta (the son of Bhagīratha).
His heir was the powerful Nābhāga, who was devoted to Bhava;
his son was Ambarīṣa, and from him Sindhudvīpa was born.
Protected by Nābhāga and Ambarīṣa with their two arms,
the earth became exceedingly free from the three types of suffering.
The valiant Ayutāyu was the son of that Sindhudvīpa;
the wise and highly illustrious Ṛtuparṇa was the son of Ayutāyu.
The powerful King, a friend of Nala, was indeed a knower of the heart of the divine dice;
in the Purāṇas, two Nalas are celebrated as being firm in their vows.
Another son of Vīrasena, born of the Ikṣvāku lineage, was the son of Ṛtuparṇa; he was Sārvabhauma, a lord of subjects.
The son of that Sudāsa was King Indrasama;
the son of Sudāsa is declared to have been the monarch named Saudāsa.
He was indeed known by the name Kalmāṣapāda and also as Mitrāsaha;
meanwhile, the highly resplendent Vasiṣṭha [beheld him] in the person of Kalmāṣapāda.
He begot Aśmaka, the enhancer of the Ikṣvāku lineage;
and from Aśmaka and Uttarā was born a son named Mūlaka.
For out of fear of Rāma, that king, surrounded by women in the forest,
wears that supreme armor of women, desiring indeed to find protection.
The righteous King Śataratha was the son of Mūlaka;
from that Śataratha was born the powerful King Ilavila.
There was a glorious and powerful elder named Vṛddhaśarman, son of Tvailavili;
his son was Viśvasaha, whom the father’s daughter begot.
Dilīpa was his son, renowned as Khaṭvāṅga;
he, having come here from heaven and obtained life for but a moment, [performed great deeds].
The three fires and the three worlds were indeed conquered by him through his intellect and truth;
from him was born a long-armed son, Raghu.
Aja was the son of Raghu, and from him was born the heroic one;
from him came King Daśaratha, the illustrious founder of the Ikṣvāku dynasty.
The heroic Rāma, knower of dharma and world-renowned, [was born] from Daśaratha;
as were Bharata, Lakṣmaṇa, and the mighty Śatrughna.
Among them, the most excellent was Rāma, possessed of great splendor and supreme heroism;
having slain Rāvaṇa in battle and performed sacrifices, he was a knower of dharma.
Rāma ruled the kingdom for ten thousand years;
to Rāma was born a son, widely renowned as Kuśa.
And Lava was most illustrious and truly wise;
Atithi was born from Kuśa, and Niṣadha was his son.
Nala was born from Niṣadha, and from him Nabhas was born;
from Nabhas came the one named Puṇḍarīka, and from him Kṣemadhanvan is remembered.
His son was the heroic and powerful Devānīka;
his son was Ahīnara, and after him came Sahasrāśva.
Śubha was born, and from him came Candrāvaloka; from him Tārāpīḍa arose.
His son was Candragiri, and from him Bhānucandra was born.
From him was born Śrutāyu, who is remembered as Bṛhadbala;
he was the one of great splendor in the Bharata lineage who was struck down by the son of Subhadrā.
These kings, the heirs of Ikṣvāku, are generally remembered as the principal figures in this lineage; they have been proclaimed here according to their preeminence.

All those followers of the Pāśupata [path], having studied the knowledge concerning the Supreme Lord, having worshipped Him according to their understanding, and having offered sacrifices according to the prescribed rules; ||| LiP_1,66.44 |||
Some high-souled ones, liberated through the yoga of the self, have gone to heaven;
yet Nṛga, by the curse of a Brahmin, became a lizard.
Dhṛṣṭa, Dhṛṣṭaketu, and the heroic Yamabāla—
these three sons of yours were exceedingly righteous and bold in battle.
The son of Śaryāti was named Ānarta, and his daughter was named Sukanyā;
Ānarta’s son was the powerful Rocamāna.
From Rocamāna came Revu, and from Revu came Raivata;
furthermore, Kakudmin was the eldest son among his hundred sons.
The daughter Revatī became the renowned wife of Rāma;
the son of Nariṣyanta was the self-controlled and mighty Jitātmā.
From Nābhāga was born the powerful Ambarīṣa, a devotee of Viṣṇu;
his son was the illustrious Ṛta, the best among those who know all dharmas.
To him was born the renowned Sudharmā, whose name was Pṛṣita;
and from Karūṣa came all the Kārūṣas, who were celebrated for their fame.
For having harmed a cow belonging to his guru, Pṛṣita incurred great sin;
it is well known that he fell into the state of a Śūdra due to the curse of Cyavana.
Diṣṭaputra was Nābhāga, and from him was born Bhalandana;
the son of Bhalandana was the powerful King Ajavāhana.
These mighty-armed sons of Manu have been described to you in brief;
now I shall tell you of the sons, grandsons, and descendants of Ikṣvāku and of Ela.
Sūta said:
O twice-born ones, the powerful Aila, named Purūravas, was a devotee of Rudra;
he ruled a kingdom free from all thorns in that most meritorious land.
On the northern bank of the Yamunā at Prayāga, frequented by sages,
there was the illustrious lord of Pratiṣṭhāna, established in Pratiṣṭhāna.
He had seven sons, all of whom possessed widespread splendor;
they were renowned throughout the world of the Gandharvas, devoted to Bhava, and endowed with great strength.
Āyu, Māyu, Amāyu, the heroic Viśvāyu,
Śrutāyu, and Śatāyu— these were the sons of Urvaśī born of the gods.
Āyuṣa had five heroic sons of great majesty;
those kings were born of Prabhā, the daughter of Svarbhānu.
Nahuṣa was the first among them, a knower of dharma renowned throughout the world;
Nahuṣa’s heirs were six in number, possessing splendor equal to that of Indra.
These highly powerful ones were born of Virajā, the daughter of the Pitṛs:
Yati, Yayāti, Saṃyāti, Āyāti, and the fifth was Andhaka.
And Vijāti—these six were all renowned for their fame;
among them, Yati was the eldest, and Yayāti was the youngest.
The eldest among them, the lord Yati, became one who had realized Brahman for the sake of liberation;
of those five, Yayāti possessed great strength and prowess.
(Yayāti) obtained Devayānī, the daughter of Uśanas, as his wife,
as well as Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of the Asura Vṛṣaparvan.
Devayānī gave birth to Yadu and Turvasu;
both of them were performers of auspicious deeds, praised, and experts in knowledge.
To that Yayāti, the powerful Śukra gave Druhyu, Anu, Pūru, and Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, along with a chariot.
Satisfied by him, the lord of brahmins, being pleased, gave him a most radiant,
divine golden quiver with excellent joints and two inexhaustible great arrow-cases.
Yoked with horses as swift as thought, he, while carrying off the maiden,
conquered the earth in six months with that preeminent chariot.
Yayāti was invincible in battle by gods, dānavas, and humans;
he was a devotee of Bhava, meritorious in soul, steadfast in dharma, and upright.
A performer of sacrifices, one who has conquered anger, and one who shows compassion toward all beings—
he was the supreme charioteer for all the Kauravas.
This concerns Janamejaya, the best of kings and a Kaurava,
who was the descendant of King Pūru and the son of Parīkṣit.
That chariot perished through the curse of the wise Garga;
for King Janamejaya had [formerly] killed the young son of Garga.
He indeed killed Akrūra and incurred the sin of killing a Brahmin;
that royal sage, smelling of iron, ran hither and thither.
Abandoned by the people of both the city and the countryside, he found no peace at any time;
thereafter, tormented by suffering, he could not attain consciousness anywhere.
Then, being distressed, he went for refuge to the sage Śaunaka,
that renowned and noble-minded seer known by the name Indrota.
And those best of the twice-born caused that king Janamejaya to perform the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) for the sake of his purification, O Indra among kings.
Freed from the smell of iron and from his sin, that highly illustrious one,
amidst the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of the sacrifice, was approached by a divine and auspicious chariot.
Falling away from that lineage, he was given again by the gratified Śakra to Vasu, the lord of Cedi; from him, Bṛhadratha obtained [the kingdom].
Then, having slain Jarāsaṃdha, Bhīma, the joy of the Kauravas, affectionately gave that excellent chariot to Vāsudeva.
Sūta said:
O best of the twice-born, the lord Yayāti, son of Nahuṣa, having been assisted by Puru himself, consecrated his son Puru as king.

And when King Puru desired to consecrate his youngest son, the social orders, headed by the brahmins, spoke these words: LiP_1,66.81: "The castes, with the brahmins at their head, addressed this speech to the king who was desirous of consecrating his youngest son, Puru."
O Lord, how is it that the younger son deserves the kingdom, bypassing Yadu, who is the grandson of Śukra and the eldest son of Devayānī?
We awaken you to these; protect the Dharma as well.
Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa* (Yayāti Revisited).
Yayāti said: "Let all the social orders, headed by the Brahmins, hear my words:
that the kingdom must never, under any circumstances, be given by me to the eldest."
My eldest son Yadu did not obey my command,
and being of a contrary mind, he is not considered a true son by the virtuous.
A son who carries out the words of his mother and father is praised by the virtuous;
he alone is a true son who conducts himself toward his parents as a son should.
Since I have been treated with contempt by Yadu, as well as by Turvasu,
Druhyu, and Anu, they have all shown me extreme disregard.
And Puru has fulfilled his word and has been especially honored;
he is my youngest heir, by whom my old age was assumed.
"Old age was ordained for me by Śukra for the sake of Devayānī;
however, when he was entreated [by me], he again made that old age transferable."
And Śukra himself, Uśanas Kāvya, granted him a boon:
"Whichever son of yours follows you shall be the bearer of your kingdom."
"Sirs, you too must grant your consent; Pūru shall be consecrated in the kingdom. The subjects said:
"He who is a son endowed with virtues and always devoted to the welfare of his parents..."
Even as the youngest, he is the lord who deserves every blessing;
Pūru is worthy of this kingdom, for he is the son who carries out your word.
"By virtue of Śukra’s boon, it is not possible to act otherwise.
Sūta said: [Thus Yayāti distributes the kingdom.]
Thus addressed by the contented people of the countryside, the son of Nahuṣa then [spoke].
Having then consecrated his own son Pūru in the kingdom,
he assigned his son Turvasu to the southeastern quarter.
Then the king appointed his eldest son, Yadu, to the south;
and both Druhyu and Anu he assigned to the west and the north respectively.
Having conquered the earth with its seven islands and its oceans, Yayāti,
the son of Nahuṣa, then divided his kingdom into three parts for his sons.
But the king, having transferred his royal fortune to his son and having entrusted the burden to his kinsmen, became full of joy, his mind overflowing with delight.
In this regard, these verses were formerly sung by the great king Yayāti,
by which one may withdraw desires from all sides, just as a tortoise draws in its limbs.
By these alone does a man become glorious, and not otherwise, even by performing ten million rites;
desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of sensual pleasures.
Like a fire with oblations, it increases all the more;
whatever rice, barley, gold, cattle, and women exist upon the earth [are increased].
Realizing that all of this is not enough for even one person, one should attain tranquility;
when one no longer harbors any evil disposition toward any living being.
Then, through action, mind, and speech, one attains Brahman when one does not fear others, nor do others fear him.
When one neither censures nor hates, then one attains Brahman—
that which is difficult for the wicked-minded to abandon, and which does not decay even as one decays.
For one who abandons that craving which is a life-ending disease, there is happiness;
as one grows old, the hair decays, and as one grows old, the teeth decay.
The eyes and ears grow old, yet craving alone remains free from affliction;
all embodied beings grow old by their very nature, and not otherwise.
The hope for life and the hope for wealth do not decay even as one grows old;
nor does the happiness of sensual pleasure in the world, nor the great divine happiness.
"This does not equal even a sixteenth part of the bliss that comes from the destruction of craving.
Having spoken thus, that royal seer entered the forest together with his wife.
Having performed austerities on Bhṛgutuṅga and having practiced fasting unto death right there, the highly illustrious one attained heaven together with his wife.
These five lineages of his are meritorious and honored by the celestial rishis;
by them the entire earth is pervaded, just as by the rays of the sun.
By reciting or hearing this meritorious account of Yayāti’s life, a wise man shall become wealthy, possessed of progeny, long-lived, and renowned.
Completely liberated from all sins, he is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Life of Yayāti," in the Soma dynasty within the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
Now listen as I proclaim, in brief and in due order, the lineage of Yadu, the eldest son of supreme splendor, as I speak.
Yadu had five sons who were like the children of gods:
Sahasrajit was the eldest, followed by Kroṣṭu, Nīla, Ajaka, and Laghu.
Sahasrajit’s son was likewise the king named Śatajit;
Śatajit had three sons of supreme fame who were well-known.
Haihaya, Haya, and King Veṇuhaya;
the heir of Haihaya was the one renowned as Dharma.
O brahmins, his son was known as Dharmanetra;
Dharmanetra’s son was Kīrti, and Saṃjaya was his offspring.
The heir of Sañjaya was the righteous one named Mahiṣmān;
the son of Mahiṣmān was the powerful Bhadraśreṇya.
The heir of Bhadraśreṇya was the king named Durdama;
the son of Durdama was the wise and renowned Dhanaka.
The heirs of Dhanaka were four, esteemed by the world:
Kṛtavīrya, Kṛtāgni, and likewise Kṛtavarmā.
Then Kārtavīrya Arjuna was born as the fourth, endowed with great vigor;
possessing a thousand arms, he became the supreme lord of the seven continents.
At that time, Rāma was his death, being of the nature of Nārāyaṇa;
he had five hundred sons there, all of whom were great chariot-warriors.
Skilled in weapons, powerful, heroic, righteous,
and high-minded were Śūra, Śūrasena, Dhṛṣṭa, and likewise Kṛṣṇa.
And Jayadhvaja was the king of the Āvantīs, a lord of the people;
Jayadhvaja’s son was the exceedingly powerful Tālajaṅgha.
He had one hundred sons here who were celebrated as the Tālajaṅghas;
among them, the eldest was the highly heroic King Vītihotra.
Vṛṣa and others were his other sons, performers of meritorious deeds;
Vṛṣa was the founder of their lineage, and his son was Madhu.
Madhu had a hundred sons, but Vṛṣṇi was the one who carried on his lineage. All the descendants of Vṛṣṇi are known as the Vṛṣṇis, while those of Madhu are remembered as the Mādhavas;
furthermore, the Haihayas are designated as Yādavas because of their descent from the lineage of Yadu.
These five groups indeed belong to those high-souled Haihayas.
The Vītihotras, the Haryātās, the Bhojas, and likewise the Āvantyas; the famous Śūrasenas, and similarly the Tālajaṅghas.
Śūra, Śūrasena, Vṛṣa, Kṛṣṇa,
and Jayadhvaja as the fifth— these were the renowned and most excellent of the Haihayas.
Śūra, Śūravīra, and the sinless Śūrasena—
the country of those great-souled ones became renowned as the Śūrasenas.
The son of Vītihotra was the renowned Narta;
and the son of Kṛṣṇa was Durjaya, the subduer of enemies.
And hear now of the lineage of the royal seer Kroṣṭu, who possessed supreme prowess,
in whose family was born Viṣṇu, the upholder of the Vṛṣṇi clan.
Kroṣṭu had one son, the highly illustrious Vṛjinīvān;
his son was Svātī, and Kuśaṅku was his son.
Then, desiring offspring, the exceedingly powerful Kuśaṅku performed various great sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
His son was Citraratha, who was endowed with meritorious deeds;
then there was the heroic Caitraratha, a performer of sacrifices who gave away abundant sacrificial fees.
King Śaśabindu, indeed, followed that supreme vow;
he was a universal monarch, a being of great essence, of great heroism, and possessed of many offspring.
Śaśabindu had one hundred thousand sons;
they proclaim that his sons were infinite and unsurpassed.
From Anantaka was born Yajña; Yajña’s son was Dhṛti;
Uśanas was his son, who indeed obtained this earth.
The most righteous king named Siteṣu, remembered as the son of Uśanas, performed one hundred horse sacrifices.
Maruta was his son, a royal sage who increased the lineage;
the heroic Kambalabarhi is remembered as Maruta’s son.
The son of Kambalabarhiṣ was the wise Rukmakavaca;
having slain armored heroes in battle, Rukmakavaca [attained his renown].
With sharpened arrows, the archer attained supreme glory;
then, at the horse sacrifice, the righteous-souled one gave the earth to the officiating priests.
From Rukmakavaca was born Parāvṛt, the slayer of enemy heroes;
and from Parāvṛta were born five sons of great being.
Rukmeṣu, Pṛthurukma, Jyāmagha, Parigha, and Hari—
his father deposited Parigha and Hari among the Videhas.
Rukmeṣu became king, and Pṛthurukma lived under his protection;
however, having been exiled by them, King Jyāmagha dwelt in a hermitage.
Though he was peaceful even while dwelling in the forest, he was exhorted by the brahmins;
taking up his bow, banner, and chariot, he went to another land.
Accompanied only by his wife, he went alone to Mount Ṛkṣavanta on the bank of the Narmadā and dwelt there, abandoned by all others.
Jyāmagha’s wife was Śaibyā, a virtuous and chaste woman;
and by means of intense austerity, that very Śaibyā gave birth.
Suta married Subhagā, who was advanced in years;
however, the king had two learned sons by his daughter, Kratha and Kaiśika.
The two sons of the King of Vidarbha were heroes skilled in battle;
Romapāda was the third, and Babhru is remembered as his son.
His son was Sudhṛti, who was learned and supremely righteous; from him came Kauśika, and from him the lineage of Caidya is remembered.
Kratha was the son of Vidarbha, and Kunti was his offspring;
from Kunti was born Vṛta, who was powerful and fearless in battle.
And the son of Raṇadhṛṣṭa was Nidhṛti, the slayer of enemy heroes;
he was known by the name Daśārha, the destroyer of hosts of great foes.
The son of Daśārha was Vyāpta; his son was Jīmūta;
Jīmūta’s son was Vikṛti; and his son was Bhīmaratha.
Now, Bhīmaratha had a son named Navaratha,
who was indeed constantly devoted to the practice of charity and righteousness, and dedicated to truth and virtuous conduct.
His son was Dṛḍharatha, and Śakuni was his son;
from him Karambha was born, and from him Devarāta arose.
From Devarāta was born King Devarāti of great fame;
he who was named Devakṣatra was born resembling the offspring of a god.
The illustrious and highly renowned Madhu, son of Devakṣatra, was the founder of the lineage of the Madhus;
from Madhu came Kuruvaṃśaka.
From Anu, who was born from the Kuru lineage, Purutvān was born; and from Purutvān, Aṃśu was born by Bhadravatī, the daughter of Vidarbha. Thus, O best of men, [the lineage continued].
Aṃśu married the princess of the Ikṣvākus, and from him Sattva was born;
from Sattva was born Sātvata, who was endowed with all virtues and increased his lineage.
I have thus described to you in detail the creation of Jyāmagha; whoever should read or even hear this account of Jyāmagha’s emanation, [shall attain merit].
By living thus, one indeed attains heaven, sovereignty, and happiness.
Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Genealogies," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
The Sātvata, endowed with truthfulness, begot four sons:
Bhajana, Bhrājamāna, Divya, and King Devāvṛdha.
And [the lineages of] the illustrious Andhaka and Vṛṣṇi, the joy of the Yadus—
listen indeed in detail to their four origins.
From Bhrājamāna, through his devotion to a woman of the Sṛñjaya clan, two sons were born who are remembered as Ayutāyu and Śatāyu; they were powerful and known for bringing joy.
Among them, King Devāvṛdha performed supreme austerity, reflecting:
"May I have a son endowed with all virtuous qualities."
It is heard that the best of kings known as Babhru was a man of virtuous fame,
and those who know the ancient chronicles of his lineage sing of him thus.
Then, proclaiming the virtues of the high-souled Devāvṛdha,
we see him from close at hand just as we hear of him from afar.
Babhru was the best among men; he was equal to the gods who increase the divine power.
There were six thousand, eight hundred, and sixty-five persons.
Those who have attained immortality even from Babhru Devāvṛdha—
may that hero, a sacrificer whose mind is intent on giving and who is devoted to Brahman, be firm in his vows.
Famous and possessed of great splendor was that great chariot-warrior (mahāratha) of the Sātvatas;
born in his lineage were the Bhojas, who were indeed like unto gods.
Gāndhārī and Mādrī were both wives of Vṛṣṇi;
Gāndhārī gave birth to Sumitra, the delighter of his friends.
And then Mādrī obtained from that god those two sons, Devamīḍhuṣa—
namely Anamitra and Śini— who were both supreme among men.
Nighna, the son of Anamitra, had two sons:
the illustrious Prasena and Satrājit.
Sūrya became a friend as dear to Satrājit as his own life;
Vivasvat gave him a jewel named Syamantaka.
He was the king of all jewels upon the earth, like a precious gem;
once, he went out on a hunt together with Prasenajit.
Having met his death at the hands of the exceedingly terrible Siṃhādeva while without any companion,
a son was then born to Śini from the youngest son of the Vṛṣṇi clan.
Satyaka was truthful in speech and perfected in truth; his son was Sātyaki, also known as Yuyudhāna, the powerful grandson of Śini.
Asaṅga was the son of Yuyudhāna, and Kuṇi was his son; Kuṇi’s son was Yugandhara; these are celebrated as the Śaineyas.
To Mādrī’s son Yudhājit was born a son, Vārṣṇi,
who became renowned as Śvaphalka and brought benefit to the three worlds.
And wherever the great king Śvaphalka, whose soul is righteous, resides,
there is no fear of disease, nor even fear of drought.
Śvaphalka obtained as his wife the daughter of the King of Kāśī;
for the King of Kāśī gave him his own daughter named Gāndinī.
Remaining indeed within her mother’s womb for many groups of years, she did not come forth; while she was still in the womb, her father spoke to her.
"Be born quickly; may it be well with you; for what reason do you remain [here]?
Then that maiden Gāndinī, staying within the womb, spoke to him.
"O father, if you were to give one cow every day to a Brāhmaṇa for three years,
then I shall emerge from your belly."
"So be it," said her father, and he fulfilled her desire;
for he was a donor, a hero, a performer of sacrifices, learned in the scriptures, and fond of guests.
Her son is remembered as Akrūra, born of Śvaphalka and endowed with great liberality;
he was also the son of Ratnā, the daughter of Śiva, whom Akrūra obtained as his wife.
Learn now of the sons he begot upon her:
Upamanyu, Māṅgu, Vṛta, and Janamejaya.
Girirakṣas, Upekṣa, Śatrughna, Arimardana, Dharmabhṛt, Vṛṣṭadharma, Godhana, and Varas; ||| 69.27 ||
Āvāha, Prativāha, and Sudhārā were his excellent wives; moreover, Akrūra had two sons by Ugrasenī who brought joy to their lineage.
Devavān and Anupadeva were born, both highly esteemed by the gods;
and Sumitra’s son was Citraka, who was of great fame.
Citraka had sons, namely Vipṛthu and Pṛthu,
as well as Aśvagrīva, Subāhu, Sudhāman, Sūka, and Gavekṣaṇa.
Ariṣṭanemi, Aśva, Dharma, Dharmabhṛt,
Subhūmi, Bahubhūmi, and two women, Śraviṣṭhā and Śravaṇā.
From Andhaka, Kāśya’s daughter obtained four sons:
Kukura, Bhajamāna, Śuci, and Kambalabarhiṣa.
Kukura’s son was Vṛṣṇi, and from Vṛṣṇi, Śūra was born; from Kapotaroman came Atibala, and his son was Vilomaka.
He had a learned son named Nala, who was a friend of Tumburu;
he is indeed renowned by the excellent name Candanānakadundubhi.
From him, moreover, Abhijit was born as his son, and from him Punarvasu;
that best of men performed an Aśvamedha sacrifice for the sake of obtaining a son.
From the midst of the sacrificial hall of that Atirātra sacrifice,
there arose the wise, omniscient, generous, and sacrificing Punarvasu.
To him also, it is said, a pair of children was born of Abhijit:
Āhuka and Āhukī, both renowned as the best among those possessed of fame.
From Āhuka, the daughter of Kaśya, two sons were born:
Devaka and Ugrasena, both equal to the offspring of gods.
To King Devaka were born sons resembling the gods:
Devavān, Upadeva, Sudeva, and Devarakṣita.
They had seven sisters; he gave them all to Vasudeva:
Vṛṣadevā, Upadevā, and likewise another, Devarakṣitā.
Śrīdevā, Śāntidevā, Sahadevā, and another,
Devakī— among them, the slender-waisted one was the most excellent.
Ugrasena had nine sons, of whom Kaṃsa was the eldest;
they, in turn, had hundreds and thousands of sons and grandsons.
The daughter of Devaka became the wife of the wise Vasudeva;
devoted to her husband, she was worthy of praise and worship even by the gods.
And Rohiṇī, the highly fortunate wife of Ānakadundubhi, was the daughter of Bāhlika and a descendant of Puru; she was honored even by the gods.
Rohiṇī gave birth to Rāma, the best of the strong, whose weapon is the plow;
he had resorted to her out of fear of Kaṃsa, and his splendor was tranquil.
Then, after Rāma was born and the exceedingly skillful Ṣaḍgarbha had been slain,
the wise Vasudeva begot Hari upon Devakī.
He alone is that Supreme Self, the God of gods, Janārdana;
he is the Blessed One Halāyudha and Ananta, who possesses the luster of silver.
Under the pretext of the curse of Bhṛgu, honoring his human form,
Janārdana became Vāsudeva through her, Devakī.
Born from the body of Umā, Yoganidrā became Kauśikī;
by the command of the God of gods, she indeed became the daughter of Yaśodā.
And that very Prakṛti is directly saluted by all the gods;
the Lord Kṛṣṇa is the Puruṣa who bestows the fruits of dharma and liberation.
Then, protecting his own son from Kaṃsa, he took that girl,
who had four arms, large eyes, and was marked with the Śrīvatsa.
Having presented Janārdana, who was bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus,
to Yaśodā, the wise Vasudeva departed.
Having given him to Nandagopa, he said, "Let him be protected," for Viṣṇu, the protector of the worlds, had assumed a physical form by his own will.
And through the grace of the god Śiva, who possesses immeasurable splendor,
he gave that boon-granting Supreme Lord to Rāma.
And since the Teacher of the World has descended for the purpose of suppressing the burden of the earth,
therefore indeed all that is auspicious shall come to pass for the Yādavas.
"This is that embryo of Devakī who will take away our afflictions;
Ānakadundubhi has given it to Kaṃsa, the son of Ugrasena."
Then he announced that a daughter of auspicious marks had been born, saying,
"O Kaṃsa of noble vows, this is the eighth pregnancy of Devakī."
"Death itself is certain, there is no doubt"—such was the ancient voice;
thereupon Kaṃsa began to strike her, leaping up into the sky.
The eight-armed goddess spoke with a voice as deep as a thundercloud:
"Protect your own body; death itself has come for you."
O fool, what evil deed was committed by you, the master of illusion in the form of Kaṃsa, while protecting your body, that you have truly become your own destroyer?
Out of fear of Devakī, Kaṃsa indeed killed the eighth [child],
for it was remembered that the death ordained for Devakī was her eighth son.
O tigers among sages, Bhoja’s effort to create a likeness of Hari was in vain, for he was rendered motionless by her very power.
Kaṃsa too was slain by that Kṛṣṇa of unwearied deeds,
as were many others who had been slayers of gods and brahmins.
The sons of that Kṛṣṇa, headed by Pradyumna, were likewise many in number; they were all reckoned to be experts in warfare.
The sons of Kṛṣṇa are celebrated as being equal to Kṛṣṇa himself;
among all these sons of Hari, Cārudeṣṇa and the others are preeminent.
The sons of Rukmiṇī and the slayers of enemies were distinguished and powerful;
they numbered sixteen thousand one hundred women.
Among all of them, Rukmiṇī was Kṛṣṇa’s most beloved and his eldest wife;
with her, Kṛṣṇa, whose actions are effortless, spent twelve years.
While dwelling there, subsisting on air alone, he worshipped Hara for the sake of sons;
[as a result, he obtained] Cārudeṣṇa, Sucāru, Cāruveṣa, and Yaśodhara.
Cāruśravas, Cāruyaśas, Pradyumna, and Sāmba—
these were obtained by Kṛṣṇa through the grace of the wielder of the trident (Śiva).
Having seen those heroic sons and the sons of Rukmiṇī,
Jāmbavatī, the wife of the wise Kṛṣṇa, spoke to Kṛṣṇa regarding Rukmiṇī.
O lotus-eyed one, being pleased, you ought to grant me a son who is distinguished, most virtuous, and equal to the lord of the gods.
Having heard the words of Jāmbavatī, Hari, the Lord of the World,
that faultless treasure of asceticism, then began to perform penance.
Then that Nārāyaṇa Kṛṣṇa, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace,
went to the excellent hermitage of the sage Vyāghrapāda.
Having seen the sage Aṅgiras and prostrated before him, Janārdana obtained the divine Pāśupata yoga by his command.
With his beard and hair shorn, anointed with ghee, and wearing a girdle of muñja grass,
the blessed Kṛṣṇa, the scorcher of foes, became initiated and performed intense austerities.
With arms raised, without support, and standing on the tips of his big toes,
Adhokṣaja subsisted on fruits, water, and air for three seasons.
Satisfied by his ascetic penance, Rudra granted him many boons,
including Sāmba, the son of Jāmbavatī, for the sake of the high-souled Kṛṣṇa.
Likewise, Jāmbavatī, the wife of Hari, obtained her son Sāmba and experienced incomparable joy, just as Aditi did upon obtaining the Sun.
And at that time, O best of sages, Bāṇa’s thousand arms were cut off by him [Viṣṇu] through the curse of the wise Rudra.
Then, accompanied by Halāyudha,
he effortlessly slew the Daityas and likewise the wicked kings upon the field of battle.
Having slain Naraka, that preeminent Daitya who was born from a god,
he did so by virtue of the boon granted to the high-souled Brāhmaṇa Urdhvacakra.
He of incomparable prowess and great strength took sixteen thousand maidens for his own enjoyment, numbering more than a hundred thousand.
Under the pretext of a curse, he brought about the destruction of the Brahmins' lineage;
having destroyed that lineage, Acyuta remained at Prabhāsa.
Then, indeed, more than a hundred years passed for Kṛṣṇa in Dvārakā, he who removes the affliction of old age.
At that time, at Piṇḍāraka, he protected himself from the curse of Viśvāmitra, Kaṇva, and the wise Nārada, as well as the words of Durvāsas.
Having abandoned his human form by means of the pretext of old age and weapons,
Kṛṣṇa also favored the hunter and departed for heaven.
By the curse of Aṣṭāvakra, all the wives of the wise Kṛṣṇa were carried off by thieves through the power of his illusory magic.
Balabhadra also departed, having abandoned his body and become a serpent;
and the auspicious queens of that Kṛṣṇa, headed by Rukmiṇī, likewise followed him.
They all entered the fire together with Kṛṣṇa of unwearied deeds,
as did the goddess Revatī with the wise Balabhadra.
Having entered the fire, O brahmins, she followed the path of her husband;
and having performed the funeral rites for Hari, the son of Pṛthā, who was possessed of supreme heroism, [proceeded].
And for Rāma, as well as for the other Vṛṣṇis,
that man of firm vows performed the ritual offerings with tubers, roots, and fruits.
Due to the absence of material wealth, Pārtha himself, along with his brothers, ascended to heaven;
thus has the account of Kṛṣṇa of unwearied deeds been told in brief.
The manifestation and the dissolution of the Great-Souled One occur by his own will alone;
O twice-born ones, such is the history of the kings of the Lunar dynasty.
Whoever should read it, or listen to it, or even cause the Brāhmaṇas to hear it, goes to the world of Viṣṇu; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Genealogy of the Lunar Dynasty," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
The sages said:
O Sūta of noble vows, you have indicated the primary creation but have not yet revealed it;
you ought now to explain it in full detail.
Sūta said: O lords of sages, the god Maheśvara, Mahādeva, the Supreme Self (Paramātman), abides as that which is beyond both Prakṛti and Puruṣa.
And from that Lord, the unmanifest (avyakta) arose as the supreme cause;
that which those who contemplate reality call Pradhāna and Prakṛti.
Devoid of smell, color, and taste, and free from sound and touch;
undecaying, stable, imperishable, eternal, and established within its own self.
The source of the world, the great element, the supreme, eternal Brahman—
the embodiment of all beings, impelled by the command of the Lord.
Without beginning or end, unborn, subtle, composed of the three qualities, the source and the imperishable,
unmanifest and unknowable, Brahman existed in the beginning.
By his own self, all this was pervaded by him through the will of Śiva;
at that time, while that [state] consisted of undifferentiated darkness (tamomaya) and the equilibrium of the qualities (guṇasāmya).
At the time of creation, when the Pradhāna is presided over by the Kṣetrajña,
the Mahat indeed manifested, becoming apparent through the state of the Guṇas.
Then, enveloped by the subtle, the great, and the unmanifest,
the Great Principle (Mahat), characterized by an excess of the quality of goodness (sattva), first manifests as mere existence.
But the mind is to be known as great; it is remembered as the single cause of that [body].
Once arisen, it is merely a subtle sign (liṅga), for it is presided over by the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).
And forms such as dharma and the rest are the causes for the purpose of the reality of the world;
impelled by the desire to create, Mahat undergoes transformation into creation.
He is remembered as the mind, the great one, the intellect, the sacred word, the fortress, the consciousness, the renown, the lord,
the wisdom, the perception, the memory, the awareness, and the sovereign of the universe.
Because it conceives of the activity and the fruit of all beings,
and because it is subtle and thus differentiated by that [activity], it is called the mind (manas).
Because he is the first-born among the principles (tattvas) and is great in terms of magnitude,
and because he is greater than even the specific qualities (guṇas), he is therefore remembered as Mahat.
The person (puruṣa) maintains pride, conceives of division, and even considers [himself as such] due to his connection with experience; for that reason, he is known as "intellect" (mati).
Because it is vast, because it nourishes all states of being, and because it is the support of everything,
Brahman is so defined since it sustains all existents.
Because he fills all the gods with his favors and leads them to the state of ultimate reality, for that reason he is called Pūri.
In this context, the person perceives all states as well as what is beneficial;
and because it causes one to perceive, it is therefore defined as "intellect" (buddhi).
Since manifestation and individual experience proceed from it,
and because enjoyment is grounded in knowledge, it is therefore remembered as "manifestation" (khyāti).
Or rather, it is manifested manifoldly through its qualities such as knowledge and the rest;
therefore, the designation for that Great One (mahat) is called "manifestation" (khyāti).
The Great-Souled One directly perceives everything, and for that reason he is the Lord;
because he follows after knowledge, he is therefore called Prajñā.
Because it accumulates forms such as knowledge and the like, as well as the many fruits of karma,
for the sake of experience, it is therefore called *citi*.
Because it remembers all actions— those of the present, those of the past, and likewise those of the future— it is called *smṛti*.
Because one obtains complete knowledge and supreme majesty from him,
he is therefore called Vindu, Vide, and Saṃvit.
Furthermore, O best of sages, it exists everywhere and one finds everything within it; therefore, it is called *saṃvit* by the great ones.
The Lord, the treasury of knowledge, has declared that "jñāna" is derived from the root "jñā" (to know);
he is called "Īśvara" by the wise because he transcends bondage and other such conditions.
The primordial and unsurpassed reality has been explained by means of synonymous terms by those who know the true nature of reality and who perceive the true essence of the Divine.
Impelled by the desire to create, he brings about the great creation;
his two functions are traditionally known as volition and determination.
From the triple-guṇa principle, when rajas predominates, the ego (ahaṅkāra) arose;
that creation, enveloped by the Great Principle (mahat), is the "origin of the elements" (bhūtādi), and it exists externally.

From that very ego (ahaṅkāra) characterized by an excess of darkness (tamas), the creation of the subtle elements (tanmātra) and the gross elements (bhūta) arose; he is indeed the Bhūtādi, belonging to the quality of darkness.
But Bhūtādi, undergoing transformation, created the subtle element of sound alone;
from that, space, characterized by sound, was produced as a hollow void.
Space, which consists of sound alone, enveloped the subtle element of touch;
and the wind, undergoing transformation, produced the subtle element of form.
Light arises from wind, and it is said to have that [wind] as its quality;
indeed, wind consists of touch alone, yet it envelops the subtle element of form.
And light, undergoing transformation, emitted the subtle element of taste;
from that, indeed, the waters came into being, and they consist of all tastes.
Those waters, consisting of the subtle element of taste, enveloped fire, which consists of the subtle element of form; and the waters, undergoing transformation, created the subtle element of smell.
From that, the aggregate (saṃghāta) is born; therefore, fragrance is considered its quality.
And because each [element] consists of that subtle element (tanmātra), it is traditionally known as "subtle element" (tanmātratā).
Because they denote without distinction, they are therefore called "undifferentiated" (aviśeṣas);
furthermore, because they are characterized by being tranquil, terrible, or deluded, they are again called "undifferentiated."
This creation of the gross elements and the subtle elements (tanmātras) should be understood as proceeding mutually from the *vaikārika* ego, which is characterized by the predominance of *sattva*.
That creation, however, which is of the nature of transformation (vaikārika), proceeds simultaneously:
[it consists of] the five sense organs and the five organs of action.
The ten deities born of *vaikārika* [rajas] are the instruments of perception, the sense organs;
therein, the eleventh is the mind, which by its own nature partakes of both [perception and action].
The ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth—
these indeed, when joined with the intellect, serve for the purpose of perceiving sound and the other sense objects.
The feet, the anus, the generative organ, the hands, and speech as the tenth; their functions are locomotion, excretion, sexual pleasure, manual skill, and speech—these are their respective actions.
Space entered into sound alone and touch alone;
from that, the twofold wind came into being, consisting of sound and touch.
In the same way, sound and both qualities of touch enter into form;
thereafter, fire arises possessing three qualities and endowed with sound, touch, and form.
And it entered into taste alone, together with sound, touch, and form;
therefore, water should be known as consisting of four qualities and having taste as its essence.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and indeed smell entered [the elements];
having combined with mere scent, they entered this earth.
Therefore, the earth-element among the gross elements is said to possess five qualities;
for that reason, its specific manifestations are recorded as being calm, terrible, and deluded.
Through their mutual interpenetration, they support one another;
within the earth, indeed, is all this [universe] encompassed by the Lokāloka mountain.
The specific qualities are perceivable by the senses and are so designated because they are restricted;
each subsequent creation attains the excellence of the preceding one.
Whatever those [qualities] are, and for as long as they exist, and whatever their extent is said to be—
should anyone perceive a scent in water, they might indeed call it a quality of water.
One should know that [the earth] exists within the earth itself due to its reliance upon water and wind;
for these seven great-souled ones exist through their mutual dependence on one another.
And because they are presided over by the Puruṣa and through the favor of the Unmanifest,
those [principles] beginning with Mahat and ending with Viśeṣa produce the Egg.
Arising simultaneously like a bubble upon water,
that great egg was produced from the subtle elements and rested upon the waters.
The egg is surrounded on the outside by water ten times its size;
that water, in turn, is surrounded on the outside by fire ten times its size.
Fire is indeed surrounded on the outside by wind ten times its size;
wind is indeed surrounded on the outside by space ten times its size.

The wind is enveloped by space, but space is enveloped by the source of the elements (bhūtādi); the source of the elements is also enveloped by the Great One (mahat), and the Great One is enveloped by the Unmanifest (avyakta).
O you of excellent vows, Śarva resides within the skull-bowl, Bhava is in the waters,
the Lord Rudra is in the midst of fire, and Ugra is remembered as being in the wind.
Bhīma resides in the midst of the earth, Maheśvara in the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra),
the Lord Īśa in the intellect (buddhi), and the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) everywhere.
The egg is enveloped by these seven primordial coverings;
and having covered one another, these eight primordial natures remain established.
But at the time of dissolution, having remained [there], they devour one another;
thus, arising from one another, they sustain one another.
(First Person): Through the relationship of container and contained, those modifications exist within the modified;
Maheśvara is beyond the unmanifest, and the cosmic egg arises from the unmanifest.
From the egg, that very Lord was born as the Puruṣa, radiant like the sun;
within him, the accomplishment of his task was perfected by his own will alone.
He is indeed the first embodied being; he is called Puruṣa. From his left side was born Viṣṇu, who is saluted by all the gods.
Indeed, by the will of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), the god Brahmā, the teacher of the world, was born from the right side of Goddess Lakṣmī along with Sarasvatī.
Within that egg were these worlds, this entire universe,
along with the moon and the sun together with the stars and planets, and together with the wind.
Indeed, within this egg, both the worlds and the non-worlds are somewhat contained.
O twice-born ones, as for that period of time which was calculated by me regarding creation:
This interval of time should be known as one day of the Supreme Lord;
and his night should be known to be of equal duration in its entirety.
The creation of that which is handless is known as night, and dissolution is known as night;
one should hold that for him there is neither day nor night.
However, this conventional designation is employed out of a desire for the welfare of the world:
[the names] "senses," "objects of the senses," and the "five great elements. (LiP 1.70.69)
Therefore, all beings, along with the intellect and the deities,
remain as non-existent within the supreme Lord, the wise one.
At the end of the day they dissolve, and at the end of the night the origin of the universe [dissolves] when the manifest,
which abides in its own self, has withdrawn its modifications.
Both Pradhāna and Puruṣa abide in similarity; endowed with the qualities of Tamas, Sattva, and Rajas, they exist in a state of equilibrium.
Those two were mutually interwoven and pervaded one another;
when there is equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas), it should be known as dissolution (laya), and when there is disequilibrium, it is called creation (sṛṣṭi).
Just as oil exists within sesame seeds, or as clarified butter resides within milk,
so too does the world abide within darkness (tamas), following after the quality of passion (rajas).
Having thus spent the entire night devoted to the supreme Maheśvarī, the Supreme One,
who is beyond the primordial nature (prakṛti), entered the mouth of Arha.
The Supreme Lord, that Great Lord Maheśvara, having entered both Pradhāna and Puruṣa, agitated them by means of his supreme yoga.
From Maheśvara, the Lord of the Universe who possesses the triple form, three gods were born—
eternal, supreme, secret, the self of all, and embodied beings.
These very three are the gods; these very three are the qualities (guṇas);
these very three are the worlds; these very three are the fires.
For these are mutually dependent and devoted to one another;
they exist by means of one another and support one another.
For these are mutual mates and depend upon one another;
indeed, there is no moment of separation for them, as they do not abandon each other.
Īśvara is the supreme deity, and Viṣṇu is beyond the Great Principle (mahat);
Brahmā, joined with the quality of passion (rajas), indeed proceeds at the beginning of creation.
That Puruṣa is to be known as the Supreme; she is remembered as the Supreme Prakṛti.
For that [earth], presided over by Maheśvara, proceeds when impelled from all sides;
and the Great One (Mahān), having entered into it, himself becomes the object of Śrī because of its long-standing stability.

Due to the imbalance of the primary qualities (guṇas) within that which consists of both the existent and the non-existent, the time of creation proceeds, preceded by the presiding of the Lord (Īśvara).
Accomplished in his task, Rudra stood at the forefront;
matchless in splendor, wise, unmanifest, yet the illuminator [of all].
He is indeed the first embodied being; he is called the Puruṣa.
Therefore, the lordly Brahmā, the four-faced Prajāpati, [proceeded from him].
Having attained perfection regarding cause and effect, Mahādeva indeed existed in that manner; though he is one alone, he is thus established in a threefold way.
They are endowed with unimpeded knowledge and sovereignty,
and they are possessed of unimpeded righteousness and dispassion.
From the unmanifest, whatever is intended by their minds arises;
for the three qualities (guṇas) have been brought under control through dependence on that [mind] and by their very nature.
As Brahmā he is four-faced, and as the Ender (Kāla) he is remembered as Antaka;
as the Puruṣa with a thousand heads, these are the three states of the Self-born One.
In the state of Brahmā he creates the worlds; in the state of Time (Kāla) he withdraws them;
and in the state of the Puruṣa he remains indifferent—these are the three states of Prajāpati.
Brahmā has the luster of the interior of a lotus; Rudra resembles the fire of cosmic destruction;
and Puruṣa is lotus-eyed—such is the form of the Supreme Self.
In one way, in two ways, in three ways, and again in many ways,
Maheśvara creates and transforms bodies.
By his own sport, Maheśvara creates and transforms bodies that possess various forms, actions, appearances, and names.
Because he exists in the world in three ways, he is called "possessing the three qualities" (triguṇa);
because he is divided fourfold, he is celebrated as the "fourfold manifestation" (caturvyūha).
Because he attains, because he takes up, because he eats these objects,
and because his state is constant, he is therefore called the Self (ātman).
And because he is all-pervading, the Seer is his embodied self, since he is its Lord;
Viṣṇu is its master because everything enters into him.
The Blessed One is remembered as Śiva because of his auspiciousness arising from his stainless nature;
he is remembered as Oṃ because he is supreme due to his excellence and because he protects (ava).
Because he is all-knowing through his universal consciousness and because he consists of everything as the All,
having divided himself threefold, he sets the three worlds in motion.
He himself creates, devours, and protects by means of these three;
because he is the beginning (ādi), he is known as Ādideva, and because he is unborn, he is remembered as Aja.
Because he protects all creatures, he is remembered as Prajāpati;
and because he is the great god among the gods, he is therefore remembered as Mahādeva.
Because he pervades all, because he is not subject to others, and because he is great, he is remembered as Brahmā; and because he has come into being, he is called Bhūta.
The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is traditionally regarded as solitary because of his knowledge of the field and his oneness;
and because he dwells within the city (puryaṃ), he is called the Person (puruṣa).
Because he is without beginning and is primordial, he is remembered as the Self-Existent (Svayambhū);
because he is worthy of sacrifice, he is called the Sacrifice (Yajña); and because his vision is all-pervading, he is the Seer (Kavi).
He is Kramaṇa because he is to be stepped upon, and Pālaka because he protects;
known by the name Āditya, Kapila is indeed remembered as the first-born Agni.
He was the embryo within the Golden Egg (Hiraṇya), and he was born from the embryo of that very gold;
therefore, his status as Hiraṇyagarbha is explained in this Purāṇa.
Even for the self-existent one who has passed away, the duration of time belonging to that Universal Soul cannot be calculated, even in hundreds of years.
A period equal to the lifespan of Brahmā is known as a *parārdha*;
an equal amount of time remains for him, at the end of which he is re-absorbed.
Indeed, thousands of millions upon millions of days have passed; such is the number of kalpas that remain, as well as those yet to come. (The Vārāha Kalpa)
Now, learn of this eon (kalpa) that is currently proceeding, which is called Vārāha.
O twice-born ones, this first aeon (kalpa) of theirs is now current,
in which there are fourteen Manus, beginning with Svāyambhuva.
By those who were in the past, those who are present, and those who will indeed be in the future,
this entire earth— with its seven continents and its mountains— [is sustained].
Indeed, for a full thousand yugas, they must be protected by the Great Lords, by their subjects, and by ascetic penance; hear now the detailed account of them.
By means of a single Manvantara, all the intermediate periods (Antaras) are described; likewise, by means of one Kalpa, the entire Kalpa is indeed explained.
A wise person should apply reasoning to the past eons, including their endings and their subsequent successions, and likewise to those yet to come.
When the surface of the earth had perished, the waters indeed came into existence first;
in this world consisting solely of tranquil water, nothing whatsoever could be discerned.
Then, when that single ocean has arisen and all things mobile and immobile have perished,
Brahmā indeed comes into being, possessing a thousand eyes and a thousand feet.
The Puruṣa with a thousand heads, golden-hued and beyond the senses,
known as Brahmā Nārāyaṇa, then slept upon the waters.
Awakened by the predominance of the quality of sattva, he beheld the world as empty;
and in this regard, they cite this verse concerning Nārāyaṇa: LiP_1,70.118 // [End of verse]
"We have heard that 'the waters are the sons of Nara' (āpo nārāḥ) is the name of the waters;
since he made for himself a path (ayana) by filling it with them."
Because he lies within the waters, for that reason he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa; he remains there during the period of night that lasts for a thousand cycles of the four yugas.
At the end of the night, for the sake of creation, he assumes the state of Brahmā;
then Brahmā, having become the wind, moved within that water.
Then, like a firefly in the night during the rainy season, he perceived the earth submerged within that water. (The earth rose up from the water. LiP 1.70.122.
Through inference, he, being undeluded, again raised himself from the earth and assumed another body, just as before at the beginnings of the kalpas.
Then the high-souled Blessed One contemplated a divine form,
having seen the earth submerged in water on all sides.
"What form indeed should I assume to lift up this earth?"— thinking thus,
he entered the form of a boar, resembling one engaged in a water-sport.
Invincible to all beings, consisting of speech and known as Brahman,
he entered the subterranean realm (rasātala) for the purpose of uplifting the earth.
Having quickly approached that earth which was covered by the waters, Prajāpati lifted it up,
and he entered into the waters as well.
Indeed, those born of the ocean [were placed] in the oceans, and those born of rivers in the rivers;
she who was submerged at the bottom of the subterranean realm (rasātala) was brought to the surface of that realm.
For the sake of the welfare of the world, the Lord, the upholder of the earth, lifted the earth with his tusk and brought it back to its own place.
Having held him for a while, that upholder of the earth released him as before;
he stood upon that flood of water like a great ship.
Indeed, because it is equal in size to that [egg] due to its vast body, the earth does not undergo submersion;
therefore, the Lord, desiring to establish the world, lifted it up.
The lotus-eyed one set his mind upon the division of the earth;
having made the earth level, he established the mountains upon it.
But when the world was being consumed by the fire of universal destruction (saṃvartakāgni) prior to the creation,
those mountains of vast extent were shattered by that fire.
Due to the coldness in that single ocean, they were gathered together by that wind;
wherever they were poured down, there they became mountains.
Because they do not move, they are called *acala* (immovable); because they possess joints (*parvan*), they are known as *parvata* (mountains).
Indeed, they are called *giri* (mountains) because they swallow (*nigīrṇa*), and *śiloccaya* (masses of rock) because they lie prostrate (*śayāna*).
Then, when those mountains had been scattered by the millions,
Viśvakarman divided them again and again at the beginnings of the kalpas.
Then he further fashioned this earth together with its oceans, its seven continents, and its mountains,
as well as the four worlds beginning with Bhūḥ.
Having fashioned the worlds,
the self-existent Lord Brahmā, desiring to create various offspring, then indeed brought forth the creation of living beings.
As in former times at the beginning of the kalpas, he emitted a creation of that same nature;
indeed, as he meditated upon the creation, it was brought forth with deliberate intent.
Simultaneously with the intellect (buddhi), that which consists of darkness (tamas) appeared:
namely, darkness (tamas), delusion (moha), great delusion (mahāmoha), gloom (tāmisra), and what is known as blind gloom (andhatāmisra).
This fivefold ignorance manifested from the Great Soul;
as he meditated with self-conceit, the creation became established in five ways.
Enveloped by darkness and covered like a seed and its sprout,
it is without light within or without, motionless, and indeed devoid of consciousness.
Because their intellects were restrained and their senses were controlled,
they are therefore proclaimed as the foremost mountains, whose very selves are restrained (saṃvṛtātman).
Having seen that primary creation to be thus ineffective and unsuccessful, Brahmā,
with a dejected mind, then reflected upon another [creation].
As he was thus meditating, the Tiryaksrotas indeed came into being;
because it proceeded obliquely from him, it is therefore known as Tiryaksrotas.
Those twice-born ones who seize upon wrong paths are known as cattle and the like;
while he was indeed meditating on another [object], the Sāttvika [quality] arose from him.
The third is the Ūrdhvasrotas (Upstreamer), who is indeed established in the upward direction;
because he proceeds upward, he is therefore known as Ūrdhvasrotas.
Abounding in happiness and joy, restrained both internally and externally,
and luminous within and without, they are known as those whose stream flows upward.

Created through the yoga of *sattva* and arising from *sattva*, they are known as those whose stream flows upward (*ūrdhvasrotas*); this is indeed remembered as the third creation, the divine creation (*devasarga*).

Those who exist both outside and inside the Light, and are born from the upward stream (ūrdhvasrotas), are known as the ūrdhvasrotas; they are remembered by the wise as those whose souls are contented.
When the gods of the upward-stream (ūrdhvasrotas) had been created, the Lord Brahmā, the granter of boons, became filled with joy; thereafter, he directed his mind toward another [creation].
Then the Lord Īśvara, the master, indeed created another creation that was effective; as he was then meditating with true meditation, [the following occurred].
Then, from the Manifested, the practitioner known as Arvāk-srotas appeared;
because they turned back toward the lower direction, they are therefore called the Arvāk-srotasas.
They abound in light yet are mixed with darkness and dominated by passion (rajas);
therefore, they experience much suffering and act repeatedly.
Those humans and practitioners who are restrained both outwardly and inwardly are successful.
Indeed, they are established in eight ways by means of their characteristics, beginning with Tāraka.
Those humans who have perfected their souls possess the same nature as the Gandharvas;
this is known as the Taijasa creation, which is proclaimed as having its flow directed downwards.
The fifth is the creation of grace, which is established as fourfold:
through error, through power, through attainment, and likewise through contentment.
In stationary beings there is a perversion [of consciousness], while in animal births it occurs according to their capacity;
but perfected souls exist among humans, and they exist in their entirety among the ṛṣis and gods.

Thus, this is known as the primary (prākṛta) creation; the ninth is considered the modified (vaikṛta) creation. That which pertains to the elements beginning with the gross elements (bhūtādi) is called the sixth creation.
Furthermore, they indeed know the past and the present of those beings beginning with the Bhūtas, as well as the seventh creation itself.
All of them are possessive and again delight in sharing;
they should be known as those who relish [objects], those lacking in virtue, and those beginning with the elements (bhūta).
In the reverse order, beginning with the primary elements (bhūta), and established through incapacity (aśakti),
this first creation of Mahat is to be known as that which is traditionally recorded as belonging to Brahmā.
The second creation is said to be that of the subtle elements (tanmātra);
the third creation is known as the Vaikārika, which pertains to the senses.
Thus this primary creation (prākṛta-sarga) has arisen as preceded by intelligence;
the fourth is the primary creation of the principal beings (mukhya-sarga), and the immovable beings are indeed known as the principal ones.
Then follows the seventh creation, that of the downward-streaming beings, which is human; the eighth is the creation of grace, which consists of both the qualities of sattva and tamas.

These five are known as the modified (vaikṛta) creations, while three are remembered as the primary (prākṛta) ones; the ninth is remembered as the Kaumāra creation, which is both primary and modified.
The first three types of creations are known as natural (prākṛta) and occur without prior conscious intent;
however, those six belonging to Brahmā proceed with deliberate intention.
Listen now as the extensive account of creation, which bestows grace, is being proclaimed;
it exists in fourfold ways throughout all beings in their entirety.
Thus, these nine are recorded as being both natural (prākṛta) and modified (vaikṛta);
they are mutually affectionate and are known by the wise through their causes.
In the beginning, Brahmā indeed created from his own mind his mental sons who were equal to himself;
these two, Ṛbhu and Sanatkumāra, were both of perpetual celibacy.
Having arisen previously, they were the first-born of all even before those [others];
having passed through eight kalpas, they are the ancient witnesses of the world.
In the Vārāha [kalpa], however, having withdrawn their splendor into the earthly world (bhūrloka), those two remained there,
both intent on the practice of liberation, having established their own selves within the Self.
Having renounced progeny, dharma, and desire, and established themselves in dispassion,
that boy is called "Kumāra" here because he remains exactly as he was when born.
Therefore, his name is proclaimed here as Sanatkumāra;
[as well as] Sananda, Sanaka, Vidvān, and Sanātana.
Having desisted from consciousness, those of great power turned back;
the perfectly awakened ones likewise ceased from manifoldness, as did the yogins.
Without having brought about the creation of progeny, they returned once more to the state of dissolution;
then, when those had passed away, [Brahmā produced] other sons who were capable of accomplishing the task.
Brahmā again created from his mind the presiding deities of the various abodes,
by whom this earth is supported until the dissolution of all beings.
