Water, fire, earth, wind, the intermediate space, and likewise heaven;
the oceans and the rivers, as well as mountains and forest trees.
Likewise, the selves of herbs, of creepers, of trees and shrubs, as well as the twigs, the wood, the digits, the moments, the junctions, the nights, and the days; LiP_1,70.180.
The half-months, months, solstices, years, and yugas—
all these are known as the "Abiding" (sthāna) and the "Named after the Abode" (sthānākhya), for they possess the conceit of abiding in their respective positions.
Listen as I recount those great gods and sages:
Marīci, Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu.
He created Dakṣa, Atri, and Vasiṣṭha—these nine from his mind;
these are determined in the Purāṇas to be the nine Brahmās.
For all those who were of the nature of Brahman and exponents of Brahman,
the lotus-born one fashioned abodes as before.
Then he created Saṃkalpa and Dharma, which brings happiness;
by means of his resolve, the god Maheśvara created Dharma.
And from that very resolve, the Grandfather of all the worlds,
the lord Brahmā, begot a mind-born son named Ruci.
From his breath Brahmā created Dakṣa, and from his two eyes Marīci;
the sage Bhṛgu was born from the heart of him who was born from the waters.
From his head he created Aṅgiras, and likewise from his ear he created Atri; furthermore, from his udāna breath he created Pulastya, and from his vyāna breath, Pulaha.
From Samāna he created Vasiṣṭha, and from Apāna he fashioned Kratu;
these are remembered as the eleven divine sons of Brahmā.
Dharma and the others were all born first as the sons of Brahmā;
however, these nine, beginning with Bhṛgu, were created [later] and are exponents of the Veda.
Those ancient householders were the originators of that dharma;
their twelve lineages were divine and endowed with celestial qualities.
Possessing ritual action and progeny, they were adorned by great seers;
both Ṛbhu and Sanatkumāra are these two whose vital seed is drawn upward.
Having arisen previously, they are the foremost of all and the first-born of everyone;
having passed through eight kalpas, these two ancient ones are the witnesses of the world.
Having withdrawn their splendor, both remained established in the world;
both, having fixed their selves within the Self, were intent on the practice of yoga.
Having renounced progeny, dharma, and desire, and having established themselves in dispassion,
he who was born in that manner is here called "Kumāra."
Therefore, his name Sanatkumāra became established here;
then, as he meditated, mental offspring were born to him.
From the limbs of that wise one, the knowers of the field (kṣetrajñas) emerged together with those effects and causes produced from his body.
Then, desiring to create the fourfold [beings]— gods, asuras, ancestors, and humans— he joined his own self to these waters.
Then, as that Prajāpati was striving with effort to bring about creation, he meditated upon that which arises from the mere state of darkness (tamas).
Then, from his thighs, the Asuras were first born as his sons.
O Brahmins, "asu" is known to mean vital breath (*prāṇa*); because they were born from that, they are called Asuras.
He cast off that body by which all the Asuras had been created; that discarded body immediately became night. (Origin of the units of time [night, etc.; = 218]) LiP_1,70.201.
Since that [night] abounds in darkness, it is therefore restrictive;
moreover, because living beings are shrouded by darkness at night, they sleep.
Having then created the Asuras, he indeed assumed another body, unmanifest and abounding in the quality of goodness (sattva); thereafter, he honored that [body].
Then, as that Prajāpati was engaged in union, it was pleasing to him;
from his mouth, as he was sporting, the deities were born.
Because they were born from him as he was playing (divyan), they are proclaimed "devas";
the verbal root *div*, which has been declared, is understood here in the sense of sporting.
Because the deities were born from him while he was playing (divyan), they are called "devas";
having created the gods, the Lord of Devas then assumed another body.
That body was cast off by him, and immediately day was produced;
therefore, the gods worship that day as being endowed with dharma.
Then he perceived another [power] consisting solely of the quality of *sattva*;
as the Lord meditated upon those sons, regarding them as his own father, [this power arose].
For the Pitṛs came into existence from the two armpits at the junction of night and day;
therefore they are the Pitṛ-devas, and by that [reason] they possess the nature of Pitṛs.
The body by which he created the Pitṛs, he cast off;
that discarded body immediately became the twilight (saṃdhyā).
Since the day is known as the deity of the gods and the night as that of the asuras,
the body of the ancestors which lies between those two is indeed the most venerable.
Therefore, all the gods, asuras, sages, and likewise human beings,
filled with joy, worship that central form during both night and day.
Then indeed, Brahmā took on yet another body;
the Lord, by means of his mind, created [the world] from that which consists of the quality of rajas.
Then he begot from his mind sons who were dear to Rajas;
from that high-minded one, the Mānavas were born as his sons.
Having created the subjects once again, he cast off that body of his;
that discarded body immediately became moonlight.
Because living beings become overjoyed at the rising of the moonlight,
these forms were indeed cast away by that Great-Souled One.
Immediately, night and day, as well as the twilight and the moonlight, were born;
the triad consisting of moonlight, twilight, and day is composed of the quality of goodness (sattva).
Night consists of the quality of darkness (tamas); therefore, it is essentially nocturnal.
Consequently, the gods were indeed created from his mouth by means of satisfaction during the day.
Because their birth was during the day, they were indeed powerful by day;
therefore, the Lord created them from his front (tanū) for the sake of the Asuras, and [the others] from his back at night.
Because they were born at night and are strong by night, they are superior to the vital breaths;
these very ones shall be the future gods together with the asuras.
Indeed, these signs appear for the ancestors and for human beings throughout all the past and future Manvantaras.
Moonlight, night, day, and twilight—these are indeed the four ambhas; because they shine (bhānti), they are called ambhas by the wise.
The root *bhāti* is declared to mean "to shine"; furthermore, Prajāpati, having created these waters, [created] gods, humans, and dānavas.
Creating various kinds of ancestors again through his own body,
that Lord then cast off that body, the moonlight, and assumed another. (The origin of the Rākṣasas) LiP 1.70.224.
He worshipped that form, which was predominantly composed of *tamas* and *rajas*;
thereafter, the Lord created others who were overcome by hunger in the darkness.
Those created by him, whose nature was hunger, were intent on seizing the waters;
however, among them, those who spoke thus: "We shall protect these waters," [were the Rākṣasas].
Because those night-stalkers, overcome by hunger, said to one another joyfully, "O Yakṣas, give us water," they were named Rākṣasas.
By that karma, they are called *yakṣas* and *guhyakas* because of their secret deeds;
furthermore, this verbal root is explained as meaning "to protect" (*rakṣa*) and "to guard" (*pālana*).
And thus, the root *yakṣati* is etymologically explained as "to devour";
for upon seeing him, the hair of that wise one indeed withered away due to his displeasure.
Those who were shattered rose upwards and indeed ascended toward the Lord;
because they were inferior to his head-hairs, they are known as *avasarpins*.
Children are known as *vyāla* because they are like beasts of prey; they are known as *ahi* because of their inferiority;
they are called *pannaga* because of their falling [from the womb], and *sarpa* because of their crawling away.
That most terrible fire born of his wrath,
whose essence was poison, entered the serpents who were born together with him.
Having created the serpents, he then became enraged and produced beings whose very nature was anger; tawny in color and fierce, those creatures were eaters of flesh.
Because they were born from *bhūta*, they are remembered as *bhūtas*; because they devour flesh (*piśita*), they are *piśācas*. When he sang with a serene mind, the *gandharvas* were born.
The verbal root *dhā* is indeed recited in the sense of drinking;
because they were born while drinking speech (*vāc*), they are therefore remembered as Gandharvas.
When these eight divine classes had been created, that Lord then,
by his own will, created other birds according to their age.
Having created the self-willed [beings] from his own will, and birds according to their age, that Lord of Gods, having created the animals, also created the flocks of birds.
Then Brahmā emitted goats from his mouth, he created sheep from his chest, cows from his belly, and he brought forth [other creatures] from his two sides.
And from his two feet [he created] horses along with elephants, donkeys, sheep, wild beasts,
camels, mules, and other species as well.
Herbs bearing fruits and roots were produced from his body hair;
having thus created animals and herbs, the Lord employed them in the sacrifice.
The cow, goat, man, sheep, horse, mule, and donkey—these they call domestic animals; now learn of those that are indeed wild.
Beasts of prey, cloven-hoofed animals, elephants, monkeys with birds as the fifth,
aquatic creatures as the sixth, and reptiles as the seventh constitute the classes of animals.
Buffaloes, gavayas, monkeys, śarabhas, and wolves—
with the lion as the seventh among them— these are remembered as the wild animals of the forest.
From his first mouth, he fashioned the Gāyatra chant, the Ṛg-veda, the Trivṛt-stoma, the Sāman Rathantara, and the Agniṣṭoma among sacrifices.
From his southern mouth, he emitted the Yajus formulas, the Triṣṭubh metre, the fifteen-fold Stoma, the Bṛhat Sāman, and likewise the Ukthya sacrifice.
From his western mouth, he created the Sāman hymns, the Jagatī meter, the seventeenfold Stoma, the Vairūpa chant, and the Atirātra sacrifice.
From his northern mouth, he created the Ekaviṃśa, the Atharvāṇa, the Āptoryāmaṇa, the Anuṣṭubh, and the Svarāja.
In the beginning of the kalpa, the blessed Lord created lightning, thunderclouds, red clouds, Indra’s bow (the rainbow), and various splendors.
High and low beings were born from the limbs of that Prajāpati Brahmā as he was creating the emanation of progeny.
Having first created the fourfold group— gods, asuras, humans, and ancestors—
he then created all beings, both stationary and moving.
[He created] yakṣas, piśācas, gandharvas, and likewise the hosts of apsarases;
nāgas, kinnaras, and rākṣasas; birds, domestic animals, wild beasts, and serpents.
Both the imperishable and the perishable—whatever exists here, whether stationary or moving—their respective actions which they undertook in a previous creation; ||| LiP_1,70.252 |||
Being created again and again, they take on those very same dispositions:
violence and non-violence, gentleness and cruelty, righteousness and unrighteousness, truth and falsehood.
Impregnated by that, they enter it; therefore, that is what pleases them, once the great elements have been created, along with the objects of the senses and material forms.
The Creator himself ordained the specific functions of all beings;
yet some wise men declare that human effort is the cause of action.
Some Brahmins say it is destiny; those who contemplate the elements say it is inherent nature; and others say it is human effort, destiny, and the nature of the manifestation of results.
The wise do not perceive it as one, nor as distinct, nor as something additional to that;
and thus, it is neither one, nor both, even by way of different names.
Those established in karma speak with partiality, while those established in sattva possess equal vision;
they [understand] the name and form of beings, as well as the elaboration of created things.
In the beginning, that Great Lord fashioned from the very words of the Veda the names of the seers and those functions which are found in the Vedas.
At the end of the night, the Unborn One gives back those very same things to those who were born;
such are the creations of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest.
At the end of the night, they are seen having attained mental perfection;
thus were created all things, both the stationary and the moving.
O best of beings, when those creatures he had created did not multiply,
Brahmā, enveloped by the quality of darkness (tamas), was then afflicted with grief.
Then he formed a resolve directed toward the determination of his purpose;
next, he perceived within himself the limiting principle consisting of pure darkness (tamas).
Having abandoned passion and goodness while abiding by his own duty,
the Lord of the World then turned that sorrow into further sorrow because of it.
He subsequently dispelled darkness, and passion (rajas) enveloped that goodness (sattva). When that darkness was indeed driven back, a pair was born.
Adharma was born from Tamas, and Hiṃsā (Violence) was born from Śoka (Sorrow).
Then, when that pair of terrible nature had come into being, [the world became filled with suffering].
(Śatarūpā) had departed; the Blessed One remained, and Prīti took refuge in him.
Thereupon, Brahmā cast off that radiant body of his own.
Having divided his own body into two parts, he became a man with one half;
with the other half he became a woman, who was born as Śatarūpā.
The Lord indeed created that Prakṛti, the sustainer of beings, out of desire;
she stands presiding over heaven and earth, pervading them with her majesty.
That former body of Brahmā remains pervading the heavens;
from half of it, as he was creating, the woman Śatarūpā was born.
Having performed a million years of penance that was most difficult to practice,
that goddess obtained as her husband a man of radiant fame.
He, the primordial Person, is indeed called Svāyambhuva Manu;
his period of seventy yugas is here termed a manvantara.
That man obtained Śatarūpā as his wife, who was not born from a womb;
he took delight with her, and for that reason she is called Rati.
At the beginning of the kalpa, he first came into being as the self of union;
Brahmā created Virāj, and he became the Puruṣa Virāj. (Manu creates the creatures) LiP 1.70.274.
The sovereign Śatarūpā was indeed that Manu known as Vairāja;
that Manu Vairāja, the Puruṣa, brought forth the creation of progeny.
From the heroic Puruṣa Vairāja,
Śatarūpā gave birth to two sons, Priyavrata and Uttānapāda, who were esteemed by the world.
And there were two highly fortunate daughters, from whom these progeny were born:
the goddess named Kūti and Prasūti; both of them were indeed such.
The Lord Svāyambhuva gave Prasūti to Dakṣa;
Prāṇa is to be known as Dakṣa, and Saṃkalpa is called Manu.
Then he bestowed Ākūti upon Ruci Prajāpati;
from Ākūti, a beautiful pair of twins was born to the mental son Ruci.
Yajña and Dakṣiṇā were born as twins;
from Yajña and Dakṣiṇā, twelve sons were born.
In the Svāyambhuva interval, the gods were known as the Yāmas;
they were the sons of this Yajña, and therefore they are remembered as the Yāmas.
Aja and Śukra were the two groups created by Brahmā;
those Yāmas who were born previously became the inhabitants of heaven.
In Prasūti, the daughter of Svāyaṃbhuva and mother of the worlds,
the lord Dakṣa begot twenty-four daughters.
All those highly fortunate ones have lotus-like eyes;
they all possess enjoyments, and they are all mothers of yoga.
And all were expounders of Brahman, all mothers of the universe:
Śraddhā, Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Medhā, and likewise Kriyā.
The Lord Dharma accepted the thirteen daughters of Dakṣa— Buddhi, Lajjā, Vapuḥ, Śānti, Siddhi, and Kīrti— as his wives.
These wives were indeed appointed for him by the Self-Existent One; from them were born eleven other younger sons of beautiful eyes.
(The daughters and granddaughters of Dakṣa were:
Satī, Khyāti, then Saṃbhūti, Smṛti, Prīti, Kṣamā, as well as Saṃnati, Anasūyā, Ūrjā, Svāhā, and Svadhā.
They consented accordingly; furthermore, other great seers did so as well:
Rudra, Bhṛgu, Marīci, Aṅgiras, Pulaha, and Kratu.
Then Pulastya, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, the Pitṛs, and likewise Agni gave Satī to Bhava,
and Khyāti to Bhṛgu.
He gave Saṃbhūti to Marīci, Smṛti to Aṅgiras,
Prīti to Pulastya, and Kṣamā to Pulaha.
He gave Saṃnati by name to Kratu, Anasūyā to Atri, Ūrjā to Vasiṣṭha, and he also gave Svāhā to Agni.
And from Svadhā, for the ancestors, learn of their offspring;
all these highly fortunate ones remain following after their progeny.
Throughout all the Manvantaras, until the dissolution of all beings, Śraddhā gave birth to Kāma; and Darpas is remembered as the son of Lakṣmī.
The son of Dhṛti was Niyama, and the son of Tuṣṭi was Saṃtoṣa;
Lobha was the son of Puṣṭi, and likewise Śruta was the son of Medhā.
From Kriyā were born two sons, Daṇḍa and Samaya;
likewise, from Buddhi was born a son, Bodha, and Pramāda also arose.
Vinaya was the son of Lajjā, Vyavasāya was the son of Vasu,
Kṣema was the son of Śānti, and Sukha was born from Siddhi.
Yaśas and Kīrti were also his sons; these were the sons of Dharma.
Harṣa was indeed the son of Kāma, born of the goddess Prīti.
Thus has this creation of Dharma, which has a virtuous future, been proclaimed;
for from Adharma were born violence, deceit, and falsehood as his son.
From Nikṛti were born two [others]: Bhaya and Naraka;
and from these two arose a pair of twins, Māyā and Vedanā.
Then Māyā gave birth once more to Death (Mṛtyu), the destroyer of beings;
and from Vedanā was born Duḥkha, as well as Raurava.
From Death were born Disease, Old Age, Sorrow, Anger, and Envy;
for all these sons are characterized by suffering and are marked by unrighteousness.
They have no wives nor sons; indeed, all these are their possessions.
Thus was this tamasic creation born, which regulates dharma.
Commanded by Brahmā, "Create progeny," Nīlalohita meditated upon his wife Satī and fashioned from himself the Rudras, who are his mind-born and immortal sons.
He created those mental beings neither superior nor inferior to himself, equal to his own mind;
indeed, he produced a thousand times a thousand of those clad in skins.
All of them were equal to himself in form, splendor, strength, and learning;
they were tawny, equipped with quivers, wearing matted hair, and crimson-hued.
He saw those distinguished ones with golden hair, those who strike with their gaze, those carrying skulls,
those of great form, those of deformed shape, those of universal form, and those of beautiful form.
Charioteers, shield-bearers, those clad in armor, and those with protective fenders;
those with a hundred thousand arms, and those who are divine, terrestrial, or moving through the atmosphere.
Those with large heads, eight tusks, two tongues, and three eyes;
those who eat food, those who eat flesh, and those who drink clarified butter and soma.
Also the Mīḍhuṣas, the Atikapālas, the Śitikaṇṭhas, the Ūrdhvaretases,
the Havyādās, the Śrutadharmas, the Dharmiṇas, and then the Barhiṇas.
He saw thousands of beings composed of the five elements— some sitting, some running, some studying, some reciting, some chanting prayers, and others practicing yoga.
Those who possess smoke, those who blaze, those possessing rivers, and those of exceeding brilliance; likewise, the aged, the wise, those most devoted to Brahman, and those of auspicious appearance.
They had blue necks and a thousand eyes; they were all capable of enduring everything, invisible to all beings, great yogis of immense power.
Wandering about, rushing forward, and leaping by the thousands,
he created these Rudras, the foremost of the gods, who are never exhausted.
Seeing this, Brahmā said to him: "Do not create such offspring;
offspring should not be created who are equal to yourself. O God, let there be salutation to you!"
Create others—blessings be upon you—for these creatures are indeed joined with death;
for if death were known by the creatures, they would not undertake any actions.
Thus addressed, he said to him: "I shall not create offspring endowed with death and old age; may you be blessed. I remain [as I am]; you, create the offspring."
These indeed, who were created by me— multiform and blue-and-red—
are thousands upon thousands of offspring issued forth from my own self.
These gods shall become known as the Rudras, possessed of great power;
they shall pervade the earth, the intermediate space, and all the directions.
"The hundred Rudras shall become equal in essence," so say the ritualists;
"they shall become partakers of the sacrifice together with all the hosts of gods."
Those gods who will exist here in the various Manvantaras,
together with them being worshipped, they shall remain here until the end of the Yuga.
Thus addressed by the wise Mahādeva, the Prajāpati Brahmā,
bowing down and rejoicing, replied.
"So be it; may you be blessed, O Lord, according to what you have spoken.
Once Brahmā had granted his permission, everything indeed came to pass exactly as he had said.
From that time forward, the Lord of Gods indeed did not procreate offspring; remaining with his vital energy drawn up (ūrdhvaretas), Sthāṇu remained steadfast until the dissolution of all beings.
Because he said, "I am standing," he is remembered as Sthāṇu.
This god, the Great God, is the Puruṣa whose radiance is like that of the sun. (Śiva transforms into Ardhanārīśvara). LiP 1.70.325.
With a body half-woman and half-man, resembling a blazing fire in its splendor, he divided himself by his own will into two distinct parts: a woman and a man separately.
That very Supreme Lord stands there with half of the eleventh;
therein she who is the highly fortunate one, forming half the body of Śaṅkara.
The great goddess previously mentioned was indeed that very same virtuous woman who became a female here;
she was formerly propitiated by Dakṣa for the welfare of the worlds.
"For the sake of her task, [the Lord] was told by the god Śambhu: 'Divide yourself; your right side shall be white and your left side likewise black. (LiP 1.70.329)
Thus addressed, O twice-born ones, she became twofold—white and black.
I shall declare her names; listen with concentrated minds.
Svāhā, Svadhā, Mahāvidyā, Medhā, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Satī, Dākṣāyaṇī, Vidyā, and she who is the power of will (icchā-śakti) whose nature is action (kriyātmikā). LiP 1.70.331.
Aparṇā, Ekaparṇā, and likewise Ekapāṭalā;
Umā, Haimavatī, Kalyāṇī, and Ekamātṛkā.
Khyāti is the illustrious Prajñā, renowned in the world as Gaurī;
she is the Mother of the Gaṇas, the Great Goddess, Nandinī, and Jātavedasī.
Furthermore, because she manifests as separate bodies from this single form,
Sāvitrī is the bestower of boons, meritorious, purifying, and world-renowned.
Ājñā, Āveśanī, Kṛṣṇā, Tāmasī, Sāttvikī, Śivā,
Prakṛti, Vikṛtā, Raudrī, Durgā, Bhadrā, and Pramāthinī.
O you of excellent vows, these are the names— Kālarātri, Mahāmāyā, Revatī, and Bhūtanāyikā— in the division at the end of the Dvāpara age.
Gautamī, Kauśikī, Āryā, Caṇḍī, Kātyāyanī,
Satī, Kumārī, Yādavī, Devī, Varadā, and Kṛṣṇapiṅgalā.
Barhidhvajā, the wielder of the trident, the supreme practitioner of celibacy,
the sister of Mahendra and Upendra, Dṛṣadvatī, who bears a single trident.
Aparājitā, many-armed, bold, borne by a lion,
the slayer of the Daityas such as Śumbha, and the crusher of the great Mahiṣa.
Amoghā, Vindhyanilayā, Vikrāntā, and Gaṇanāyikā—
these are the various names of the Goddess in their proper order.
Those men who recite these words spoken by me to Bhadrakālī, which grant perfect fruit, for them no sin exists.
One should employ this protection in the forest or on a mountain, in a city or even in a house, whether in water or on land.
In places of fear from tigers, jackals, and thieves, and especially during all kinds of calamities, one should chant the names of the Goddess.
One should employ this protection for children who are afflicted by noble ancestors, seizing spirits, ghosts, and the Pūtanā mothers.
The two portions of Mahādevī are proclaimed as Prajñā and Śrī;
by these two, thousands of goddesses are manifested, by whom the entire world is pervaded.
By means of this [truth], that god of gods, the truthful Rudra Maheśvara,
the Supreme Lord, established himself for the welfare of all the worlds.
In ancient times, Rudra was Paśupati; by his splendor, the three cities were consumed, and all the gods became his subjects (paśus).
Whoever should read or even hear this auspicious sequence of the primordial creation,
or cause the best of the twice-born to hear it, goes to the world of Brahmā.
Thus ends the seventieth chapter, titled "The Expansion of Creation," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
The sages said:
The auspicious creation has been described by you both in brief and in detail;
how was it that Maheśvara became Paśupati in order to burn the city?
And how did the animals, along with the gods and Brahmā, formerly come to dwell in that city built by Maya through his ascetic power—a city so difficult to enter? O Lord!
We have heard that the unsurpassed divine city, made of gold, silver, and iron, which was so difficult to assail, was utterly consumed by the God of gods.
How did the Blessed One, the destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes,
burn him then with a single discharge of his divine arrow?
That triple city was not consumed by the beings produced by Viṣṇu;
the entire origin of that city and its former attainment of boons have been heard [by me].
"Now, O observer of noble vows, you ought to explain the entire process of cremation.
Having heard those words of theirs, Sūta, the best of Paurāṇikas, [replied].
Sūta said: Just as he had heard it from Vyāsa, the indicator of the welfare of the universe, he spoke accordingly:
"Indeed, due to the curse of this triple world arising from [faults of] mind, speech, and body..."
When the Daitya Tāraka had been slain along with his son Tāra and his kinsmen by Skanda through great effort, his sons, who were possessed of great strength, [arose].
Vidyunmālī, Tārakākṣa, and the heroic Kamalākṣa—
those great-souled ones of immense strength and prowess— performed austerities.
Having undertaken fierce austerity and remaining fixed in supreme discipline,
those best of Dānavas emaciated their own bodies through penance.
Their grandfather, being pleased and desiring to grant a boon, bestowed a favor upon them.
The Daityas said:
"Grant us invincibility against all beings at all times."
Together they chose the Grandfather of all the worlds;
then the imperishable God, the Lord of the worlds, spoke to them.
"There is indeed no such thing as immortality for all; therefore, O Asuras, desist from this!
Choose another boon, whatever may be pleasing to you."
Then those Daityas, having deliberated together with one another,
bowed down to Brahmā, the teacher of the world, and spoke to him.
"O Lord of the World, O Teacher of the Universe, by your grace we shall traverse this earth, having established ourselves in three cities."
Likewise, O sinless one, after thousands of years we shall meet with one another; these ancient cities shall also attain a state of oneness.
O Blessed One, if a god were then to strike these who have gathered together with but a single arrow, he would become our death.
Having replied to them, "So be it," the god entered heaven;
thereafter, the heroic Maya, by means of his own ascetic power, constructed the cities.
There was a golden city of theirs in heaven, one of silver in the intermediate space, and one of iron upon the earth, belonging to those great-souled ones.
Each is one hundred yojanas in equal width and length;
that of Tārakākṣa is made of gold, and that of Kamalākṣa is made of silver.
The iron fort of Vidyunmālin was indeed threefold and most excellent;
and there dwelt the powerful Maya, who is worshipped by the Daityas and Dānavas.
Having made his abode in gold, silver, and likewise in iron,
the powerful one then dwelt there.
O best of Brahmins, thus did the Daityas come to possess three cities that were exceedingly difficult to assail, like a second triple-world, O observers of excellent vows.
When the three cities had thus come into existence within the three worlds, all the Daityas entered those three cities and became superior in strength.
It was filled with wish-fulfilling trees (kalpadruma), crowded with elephants and horses,
interspersed with various palaces, and covered with networks of jewels.
It was adorned with celestial chariots resembling the solar disc, facing every direction,
made of rubies, brilliant, and shining like the moon.
Their three cities were adorned with divine palaces and gate-towers that resembled the peaks of Mount Kailāsa, each one individually unsurpassed.
It was completely filled with celestial women, Gandharvas, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas;
and in every house, O best of the twice-born, were temples of Rudra accompanied by the Agnihotra fire.
It was adorned on all sides with ponds, wells, lakes, and oblong pools,
as well as by herds of rutting elephants and magnificent horses.
And with chariots of various forms, diverse and facing every direction, as well as with assembly halls, porticos, and separate pleasure grounds.
Surrounded on all sides by various halls for Vedic study,
it was unassailable even in thought by others, owing solely to the illusory power of Maya.
O best of sages, this piety of the inhabitants of Tripura is practiced everywhere by women devoted to their husbands;
even after committing very great sins, they become free from sin through the worship of Śaṅkara.
O twice-born ones, [he was attended] by the illustrious lords of the Daityas, together with their wives and sons,
who were always devoted to that dharma and were knowers of the meaning and duty of the Śrauta and Smārta rites.
Having abandoned any other deity than Mahādeva, they remain intent upon his worship—
men with broad chests and shoulders like bulls, who always carry all manner of weapons.
[He was surrounded] at all times by those who were hungry, whose eyes resembled forest fires,
by those who were tranquil and those who were enraged, as well as by hunchbacks and dwarfs.
With hair as dark and curly as the petals of the blue lotus,
resembling the dark-blue peaks of Mount Meru, with voices like the roar of clouds,
all of them protected by Maya, well-trained, and eager for battle.

Then, that place was well-served by those who delight in battle, who have always attained valor through the worship of Śiva’s feet on all sides, who resemble the Sun, the Maruts, and Indra, and who are the destroyers of the gods, firm and steadfast.
O best of the twice-born, the gods, including Indra, were consumed by the fire of the three cities due to the power of the Daityas, just as trees are consumed by a forest fire.
Then, having been thus consumed, those gods paid homage to Hari, the Lord of Gods, and spoke to him of incomparable splendor.
That glorious Nārāyaṇa, the Lord, also reflected in his mind:
"What task among the duties of the gods remains for the Blessed One?"
Then Janārdana, whose form is sacrifice, remembered the sacrifice—
he who is the sacrificer, the enjoyer of the sacrifice, the sovereign lord, and the master who bestows the fruits upon those who perform sacrifices.
Then, for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods' work, sacrifice was ordained by him;
at that time, they bowed down to the God and the Puruṣa and praised them.
The Blessed One, having seen that sacrifice, spoke to Sanātana;
then the infallible Sanātana, looking toward the gods including Indra, [spoke].
The illustrious Viṣṇu said:
"O gods, with this *upasad* rite, worship the Supreme Lord for the destruction of the three cities and for the prosperity of the three worlds."
Sūta said: Then, having heard those words of the wise God of gods,
the deities let out a great lion’s roar and praised the Lord of Sacrifice.
Then, having reflected, the Blessed One Janārdana himself,
the lord of the thirty gods, spoke again to all those deities.
Even if one has killed or burned living beings, or consumed [food] unjustly, if one worships Mahādeva, one becomes sinless; of this there is no doubt.
Those who are sinless must certainly not be killed, while those who are sinful must be killed without a doubt;
yet, O best of gods, how can they be slain with all one's effort? How can they be put to death?
Although the Asuras are intoxicated with pride and wicked, they are not to be slain by the gods of great strength, because of the power of Rudra, the Supreme Lord.
Who am I— whether Brahmā, or the gods, or the Daityas who are the slayers of the enemies of the gods,
or even the high-souled sages— without the grace of the Lord?
He who is the twenty-seventh, eternal, the Lord higher than the highest,
the sovereign of all the immortals, the one worthy of worship, the support of the universe, the Great Lord (Maheśvara).
He alone is the Lord of all gods and the benefactor of all;
by his divine play, the Destroyer made the distinction between the lords of gods and daityas.
By worshipping one part of that [being], the gods attained godhood;
Brahmā attained the state of Brahmā, and I likewise attained the state of Viṣṇu.
In this world, what man desiring success would fail to worship him?
Therefore, by the power of the ritual for the worship of the *liṅga*, he alone must be slain.
All of them were devoted to the Dharma and established in the performance of rites prescribed by the Vedas and the Smṛtis;
nevertheless, having worshipped the Lord Rudra according to the rules with a fierce *upasad* sacrifice, we shall conquer the foremost of the Daityas.
Who indeed, other than the one blessed Lord with three eyes, is capable of destroying Tripura— which is protected by Maya with his starry eye, self-contained, hidden, and singular like a crystal?
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus and having performed the sacrifice with the Upasad rite for the Lord,
Hari sat down and then beheld hosts of beings by the thousands.
At that time, they were equipped with various weapons and wore diverse garbs, holding spears, javelins, and clubs in their hands, as well as axes, stones, and rocks.
Then the Lord Hari, the Master himself, spoke to those who stood before him prostrate, who resembled the Rudra of the Kālāgni fire and were like Kālarudra.
Viṣṇu said:
"O heroes, having burned, pierced, and consumed the three cities of the Daityas,
you ought to return as you came for the sake of our prosperity."
Then, having bowed to the Lord of Gods, all those hosts of beings entered the three cities and perished like moths in a fire.
Then, by the command of the Lord of Gods, all those beings vanished;
meanwhile, thousands of Daityas danced, rejoiced, and sang.
They praised the Lord of the gods of gods, the Supreme Self, the Sovereign;
then, in an instant, the gods were utterly defeated and their prowess destroyed.
Accompanied by Indra, they gathered and stood before Upendra, the lord of gods, out of fear;
seeing them, the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, reflected.
Burning with anxiety as to what ought to be done, he pondered for a moment over those who were themselves tormented, including Indra, thinking:
"How indeed can I, through diligent effort, destroy the strength of those Daityas?"
"By the grace of the Supreme Lord, I shall perform the work of the gods;
for those who are most righteous, there is no sin when acting with discernment—of this there is no doubt."
Therefore, those Daityas cannot be slain by beings born from the Upasadas;
for one dispels evil through dharma, and everything is established in dharma.
"Sovereignty comes from dharma"—this is the eternal Vedic revelation;
for all these Daityas, the inhabitants of Tripura, are indeed most righteous.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, they have attained invincibility and not otherwise;
for those who worship Rudra remain so even after committing very great sins.
They are liberated from all sins, just as a lotus leaf is untouched by water;
through worship, O twice-born ones, the attainment of enjoyments necessarily arises.
Therefore, those Daityas, who were devoted to the worship of the *liṅga* and possessed of enjoyments,
created an obstacle to dharma for me by means of their own *māyā*, O gods.
"For the sake of the gods' purpose, I shall conquer Tripura from the Daityas in an instant.
Sūta said:
Having reflected thus, the Blessed One, Puruṣottama, [spoke] to them.
And he resolved to create an obstacle to the dharma of the enemies of the gods.
And the one of great splendor,
the infallible master of illusion, created from himself a person composed of illusion for the purpose of obstructing their dharma.
Assuming forms at will, the Illusionist Teacher, who deludes all beings, composed the scripture for everyone, accompanied by visible proofs.
Having taught this scripture consisting of sixteen hundred thousand verses, which is composed of illusion, to the Puruṣa who was born from his own body, the Illusionist [departed].
That which contradicts the Śruti and Smṛti, which is devoid of the system of castes and stages of life,
and which presents heaven and hell as occurring right here— such a thing is not otherwise.
Having personally taught that scripture to the Puruṣa,
Hari, the Infallible One, spoke to that Puruṣa for the sake of destroying the three cities.
O Lord, you ought to go swiftly for the destruction of the city-dwellers;
let the duties prescribed by the Vedas and the Smṛtis perish without a doubt.
Then, having bowed to him, that master of illusion, the sage who was highly skilled in the science of magic,
quickly entered that city and performed his magical arts.
Through his illusory power, those Daityas residing in the three cities abandoned the Vedic and Smṛti traditions and then became his disciples.
And they abandoned Mahādeva, Śaṅkara, the Supreme Lord;
and then Nārada too, the master of illusion, [did so] by the command of the Lord who is the master of illusion.
Having entered that city with that master of illusion,
the sage himself, surrounded on all sides by his disciples and grand-disciples, was initiated.
And he established the dharma of women, which brings about the attainment of the fruits of even evil conduct;
having obtained it, those women always immediately received its results.
Having reviled those women who held their husbands as deities, they became attached to men;
even today, O Sage, this is due to the weight of that sage Nārada’s influence in the Kali age.
Wretched and base women wander about at will, abandoning their husbands;
for women, the mother, father, kinsman, companion, friend, and relative are all [mere sources of attachment].
"He is indeed her husband, there is no doubt; nevertheless, even if she has committed a very great sin through deceit, she who is filled with love for her husband [is purified]."
One would attain the supreme heaven, and by the opposite course, hell;
O tigers among sages, in former times a certain woman always [sought] all dharmas from her husband.
Having abandoned [other gods] and worshipped no other deities who are the teachers of the world,
those virtuous women reach the heavenly realm and rejoice, freed from all distress.
Another went to hell; therefore, the husband is the supreme refuge.
Nevertheless, they abandoned their own husbands and became self-willed in their conduct.
By the power of the illusion of Viṣṇu, the God of gods, and by the command of that Lord,
Alakṣmī herself went to Tripura at his direction.
That fortune which they had obtained through their ascetic penance from the Lord of the Gods was cast out by the command of the sovereign Brahmā.
Having bestowed upon them that state of mental delusion produced by the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu, the god and the illusory Nārada remained there for a moment, O Nārada.
Seated comfortably and unperturbed, the two imperishable ones were intent on obstructing the Dharma;
thus, at that time, the most beautiful Dharma of the Śruti and Smṛti was destroyed.
When that heresy had been proclaimed by Viṣṇu, the source of the universe, and when Maheśvara was abandoned as well as the worship of the liṅga by the Daityas; 71.94.
When the entire dharma of women had perished and wicked conduct was established,
the Lord of the Gods, as if his purpose were fulfilled, [approached] Umāpati together with the gods.
Having attained the Omniscient One through austerity, Puruṣottama offered praise.
The Blessed Lord said: "Salutations to you, Maheśvara, the divine, the Supreme Self."
Salutations to you, who are Nārāyaṇa, Śarva, and Brahmā in the form of Brahman; salutations to you, the eternal, the infinite, and the unmanifest.
Sūta said:
Having thus praised Mahādeva and prostrated himself like a staff,
the Blessed One remained in the water and recited the Rudra-mantra ten million times.
And all those gods, including Indra, the Sādhyas, Yama, the Rudras, and the hosts of Maruts, praised the Supreme Lord.
The gods said:
"Obeisance to you, the soul of all, to Śaṅkara, the remover of affliction;
to Rudra, Nīlarudra, Kadrudra, and Pracetas."
The crusher of the enemies of the gods is our refuge at all times; he is to be worshipped by us.
You are the beginning, you are the infinite, the endless, and the imperishable Lord.
O Teacher of the World, you are Prakṛti and Puruṣa manifest; you are the creator, the destroyer, the protector, and the leader in this world, O lover of the twice-born.

The bestower of boons, consisting of speech, yet expressible as that which is spoken, he is devoid of both the expressed and the expression; the Lord is to be worshipped by yogis through the various manifestations of yoga for the sake of liberation.
The wise declare that the existent one, whose nature is the supreme Brahman, always resides within the hollow of the heart-lotus of yogins.
"O Lord, in this world, the noble ones call you the Reality, the mass of splendor beyond the supreme, and the Supreme Self. (LiP 1.71.105)
O Teacher of the World, everything seen, heard, and existing, and all that is being born,
is said to be smaller than the smallest and greater than the greatest.
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces on all sides, and with ears everywhere in the world, You abide pervading everything.
To you, the Great God, the indefinable, the omniscient, the one free from affliction;
to the one whose form is the universe, the three-eyed one, the eternally auspicious, the one free from affliction—[I bow].
Resembling ten million suns, resembling ten million moons,
and resembling ten million fires of cosmic destruction, he is the twenty-sixth principle, the Lordless One.
They call him the initiator in this world, the great-grandfather of primordial nature (prakṛti),
the boon-granting god, the abode of all, and the self-existent one.
People who know the essence of the Vedas recognize you, the essence of the Vedas, through the Vedas themselves.

O you of manifold forms, that which has never been seen by us in this world has now been brought about by you alone— the hosts of Daityas, Asuras, and spirits, as well as gods, humans, and all things mobile and immobile.
"Protect us, O Śambhu; there is no other refuge for us after you have struck down the foremost of the Asuras, for all of us have been deluded by your Māyā, O Supreme Lord."
Just as waves and masses of billows fight one another within the ocean,
yet remain inert because they are supported by water, so too is everything of the Unborn (Ajā).
Sūta said:
The man who, having risen at dawn and become pure, should recite or listen to this meritorious hymn shall obtain all his desires.
Thus praised by the gods and through the chanting of Viṣṇu’s name, Maheśvara,
smiling and placing Nandin’s hand in his own, then embraced Soma.
Looking upon the gods, Śaṅkara spoke with a profound voice:
"O lords of the gods, this task of the gods has now been understood by me."
O best of gods, [you witnessed] the power of Viṣṇu’s māyā and that of the wise Nārada against those Daityas who were devoted to unrighteousness.
"And I shall bring about the destruction of the three cities, O best of gods.
Sūta said:
Then the gods, together with Brahmā, Indra, and Upendra, assembled.
Having heard those words of the Lord, they then bowed down and offered praises;
meanwhile, in that interval, the Goddess, beholding the God, was filled with wonder.
Striking him with a toy lotus, she spoke these words to the bull-bannered god:
"O Lord, behold the six-faced one playing, resplendent like the sun. Thus the goddess said.
[He saw] his son, the best among those who have sons, adorned with auspicious ornaments— namely,
crowns, bracelets, earrings, and beautiful bangles.
With anklets, covered bracelets, as well as waist-bands, with many small bells, and with golden leaves of the *aśvattha* tree; LiP_1,71.123 //

Adorned with auspicious locks of hair beautified by flowers born from the wish-fulfilling trees, and likewise with necklaces, armlets, and various gems such as those of the color of lotuses; ||| LiP_1,71.124 |||
O Mahādeva, behold your son, who is most beautiful, adorned with necklaces made of pearls that possess a luster equal to the full moon, and with forehead marks.
O Lord, behold the multitude of faces marked with saffron and other pigments, fashioned from ashes in a circular form, like a cluster of *kāmalaka* flowers.
And behold, O Lord, the auspicious eyes and the various ointments brought by the Mothers for the sake of auspiciousness.
Thus Śiva was awakened by the words of the Mother of the World, specifically by Gaṅgā and the others, Kṛttikā and the others, and Svāhā.
Drinking the nectar from Skanda’s mouth, the Lord did not reach satiety,
nor did he remember those gods who had been oppressed by the weapons of the Daityas.
Embracing Skanda and smelling his head, he said, "Dance, my son!
And that Lord, the remover of suffering, being playful and graceful, began to dance as a child.
Other lords of the Gaṇas danced together with him;
at the command of the Lord, the entire three worlds danced there for a moment.
All the nāgas danced, and the gods, led by Indra, praised Skanda; the hosts of attendants and the mothers rejoiced.
The Gandharvas and Kinnaras showered rains of flowers and sang;
having then drunk that nectar of dance, Pārvatī and the Supreme Lord attained satisfaction, as did Nandin and the lords of the Gaṇas.
Then Nandin, together with the six-faced one (Kārttikeya) and likewise with the daughter of the King of Mountains, entered the divine abode;
and Bhava too, resembling a cloud, entered like one cloud merging into another.
Standing by the side of the door of that wise god,
the deities praised Mahādeva with their minds somewhat anxious.
But some, looking at one another and saying "What? What?", were thus distressed;
others said, "We are indeed sinners," while still others said, "We are unfortunate."
"Other lords of the gods say that the lords of the Daityas are fortunate;
others say this is the fruit of their worship, while still others say it is not."
In the meantime, having heard their various cries,
the highly effulgent Kumbhodara struck the gods with his staff.
Overcome by fear, the gods fled, crying out "Alas! Alas!", while other sages and deities fell to the surface of the earth.
"Aho! Such is the power of destiny," said the sages, Kaśyapa and the others, even after beholding the Lord of the gods and the enemies of the Asuras.
"Due to misfortune, the task was not completed," said other twice-born ones;
having worshipped [the mantra] "Namas Śivāya" within their hearts, they performed it in a much more abbreviated manner.
Then there was the matted-haired Nandīśa, the sage beloved of Mahādeva,
bearing a trident, wearing a garland, likewise carrying a plow, adorned with earrings and bracelets, and holding a club.
Then, by his command, he mounted a very white bull and departed;
thereafter, seeing Nandin, that Gaṇa Kumbhodara also [set out].
Having bowed his head to Nandin, he departed in haste along with him;
Nandin, of great splendor and bearing the bull-banner, shone resplendent upon the back of the bull.
Accompanied by his retinue, the commander of the host was like Bhava upon the back of a cloud;
[the chariot] was ten yojanas in width and adorned with nets of pearls.
That white umbrella shines like the sky above a mountain;
within it is fixed a beautiful garland made of pearls.
Just as the Gaṅgā falling from the sky shines upon the head of the All-pervading Lord, so too,
having seen the leader of the Gaṇas, the auspicious celestial drums resounded.

At the command of the Wielder of the Thunderbolt (Indra), all the preeminent sages broke into applause and praised the auspicious Lord of the Gaṇas, the bestower of desired boons, with pleasing words.
Just as the gods, upon seeing Bhava, had their skin bristle with joy,
so too did the sky-dwellers, by the command of the wielder of the thunderbolt, shower a rain of flowers upon his head.
And the delighted clouds rained down a fragrant shower from the sky;
satisfied by that rain, he then shone with a contentment that was truly nourishing.
May Nandin go forth from existence after bathing with fragrant water;
there, that back of the bull shines with various kinds of flowers.
O you of excellent vows, Nandin, covered with flowers, shone upon the back of the bull like the surface of the sky crowded with stars.
Just as the moon on the back of the sky is surrounded by the stars, O you of excellent vows,
so did the gods, including Indra and Upendra, behold Nandin in that manner.
They praised the Lord of the Gaṇas, as if he were another God of Gods.
The gods said:
"Salutations to you, the devotee of Rudra and one who delights in the recitation of the Rudra-mantra."
Salutation to you, the lord of the hosts of Kūṣmāṇḍas, the master of yogins, who delights in fierce deeds for the sake of destroying the suffering of those devoted to Rudra.
Salutations to you, the giver of all, the refuge, the omniscient, the remover of suffering,
the Lord of the Vedas, and the one known through the Vedas.
To you, the wielder of the thunderbolt, with thunderbolt-like fangs, who wards off the thunderbolt of the wielder of the thunderbolt;
whose body is adorned with the thunderbolt, and who has been propitiated by the wielder of the thunderbolt.
Salutations to you who are red, with red eyes, and wearing red garments;
to you whose lotus feet are the refuge of those who are red, and who bestow the world of Rudra.
Salutation to the Lord of the armies, salutation to the Lord of the Rudras;
salutation to the Lord of the spirits and the lords of the worlds, the remover of sin.
Salutations to you, Rudra, the Lord of Rudras, who removes terrible sins;
salutations to you, the auspicious and gentle one, devoted to Rudra.
Sūta said: Then the leader of the Gaṇas, the son of Śivā, being pleased, spoke to the gods regarding the chariot, the charioteer, the bow, and the excellent arrow of Śambhu.
"You ought to strive to restore the three cities, considering them as lost.
Then they, together with Brahmā and likewise with Viśvakarman, [set about this task].
Greatly exerting themselves, they fashioned a chariot for the wise God of gods.
Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, titled "The Words of Nandikeśvara during the Burning of the City," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
(Śiva’s chariot for the destruction of Tripura) Now, a divine chariot composed of all the worlds was constructed with great care and reverence by Viśvakarman for the god Rudra. LiP 1.72.1.
He consists of all beings and is saluted by all the gods;
he consists of all the gods, is golden, and is honored by everyone.
The right side of the wheel is Sūrya, and the left side is indeed Soma;
for the right has twelve spokes, while the upper (left) has sixteen.
O best of brahmins, the twelve Ādityas are in those [twelve] spokes;
O you of excellent vows, the sixteen digits (kalās) of the moon Vāma are in the sixteen spokes.
And at that time,
O best of brahmins, the stars were the ornaments of his left side, while the six seasons were the rims of those two wheels.
The Puṣkara island is indeed the interior of the chariot, and Mount Mandara is the chariot-box;
both the Sunset Mountain and the Sunrise Mountain are known as the two poles.
Mount Meru is its foundation, the Kesara mountains are its supports;
its speed is a year, and its two solstices are the junctions of its wheels.
The *muhūrta*s are known as his neck; the *kalā*s are his yoke-pins (*śamyā*);
the *kāṣṭhā*s are known as his nostrils, and the *kṣaṇa*s are indeed his axle-shafts.
The twinklings of his eyes and the subsequent pullings of the reins are known as his *lava*s;
the sky is the fender of this chariot, and both heaven and liberation are its two banners.
Dharma is his detachment; his staff is known as sacrifice, upon which the staffs depend.
His sacrificial fees are the joints, and the fifty fires are his metals.
Both his dharma and kāma are remembered as the two ends of the yoke-pole at the end of the eon;
likewise, the unmanifest (avyakta) is its shaft, and his intellect (buddhi) is the reed-bed (naḍvala).
Likewise, the corners are the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), and the elements are known as his strength;
the sense organs are his ornaments on all sides.
Faith is his vehicle, and the Vedas are known as his horses;
the [Vedic] words are his ornaments, while the six auxiliary sciences (ṣaḍaṅga) are his secondary ornaments.
O you of excellent vows, the Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, and the Dharmaśāstras,
as well as the Vālakhilyas and the Paṭas, are all endowed with every auspicious characteristic.
The mantras are known as the bells; their phonemes are the feet, as well as the stages of life (āśramas).
The infinite Avaccheda is indeed adorned with a thousand hoods.
The cardinal directions are the feet of this chariot, as are the intermediate directions;
its banners, beginning with the lotus, are made of gold and adorned with jewels.
The four oceans are known as his chariot blankets;
the Ganges and other excellent rivers are all adorned as his ornaments.
With the tips of their hands grasping chowries, all of them, adorned with the beauty of feminine forms,
stood here and there and graced the chariot.
Likewise, there are seven steps beginning with Āvahā, made of excellent gold;
the Lord Brahmā is known as the charioteer, and the gods are remembered as the holders of the reins.
The *praṇava* is the goad of that Brahman, whose deity is Brahman;
the Lokāloka mountain stands all around it as its surrounding staircase.
At that time, the external Mānasādri is uneven, yet it is exceedingly beautiful; all the mountains surrounding its nose are likewise recorded as being such.
The *tala* mountains were the pigeons (*kapota*), and all those dwelling upon the *tala* mountains were the *kāpota* birds;
Mount Meru was the great umbrella, and Mandara was the side-drum.
The Lord of Mountains [became] his bow, the King of Serpents himself became the bowstring,
and likewise here, Kālarātri as well as Indrāyudha [became the arrows].
The goddess Sarasvatī is the bell, appearing as the sacred revelation (Śruti) of the bow;
Viṣṇu of great splendor is the arrowhead, and Soma is the shaft of the arrow.
The fire of time (Kālāgni) is the sharp and most terrible arrow of that [deity] himself;
the army is produced from poison, and the winds are known as the horses.
Having thus fashioned the divine chariot, as well as the bow and the arrow,
he likewise appointed Brahmā— the Lord and Sovereign— as the charioteer of the worlds.
Bhava, the ornament of the battlefield, ascended his divine chariot,
which was yoked with all the hosts of gods, as if making heaven and earth tremble.
(Śiva mounts the chariot) While being praised by the sages and lauded by the bards,
he was accompanied by throngs of Apsarases skilled in the dance, who performed before him.
Looking upon his charioteer, the boon-granting Lord, shining with great splendor,
ascended that prepared chariot which was provided for the sake of the world.
The horses born of the Vedas fell to the earth with their heads bowed;
then, beneath this chariot, the Blessed One, the upholder of the earth, appeared.
Having raised him up in the form of a lordly bull, he indeed caused him to stand for a moment;
in another moment, the lordly bull also went to the ground upon his knees.
With reins in hand, the Lord, the omnipresent one, raised the horses and,
by the command of the God, stationed the auspicious chariot.
Then he urged on the horses, which possessed the speed of thought and the wind,
toward the cities situated in the sky belonging to the powerful Dānavas.
Then the Blessed Lord Rudra, the benefactor Śaṅkara, looking toward the gods, said:
"The lordship over all creatures has been granted to me; therefore, I shall slay the asuras."
O best of gods, having conceived the state of being a separate sacrificial animal for the gods as well as for others, they are to be slain; it cannot be otherwise, O most excellent ones.
Having heard all these words of the wise God of gods,
they all fell into despondency, apprehensive regarding their state as sacrificial animals.
Having understood their state from that, the God spoke this to them:
"O best of the gods, let there be no fear in you regarding this state of being cattle."
Listen to the liberation from the state of being a beast, and let it be performed:
whoever shall practice the divine Pāśupata [vow] will indeed be liberated.
"O you who are composed, it is true that I have vowed this because of my state as a *paśu*;
and so too shall others who shall practice my Pāśupata vow."
O best of gods, there is no doubt that they shall be liberated from their state as animals after observing the vow for twelve years, or its half, which is three years.
He who causes [others] to perform service is liberated from the state of a beast;
therefore, O best of gods, you shall practice this supreme, divine [duty].
"So be it," the gods replied to Śiva, who is honored by the worlds;
therefore, O Lord, all beings—gods, asuras, and humans—are indeed his cattle (paśus).
Rudra is indeed Paśupati, the liberator from the bonds of the bound soul (paśu); by means of this vow, one should renounce both that which is the bound soul and its state of being bound.
"Having performed that, one does not become more sinful"—such is the certainty of the scripture.
Then Vināyaka appeared in person as a boy, yet possessing the prowess of one who is no child. (Ganesha was pacified. LiP 1.72.44.

Then, not being worshipped by the gods, Śrī Vināyaka spoke, restraining the gods: "Without worshipping me in this world with auspicious foods, both solid and soft, [you shall not succeed]. (LiP 1.72.45)
"Who among men attains perfection—a god or even a dānava?
Then, at that very moment, regarding that task of the gods, the lords of the deities [spoke].
"O Lord of Gods, how shall I create an obstacle for those who are prepared to act?
Then all the gods, including Indra, became afraid and worshipped that Lord.
With various kinds of foods, both hard and soft, as well as with sweets and *uṇḍaras*,
they addressed Gaṇeśāna, saying, "May we always be free from obstacles."

Then Bhava, the foremost of all the lords of the gods, having embraced and smelled his son, worshipped Gaṇeśa with many flowers and with various savory, fragrant foods fit for eating and chewing. Having thus worshipped Vināyaka, the worshipful one and the leader of the lords, together with the hosts of deities, [he departed].
Accompanied by the lords of the Gaṇas, he, whose bow was as great as the king of mountains, went forth to burn the three cities.

Then the hosts of gods and siddhas, all the multitudes of spirits, and the lords of the gaṇas headed by Nandin— those sovereigns— followed that Lord of Gods, Maheśvara, the Lord, each with his own vehicle.

Then, at the head of the hosts of gods and lords of the Gaṇas, Nandin mounted a celestial chariot resembling the king of mountains and went forth to strike the city, like the Lord Viṣṇu approaching Death.
Then, as the son of Śilāda departed, having mounted the best of serpent-kings, bull-kings, and horse-kings,
all the gods and the leaders of the Gaṇas went forth, their hands bearing the marks of their own weapons.

Mounting the king of birds, who resembled the king of mountains, the one whose banner is a bird— his power undiminished— proceeded to the left of Śambhu for the sake of the welfare of the worlds in order to burn the three cities. All the gods followed that immeasurable lord of the world of the gods from every side.
The thousand-rayed Lord, the fierce one, [shone] as the sovereign of the gods and demons;
the Lord, whose color is like the petals of a lotus, shone in the midst of the gods like a wedding procession,
just as the thousand-rayed Lord, the fierce one, shines when mounted upon the peak of Mount Sumeru.
The thousand-eyed Indra, the foremost of the gods, mounted the lord of elephants and went to the city of Rudra on its right side to slay him, just as Vainateya goes there to slay serpents.

The heroes among the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and lords of the gods praised from all sides that Indra, the lord and sovereign over the hosts of the gods, the bestower of desired boons; they hailed Śakra with cries of "Victory! amidst a rain of excellent flowers.

Then, seeing the Lord of the Gods, the Lord of the World— who had been Ahalyā’s paramour— the inhabitants of heaven prostrated before the thousand-eyed one, just as Ambā playfully bows to her son Indra.
Yama, Agni, Kubera, Vāyu, and Nirṛti likewise [paid homage].
Likewise, Apāmpati, Īśāna, and Bhava have also assembled together.
Vīrabhadra, auspicious in battle, was indeed at the southwest of the chariot;
he had mounted the lord of bulls and was covered with hair.
Possessing great splendor, like another Mahādeva, Mahākāla performed service to the three-eyed God of gods in order to destroy Pura.
In the northwestern direction, he performed the service of the chariot together with his attendants.

The six-faced one, resembling the king of mountains, was accompanied by the Siddhas and Cāraṇas and his army; likewise, the one born from fire was surrounded by the hosts of the gods' lords and mounted upon an elephant.
Having removed the obstacles of the lords of the asuras and ensuring there were no obstacles for the gods, the Lord Gaṇeśa,
the Master of Obstacles, together with his hosts of attendants, went to that place, the abode of Īśāna.

Then Kālī, adorned with a skull-ornament and intoxicated by drinking the honey-wine of the great asuras' blood, brandished with her hand a trident that possessed the luster of the night of destruction, while shaking the lords of the gods.

With eyes rolling from intoxication, she who moves like a rutting elephant went before the Lord of the Gaṇas, her body draped in garments of the skins of intoxicated elephants, accompanied by intoxicated Piśācas and hosts of Gaṇas.
The foremost among the Siddhas, Gandharvas, Piśācas, Yakṣas, Vidyādharas, lords of serpents,
and lords of gods, bowed deeply to her and loudly praised the goddess, the daughter of the Snow Mountain, saying, "Victory!"
The Mothers, who destroy the enemies of the foremost gods and are duly honored by the hosts of deities,
then proceeded toward their Mother on their own vehicles, surrounded on all sides by their own attendants bearing banners.

Mounted upon a lion that was difficult to approach, the goddess Śivā— unassailable even by hosts of mighty arms, bearing a goad, a trident, a noose, an axe, a discus, a sword, and a conch as her weapons,
and scorching the path with eyes resembling a thousand full-grown suns— set out to strike down the Daityas, she who possesses the prowess of a child yet is beyond childhood.
Then those leaders of the Gaṇas, resplendent like the lord of gods and the sun, set out on elephants, horses, excellent lions, chariots, and bulls to slay that god, the Lord of Tripura.
With plows, spikes, clubs, and *bhuśuṇḍi* weapons, as well as with mountain peaks resembling great mountains,
those lords of the gods and lords of the hosts of spirits marched in front of Maheśvara.

Likewise, the gods headed by Indra, Padmodbhava, and Viṣṇu, as well as the lords of the Gaṇas, spoke to the Lord Gaṇeśa from all sides with their hands joined in reverence upon their crowns, saying, "Victory! to the Blessed One.
All the sages, staff in hand and wearing matted locks, danced;
the Siddhas and Cāraṇas moving through the sky rained down showers of flowers;
and likewise, O best of Brahmins, the three cities resounded on all sides.
Surrounded by the lords of the Gaṇas and the hosts of gods, Bhṛṅgin— the preeminent leader of all the Gaṇas—
ascended his celestial chariot like Mahendra and went forth as a yogi to destroy Tripura.
Keśa, Vigatavāsa, Mahākeśa, Mahājvara,
Somavallī, Savarṇa, Somapa, and likewise Senaka.
Somadhṛk, Sūryavāc, Sūryapeṣaṇaka, Sūryākṣa, the one named Sūri, the god Surasundara, and Sundara as well; LiP_1,72.77 //
Prakuda, Kakudanta, Kampana, Prakampana,
Indra, Indrajaya, Mahābhi, and likewise Bhīmaka.
Śatākṣa, Pañcākṣa, Sahasrākṣa, Mahodara,
Yamajihva, Śatāśva, Kaṇṭhana, and Kaṇṭhapūjana.
O twice-born ones, he has two crests, three crests, and likewise five crests;
he is shaven-headed, half-shaven, long-bodied, with the face of a Piśāca, and the bearer of the Pināka bow.
Pippalāyatana, likewise Aṅgārakāśana,
Śithila, Śithilāsya, Akṣapāda, Aja, and Kuja.
The goat-faced, the horse-faced, the elephant-faced, and the upward-facing one—
these and others surround the Lord, free from both the characterized and the characteristics.
Surrounded by their hosts, they went to Soma, encompassing him in multitudes;
there were thousands upon thousands of Rudras whose vital seed is drawn upward.
Having returned to Mahādeva, the God of gods, Maheśvara,
they went forth to burn the three cities, surrounded by hosts numbering in the tens of millions.
The gods of the Thirty-three, as well as three hundred and thirty,
and three thousand gods, went forth in every direction.
The mothers of all the worlds, the mothers of the Gaṇas,
and the mothers of all beings followed behind the god.
And the Lord of the Gaṇas shines in the midst of the hosts within his chariot,
like the King of Stars in the midst of the stars in a cloudless sky.
Then the goddess Girijā, standing by the side of the god,
shone forth as Gaurī, who, through her power, was like Bhava himself, composed of the entire universe.
Then the goddess Śubhāvatī shone, seated at his side, her fingertips grasping a chowrie; she was the color of a golden lotus.
Then the bright body of the All-pervading Lord, illuminated by that Mother Ambikā with her ash-smeared form,
shone forth like a white cloud accompanied by lightning in the sky of the Supreme Lord, the Sovereign of the Gods.
The sky shone with the rainbow as the world shines with Mount Meru;
the gentle form of Śambhu, possessing the luster of the moon, shone with its golden bow.
The white parasol of the Supreme Lord, mingled with the rays of jewels,
shines like the unbroken orb of the moon at its rising.
O Śivā, this beautiful red garland, suspended from the edge of the parasol,
shines like a supreme river falling from the sky through the lattice-work of jewels.
Then, with his lotus feet bowed to by Mahendra, Viriñci, Vibhāvasu, and others,
he went together with his mother to the Triple City for the welfare of all the worlds.
The wielder of the trident is capable of burning all this world, including the moving and the unmoving, with his mind in an instant;
why then did the wielder of the Pināka bow go there in person, along with his attendants, to burn Tripura?

"What is the use of his chariot, his excellent arrows, or his hosts of attendants and the hosts of gods for Śambhu, whose power is undiminished? Why has he burnt down the three cities?"—thus spoke the leaders of the immortals.
We consider that the Lord Pinākin has surely set all this in motion for the sake of sport; whether he remains thus or otherwise, what other fruit could there be than his mere manifestation?

Near this triple city, Nandin, the lord of the Gaṇas, shone with the lords of the gods and the Gaṇas headed by Nandi; he, the chariot of the world for the Goddess, was like Mount Meru with its eight peaks.
Then, having beheld the Lord of the Gods, the Sovereign, together with his attendants and the Daughter of the Mountain,
the host of gods stationed upon the stage of the triple city likewise followed him in person.
O lords of sages, those three cities shine there perfectly like another entire triple-world,
filled with kings, hosts of attendants, gods, and the three kinds of non-gods.
(Śiva burns Tripura) Then, having strung his bow and fixed that arrow, Śarva, having joined it with the Pāśupata weapon, meditated upon Tripura.
While that great god Rudra stood with his bow drawn,
during that time the cities indeed quickly attained oneness.
And when Tripura had indeed become one and arrived,
there arose a tumultuous joy among the high-souled deities.
Then all the hosts of gods, the Siddhas, and the supreme ṛṣis uttered cries of "Victory! while praising the one of eight forms.
Then the Blessed Brahmā spoke regarding the casting down of Bhaga’s eyes,
even when the conjunction of Puṣya had arrived, [concerning] the Lord of Umā who was acting out of his own playful whim.
O Mahādeva, O Supreme Lord, this action of yours is indeed fitting, since,
O Master, both the former gods and the current gods are equal to you.
Nevertheless, O Lord of the World, the current gods are most righteous while the former gods were sinful; therefore, you ought to abandon your divine play here.
O Lord, what need have you for a chariot or a banner to burn the three cities?
O Master, [you require] only an arrow, along with the hosts of beings, Viṣṇu, and myself.
O Lord of Gods, when the conjunction of Puṣya has arrived, you ought to burn the city while they have not yet departed into separation.
"You ought to burn these three cities quickly.
Then the god Mahādeva, the omniscient one, looked upon them.
At that very moment, Virūpākṣa reduced the three cities to ashes;
so too did the Lord Soma, Viṣṇu, Kālāgni, and Vāyu.
All of them, stationed upon the arrow, bowed down to that god and said to him:
"O Lord of Gods, even though the three cities have been burnt by your glance..."
"O Lord of Gods, you ought to discharge an arrow here for our benefit.
Then, having wiped the bowstring, the Destroyer of Tripura smiled.
O best of Brahmins, the Lord drew his arrow back to his ear and released it;
in that very instant, the arrow, which brings about the end of Tripura, consumed the triple city.
Having approached the God of gods and paid homage, he stood there; the three cities, though surrounded by hundreds of millions of Daityas, shone even as they were being consumed by fire.
With that arrow, as Rudra at the end of the eon [consumes] the three worlds,
even there the Daityas along with their kinsmen worshipped Rudra.

Then, by the power of the ritual of worship, the gods—including Indra and Upendra—along with the lords of the Gaṇas, attained the status of leaders of the Gaṇas under Śambhu; they said nothing at all.
Having observed the god out of fear, and seeing the daughter of Himavat, the goddess, that host of gods was then terrified; [thereupon] the bull among gods [spoke].
Furthermore, he said: "Then the gods bowed down to him from all sides."
The hosts of gods paid homage to Nandin, who is adorned with the moon; they paid homage to her who was born from the king of mountains;
they paid homage to the Lord, the son of the mountain’s daughter; and they paid homage to Maheśvara.
Together with the gods and Viṣṇu, Brahmā, composed in mind, praised the god Bhava, the Lord and enemy of Tripura.
The venerable Grandfather said:
Be gracious, O Lord of the gods; be gracious, O Supreme Lord. Be gracious, O Protector of the worlds; be gracious, O imperishable bestower of bliss.
Salutation to you, the five-faced Rudra, the Rudra of fifty crore forms, who is seated upon the three selves, the essence of knowledge (vidyātattva).

Salutations again and again to Śiva, to the principle of Śiva (śivatattva), to Aghora; salutations to the one whose nature consists of the twelve-fold self, the essence of the eightfold Aghora-mantra.
To the one whose self is Śiva, who has assumed a form in this world that is exceedingly beautiful, possessing eight faces and resembling ten million flashes of lightning; LiP_1,72.125.
To the one with the color of fire, the fierce one, whose body is half-formed by Ambikā, the god who bestows liberation upon those who are white, dark, and red; and to the immortal one.
Salutation indeed to the Eldest, who has the form of Rudra, to Soma, the giver of boons,
to the one who is the three worlds, the three gods, and the Vaṣaṭkāra.
Salutation to you who are of the nature of space in the center and who abide in space;
salutation to you who possess the eight forms of the eight fields and who are the eight principles.
To him who is established in fourfold ways, fourfold ways, and fourfold ways;
to him whose body consists of five mantras, fivefold and indeed fivefold.
Homage again and again to the letter *A*, which consists of sixty-four aspects; homage again and again to the letter *U*, which is the form of the thirty-two principles (*tattva*).
Salutations again and again to the syllable *ma*, whose essential nature consists of sixteen parts;
salutations to the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*), whose essential nature consists of eight parts.
Salutations to you, O Oṃkāra, who are established in fourfold form;
salutations again and again to the divine Lord of the Sky and the Lord of Heaven.
Salutations indeed to the one who is the seven worlds, the lord of the netherworlds and hells;
to the one who possesses eight fields and eight forms, and who is higher than the highest.
Salutations to you who possess a thousand heads, and salutations to you who possess a thousand [eyes];
to Śarva, the supreme lord, who is endowed with a thousand feet.
To the one whose form consists of the ninefold self-principle, whose power is the self-nature of the nine and eightfold [principles],
who again shines forth in eight ways, and who possesses the form of the sixty-four [manifestations].
Salutations to you, whose self-nature consists of the sixty-four [principles], who are again eightfold,
who are enveloped by the eight qualities, yet who are yourself devoid of qualities.
Salutations to you who abide in the root, who dwell in the eternal station,
who reside in the circle of the navel, and who produce the soundless resonance within the heart.
To him who is stationed in the throat, to him who is stationed in the cavity of the palate,
to him who is stationed between the eyebrows, and to him who is stationed in the midst of the primordial sound (nāda).
To Śiva himself, who abides in the lunar orb, whose form is auspiciousness, who consists of the nature of fire, moon, and sun, and who embodies the thirty-six powers; ||| LiP_1,72.139 |||
Salutations to you who, having withdrawn the three worlds through the threefold concealment,
abide in the form of the three sacrificial fires, like a serpent lying dormant.
Salutations indeed to Sadāśiva, the peaceful one, the Great Lord who wields the Pināka bow,
the omniscient refuge, and to Sadyojāta.
Salutation to you, Aghora; salutation to you, Vāmadeva;
let there be salutation to Tatpuruṣa; repeated salutations to Īśāna.
Salutations to the one who illuminates the thirty [principles], salutations indeed to the one who has transcended tranquility;
salutations be to you, Ananteśa, Sūkṣma, and Uttama.
Salutations to you, the one-eyed; salutations to you, the single Rudra. Salutations to you, the triple-formed; salutations to Śrīkaṇṭha, the crested one.
Salutation to you who are seated upon the infinite throne, the infinite one who brings an end to all, the stainless, the vast, and the one of pure limbs.
To him who is seated upon a stainless throne, whose form is the essence of the stainless meaning,
who dwells within the seat of yoga, who is the yogi, and the bestower of yoga.
Always abiding in the hearts of yogins like the awn of wild rice,
you are ever devoted to the withdrawal of the senses for those who delight in that withdrawal.

Salutations to you who delight in the withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), who abide in the stage of steadiness (pratisthāna), who are the very essence of concentration (dhāraṇā), and who take pleasure in those concentrations.
Salutations to you who stand before those engaged in the practice of *dhāraṇā*, who are meditation itself, whose form is meditation, and who are attainable through meditation.
Salutations to you, the object of meditation, who are accessible through meditation, and who are both the meditator and the act of meditation;
salutations to you, the object of meditation even for those things that are themselves objects of meditation, the most supreme object of meditation.
Homage to you, who are accessible through meditative concentration,
who are yourself meditative concentration, and who possess the nature of the non-conceptual object for those who delight in meditative concentration.

O Rudra, having burnt and extracted all this—the three worlds and indeed the triple city—today, who would wish to praise you? How indeed shall I praise such a one as you, for the sake of propitiating you, Śiva?
O God of gods, through devotion, satisfaction, and the sight of wonders, these mortals— even the immortals—
these hosts, O Lord of gods, O Lord of Gaṇas, offer salutation to you along with the hosts of Siddhas.
O Lord, by a mere glance you were able to burn both the three cities and the three worlds;
yet, while you were playfully at ease with Ambikā, they were indeed consumed in an instant, and only then was the arrow released.
The chariot has been prepared, the excellent arrow is ready, and your bright bow is set for the destruction of Tripura;
yet, despite my many efforts, as well as those of the hosts of gods and siddhas, no fruit has been seen by you.

The chariot, the charioteer, the best of gods, and the horse—Rudra himself, Śakra, and the Grandfather (Brahmā)—all these are you alone, O Blessed One; how then shall I praise you, who are beyond being praised, while prostrating with my head?
You have infinite feet, infinite arms, infinite heads, and you are the auspicious one who brings an end;
you possess infinite forms. How shall I satisfy you who are such as this? For how can I satisfy you who are thus beyond being satisfied?
Salutations again and again to you, the all-knowing Śiva, Rudra, Śarva, and Bhava;
to you who are gross, subtle, and subtler than the most subtle, the knower of the subtle reality, and the Ordainer.
Salutations to the Creator, the sustainer and destroyer of all gods and demons, the ordainer of the worlds,
the leader of the gods and lords of the asuras, the giver, the instructor, and my teacher in all scriptures.
Salutations to you, Bhava, who are to be known through the Vedānta, who are perfectly pure, who are constantly praised by those who know the meaning of the Vedas,
whose nature is the very soul of the Veda, and who are the end, the middle, and the most excellent center.
