Salutations to you who are empty of beginning and end, yet established as non-empty; to you who possess marks, yet are markless; to you who consist of marks, to you who are the manifest mark itself, and who are the direct embodiment of the Vedas and all else.

O Lord, for the sake of destroying my darkness, you who are the primordial god Rudra and the very embodiment of sacrifice, merely upon seeing me, you severed my head with the tip of your fingernail on the ground.
"O God of gods, Lord of all gods and asuras, how wondrous is your activity!
Though you are the reality whose nature is beyond the qualities (nirguṇa), you will perform the work of the gods like an embodied being together with the deities."
One is gross, one is subtle, and one is most subtle; one is both formed and formless, while one is indeed formless;
one is seen, one consists of speech, and one is the Lord to be meditated upon—this reality here is wonderful to you.
Whatever object is seen in a dream appears indeed as unperceivable; I think it does not even exist.
O Lord of Devakī, how could our form be unperceivable by the gods, even with great effort, when it is surely visible?
O Lord of Gods, where is Your divine power, and where are we? Where is our devotion, and where is our praise?
Nevertheless, O Blessed One, O Lord, forgive me, the Grandfather, as I lament out of devotion.
Sūta said:
O best of the twice-born, whoever on earth should hear this or recite it after prostrating before the God,
he shall be released from the bonds of sin by means of devotion to Bhava through this hymn of praise to the Subduer of Cities.

Having heard this and being praised with devotion by the four-faced Brahmā, the mighty-armed one who dwells on the peak of Mount Mandara smiled, looked at the daughter of the mountain, and then spoke this hymn of great majesty.
Śiva said:
"O Lotus-born One, I am pleased with this hymn and with your devotion.
Choose boons, as you desire, for the gods; may it be well with you."
Sūta said:
Then, having bowed to the Lord of Gods, the Blessed One born from the lotus,
with palms joined in reverence and a joyful heart, spoke as follows.
The venerable Grandfather said: "O Blessed One, Lord of the gods, Śaṅkara, destroyer of Tripura!
O Supreme Lord, be gracious to me today; grant me supreme devotion unto you."
O Lord who grants all goals, may you be gracious toward all the gods through the yoga of devotion and by always acting as their charioteer.
The Blessed Janārdana, having also paid homage to Maheśvara,
joined his palms in reverence and spoke to the three-eyed Lord who was with Sāmba.
O Īśāna, I eternally desire to be your vehicle; be gracious to me. O Lord of Gods, O God of gods, may there be homage to you, and may there be devotion unto you. LiP_1,72.174.
And may there always be in me the power and the capacity to carry you,
O Giver of Boons, O Śaṅkara, who are omniscient and omnipresent.
Sūta said: Having heard their petition, Mahādeva, the Supreme Lord Bhava, appointed them to the roles of charioteer and vehicle.
Having bestowed [the boon] upon that Brahmā and Viṣṇu, and having incinerated the Daityas, the high-souled Śarva, the god of gods,
caused himself to vanish along with the Goddess, Nandin, and the hosts of spirits.
Then, when Maheśvara had departed from the battlefield along with his attendants,
the lords of the gods, greatly amazed, bowed down to Bhava and Pārvatī.
Then, freed from suffering, the lords of the gods, the lords of the sages, the lords of the Gaṇas, and the suns departed for heaven on their own vehicles.
Or if one causes the twice-born to hear it with devotion, he goes to the world of Brahmā;
likewise, he is freed from mental, verbal, and physical sins.

O best of the twice-born, [beings are afflicted] by gross, subtle, and extremely subtle sins arising from the great transgressions (mahāpātaka), as well as by those arising from the minor transgressions (upapātaka).
By hearing this auspicious chapter, a living being is liberated from sins;
enemies meet their destruction, and one becomes victorious in battle.
He shall not be afflicted by any diseases, nor shall calamities touch him;
he shall obtain wealth, long life, fame, knowledge, and incomparable power.
Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, titled "The Hymn of Brahmā," in the section on the Burning of Tripura within the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
When the god Maheśvara had departed after burning Tripura in an instant,
the Blessed One Padmasambhava spoke to the assembly of the lords of the gods:
The Grandfather said:
Having abandoned Maheśvara, the Lord of the gods of gods, who exists in the form of the *liṅga*,
the grandson of Tāra, the mighty son of Tāraka, possessed of great splendor— *LiP_1,73.2*.
Tārakākṣa, the son of Diti, as well as the heroic Kamalākṣa,
Vidyunmālī the lord of the Daityas, and others too along with their kinsmen.
Having abandoned the god Mahādeva through the illusory power (māyā) of the lord Hari,
they were all destroyed and ruined along with their cities and everything contained within them.
Therefore, Sadāśiva in the form of the *liṅga* should always be worshipped;
for as long as there is worship of the lords of the gods, so long does their existence endure.
Śiva is to be worshipped constantly with faith by the foremost of the gods;
the world consists of all *liṅgas*, and everything is established within the *liṅga*.
Therefore, one who desires his own perfection should worship the *liṅga*;
for it is solely through the worship of the *liṅga* that all gods, daityas, and dānavas [attain their goals].
Yakṣas, vidyādharas, siddhas, rākṣasas, flesh-eaters,
ancestors, sages, as well as piśācas, kinnaras, and others.
Having worshipped the form of the Liṅga, one attains perfection; there is no doubt about this.
Therefore, O gods, one should always worship the Liṅga by whatever means possible.
And we are the cattle of that wise God of gods;
having abandoned our state as cattle, we have then performed the Pāśupata [vow].
The eternal Mahādeva, whose form is the *liṅga*,
is to be worshipped after having purified the elements with the five *praṇavas*.
O best of gods, by means of five combined breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and four *praṇava*s, those devoted to breath-restraint [attain their goal].
And by means of three *praṇavas* and likewise three such *prāṇāyāmas*,
having performed the twofold placement (*nyāsa*) of the syllable *oṃ*, one should be devoted to *prāṇāyāma*.
Then, having uttered the syllable *Oṃ* and having restrained the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths,
one should fill all the limbs with the nectar of knowledge by means of the *praṇava*.
O you of excellent vows, [he created] the three qualities known as the fourfold [ego], the ego (ahaṅkāra),
the subtle elements (tanmātras), the gross elements (bhūtas), and the organs of perception (buddhīndriyas).
Having purified the organs of action as well as the pair of the individual soul (puruṣa) and the intellect (yugala),
and having made the conscious self (cidātman) his body, he should touch [the ashes] with the mantra "Agni bhasma" (Fire is ash).
He who smears himself with ashes at the three junctions of the day, saying, "The wind is ashes, and likewise the sky, the water, and the earth," [attains] the triple longevity.
O best of gods, that yogin who knows all principles should observe this Pāśupata vow, which was taught by Bhava for the sake of liberation from the bonds.
Having thus performed the Pāśupata rite and worshipped the Supreme Lord,
[I saw him] in the form of a liṅga, which was previously seen by me and by the high-souled Viṣṇu.
O deities, cattle are not born merely by rain;
rather, all our undertakings [are successful] by worshipping the god with diligence.
"O best of gods, I believe that the Lord must be fashioned both externally and internally; this is the divine vow of both myself and Viṣṇu."
And for sages there is no doubt; therefore, one should worship Śiva.
That [failure] is a loss, that is a great flaw, that is delusion, and that is muteness.
Those who are devoted to Bhava and whose minds are bowed in salutation to Bhava should contemplate Śiva for even a single moment or a single muhūrta.
Those who are intent on recollecting their past lives are not vessels for suffering;
they possess delightful palaces, divine ornaments, and women.
Those who desire wealth up to the limit of satisfaction as the fruit of the ritual of Śiva’s worship,
or those who long for great enjoyments and sovereignty in the abode of the thirty gods,
let them always worship Maheśvara in the form of the Liṅga.
Having slain and pierced living beings, and having burnt this entire world; LiP_1,73.26 //
One should worship the single Virūpākṣa; he is not defiled by sins, for my Śaila-liṅga is indeed saluted by all the gods.
Having spoken thus and first worshipped Rudra, the Lord of the three worlds,
he praised the God of gods, Tryambaka, with pleasing words.
From that time forward, Śakra and the other gods worshipped the Lord,
having personally adopted the Pāśupata state with their bodies smeared with ashes.
Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Worship of the Liṅga as Proclaimed by Brahmā," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
Having thus fashioned the lingas according to their respective capacities,
Viśvakarman gave them to them by the command of the Lord Brahmā. (LiP 1.74.1)
The linga made of sapphire was always worshipped by Viṣṇu;
that made of ruby by Śakra; and that made of gold by the son of Viśravas.
Likewise, the Viśvedevas [preside over] silver; the Vasus, over beautiful gold;
Vāyu, over brass; and the Aśvins, always over earth.
King Varuṇa [worships] one made of crystal,
the wise King Soma [worships] one fashioned from copper, and likewise the supreme liṅga is made of pearl.
The great nāgas, beginning with Ananta, [worship] an auspicious liṅga made of coral;
the Daityas [worship] one made of iron, as do the high-souled Rākṣasas.
The Guhyakas [worship] with an image made of the three metals, the Gaṇas with one made entirely of metal, Cāmuṇḍā with sand, and the Mātṛs directly, O best of the twice-born.
Nairṛti [worships] one made of wood with devotion; Yama, an auspicious emerald;
the Rudras beginning with Nīla likewise [worship] one made of pure, auspicious ashes.
Lakṣmī [should worship] an image made of the Lakṣmī-tree, Guha indeed one made of cow-dung,
and the sages, O tigers among sages, the supreme one made of the tips of Kuśa grass.
Vāmā and the others [worship] the flower-liṅga; Manonmanī, Sarasvatī, and Vāgbhavā of Rudra [worship] the fragrance-liṅga and that which is made of jewels.
Durgā [should be fashioned] from gold as the unsurpassed Mahādeva together with his altar;
Ugrā [should be made] from flour, while all the auspicious mantras consist of clarified butter.
By the grace of Brahmā, all the Vedas obtained a form made of curd, the Piśācas one made of lead, and each attained their respective station as was appropriate.
What is the use of saying more here? This entire world, both moving and unmoving, stands here as the Śivaliṅga after having been worshipped; of this there is no doubt.
They say that the *liṅga* is of six kinds according to the classification of materials;
the subdivisions of these are traditionally recorded as forty-four.
The first is said to be stone-born, for that is indeed directly of four kinds;
the second, O best of sages, is jewel-born, and that is of seven kinds.
The third type of liṅga, made of stone, belongs to Parameṣṭhin and is said to be of eight kinds;
the fourth type, made of wood, is said to be of sixteen kinds.
O best of the twice-born, the fifth type of linga is made of clay and is divided into two kinds;
the sixth is the momentary linga, which is proclaimed to be of seven types.
A linga made of gems bestows prosperity; one made of stone grants all perfections (siddhis);
one made of metal directly bestows wealth; and one made of wood grants the attainment of enjoyments.
O best of Brahmins, an image made of clay is auspicious and brings about all spiritual accomplishments;
one made of stone is said to be the most excellent, while that made of metal is considered middling.
There are many varieties of linga-differences, which in brief are nine;
at the base is Brahmā, and likewise in the middle is Viṣṇu, the lord of the three worlds.
Above Rudra is Mahādeva, known as Praṇava, who is Sadāśiva;
the pedestal of the liṅga is Mahādevī, the Mother (Ambikā) who consists of the three qualities and the three aspects.
And whoever worships with that [image], both the Goddess and the God are worshipped—
whether it be made of stone, or of jewels, or of minerals, or even of wood.
Even by installing [an image] made of clay or that which is momentary with devotion, one obtains auspicious fruit; [worshipped] by the lords of the gods, Brahmā, Agni, Yama, Varuṇa, and Kubera.
The one of great merit was being praised by perfected beings, vidyādharas, lords of serpents, yakṣas, dānavas, and kinnaras, amidst the sounds of celestial drums.
Having ascended in succession through the worlds of Bhūr, Bhuvas, Svar, and Mahar, and beyond Janas,
Tapas, and Satya, he illumined them with his own splendor.
With his long sword firmly set in the right path for the installation of the *liṅga*,
he quickly split open the cosmic egg and emerged without hesitation.
Having set aside that which is made of stone, or born of jewels, or born of minerals, or born of wood, or made of clay, or even that which is temporary, one should install the entire form.
And having performed the rite according to the injunctions, that man who installs an auspicious linga accompanied by Skanda and Umā, resembling the jasmine flower or cow’s milk; LiP_1,74.27.
Having assumed a human body, Rudra remains there; of this there is no doubt.
By seeing him and by touching him, men obtain liberation.
O best of Brahmins, it is not possible for me to describe his merit correctly even in hundreds of yugas; therefore, one should indeed establish it in that manner.
For all mortals, the auspicious divine body of the Lord is with parts (sakala) and fit for meditation; for yogis alone, it is without parts (niṣkala).
Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Classification and Installation of Śiva-liṅgas," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
The sages said:
"Being partless, stainless, and eternal, how did you come to possess parts?
You should explain this to us just as it was previously heard."
Sūta said:

O best of Brahmins, some who know the supreme truth, having heard that the Unborn One resides at the head of the Vedas, spoke of him as being of the nature of the *praṇava* and as pure consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Cognition whose object is sound and so forth is designated as "knowledge";
some maintain that such knowledge is free from error, while others say it is not. (LiP 1.75.3)
"O twice-born sages, other seers say that knowledge is that which is stainless, pure, free from conceptual construction, and without support— the knowledge that illuminates the Guru."
Liberation occurs through knowledge alone; grace leads to the attainment of knowledge.
Through both, the yogi is liberated and therein becomes filled with bliss.
Some sages say that his connection with action occurs only by his own will, having withdrawn the form fashioned by conceptual construction.
The sky is the head of that pervasive Lord, and space is the navel of the Supreme Being;
the moon, sun, and fire are the eyes of the Great Soul, and the quarters of space are his ears.
His two feet are the netherworld (pātāla), the ocean is his garment,
all the gods are his arms, and the stars are his ornaments.
Prakṛti is his wife, and Puruṣa is said to be the *liṅga*.
Indeed, all Brāhmaṇas arose from his mouth, as did the Lord Brahmā, the sovereign master.
From the two arms of the high-souled wielder of the Pināka bow came Indra and Upendra; from his thighs came the Kṣatriyas, from his thighs the Vaiśyas, and from his feet the Śūdras.
The Puṣkarāvartaka and other winds are proclaimed to be his hair;
the sense of smell is his breath, and his movement is both revealed scripture (śruti) and tradition (smṛti).
Now, by this very [power], the self consisting of action is the instigator of primordial nature;
yet the glorious Puruṣa of men is to be reached through knowledge, and not otherwise.
A sacrifice of austerity is superior to thousands of sacrifices of ritual action;
a sacrifice of recitation is superior to thousands of sacrifices of austerity.
The sacrifice of meditation excels thousands of sacrifices of recitation;
there is nothing superior to the sacrifice of meditation, for meditation is the means to knowledge.
When the yogi, established in the state of equanimity, perceives through meditation,
then Śiva is present before him as he delights in the sacrifice of meditation.
For those who possess true knowledge, there is no ritual purity nor injunctions for expiation;
all people who know the wisdom of Brahman are purified by that very knowledge.
Upon reflection, there is no action in the worlds, nor pleasure or pain;
for those who meditate, dharma and adharma, recitation, fire-offerings, and their very presence are always one.
The Linga, which consists of supreme bliss, is pure, auspicious, and imperishable;
it is partless, all-pervading, and should be known as abiding in the hearts of yogins.
The twice-born say that the *liṅga* is of two kinds:
external and internal, O best of sages; the external is gross, O twice-born, while the internal is subtle.

Those who are coarse, devoted to ritual sacrifices and intent on the worship of the gross liṅga, [do so] for the sake of the mental cultivation of the unenlightened; otherwise, there would be no gross form.
He for whom the internal sign is not directly perceived is a fool; he conceptualizes everything externally and nothing else.
To the wise, it becomes subtle, stainless, perceptible, and imperishable;
whereas to those who are unrefined, it appears gross, fashioned from clay, wood, and the like.
Others who know the true nature of reality maintain that, upon investigation, no objective entity exists;
therefore, everything—both the partless and the possessed of parts—is composed of Śiva.
O practitioners of excellent vows, even the single sky is indeed perceived as distinct for each individual bowl;
and others say that this applies to Śaṅkara as well, both in terms of distinction and non-distinction.
For the sake of providing conditions for the world, O you of noble vows, even though the sun is situated in one place,
it is seen as many in various reservoirs of water, even though it is but one.
All living beings, both in heaven and on earth, are indeed composed of the five elements;
nevertheless, they are seen to be manifold due to the distinctions of genus and individual manifestation.
Whatever is seen or heard, know that each and every thing is of the nature of Śiva;
for upon investigation, the perception of difference among people in this world vanishes.
And having enjoyed vast pleasures in a dream, a mortal becomes happy;
yet, upon reflection, he does not experience the pleasure or the suffering that was [merely] experienced.
Thus have others spoken, and all those who have realized the true essence of the Vedas:
"The Supreme Lord, in his entirety, is directly present within the hearts of those transmigrating beings."
For yogins, the God is partless; for the wise, He is identical with the universe.
Thus, the threefold form of the Supreme Lord is praised in the world.
O best of the twice-born, the first is partless (niṣkala), the second is both with and without parts (sakalaniṣkala), and the third is indeed with parts (sakala); it is not otherwise.
Some constantly worship him who is both with parts and without parts; some worship the omniscient one in their hearts, in the *śivaliṅga*, or in the sacrificial fire.
Some sages remain forever within the cycle of worldly existence;
likewise, men together with their wives and sons worship [the deity] in this very manner.
As is Śiva, so is the Goddess; as is the Goddess, so is Śiva.
Therefore, through the cognition of non-difference alone, [the worship is performed] according to twenty-seven divisions.
They sacrifice in the body and externally upon the four-cornered, six-cornered,
ten-cornered, twelve-cornered, sixteen-cornered, and three-cornered [mandalas].
That Lord Śiva, who is by nature devoid of the manifestation of existence and non-existence, dwells in person together with the Goddess according to his own will for the sake of delivering [beings].
Some say that he is one; some say he is twofold; and some say he consists of three qualities (guṇas).
Likewise, others call him Śiva, while those who know the Vedas declare him to be the transmigrating soul (saṃsārin).
Endowed with devotion and auspicious yoga, the distinguished brahmins, ever devoted to dharma,
worship the Lord himself— the master of yoga whose form is all-encompassing— within the center of the hexagon.
Those who perceive Śiva there—in the triangle of the three times, in the midst of the three principles, possessing the three qualities and the three eyes—they go to Him;
but other yogis do not, nor do they reach the Ancient Puruṣa through that Goddess.
Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Non-duality of Śiva," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
Henceforth, for the benefit of all the worlds, I shall proclaim the entire fruit of consecration, which arises from the manifestation of one's own will-formed body.
Having devoutly fashioned and installed the God seated upon the supreme throne together with Skanda and Umā, one shall attain all desires.
Having worshipped the God together with Skanda and Umā once according to the prescribed rite,
I shall describe what fruit a mortal obtains, exactly as I have heard it.
With celestial palaces resembling ten million suns, fulfilling all desires, crowded with Rudra-maidens, and accompanied by song and dance; 76.4.
The yogin sports like Śiva until the dissolution of all beings;
having enjoyed great pleasures there in celestial chariots that fulfill all desires, he remains.
The one of great splendor [attained] the worlds of Aum, Kaumāra, Aiśāna, Vaiṣṇava, Brāhma, Prājāpatya, Janaloka, and likewise Mahas.
Having attained the status of Indra and having exercised that sovereignty for ten thousand years,
he then enjoyed most beautiful divine pleasures in the Bhuvarloka.
Having reached Mount Meru, he rejoices in the abodes of the gods;
he has one foot, four arms, three eyes, and is equipped with a trident.
Having created Hari, who stands on his left, and the four-faced Brahmā on his right,
he [shone] with the brilliance of twenty-eight crores of Rudras pervading all his limbs.
Likewise, one should visualize the twenty-fifth principle, the Puruṣa, directly from the heart;
Prakṛti to the left, and indeed Buddhi at the location of the intellect.
From the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra) indeed arise the subtle elements (tanmātrāṇi), and from the senses themselves arise the organs; thus the Supreme Lord [manifests] through his divine play.
From the base of the feet, one should contemplate the earth; likewise, water from the region of the secret parts;
fire from the region of the navel; and likewise, the sun from the heart.
Having thus emitted Soma from his throat, the Self from the middle of his eyebrows, and the heavens from his head,
he directly established the entire world of moving and unmoving beings.
Having fashioned the all-knowing, all-pervading God according to the ritual rules of the Vidyā,
and having installed him according to the proper method, one shall attain union with Śiva.
Having fashioned the Lord of Sacrifice, Īśāna, with three feet, seven hands, four horns, and two heads, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Having enjoyed great pleasures there for a hundred thousand kalpas, that man, living in happiness,
eventually returns to this world and becomes a performer of all sacrifices.
He who should depict Soma, adorned with the crescent moon, mounted upon a bull,
attains that merit which is acquired by performing ten thousand horse sacrifices.
Having traveled by means of a golden celestial chariot garlanded with networks of tinkling bells to the divine city of Śiva, he is liberated right there.
I shall describe, exactly as I have heard it, the fruit that one obtains by representing the Lord accompanied by Nandin, along with Ambā, and surrounded by all his attendants.
With celestial chariots resembling the solar disc, yoked to bulls, crowded with throngs of apsaras, and difficult even for gods and dānavas to obtain; LiP_1,76.20 //
Surrounded on all sides by throngs of dancing Apsarases who are most beautiful in every way,
he shall go to the divine city of Śiva and attain the status of a Gaṇapati.
[He saw] the Lord of the gods of gods, the Sovereign accompanied by the Daughter of the Mountain, dancing—
whether he had a thousand arms or four arms, being the omniscient one.
The Supreme Lord, the bull-bannered Īśvara himself, was surrounded by Bhṛgu and other hosts of beings,
together with the daughter of the mountain.
The Supreme Lord was always saluted by Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, Soma, and all others,
and was surrounded by the Mothers and the sages.
I shall now declare the fruit that comes from performing [this rite] with devotion and installing [the image],
as well as the fruit found in all sacrifices, austerities, gifts, pilgrimages, and deities.
Having obtained that fruit multiplied ten millionfold, he goes to the state of Śiva;
having enjoyed great pleasures there until the dissolution of all beings (ābhūtasaṃplava), he remains.
When another creation has begun, he shall attain the state of a human being;
[he will appear] naked, four-armed, white, with three eyes, and having a snake for a girdle.
Having fashioned an image of the Lord of Gods with a skull in his hand and dark, curly hair,
and having installed it with devotion, one shall attain union with Śiva.
The Lord Sāmba, the son of the king of elephants, the bestower of success, the sovereign,
who is smoke-colored, red-eyed, three-eyed, and adorned by the moon.
Hara bears the feathers of a crow upon his head and carries the chisel of an elephant-carver;
the Lord wears a lion’s skin as an upper garment and a deer’s hide as his clothing.
With sharp fangs, a mace in hand, and a skull held aloft in his paw,
he makes all the quarters of the sky resound with the great sounds of "huṃ" and "phaṭ."
Holding a white lotus and a deer-skin with his two arms,
as well as a conch shell, he was laughing and roaring while drinking up the dark ocean.
Having danced while adorned by hosts of spirits and groups of attendants, and having installed [the deity] with devotion according to the full extent of one's wealth; LiP_1,76.33.
Having transcended all obstacles, he is glorified in the world of Śiva;
having enjoyed great pleasures there until the dissolution of all beings, he remains.
Having obtained knowledge through inquiry from the Rudras, one is liberated there [from that state];
[one beholds] the unsurpassed four-armed Lord, Ardhanārīśvara.
The Lord has his hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, holds a trident and a lotus,
exists in both male and female forms, and is adorned with all ornaments.
Having performed [this] with devotion and having consecrated it, one is glorified in the world of Śiva;
having enjoyed great pleasures there, one is endowed with the powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest.
Having thereby obtained knowledge that lasts as long as the moon and stars, one who makes Lakulīśvara— the omniscient Lord of the gods of gods— is liberated.
Having devoutly established one who is surrounded by disciples and grand-disciples and whose hand is raised in the gesture of exposition, he goes to the world of Śiva.
Having enjoyed abundant pleasures there for a hundred yugas,
a person attains the yoga of knowledge and is liberated right there.
And that place which was desired by all the former gods and immortals has now become the abode of the god whose seal is made, who is smeared with the ashes of the funeral pyre.
Among them, there was one who wore the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), who bore a garland upon his head,
who possessed the hair of Brahmā, and who wore a single sacred thread.
Holding in his left hand the skull of Brahmā as a boon,
and likewise bearing the body of Viṣṇu, [he is] the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin).
Having performed [this] with devotion and having installed it, one is liberated from the ocean of existence;
"Oṃ namo nīlakaṇṭhāya" is the eight-syllable mantra of merit.
He recites the mantra once, and he is liberated from all sins;
with this mantra, one should worship with perfumes and other offerings out of devotion, according to one's means.
Having worshipped the Lord of the gods of gods, the Lord who holds the Sudarśana discus and is the destroyer of Jālandhara, one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Having worshipped with devotion and installed Jalandhara, who has been split in two, one attains union with Śiva; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
The god who bestows the Sudarśana, possessing the characteristics previously described,
was worshipped by the god with the worship of his own eyes.
Having performed this with devotion and installed it, one is glorified in the world of Śiva;
thereafter, the lotus-foot [of the Lord] rests upon the back of Nikumbha as he stands.
Having properly positioned his right arm and embracing the Daughter of the Mountain with his left,
he should place his elbow upon the tip of the trident, which has a serpent fashioned as its small bells.
And having observed Andhaka standing at his side with palms joined in reverence,
he assumed his true form as is fitting, and [Andhaka] attained union with Śiva.
Whoever should fashion the Lord of the God of Gods, the Sovereign who brought an end to Tripura,
equipped with bow and arrow, accompanied by Soma, and adorned with the crescent moon;
The god well-established in the chariot, with the four-faced one as his charioteer—
having gone to the city of Śiva by means of that very form, he too becomes happy.
He sports there, of this there is no doubt, like a second Śaṅkara;
having enjoyed great pleasures there for as long as he desires, O best of the twice-born.
Having attained the knowledge that has been investigated, he is liberated right there.
[He saw] Gaṅgādhara seated comfortably, and likewise Candraśekhara.
Likewise, one should place Gaṇeśa together with Gaṅgā on the left lap, accompanied by Ambikā;
and similarly Skanda, the eldest, along with the most beautiful Durgā.
And likewise Bhāskara, Soma, Brahmāṇī, Maheśvarī,
the goddess Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, and Vārāhī, the giver of boons.
The wise person who [worships] Indrāṇī, as well as Cāmuṇḍā accompanied by Vīrabhadra, and Vighneśa, shall attain union with Śiva.

Having placed the Lord who bears the moon on his crest in the center of the liṅga— one who is the embodiment of the liṅga, possessed of great flames, enveloped in radiance, and imperishable— LiP_1,76.60.
Likewise, one should fashion in the sky the Liṅga, with Brahmā in the form of a swan and Viṣṇu in the form of a boar, facing downward beneath the Liṅga.
To his right stood Brahmā with palms joined in reverence;
in the center was the most formidable Linga, established within the great waters.
Having performed [the rite] with devotion and having installed the Lord who protects the sacred field, as well as the Lord Pāśupata, one shall attain union with Śiva.
Having performed [this] with devotion according to the rule, one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Fruits of the Installation of the Forms of Śiva," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
The sages said:
The merit of installing a liṅga, the very act of establishing a liṅga,
and the various classifications of liṅgas have been heard by me here from your own mouth.
O you who have attained the state of Śiva, it behoves you to declare the fruit that a mortal obtains by constructing a temple of Śiva using materials ranging from clay up to precious gems.
Sūta said:
Even one who is devoted to him in this world, though possessed of knowledge, is tormented by children, wife, home, and so forth; yet for such a person, what need is there for houses?

Nevertheless, the devotees of the Supreme Lord, even by means of fashioned clay lumps [as offerings], go to the divine world of Rudra in an excellent celestial chariot, which is indeed worshipped by the Lord of the Gods and the Lotus-born Brahmā.
Even children, having fashioned an image of the Primordial God with a clod of earth, clay, or dust,
and likewise constructing a house for Śambhu and worshipping it, attain the state of Rudra.
Therefore, with every effort and with devotion, devotees [should honor] the abode of Śiva.
This should be performed with every effort for the sake of accomplishing dharma, pleasure, and wealth.
Having constructed a temple for Rudra with keśara, nāgara, drāviḍa, or other styles, one is glorified in the world of Śiva through devotion.
And he who constructs a temple for the Supreme Lord known as Kailāsa rejoices happily in celestial palaces shaped like the peaks of Mount Kailāsa.
Or one should construct a Mandara for Śiva according to the prescribed rites,
with devotion and in accordance with one's wealth, whether it be of superior, inferior, or middling quality.
With celestial chariots resembling Mount Mandara, facing every direction, crowded with throngs of Apsarases, and difficult even for gods and Dānavas to obtain; LiP_1,77.10 //
Having gone to the beautiful city of Śiva and having enjoyed pleasures as desired,
a man attains the yoga of knowledge and gains the status of a leader of the Gaṇas.
Whatever fruit one who builds a temple named Meru for the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin) obtains, that cannot be attained even by all the great sacrifices.
Having obtained the entire fruit that is found in all sacrifices, austerities, gifts, sacred fords, and the Vedas, he rejoices for a long time like Śiva.
The wise person who devoutly constructs a temple named Niṣadha attains the world of Śiva and rejoices there for a long time like Śiva himself.
Or, O Brahmins, he who performs an auspicious act for the unsurpassed Himavat mountain shall go to the auspicious city of Śiva by means of celestial vehicles resembling the snowy peaks.
Having attained the yoga of knowledge, one shall obtain the status of a Gaṇapati,
as well as a most beautiful temple known as Nīlādriśikhara.
Having performed [this] with devotion according to one's wealth for Rudra Śambhu,
I shall declare the fruit that a mortal obtains.
Having obtained that entire fruit which was previously declared by you regarding what is gained through devotion on the Himālaya mountain, he will be saluted by all the gods.
Having reached the world of Rudra, he rejoices together with the Rudras in the palace named Mahendraśaila, which is esteemed by Rudra.
I shall declare the fruit that one obtains by performing this:
one travels in celestial chariots resembling Mount Mahendra, yoked with bulls.
Having gone to the divine city of Śiva and enjoyed pleasures as they desired,
those foremost of sages attained the knowledge deliberated upon by the Rudras.
Having abandoned sense objects as if they were poison, one may attain union with Śiva;
likewise, he who would construct a temple adorned with jewels out of gold [attains the same].
Whether it be in the Drāviḍa, Nāgara, or Kesar style, according to the prescribed rules,
the structure may be a peaked roof (kūṭa) or a pavilion (maṇḍapa), and it may be either square or rectangular.
It is not possible to describe his merit even in a hundred yugas,
whether [the image] be worn out, fallen, broken, or cracked.
O twice-born ones, he who should have a temple, a pavilion, a wall, or a gate-tower made very beautiful with doors and other features as previously described, [attains great merit].
A man who performs work in a temple of Śiva, whether for his own livelihood or otherwise, obtains even greater merit than the builder; of this there is no doubt.
He who, even for the sake of achieving his own enjoyment, goes but once to the abode of Rudra, goes to the heavenly world along with his kinsmen; of this there is no doubt.
If one performs a ritual action and rejoices even upon obtaining happiness,
therefore, O best of sages, he who would build a sanctuary with devotion [attains great merit].
O best of sages, by means of wood, bricks, and other materials, a mortal who builds a temple for the sake of propitiating Maheśvara is glorified in the world of Śiva.

O best of sages, it should be constructed with every effort for the sake of dharma, pleasure, wealth, and liberation; however, if one is unable to build a supreme temple, [one should perform other meritorious acts].
Or by means of sweeping and other such acts, one may obtain all desires;
for he who performs the sweeping with a soft and fine broom [attains these].
The fruit of a thousand cāndrāyaṇa fasts is obtained in a single month by one who performs [the rite] with water scented with cow dung that has been filtered through a cloth.
By applying an ointment according to the prescribed rule, one obtains the merit of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance performed for a year;
the sacred field of Śiva extends half a krośa in every direction from the Śivaliṅga.
He who would renounce his life-breaths, so difficult to give up, shall attain union with Śiva;
for such was the measure of Svāyaṃbhuva and likewise of Bāṇa, O you of excellent vows.

O best of the twice-born, in the Svāyambhuva [Manvantara] that measure would be half; in the Ārṣa it would be half of that; and in the Mānuṣa it would be half of that—such is the measurement of the field.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, is the measurement of the sacred field (kṣetra) in the dwellings of ascetics,
as well as in the first incarnation of Rudra, and likewise among disciples and grand-disciples.
O twice-born ones, [this occurred] during the descent of Nara, in his disciple, in that disciple's disciple,
and in the great and meritorious Śrīparvata, or in its vicinity.
Or whoever should give up their life there, would attain union with Śiva;
likewise in Vārāṇasī, and especially so in Avimukta.
He who gives up his life at the great field of Kedāra, especially at Prayāga, and at Kurukṣetra, attains final liberation.
One who dies at Prabhāsa, Puṣkara, Avantī, as well as at Amareśvara,
and at Vaṇīśailākula, attains the nature of Śiva.
A living being who dies in Vārāṇasī shall never again enter the state of a sentient creature;
the same applies to one who dies in Triviṣṭapa, Vimukta, Kedāra, or Saṃgameśvara.
One may likewise abandon one's life at Śālaṅka, or at Jambukeśvara,
or at Śukreśvara, Gokarṇa, Bhāskareśa, or Guheśvara.
He who, having dried up his body through observances, casts it off in a sacred field of Śiva, attains the supreme goal in Hiraṇyagarbha and Nandīśa.
O best of sages, that yogi attains the state of Śiva whether among humans, gods,
ṛṣis, or even among the self-born (Svāyambhuvas).
Likewise, regarding the self-existent deity, no deliberation should be made here;
having established the fire in a sacred field of Śiva and having worshipped the Supreme Lord, [one should proceed].
He who offers his own bodily mass as an oblation attains the supreme goal;
having remained without food for that long, he should eventually relinquish his life-breaths.
O best of sages, one who has even cut off both his feet and dwells in a sacred field of Śiva shall attain union with Śiva.
He attains the state of Śiva; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Merely seeing the sacred field (kṣetra) is meritorious, while entering it is a hundred times more so.
The merit of touching [the image] and circumambulating it is a hundred times greater than that;
and the merit of bathing in water thereafter is a hundred times greater still.
Then, O brahmins, a bath with milk is unsurpassed and yields more than a hundredfold merit;
a bath with curd is said to yield a thousandfold, and one with honey yields more than that by a hundred.
Through a bath with ghee, the merit is infinite; through one with sugar-cane juice, it is a hundred times more than that.
Having reached and immersed oneself in a river situated near a sacred field of Śiva, [one obtains this fruit].
Having abandoned food and cast off the body, one is glorified in the world of Śiva;
all rivers situated near a sacred field of Śiva are exceedingly beautiful.
O best of the twice-born, ponds, wells, and tanks are known as the sacred sites (tīrthas) of Śiva; having bathed with devotion in those sacred sites, a man [attains merit].
O best of sages, a human being who bathes in the morning at the Śiva-tīrthas is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa; of this there is no doubt.
Having obtained the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice, that man goes to the world of Rudra,
provided he bathes with devotion even once at the Śiva-tīrthas at midday.
One obtains merit equal to bathing in the Gaṅgā; there is no doubt about this.
Likewise, having bathed when the sun has set, one shall go to the auspicious state.

Having cast off the cloak of evil, a man who bathes three times a day at the sacred sites of Śiva becomes equal to the twice-born; indeed, a man who bathes even once at a sacred site of Śiva attains the same state.
One attains union with Śiva; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Formerly, a certain boar, seeing a dog on the path out of fear, [fled]. (LiP 1.77.58)
O best of the twice-born, having incidentally bathed once at Śivatīrtha, he died and attained the status of a Gaṇapati.
He who beholds in the morning Śiva, the Lord of the gods, in the form of the Liṅga, attains a state that is indeed superior to all others.
By beholding Mahādeva at midday, one obtains the fruit of sacrifice;
by beholding him in the evening, having attained the fruit of all sacrifices, one is liberated.
From mental, verbal, and great physical sins,
as well as from minor offenses (upapātaka) and even lesser offenses (anupātaka).
At the Saṃkrama, having beheld the Lord Īśāna in the form of a liṅga,
one abandons whatever sin has been committed during a month and goes to the auspicious state of Śiva.
By worshipping during the solstices, during the half-months, during the southern course, during the northern course, and likewise during the equinoxes, one attains the supreme goal.
A pure man, moving with gentle steps in a clockwise direction, should perform three circumambulations around the temple from all sides, following the method of alternating between left and right.
He who constantly utters "Śiva" with his speech as the Supreme Lord shall obtain at every step the fruit of the horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha).
Even he goes to the auspicious abode; how much more so, then, for one who has prepared a mandala-field with water scented with cow dung?
With powders made of pearls, as well as those made of sapphires,
rubies, and beautiful crystals.
Likewise, with emeralds, gold, and silver,
as well as with powders of those colors found in the world, even by those devoid of wealth.
O fortunate ones, having drawn an auspicious lotus measuring ten cubits,
complete with a pericarp, in the presence of Mahādeva;
There, one should invoke Mahādeva, who is endowed with nine powers,
and who is the supreme bestower of desired fruits through five, six, or eight [mantras].
Furthermore, having worshipped Īśāna with eight [offerings] on the ten-spoked [wheel], and likewise with ten on the next,
and again with ten on the outermost, one should prostrate.
By offering this to the God of gods, one obtains the fruit of gifting land;
or even a poor person, having drawn a lotus with rice-flour and other materials, [attains the same].
One obtains all the merit previously described; there is no doubt about this.
Likewise, having drawn the twelve-spoked mandala, which is the supreme station— LiP 1.77.74.
With powders such as powdered jewels and likewise with the twelve forms,
one should place the Sun in the center of the mandala and worship him.
Or even if it is surrounded by the planets, [one attains] the supreme union with the Sun;
likewise, having fashioned the six-sided [diagram] for the Prākṛta and Ārṣī [mantras].
And in the middle region, he [should worship] the Goddess of the gods, Prakṛti, whose form is Brahman;
to the south, the embodiment of Sattva, and to the left, the quality of Rajas.
In front [he should place] him whose form is darkness (Tamas), and in the middle the goddess Ambika;
likewise, the five gross elements and the pentad of subtle elements (tanmātra) on the right.
Having duly worshipped the five organs of action and likewise the five organs of perception,
one should worship them in the six-cornered [figure] according to the prescribed rule.
By [worshipping] the self, the inner self, the pair, the intellect,
and the ego along with the Great Principle (mahat), one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices.
Thus has the supreme mundane mandala been described to you in its entirety;
therefore, O best of Brahmins, I shall now speak of that which accomplishes all desires and goals.
Having drawn a mandala the size of a cow's hide with cow dung,
the knower of mantras should fashion it into a square according to the rules and sprinkle it with water.
Having adorned it with canopies and the like, or with beautiful parasols,
as well as with golden ornaments in the shape of bubbles, half-moons, and leaves of the *aśvattha* tree.
With white and blooming lotuses, as well as red and blue water-lilies,
with strings of pearls, and with white banners hanging from the edge of the canopy.
With white earthen vessels, very smooth full jars, garlands of fruits and sprouts, victory banners, and silken cloths; LiP_1,77.85.
One should draw an excellent lotus endowed with fifty petals, adorned with garlands of fifty lamps and likewise with five kinds of incense.
Having fashioned a lotus according to the prescribed rite, measuring one cubit in size, using powders of various colors or even white powder; ||| LiP_1,77.87 |||
One should place the god Bhava, the Lord of Gods, together with the Goddess upon the pericarp;
and one should place the seed-syllables on the petals, starting from the east in sequence, accompanied by the Rudras.

O best of sages, O you of excellent vows, having thus worshipped all the letters, beginning with *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*, in their proper order with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings; LiP_1,77.89.
There, one should feed fifty Brahmins according to the prescribed rites,
and [bestow upon them] a rosary of seeds, a sacred thread, earrings, and a water-pot.
Having thus offered the great sacrificial pap (mahācaru) as well as a pair of black cows to Kṛṣṇa,
one should finally cause a powder-mandala to be presented to the God of gods.
The wise one should offer the substances used in the sacrifice to Śiva,
reciting the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning and repeating it for each letter in successive order.
I shall now describe in brief the fruit that a mortal obtains by thus painting this supreme mandala with devotion.
Having studied the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs according to the rule and in accordance with the prescribed ordinances,
and having performed sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and others in due order and according to the rule;
Then, having fathered sons such as Viśvajit and others like them,
he entered the forest-dwelling stage of life (vānaprasthāśrama) together with his wife and his sacred fires.
Having performed all the rites such as the Cāndrāyaṇa and having deposited them [in the fire], O twice-born ones,
and having studied the Brahmavidyā, one should diligently attain knowledge.
Whatever desired object a yogi may obtain by perceiving the knowable through knowledge,
he attains all that fruit simply from the vision of the maṇḍala of the castes (varṇa).
O best of the twice-born, by whatever means a mortal may smear [the ground] in front of the sanctuary, or to the north, the south, or even behind it; ||| LiP_1,77.99 |||
Or, having decorated a square area on all sides with colored powders and having worshipped it with flowers, unbroken rice, and other offerings, one is liberated from all sins.
Having scattered fragrant flowers and having perfumed [the area] with four kinds of incense, he should pray to the Lord Īśāna; he goes to the world of Śiva.
Having enjoyed great pleasures there for a hundred million kalpas,
that man shall fill the temple of Śiva with flowers having the fragrance of his own body.
Having gradually attained the state of a Gandharva and being well-honored by the Gandharvas,
he eventually returns to this world and becomes a powerful king.
The primordial god, the great god, the cause of dissolution and maintenance,
the creator, the lord of the worlds, the all-pervading Śarva, Sadāśiva—
the nectar of Śiva-Brahman is to be grasped as the supreme means for liberation.
One should always worship the Lord, who is both manifest and unmanifest, eternal, and inconceivable.
Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Smearing and Other Rites," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
O best of sages, in a sacred field of Śiva, all tasks such as smearing [the ground] must be performed with water filtered through a cloth; otherwise, success is not desired.
O tigers among sages, these waters become pure when they are drawn up, filtered through a cloth, and free from foam; this is especially true for water taken from rivers.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, all rites pertaining to the divine should indeed be performed with pure water for the successful accomplishment of every undertaking.
For water is indeed mixed with living beings; having killed those subtle creatures, one would incur all the sin that comes from using water that has not been purified for a long time.
Likewise, during the sweeping of the house, especially during the cleansing of people, at the fire, while pounding, grinding, and collecting water; // LiP_1,78.5 //
Violence is ever present for householders; therefore, one should avoid violence.
O twice-born ones, this non-violence is the supreme dharma for all living beings.
Therefore, with every effort, one should practice straining water through a cloth;
that gift of fearlessness is meritorious and the most excellent among all gifts.
Therefore, one must avoid violence at all times and in all places;
one should always avoid a person who is violent in thought, deed, or speech.
All living beings protect one another and afflict the violent;
yet the fruit that belongs to one who has mastered the Vedas is equal to giving away the entire three worlds.
A person who refrains from violence and delights in the welfare of all beings through thought, deed, and word obtains that fruit multiplied ten millionfold.
Those who have shown the path of compassion go to the world of Rudra,
and like their own master, they protect many various things.
Those who, out of affection for their sons and grandsons, go to the world of Rudra—
therefore, with every effort, one should [bathe] with water filtered through a cloth.
The daily sprinkling and especially the ritual bathing of the image should always be performed;
the fruit of this is proclaimed to be equal to that which is attained by destroying the entire triple world.
By destroying even a single [insect] in the abode of Śiva, one obtains all of that;
O best of the twice-born, for the sake of Śiva, the destruction of flowers should always be performed.

The killing of animals for the sake of sacrifice and the punishment of the wicked by Kṣatriyas—these exist; however, for yogins who proclaim Brahman, there is neither that which is prescribed nor that which is forbidden.
Therefore, they must not be killed because of their indulgence in forbidden acts; having renounced all ritual actions, these expounders of Brahman have truly taken up the life of renunciation.
Women born in the lineage of Atri are always pure and worthy of worship; they must never be harmed, even if they are devoted to sinful deeds.
The sin of killing an Ātreyī woman is equal to the murder of a Brāhmaṇa;
therefore, no women should be killed, even those devoted to sinful deeds.
O best of Brahmins, women should not be taken for the sake of sacrifice by anyone, anywhere, or at any time— even from among all social classes, even if they are devoted to sinful deeds.
Whether they are beautiful or ugly, dirty or dressed in soiled garments,
they must never be harmed by mortals, out of fear of Śiva and likewise of Śaṅkara.
Those whose vows and conduct lie outside the Vedas and who are excluded from the Śrauta and Smārta rites are known as heretics (pāṣaṇḍins); they should not be conversed with by the twice-born.
She is not to be touched nor is she to be looked upon; yet, having seen the sun, she gazes at it, and nevertheless, she is to be slain by him, by kings, and by other creatures.
O twice-born ones, even that mortal who, by chance,
worships Maheśvara even once, attains the world of Rudra.
O best of sages,
all those men who are devoid of devotion toward Bhava, the supreme cause, become utterly miserable and heartless.
Those devotees of Śiva, the God of gods and the Supreme Lord,
who are fortunate, are liberated after having enjoyed worldly pleasures right here in this world.

Just as the minds of men are devoted to sons, wives, and homes, so too is the mind of those great ascetics directed toward the Primordial God; for them, through even a single instance of such attachment, the realm of the Supreme Lord is not far off.
Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Devotion," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
The sages said:
O high-minded one, how is Mahādeva, the Lord of Creatures, to be worshipped by mortals who are dull-witted,
whose lifespans last but a single kalpa, and who possess little vigor and little strength?
Even after worshipping Śaṅkara with ascetic penance for thousands of years, the gods do not see him; how then can they worship the Lord?
Sūta said:
O eminent sages, what you have spoken here is indeed the truth;
nevertheless, he is to be beheld, worshipped, and conversed with with faith.

And by way of incidental mention, O twice-born ones, it is proclaimed that even those devoid of devotion, having performed worship, obtain fruits according to their inner disposition, for the Blessed Lord is the bestower of results in accordance with one's state of being.
O twice-born ones, the lowest of the twice-born who worships while impure reaches the realm of the Piśācas;
the fool whose mind is deluded, being full of anger, shall attain the station of the Rākṣasas.
By consuming what is unfit for consumption, the wicked person attains the realm of the yakṣas after performing worship;
likewise, one who is habitually fond of singing attains the realm of the gandharvas, as does one habitually fond of dancing.
Likewise, the lowest of men who is devoted to women, though possessing fame and virtue,
and who, afflicted by intoxication, worships Rudra, shall attain the abode of Soma.

Having worshipped the deity with the Gāyatrī, one obtains the state of Prajāpati; indeed, by means of the Praṇava alone, one attains the state of Brahmā, and by praising [the deity] as Vaiṣṇava, one attains the state of Viṣṇu.
Even by worshipping Maheśvara just once with faith,
one reaches the world of Rudra and rejoices together with the Rudras.
Having purified the auspicious *liṅga* worshipped by gods and asuras, he should then,
with devotion, invoke the God onto the pedestal with pure waters.
Having seen the god Śaṅkara, he prostrated according to the prescribed rule and established him upon a beautiful throne fashioned from the essence of the knowledge of Dharma.
In him who is endowed with dispassion and sovereignty, who is saluted by all the worlds, and who is born from the moon, sun, and fire within the lotus of the syllable Oṃ; LiP_1,79.12.
Having offered water for the feet, water for sipping, and the arghya offering to Rudra Śambhu,
one should bathe him with divine waters, as well as with ghee and milk.
One should bathe Rudra with curd and purify him according to the prescribed rite;
then, having bathed him with pure water, one should worship him with sandalwood paste and other offerings.
Having worshipped with yellow pigment (rocanā) and other substances, one should worship with divine flowers,
with unbroken bilva leaves, and likewise with various kinds of lotuses.
With blue lotuses, red lotuses, water-lilies, and mallikās;
with campakas, jasmine flowers, bakulas, and karavīrakas.
With *śamī* flowers, *bṛhat* flowers, as well as those from the *unmatta* and *agastya* plants,
with *apāmārga* and *kadamba*, and with beautiful ornaments.
Having offered five kinds of incense, one should present milk-rice (pāyasa),
and thereafter, rice mixed with curd and saturated with honey and ghee.
One should offer pure rice and mung-bean rice in six varieties;
or alternatively, one may offer five varieties along with clarified butter.
One should cook one āḍhaka of pure rice alone;
having done so, one should circumambulate it at the end, bowing down again and again.
Having praised the Lord Īśāna and once again worshipped Śaṅkara—
namely Īśāna, Puruṣa, Aghora, and Vāma— [he should proceed].
Reciting the Sadyojāta mantra, one should also worship Śiva with the five [mantras];
by this procedure, the god Maheśvara becomes propitious.
O best of the twice-born, trees that have been utilized with flowers, leaves, and so forth for the worship of Śiva, as well as cows, attain the supreme goal.
Whoever worships Śiva, Rudra, Śarva, Bhava, and the Unborn even once,
attains union with Śiva from which there is no return.
By seeing the worshiped Supreme Lord Bhava, Śarva, the consort of Umā, even once by chance, one is liberated from all sins.
Having seen Mahādeva worshipped, or even being worshipped himself, a mortal indeed goes to the world of Brahmā; of this there is no doubt.
Having heard this, one should rejoice;
he who offers a lamp of ghee even once before the Liṅga attains the supreme goal.
He attains that stable state which is difficult to reach even through one's own religious stages of life (āśramas)—
by offering a lamp-stand made of earth, wood, or stone in a temple of Śiva.
Having given [a vessel] made of iron, copper, silver, or likewise gold, one is honored in the world of Śiva for more than a hundred generations of one's lineage.
Whoever offers a lamp to Śiva according to the prescribed rite or with devotion shall go to the city of Śiva in smooth vehicles equal to ten thousand suns.
He who, in the month of Kārttika, offers a ghee lamp before Śiva,
or beholds the Supreme Lord worshipped according to the prescribed rite, [attains great merit].
O best of sages, through faith he goes to the world of Brahmā;
[he performs] the invocation, the presence, the installation, and likewise the worship.
The seat is prescribed with the Rudra-gāyatrī and indeed with the Praṇava;
the ritual bathing is prescribed with the five [mantras] beginning with the Rudras, especially.
Thus one should constantly worship the God of gods, the Lord of Umā;
one should worship Brahmā to his right with the syllable Om (praṇava).
In the north, one should worship Viṣṇu, the Lord of the gods of gods, with the Gāyatrī mantra;
having offered oblations into the fire according to the rule with the five [mantras] and the Praṇava.
Having thus worshipped Śaṅkara, he attains union with Śiva;
such, in brief, is the sequence of the ritual for the worship of the Liṅga.
It was previously told by Vyāsa, having heard it himself from the mouth of Rudra.
Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Worship of Śiva," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
The sages said:
How is it that upon seeing Paśupati, the gods attained liberation from the bonds of the bound (paśu) and abandoned their state as bound souls? You ought to tell us this here.
Sūta said:
Formerly, on the peak of Kailāsa, in his own city named Bhogya,
the gods, having assembled by his grace, approached the omniscient one.
For the welfare of all the gods, Janārdana,
the Supreme Person, mounted the shoulder of Garuḍa at the command of Brahmā.
Hari indeed went to the presence of the God of gods along with the deities;
having all arrived together with the Lord, they reached the auspicious, excellent mountain.
Accompanied by the Sādhyas and the Yamas, they, together with Indra, bowed down before that supreme mountain. Then the Blessed Vāsudeva, whose banner bears Garuḍa,
descended from Garuḍa and ascended Mount Meru along with the best of the gods.
Free from all misfortune, bestowing all things, and preeminent in enjoyment; resounded by flocks of joyful *kurara* birds and by throngs of serpents;
filled with sweet-sounding songs, accompanied by favorable darkness, its forest edges laid out with lotuses, and its waters stirred by lovely breezes. (LiP 1.80.6)
It was graced by hundreds of thousands of celestial abodes resembling the sun, and interspersed with flocks of swans, graceful and clever in their flight;
it was filled with trees such as dhava, khadira, palāśa, and sandalwood, and with multitudes of excellent birds like cuckoos and swarms of bees.
In some places, that best of mountains was crowded with every kind of celestial tree, as well as *kurabaka*, *priyaka*, and *tilaka* trees;
it was likewise covered by many *kadamba* and *tamāla* creepers, and possessed various kinds of peaks.
On the summit of the mountain, a supreme city belonging to Śiva was fashioned by Viśvakarman for the sake of the sport of Bhava, the god of gods and the Supreme Lord.
Not seeing that city, the gods, including Indra and Upendra, remained composed;
they bowed from afar out of sheer reverence for the power of the wielder of the trident.
Resembling a thousand suns, vast, and distinguished by thousands of all virtues,
that Great-Souled One, the Primordial God, went to the city on Mount Kailāsa, which was situated on a portion of Meru.
Then, O slayer of the enemies of the gods, the unborn Hari, accompanied by women, elephants, and horses, and with many chariots,
as well as by the Gaṇas and the lords of the Gaṇas, approached the gate of the great city which resembled the king of mountains.
Then it was surrounded by palaces made of Jāmbūnada gold adorned with jewels,
by celestial chariots of various forms, and by ramparts.
Having beheld the outer city of Śambhu, Hari, together with the gods including Brahmā,
became joyful of countenance and then entered that city.
The second [palace] of the God of gods is crowded with mansions and palaces, provided with great turrets, and is very beautiful with four gates.
It is completely covered with nets of diamonds, lapis lazuli, rubies, and jewels;
it is equipped with swinging swings and adorned with bells and chowries.
It was graced by mṛdaṅga and muraja drums and resounded with the music of lutes and flutes;
it was surrounded by throngs of dancing apsarases and hosts of spirits,
and filled with palaces resembling the abodes of the lords of the gods that captivate the sight.
Then, thousands of city women stood upon the turrets of the palaces and, with their hands, scattered flowers, fruits,
and unbroken grains all around the head of that Hari, just as they do for Bhava.
Then, having seen Viṣṇu, the women had their eyes rolling with intoxication.
Upon seeing Hari, some women with broad hips immediately began to dance, rejoiced, and sang, their faces slightly smiling.
With their garments slightly disheveled and their girdles slipping down,
they sang the fourth, fifth, sixth, and likewise the seventh [notes].
Having passed beyond the eighth, the ninth, and the tenth supreme city, he reached the most beautiful city of the god Śambhu.
It was perfectly circular and exceedingly bright upon the auspicious peak of Kailāsa,
adorned with celestial chariots resembling the orb of the sun.
It was adorned in all directions and intermediate points with bright pavilions made of crystal, as well as those fashioned from gold and various kinds of jewels.
With many gate-towers of Śambhu, the Lord of the Earth, adorned with various ornaments, auspicious on all sides, and composed entirely of every kind of gem; LiP_1,80.25.
It was surrounded by twenty-eight ramparts of various forms,
with diverse and sturdy secondary gates and great gates at the intermediate directions.
O highly fortunate ones, [they were adorned] with secret abodes, secret houses, and the auspicious palaces of Guha,
as well as other village dwellings and pearl ornaments that captivate the eye.
It was likewise adorned with divine abodes of Gaṇeśa made of rubies,
with sandalwood trees of various forms, and with beautiful flower gardens.
It was surrounded on all sides by ponds and oblong lakes with rows of golden steps, frequented by swans that surpassed the gait of women.
It was adorned with peacocks, kāraṇḍava ducks, cuckoos, and ruddy geese,
as well as by beautiful ponds filled with divine nectar-like water.
Skilled in conversation and discourse, adorned with every ornament,
they were bent low by the weight of their breasts, their eyes rolling with intoxication.
By thousands of divine Rudra-maidens who delighted in singing,
and by throngs of Apsarases dancing— beings difficult even for the immortals to attain.
It was likewise filled with clusters of blossoming lotuses and other such flowers, as well as by the best of the twice-born,
who were mingled with hosts of Rudra’s wives and intent upon sporting in the water.

And with those who were devoted to the festivals of love, graceful at every step, impassioned by the melodies of the musical scales (*grāmarāga*), and possessing a radiance like that of rubies; 80.34.
Having seen the hosts of women belonging to Bhava, the God of gods and Supreme Self, the deities were struck with wonder and stood on all sides.
Right there, the gods beheld a multitude of Rudra’s attendants,
as well as thousands of groups of heroic lords of the Gaṇas.
They beheld the celestial palaces of the God of gods, featuring staircases made of gold and adorned with diamonds and lapis lazuli, as well as crystal structures.
And upon their peaks were joyful women with lotus-like eyes,
as well as yakṣas, gandharvas, and apsarases with broad hips.
Kinnarīs and Kinnaras, serpents and Siddha maidens,
as well as others wearing various garments and adorned with diverse ornaments.
Endowed with various powers, fond of diverse enjoyments and pleasures,
they resemble the petals of the blue lotus, with eyes as long as lotus leaves.
They were exceedingly beautiful with garments resembling the filaments of a lotus,
as well as with bracelets, anklets, necklaces, variegated umbrellas, and likewise with fine cloths.

Adorned with various ornaments and decorated with other finery, those who delight in adornment beheld the host of celestial beauties belonging to the lords of the Gaṇas; then the lords of the gods, led by Śakra, went to the city of the lord of the Gaṇas, the enemy of the cities.

And having seen it, the hosts of gods and Siddhas, led by Indra, stood in the midst of the city before the primordial celestial chariot of Bhava, the Supreme Lord, which possessed the color of a thousand rising suns.
Then all the gods, led by Śakra, beheld Nandin, the lord of the Gaṇas, stationed at the gateway of that celestial palace.
Seeing Nandin, all the gods bowed to the Lord of the Gaṇas and cried, "Victory! Upon seeing them, the Lord of the Gaṇas also spoke.
O gods, O highly fortunate ones, all of you whose taints have been shaken off,
who have attained lordship over all the worlds and are firm in your vows, you ought to speak.
They call him the God who grants boons, whose splendor is equal to that of the lord of elephants;
show us Maheśvara for the sake of liberation from the bonds of the individual soul (paśu).

"O observer of noble vows, in the past, when you were designated as the sacrificial animal (paśu) in order to burn down the three cities, we too became apprehensive regarding that state of being an animal."
The Pāśupata vow was proclaimed by Bhava, the Supreme Lord;
by this vow, O Lord of Beings, the state of being a bound soul (paśutva) no longer exists.
Then, having performed that supreme vow for twelve years, or for twelve months, or even for twelve days; LiP_1,80.50.
"All the bound souls (paśu) are indeed liberated from the bonds of Bhava.
He then showed those gods, headed by Nārāyaṇa, [the state of liberation].
Nandin, the son of Śilāda and leader of all the hosts of spirits,
beheld that imperishable Lord Īśāna together with Ambā and his attendants.
With their skin bristling with joy,
they prostrated and offered hymns of praise after requesting Śitikaṇṭha for the liberation of the bonds of the individual soul (paśu).
They stood then before Śambhu, prostrating themselves again and again;
then, having gazed upon them all, the God of gods, whose banner is the bull, spoke.
Having purified those gods of their state as sacrificial victims, the Supreme Lord,
the God Maheśvara himself, [bestowed] the Pāśupata vow.
Having instructed the sages, Bhava remained there together with Ambā;
from that time forward, all those gods are remembered as Pāśupatas.
Because he is the Lord of beasts (paśu) and their manifest deity, they are therefore called Pāśupatas; and they again performed austerities.
Then, at the end of twelve years, those supreme gods, their bonds released,
all departed as they had come, together with Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
All this has been told to you, as it was heard from the mouth of the Grandfather (Brahmā) in the past by Sanatkumāra, and from him by the wise Vyāsa.
The man who, being pure, causes the Brahmins to hear this, or who hears it himself while being pure,
shall, upon the dissolution of the body, be liberated from the bonds of the individual soul (paśu-pāśa).
Thus ends the eightieth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Pāśupata Vow," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
The sages said:
This vow which has been proclaimed by you is the liberation from the bonds of the individual soul (paśu);
it is the Pāśupata vow of the Liṅga, which was practiced by the gods in ancient times.
"You ought to tell us how it was heard by you in the past.
Sūta said:
"In ancient times, Śailādi was respectfully questioned by Sanatkumāra."
Nandī spoke these words to him in brief:
"By the gods, the daityas, as well as the siddhas, gandharvas, and siddha-cāraṇas... (the result of liṅga worship).
And this unsurpassed vow known as the Twelve Liṅgas, which effects liberation from the bonds of Paśu, was practiced by the highly fortunate sages.
It bestows enjoyment and yoga, grants desires and liberation, is auspicious,
brings about non-separation, is meritorious, and destroys the fears of devotees.
Having churned the Vedas together with their six auxiliary limbs,
he fashioned by means of that [knowledge] a merit which is the highest of all gifts and exceeds ten thousand horse-sacrifices.
It bestows all auspiciousness, is meritorious, destroys all enemies,
and grants liberation even to living beings submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra.
It removes all diseases and destroys all fevers;
it was formerly practiced by the gods, as well as by Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
Having fashioned a small liṅga and bathed it with sandalwood water,
O best of Brahmins, one should observe the Śivaliṅga vow beginning from the month of Caitra.
Having fashioned an auspicious golden lotus, complete with a pericarp and filaments,
and inlaid with the nine gems upon its eight petals according to the prescribed rite.
One should place a crystal liṅga together with its pedestal upon the pericarp;
there, one should worship it with devotion according to the rule using bilva leaves.
With white thousand-petaled lotuses, red and blue water-lilies,
white arka flowers, karṇikāras, karavīras, and bakas as well.

O best of the twice-born, one should offer the great Lord Maheśvara in the form of the Liṅga with the rite of lustration (nīrājanā) and other ceremonies, and one should offer aloe-wood (agaru) to the south while reciting the Aghora mantra.
In the west, one should cause divine red arsenic (manaḥśilā) to be offered with the Sadyojāta mantra;
in the north, one should likewise cause sandalwood to be offered with the Vāmadeva mantra.
O best of sages, a man [should offer] yellow orpiment in the east;
O brahmins, likewise [incense] derived from white agallochum and that derived from black agallochum.
Likewise, one should devotedly offer to Īśa incense made of guggulu, the unsurpassed saugandhika, and the incense known as sitāra.
A great sacrificial porridge (mahācaru) should be offered, or else a measure of cooked rice (āḍhaka);
this meritorious Great Vow of the Śiva-liṅga has thus been described to you.
(The time for this vow:
The general [rule] for all months is stated, as well as the specific [rules].
In Vaiśākha, there is a vajra-liṅga, and likewise an emerald one in Jyeṣṭha.
In Āṣāḍha, the linga is made of pearl; in Śrāvaṇa, it is fashioned from sapphire;
in the month of Bhādrapada, the auspicious linga consists of ruby.
O best of Brahmins, in the month of Āśvina, it should be auspiciously made of *gomedaka*;
likewise, in Kārttika and Mārgaśīrṣa, it should be made of coral.
The material for the *liṅga* is as follows:
a *liṅga* made of beryl (*vaiḍūrya*) in the month of Puṣya,
one of topaz (*puṣparāga*) in the month of Māgha, and one of sun-crystal (*sūryakānta*) or rock crystal (*sphāṭika*) in the month of Phālguna.
In all months, a single golden lotus is prescribed;
in its absence, one may use a silver one, or even a lotus made of any material at all.
If even gems are not available, one should have [the image] made of gold or silver;
if even silver is not available, one should have it made of copper or iron.
One should fashion a temporary [image] made of stone, wood, or clay, provided with a pedestal, or even composed entirely of fragrant substances.
In the winter season, one should worship Mahādeva with a lotus made of gold;
in all months, however, a lotus may be made either of gold or even of a single leaf.
Or one may offer an excellent silver lotus with a golden pericarp;
however, in the absence of even a silver one, one should worship with bilva leaves.
If one cannot obtain a thousand lotuses, one should worship Rudra with even half of that number,
or half of that again, or with one hundred and eight.
Goddess Lakṣmī, endowed with all auspicious marks, resides in the *bilva* leaf; Ambikā herself is present in the blue lotus, and Ṣaṇmukha himself is in the *utpala*. (Flower = Deity) LiP 1.81.29.
The Great God Śiva, the lord of all deities, is seated upon a lotus;
therefore, a wise person should, with every effort, never discard a leaf of the *śrī* plant.
The blue lotus, the utpala, and especially the kamala;
the lotus brings all things under control, and the stone grants the accomplishment of all goals.
The offering of black agalloch wood, which destroys all sins,
as well as the presentation of lamps made from guggulu and other such substances.
Sandalwood brings about the destruction of all diseases and grants all accomplishments;
likewise, the fragrant incense accomplishes all desires and goals.
That which arises from white agallochum, as well as that arising from black agallochum,
the gentle incense of *sītāri*, directly bestows the accomplishment of nirvāṇa.
In the white *arka* flower, Prajāpati himself, the four-faced one, is directly present;
in the flower of the *karṇikāra*, wisdom itself is established.
Gaṇādhyakṣa resides in the karavīra, Nārāyaṇa himself in the baka,
and the Daughter of the Mountain (Umā) in all fragrant flowers.
Therefore, with whatever auspicious flowers, incense, and other offerings one may obtain,
one should worship the Lord of the Gods with devotion, according to one's means.
Then, with devotion, one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) and the great sacrificial oblation (mahācaru),
together with clarified butter, side-dishes, and all other necessary ingredients.
One should devotedly offer him pure rice or mung-bean porridge, either a full āḍhaka or half an āḍhaka, as well as a yak-tail whisk and a palm-leaf fan.
The offerings, meritorious and even those acquired through righteous means,
being of various kinds and worthy, were further sprinkled with water.
And one should offer it to Rudra with a mind full of devotion,
for from milk indeed comes the eternal nectar for the sustenance of all the gods.
Everything is established in food, which is Viṣṇu himself, the victorious;
through the gift of food to living beings, satisfaction arises for Śaṅkara.
Therefore, one should worship the God; for the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are established in the food.
Likewise, satisfaction arises from the offering, and the Wind himself resides in the condiments.
Mahādeva is the soul of all; indeed, the Lord of Waters is present in the fragrant water.
On the seat (pīṭha), Prakṛti herself is directly established along with Mahat and the other principles.
Therefore, one should worship the God with devotion every month according to the prescribed rule;
on the full moon day, the vow should be performed for the sake of attaining all desires and goals.
Truthfulness, purity, compassion, tranquility, contentment, and generosity—
these one should practice, as well as fasting on the full moon and the new moon days.
At the end of the year, one should especially perform the gift of a cow and the ritual release of a bull;
one should devoutly feed Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the Vedas and have mastered them.
That linga, worshipped by him and provided with all necessary materials,
he should either install in a sacred field of Śiva or cause it to be given to a Brāhmaṇa.
O best of sages, he who performs this great vow of the Śiva-liṅga with devotion in this manner throughout all the months is indeed the foremost among those who practice austerities.
Having traveled to the divine city of Śiva in celestial chariots adorned with jewels and resembling ten million suns, he never returns here again.
Or indeed, by practicing this supreme vow for even one month, one attains the world of Śiva; there is no need for deliberation on this point.

Alternatively, if his mind is attached [to worldly desires], whatever boons he might contemplate, he should practice in this manner for one year; having attained those various [results], he shall go to Śiva.
Even a man who is attached to worldly desires may attain the state of a god, the state of a progenitor, the sovereignty of the gods, or even the rank of a leader of the Gaṇas.
One seeking knowledge shall obtain knowledge; one seeking enjoyment shall attain enjoyment;
one seeking wealth shall behold a treasure; and one desiring long life shall attain longevity.
Whatever desires he contemplates, those very things he attains here and rejoices in;
by the mere observance of this vow for one month, he shall attain the state of Rudra at the end.
This supreme purifier, this secret, this most excellent vow was created even by the Creator of the universe for the welfare of gods, asuras, siddhas, mortals, and vidyādharas, by Śiva himself.
Having thus worshipped the worshipful Lord according to the prescribed rite, and having bowed his head along with his servants and sons,
he should diligently perform circumambulation of Śiva and recite the hymn named *Vyapohana*.
