This highly precious hymn was formerly composed for the benefit of the three worlds by the Creator, the God,
the Grandfather himself, together with the gods, who is possessed of great majesty.
Thus ends the eighty-first chapter, titled "The Narration of the Worship of the Liṅga and the Liberation from the Bonds of Paśu," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅgamahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
I shall now proclaim the auspicious hymn of praise for the Dispeller (*Vyapohana*), which bestows all accomplishments,
as it was heard from the mouth of Nandin by the high-souled Kumāra.
Therefore, out of great respect, I have related this to Vyāsa;
salutations to Śiva, the pure, the stainless, and the glorious.
Salutation to the one whose body is the Destroyer of the wicked, to existence itself, to the Supreme Self;
who indeed has five faces and ten arms, and is endowed with fifteen eyes.
Resembling pure crystal, adorned with all ornaments,
omniscient, omnipresent, peaceful, and firmly established above all.
May Someśa, seated in the lotus posture, swiftly dispel my sin—
He who is Īśāna, Puruṣa, Aghora, and Sadyojāta.
And may the blessed Vāmadeva swiftly dispel my sin;
he is Ananta, the lord of all sciences, the omniscient, the all-bestowing, and the sovereign Lord.
May he, who is perfected solely through meditation on Śiva, may he— subtle, the lord of gods and asuras, the lord of the universe, worshipped by the Gaṇas— dispel my sin.
May he, who is fully accomplished solely through meditation on Śiva, may he remove my sin—
he who is the supreme Śiva, worthy of great worship, and devoted to the meditation on Śiva.
All-pervading, all-bestowing, and peaceful, may he remove my sin;
the one-eyed Lord Īśa, who is solely devoted to the worship of Śiva.
May that Lord Īśa, who is the embodiment of the three forms and the awakener of devotion to Śiva, being perfected solely through meditation on Śiva, dispel my sin.
May he, who is solely perfected through meditation on Śiva— Śrīkaṇṭha, the Lord of Śrī, the illustrious one, who is ever devoted to the meditation on Śiva— dispel my sin.
May that illustrious one, devoted to the worship of Śiva, dispel my sin;
may the ancient Goddess, who is saluted by the three worlds and whose form is like a flaming torch, do the same.
May that glorious one, devoted to the worship of Śiva, remove my sin;
may the ancient Goddess, who is saluted by the three worlds and whose form is like a flaming torch, [grant me protection].
Dākṣāyaṇī, Mahādevī, Gaurī, Haimavatī, Śubhā,
Ekaparṇā, Agravajā, Saumyā, and likewise Ekapāṭalā.
Aparṇā, the goddess Varadā, who is solely intent upon the granting of boons; Umā, the destroyer of the gods, she who is manifest as Kauśikī or Kapardinī.
Divine, bearing a skull-topped staff, with the sprouts of trees upon the tips of her hands,
she is surrounded by four divine sons, Naigameya and the others.
The goddess Menā was the daughter of Vārija, who had lotus-like eyes;
she was the mother of the high-souled Nandin, whose sorrow had departed.
Śāntā, Pañcacūḍā, and Varapradā are the companions of Śubhāvatī;
for the sake of the creation of all beings, the imperishable one has assumed the state of primordial nature (prakṛti).
She who is manifested through the twenty-three principles beginning with the Great One (mahat),
who is eternally bowed to by Lakṣmī and the other Śaktis, and who delights in the Nandana grove— salutations to her.
The great goddess Manonmanī is the master of illusion and fond of adornment;
by means of her illusory power (māyā), she [creates] the entire universe, beginning with Brahmā, including all that is moving and unmoving.
Ever agitating and deluding, she dwells within the hearts of yogins;
though one, she exists as many in the world, her eyes resembling blue lotuses.
She is eternally praised with supreme devotion by all the gods,
headed by Gaṇendra, Ambhojagarbha, Indra, Yama, and Vitteśa.
Their mother is praised as the destroyer of all calamities;
she is the remover of the distress of devotees, auspicious, and the annihilator of the state of worldly existence.
May that divine Great Goddess, who effortlessly bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon her devotees, swiftly dispel my sin in person.
May the illustrious Caṇḍa, the lord of all the Gaṇas, who emerged from the mouth of Śambhu and is devoted to the worship of Śiva, dispel my sin.
But the son of Śālaṅkāyana was the lord who rose from the path of the plow;
he was the divine son-in-law of the Maruts and the great sovereign of all beings.
The all-pervading, all-seeing Śarva, the Lord who resembles the Lord of all,
[is worshipped] by the gods including Nārāyaṇa, along with Indra, the Moon, and the Sun.
And by the Siddhas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Bhūtas who ordain the elements,
as well as by the Uragas, the Ṛṣis, and the high-souled Brahmā.
May Nandin, the lord of the three worlds, who is praised and dwells within the inner sanctum of the Sage,
and who is ever worshipped by all— may he dispel our sin.
Possessing a great body and great splendor, like another Mahādeva,
that illustrious one who is devoted to the worship of Śiva may dispel my sin.
He shatters the peaks and slopes of Meru, Mandāra, and Kailāsa,
and is well-honored by the divine elephants of the quarters, such as Airāvata and others.
Śiva has the seven netherworlds as his feet, the seven continents as his thighs and shanks,
the seven oceans as his goad, and all sacred fords as his belly.
His body is space, his arms are the directions, and his eyes are the moon, the sun, and fire;
he has struck down the great tree of the asuras and is intensely exalted by the supreme knowledge of Brahman.
Bound by divine elephant-drivers beginning with Brahmā, who are equipped with the nooses of yoga,
he has suppressed his mental fluctuations within the pillar known as the heart-lotus.
May he who has the face of the Lord of Serpents, who is surrounded by hundreds of millions of Gaṇas in person,
and who is perfected solely through meditation on Śiva, dispel my sin.
May that illustrious Bhṛṅgīśa— whose eyes are tawny, who consumes ashes, whose body is adorned with them,
and who is devoted to the worship of Śiva— dispel my sin.
With four bodies, he is the eternal destroyer of all asuras;
Skanda, the wielder of the spear, the peaceful one, the leader of the army, whose vehicle is the peacock.
May the glorious Deva-senāpati dispel my sin;
likewise Bhava, Śarva, Īśāna, Rudra, and Paśupati.
The fierce Bhīma, the Great God who is ever devoted to the worship of Śiva—
may these forms of the Supreme Lord dispel our sin.
Mahādeva, Śiva, Rudra, Śaṅkara, Nīlalohita,
Īśāna, Vijaya, Bhīma, Devadeva, and Bhavodbhava.
And Kapālīśa is to be known; these Rudras, born from portions of Rudra and perfected by prostration to Śiva, may they remove my impurity.
Vikartana, Vivasvat, Mārtaṇḍa, Bhāskara, Ravi,
Lokaprakāśaka, Lokasākṣin, and Trivikrama.
Āditya, Sūrya, Aṃśumat, and Divākara—
may these twelve Ādityas indeed dispel my impurity.
Space, touch, fire, taste, and earth,
as well as the moon, the sun, and the self— these are the subtle bodies spoken of by Śiva.
May they dispel my evil and utterly destroy my fear:
Vāsava, Pāvaka, Yama, and Nirṛti as well.
Varuṇa, Vāyu, Soma, the Lord Īśāna, Hari,
and the Blessed Grandfather (Brahmā) were all intent upon meditation on Śiva.
May these— Nabhasvān, Sparśana, Vāyu, Anila, and likewise Māruta— dispel the evil committed by me through thought and deed.
May Prāṇa, Prāṇeśa, Jīveśa, and Māruta, as spoken by Śiva—
all of whom are devoted to the worship of Śiva— dispel my impurity.
Khecarī, Vasucārī, Brahmeśa, Brahmabrahmadhī, Suṣeṇa, Śāśvata, Pṛṣṭa, Supuṣṭa, and Mahābala.
"These attendants of Śambhu, who are deeply devoted to his worship,
shall surely remove all impurity and every sin committed by me."
He is the knower of mantras, the master of mantras, the wise one, the king of mantras, and the one worshipped by the Siddhas;
he is the supreme among the Siddhas, the perfected one, and the bestower of all accomplishments.
May all the Siddhas, who worship the state of Śiva, dispel every impurity;
as do the Yakṣa, Dhanada the lord of Yakṣas, Jṛmbhaka, and Maṇibhadra.
May Pūrṇabhadreśvara, Mālī, Śitikuṇḍali, and Narendra—
the lords of the Yakṣas— dispel my impurity.
Ananta, Kulika, Vāsuki, Takṣaka,
Karkoṭaka, Mahāpadma, and the very powerful Śaṅkhapāla.
May those who are perfected by prostrations to Śiva and who adorn the body of Śiva dispel my sin and neutralize all poison, both stationary and mobile.
Vīṇājña, Kinnara, Surasena, Pramardana,
Atīśaya, Sa-prayogī, and Gītajña— these are the Kinnaras.
May these, who are perfected through prostration to Śiva— the Vidyādhara, the Vibudha, the Vidyārāśi, and the best among the knowers— dispel my impurity.
Awakened, wise, illustrious, grateful, and of great renown—
all these Vidyādharas are devoted to meditation upon Śiva.
By the grace of Mahādeva, may Vāmadevī, Mahājambha, and the mighty Kālanemi dispel this terrible impurity.
Sugrīva, Mardaka, Piṅgala, Devamardana, Prahrāda, Anuhrāda, Saṃhrāda, and indeed Bāṣkala; // LiP_1,82.60 //
Jambha, Kumbha, Māyāvī, Kārtavīrya, and Kṛtañjaya—
these high-souled Asuras were devoted solely to Mahādeva.
May Garuḍa, the king of birds who moves through the sky and crushes the serpents, dispel this terrible fear as well as the demonic disposition.
Nāgaśatru, Hiraṇyāṅga, Vainateya, Prabhañjana, Nāgāśīrviṣanāśa, and Viṣṇuvāhana.
May these golden-hued Garuḍas, the vehicles of Viṣṇu,
adorned with various ornaments, remove my impurity.
Agastya and Vasiṣṭha, Aṅgiras and Bhṛgu,
Kāśyapa and Nārada, as well as Dadhīca and Cyavana.
May Upamanyu and the other sages,
who are permeated by Śiva and entirely devoted to the worship of Śiva, remove my impurity.
The fathers, the grandfathers, and likewise the great-grandfathers;
the Agniṣvāttas and the Barhiṣads, as well as the maternal grandfathers and the others.
May Lakṣmī, Dharaṇī, Gāyatrī, and Sarasvatī— who are devoted to the meditation on Śiva— dispel all fear and evil.
Durgā, Uṣā, Śacī, Jyeṣṭhā, and the Mothers worshipped by the gods;
likewise, the mothers of the deities and the mothers of the Gaṇas.
May all those who are the mothers of beings, wherever they may be— the Mothers of the Gaṇas—
through the grace of the God of gods, remove my impurity.
Urvaśī, Menakā, Rambhā, Ratī, Tilottamā, Sumukhī, Durmukhī, Kāmukī, and Kāmavardhanī.
Likewise, other divine apsarases from all the worlds,
being intensely devoted, constantly perform the tāṇḍava dance for the sake of Śiva.
May the goddesses devoted to the worship of Śiva remove my impurity;
may Arka, Soma, Aṅgāraka, Budha, and Bṛhaspati [do the same].
May Śukra, Śanaiścara, Rāhu, and likewise Ketu—
those who worship Śiva— dispel this terrible fear and the affliction of the planets.
Aries, Taurus, Gemini, and likewise auspicious Cancer;
Leo, Virgo, Libra, and likewise Scorpio.
The bow, the crocodile, the water-jar, and likewise the fish—
these are the twelve zodiac signs, devoted to the worship of Śiva.
By the grace of the Supreme Lord,
may Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, and likewise Rohiṇī dispel fear and evil.
The illustrious asterisms Mṛgaśiras, Ārdrā, Punarvasu, Puṣya, Āśleṣā, Maghā, Pūrvaphalgunī, and likewise Uttaraphalgunī; LiP_1,82.78 //
Hasta, Citrā, as well as Svātī, Viśākhā, Anurādhikā, Jyeṣṭhā, Mūla, O highly fortunate one, and likewise Pūrvāṣāḍhā; // LiP_1,82.79 //
Uttarāṣāḍhā, Śravaṇa, Śraviṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣaj, Pūrvabhadrā, and likewise Proṣṭhapadā; // LiP_1.82.80 //
And may the goddesses of the constellation Pauṣṇa constantly dispel my impurity;
as well as Jvara, Kumbhodara, and the mighty Śaṅkukarṇa.
Mahākarṇa, Prabhāta, Mahābhūtapramardana,
Śyenaji, and Śivadūta are the Pramathas who increase joy.
May the Mothers of beings, by hundreds of millions upon millions,
always dispel fear and evil through the grace of Mahādeva.
Perfectly endowed with meditation on Śiva, he resembles the king of snow-mountains (Himavat) and is like water;
his form is like the kunda flower and the moon, and he is adorned with the kumbha, the kunda flower, and the moon.
He who is the enemy of the submarine fire (vaḍavānala), the piercer of the mouth of the mare,
endowed with four legs, and white like the Ocean of Milk.
Ever abiding in the world of Rudra together with the Rudras and the lords of the Gaṇas,
the bull-bannered god is the sustainer of the universe and the father of the entire world.
May he who crushes the sacrifice, who is constantly surrounded by his mothers beginning with Nanda,
and who is ever devoted to the worship of Śiva, remove my sin.
Gangā, the mother of the world, is established in the realm of Rudra;
may that Nandā, who is devoted to Śiva, dispel my sin.
The auspicious goddess Bhadrapadā, established in the world of Śiva,
the highly fortunate mother of cows— may she dispel my sin.
May she who is fragrant, auspicious in every way, the destroyer of all sins,
and eternally devoted to the worship of Rudra, remove my sin.
May she who is well-behaved, endowed with virtue, the bestower of prosperity, and meditated upon as auspicious— she who dwells eternally in the world of Śiva— dispel my sin.
He knows the true meaning of the Vedas and the Shastras; he is the deliberator of all duties;
he is endowed with every virtue; and he is the son of the Lord of all the gods.
The eldest, the Lord of All, gentle, himself the body of Mahāviṣṇu,
the noble one, the commander-in-chief, manifest as Gahana, the destroyer of sacrifices.
Mounted upon the elephant Airāvata, with black, curly hair,
a dark body, and red eyes, he is adorned with the moon and serpents.
Surrounded by bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and kūṣmāṇḍas,
may he who is visibly devoted to the worship of Śiva dispel my sin.
Brahmāṇī, Māheśī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī;
likewise Vārāhī, Māhendrī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Āgneyikā.
May all these Mothers, who are honored by all the worlds,
being composed in meditation, dispel great sin through their power as Yoginīs.
Vīrabhadra, of great splendor, resembling snow, the kunda flower, and the moon,
is the fierce son of Rudra, with his great hand grasping a trident.
The thousand-armed, omniscient Lord himself, bearing all weapons,
with the three sacred fires as his eyes, is the sovereign who grants fearlessness to the three worlds.
The constant protector of the Mothers, whose vehicle is the great bull,
he is honored by the three worlds, glorious, and devoted to the worship of Śiva’s feet.
He was the one who severed the head of the sacrifice, the destroyer of Pūṣan’s teeth,
the direct snatcher of Agni’s hands, and the one who struck down Bhaga’s eyes.
With his big toe, he is the crusher of Soma’s body and is known as Prabhu;
he is the protector of the limbs of the gods, including Upendra, Indra, Yama, and the others.
May that Lord of the Gaṇas, the commander of the army, who had his nose and lips cut off by the great goddess Sarasvatī, dispel my sin.
May Mahālakṣmī, the mother of the world, who is the eldest, the most excellent, the giver of boons, and adorned with choice ornaments, dispel my sin.
May she, Mahāmohā, of great fortune, surrounded by hosts of great beings and ever devoted to the worship of Śiva, dispel my sin.
May the goddess Lakṣmī— who is endowed with all virtues, possessed of all auspicious marks,
and who is ever-present everywhere— dispel my sin.
The great goddess mounted upon a lion, the imperishable daughter of Pārvatī,
is the sleep of Viṣṇu, the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), the power of Viṣṇu (Vaiṣṇavī) worshipped by the gods.
May that goddess Durgā— the three-eyed, boon-granting one who crushes the demon Mahiṣāsura and is devoted to the worship of Śiva— dispel my sin.
May the Rudras, the upholders of the cosmic egg, who are worshipped by all the worlds,
and all those who are truthful and born of the mind, dispel my fear.
May the Bhūtas, Pretas, Piśācas, and the leaders of the hosts of Kūṣmāṇḍas—
may those Kūṣmāṇḍakas, being composed in mind, dispel my sin.
Having praised the God with this, O best of the twice-born, one should conclude everything at the end by bowing with the head to the ground every month.
Whoever recites or even hears this divine hymn of dispelling shall shake off all sins and be glorified in the world of Rudra.
One desiring a daughter obtains a daughter; one desiring victory obtains victory;
one desiring wealth obtains wealth; and one desiring sons obtains many sons.
A seeker of knowledge obtains knowledge, and one who seeks enjoyment shall attain enjoyment;
whatever desires a person prays for here through listening [to this teaching], he shall obtain them.
One quickly attains all of those and becomes beloved by the gods;
this merit, while being recited, accrues to whomever it is recited for.
Diseases arising from wind, bile, and other humors do not afflict him;
he does not meet an untimely death, nor is he bitten even by serpents.
Whatever merit belongs to sacred fords, whatever fruit belongs to sacrifices, whatever merit belongs to gifts, and especially to vows; [all that is obtained by this].
By reciting it ten million times, a human being obtains that merit multiplied by ten million;
yet one who kills a cow, one who is ungrateful, a slayer of heroes, or a slayer of a Brahmin shall [fall].
One who kills those who have sought refuge, one who betrays the trust of friends, one who is wicked and of sinful conduct, as well as a killer of mother or father; LiP_1,82.119 //
Having cast off all evils, one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Praise of Vyapohana," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
The sages said:
We have heard with devotion this meritorious hymn of Vyapohana;
now, in connection with the granting of the liṅga, please tell us also about the vows.
Sūta said:
O best of sages, I shall proclaim to you the auspicious vows that were recounted here by Nandin to the wise son of Brahmā.
Having heard them in detail from Vyāsa, I shall relate them to you:
on the eighth and the fourteenth days of both fortnights.
He who worships Śiva at night for one year,
having obtained the fruit of all sacrifices, goes to the supreme goal.
Having used the earth as his vessel and having eaten on the sacred festival days (parvan),
a man enjoys the fruit of a three-night fast by means of a single day and night.
If a man observes the milk-drinking vow on the two fifth days and the two first days of the month, he shall obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
By eating only at night from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
one obtains enjoyments and goes to the world of Brahmā.
He who for one year observes the practice of eating only at night on every lunar festival day,
remaining celibate, conquering anger, and devoted to meditation upon Śiva;
At the end of the year, one should feed the foremost of Brahmins according to the prescribed rites;
he goes to the world of Śaṅkara—of this there is no doubt to be made.
Alms-gathering is superior to fasting; not begging is superior to alms-gathering; eating at night is superior to not begging; therefore, one should subsist by eating at night.
The gods partake [of it] in the forenoon, likewise the sages at midday,
the ancestors in the afternoon, and the Guhyakas and others at twilight.
Transcending all other times, eating only at night is supreme;
so too are the consumption of sacrificial food (haviṣya), ritual bathing, truthfulness, and moderation in diet.
One should perform the fire-ritual, sleep on the ground, and eat only at night;
I shall now describe month by month the unsurpassed Śiva-vow.
For the sake of dharma, desire, wealth, and liberation, and for the purification of all sins,
he who performs the practice of eating only at night while making full offerings during the month of Puṣya— // LiP_1,83.14 //
Speaking the truth and having conquered anger, one should diligently observe a fast on the eighth day of both fortnights, subsisting on rice, wheat, and dairy products.
And at the end of the month, on the full moon day, having bathed Rudra Mahādeva with ghee and other substances, one should worship him according to the prescribed ritual while lying upon the ground.
O twice-born ones, having given barley-gruel and boiled rice with milk and ghee,
one should feed the remaining Brahmins and especially recite pacifying prayers.
Likewise, one should present a pair of tawny cows to Bhava,
the God of gods, to Śiva, the Supreme Lord.
O tiger among sages, he goes to the supreme world of Vahni;
having enjoyed vast worlds there, he is liberated right then and there.
Having performed worship in the month of Māgha, he who observes the practice of eating only at night, consuming *kṛśara* mixed with ghee while his senses are restrained; ||| LiP_1,83.20 |||
One should observe a fast on the fourteenth day of both fortnights;
then, on the full moon day, one should indeed offer a "blanket of ghee" to Rudra.
One should give a pair of black cattle, worship Śaṅkara,
and feed the Brāhmaṇas according to the extent of one's wealth.
Having reached the southern world, he indeed rejoices together with Yama;
when the month of Phālguna has arrived, one should indeed observe the practice of eating only at night.
Having conquered anger and mastered the senses, one should observe a fast on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days, subsisting on śyāmāka grain with ghee and milk.
On the full moon day, having bathed and fully worshipped Mahādeva Śaṅkara,
one should also present a pair of copper-colored cows to the wielder of the trident.
Having fed the Brahmins, one should pray to the Supreme Lord;
he attains union with the Moon—of this there is no doubt.
In the month of Caitra as well, having worshipped Rudra, one should indeed observe eating only at night,
consuming śāli rice mixed with milk and ghee according to one's pleasure.
O best of sages, one who sleeps in a cow-pen should remember Śiva while lying on the ground at night;
having bathed Śiva on the full moon day, he should present a pair of white cows.
One should feed the Brāhmaṇas and shall attain the abode of Nirṛti;
likewise, having observed the practice of eating only at night during the month of Vaiśākha, one attains that same state.
Having bathed the image on the full moon day with the five products of the cow, clarified butter, and other substances,
and having given a pair of white cows, he shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
And in the month of Jyeṣṭha, having worshipped Bhava, Śarva, the Lord of Devas and Lord of Umā with faith and devotion, one should indeed observe the practice of eating only at night.
He should eat red śāli rice with honey purified by water and clarified butter;
he should remain in the vīrāsana posture for half the night and be devoted to the service of cows.
On the full moon day, having worshipped the God of gods, the Lord of Umā,
and having bathed him according to rule and according to one's means, one should offer sacrificial pap (caru) to the Wielder of the Trident.
Having fed the Brahmins according to the full extent of his wealth and having given a pair of smoky-colored cows, he is honored in the world of Vāyu.
Likewise, in the month of Āṣāḍha, being intent on eating only at night,
one should offer cow's milk mixed with abundant sugar, ghee, and parched grain flour.
On the full moon day, having bathed [the image] with ghee and other substances and worshipped it according to the rules,
one should feed Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the Vedas and have mastered them.
O twice-born ones, having observed the practice of eating only at night during the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should give a pair of white cows; such a person shall attain the world of Varuṇa.
Having worshipped the Bull-bannered Lord with a meal of milk and sixty-day rice on the full moon day, one should bathe Him with ghee and other substances and worship according to the prescribed rite.
And having fed Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the Vedas and have mastered them,
one should further give a pair of cattle consisting of a white-tipped-footed bull and a Pāṇḍu cow.
Having observed this practice of eating only at night during the month of Bhādrapada, he attains union with Vāyu and becomes all-pervading like the wind.
Resorting to the roots of trees during the day, he should eat the remnants of the oblation offered to the foremost of Brahmins;
and on the full moon day, having bathed and fully worshipped Śaṅkara, the Lord of Gods.
Having devoutly given a bull with a blue hump and a cow according to the prescribed rite, and having fed Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences; LiP_1,83.42.
Having reached the world of the yakṣas, that man shall become a king of the yakṣas;
thereafter, having likewise observed the practice of eating only at night during the month of Āśvayuja, he attains this state.
Having worshipped Śaṅkara with ghee on the full moon day as before, and having fed the Brāhmaṇas who are devotees of Śiva and ever pure; LiP_1,83.44.
By giving a bull that has the luster of a dark-blue color and a high-humped chest,
as well as a cow, according to the prescribed rule, one shall attain the world of Īśāna.
And likewise, having observed the practice of eating only at night during the month of Kārttika,
one should worship the Lord Bhava with milk-rice mixed with clarified butter.
And on the full moon day, having bathed [the image] according to the rules and offered the sacrificial porridge (caru),
one should feed the Brahmins to the extent of one's wealth and means.
O twice-born ones, by giving a pair of Kapila-colored cows as before, one attains union with the Sun; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
And in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa as well, having likewise observed the practice of eating only at night,
one should do so according to rule with barley food, together with clarified butter, milk, and other such items.
And on the full moon day, having performed what was previously described for Śarva Śambhu,
one should feed Brāhmaṇas who are poor yet masters of the Vedas.
Having given a pair of white cows according to the prescribed rite,
one reaches the world of Soma and rejoices together with Soma.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, forbearance, compassion,
bathing three times a day, maintaining the sacred fire, sleeping on the ground, and eating only at night.
And one should observe fasting on both fortnights, as well as on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days.
Thus has this entire Śiva-vrata for each month been proclaimed.
O twice-born ones, he may perform [the rite] for a year either in regular order or even in reverse order;
he shall attain union with Śiva and obtain the yoga of knowledge.
Thus ends the eighty-third chapter, titled "The Narration of the Śiva Vow," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
O best of sages, I shall describe the Umāmaheśvara vow as spoken by the Lord, for the benefit of all beings, including men and women.

On the full moon day, the new moon day, and on the fourteenth and eighth days of the lunar fortnight, one should observe the practice of eating only at night for a year, subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya), and worship Bhava.

Having fashioned a very beautiful image of Umā and Maheśvara out of gold, or else of silver, and having installed it according to the prescribed rites at the end of the year, [one should perform the worship].
Having fed the Brahmins and given them sacrificial fees according to one's ability, or having carried the Lord of Gods on chariots and other vehicles toward the temple of Rudra; ||| LiP_1,84.4 |||
One should offer the vow to Śiva, the Supreme Lord, with parasols, chowries, and ornaments endowed with every excellence.
O Lord, if a woman, self-restrained and observing celibacy, does so on the eighth or the fourteenth lunar day, she attains union with Śiva, the Goddess.
For one year, neither a maiden nor even a widow shall eat [meat];
then, at the end of the year, having fashioned an image according to the previously mentioned procedure, she should proceed as follows.
Having installed [the image] according to the rule and having offered it again in the temple of Rudra,
and having fed the Brahmins, he rejoices together with Bhavānī.

O twice-born ones, whatever woman should thus observe the single fourteenth day of the dark fortnight for a year, at the end of the year she should fashion an image, even if it be made of anything whatsoever.
Having performed everything previously described, he rejoices together with Bhavānī;
for one year, she should remain well-restrained and abstain from food on the new moon day.
Having fashioned a trident according to the prescribed rite, one should offer it at the end of the year;
having bathed Īśāna, one should worship him with devotion using thousands of white lotuses.
Having given a silver lotus with a beautiful pericarp made of gold to the Brahmins for Bhava, one should also bestow a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Whatever sin has been committed even out of desire, such as the killing of a fetus and so forth,
a woman shall undoubtedly destroy all of that by the gift of a trident.
O best of the twice-born, in this way one attains union with Bhavānī;
or whatever else a man may do, he too shall attain union with Rudra.
O best of the twice-born, for one year, a woman— or even a man— free from sloth and devoted to fasting on the full moon and the new moon days, [attains the fruit].
O best of the twice-born, that duty must be performed solely by the command of their husbands;
for women are not independent in respect to recitation, charity, or austerity.
At the end of the year, she who is firm in her vows should present an image enriched with all kinds of perfumes; she shall attain both union with Bhavānī and her very form.
She obtains [this], there is no doubt here; I speak the truth, the absolute truth:
whatever woman observes the practice of eating only one meal on the full moon day of Kārttika, [she attains the fruit].
Endowed with the restraints of forbearance, non-violence, and so forth, practicing celibacy,
and remaining unwearied, she should give one *bhāra* of black sesame seeds.
Having given rice mixed with ghee and jaggery to the supreme Lord and to the Brāhmaṇas, according to the extent of one's wealth; LiP_1,84.20.
Devoted to fasting on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days,
that woman of virtuous vows rejoices together with Bhavānī after attaining a form identical to hers.
Forgiveness, truthfulness, compassion, generosity, purity, and restraint of the senses—
this is the common dharma in all vows, as is the worship of Rudra.
I shall explain to you in brief, in due order, [the rites] for each month,
starting from the month of Mārgaśīrṣa and ending with Kārttika, according to their sequence.
Then, Nandin described the very extensive and meritorious vow for the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, known as the Vṛṣa, which is complete in all its parts and supreme.
Having adorned her according to the prescribed rule, one should offer her to Śiva;
she indeed rejoices together with Bhavānī—of this there is no doubt.
Having installed the Śūla in the month of Puṣya and offered it,
and having performed everything previously mentioned, one rejoices together with Bhavānī.
Having constructed a chariot endowed with all auspicious characteristics in the month of Māgha,
one should give it after worshipping the Lord of Gods, and likewise feed the Brāhmaṇas.
And that highly fortunate lady rejoices with the Goddess; of this there is no doubt—having fashioned an image out of gold according to the prescribed rite during the month of Phālguna.
Having established it in silver or copper according to the extent of one's wealth,
and having worshipped it thoroughly, one should install it in the abode of Śaṅkara.
And she rejoices together with Mahādevī; of this there is no doubt—[having worshipped] Bhava, Kumāra, and Bhavānī in the month of Caitra according to the prescribed rite.
Having fashioned [an image] out of copper or other materials according to the rules and having installed it according to the prescribed rite,
one rejoices together with Bhavānī after offering it to Śambhu, the Lord Rudra.
Having indeed made a silver abode for Kubera, it should be fashioned with silver and joined on all sides by the Lord Umā and the Gaṇeśas.
Having installed it according to the prescribed rite, equipped with all kinds of jewels,
one should place it in the auspicious temple of Bhava, the Supreme Lord.
In the month of Vaiśākha, one should indeed perform this supreme vow called Kailāsa;
having reached Mount Kailāsa, he rejoices together with Bhavānī.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, Mahādeva, the Lord of Umā in the form of a liṅga,
was worshipped with palms joined in reverence by both Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
O best of the twice-born, one should fashion an auspicious image of the Liṅga in the form of a Haṃsa and a Varāha, joined in the middle, out of copper or other such materials.
Having installed [the image] according to the rule, he should then feed the Brahmins at the shrine of Śiva,
having attained auspiciousness for Śiva, in accordance with the prescribed ritual.
Having established [the image] together with Brāhmaṇas, one shall attain union (sāyujya) with the Goddess;
and in the auspicious month of Āṣāḍha, having constructed a most beautiful house.
It should be constructed according to rule with baked bricks, as extensively as one's means allow,
and filled with all kinds of seeds and juices, as well as every kind of beautiful ornament.
And with household utensils such as pestles and mortars,
as well as female and male servants, beds, food, and so forth.
Having covered the house on all sides with complete garments,
one should bathe the god Mahādeva, the Lord of Umā, with clarified butter and other substances.
And having fed a thousand Brahmins according to the prescribed rite,
[he should honor] a Brahmin endowed with learning and discipline who has mastered the Vedas.
Having worshipped the student of the first stage of life with devotion according to the prescribed rule,
[he should give] a slender-waisted maiden who is endowed with a long life.
One should likewise present a field and a pair of cattle in his house,
along with various divine vehicles resembling Mount Meru.
Having reached Goloka, she rejoices together with Bhavānī;
having become equal to Bhavānī, she remains imperishable throughout all kalpas.
He attains union with Bhavānī herself; of this there is no doubt.
[The temple] is strewn with all kinds of minerals and adorned with variegated banners.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should offer a mountain of sesame seeds to Śarva;
one should present it with canopies, banners, cloths, and other items, as well as with minerals.
And having fed the Brahmins, everything previously mentioned shall come to pass;
likewise, having fashioned a beautiful mountain of rice in the month of Bhādrapada.
One should offer canopies, banners, cloths, and other such items, as well as relics;
and having fed the Brāhmaṇas, one should cause gifts to be given according to the prescribed rule.
Resplendent like the rays of the sun, she rejoices together with Bhavānī after having fashioned a vast mountain of grain in the month of Āśvayuja.
Having given [the gift] together with gold and garments, having worshipped Śaṅkara,
and having fed the Brāhmaṇas, everything previously mentioned shall come to pass.
It is provided with all kinds of grain, with all seeds, juices, and so forth;
it is endowed with all minerals and adorned with all jewels.
It was endowed with four horns, adorned with canopies and umbrellas,
and beautifully decorated with perfumes, garlands, and various incenses.
It was endowed with eight great banners, radiant with various flowers,
the king of mountains named Meru, the supreme support of the three worlds.
One should place Śiva upon its top, with the [linga] material itself in the center,
and Brahmā, four-faced, on the right according to the rule.

In the north, having installed Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the gods of gods, who is free from all ailment, as well as Indra and the other guardians of the world, with devotion according to the prescribed rite; ||| LiP_1,84.57 |||
Then, having installed Maheśvara, bathed him, and worshipped him thoroughly,
one should place the trident honored by the thirty gods in the right hand of the deity.
In the left [hands], one should diligently place a noose for Bhavānī and a gold-adorned lotus;
and for Viṣṇu, a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus.
And [he gave] to Brahmā a rosary of beads and an unsurpassed water-pot;
to Indra, the thunderbolt; and to Agni, the supreme weapon called Śakti.
The staff of Yama, the sword of Nirṛti,
the noose of Varuṇa known as Nāga, and the wonderful [trident] of Rudra.
Having offered the staff of Vāyu, the mace of Kubera worshipped by the world, and the axe of the god Īśāna, one should proceed in this manner in due order.
Having performed a grand worship of Śiva accompanied by the *caru* oblation,
one should worship all the gods according to the extent of one's means.
Having fed the Brahmins and having performed worship with great care,
and having undertaken the Mahāmeru-vow, one should cause it to be offered to Mahādeva.
Having reached Mount Mahāmeru, he rejoices with the Great Goddess;
he attains eternal union with the Great Goddess, of this there is no doubt.
On the full moon day of Kārttika as well, whatever woman, having fashioned the auspicious Goddess Umā,
complete with all ornaments and endowed with all auspicious marks, [worships her]...
Having installed [the image] according to the prescribed rite using materials such as copper or red gold,
one should fashion the Lord of Gods, endowed with all auspicious characteristics.
In front of those two, he saw the sacrificial fire, the Grandfather (Brahmā) with a *sruva* ladle in his hand,
and Nārāyaṇa, the giver, adorned with all ornaments.
Having diligently established him, surrounded by the world-protectors and the Siddhas,
one should cause him to undertake the vow in the temple of Rudra with devotion.
Having entered the body of Bhavānī, she rejoices together with Bhava;
[this is the merit of] the vow of single-minded devotion performed month by month in succession.
O best of sages, this was inaugurated for the benefit of all beings, including men and women, beginning from the month of Mārgaśīrṣa and ending with Kārttika.
A man who performs this vow shall attain union with Śiva;
for a woman, she attains union with the Goddess—of this there is no doubt, as declared by Śiva.
Thus ends the eighty-fourth chapter, titled "The Umā-Maheśvara Vow," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
O best of the twice-born, having fully worshipped the God of gods, the Lord of Umā, in all vows, one should recite the five-syllabled mantra according to the prescribed rule.

There is no doubt that through recitation alone—and especially through vows—the completion [of the goal] occurs; it does not happen otherwise. Therefore, one should recite the auspicious five-syllabled mantra.
The sages said:
"O illustrious one, tell us how the five-syllabled mantra functions and what its power is; for we have a great curiosity to hear the method of its sequential practice."
Sūta said: Formerly, that which was told by the god Rudra, the god of gods, Śambhu,
to Pārvatī— meritorious, I shall relate it in brief.
The Goddess said: O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Great Lord of all the worlds,
I desire to hear the majesty of the five-syllabled mantra according to its true nature.
The Blessed Lord said:
"The greatness of the five-syllabled mantra cannot be fully described even in hundreds of millions of years."
It is not possible to describe it in full, O Goddess; therefore, listen to it in brief.
When the dissolution has arrived, when the moving and the stationary have perished,
when gods and asuras have vanished, and when serpents and rākṣasas have likewise perished.
Everything that has returned to its primordial nature shall undergo dissolution by you;
O Goddess, I alone remain established, for there is no second anywhere.
In that five-syllabled mantra, the Vedas and the Śāstras are established;
they have not met with destruction at all, for they are protected by my power.
I alone existed in two ways, through the natural differentiation of my own self;
that god Nārāyaṇa lies there, possessing a body composed of māyā.
Seated upon his yogic cross-legged posture on a bed in the midst of the waters,
the five-faced Grandfather was born from the lotus at his navel.
Desiring indeed to create the three worlds, Brahmā was unable to do so, being without assistance.
In the beginning, Brahmā created ten mind-born sons of immeasurable luster.
For the sake of accomplishing their creation, the Grandfather spoke to me:
"O Mahādeva, O Maheśvara, grant power to my sons."
Thus instructed by him, I, who indeed bear five faces,
proclaimed the five syllables with my five mouths to the one born from the lotus.
Grasping them with his five faces, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
came to know the Supreme Lord through the relationship of the signified and the signifier.
O Goddess, Śiva, who is worshipped by the three worlds, is to be expressed by means of five syllables;
his supreme expressive mantra exists as that very five-syllabled one.

Having understood the ritual application and attained accomplishment according to the prescribed method, the great-souled Pañcamukha indeed spoke this mantra of great significance and five colors to his sons for the welfare of the world.
Having obtained that jewel of a mantra directly from the Grandfather of the World,
they sought to propitiate that god Śiva, who is higher than the highest.
Then the Blessed One, Śiva, who is beyond the three forms, was pleased;
he bestowed upon him complete knowledge and the eight supernatural powers, beginning with *aṇiman*.
Having obtained those boons, those brahmins, desiring to propitiate him,
went to the mountain named Muñjavat on the delightful peak of Meru.
Near him, who is ever dear to me, glorious, and protected by my own manifestations,
those eager for the creation of the world performed intense penance.
O Goddess, in former times those sages remained for a thousand divine years subsisting only on air, acting for the sake of bestowing grace.
Seeing their devotion, I immediately became manifest before them,
[revealing] the five-syllabled mantra along with its seer, meter, deity, power, and seed-syllable.

Out of a desire for the welfare of the noble ones and the worlds, I have fully explained the ritual placement (nyāsa), the six-limbed rite (ṣaḍaṅga), the binding of the directions (digbandha), and the application (viniyoga).
Having heard that greatness of the mantra, those sages whose wealth is austerity performed the application of the mantra and carried out everything accordingly.
By virtue of his majesty, he then [established] the worlds together with the gods, asuras, and humans;
the social classes and the divisions of those classes; and all the auspicious dharmas.
Just as in former times, those who have heard [the tradition] know that the worlds, the Vedas, and the great sages arose from the power of the five syllables in a previous kalpa.
(Description of the Pañcākṣara Mantra) "The eternal dharmas, the gods, and this entire world abide [by it]. Therefore, I shall now proclaim it; listen with complete attention. (LiP 1.85.28)

This statement, which consists of the essence of Śiva, is composed of few syllables yet possesses great meaning; it is the core of the Vedas, bestows liberation, is established by direct command, and is free from doubt.
My supreme lordly speech is endowed with various supernatural powers, divine, pleasing to the minds of the world, profound, and its meaning perfectly certain.
The mantra, which is easily pronounced from the mouth and accomplishes all purposes,
is the seed of all vidyās, the first and most beautiful of mantras.
That which is to be known is exceedingly subtle and of great significance, like the seed of a banyan tree;
he is the Veda, beyond the three qualities (guṇas), the omniscient Lord who is the creator of all.
Śiva, who is omnipresent, abides as the single-syllable mantra *om*;
in the subtle six-syllable mantra, Śiva has a body of five syllables.
Established directly by their very nature in the relationship of the signified and the signifier,
Śiva is the signified because he is the object of knowledge, and the mantra is traditionally held to be its signifier.
This relationship of signifier and signified between these two is established as beginningless,
whether in the Veda or in the Śiva-āgama, wherever the six-syllabled mantra occurs.
The five-syllabled mantra is considered the foremost and eternally present in the world;
what need has he for many other mantras or for scriptures of great extent?
He in whose heart this mantra of the Supreme Lord is thus established has studied, he has heard, and by him everything has been performed.
The wise one who, having studied it thoroughly according to the prescribed rules, recites it correctly—this indeed is the entirety of the knowledge of Śiva; this is the supreme state.
This much is the knowledge of Brahman; therefore, the wise man should recite it constantly.
This mantra, consisting of five syllables with the *praṇava*, is my heart.
I shall declare the seer, the meter, and the presiding deity of this mantra, which is the supreme knowledge of liberation, more secret than the secret itself.
Regarding the seed-syllable, the power, the vowel, the consonant, the position, and the syllable itself,
the seer (ṛṣi) is named Vāmadeva, and the meter (chandas) is declared to be Paṅkti.
"O fair-faced one, I myself am Śiva, the deity of this mantra;
and the seed-syllables beginning with the letter *na* consist of the five elements."
Know yourself to be the *praṇava*, the all-pervading and imperishable;
you alone, O Goddess of gods, are the power (*śakti*) who is saluted by all the deities.
O Goddess, your *praṇava* is something, and my *praṇava* is likewise;
there is no doubt that yours is the source of power for all mantras.
The syllables *a*, *u*, and *m* reside within my *praṇava*;
indeed, they are situated there in sequence as *u*, *m*, and *a*.
Know that your *praṇava* is the supreme *pluta* vowel consisting of three measures (*trimātra*).
Of the syllable *oṃ*, its accent is acute (*udātta*), its seer (*ṛṣi*) is Brahman, and its form is white.
The goddess Chandas is Gāyatrī, whose presiding deity is the Supreme Self;
likewise, the first, fourth, and second [syllables] are the udātta accent.
The fifth [vowel] is the svarita, and Niṣadha is known as the middle;
the letter *na* is yellow in color, and its position is remembered as facing the east.
Indra is the presiding deity, the Gāyatrī the metre, Gautama the seer;
its syllable is *makāra*, its color is black, and its position is indeed facing south.
The metre is Anuṣṭubh, the seer is Atri, and Rudra is said to be the deity;
its seed-syllable is Śikāra, its color is smoky, and its location is indeed the western face.
The seer is Viśvāmitra, the metre is Triṣṭubh, and the deity is Viṣṇu;
the syllable is *vā*, its color is golden, and its location is the northern face.
Brahmā is the presiding deity, the Bṛhatī is the meter, Aṅgiras is the seer;
the letter Ya is red in color, its location is above, and its face is that of Virāṭ.
Chanda is the seer, Bharadvāja is the lineage, and Skanda is said to be the deity.
I shall now proclaim its auspicious ritual placement (*nyāsa*), which brings about all accomplishments.
The threefold nyāsa is said to remove all sins; it is indeed the destroyer of every evil.
It is traditionally held to be threefold, according to the distinctions of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal.
For celibate students, householders, and ascetics, there should be [the stages] in succession;
for celibate students there is origination, and for householders there is always stability.
For ascetics, the withdrawal of the senses is *nyāsa*; success (*siddhi*) occurs [through this] and not otherwise.
It is threefold: *aṅganyāsa*, *karanyāsa*, and *dehanyāsa*.
O fair-faced one, it shall be explained to you according to the threefold division beginning with origination:
first one should perform the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa), and immediately thereafter the ritual placement on the body (dehanyāsa).
Thereafter, the placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) of the syllables according to the prescribed sequence,
from the head down to the feet, is called the nyāsa of origination (utpattinyāsa).
O Dear One, the withdrawal (saṃhāra) occurs from the feet up to the crown of the head;
the placement (nyāsa) upon the heart, mouth, and throat is declared to be the placement of maintenance (sthiti).
O beautiful one, for those who are celibate students, householders, and ascetics alike,
one should then touch the entire body, including the head, with the mantra.
This is called the "renunciation of the body" (dehanyāsa), and it is the same for everyone;
indeed, it begins from the right big toe and ends at the left big toe.
That which is deposited is its emanation, while the reverse is its withdrawal;
it is deposited on both hands, beginning from the thumb and ending with the little finger.
O Goddess, the ritual placement of stability (sthitinyāsa) brings great wealth to those with families;
having first performed the placement on the hands (karanyāsa), one should thereafter perform the placement on the body (dehanyāsa).
Afterwards, one should perform the ritual placement (aṅganyāsa); this is the general rule.
Having encased the syllable Oṃ, one should place it upon all the limbs.
Having washed both hands, including the ten fingertips in due order, and having rinsed his feet and sipped water, he should become pure and composed.
Facing either east or north, one should perform the rite of ritual placement (nyāsa);
first, one should recollect the seer (ṛṣi), the meter (chandas), the deity (daivata), and the seed-syllable (bīja).
O fair-faced one, having rubbed the hands together with the mantra— [visualizing] Śakti, the Supreme Self, and the Guru— one should place the Praṇava upon the two palms.
And likewise, on all the fingers, at the first and last joints,
there are the five seed-syllables with the nasal bindu, while they are placed on the middle joints.
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) according to the three divisions beginning with origination, following the sequence of the stages of life (āśrama),
using both hands from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head.
One should touch the body with the mantra, encased by the *praṇava* (Oṃ),
at the head, the mouth, the throat, the heart, and likewise at the secret place.
One should place the syllable Om (praṇava) and the others upon both feet, the secret place, the heart, the throat, the middle of the face, and the head.
One should indeed perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the heart, the secret place, the feet, the head, the speech,
and the throat, according to the threefold division beginning with the syllable Om (praṇava).
Having thus performed the assignment of the limbs (aṅganyāsa), one should indeed assign the faces,
starting from the east up to the zenith, in sequence beginning with the letter *na*.
Thereafter, one should beautifully place the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) in their respective locations,
together with the utterances *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ*.
One should know the Praṇava to be the heart; the syllable *na* is said to be the head;
the syllable *ma* is declared to be the tuft (*śikhā*); and likewise, the syllable *śi* is the armor (*kavaca*).

The letter Ā is proclaimed as the form, the eye, and the weapon, while the letter Ya is likewise celebrated [as such]. Having thus performed the placement of the limbs (aṅga-nyāsa), one should then bind the directions.
Vighneśa, the Mothers, Durgā, Kṣetrajña, and the deities of the directions are to be worshipped in sequence in all four corners, beginning with the southeast.
Having placed the tips of the thumb and forefinger together in an auspicious and beautiful manner,
and having said, "Protect [me]," one should pay homage to each [deity] individually.

The wise practitioner should perform the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa) upon the throat, the center [of the chest], the thumb, and the fingers beginning with the index finger, using the thumb.
Thus has this auspicious nyāsa been proclaimed, which removes all sins,
bestows all siddhis, is meritorious, provides all protection, and is conducive to well-being.
Then, O fortunate one, when the mantra has been deposited, one becomes equal to Śaṅkara;
even the sin committed in previous births perishes at that very moment.
Having thus performed the ritual placement, the wise one, with a purified body and firm vows,
should recite the five-syllable mantra after having received it through the grace of the preceptor.
Henceforth, O auspicious one, I shall proclaim the compendium of mantras,
without which [practice] is eternally fruitless, and by means of which it becomes fruitful.
That which is devoid of the command, devoid of ritual action, devoid of faith, lacking mental focus,
commanded [at an improper time], and devoid of the sacrificial fee— such recitation is always fruitless.

A mantra is perfected because it is accomplished through command, accomplished through ritual action, accomplished through faith, accomplished through a noble mind, and likewise accomplished through sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Thus, from whichever source it may come, the mantra is perfected.
Having approached the guru, a brahmin who knows the true meaning of the mantras, who is wise, endowed with excellent qualities, and devoted to the yoga of meditation; LiP 1.85.86.
Endowed with purity of intention, one should strive to please him through speech, mind, body, and material wealth.
A disciple should always worship the teacher with the utmost diligence,
[offering] elephants, horses, chariots, jewels, fields, and houses.
Ornaments, garments, and various kinds of grain—
one should give these to the preceptor with devotion, provided one has the means.
One should not practice stinginess regarding wealth if one desires success for oneself;
O Goddess, one should later offer up oneself along with one's retinue.
Having thus worshipped according to the rule and to the best of one's ability, without deceiving [the teacher],
one should receive the mantra and the knowledge from the guru in due order.
Thus satisfied, the Guru [should initiate] the disciple who has been honored, has resided there for a year,
is desirous of service, free from egoism, emaciated by fasting, and pure.
Having caused the disciple to bathe and having honored the Brāhmaṇas as well,
[one should perform the rite] on the seashore, by a river, in a cow-pen, or even in a temple.
In a pure place or even within a house, at a time that brings success, on an auspicious lunar day,
under a favorable constellation and yoga, and always free from defects.
Then, having shown favor, he should bestow the unsurpassed knowledge of Śiva;
with a clear mind, he should properly recite it aloud even in a secluded place.
Having recited it again and again, the preceptor himself becomes the bestower of success;
[he should say: "May there be Śiva, may there be auspiciousness, may there be well-being, and may there be what is dear."
Having thus obtained the supreme mantra and knowledge from the guru,
one should daily perform the recitation with firm resolve, as well as the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa).
One should recite it daily for as long as one lives, eight hundred and more times;
by becoming intent upon that practice while fasting, one attains the supreme goal.

One who eats only at night, remains self-restrained, and performs the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa) is said to be one who should recite the mantra four hundred thousand times with devotion, totaling one hundred thousand syllables.
Whether one is a practitioner of the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) or a regular reciter,
one of these two should be desirous of attaining success before long.

The man who, having performed the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*), becomes a practitioner of constant recitation (*nityajāpī*), has no equal in the world; he is perfected, a bestower of perfection, and self-controlled. (LiP 1.85.101)
Having assumed a beautiful posture, remaining silent and with a one-pointed mind,
facing either east or north, he should mutter the unsurpassed mantra.
One should indeed perform breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) at both the beginning and the end of the recitation;
likewise, at the conclusion, one should recite the seed-syllable one hundred and eight times for auspiciousness.
Having performed forty repetitions and restrained the breath, one should meditate;
this is declared to be the breath-restraint (prāṇāyāma) for the five-syllable mantra.
Through breath control (prāṇāyāma), there quickly occurs the complete destruction of all sins and mastery over the senses; therefore, one should restrain the vital breaths.
One should know that recitation performed at home yields an equal result; in a cow-pen it becomes a hundredfold;
by a river it is a hundred-thousandfold; and in the presence of Śiva, it is infinite.
On the shore of the ocean, at a divine lake, on a mountain, in temples,
and in all sacred hermitages, the recitation of mantras becomes ten million times more efficacious.
The practice of recitation (japa) is highly commended when performed in the presence of Śiva, before the Sun, or even before one's Guru, as well as by a lamp, a cow, or water.
O fair-faced one, counting by means of finger-joints is said to be single-fold;
by means of lines it is eightfold, and by means of *putrajīva* seeds it is tenfold.
A hundred [is the value] for conch shells and gems; a thousand for coral;
ten thousand for crystals; and a hundred thousand is said for pearls.
With lotus seeds, ten lakhs [of recitations] are performed; with golden beads, it is said to be ten million; and with knots of *kuśa* grass or *rudrākṣa* beads, it is said to yield infinite merit.
Twenty-five [verses] are for the sake of liberation; twenty-seven for nourishment;
thirty for the attainment of wealth; and fifty for malevolent rites.
One should know that facing east brings subjugation, facing south brings malevolent rites (abhicāra),
facing west bestows wealth, and facing north brings pacification (śāntika).
One should know that the thumb bestows liberation, the index finger destroys enemies,
the middle finger grants wealth, and this ring finger brings about peace.
The little finger is to be protected during the auspicious rite of recitation;
one should perform the recitation with the thumb together with the other fingers.
Since an action performed without the thumb is fruitless, listen: among all sacrifices, the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*) is preeminent. (LiP 1.85.116)
They engage in those [other rites] through violence; the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*), however, is not performed through violence.
Whatever sacrifices of action (*karmayajña*) there may be, as well as offerings and ascetic penances—[all these are surpassed by it].
All of them are not worth even a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of recitation;
thus has been proclaimed the majesty of the vocal sacrifice of recitation alone.

Therefore, the whispered recitation is said to be a hundredfold more effective than that, and the mental recitation a thousandfold; whereas [the loud recitation] is performed with words in high, low, and circumflex tones, with clear syllables and distinct phrases.
One should recite the mantra with speech; that is the vocal sacrifice of japa.
One should recite the mantra softly, moving the lips only slightly.
One should know that a slight interval [between the breaths] is the whispered recitation (*upāṃśujapa*);
that which is performed mentally through the sequence of syllables—syllable by syllable and word by word—is the mental recitation (*mānasajapa*). (LiP 1.85.121)
One should further contemplate the meaning of the words; that is called mental recitation (*mānasa-japa*).
Among the three types of sacrificial recitation (*japayajña*), each subsequent one is superior to the preceding.
The excellence of that fruit may arise from a specific sacrifice;
however, the deity, being constantly praised through recitation (*japa*), becomes pleased.
Being pleased, she bestows vast enjoyments and eternal liberation.
Yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and all terrifying grahas do not approach the one who recites [the mantra], being terrified by fear from every side.
"By recitation one may pacify all sins whatsoever committed throughout a succession of births;
by recitation one conquers enjoyments and death, and by recitation one attains perfection and liberation.
Having thus obtained the knowledge of Śiva and understood the sequence of the rules for recitation,"* LiP_1,85.125–126 *
One who always practices right conduct, constantly reciting prayers and meditating on what is auspicious, attains well-being.
I shall now fully declare right conduct, which is the means for accomplishing Dharma.
Since the practice of one devoid of proper conduct becomes fruitless, right conduct is the supreme dharma; right conduct is the supreme austerity.
Conduct is the supreme knowledge; conduct is the supreme goal.
For men who possess good conduct, there shall be fearlessness everywhere.
In the same way, O fair-faced one, those devoid of proper conduct shall experience fear everywhere; through good conduct, however, one attains the state of a god or a seer.
In the same way, by transgressing proper conduct, one enters into a base womb;
a man devoid of proper conduct becomes censured in the world.
Therefore, one who seeks perfection should be perfectly observant of proper conduct;
for one of evil conduct, though perhaps full of ritual purity, is a sinner who defiles knowledge.
One should diligently perform the dharma as prescribed by the rules for the castes and stages of life.
Performing whatever action is prescribed for him, he is always dear to me;
he should be devoted to the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana), with a serene mind, both evening and morning. (Sandhyā 85.134)
Beginning from before sunrise and following the prescribed rule,
a pure twice-born man should not neglect the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) out of desire, delusion, fear, or greed.
Since a Brahmin falls from his status as a Brahmin by transgressing the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā),
he should not speak anything untrue, nor should he abandon the truth.
That which they call "truth" is Brahman; untruth is the defilement of Brahman—namely, falsehood, harshness, deceit, and slander, all of which have sin as their cause.
One should never, whether by speech or by thought, commit adultery with another's wife, seize another's property, or inflict injury upon another, even on any occasion whatsoever.

One should avoid the food of a Śūdra, food that has been left over, food offered as a sacrificial oblation, food from a funeral rite (śrāddha), food belonging to a group, food belonging to a collective, and the food of a king. (Rules concerning food and a meal) LiP 1.85.139.
The purification of the inner being does not occur through earth or water alone;
when the inner being is purified, perfection arises—therefore, one should thoroughly purify the food.
For Brahmins who expound the Veda but have been consumed by accepting gifts from kings,
there is no rebirth, even as there is none for seeds that have been scorched.
Having understood that accepting gifts from a king is terrible and, at first sight, like poison, a wise man should avoid it; he should also avoid the flesh of dogs.
One should not eat without having bathed, nor without reciting prayers, nor without honoring the fire;
one should not eat from the back of a leaf, nor likewise at night without a lamp.
One should not eat the remnants of a Śūdra, nor food shared with children, from a broken vessel or from what has fallen on the road.
One should eat pure, unctuous food that has been prepared and consecrated with mantras;
the eater, remembering "I am Śiva," should remain silent with a one-pointed mind.
One should not drink water from the mouth, nor while standing with joined palms, nor from the left hand, nor while lying on a bed, nor likewise from the lap of another.
One should not take shelter in the shade of the *vibhītaka*, *arka*, *kārañja*, or *snuhi* trees,
nor in that of pillars, lamps, humans, or other living beings.
One should not travel alone on a journey, nor cross a river with one's arms;
one should not descend into wells and such, nor climb high trees.

In this world, during an auspicious time, one who has turned away from the sun, fire, water, deities, and teachers should not perform any activities, nor the practice of recitation (*japa*), nor any other auspicious rites.
One should not warm one's feet over the fire, nor touch the hands with the feet;
one should not sit facing the rising flame of the fire, nor should one discard any kind of impurity into the fire.
One should not strike the water with one's feet, nor should one discard bodily impurities into the water;
one should wash off the impurities on the bank, and having washed them off, perform the ritual bath.
If one should touch the water from a jar used for bathing, which has been discarded along with fingernail clippings and hair,
it is inauspicious for humans and impure.
If a foolish person touches the dust raised by the hooves of goats, horses, or camels, he destroys even the prosperity of Hari. (No pets. LiP 1.85.153.
The man in whose house there is a cat is equal to an outcaste;
yet, O best of Brahmins, he who would feed [guests] in the presence of a cat [attains merit].
That should be known as equal to an outcaste; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
[One should avoid] the wind from the buttocks, the wind from a winnowing fan, and the breath from the mouth.
When touched by these, they carry away the merits of a man:
one wearing a turban, one in a bodice, one naked, one with disheveled hair, and one covered in filth.
With impure hands or while being unclean, one should never mutter prayers while talking;
nor should one do so when overcome by anger, intoxication, hunger, drowsiness, spitting, or yawning.
Seeing dogs, low-caste people, sleep, and incoherent speech—these are enemies of recitation;
even when these occur, one should look at the sun or other bright objects.

Having sipped water (ācamana), one should recite the remainder; or, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), [one should know that] the sun, fire, the moon, as well as the planets, lunar mansions, and stars [are present].
These are declared by learned Brahmins to be the luminaries;
one should not recite [the mantra] with the feet extended, nor while in the cock-sitting posture.
(Performing the *āsana*:

A practitioner of recitation (*jāpaka*) should likewise not perform recitation while sitting without a seat, while lying down, on a road, in the presence of a *śūdra*, on red ground, or on a bedstead. *LiP* 1.85.161.
Seated upon a seat, one should recite the mantra correctly with a mind focused on the meaning of the mantra,
whether on silk, tiger-skin, cotton, or even woolen cloth.
One should prepare a seat made of wood or a palm leaf;
and one who desires his own welfare must perform worship of the Guru at the three junctions of the day.
He who is the Guru is declared to be Śiva; he who is Śiva is remembered as the Guru.
As is Śiva, so is the Vidyā; as is the Vidyā, so is the Guru.
O Goddess, from that Guru of Śiva-vidyā, one obtains a fruit equal [to that of worshipping all gods] through devotion;
for he embodies all the gods and indeed possesses all powers.
Whether he possesses attributes or is devoid of them, one who seeks his own welfare should bear his command upon his head and should not transgress the guru’s command even in thought.
One who properly observes the command of the guru attains the perfection of knowledge;
whether walking, standing, sleeping, eating, or whatever action one may perform.
If all that is to be performed in the presence [of the deity], it must be done with the permission of the guru;
or [it may be done] in the presence of the guru or the deity, but one should not sit as one pleases.
Since the Guru is the deity manifest, his house is a temple of the gods;
yet through association with a sinner, one may fall due to that person's sins.
In the same way, through association with a teacher, one becomes a partaker of the fruits of his dharma;
just as gold sheds its impurity through contact with fire.
In the same way, through contact with a guru, a human being abandons sin,
just as a pot of ghee melts when placed near a fire.
In the presence of the teacher, evil is dissolved just as a blazing fire consumes excrement and wood.
When the Guru is pleased, he burns away evil in this way through the power of his mantra;
so too do Brahmā, Hari, Rudra, the gods, and the sages.
When the Guru is pleased, they grant grace; of this there is no doubt.
One should not provoke the anger of the Guru through action, mind, or speech.
By his anger, longevity, prosperity, knowledge, and meritorious deeds are consumed;
for those who harbor that anger, even their sacrifices become fruitless.
One should not entertain any doubt regarding the observances of the Japas;
one must, with every effort, avoid speaking any word that is contrary to the Guru.
If one should speak out of great delusion, O observers of good vows, he shall go to the Raurava hell by means of his mind, his wealth, and likewise his speech.
O Goddess, one should never falsely act against the guru through one's conduct;
if his faults are proclaimed, one shall partake in a hundredfold lack of virtue.
When his virtues have been proclaimed, he shall obtain the fruit of possessing all virtues;
he should always do what is beneficial and pleasing to the guru, whether commanded or not.
Whether in the presence or absence of the guru, one should perform one's duties;
one should do what is beneficial and pleasing to the guru through the actions of mind, speech, and body.
One who acts [otherwise] falls downward and, having gone there, revolves in that very place;
therefore, he (the Guru) is to be worshipped at all times and saluted at all times.
Even when standing nearby, he should speak after having obtained permission, turning his back toward the guru;
thus possessed of proper conduct, devoted, and constantly intent upon recitation.
One who acts to please the Guru is then worthy to employ the mantra;
I shall now declare the application (viniyoga), which is the purpose for employing the perfected mantra.
The mantra of one who does not know its application (viniyoga) becomes weak,
especially when it is employed for a purpose other than that for which it was specifically intended.
That application (viniyoga) should be understood as having results pertaining to both this world and the next;
from such application arises longevity, health, and eternal union with Him.
Sovereignty and lordship, wisdom, heaven, and even nirvāṇa;
as well as sprinkling, consecration, and the Aghamarṣaṇa rite—these are [attained].
One should indeed perform the ritual at the time of bathing and during the two twilights with the eleventh [mantra];
being pure and free from sloth, one should ascend a mountain and recite it one hundred thousand times.
By [performing this] at the Mahānadī river, one shall obtain a lifespan of two hundred thousand years;
likewise, pills made of dūrvā sprouts, sesame seeds, vāṇī, and guḍūcī [yield the same result].
For them, ten thousand oblations increase longevity;
a wise person should recite [the mantra] two hundred thousand times while taking refuge under an Aśvattha tree.
On the day of Saturn, a man who touches [the tree] shall obtain long life;
on the day of Saturn, the wise man should touch the *aśvattha* tree with both hands.
One should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times; thus one becomes a remover of death by means of Soma.
Facing the Sun, one should recite it one hundred thousand times with undistracted mind.
Having recited the *arka* mantra one hundred and eight times while offering oblations with *palāśa* wood fuel, a person is liberated from disease for the sake of pacifying all illnesses.
Having offered ten thousand oblations, a person shall become free from disease;
having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times daily, he should drink water in the presence of the sun.
One is liberated from all diseases caused by gluttony within a single month;
on the eleventh day, one should consume food that has been consecrated with mantras.
Furthermore, whatever else is to be eaten or drunk—even poison—shall become nectar;
one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times in the forenoon, having indeed offered oblations eight hundred times.
By constantly worshipping the sun and touching a beautiful jar filled with river water, one shall attain perfect health.
By reciting it ten thousand times and bathing with that [water], it becomes a remedy for diseases;
having purified oneself, one should eat food every day after reciting it twenty-eight times.
And having offered oblations with palāśa wood in this manner, one attains freedom from disease;
likewise, having fasted beforehand during an eclipse of the moon or sun, being pure and acting according to the prescribed rule.
Until the release from the planetary seizure, one should remain concentrated and recite [the mantra] by a river flowing toward the ocean; indeed, this is done until the release of the seizure.
O twice-born ones, by drinking the juice of brāhmī one thousand and eight times,
one obtains auspicious intelligence in this very life that retains all the scriptures.
The goddess Sarasvatī shall become his superhuman speech;
during afflictions caused by planets and constellations, a man should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times with devotion.
Having offered eight thousand oblations, one dispels the affliction caused by the planets;
upon seeing a bad dream, a man should bathe and indeed recite the mantra ten thousand times.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter, immediate peace will be attained;
likewise, during an eclipse of the moon or sun, having worshipped the Linga according to the prescribed rite.
O Goddess, whatever one may desire, one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times with devotion,
remaining pure and with a restrained mind in the presence of this deity.
A person attains all desires; there is no doubt in this matter—especially those of elephants, horses, and cattle.
Upon the onset of a disease, having become pure, one should offer oblations of sacrificial fuel-sticks for a month according to the prescribed rite, ten thousand times, endowed with devotion.
For them, there will be supernatural power and peace; of this there is no doubt.
During a portent or when oppressed by enemies, one who is pure should perform ten thousand oblations.
O Goddess, through fuel-sticks of *pālāśa* wood, his peace shall be attained;
O Goddess, one should perform this in the case of affliction caused by malevolent magic.
That power turns inward and there will be suffering for the enemy;
for the purpose of inciting enmity, one should offer eight pieces of *vaibhīta* wood as oblations.
By writing [the name] in reverse order with moist blood or poison smeared with blood, one causes hatred among men.
I shall proclaim the expiation for the purification of all sins,
so that a man intent on performing it may achieve the complete purification of his transgressions.
Since the purification of sin is the cause for the perfect attainment of knowledge,
if a person has no purification of sin, all their actions are fruitless.
Therefore, knowledge is lost; hence, one must perform the purification of sin.
O auspicious lady, for the sake of purifying learning and prosperity, one should meditate upon me with palms joined in reverence.
One should sprinkle [the disciple] from all sides with water using the eleven-fold Śiva-mantra;
one should bathe with exactly one hundred and eight repetitions for the purification of sins.
That [mantra] yields the fruit of all sacred fords, removes all sins, and is auspicious;
a man should recite it one hundred and eight times when there is an interruption in the performance of the twilight devotions (saṃdhyopāsana).
One should not eat food touched by village pigs, Cāṇḍālas, wicked people, or even by cocks; if one has eaten such food, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
For the sake of purification from the murder of a Brahmin, a man should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times;
for other sins, it shall be half of that—no deliberation is required in this matter.
For those defiled by minor offenses (upapātaka), half of that is prescribed;
for all other sins as well, one should recite five thousand [times].
This supreme secret, which leads to self-realization and illuminates the realization of Śiva—one should become Śiva;
undisturbed, one should recite the mantra five hundred thousand times.
O auspicious lady, a person who has conquered the five vital airs attains happiness;
being pure and having restrained the senses, he should perform five hundred thousand recitations.
O fair-faced one, victory over the five senses will be attained by him who,
disciplined in meditation and free from agitation, recites [the mantra] five hundred thousand times.
A person who, endowed with devotion, recites the fourth [chapter] five hundred thousand times attains mastery over the five sense objects.
A person who restrains his mind with effort and recites [the mantra] four hundred thousand times shall attain victory over the five elements here in this world.
O fair-faced one, O lotus-faced one, by reciting [the mantra] twenty-five hundred thousand times, one attains complete victory over the senses.
A person shall obtain victory over the twenty-five principles;
at midnight, in a place free from wind, one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times with devotion.
O beautiful one, by means of this vow one attains the perfection of Brahman; one should recite [the mantra] a hundred thousand times without laziness, in a windless place free from noise.
And at midnight, one beholds the two Śivas; of this there is no doubt.
It is like the destruction of darkness and the manifestation of light from a lamp.
Whether within the heart or externally, there will be no doubt;
for the sake of the prosperity and abundance of all wealth, the self-possessed practitioner should recite it ten thousand times.
Pure and full of devotion, one should recite the mantra with its seed-syllable and its encapsulation a hundred lakhs of times; he attains union with me—what could be greater than this?
Thus, I have explained to you the entire sequence of the ritual for the five-syllabled mantra;
whoever reads or even hears it attains the supreme goal.
And he should cause pure twice-born men to hear the procedure for the five-syllabled mantra during rites for the gods or the ancestors; such a person is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Thus ends the eighty-fifth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Five Syllables," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
The sages said:
Brahmins whose sins have been burnt away declare that for those who are dispassionate and awakened, the sacrifice of meditation is most excellent and most beautiful, surpassing even recitation.
