Therefore, O Sūta, speak today in full detail and with every effort regarding the sacrifice of meditation for the sake of the dispassionate great-souled ones.
Having heard those words of the high-souled sages engaged in long sacrificial sessions, Rudra, having reached the cave, spoke.
Having withdrawn the poison known as Kālakūṭa by means of Viśvakarman,
Sūta said:
"Śaṅkara, having reached the cave and sitting comfortably together with Bhavānī..."
The sages, whose souls were firmly disciplined, bowed down to him who dwells in the cave; then they all praised Nīlakaṇṭha, the lord of Umā.
O Blessed One, that most terrible poison called Kālakūṭa was swallowed by you;
therefore, O God whose banner is the bull, everything has been established by you.
Having heard those words of theirs, the Lord Nīlalohita,
the soul of the universe, smilingly spoke to those led by Sanandana.
O best of the twice-born, what is the use of this? I shall speak of a most terrible poison;
for one who can neutralize that poison—what indeed is the need for this?
(On the Curse of Saṃsāra:
That which is called the Kālakūṭa poison is not truly poison; it is saṃsāra that is called poison.
Therefore, with every effort, one should destroy this most dreadful thing.
Saṃsāra is said to be of two kinds, according to one's own specific office:
for men whose minds are utterly deluded, it is inexhaustible and most terrible.
O you of good vows, creation proceeds through the fault of desire and passion, while it is sustained by knowledge;
by their power alone, for all beings, dharma and adharma arise—of this there is no doubt.

O twice-born ones, even regarding an object that is not present before them, the scripture certainly generates understanding in the wise who have heard it, as they dwell within this cycle of worldly existence.
Therefore, one who is dispassionate should abandon with every effort that which is both perceptible and scriptural, as it is flawed; he is thus called "dispassionate."
O twice-born ones, this scripture is said to be that portion of the Veda concerning ritual acts;
it is the head of Brahman, the essence of the sages, and the fruit of their labor.
Surely, desire is observed to be the inherent nature of all beings, and not otherwise;
it is the sacred revelation (śruti) that impels them toward action, according to those who do not know this [reality].
The Dharma characterized by cessation is taught here for those who are capable;
therefore, the saṃsāra of all embodied beings has its root in ignorance.
Through action and by the nature of another, the *kalā* undergoes complete drying up;
thus the embodied soul (*sakala-jīva*), devoid of knowledge due to ignorance, is of three kinds.
The hell-being is the doer of evil; the celestial being is the doer of merit through the weight of merit;
and the living soul is established in four ways according to their mixed nature.
Born from sprouts, born from sweat, born from eggs, and indeed born from a womb—
thus is the embodied soul situated, ignorant due to karma and lacking in peace.
For the virtuous, liberation does not come through progeny, ritual action, or even through wealth;
rather, liberation occurs through renunciation alone. In the absence of that, one wanders in delusion.
Thus, through the fault of ignorance and by the power of various karmas,
this [being] assumes a body composed of the six sheaths.
There are manifold sufferings in the womb, on the path through the birth canal, and upon the earth;
likewise in childhood, youth, old age, and even at death.
O twice-born ones, for the virtuous, suffering arises from reflection upon such things as association with women;
yet in this world, the suffering of one who is afflicted is indeed pacified by a single instance of suffering.
Desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of desired objects;
rather, it increases all the more, like a fire fed with clarified butter.
Therefore, upon investigation, there is no [satisfaction] for men even through union; likewise, it exists neither in the acquisition of objects, nor in their preservation, nor in their expenditure.

O best of the twice-born, there is suffering in the realms of the Piśācas and Rākṣasas, and likewise in the realm of the Yakṣas when one reflects upon it; and similarly in the realm of the Gandharvas, in that of the Moon, and in the world of Soma.
O you of excellent vows, in the realms of Prajāpati, Brahmā, Prakṛti, and Puruṣa, there are sufferings within sufferings due to decay, excess, and other such conditions.
One should abandon those impure fortunes as well as wealth;
therefore, one should [renounce] enjoyment eightfold, and likewise established in sixteen ways.
O you of excellent vows, it is established in twenty-four ways;
O sinless ones, it further possesses thirty-two divisions and forty qualities.
Likewise, for the discerning person, suffering itself consists of forty-eight, fifty-six, and sixty-four varieties.
One should contemplate them in their proper order: the earthly, the watery, the fiery, the airy, the ethereal, and the mental.

Likewise, for yogins who proclaim Brahman, suffering—whether it be that arising from conceit, that pertaining to the Buddha, or even that of ordinary folk—is nothing but suffering; of this there is no doubt.
Upon reflection, even for the lords of the Gaṇas, suffering alone prevails—
at the beginning, in the middle, and likewise at the end, throughout all worlds and at all times.
Present sufferings and future ones exactly as they are,
as well as various sufferings in regions corrupted by defects.
For those who, out of ignorance, pride themselves on their knowledge, do not cultivate [wisdom regarding] past deeds;
food is said to be for the sake of pleasure, not merely for the purpose of warding off the affliction of hunger.
Just as medicine for other diseases does not lead to happiness for embodied beings during their respective seasons due to cold, heat, wind, rain, and so forth; LiP_1,86.36.
It is indeed suffering, there is no doubt; for the unwise do not understand this.
Even in heaven, O best of sages, it is likewise [suffering] due to impurity, exhaustion, and other such states.
Seized by various kinds of diseases, such as passion, hatred, fear, and the like,
one falls helplessly to the earth like a tree whose roots have been severed.
In the same way, when the tree of merit is exhausted, the denizens of heaven fall to the earth;
for those whose ultimate aim is the longing for pleasure, there is only the abundance of experiencing suffering and the like.
But for those celestial dwellers falling from heaven, there is painful suffering;
here, however, there is only suffering due to the constant haunting of the hells.
And also because of the non-performance of prescribed duties, O best of sages, for those belonging to the social classes.
Just as a deer, terrified by the fear of death, finds no sleep because its dwelling has been destroyed,
so too a high-souled ascetic devoted to meditation, fearing the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), finds no sleep.
Suffering is indeed seen among insects, birds, wild animals, domestic cattle, elephants, and horses; therefore, for one who renounces [worldly life], there is supreme happiness.

O you of excellent vows, even for the inhabitants of celestial palaces who preside over the kalpas, as well as for those who dwell in the higher realms and for Manu and the others, suffering is likewise present.
Due to their mutual desire for victory, there was only suffering among the gods, the Daityas, the kings, and the Rākṣasas throughout the three worlds.
In the ultimate sense, the stage of life (āśrama) is for the sake of exertion among the social classes (varṇas);
it is not [attained] by means of stages of life, nor by gods, nor by sacrifices, nor by Sāṃkhya, nor likewise by vows.
Through fierce austerities and various kinds of gifts, even those of many sorts, people do not attain the Self in that way; rather, the possessors of knowledge attain it by themselves.
Therefore, with every effort, one should practice the Pāśupata vow;
in the Pāśupata vow, the wise man should always lie upon ashes. (LiP 1.86.48)
Endowed with the knowledge of the five objects and absorbed in the principle of Śiva,
the wise man [should practice] that which effects liberation and cuts through the ritual actions of yoga.
The wise one, perfected through the yoga of the five objects, attains the end of suffering;
that which is to be known is realized through the supreme Vidyā, for it is not realized by the inferior one.
Indeed, two types of knowledge are to be known: the higher (parā) and likewise the lower (aparā).
Among these, O best of the twice-born, the lower consists of the Ṛgveda and the Yajurveda.
Likewise, there is the Sāmaveda and the Atharvaveda, which accomplishes all aims;
as well as Śikṣā, Kalpa, Vyākaraṇa, Nirukta, and Chandas.
And the science of astrology is established as the lower knowledge (*aparā vidyā*), whereas the supreme syllable (*parākṣara*) is this:
it is invisible, ungraspable, without lineage, and without color.
O best of the twice-born, that is without eyes, without ears, without hands, and without feet; it is unborn, unbecome, and without sound.
It is intangible and formless, devoid of taste and smell;
it is imperishable, without support, eternal, all-pervading, and omnipresent.
O twice-born ones, that is great and vast, unborn and consisting of consciousness;
it is without breath or mind, and it is neither oily nor red.
That is immeasurable; it is neither gross nor long, neither thick nor short;
it is boundless, blissful, and immutable.
Unobstructed, non-dual, infinite, beyond the reach of the senses, and unconditioned—that alone is the one Self; this is supreme knowledge, and not otherwise.
The distinction between the higher and the lower is spoken of here, but not from the perspective of ultimate reality;
I alone am the entire universe, and the whole universe exists within me.
It arises from me, it abides in me, and it dissolves into me alone;
one should perceive that there is nothing other than me through mind, speech, and hands.
One who is composed should perceive everything—both the existent and the non-existent—within the self;
for by perceiving everything within the self, one does not direct the mind toward the external.
One should know that the heart, situated at a distance of one span above the navel and below the gaze, is the great abode of the universe. (4 states of mind) LiP_1,86.62.
In the center of this heart, however, resides a lotus,
born from the root-stalk of Dharma, with a beautiful stalk of knowledge.
The eight-petalled lotus of sovereignty is white, with supreme detachment as its pericarp;
its apertures are the directions, and the vital breaths (prāṇa) and others are established therein.
Joined with the vital breaths (prāṇa) and the rest, one perceives [them] in many ways in succession;
O best of sages, there are ten channels for each of the vital breaths.
Seventy-two thousand channels have been fully described;
one should know that the waking state resides in the eyes, and one should indicate the dreaming state as being in the throat.
Deep sleep resides in the heart, while the fourth state (turīya) is situated in the head;
Brahmā and Viṣṇu preside over the waking state and the dreaming state respectively, in due order.
Others, however, say that in deep sleep he is Īśvara, and in the fourth state (turiya) he is Maheśvara; thus they describe the Person by means of all the faculties.
When these are active at that time, it is designated as his waking state;
this consists of the fourfold group: mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṅkāra), and consciousness (citta).
O you of firm vows, when one is established in these states and the instruments [of perception] have dissolved into one's own self, that is designated as "dream."
Deep sleep is distinguished by the instruments [of perception]; the fourth state (turīya) is proclaimed as that which transcends this. Beyond the fourth is Śiva, the supreme cause.
O best of Brahmins, the waking state, the dreaming state, the deep sleep state, and the fourth state are said to be the physical (ādhibhautika),
the personal (ādhyātmika), and the divine (adhidaivika).
All that, O best of Brahmins, as well as the organs of perception and the organs of action, should be known by the wise one as being none other than myself.
The intellect, the ego, and the mind— this fourfold group is traditionally held to be the fourteenfold internal [organ], each distinct from the others.
O best of sages, that which is to be seen, heard, and smelled should be experienced in due order, as well as that which is to be tasted and likewise that which is to be touched.

O best of sages, that which is to be deliberated upon, that which is to be understood, that which is to be performed as the ego-maker, as well as that which is to be willed and that which is to be spoken— [all these belong to me].
That which is to be taken up, that which is to be gone toward, that which is to be emitted,
and that which is to be rejoiced in— these, indeed, are the *adhibhūta* (objects of experience) in their respective order.
The Sun, as well as the quarters, the Earth, Varuṇa,
Vāyu, the Moon, Brahmā, Rudra, and indeed the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña).
Agni, Indra, Viṣṇu, Mitra, and the god Prajāpati—
thus, in sequence, the divine [manifestation] is indeed of fourteen kinds.
O best of the twice-born, Sudarśanā, Jitā, Saumyā, in due order, as well as Moghā, Rudrā, Amṛtā, Satyā, and Madhyamā are the queens.
Nāḍī, Rāśiśukā, Asurā, Kṛttikā,
and Bhāsvatī— these are the channels (nāḍīs) bound by fourteen [knots].
The fourteen winds situated within the channels are the carriers;
they are Prāṇa, Vyāna, Apāna, Udāna, and Samāna.
Vairambha, as well as Mukhya, Antaryāma, Prabhañjana, Kūrmaka, Śyena, Śveta, and likewise the wind Kṛṣṇa.
O you of good vows, the fourteen winds are indeed called *nāgas*,
as well as those located in the eyes, in the objects of sight, and likewise in the sun.
In the channel, in the vital breath, in consciousness, and in bliss— in this sequence—
he is the Supreme within all this, in the space of the heart.
The Self moves alone; one should worship Me as that Lord—undecaying, infinite, free from sorrow, immortal, and eternal.
He alone wanders through these fourteen kinds of states;
they dissolve back into him alone, O twice-born ones, for there is indeed nothing else.
For he alone is the omniscient one, and he alone is the Lord of all;
this god is the sovereign of all, the inner controller of great splendor.
O best of the twice-born, although he is the eternal source of all happiness for everyone when worshipped, he himself does not experience any happiness here while being worshipped.
Even while being worshipped by the Vedas and various kinds of scriptures,
this omniscient Lord will not indeed go to the Vedas and scriptures [for knowledge].
All this is food for him alone; he himself does not become food.
He should eat that which has been protected by his own self and has become food, and never anything else.
I am the food for all living beings everywhere; I am the knot of living beings; I am the ruler and the guide, fivefold in my nature according to my divisions.
This elemental self (bhūtātman) consists of food, for it consumes food;
the self consisting of vital breath (prāṇamaya) is the nature of the senses; and the self consisting of mind (manomaya) is the nature of volition.
In this world, Soma himself, whose nature is Time, is said to consist of consciousness;
having become composed of eternal bliss, he is Maheśa, the Supreme Lord.

Thus, I [realize] that this entire world, being dependent upon me alone, exists entirely within me; for through investigation, it is seen that since it lacks independent existence, it is not autonomous even though it appears as such.
Even unity does not exist at all; how then, alas, could there be duality therein?
Thus, since even mortality does not exist, how could there be the birth of the immortal from the Unborn?
(ignorance is the source of saṃsāra:
He is neither one whose consciousness is internal, nor one whose consciousness is external, nor likewise one whose consciousness is directed toward both;
he is not a mass of pure consciousness, nor is he a wise man preceded by knowledge.
From the perspective of ultimate reality, there is nothing to be known and no object of knowledge;
indeed, Nirvana is absolute liberation, the supreme good, and free from all affliction.
Amṛta, the imperishable (akṣara), Brahman, the Supreme Self (paramātman), the higher and the lower (parāpara),
the non-conceptual (nirvikalpa), and the non-manifest (nirābhāsa)— these are synonyms for knowledge (jñāna).
That which is serene and one-pointed is known as knowledge;
everything else is ignorance—no deliberation need be made on this point.
In this way, consciousness, which is born from contact with a guru, becomes firmly serene, always free from passion,
hatred, falsehood, anger, sensual desire, thirst, and the like.
This very [teaching], untouched [by error], should be known today as the bestower of liberation;
however, because it was preceded by the impurity of ignorance, the person is considered defiled.
For liberation arises from the destruction of that [karma], and not otherwise even in ten million births;
without singular knowledge, there is no exhaustion of merit and sin.
Therefore, O best among the knowers of Brahman, one should practice knowledge alone for the sake of liberation;
for through the practice of knowledge, the intellect of men indeed becomes stainless.
Therefore, one should always practice knowledge, being established in it and devoted to it;
for the yogin who is satisfied by knowledge alone and has abandoned all attachment.
O best of Brahmins, there is nothing further to be done; if there were, one would not be a knower of reality.
Indeed, for such a person, there is nothing to be done in this world or in the next.

Therefore, one who knows Brahman is liberated while living; in the ultimate sense, he is constantly devoted to the practice of knowledge and is himself a knower of the true meaning of the reality of knowledge.
O best of the twice-born, he who has abandoned anger and relinquished pride in his caste and stage of life attains knowledge itself by casting off the habitual performance of ritual duties.
The fool who delights elsewhere is ignorant; of this there is no doubt.
Ignorance is the cause of saṃsāra, and saṃsāra is the assumption of a body.
Likewise, knowledge is the cause of liberation; one who is liberated abides in his own self.
O best of Brahmins, when ignorance exists, anger and other passions arise—of this there is no doubt.
O best of the twice-born, anger, joy, greed, delusion, and hypocrisy—
these indeed constitute dharma and adharma for them, and under their influence occurs the assumption of a body.
As long as there is a body, there is indeed affliction; therefore, the wise man should completely abandon ignorance.
Having discarded ignorance through knowledge, the yogin remains established in that very state.
O twice-born ones, anger and the like come to an end, as do both dharma and adharma;
and through their destruction, one is no longer joined with a body.
He alone is liberated from saṃsāra and freed from the threefold suffering;
O best of the twice-born, without such knowledge, there is no meditation for the meditator.
For knowledge arises from contact with the guru, not merely through words in the ultimate sense;
having understood the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha), the meditator should practice meditation.
The fire of knowledge quickly consumes both innate and adventitious evil, as well as that arising from bone and speech, just as fire burns dry fuel.
There is nothing superior to knowledge for the destruction of all evils;
one should always practice knowledge, free from all attachments.
The wisdom of the knower digests all sins; there is no doubt in this.
Even while playing, he is not tainted by various kinds of evils.
As is knowledge, so is meditation; therefore, one should practice meditation thoroughly.
Meditation is said to be initially with an object, and likewise, it is described as being without an object.
Having practiced in six ways, then likewise in four, six, and ten;
and likewise in twelve ways, and again in sixteen ways in succession.
By practicing these two ways, the lord of yogins is liberated; of this there is no doubt.
[He perceives it] having the appearance of pure gold, resembling smokeless embers.
Yellow, red, or white, with a radiance equal to tens of millions upon tens of millions of lightning bolts;
or else, having diligently fixed the mind at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
The knower of Brahman should not recall what has been eaten, smelled, or drunk;
he should be non-violent, truthful in speech, and refrain from theft with every effort.
Free from possessions, practicing celibacy, firm in his vows,
contented, endowed with purity, he is always devoted to the private recitation of the Vedas.
One who is devoted to me should certainly practice the meditation born from contact with the Guru;
yet, O best of the twice-born, the meditator does not perceive it while fixing the mind in that way.
The yogi does not conceive of himself, nor does he see anything on all sides;
he neither smells nor hears at all, being absorbed within his own self by his very nature.
And he does not perceive touch; he is indeed remembered as being of equal flavor (samarasa).
In the earthly layer Brahmā resides, and Hari himself in the watery element.
One should contemplate them in this sequence: Kālarudra in the fire element, Maheśvara in the air element, and Śiva himself directly in the cavity. LiP 1.86.128.
On earth the god is remembered as Śarva; in the waters he is remembered as Bhava;
likewise Rudra is established in fire, and Ugra resides in the wind.
Bhīma resides in the hollow of the sky; he is stationed in the orb of the sun, and as Īśāna in the lunar disc, he is known as Mahādeva.
For men, the god Paśupati is established as myself in eight forms.
That which is hardness in the body is proclaimed to be entirely the element of earth.
That which is fluid is called water; that which is designated by color is said to be fire;
O best of the twice-born, that which moves is wind, and that which is hollow is space.
Likewise, O Brahmins, consciousness born from space arises from sound;
similarly, consciousness known as touch arises from wind.
O twice-born ones, one should contemplate that form is fiery, taste consists of water, and that which is called smell is earthy; furthermore, one should meditate on the Sun in this sequence.

O twice-born ones, one should contemplate Soma in the right and left eyes, and the all-pervading Lord in the heart; the earth element extends as far as the knees, and the sphere of water from the navel upward.
O best of the twice-born, the fire element (vahnitattva) extends from the throat to the forehead;
the wind element (vāyavya) begins at the forehead, while that called space (vyoma) reaches the tip of the crest-lock.

Then one should remember the Brahman called Haṃsa, which is beyond the sky; then that which is even further beyond, called Vyoma, situated in the midst of the sky—this is indeed the primordial [Brahman].

Neither the individual soul (jīva), nor primordial nature (prakṛti), nor goodness (sattva), passion (rajas), nor again darkness (tamas); nor the great principle (mahat), nor likewise the ego-sense (abhimāna), nor the subtle elements (tanmātras), nor the sense organs (indriyas).
The elements, beginning with space, do not exist here in the ultimate sense;
rather, because he remains pervading the entire universe, he is designated as "Sthāṇu" (the Immovable).
The sun rises, and the wind blows in fear;
the moon shines, fire blazes, and the waters flow.
The earth provides support and space provides room; everything is pervaded by His command. Therefore, O twice-born ones, one should indeed meditate upon Him.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, having realized that all this is presided over by Him alone—
that Śarva consists of every form— one should meditate upon Bhava.
O best of the twice-born, for those scorched by the poison of saṃsāra, the remedy is indeed declared to be the nectar of knowledge and meditation; it is not otherwise.
Knowledge arises directly from dharma; from knowledge, detachment is born;
from detachment comes supreme knowledge that illuminates the ultimate reality.
O best of the twice-born, for one endowed with knowledge and dispassion, there is the perfection of yoga;
through the perfection of yoga, liberation occurs for one established in *sattva*, and not otherwise.
O twice-born ones, having established oneself in the power of pure being (*sattva-śakti*), one should worship Śiva— that wondrous, immutable state which is shrouded by the darkness of ignorance.
He who is devoted to living beings, my devotee, intent upon my worship, steadfast in dharma in every respect, always energetic, and composed; LiP_1,86.147 //
The steadfast one endures all dualities, is devoted to the welfare of all beings,
is always upright by nature, composed in mind, and ever gentle.
O best of the twice-born, he is free from pride, wise, tranquil, and has abandoned all rivalry;
he is ever seeking liberation, a knower of dharma, characterized by the defining marks of his own self.
Freed from the three debts and possessing merit from previous births,
he became a twice-born man endowed with old age, and through faith in his guru, he followed the traditional sequence.
Or otherwise, having performed service free from artifice,
one reaches the heavenly world and enjoys pleasures in due succession.
Having reached the land of Bhārata, O twice-born ones, the knowledge of Brahman arises;
having attained wisdom through such contact, the wise man becomes a knower of yoga.
O best of the twice-born, this is the sequence for one filled with impurity to attain knowledge;
therefore, by this path, one who has abandoned attachment and is firm in his vows [should proceed].
O best of sages, one is liberated from what is called the kālakūṭa poison of saṃsāra;
thus has this infallible [teaching] been briefly proclaimed by me to you.
The greatness of knowledge alone is beautiful here by virtue of this context;
thus has the Pāśupata yoga been described by the Lord.
O best of sages, that which has been spoken by Śiva must not be given to just anyone;
it should always be given with great affection to a yogin who is firmly established in the sacred ash.
The man who reads or even hears this [text] which pacifies the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) attains union with Brahman; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
Thus ends the eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Poison of Saṃsāra," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
Having heard this, those highly wise youths, led by Kumāra, bowed down to the wielder of the Pināka bow and, being terrified, spoke to the gracious Supreme Lord.
If, O Maheśvara, you thus sport with this goddess Haimavatī in various enjoyments, how can you possibly justify yourself here?
Sūta said:
Having been addressed thus, the Lord Pinākin, who is blue-and-red (Nīlalohita), laughed and,
looking at Ambikā, spoke to the twice-born ones who stood there prostrate before him.
In this world, bondage and liberation do not belong to me, for I am the embodied one who acts according to my own will;
the individual soul is an ignorant beast, yet it is all-pervading, the enjoyer, and atomic in size.
The one possessed of illusion is bound by illusion, and he is indeed joined with karmas;
O twice-born ones, knowledge, meditation, bondage, and liberation do not belong to the Self.
When even for that learned man who knows me thus, this knowledge is not complete in every respect, I am indeed the one to be known; I am this wisdom, and I am the Śruti and the Smṛti.
This is my steadfastness, my final goal, as well as the power of knowledge and action;
likewise, that which is called will and the Command—these two are the Vidyās, without a doubt.
For this is neither the primordial nature (prakṛti) nor a transformation (vikṛti) when examined;
it is not a modification at all, but rather Māyā, devoid of the manifestation of being and non-being.
In the past, the eternal and highly fortunate five-faced Command issued from my mouth, bestowing fearlessness upon the worlds.
Having entered that command and contemplating the welfare of the worlds, I,
Śiva, pervaded everything in twenty-seven ways by means of this [power].
"O best of the twice-born, from that time forth indeed began the practice of liberation.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus, the Supreme Lord then beheld Bhavānī.
And Bhavānī, the imperishable one, having looked at him, removed that illusion;
those sages, freed from the stain of illusion, beheld Pārvatī.
They became joyful and were liberated from that; therefore, this is the supreme goal.
In ultimate reality, there is no difference whatsoever between Umā and Śaṅkara.
He remains established in two forms, without a doubt,
when the wise one becomes free from attachment through the command of the Supreme Lord.
Then liberation occurs in an instant, and not otherwise even through millions of karmas;
the sequence of the Supreme Lord, increased by the elements, is not intended to be expressed here.
Through grace, liberation occurs in an instant; this is my promise, there is no doubt.
Whether one is still in the womb, being born, a child, or even a youth—LiP_1,87.16.
Whether an old being or one who is young, whether born from an egg, born from a sprout, or born from sweat, every creature is liberated through the grace of the Supreme Lord.
By the grace of the God of gods, there is no need for deliberation here;
he alone is the Lord of the World, Śiva, who effects both bondage and liberation.
Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svar, and Mahas, as well as Jana, Tapa itself,
and Satyaloka, along with hundreds of millions upon millions of cosmic eggs.
The form of the God of gods, as well as the eightfold covering of the cosmic egg,
[is present] in all the seven continents, on the mountains, and in the forests.
And in all the oceans, in all the masses of wind everywhere,
and likewise in other worlds, both moving and non-moving beings dwell.
All states of existence are surely born from him; he indeed is their goal.
All is Rudra; salutations to that Great-Souled Puruṣa.
The entire universe, as it has come to be and is born in manifold ways, is indeed Rudra;
this Goddess, established by the command of Rudra, is Ambikā, through whom liberation is attained.
Thus did the perfected beings (siddhas) who move through the sky speak with delighted minds,
when Ambikā, out of her grace, looked upon them all.
Then those sky-dwellers, having attained union (sāyujya) with the Lord, abide [there].
Thus ends the eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Quelling of the Sage’s Delusion," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
The sages said:
O Sūta, by what yoga do the virtuous attain the qualities here in this world? How is it that yogins become endowed with the powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest?
O Sūta, you ought to explain all of that in detail now.
Sūta said:
Hereafter I shall proclaim the yoga that is most difficult to attain;
first, one should establish the Eternal One in the mind and contemplate him in five ways.
O best of the twice-born, one should fashion a lotus seat joined with the moon, sun, and fire, endowed with twenty-six powers, and arranged in eight ways.
Then, O twice-born ones, one should likewise remember that god, the Lord of Umā, sixteenfold and again twelvefold within the center of the Goddess.
The unborn Lord, who possesses eight forms, is endowed with eight powers;
through those [powers], the Rudras are of eight kinds, and furthermore, of sixty-four kinds.
And likewise, one should remember all the Śaktis as endowed with the eight qualities,
having thus attained supreme knowledge in this very sequence.
Thus, O Brahmins, the Pāśupata yoga bestows the attainment of liberation; through it, one gains the powers such as *aṇimā*, and not otherwise by means of millions of ritual acts.
(Īśvaratva): In that regard, the eightfold sovereignty of yogins has been proclaimed;
understand now all of it as it is being described in its proper sequence. LiP 1.88.8.
Atomicity, levity, and indeed magnanimity, as well as attainment;
mastery over all things, and sovereignty everywhere.
Furthermore, mastery everywhere, wherein there is the power to bring desires to their fulfillment—
that sovereignty which grants all wishes is also to be known as threefold.
It proceeds as both faulty and faultless, and indeed as subtle;
that which is called "faulty" therein is traditionally held to consist of the five elements.
The sense organs, the mind, and that which is known as the ego—
within these, moreover, resides the subtle activity consisting of the five elements.
The sense organs, the mind, that which is designated as consciousness, intellect, and ego,
as well as everything composed of these, and even manifestation itself, reside within the Self.
Union itself is threefold and operates only among subtle things;
furthermore, it is also prescribed as eightfold only among subtle things.
I shall describe his form as the Lord, the Master, has declared it,
and how his ordinance is remembered among all beings in the three worlds.
Likewise, the unmanifest, beginning with the power of atomization (aṇimā) and so forth, is established everywhere;
it is declared to be difficult to attain for all beings within the three worlds.
That becomes the first power to be attained by yogins;
his form shall always be capable of leaping and bounding throughout the world.
Swiftness among all beings is remembered as the second station;
it is honored by the majesty of all beings throughout the three worlds.
And greatness in this world is called the third yoga;
it is traditionally defined as the power to go wherever one desires throughout the three worlds and among all beings.
He enjoys objects of desire to his heart's content, being unimpeded anywhere;
thus, the happiness and suffering of all beings in the three worlds proceed from him.
The knower of yoga becomes a lord everywhere through his discernment;
and all beings in the three worlds, including the moving and the unmoving, come under his control.
By his will, his forms come into being and cease to be; he possesses the power to resolve his desires at will throughout the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile.
Sound, touch, taste, smell, form, and likewise the mind—
these function according to his will, yet they do not exist merely by his mere wish.
(The yogin is freed from attachment:
He is neither born nor does he die; he is neither cut nor divided; he is not burned, nor is he deluded; he is not dissolved, nor is he stained. LiP_1,88.24.
It is neither exhausted nor does it perish; it never suffers weariness.
It is not acted upon anywhere, nor is it ever transformed.
But he is without smell, taste, or form; he is intangible and devoid of sound;
for he is without color, without voice, and never possesses any complexion.
He experiences the objects of the senses, yet he is not joined with them;
because of his atomic nature, he is supreme and subtle, and because of his subtlety, he is destined for liberation.
He is considered all-pervasive because of liberation, and from that which is all-pervasive, he is known as Puruṣa;
yet Puruṣa, by virtue of his subtle nature, abides in supreme sovereignty.
Then, having attained unsurpassed yoga characterized by supreme qualities and sovereignty that is subtle in every respect, one attains an unimpeded mastery.
From that, one should go to liberation, that subtle and supreme state;
thus, O best of sages, is the Pāśupata yoga to be known.
It bestows the fruits of heaven and liberation, and is the cause of union with Śiva;
or else, one whose wisdom has departed may perform ritual action out of passion.
Even after consuming that which is rajasic or tamasic, one is liberated right there;
likewise, one who has performed virtuous deeds enjoys the fruit thereof in heaven. (Brahmā guarantees liberation. LiP 1.88.32.
From that state, one is reborn again as a superior human;
therefore, Brahman is the supreme bliss, the eternal and highest Brahman.
One should indeed serve Brahman alone, for Brahman alone is the supreme bliss;
for the labor involved in sacrifices proceeds only for the sake of a great purpose.
He falls again under the power of death; therefore, liberation is the supreme happiness.
Alternatively, one who is united with meditation and devoted to the reality of Brahman [attains it].
But he cannot be made to fall even in hundreds of Manvantaras,
having beheld the divine Person, named Viśva, whose faces are on all sides.
The Lord whose feet, heads, and necks are universal, the Lord of the universe, who possesses a universal form;
who has universal fragrance and universal garlands, and who wears universal garments.
With his rays he pervades the great earth like winged birds; thus he generates [the world] repeatedly, even in this very way.
[He is] the ancient seer, the instructor, subtler than the subtle and greater than the great. (LiP 1.88.38)
Through yoga, and not with the eye, one should behold the Person who is devoid of senses, golden-hued,
signless, free from qualities, conscious, eternal, ever omnipresent, and the essence of all.
For those who are purified by that light perceive, through reasoning, that immovable radiance blazing with splendor;
it is without hands, feet, belly, sides, or tongue, beyond the senses, exceedingly subtle, and one.
Though eyeless, he sees; though earless, he hears; there is nothing unperceived by him, nor is there any perception apart from him.

He knows everything, yet he is not an object of universal knowledge; they call him the foremost, the Great Puruṣa. (LiP 1.88.41) Yogis, when disciplined, perceive Prakṛti—the unconscious, all-pervading, subtle, and productive source of all beings. (LiP 1.88.42)
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces everywhere,
and with ears everywhere in the world, it stands pervading all.
One who is disciplined through yoga perceives the eternal Īśāna, the Puruṣa of all beings; knowing him, one is not deluded.
The meditator who contemplates the self of all beings, the great self, the supreme self, the imperishable, the self of all, the highest Brahman— indeed, such a person is not deluded.
Just as the wind, moving through all forms, is easily grasped, yet when it rests within the city [of the body], it is very difficult to grasp; therefore, it is called *puruṣa*.
(Development of the embryo: Then, she whose nature is obscured by her own remaining karmas enters into the womb of Brahmā, which is joined with semen and blood. LiP 1.88.47.
For when a woman and a man unite, from that a lord (the embryo) is born;
then, through the period of gestation, it becomes what is called the *kalala*.
In due time, the *kalala* and the *budbuda* are produced,
just as a lump of clay is compressed on a wheel by the rotation of the wheel.
Just as [clay] being worked by the hands attains the state of an image,
so too [the body], joined with internal [elements] and fully filled by the wind, [attains its form].
"If I am released from the womb, I shall then take refuge in Maheśvara,
before the wind of Viṣṇu touches me as soon as I am born."
One should think, "I shall worship Mahādeva for that length of time";
there, a human is born with a form and age corresponding [to that intention].
Wind arises from space, and from wind indeed comes water;
from water arises the vital breath (prāṇa), and from the vital breath semen increases.
The portion of blood consists of thirty-three parts, and the portion of semen consists of fourteen;
having made the fruit half [in size] according to these portions, the embryo is then infused.
Then, joined with the embryo and enveloped by the five vital airs (vāyus),
his form is produced limb by limb from the body of the father.
Then, from his mother’s food—through its being drunk, licked, or swallowed—the vital breaths enter him by way of the navel region; for these are indeed the support of embodied beings.
Afflicted for nine months,
with his neck encircled and all his limbs wrapped around, he finds no room to enter.
Having remained for nine months with head downward through the opening of the womb,
he then, by his own evil deeds, falls into hell.
The Forest of Sword-leaves, the Shattering of the Silk-cotton Tree,
as well as the Beating, the Devouring, and the Eating of Pus and Blood.
For just as waters that have been divided come together once more,
so too do those who are cut and shattered, having arrived at the place of torment.
In this way, living beings, tormented by those sins committed by themselves,
shall experience suffering or its opposite through the remnants of their karma.
Indeed, one must depart alone, having abandoned all people; likewise, one must enjoy [the fruits of action] alone. Therefore, one should practice virtuous deeds.
For no one follows him as he sets out and goes;
rather, it is the karma that he has performed which follows him.
Constantly engaged in the realms of Yama, they cry out perpetually due to their association with what is undesirable;
their bodies, overwhelmed by suffering, wither away through many extremely intense and endless torments.
Whatever one habitually practices through action, mind, or speech,
that very habit carries one away; therefore, one should practice what is virtuous.
The continuum of the embodied being’s prior karma is beginningless;
it leads them into the sixfold, terrible, and dark cycle of transmigration.
From the human state one becomes an animal, from the animal state one becomes a wild beast; from the state of a wild beast one becomes a bird, and from that indeed one becomes a reptile.
Due to being a crawling creature, he will indeed attain the state of an immobile being; of this there is no doubt.
Once the state of an immobile being has been reached, he remains as long as people keep their eyes open.
"Whirling like a potter's wheel, he revolves right there;
thus indeed consists the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) for humans and others, ending with the stationary beings."
That which is to be known as tāmasa revolves right there;
the sāttvika cycle of existence (saṃsāra), beginning with Brahmā, is likewise proclaimed.
Among embodied beings in the abodes of heaven, he should be known as ending in the state of a Piśāca;
in the realm of Brahmā there is pure Sattva, while in the stationary [beings] there is pure Tamas.
Among the fourteen locations, the obstructing *rajas* [is active] when the vital points (*marmans*) of the embodied being, afflicted by pain, are being severed.
Then how will the Brahmin remember that supreme Brahman?
For the cycle of existence is driven away by the meditations on his former dharma.
One always encounters the human state; therefore, one should practice meditation, having understood this fourteen-fold sphere of worldly existence.
One who is oppressed by the fear of saṃsāra should constantly undertake the practice of dharma;
thus, through gradual transformation, he crosses over saṃsāra.
Therefore, one who is constantly disciplined, intent on meditation,
and devoted to yoga should undertake the practice in such a way that he perceives the Self.
This is the waters, this is the supreme light; this is the unsurpassed bridge, for by its opening there is the union of all beings, and it is eternal.
Therefore, one should worship this Great Lord, the Self, as the bridge, the fire whose face is turned in every direction, and who resides in the hearts of all beings.
Likewise, one should contemplate the God stationed within, adorned by His own power,
in eight ways, in another eight ways, and likewise in an eightfold manner.
Having withdrawn the fire that was established for the purpose of creation and situated within the heart,
one should meditate correctly upon Rudra, the Lord of Gods and the sovereign of the worlds.
Having properly offered five oblations while his mind is absorbed in contemplation of that [deity], he should [worship] Vaiśvānara, who resides in the heart, in due order and according to the rules.
Having sipped the purified water once and offered oblations silently, they sat down;
that first oblation of his is remembered as being for "Prāṇa. (LiP 1.88.82)
The second is for Apāna, and likewise the next for Vyāna;
the fourth should be for Udāna, and the fifth for Samāna.
Having offered the oblations separately with the utterances of *svāhā*, he should eat the remainder according to his desire;
then, having sipped water once and performed the ritual sipping (*ācamana*), he should touch his heart.
The self is the knot of the vital breaths; indeed, Rudra is the self that destroys all beings.
Rudra is truly the vital breath of the self; thus one should cause oneself to swell with strength.
Rudra is indeed established in the vital breath (prāṇa); therefore, he himself consists of the vital breath.
For the sake of Prāṇa and for Rudra, one should offer the supreme nectar (amṛta).
"O Śiva, enter me here, O Lord; Svāhā! To the Self that is Brahman, by itself!"—with these five oblations, may the eternal Lord be pleased.
You are the Puruṣa; you reside within the city [of the body] with the measure of a thumb.
You are the Lord, the supreme cause, who rests upon the very thumb.
May the eternal Lord, the master of the entire world, be pleased;
you are the eldest of the gods, and you, O Bull, are Rudra before all.
"O gentle one, may this food be offered to us for you.
Thus everything was spoken, according to the specific attainment of qualities.
The practice of yoga was previously taught by that very Brahmā himself;
thus, the knowledge of Pāśupata should be understood with diligent effort.
One should always bathe in ashes and remain constantly smeared with ashes;
whoever reads this, or listens to it, or causes the best of the twice-born to hear it, [attains the highest state].
Whether at a rite for the gods or one for the ancestors, he attains the supreme goal.

Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Eight Siddhis such as Aṇimā, the Three Guṇas, Saṃsāra, and the Oblation into the Primordial Fire," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the characteristics of pure conduct,
by the performance of which a purified soul may attain the supreme goal after passing away.
Formerly, for the benefit of all beings, Brahmā indeed spoke this compendium of the meaning of all the Vedas, which is the collection of the teachings of those who discourse on Brahman.
But for the sake of the arising of purities, the supreme state belongs to the sages;
he who is then heedful therein, that sage does not perish.
These two, honor and dishonor, are said to be poison and nectar;
therein, dishonor is the nectar, while honor is called the poison.
But he who is intent on the welfare of his guru shall dwell with him for one year, remaining vigilant in the observances (niyamas) and always steadfast in the restraints (yamas).
Then, having obtained permission, he should wander this earth practicing the unsurpassed yoga of knowledge in a manner that is not in conflict with dharma.
One should walk along a path purified by the sight; one should drink water purified by a cloth;
one should speak words purified by truth; and one should act with a mind that is pure.
Whatever sin would accrue within six months from one who catches fish, that same [sin] is known to be incurred by water that remains impure for even a single day.
But if one drinks unpurified water, one should recite the Aghora mantra, characterized by its specific marks, five hundred times; thereby, one shall attain purification.
Alternatively, one should worship Śambhu with elaborate rites such as bathing him with ghee;
having circumambulated him three times, one is purified—of this there is no doubt.
A knower of yoga should never go to rites for guests, ancestral offerings, or sacrifices;
for it has been determined that in this way the yogin becomes non-violent.
(Rules for wandering for alms:

A wise man should wander for alms when the fire has gone out, when the embers have subsided, and when all the people have finished their meal; however, he should not do so constantly among those very same people.
Then others may despise him and treat him with contempt;
under such circumstances, he should practice begging for alms in a manner consistent with the conduct of the virtuous, without violating the dharma of the good.
He should practice begging for alms among forest-dwellers and among the households of wandering ascetics;
indeed, this first mode of livelihood is considered the most excellent for him.
From this point forward, O twice-born ones, one should move among householders who are virtuous, faithful, self-controlled, learned in the Vedas, and high-souled.
Furthermore, beyond this, even among those who are neither corrupted nor fallen,
the practice of wandering for alms among the social classes is said to be the lowest mode of livelihood.
Alms-food, rice-gruel, buttermilk, milk, or barley-meal;
or cooked fruits, roots, and the like; or broken grains, oil-cakes, and parched flour.
Thus have these foods that increase the success of yogins been declared by me; among those perfected ones, alms-food is traditionally held to be the best.
He who subsists on a single drop of water with the tip of a blade of kusha grass month after month is superior to one who lives according to the rules by begging for alms, as previously described.
For one who is afraid of old age, death, and the womb, as well as of the hells and other such states, it provides sustenance in this way; therefore, it is traditionally known as *bhikṣā* (alms).
Those who subsist on curd, those who subsist on milk, and others whose lives are sustained by [these]—
all of them are not worth even a sixteenth part of one who subsists on alms.
He who desires the supreme state should always lie upon ashes, subsist on alms, and have his senses subdued; he should practice the Pāśupata vow.
And for all yogins, the Cāndrāyaṇa fast shall be the most excellent;
one should perform it once, twice, thrice, or four times, according to one's capacity.
Non-stealing, celibacy, non-greed, renunciation, and [non-violence]—these are the five vows of monks; among them, non-violence is supreme in this world.
Absence of anger, service to the teacher, purity, moderation in food,
and constant study— these are proclaimed as the observances (niyamas).
The substance of the seed-source and its qualities, as well as bondage through actions,
are ordained for human beings just as wild elephants are in the forest.
All sacrificial rites are equal to the gods; yet they say that from sacrifice comes recitation, and from recitation comes knowledge.
From knowledge comes meditation free from attachment to worldly ties; when that is attained, there is the realization of the eternal.
Self-restraint, tranquility, truthfulness, freedom from blemish, silence, and straightforwardness toward all beings—
those whose intellects are purified by knowledge declare this to be suprasensory wisdom and likewise auspicious.
Concentrated, devoted to Brahman, heedful, pure, delighting in solitude, and having conquered the senses—
the high-souled one, as well as the blameless and stainless great seers, shall attain this yoga.
Just as one who is restrained by a goad reaches his desired destinations, so too does he reach his goal.
By this pure path, indeed, one whose seeds are burnt becomes free from stain.
Devoted to virtuous conduct, peaceful, and protectors of their own dharma,
they conquer all worlds and proceed to the world of Brahmā.
(Prostration to Superiors) The eternal Dharma was taught directly by my grandfather;
for the benefit of all the worlds, listen as I proclaim it to you. (LiP 1.89.32)
One should cause those who are endowed with the teacher’s instructions, who are elders, and who follow the traditional sequence,
to perform all acts such as rising from their seats and prostration.
O you of excellent vows, the Guru of Brahmā is indeed to be saluted by performing a prostration with eight limbs placed three times and by the practice of circumambulation three times.
Furthermore, all those who are senior are to be saluted by one who possesses discernment;
one should not disobey their command if one desires the highest accomplishment.
One should avoid with every effort subsisting on the elements, empty cavities, fields, and minor mantras, as well as [dealing with] poisons, planetary seizures, sorcery, and the like.
One should always avoid deceit, stinginess with wealth, and backbiting; as well as excessive laughter, arrogance, and acting according to one's own whims for mere sport.
One should avoid with every effort that which is contrary to the words of the guru, even in the presence of one's teachers; for the word of a guru is indeed not to be disregarded.
One should not speak [of these] with any effort, nor should one ever think of what is undesirable:
the seat, clothing, staff, and so forth, as well as the sandals of ascetics.
One should not touch with one's foot a garland, a place where one has slept, an alms-bowl, a shadow, nor the components of sacrificial implements, even with great effort.
One should not commit an offense against the gods or an offense against one's guru by any means whatsoever;
O Brahmins, having committed such an offense through negligence, one should recite the Praṇava ten thousand times.
One is purified from treason against the gods or treason against one's guru by means of ten million [recitations];
likewise, for the sake of purification from the great sins (mahāpātaka), one should proceed according to the prescribed rule.
A sinner who maintains good conduct is purified by half of that [penance];
all those who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin) are purified by half of that [again], provided they are observant of their vows.
If the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) have been omitted, a Brahmin is purified by performing them three times;
if the daily ritual (āhnika) has been interrupted, it is declared that one hundred [repetitions] must be performed.
For transgressing established rules, for eating what is forbidden to eat,
and for speaking what should not be spoken, purification is said to require one thousand [repetitions].
Even for the killing of crows, owls, pigeons, or other birds, one is liberated by reciting [the mantra] one hundred and eight times; there is no doubt about this.
Furthermore, one who knows reality, a knower of Brahman, and the best of Brahmins, attains purification through mere remembrance; no deliberation need be made on this point.
For those who know the Self, there are no such expiations nor any injunctions;
for those people who know the knowledge of Brahman are pure by their very nature.
Those who are solely devoted to the meditation of yoga are stainless like gold;
for those who are pure, there is no further purification, as they are already purified by the knowledge of Brahman.

(Regarding the purification of water: One should perform all [ritual] acts with waters that have been drawn up, are cool and free of froth, and are purified by the "cloth-eye" [filter]; one should avoid turbid water.
Water from the ocean or from a pond that is tainted by foul odors, colors, and tastes; situated in an impure place; or defiled by mud and stones [is unfit].
One should avoid [water] that is covered with moss or otherwise defiled by impurities;
O twice-born ones, one should perform all ritual activities while maintaining the cleanliness of one's garments.
All acts such as prostrations and service to the guru will be in vain for one whose self is devoid of the purification of clothing; he is indeed impure—of this there is no doubt.
For garments used for the sake of the gods, daily purification is prescribed;
for other garments, however, purification should be performed whenever dirt appears.
O twice-born ones, one should avoid with every effort clothing worn by others;
likewise, silk and woolen garments should be treated with rough substances, and linen garments with white mustard seeds.
The rules for *śrīphala* fruits, *aṃśupaṭṭa* cloths, *kutapa* woolens, *ariṣṭaka* fibers,
hides, bamboo vessels, and rattan are considered to be the same as those for ordinary garments.
The purification for all types of bark garments, as well as for umbrellas and chowries,
is declared by the lords of sages who know the Veda to be the same as that for cloth.
(Regarding the purification of objects:
"Brass is purified by ash, iron is said to be purified by alkaline salt, and copper, O Brahmins, as well as tin and lead, are purified by acid. (LiP 1.89.58)

O best of the twice-born, the purification of a beautiful golden vessel with water, as well as that of a silver vessel, and of vessels made of gems, stones, conch shells, and pearls, is declared to be like that of metallic objects.
In this world, for all liquids that have been severely defiled through contact with fire or water, purification is traditionally held to be by means of boiling.
The purification of objects such as grass and wood is prescribed by sprinkling them with pure [cow-dung] water;
likewise, the purification of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles is performed with warm water.
In the same way, the purification of sacrificial vessels, as well as of pestles and mortars, and of objects made of horn, bone, wood, or ivory, is accomplished solely by means of planing.
O highly fortunate ones, sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) is prescribed for objects that are aggregated;
for objects that are not aggregated, purification is said to be performed individually.
If a portion of grain belonging to a heap that has not yet been consumed becomes defiled,
one should remove only that much and sprinkle it with water infused with *kuśa* grass.
The purification of vegetables, roots, fruits, and the like is desired to be as that of grain; likewise, a house is purified by sweeping and scrubbing, and an earthen vessel by re-firing.
The earth is traditionally held to be purified by scraping, by applying collyrium, by sweeping, by the dwelling of cattle, and by sprinkling water.
Water situated on the ground is pure when it is sufficient to quench the thirst of a cow; it is unpolluted by impurities and endowed with excellent fragrance, color, and taste.
A calf [is the best] at the spring, a bird in causing fruit to fall;
for householders, one's own wife is the best during sexual union out of a longing for a spouse.
The best knower of Dharma should take up the cloth that has been washed by hand and with care according to the rules, having thoroughly sprinkled it with water infused with *kuśa* grass.
Merchandise displayed for sale according to the divisions of caste and stage of life is pure, as is that which originates from mines; among these, a dog is pure when it seizes game.
O best of the twice-born, O brahmins, shadow, sparks, flies and the like,
dust, earth, wind, and fire are always pure to the touch.
O Brahmins, having slept, eaten, sneezed, or drunk, as well as after spitting or beginning Vedic study, one should sip water again for purification, even if already pure.
Even those drops of water from the rinsing of the mouth that touch the feet should be known as equal to earth; one does not become impure because of them.
And having engaged in sexual intercourse, or having touched a fallen cock or the like, a pig, a crow or the like, a dog, a camel, or likewise a donkey; LiP 1.89.74.
Having touched a sacrificial post, a Caṇḍāla, or others of that sort, one becomes pure by bathing;
however, one should not touch a woman in her menses, a woman who has recently given birth, or even an outcaste.
One who is affected by the impurity of childbirth or joined by the impurity of a corpse should not touch those women during their menses;
having touched them, one becomes pure only after bathing.
O observers of good vows, there is no impurity for ascetics, forest-dwellers, celibate students, lifelong students, kings, and members of a circle of rulers.
Therefore, due to the conflict with their duties, this cannot be otherwise for kings;
for it is impossible for Vaikhānasa Brahmins to become outcasts.
For the twice-born who possess no stores, purification occurs by mere bathing and not otherwise;
likewise for those who have gathered together for the sake of a sacrifice, and for one who has been initiated.
The Self-Existent One has declared that purification for those who perform sacrifices occurs after one day;
however, for all embodied beings who have studied their own Vedic recension, it occurs after four days.

O best of the twice-born, for relatives, there is no impurity (*sūtaka*) or impurity due to death (*pretaka*) beyond three days in that case; however, it lasts until the end of the eleventh day for those who are near.
When death has occurred, purification is indeed achieved by mere bathing;
therefore, it is proclaimed that for the period prior to three menstrual cycles, purification takes one day.
For those who have died before the age of seven, the impurity lasts for three nights;
beyond that, it is ten days for Brāhmaṇas, or alternatively, only on the first day for the father.

The impurity for a mother due to childbirth lasts ten days, as do those for other relatives; however, for relatives under three years of age, purification occurs through bathing, while for the father it is always immediate.
For a kinsman, purification occurs after one night for those aged eight years or more;
for women, O observers of good vows, it is three nights before the age of twelve.
The sapinda relationship ceases with the seventh person;
however, once ten days have passed, one shall remain impure for three nights.
Then, O Brahmin, that same person who was previously present becomes pure merely by bathing once a year has passed.
(Regarding purification after touching a corpse:
Having touched a corpse, bathing for the sake of dharma is prescribed after three nights;
for those who carry or burn the body, however, mere bathing suffices if they are not blood relatives.
Having followed [the corpse] and bathed, one becomes pure by consuming clarified butter;
likewise, upon the death of a teacher, or when a Śrotriya has died, one must observe impurity for three nights.
O twice-born ones, [this applies] to maternal uncles, brothers,
kings, and circles of vassals who reside within one's own kingdom, as well as to birds, immediately.
O best of the twice-born, for Kṣatriyas there is impurity for only twelve days;
however, there is no impurity for one who has been consecrated in the event of a battle or in cases of accidents.
A Vaiśya is purified in fifteen days, and a Śūdra in a month;
thus has the unsurpassed purification of objects been briefly described.
Impurity does not exist at all for ascetics in its successive stages;
O twice-born ones, from the Tretā age onwards, women experience the menstrual flow month after month.
In the Kṛta age, by the power of the yuga, they are indeed born together at once;
and those highly fortunate ones pass away together with their wives, just like the Kurus.
And the system of the castes and stages of life, O observers of good vows, has existed since the Tretā age in the southern region of Bhārata, but not in the other regions.
In Mahāvīta and Suvīta, as well as in Jambūdvīpa and the eight [other continents] such as Śākadvīpa, the Dharma was indeed proclaimed just as it is in Bhārata.
In the Kṛta age, the mode of subsistence was based on the essence of flavors; in the Tretā age, it arose from houses and trees.
This very same [mode] arose among men due to the defects produced by the seasons, as well as through passion, hatred, and so forth.
O Brahmins, from sexual desire and likewise from harsh words and the like,
the fourteen types of grain— both cultivated and wild— such as barley and others, are produced.
Herbs are defiled by dust, and women by the impurities of passion and the like;
likewise, men are corrupted when crops are harvested out of season, when they are destroyed, or when they are replanted prematurely.
Therefore, with every effort, a woman in her menses must not be spoken to;
on the first day, she is to be avoided just as a Cāṇḍālī woman is.
On the second day, O Brahmins, she is indeed like a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa;
on the third day, she is half that [sin]; and on the fourth day, O men of good vows, she is purified.
Having bathed after half a month, she shall become completely purified;
thereafter, for women until the age of sixteen, purification is prescribed to be like that for urine.
Likewise, if she remains untouchable due to her menstrual flow for five nights,
then after twenty days, she becomes as before because of that flow.
Bathing, purification, as well as singing, weeping, laughing, traveling, anointing the body, women, gambling, and likewise the application of unguents; LiP_1,89.104.
One should especially avoid sleeping during the day, as well as cleaning the teeth,
sexual intercourse— whether mental or verbal— and the worship of deities [at improper times].
A woman who is menstruating should avoid prostrating with every effort;
likewise, she should avoid touching or conversing with another woman who is menstruating.
She should avoid, with every effort, the discarding of her garments;
having bathed, a woman in her menses must not touch another man.
One should gaze upon the Sun-god and then drink the *brahmakūrca* mixture;
or else, for the sake of self-purification, one should drink pure *pañcagavya* or milk.

On the fourth lunar day, however, a woman must not be approached; one who approaches her on that day gives birth to a child of short lifespan, one devoid of learning, one fallen from his vows, an outcast, or an adulterer.
And she gives birth to a son submerged in an ocean of poverty;
therefore, one who desires a daughter should again go according to the rules on the fifth lunar day.
From an excess of blood a female is born; from an excess of semen a male is born;
when they are equal, a neuter is born, and on the fifth day, a girl is born.
On the sixth day, the highly fortunate woman may be approached; she shall become the mother of a virtuous son.
Once the son is born, he of great splendor will manifest his status as a true son to him.
"Puṃs" is the name for hell, and they know hell to be suffering;
such a son, endowed with protection for his father, is thus born.
On the seventh day, one seeking a daughter should go; she herself will give birth [to one]. On the eighth day, one gives birth to a son endowed with all perfections.
On the ninth [lunar day], one seeking a daughter will obtain her; on the tenth, he shall become wise;
and on the eleventh, she shall likewise give birth to a woman, as previously described.
On the twelfth day, [he saw] one who knows the reality of dharma and who promotes the rites prescribed by revelation and tradition;
on the thirteenth day, a dull-witted woman who causes all kinds of confusion.
Since a woman gives birth [to a child] because of this, she should not go [to him] by all possible effort;
however, if she should go on the fourteenth day, she will become a mother of a son.
On the fifteenth day, the child is righteous; on the sixteenth, it has reached the further shore of knowledge.
Indeed, during the time of sexual union for women, the wind [of the embryo] resides on the left side.
If a woman should perform [this rite], she shall obtain a male child;
for women, however, at the time of sexual union, provided they are free from malefic planets.
"Having become pure at the prescribed time, he should approach a pure woman of bright smiles.
Thus, in this manner, within the compendium of dharma for ascetics, [the topic continues] by way of incidental discussion.
Good conduct has been proclaimed as the duty for all beings alike;
the pure man who either recites or even hears this account of good conduct [attains merit].
Or, having caused the Brāhmaṇas, whose sins have been burnt away, to hear it according to the rule,
he reaches the world of Brahmā and rejoices together with Brahmā.
Thus ends the ninety-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Right Conduct," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
Henceforth,
I shall declare here the definitive penance for ascetics as proclaimed by Śiva, which effects the purification of the sins of ascetics.
For evil should be known to be threefold, arising from speech, mind, and body;
it is that which constantly, by day and by night, envelops this world.
The supreme Śruti states that this [prāṇa] remains even without that [specific] action;
however, one should employ it for a moment as a means of sustaining the life-force (āyuṣya).
Yoga belongs to one who is vigilant, for yoga is indeed the supreme strength;
indeed, nothing more auspicious than yoga is seen for human beings.
Therefore, wise men endowed with righteousness praise yoga;
having conquered ignorance through knowledge, they attain unsurpassed sovereignty.
Having perceived the higher and the lower, the wise go to that supreme state;
such are the vows of the monks, as well as the secondary observances.
A penance is prescribed for each one of these transgressions;
however, having approached a woman out of lust, one should prescribe a specific penance.
One should perform the Sāṃtapana vow conjoined with breath control (prāṇāyāma);
thereafter, being composed, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance at the conclusion according to the instruction.
Having returned again to the hermitage, the mendicant should practice without sloth;
for the wise maintain that a falsehood joined with dharma does not cause harm.
Nevertheless, it must not be performed, for this is a terrible consequence;
likewise, there would be fasting for a day and night, as well as a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).
A mendicant who desires the Dharma should not engage in false speech;
nor, even when fallen into the greatest distress, should he commit theft.
(On the importance of possession:
"There is no unrighteousness greater than theft," so says the Śruti; for this theft is indeed declared to be the supreme form of violence. LiP 1.90.12.
That which is called wealth is indeed these vital breaths moving outside;
he who takes away another's wealth takes away his very life-breaths.
Having acted thus, that evil-minded one, whose conduct has become corrupted and who has fallen from his vow,
should again attain a sense of renunciation and perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
"According to the procedure seen in the scriptures, [he remains thus] for a year," so says the Śruti.
Then, at the end of that year, having further diminished his impurities and having attained renewed world-weariness, he should practice as a mendicant without sloth.
Non-violence toward all living beings through action, mind, and speech is the rule;
yet if a monk should harm animals or insects even unintentionally, [he incurs sin].
If an ascetic should emit semen upon seeing a woman due to weakness of the senses, he should perform the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra penance or the Cāndrāyaṇa.
Therefore, sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) must indeed be performed as the prescribed expiation for a Brahmin who has emitted [semen] during the day.
There shall be three nights of fasting as well as one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas);
if it is emitted at night, one becomes pure by bathing and performing twelve dhāraṇās.
O twice-born ones, one whose self is purified by breath control becomes free from passion;
likewise, [one is purified from] eating food belonging to a single person, honey, meat, or even uncooked food.
Furthermore, salt that is visible [to the eye] is unfit for ascetics to consume;
for each of these transgressions, an expiation is prescribed.
By means of the Prājāpatya penance, one is then liberated from that sin,
as well as from whatever transgressions may have arisen through speech, mind, or body.
Having deliberated together with the virtuous, one should act upon what they say.
One should live pure, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, and being perfectly composed toward all beings;
having gone to that supreme, certain, eternal, and imperishable station, one is indeed not born again.
Thus ends the ninetieth chapter, titled "Atonement for Ascetics," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
Henceforth I shall proclaim the signs of approaching death;
learn them, by which specific knowledge yogins perceive death.
A man who does not see Arundhatī, Dhruva, the shadow of the moon (Somachāyā), and the Great Path (Mahāpatha) shall not live beyond one year.
He who sees the sun with its rays and the fire with its flames shall certainly not live beyond eleven months.
If one vomits urine and feces, or likewise gold and silver,
whether witnessed directly or in a dream, one will not live for ten months.
If one sees a golden-colored tree and cities of the Gandharvas,
and sees pretas and piśācas, he shall live for nine months.
If one suddenly becomes stout and suddenly becomes emaciated,
and if one deviates from their natural constitution, they will live for eight months.
If one's footprint should appear incomplete either in front or behind,
whether on dust or in mud, such a person lives for seven months.
If a crow, a pigeon, a vulture, or a carnivorous bird should alight upon someone's head and does not depart for six months, [that person will die].
Or if he should pass through a flight of crows or a shower of dust,
or if he should see his own shadow distorted, he shall live for four or five days.
If one should see lightning in a cloudless sky situated in the southern direction,
or the bow of Indra in the water, he lives for three or two years.
Whether in water or in a mirror, he who does not see his own reflection,
or sees it without a head, shall not live beyond a month.
If his body should smell of a corpse or even of fat, death has indeed approached him; he will not live for more than half a month.
If, immediately after bathing, one's heart dries up or if one sees smoke emanating from the head, that person will not live for ten days.
When his vital airs are disordered and they cut through his vital points (marmasthāna),
and he does not experience a thrill when touched by water, death has arrived for him.
If one dreams that they are traveling toward the southern direction in a chariot yoked with bears and monkeys, while singing and dancing, one should know that death has arrived.
If a woman wearing black garments, dark-complexioned, or singing,
leads one toward the southern direction in a dream, even he does not live.
If a man sees a hole in his own throat in a dream,
or sees a naked ascetic, he should know that death has arrived.
But he who sinks into an ocean of mud up to the surface of his head,
having seen such a dream, does not live even for an instant.
He who sees ashes, charcoal, hair, a dried-up river, or serpents for ten nights will not live.
He who is struck with stones in a dream by hideous, dark men with uplifted weapons does not live long.
If jackals howl directly in front of a man at sunrise or at dawn, he shall indeed be one whose life has reached its end.
Or, if immediately upon bathing his heart is severely distressed and his teeth tingle, one should declare that his life has come to an end.
He who trembles again and again, whether by night or by day,
and does not perceive the scent of a lamp, should know that death has arrived.
If one should see a rainbow at night or a circle of stars during the day,
or if one does not see oneself in the eyes of others, that person does not live.
He whose one eye flows with tears, whose ears have fallen from their places,
and whose nose has become crooked, should be known as one whose life has departed.
He whose tongue is black and rough, whose face has the luster of a lotus, or whose cheeks are red like a ball of meat— for him, death has arrived.
That man who goes toward the southern direction with disheveled hair, laughing, singing, and dancing, his life comes to an end there.
For one whose white form repeatedly appears like a mass of white clouds or resembles a white mustard seed, death has indeed arrived.
If in a dream one sees camels or donkeys yoked to a chariot,
that person will not live, even if he has gone facing south.
Or else, when the two supreme vital breaths have become one in the *ariṣṭa* [the heart], he becomes transcendent;
he hears no sound in his ears, nor does he see light with his eyes.
If one falls into a chasm in a dream, and the door is closed,
and he does not emerge from that chasm, his life has reached its end.
The gaze is upward and lacks stability; the face is flushed and repeatedly turning;
there is dryness of the mouth, a sunken navel, and urine that is excessively hot; he remains in a state of extreme instability.
Whether by day or by night, he who is visibly struck down [by these signs]...
And he shall not see his slayer; having reached the end of his life, he does not live on.
That man who enters the fire at the end of a dream,
and no longer retains his memory, his life ends there.
But that man who, while seeing his own upper garment as white,
perceives it in a dream as black or even red— for him, death has arrived.
(Preparation for Death) When the body has been signaled by the omens of death and that time has arrived,
a wise man should abandon weariness and despondency and remain equanimous.
Having gone out toward either the eastern or the northern direction, being pure,
he should stand in a level, stable, secluded place, free from living beings.
Facing either north or east,
composed and having sipped water, one should sit in the svastika posture and pay homage to Maheśvara.
Keeping the body, head, and neck straight, one should not look about;
like a lamp placed in a windless spot that does not flicker—this is the simile taught.
In a region sloping toward the northeast, one who knows the scriptures should likewise apply himself;
[he should master] desire, discursive thought, joy, and both pleasure and pain.
Having restrained everything with the mind, one should constantly recollect pure meditation in the nose, the tongue, as well as in the eyes and the sense of touch.
One should fix [the mind] there upon the ears, the mind, and the intellect, and always upon the chest;
having understood the actions of time, one should remain constantly amidst the multitudes.
"Twelve internal"—thus is the practice of yoga-dhāraṇā described.
One should maintain the dhāraṇā upon the crown of the head for either one hundred or fifty [breaths].
For one who is weary, through the practice of retention (dhāraṇā), the vital air moves upward;
then, accompanied by the syllable OṂ, one should fill the body with it.
Likewise, the yogin who consists of the syllable Oṃ becomes imperishable within the Imperishable.
(Oṃkāra) Hereafter, I shall explain the characteristics of attaining the syllable Oṃ.
This should be known as having three measures (mātrās), and the consonant here is the Lord (Īśvara).
The first measure is called Vidyutī; the second is remembered as Tāmasī.
The third measure, which is indeed devoid of qualities and leads to the Imperishable,
should be known as Gāndhārī, originating from the Gāndhāra note.
The touch of the movement of an ant applied to the head is perceived;
just as the syllable *oṃ* when applied issues forth from the head.
Likewise, the yogi who consists of the syllable *oṃ* becomes imperishable,
