for the *praṇava* is the bow, the self is the arrow, and Brahman is said to be the target.
One who is vigilant should pierce [the target] like an arrow and become absorbed in that;
for this single syllable "Om" is the state hidden within the cave of the heart.
The syllable "Om" is these three worlds, the three Vedas, and the three fires;
it is also these three strides of Viṣṇu, as well as the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus verses.
In the ultimate sense, one should know that there are three [measures], namely the measure (mātrā), the half-measure (ardha), and the third;
the yogin who is devoted to them shall attain residence in the same world (sālokya) as [the deity].
The syllable *a* is to be known as the imperishable (*akṣara*); *u* is remembered as being conjoined;
and *m* together with *o* is designated as the three-measured (*trimātra*).
The letter *a* is said to be the world of the earth (*bhūrloka*); the letter *u* is called the world of the atmosphere (*bhuvar*).
But the letter *m*, together with its consonant, is sung as the world of heaven (*svarloka*).
The syllable Oṃ is indeed the three worlds; its head is the triple heaven (Triviṣṭapa), and all the worlds are its limbs—that is called the state of Brahman.
The world of Rudra consists of measured steps, whereas the state of Śiva is beyond measure;
thus, through the excellence of knowledge, that state is fully attained.
Therefore, one who desires eternal happiness should always take delight in meditation; for that syllable is immeasurable and should indeed be worshipped with effort.
The first measure is short, and immediately after that, the long;
thereafter, the third is taught as being protracted (pluta).
These measures should be understood correctly and in their proper sequence;
indeed, they should be maintained only as long as they can be sustained.
Listen now to the fruit that one obtains who always meditates upon the senses, the mind, and the intellect within the Self, even for half a *tanmātra*.
Whatever merit one might obtain by performing the horse sacrifice every month for a hundred years,
one may attain that same measure of merit [by this].
One shall obtain that fruit which is properly attained through intense austerity or through sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees; indeed, one may attain it with ease.
And in that regard, this measure which is taught as being "protracted" (pluta) should indeed be performed by householders who are practitioners of yoga.
And specifically regarding their eightfold sovereignty beginning with *aṇimā*, these should be understood; therefore, O twice-born ones, one should practice that [concentration].
For thus, O twice-born ones, he who is endowed with yoga, pure, self-controlled, and has conquered his senses— he who knows the Self, finds everything.
Therefore, the wise person should contemplate the Self through the Pāśupata yogas;
those who know the Self are pure, of this there is no doubt.
Through the knowledge of yoga, the Brahmin who contemplates the supreme self attains the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, as well as the Upaniṣads.
Having become composed of all the gods, he is born though he was previously non-existent;
having abandoned the transition through a womb, he indeed goes to the eternal state.
Just as ripe fruit falls from a tree when stirred by the wind,
so too is sin destroyed by a salutation to Rudra.
Wherein the salutation to Rudra is certain to yield the fruit of all actions;
one would not obtain such a result from salutations to other deities.
Therefore, the yogin should worship Maheśvara three times a day;
likewise, he should [worship] the ten-fold extensive Brahman with the expansions of the Veda.
Thus, he who, endowed with meditative concentration, should renounce his own body,
attains union with Śiva, having uplifted the three lineages.
Alternatively, when death is imminent upon perceiving an ill omen,
one should go to Avimukteśvara in Vārāṇasī for purification.
O best of Brahmins, by abandoning his body anywhere at all, a man is liberated;
or a man may abandon his own body on Śrīparvata.
He attains union with Śiva; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
Avimukta is the supreme sacred field, which always grants liberation to living beings.
The wise person should constantly practice this, especially when death is near.
Thus ends the ninety-first chapter, titled "The Narration of Ariṣṭa," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
The sages said:
"O Sūta of great intelligence, if Vārāṇasī is thus meritorious,
you ought to describe its power to us now."
We indeed have a great curiosity to hear, in detail and according to the proper method, the beautiful majesty of this sacred field, Avimukta.
Sūta said:
I shall describe succinctly and correctly the most beautiful [site] of Vārāṇasī, known as Avimukta.
The greatness of the Unliberated One is as the Blessed Lord Bhava has declared:
O best of Brahmins, it is not possible for me, nor even for the high-souled Brahmā, to describe this in detail even in hundreds of millions of years.
Long ago, the god Śaṅkara, who is blue-and-red (nīlalohita),
having performed his marriage with the goddess Haimavatī on a peak of the Himavat, [departed] with the lords of his hosts.
Having reached Vārāṇasī, Śaṅkara revealed the Avimukteśvara Liṅga and made his residence there.
In the Pāśupata yoga, one should become an ascetic for even a single day;
therefore, having renounced everything, one should practice the Pāśupata vow.
There, in the celestial garden, Rudra dwelt; that unsurpassed garden of Śarva, as well as a most beautiful celestial chariot, he fashioned by his mind.
And then the Supreme Lord himself, accompanied by Nandin, showed the unsurpassed celestial garden of Haimavatī.
And Śaṅkara, the Supreme Lord Bhava, spoke of the majesty of this sacred field, Avimukta, for the pleasure of Pārvatī.
Outside, it was adorned with various kinds of flowering shrubs and made enchanting by the spreading of creepers;
it was surrounded on all sides by *priyaṅgu* trees with fully grown blossoms, and by well-flowered, thorny *ketaka* trees.
It was covered everywhere with fragrant tamāla thickets and vakula trees in full bloom,
as well as hundreds of aśoka and punnāga trees in exquisite flower, their clusters of blossoms swarming with swarms of bees.
In some places it resounded on all sides with birds adorned by the pollen of full-blown lotuses and uttering melodious cries,
as well as with cranes and ruddy geese, and excellent, intoxicated gallinules.
In some places it was auspiciously resounded with the cries of peacocks; in other places it echoed with the calls of water-fowls;
and in others it was filled with swarms of intoxicated bees and female bees agitated by passion.

It was frequented by beautiful, fragrant flowers, in some places by well-flowered mango trees, and in others by *tilaka* trees entwined with creepers; it resounded with the songs of *vidyādhara*s, *siddha*s, and *cāraṇa*s.
It was attended by throngs of Apsarases engaged in dancing, frequented by various kinds of joyful birds,
resounded by the singing of dancing Hārītaka flocks, and filled with the roars of lions and the minds of the intoxicated.
In some places, the heaps of darbha grass sprouts and flowers were being browsed by herds of musk deer;
and in other places, it was adorned with lakes and ponds filled with various kinds of blossoming and beautiful lotuses.
It was dense with clusters of branches, delightful with peacocks, and charming with the songs of birds intoxicated with joy;
it was graced by bees clinging to the flowering tree-branches and beautified by the splendor of fresh sprouts, its lofty boughs reaching high.

In some places it had beautiful creepers marked by the tooth-bites [of celestial beings], and in others lovely young trees embraced by climbing vines; in other parts it was frequented by the wives of the *kiṃpuruṣas*, moving with the languid grace of amorous play.
With its cloud-scraping peaks, white and enchantingly beautiful in form, it was made charming by the warbling cries of pigeons.
It was made resplendent by numerous divine throngs of the thirty gods, with swans distinguished by the abundance of scattered flowers.
The royal road was graced by reservoirs of water adorned with thousands of canopies of blooming blue and white lotuses;
it was further endowed with various shrubs and branches interconnected by rows of diverse flowers set along the intervals of the path.

The area was illuminated at night by lovely *aśoka* trees with lofty tops and long branches bent down by the weight of clusters of blue flowers, which produced a pleasant sound from the ends of their swaying swings; these trees, blossoming like *tilaka* marks, attained a unity with the light of the moon, while the tips of the *dūrvā* grass shoots were nibbled away by herds of deer who had fallen asleep in the shade, only to wake and stand up again.
Its vast waters were clear from the lotuses stirred by the wind from the wings of swans; on its banks, peacocks danced with the grace of trembling plantains;
in some places, the ground was colored by the moon-like feathers of peacocks resting upon it; and in every region, flocks of intoxicated hārīta birds frolicked and rejoiced.
In some places its regions were graced by *sāraṅga* deer; in others it was hidden by various heaps of flowers;
and in yet other places, the throats of joyful *kinnara* maidens were sweet with song and dance accompanied by lutes.
In some places, it was surrounded by the dwellings of sages, where flowers were strewn and scattered upon the ground;
in other places, it was endowed with vast and towering jackfruit trees that were laden with fruit from their very roots.

It was delightful with the sound of golden anklets from the *siddhas* and *siddha-aṅganās* brought within the bowers of flowering *atimuktaka* creepers; it was beautiful with bees clinging to the clusters of blossoms on the *priyaṅgu* trees, and with *āmra* and *kadamba* flowers being devoured by swarms of bees.
It was charming with waters stirred by the wind from heaps of flowers, and lovely with sweet thickets where bees were falling.
It was like a herd of does terrified by a sudden predator within a thicket, driven by the wind, bestowing liberation upon embodied beings.
It was filled with beautiful *tilaka* trees variegated by webs of moonbeams, with *aśoka* trees resembling vermilion, saffron, and safflower,
and with *karṇikāra* trees possessing vast branches and clusters of blossoms equal in luster to refined gold.
In some places the ground was covered with flowers resembling powdered collyrium, in some places like coral, and in other places like gold.
There were hundreds of birds warbling among the *punnāga* trees; the red *aśoka* trees were bent low under the weight of their clusters of blossoms;
the pavilions at the lovely outskirts were filled with the sounds of revelry; and the bees sported among the full-blown lotuses.
Then the Lord of the World, the sustainer of all the universe, together with the daughter of the Snow-Crested Mountain and his beloved lords of the Gaṇas,
showed the Goddess a most delightful grove, vast with various trees and filled with birds intoxicated and nourished by food.
With wild flowers, both auspicious and most auspicious, fashioned with divine ornaments, Śarva adorned the divine goddess who had gone to the grove;
and she too, the daughter of the Snowy Mountain, with devotion adorned Śaṅkara, the god of gods, with divine flowers that were most exceedingly auspicious.
Having worshipped the one worthy of worship among the lords of the thirty gods, and having beheld the exceedingly beautiful garden,
the Goddess prostrated before the God and spoke together with the lords of the Gaṇas, headed by Nandin.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, you have shown me the garden endowed with supreme splendor;
you ought to tell me once more all the qualities of this sacred field."
O Lord of Gods, God of gods, Bull-bannered One, you ought to describe in every way the majesty of this sacred field, Avimukta.
Sūta said:
Having heard those words of the Goddess, the God of gods, the Lord who grants boons,
smelled her lotus-like face and then spoke to Girijā with a smile.
(The Holiness of Avimukta) The Blessed One said:
"This most secret field, Vārāṇasī, is always mine."
It is always the cause of liberation for all living beings indeed.
O Goddess, those perfected ones who have always remained established in my vow,
constantly assuming various outward forms, are ever desirous of my world.
With their minds disciplined and their senses conquered, they practice the supreme yoga in that place crowded with various trees and adorned by various birds.
It was beautifully adorned with lakes abundant with lotuses and water-lilies,
and was always frequented by hosts of Apsarases and Gandharvas in that auspicious place.
I always delight in his dwelling; hear now for what purpose: he whose mind is fixed on me, who is my devotee, and who has eternally offered all his actions to me.
Just as one attains liberation here, it cannot be so anywhere else;
for indeed, O Goddess, a living being who dies here at will is fit for liberation.
This is my divine city, the great secret more secret than all secrets;
it is known by Brahmā and others, as well as by the perfected ones (siddhas) who seek liberation.
Beyond this, this is my field and this is my supreme goal;
for it has never been abandoned by me, nor will it ever be abandoned.
Therefore, this field of mine is known as Avimukta;
likewise [it is found] at Naimiṣa, Kurukṣetra, Gaṅgādvāra, and Puṣkara.
Since liberation is not attained either through ritual bathing or through service,
that by which it is attained here is therefore superior to those.
"Whether liberation occurs at Prayāga or here, it is through my acceptance [of this place];
for this auspicious Avimukta is superior even to Prayāga, the foremost of sacred sites."
Truth is the secret essence of dharma; tranquility is the secret essence of liberation;
yet even the most excellent of the wise do not know the secret essence of sacred fields and pilgrimage sites.
Whether eating, sleeping, playing, or performing various activities,
if a person gives up their life-breaths in Avimukta, they become fit for liberation.
Even after committing thousands of sins, it is better for men to attain the state of a piśāca than to possess the status of a thousand Indras in heaven without the city of Kāśī.
Therefore, Avimukta should indeed be frequented for the sake of liberation,
where Jaigīṣavya, the great ascetic, attained supreme perfection.
Due to the majesty of this sacred field and through my grace,
the excellent Jaigīṣavya Cave is desired as a dwelling place for yogins.
Meditating upon me there constantly, the fire of yoga blazes intensely;
one attains supreme liberation, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
Liberation, which is difficult to attain anywhere else at any time, is achieved here by sages whose outward signs are unmanifest and who know all philosophical systems.
And to them I shall proclaim the unsurpassed sovereignty of yoga,
as well as union with my own self and the desired state.
Kubera, having dedicated all his actions to me in this field of mine,
indeed attained the status of Lord of the Gaṇas (Gaṇeśa) simply by cultivating that field.
And he who shall become Saṃvarta—he too shall indeed be devoted to me;
having propitiated me right here, O Goddess, he shall attain unsurpassed perfection.
The son of Parāśara, the yogi, the seer Vyāsa of great asceticism,
shall be my devotee and the one who establishes the system of the Vedas.
O lotus-eyed one, that bull among sages— whether Brahmā together with the celestial rishis, or Viṣṇu, or even the Sun— will also take delight in this sacred field.
Śakra, the king of the gods, as well as the other inhabitants of heaven—
all these high-souled ones attend upon me here, O lady of excellent vows.
Other divine yogins as well, great-souled ones whose forms are concealed,
always worship me here, having become single-minded.
Even a man whose mind is attached to sense objects and who has abandoned delight in the Dharma,
if he dies in this field, shall not be born again in saṃsāra.
Furthermore, those wise ones who are free from possessiveness, established in the welfare of beings, with their senses conquered,
observant of vows, and free from worldly undertakings— all of them have been cultivated within me.
O lady of excellent vows, having approached the God of gods, the wise who are free from attachment have attained supreme liberation here through my grace.
O lady of excellent vows, by my grace, you shall attain in this very life that supreme liberation which a yogi might not achieve even in thousands of other births.
This field, Goprekṣaka, was established by Brahmā in ancient times;
and here, O lady of beautiful countenance, behold the divine abode of Kailāsa.
Furthermore, having come to Goprekṣaka and seen me here,
a person does not fall into an evil state and is liberated from all taints.
Thus, indeed, Brahmā created the great and most meritorious sacred ford known as Kapilāhrada with the water produced from the milk of cows.
In this place as well, O Goddess, I myself am known as Vṛṣadhvaja; I have established my presence here, and I am always seen by you.
Behold here, O Goddess, this auspicious water and the lake created by Brahmā;
in this place, O Goddess, I was propitiated by all the gods.
"Go to tranquility, O Lord; Śiva is likewise tranquil.
Here I have been brought and established by Brahmā, the Supreme Lord."
Having been taken up by Brahmā, he was then established again by Viṣṇu;
thereafter, Viṣṇu was addressed by Brahmā with an agitated mind.
"Why have you installed this linga brought by me?
Viṣṇu spoke again to Brahmā, whose face was contorted with anger.
"O Lord Rudra, my devotion toward you is exceedingly great.
This liṅga installed by me shall bear your name."
"Thus, having established myself here as Hiraṇyagarbha,
even by beholding this Lord of Gods, a man shall go to my world."
Then, once again, Brahmā, endowed with supreme devotion, duly installed this auspicious liṅga of mine according to the prescribed rites.
"I myself have come here to this very place called Svarlīneśvara;
a man who gives up his life here shall never be born again anywhere."
"That goal which is remembered for yogins is indeed not different from his;
even in this region, I [slew] a Daitya who was a thorn in the side of the gods. (Vyāghreśvara) LiP 1.92.79.
Having assumed the form of a tiger, the proud and powerful one was slain;
known as Vyāghreśvara, I am ever established here.
Furthermore, having seen this Lord Vyāghra, the two Daityas Utpala and Vidala who were formerly created by Brahmā do not go to an evil rebirth.

Seeing those two arrogant men who were to have been slain by a woman, you yourself killed them in battle; it was with contempt that you struck them here with a ball, and this [demon] has now taken possession of his body.
"Having come here at the beginning, I set out together with the lords of the Gaṇas;
therefore, this is the station of the Eldest, and thus it is a sight of merit for me."
Since these lingas have been established on all sides by the gods,
even a mortal who sees them will certainly become a member of the Gaṇas upon the dissolution of the body.
In former times, your father Himavat, the king of mountains,
having himself recognized this place as dear and beneficial to me, installed a liṅga there.
"Behold with reverence here that which is known as Śaileśvara;
having seen this, O Goddess, a man shall not go to an evil state."
This divine river Varuṇā is holy and a liberator from sin;
having adorned this sacred field, she has united with the Jāhnavī.
An excellent liṅga was also established by Brahmā at the confluence;
let it be seen in the world as renowned by the name Saṃgameśvara.
Indeed, for that pure person who, having bathed at the confluence of the celestial river,
worships Saṅgameśvara, whence can there be any fear of rebirth?
I consider this to be a great field, the supreme abode of yogins,
wherein I myself have become present and occupy the foremost position in the midst of that field.
Thus it is renowned by all the gods and asuras as Madhyameśvara;
for this is the abode of the perfected ones who observe my vows.
Having seen this Madhyameśāna, the yogins who desire liberation and whose souls are devoted to the yoga of knowledge do not grieve over birth.
This installed linga was established by Śukra, the son of Bhṛgu;
it is known by the name Śukreśvara and is worshipped by all the Siddhas and immortals.
Upon seeing him, one who is self-restrained is immediately liberated from all sins;
and when dead, that person shall not again become a transmigrating being.
Formerly, an asura who was a thorn to the gods took the form of a jackal;
having obtained a boon from Brahmā, he became apprehensive of being bound.
"O daughter of Himavat, I am therefore known as Jambūkeśa;
even today I am celebrated throughout the world and worshipped by gods and asuras."
Having beheld even this Lord of the Gods, one shall obtain all desires;
for these [images] were indeed installed by the planets, with Venus at their head.
Behold these meritorious lingas that grant all desires;
such are these holy places where I dwell, O Pārvatī.
These have been declared within my field; now hear this other secret:
this field is proclaimed to extend four krośas in each of the four directions.
O lady of beautiful limbs, know that I, who am situated on Mount Mahālaya and established at Kedāra, bestow immortality at the time of death for one who travels a yojana [to reach me].

For by seeing this, one attains the state of being a Gaṇa, and indeed liberation is attained therein; since one thereby obtains the status of a leader of the Gaṇas (Gāṇapatya), that is the supreme liberation.
Therefore, O fair-faced one, the field known as Avimukta is remembered as more meritorious even than that great Mahālaya and the Madhyama Kedāra.
Kedāra is a middling field and Mahālaya is a sacred site;
these are my meritorious places in the world of mortals, but this [place] is indeed the most excellent among them.
Since these worlds were created from that [place], this field is auspicious;
because it was never abandoned by me at any time, it therefore became known as Avimukta (the Unabandoned).
Having beheld the Avimukteśvara Liṅga here,
a human being is instantly liberated from sin and released from the bonds of Paśu.
Śaileśa, Saṅgameśa, Svarlīna, Madhyameśvara,
Hiraṇyagarbha, Īśāna, Goprekṣa, and Vṛṣabhadhvaja.
[He visited] Upaśānta and Śiva, who dwells in the Jyeṣṭha station,
as well as the renowned Śukreśvara, Vyāghreśa, and Jambukeśvara.
"Having seen [this], a mortal is not born again in the ocean of suffering that is saṃsāra.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus, Mahādeva gazed in all directions.
When Maheśvara, the God of gods, had looked on and remained there,
that entire region suddenly became as if set ablaze.
Then there were the perfected Pāśupatas, white with the luster of smeared ashes,
as well as the high-souled Māheśvaras who were firm in their vows.
Many hundreds approached and paid homage to Maheśvara;
having gazed again upon the Lord of Yoga, they [praised] the entirety of the yoga of meditation.
They remained, established in their own selves as if dissolving into the Lord;
while they were thus situated, the God of gods, the Lord of Umā, [spoke].
Bearing that supreme form, he became the Lord Puruṣa,
as if stationed at the end [of time] in order to draw the entire world into himself.
As the Lord of the World remained in that supreme form,
the Daughter of the Mountain King, her hair standing on end with joy, was unable to look upon him again.
Then, having perceived that unseen form, the Supreme Goddess, by means of yoga, assumed a physical form from primordial nature (prakṛti) while abiding within that very nature.
They were able to behold him again, as well as the high-souled Hara;
thereafter, those yogins merged into that Supreme Person.
Having burned away the seeds of worldly existence, they all entered his heart while recollecting the most beautiful seed-syllable of the five-syllabled mantra.
This divine [teaching], which removes all sins, was indeed revealed in the past;
then, abiding in the form of Nīlalohita, he again assumed an auspicious body.
Seeing him, Śailajā, her hair standing on end with joy, bowed at his feet and, offering praise, asked: "O Blessed One, who are these?"
Then the Supreme Lord, the best of gods, spoke to that goddess, the daughter of the mountain king:
"The Blessed One said:
'By resorting to my vow, the most excellent of the twice-born who are possessed of devotion [shall attain their goal]...'"
O beautiful lady, by whatever yogas have been practiced here, they [attain perfection] in a single birth through the power of this sacred field and my grace.
For in this way, I myself grant grace through my own form;
therefore, this is a great field of merit, frequented likewise by Brahmā and the other gods.
And by the foremost of Brahmins learned in the Vedas, by those who have attained perfection, and by ascetics,
[this should be done] every month on the eighth day and every month on the fourteenth day.
O Goddess, [this] is worshipped in both fortnights in Vārāṇasī,
especially during an eclipse of the moon or sun and on the full moon day of Kārttika.
On all auspicious festival days, at the equinoxes and solstices,
all the sacred fords on earth are present in Vārāṇasī, yet the Jāhnavī herself is superior there.
She is the meritorious daughter of your father Himavat, the king of mountains, who flows toward the north and issues from my own crest.
O fair-faced one, listen to those who, having approached from all directions, always resort to her who dwells in a holy place, who is herself meritorious, and who flows toward the auspicious quarter.
Having gathered together at Kurukṣetra along with hundreds of other sacred fords (tīrthas),
as well as Puṣkara, Nimiṣa, Prayāga, and Pṛthūdaka;
Drumakṣetra, Kurukṣetra, and Naimiṣa together with its sacred fords— O Goddess, all these holy sites, as well as the deities and the sages, [are present] everywhere.
The twilights, the seasons, all the rivers and lakes,
the seven oceans, and all the divine tirthas are present here in their entirety.
O lady of virtuous vows, they shall reach the Bhāgīrathī on all festival days after having beheld Avimukteśvara and Triviṣṭapa.
O Goddess of the Suras, having approached Kālabhairava on every festival day, one's sins are indeed washed away in every respect.
Whatever great and meritorious shrines exist upon the earth always enter this supreme field, Avimukta, which destroys great sins, on every sacred festival day.
The liṅga that is at Kedāra and the liṅga that is at Mahālaya; ||| LiP_1,92.134 |||
And [the shrine] known as Madhyameśvara, as well as Pāśupateśvara,
Śaṅkukarṇeśvara, and likewise both Gokarṇas.
Drumacaṇḍeśvara by name, the unsurpassed Bhadreśvara,
Sthāneśvara, likewise Ekāgra, Kāleśvara, and Ajeśvara.
Bhairaveśvara, Īśāna, as well as the one known as Oṃkāra,
Amareśa, Mahākāla, Jyotiṣa, and Bhasmagātraka.
And whatever other meritorious sites exist upon my earth,
numbering sixty-eight, all others are fully established there.
All of them, without exception, enter me at Vārāṇasī on all meritorious festival days; this is declared to be a secret.
Therefore, O auspicious one, by my very sight and because he has bathed in the Gaṅgā, this living being, upon death, attains the divine immortal state.
One immediately attains the equivalent of the fruits of hundreds of thousands of desired sacrifices;
what could be more wonderful than that?
"O Goddess, understand that which is higher than the highest, present in all the principal abodes— whether in heaven, on earth, or even in the mountains"— thus was it spoken by me.
By the word "avi," evil as declared in the Vedas is spoken of by the twice-born;
because it is freed from that and is inhabited by me, it is therefore called Avimukta.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Rudra, the Great Lord of all the worlds, said:
"O Goddess of the gods, look well upon my abode, Avimukta."
Having said, "Śrīśaila," the Blessed Lord, the husband of Umā, together with her,
showed the Blessed One the unsurpassed Śrīparvata.
He dwelt eternally and always with her in Avimukteśvara;
because he is omnipresent and all-pervading, he is the self of all, consisting of both being and non-being.
Having reached Śrīparvata, Hara, the Lord of Gods, Bhava,
the Master of all beings, showed the sacred sites to the Goddess.
And the supreme, divine Kuṇḍīprabha; Vaiśravaṇeśvara;
the divine Āśāliṅga, the Lord of Gods; and that which is Bileśvara.
And there is Rāmeśvara, the supreme [liṅga] which was installed by Viṣṇu;
and on the side of the southern gate is the Lord Kuṇḍaleśvara.
Near the eastern gate stands the supreme Tripurāntaka,
who has grown together with the mountain and is saluted by the God of gods.
It is called Madhyameśvara, renowned throughout the three worlds;
and there is Amareśvara, the granter of boons, formerly established by the gods.
Gocarmeśvara, Īśāna, as well as the wonderful Indreśvara,
and the vast Karmeśvara, which was created by Brahmā for the sake of his task.
And Śrīmatsiddhavaṭa is my eternal abode in the Imperishable; it is a divine place fashioned by the Unborn One, auspicious and manifest as the very cave of Aja.
Right there are my two divine sandals and the Bileśvara [liṅga];
and right there, in the center of Śṛṅgāṭa mountain, is the place shaped like a water-chestnut (śṛṅgāṭaka).
Śṛṅgāṭakeśvara was established by the illustrious Goddess, as was Mallikārjuna; this is my auspicious abode.
And Rajeśvara, well-established by Rajas in the Paryāya;
Gajeśvara in Vaiśākha; and the imperishable Kapoteśvara.
O Goddess, behold today Koṭīśvara, the great sacred ford, which was formerly frequented by hosts of ten million Rudras; it is more auspicious than all others.
And the auspicious mountain known as Dvidevakula was established by Brahmā on the south,
while that which is made of stone was established by Viṣṇu on the north.
And behold the great-liṅga Mahāpramāṇa, which was formerly established by me on the western mountain, as well as Brahmeśvara and Aḷeśvara.
"O Brahmin, it was adorned by you in the past together with the sages";
having said this, he remained in that house, and thus it is remembered as "Alaṅgṛha" (the Adorned House).
Even there, O knower of sacred sites, behold my *vyomaliṅga* at that very site;
for this Kadambeshvara was indeed established by Skanda himself.
And Gomaṇḍaleśvara was well-established by Nanda and others;
all these were installed by the gods, beginning with Śakra, O fair-faced one.
"O Goddess, behold these places of mine on the shores of the illustrious Devahrada, as well as in Hārapura, where your necklace was cast down."
O lady of excellent vows, for the welfare of the worlds, you have fashioned this necklace and earring upon his body in Śivarudrapura.
There, O Brahmā, the Lord of the Mountain (Tvacaleśvara), who had been installed by my father Suśaila, was adorned by me in the presence of the sages.
O Goddess, Caṇḍikeśvaraka is there, and Caṇḍikeśa is your son;
this excellent Ambikātīrtha is a place created by Caṇḍikā.
And Rucikeśvaraka—this is the auspicious Kapilā Dhārā;
O Goddess, in these places and in various sacred bathing sites (tīrthas), [one should perform rites].
One should always worship me with devotion, for one rejoices together with me;
a Brahmin whose sins have been burnt away should cast off his body at Śrīśaila.
One is liberated from this, there is no doubt, just as there is auspiciousness in Avimukta;
and he who performs the great ablution with ghee according to the prescribed rite [attains the same].
O you of virtuous vows, he attains union with me in these places;
bathing is known to consist of a hundred palas, while anointing consists of twenty-five.
A great ablution is proclaimed to require two thousand palas;
having bathed my liṅga with cow-derived ghee alone, [one should proceed].
Having purified him with all ritual substances, he sprinkles him with waters;
thus, by this bathing, he attains the merit of a hundred sacrifices and likewise that of a million.

Through worship, [the merit] is a hundred thousandfold; through song and instrumental music, it is infinite. But when one is intent upon the Great Bath (mahāsnāna), the bath itself is remembered as being eightfold [in merit].
With devotion, one should perform an anointing with pure water alone, or with fragrant water;
indeed, that entire anointing should be done with twenty-five palas [of the substance].
One should offer the śamī flower according to the prescribed rite, as well as bilva leaves, lotuses, and other flowers; one must never abandon the bilva leaf.
One should offer four *droṇas* to Mahādeva, or even eight;
the food offering (*naivedya*) should consist of ten *droṇas*, or even eight.
The same merit as that of a hundred *droṇas* is ordained even for a single *āḍhaka* given by a Brahmin who lacks wealth; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
With kettledrums, clay drums, murajas, timiras, paṭahas, and other such instruments, as well as with various other musical instruments and diverse sounds; LiP_1,92.178 //
He who causes the vigil to be performed and makes requests in the proper sequence,
together with his servants, sons, wives, as well as his kinsmen and relatives, [attains the fruit].
Having performed a circumambulation together with it, one should pray to the supreme liṅga:
"O Lord of the Gods, [whatever has been done] deficient in materials, deficient in ritual action, or deficient in faith..."
"O Śaṅkara, you ought to forgive whether [the offense] was committed or not committed";
having spoken thus, one should quickly recite the Rudra-mantra and likewise for peace.
Having thus recited this great seed-syllable as well as that of the five syllables,
one obtains that very fruit which is found at all sacred fords and in all sacrifices.
One obtains that same fruit as one who dies in Vārāṇasī;
likewise, one attains union with me—of this there is no doubt.
This task must be performed by my devotees according to the prescribed rites for the sake of my pleasure;
those who do not perform it are not true devotees—of this there is no doubt.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words, the goddess went to the city of Vārāṇasī and [worshipped] the Avimukteśvara Liṅga with milk and ghee.
He worshipped Rudra, the lord of gods and leader of the worlds,
through ascetic penance at Avimukta, [the abode] of the high-souled Mandara.
The Lord indeed prepared a field on Mount Mandara, which has beautiful caves;
there, he [confronted] Andhaka, the great Daitya and son of Hiraṇyākṣa.
Having favored him, he effortlessly caused him to attain the status of a Gaṇa.
Thus, I have related to you with reverence this entire essence of the narrative.
Whoever should read or even hear this supreme majesty of the sacred field (kṣetra-māhātmya),
shall immediately obtain all the merit that exists in all sacred fields.
Or, if he causes all the twice-born— those who have performed their purifications and have conquered their senses— to hear it,
that man obtains the fruit of every sacrifice.
Thus ends the ninety-second chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of Vārāṇasī and Śrīśaila," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
The sages said:
How did the lord of the Daityas named Andhaka, who was subdued on Mount Mandara with its beautiful caves, obtain the status of a Gaṇapati from Maheśvara?
"You ought to tell us exactly what happened and what was heard.
Sūta said:
"The favor shown to the Andhakas, as well as the drying up [of the ocean] on Mount Mandara."
And I shall briefly proclaim the entirety of the attainment of boons:
the son of Hiraṇyākṣa, who resembled Hiraṇyanayana.
Formerly, there was one known as Andhaka, who had acquired prowess through ascetic penance and had obtained invincibility directly from the grace of Brahmā himself.
Having formerly enjoyed the entire three worlds and conquered the city of Indra,
he terrified Vāsava with ease and without effort.
Oppressed, struck, bound, and cast down by him, those gods,
led by Nārāyaṇa, entered Mount Mandara in fear.
Having thus oppressed the gods, the great asura Andhaka reached Mount Mandara by chance, a mountain with beautiful caves.
Then all those lords of the gods, together with the Sādhyas, spoke thus to Maheśa, the lord of the gods:
"We have been swiftly shattered by the weapons of the king of the Daityas; our bodies are broken and our strength is diminished."
Having heard this entire, incomparable account of the Daitya’s arrival,
the Blessed One set out toward Andhaka accompanied by the lords of the Gaṇas.

Thereupon, all the lords of the gods, headed by Indra, Padmodbhava, and Viṣṇu, as well as the foremost of the Brahmins, spoke the word "Victory! to the Blessed One from all sides with their hands joined in reverence upon their crowns. Then, [he was surrounded] by hundreds of millions upon millions of all the Asuras.
Having reduced him to ashes, Mahādeva then pierced Andhaka.
Having seen Andhaka, whose garment of sin had been burnt away and who was impaled upon the trident by the Trident-bearer, the Grandfather (Brahmā) prostrated himself and uttered a cry of praise.
Upon hearing that sound, the gods bowed down to the God and rejoiced;
all the sages danced, and the leaders of the Gaṇas were filled with delight.
Then the gods released showers of flowers over Śambhu;
the entire three worlds rejoiced with joy and let out a great roar.
Burned by fire and impaled on a stake like the blind demon Andhaka, he,
assuming a state of sattva, reflected thus in his mind.
"Because Śiva indeed burnt me even in another birth,
Maheśvara himself was propitiated by me in the past."
Therefore, this has been obtained by me; otherwise it would not be possible:
whoever should remember Rudra in their mind even once at the end of life.
He attains union with Śiva; how much more so one who remembers [him] repeatedly!
So too do Brahmā, the Lord Viṣṇu, and all the gods together with Indra.
Having found refuge, they remain there; one should likewise go for refuge to Him alone.
Having reflected thus, Andhaka, with a satisfied soul, [sought refuge] in that slayer of Andhaka.
Out of the weight of their merit, they praised Śiva, the Lord Īśāna, together with his retinue;
thus entreated by him, the Blessed Hara, the remover of supreme suffering, [responded].
Beholding the son of Hiraṇyanetra impaled on the tip of the trident, Nīlalohita, the lord of the gods, spoke to the Dānava out of compassion.
"I am pleased, my child; may it be well with you. What desire shall I fulfill for you?
Choose boons, O Lord of Daityas, for I am the granter of boons to you, O Andhaka."
Having then heard those words of Śambhu, the son of Hiraṇyanayana spoke this to Maheśvara with a voice faltering with joy.
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Śaṅkara, remover of the suffering of devotees!
O Lord, may you be gracious toward my devotion to you, if a boon is to be granted to me.
Having heard the words of the high-souled Andhaka, Bhava,
of great splendor, granted to the lord of the Daityas that faith which is so difficult to attain.
And having deposed him, he bestowed the status of a Gaṇapati upon the Daitya;
Indra and the other lords of the gods bowed down to him as he was established in the rank of a Gaṇapati.
Thus ends the ninety-third chapter, titled "The Andhaka-Gāṇapatya Episode," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
The sages said:
How was his father, the most terrible Daitya Hiraṇyākṣa, slain by Viṣṇu? And how did Viṣṇu assume the form of a boar?
O Sūta, you ought to explain here in detail how that horn of Maheśa came to serve as his ornament; you should tell us all of this specifically.
Sūta said: Hiraṇyākṣa was known as the brother of Hiraṇyakaśipu;
in ancient times, he was the father of the lord of the Asuras, Andhaka, and was like the Destroyer at the end of time.
Then, having conquered the gods and bound this earth, the lord of the Daityas took her to the subterranean realm (rasātala) and made her, who possessed the luster of a blue lotus, his captive.
Then the gods, including Brahmā, their facial splendor withered,
were indeed oppressed, struck, and bound by that Hiraṇyākṣa.
The powerful and cruel Daitya chief, who was extremely wicked-minded,
bowed his head to Viṣṇu, the crusher of tens of millions of Daityas.
They all made their request regarding the binding of the Earth by Hari;
having heard this, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, Hari, [responded] concerning the binding of the Earth.
Having become the Sacrificial Boar, just as [described] in the *Liṅgodbhava*,
he [fought] with the Daityas and the mighty Daitya-lord Hiraṇyākṣa.
Having struck him with the tip of the point of his tusk, the Lord, the destroyer of the Daityas, shone forth;
and as at the beginning of the kalpas, he entered the subterranean realm (rasātala) as before.
Having brought the goddess Vasudhā outside and placed her upon his lap,
the Grandfather, the god of gods, then offered praise to the Lord of Gods.
Accompanied by Śakra and the other gods, he spoke with a voice faltering with joy:
"Homage to the eternal Boar, the tusked one, the wielder of the staff!"
Salutations to Nārāyaṇa, the All-pervading, the Brahman, the Supreme Self;
to Him who is Himself the creator, the sustainer, and the destroyer of the enemies of the gods,
as well as the creator and leader of the lords of the gods, and the teacher of everything.
You are the eight-formed one; you are the one of infinite forms; you are the primordial god, known by infinite wisdom.
All this has been created by you; be gracious, O Lord of gods, Lord of the world, Varāha, Viṣṇu!
Likewise, O Viṣṇu, granter of desires, by a portion equal to half of a single part of the tip of the point of one of Your tusks,
the chief Daityas were struck down in an instant along with their sons and servants by the very edge of Your tusk.
O God, Lord of the Earth, you who possess the form of a mountain and hold the tip of your tusk aloft, the earth was lifted up by you;
O moon-faced one, you are served by all the mountains, by all people, by the oceans, and by the gods and asuras.
O Lord of Gods, O All-pervading One, victory over the lords of the asuras was achieved by the gods through you alone;
oh, the boon has been granted! Be gracious, O Goddess of Speech, to the one born from the lotus.
In your hair are all the lords of the immortals; in your two eyes are the moon and the sun;
in your two feet is the earth situated in the netherworld (rasātala); and on your back are all the stars and other celestial bodies.
O Blessed One, for the welfare of the worlds, the earth was then brought by you from the depths of the netherworld.
And that which was lifted up by a woman, O Blessed One, is indeed entirely held by you alone, O Teacher of the World.
Thus Vākpati, the Prajāpati, having prostrated before Viṣṇu with various modes of worship along with the gods,
obtained diverse boons from the mouth of Hari himself, who bears the body of the lotus-navelled one.
Then, O gods and lords of sages, having placed that earth which had been lifted up by him upon their heads, they offered salutations in the presence of the Wielder of the Discus.
O bestower of boons, you were uplifted by this very Varāha—
by Viṣṇu, who is Kṛṣṇa, whose actions are effortless, and who possesses a hundred cubits.
O Earth, you are the source of great enjoyment; O imperishable one, you are the earth and the cow.
For you are the sustainer of the worlds; O Mṛttikā, take away my sin!
O giver of boons, O lotus-eyed one, through your grace we live on, our sins destroyed by you in thought, deed, and word.
O twice-born ones, having been addressed thus by the gods, the goddess Earth then spoke while the earth was being pierced by the tusk of the Boar: "The clay [from this spot]... (LiP 1.94.24).
He who bears this mantra upon his head is liberated from sin;
he becomes long-lived, powerful, fortunate, and endowed with sons and grandsons.
Having gradually ascended from earth to heaven at the conclusion of his karma, he rejoices with the gods;
then, when the god has departed, he leaves the Varāha and the ocean of milk.
The earth, burdened by the weight of the tusks of that wise god of gods, shook again as he assumed his sinless boar-form.
Beholding Bhava by chance, the Lord of the World departed;
seeing her, he seized her tusk for the sake of his own ornament.
And Mahādeva held [the weapon] at the tip of his beard upon his great chest;
and the gods, together with Indra, praised the majesty of the God of Gods.
Thus the earth was established by the God of gods through his divine play;
and even during the dissolution of all beings, it remains as the very body of Viṣṇu.
How can there be liberation for the brahmins? Therefore, Maheśvara is the one with fangs.
Thus ends the ninety-fourth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Varāha," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
The sages said:
It has been heard that in the past, Hiraṇyākṣa’s elder brother was slain by Nṛsiṃha;
tell me how Hiraṇyakaśipu was destroyed by him.
Sūta said:
The son of Hiraṇyakaśipu was renowned as Prahlāda.
He was a knower of dharma, perfected in truth, an ascetic, and highly wise.
From birth onwards, he worshipped the imperishable Lord of Gods,
Viṣṇu— the omniscient, omnipresent one, who is the source of the existence of all the gods.
With devotion, [one should worship] that primordial Person, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman,
the Lord of Brahmā, and the cause of creation, preservation, and destruction.
He too, seeing his son in such a state of meditative absorption, repeatedly uttered, "Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa! and "O Govinda! (LiP 1.95.5).
As he was praising him, the enemy of the gods, evil-minded as if burning with rage, said:
"O wicked-minded one, you do not know me, the lord of all the Daityas and the immortals."
"O hero Prahlāda, who is this wicked son who causes distress to the twice-born and the gods? Is he Viṣṇu, or the lotus-born Brahmā, or Śakra, or Varuṇa?"
Vāyu, Soma, as well as Īśāna and Pāvaka are equal to me;
therefore, always worship me alone with devotion, and [worship] Nārāyaṇa only slightly.
"O Prahlāda, listen if you still have this desire for life;
having heard those words of Hiraṇyakaśipu, the wise one [remained silent]."
Prahlāda worshipped him, saying "Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa," and he caused all the sons of the Daityas to say, "Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa."
And he taught her that most beautiful knowledge of Brahman,
which he himself saw to be difficult to master even for Śakra and the other gods.
Hiraṇya said to the Dānavas regarding his command, which had been transgressed by his son:
"You ought to kill this wicked son, who deserves to be slain by various means."
Having been addressed thus by that wicked-souled Daitya, they then struck Prahrāda, the imperishable servant of the God of gods.
O best of the twice-born, at that time the image fashioned by the gods against the son of the Daitya king became fruitless before the splendor of the Lord who reclines upon the ocean of milk.
Then, the Lord appeared right there in the form of a man-lion (Nṛsiṃha) to slay Hiraṇyakaśipu, whose pride had been shattered.
And seeing his father, that lowest of Dānavas, he struck him;
at that very moment, he pierced him with hundreds of sharp claws.
Then, having slain that Daitya along with his kinsmen,
the destroyer of sins tormented the lord of the Daityas like another fire at the end of an eon.
O Brahmins of firm vows, the world was terrified by the terrible roars of that Nṛsiṃha, and everything trembled as far as the realm of Brahmā.

Seeing Nṛsiṃha at that moment, the gods, asuras, great serpents, siddhas, and sādhyas—headed by Hari and Viriñci—regained their courage and strength; they departed, leaving him while remaining intent on protecting the asuras from the very ends of the quarters.
Then, after they had departed, this god Nṛsiṃha, possessing a thousand forms, with all feet and all arms,
with a thousand eyes and eyes like the moon, the sun, and fire— the master of illusion— remained there, pervading everything.
The best of the gods, together with Brahmā, the Sādhyas, Yama, and the hosts of Maruts, praised him as they stood upon the Lokācala mountain.
You are the Brahman higher than the highest, the reality beyond all realities;
you are the supreme light among lights, the Supreme Self who pervades the universe.
He consists of the auspicious Śabdabrahman, which is gross, subtle, and most subtle;
he transcends speech, is without support, free from dualities, and undisturbed.
You are the enjoyer of sacrifice, the embodiment of sacrifice, the Lord who bestows the fruits upon those who perform sacrifices;
you exist in the world having assumed the forms of the Fish and the Tortoise.
Having assumed that form of Vārāhī as well as that of Siṃhī,
he remained here for the protection of the gods, having slain the lord of the sons of Diti.
Thus you have descended through sport under the pretext of a Brahmin’s curse;
for nothing among all things moving and stationary has been seen that is other than you.
You are Viṣṇu, you are Rudra, and you alone are the Grandfather (Brahmā);
you are the beginning, you are the end, and you alone are we, O All-pervading Lord.
O Lord, you alone are the entire universe; what is the use of this idle talk? O Master, it exists in many forms through māyā, yet its essence is non-dual.
O God of gods, Lord of beasts, how shall we praise you?
For even when praised by various means of eulogy and manifold states of being, the Lord remains as he is.
O twice-born ones, he who recites the hymn to Nṛsiṃha with devotion and reflects upon its meaning does not find peace, honoring his own spiritual lineage.
Or if he causes all the twice-born to hear it, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
In that interval, the gods, including Indra and Brahmā, took refuge in the Lord Śiva.
Having reached him and informed him of everything regarding those in the form of deer,
Brahmā and the others then quickly offered praise to the Supreme Lord.
For their own protection, they went for refuge to the Supreme Cause,
Mahādeva, who was sporting with Umā while seated upon Mount Mandara.
Attended by hosts of Gaṇas and Gandharvas, by Siddhas and throngs of Apsarases,
and together with the deities, Brahmā— extremely terrified and with a faltering voice—
prostrated himself like a staff upon the ground and praised the Supreme Lord.
Brahmā said:
Salutations to you, the Death of Death; salutations to you, O Rudra, to your wrath.
Salutations to Śiva, to Rudra, to Śaṅkara, and to you, the Auspicious One.
You are fierce toward all beings, you are their restrainer, and you are auspicious for us. Homage to Śiva, to Śarva, to Śaṅkara, the remover of suffering!
Salutation to Viṣṇu, the creator of all, the universal Brahman;
salutation to you, the Ender; salutation to the Lord of Umā.
Salutations to the golden-armed one, the manifest lord of gold;
repeated salutations to Śarva, who possesses all forms, the Supreme Person.

Salutations to you, the cause of the Great Principle (mahat), who are devoid of the manifestation of existence and non-existence; salutations to you, the eternal one, whose form is the universe, and who are ever being born.
Homage again and again to him who is born in many ways throughout the world and has become manifold;
to Rudra, to Nīlarudra, to Kadrudra, and to Pracetas.
Salutation to Kāla, to him whose form is Time, salutation to the one who seizes the limbs of Time;
salutation to you, the most bountiful god, the blue-throated one.
Homage to you, the Great One, the eternal slayer of the enemies of the gods;
homage again and again to Tāra, Sutāra, and Tāraṇa.
Salutations to the golden-haired god, to Śambhu, the Supreme Self;
salutations to you, the source of well-being for the gods, the source of well-being for all beings.

Salutations to you, the source of bliss; salutations to the one who is the wrath of Haimavatī; salutations to you in the form of Rudra; salutations to you, the one with matted hair; salutations to you, the blue-throated one.
Salutations again and again to Hiraṇya, to Maheśa, and to Śrīkaṇṭha; salutations to him whose body is smeared with ashes, and to Daṇḍamuṇḍīśvara.
Homage to the short one, to the long one, and repeated homage to the dwarf;
homage to the fierce one with the trident, and repeated homage to the formidable one.
Salutations to you, who are Bhīma, of terrifying form, and devoted to fearsome deeds;
salutations to you who strike down those nearby and those far away.
Salutations to you, the wielder of the bow, the trident, the mace, and the plough; salutations always to the bearer of the discus and armor, the destroyer of the deeds of the Daityas.
Salutation to you, Sadya, who possesses the form of Sadya, and to you, Sadyojāta;
salutation to you, Vāma, who possesses the form of Vāma, and to you, Vāmanetra.
Salutation to you of non-terrible form, the formidable one with a formidable body;
salutation indeed to the one in human form, the sole Supreme Person (Tatpuruṣa). Salutation to the Lord, the Parameṣṭhin, who bestows the goals of human existence.
Salutations to you, O Īśāna; salutations again and again to the Lord (Īśvara).
Salutations to you, Brahmā, who possesses the form of Brahman, the manifest Śiva;
salutations to Viṣṇu, the creator of the universe, who has assumed the form of Nṛsiṃha.
Having slain Hiraṇyakaśipu himself with his sharp claws,
the Lord, for the sake of the welfare of the worlds, [did so] together with many lords of the Daityas.
Assuming the form of a lioness, she oppresses the entire world;
O Lord of Gods, perform here whatever task must be done in this matter.
You are fierce toward all the wicked, yet you are the restrainer and our auspicious protector; with a form such as that of the Kālakūṭa poison, protect us who have come to you for refuge.
But O Lord of All, this circular form of Śukra is indeed merely our play;
through Your opening and closing of the eyes, there are our dissolution and emergence.
"O Brahman, you shall open [your eyes] for him; there is no destruction for you, O Śiva.
O Lord, we are tormented by Hari of immeasurable splendor."

Having been thus informed, the God, smiling, spoke to those deities.
And the Lord granted them freedom from fear, saying, "I shall slay him.
Then Śakra, together with the gods, prostrated themselves and departed as they had come.
The blessed Brahmā and the other supreme gods departed;
then Mahādeva arose and assumed the form of a Śarabha.
Then the śarabha,
honored by the gods, took away the life-breaths of that proud lion, the eater of deer, at the very end.
Then, having become a man from the lion, he proceeded in due order;
thus praised by the gods, he then departed in due order.
Whoever should recite or even hear this supreme hymn to Śarva,
having reached the world of Rudra, rejoices together with Rudra.
Thus ends the ninety-fifth chapter, titled "The Nārasiṃha," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
The sages said:
How did the god Mahādeva, the agent of the universal dissolution,
assume that most terrible and deformed form known as Śarabha?
"What and what fortitude was exercised by him? Tell us everything without omission.
Sūta said:
"Thus entreated by the gods, the abode of compassion formed a resolution."
Then, for the purpose of destroying that splendor known as Nṛsiṃha, the Supreme Lord Rudra called to mind the exceedingly powerful Vīrabhadra.
In former times, the form of Bhairava himself, the cause of the great dissolution, suddenly appeared laughing before the Gaṇas. (LiP 1.96.4)
He was surrounded by tens of millions of the most excellent hosts, who were leaping here and there with loud laughter and appearing in the extremely fierce forms of man-lions.
Surrounded by as many heroic and highly steadfast beings, beginning with Brahmā, who were filled with joy, dancing and playing like balls.
Surrounded by others never seen before, he who is honored by heroes blazed with the flames of the fire at the end of an aeon, his three eyes gleaming.
Wielding a weapon, adorned with a mass of matted locks graced by the blazing crescent moon,
he possesses two sharp sprouts of fangs shaped like a pair of crescent moons.
Possessing creeper-like eyebrows resembling fragments of Indra’s bow,
he deafened the quarters of the sky with his exceedingly fierce *huṃ* sounds.
Terrible with a beard like a dark cloud or collyrium,
he was extraordinary as he repeatedly brandished his three-pointed trident with two unbroken blades.
The blessed Vīrabhadra, manifested through the power of the Hero (Vīraśakti), himself made this inquiry: "What is the cause for remembering [this] here?"
"Command me, O Lord of the World; let your grace be bestowed upon me.
Thus [requested], the Blessed One said: (Śiva orders the destruction of Nṛsiṃha).
O Bhairava, a danger has arisen at an improper time, even for the gods.
That fire of Nṛsiṃha is ablaze; pacify this one who is difficult to approach.
By first conciliating and awakening him, why would he not be appeased?
Then, manifest that state which is supreme to me, the Bhairava;
having withdrawn the subtle with the subtle and the gross with your gross splendor.
"Bring the mouth and the hide, Vīrabhadra, by my command!
Thus instructed, the leader of the Gaṇas remained there with a tranquil form.
He went with great speed to where the man-lion was;
then Vīrabhadra, the destroyer, awakened Hari.
The Lord spoke these words, like a father to his own biological son.
Śrī Vīrabhadra said:
O Blessed One, O Mādhava, you have descended for the sake of the happiness of the world.
And you are joined with the highest Supreme Lord for the purpose of preservation;
the wheel of living beings was protected by the Blessed One in the form of a fish.
In ancient times, while wandering upon the single ocean, you supported [the earth] in the form of a tortoise after binding it with your very tail;
and in the form of a boar, the earth was uplifted by you.
In this form as Hari, Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain;
by you, moreover, as Vāmana, Bali was bound through your strides.
You alone are the power, the lord, and the imperishable one of all beings;
for whenever any suffering whatsoever arises in the world, [you manifest].
At each such time, you, having descended, will make [the world] free from affliction;
O Hari, devoted to Śiva, there is no one superior to you, nor even anyone equal to you.
O auspicious Keśava, by you the Dharmas and the Vedas have been established on the path of righteousness; he for whose sake this incarnation occurred has also been slain.
O Blessed One, O Soul of the Universe, withdraw this exceedingly terrible form of yours as Narasiṃha right here in my presence.
Sūta said:
Having been addressed thus by Vīrabhadra with peaceful words,
Hari then kindled an even more intensely terrible wrath.
The illustrious Nṛsiṃha said:
"Go back to where you have come from; do not speak what is beneficial [to me].
Now I shall destroy this entire world, both moving and unmoving."
For the destroyer, there is no destruction either by himself or by another;
this has been taught by me everywhere, and no teacher whatsoever exists [other than me].
By my grace, everything proceeds according to its boundaries;
for I am the one who sets all powers in motion and withdraws them.
Whatever being possesses majesty, or is endowed with splendor or power, know that, O Lord of the Gaṇas, to be a manifestation of my own brilliance.
Those who know the supreme reality of the deities know me alone as the highest; the gods, such as Brahmā, Śakra, and others, are my own portions, endowed with power.
In ancient times, the four-faced Brahmā was born from the lotus at the navel of Manu;
from his forehead was born the Lord whose banner is the bull.
Presided over by *rajas*, the creator Rudra is said to be characterized by *tamas*;
I am the controller of all, and there is no deity higher than me.
He is superior to all, independent, the creator and destroyer, and the Lord of all;
who, moreover, would wish to hear further of this supreme splendor beyond me?
Therefore, having come to me for refuge, go forth free from all feverish distress;
know this to be my supreme state, for I am the Great Lord of all beings.
"I am Time, the cause of the destruction of Time; I have set out to withdraw the worlds.
Know me, O Vīrabhadra, to be the death of Death itself; these gods live by my grace."
Sūta said:
Having heard this with its display of pride, Hari, of immeasurable prowess,
laughed and spoke with contempt, his lips quivering.
Śrī Vīrabhadra said:
Do you not know the Lord of the Universe, the wielder of the Pināka bow, who is the destroyer?
This false speech and this dispute will result only in your own destruction.
What other incarnations of yours remain at present?
By whomsoever they may be performed, the narrative will reach its conclusion.
"Behold this fault; you have come to such a state as this.
By him, who is skilled in destruction, you shall be utterly annihilated in an instant."
You are Prakṛti, and Rudra is the Puruṣa; within you, virility is concentrated.
From the lotus of your navel was born the five-faced Grandfather (Brahmā).
For the purpose of creation, he who was established in fierce austerity first meditated upon Śaṅkara, the blue-and-red one, upon his forehead.
That [fire] emerged from the forehead of Śambhu for the sake of creation; it is not a fault.
I am a portion of the God of gods, who has assumed the form of Mahābhairava.
"I have been appointed by Vinaya and Bala for your destruction;
thus, O Rākṣasa, you shall be torn asunder while joined with a portion of Śakti."
"Arrogant with pride, you roar tirelessly;
for any assistance rendered to the wicked serves only to bring them harm."
O Siṃha, if you consider Maheśāna to be your own rebirth,
you are neither the creator nor the destroyer, for you are certainly not independent in any respect.
Impelled by the power of the wielder of the Pināka bow like a potter’s wheel,
even now the skull of you who have taken the form of a tortoise remains placed upon you.
O innocent one, why do you not realize that you are in the midst of Hara’s garland of necklaces? Have you forgotten how you were once tormented by the uprooting of his fangs?
Today, you who have assumed the form of a boar have been burnt with cries of lamentation by the enemy of Tāraka, under the pretext of being Viṣvaksena, upon the tip of his trident.
At Dakṣa’s sacrifice, the head of you who were in the form of the sacrifice was severed by me;
even today, the fifth head of your son Brahmā remains [unsevered].
That very portion of his power, which was the aim [of your attack], has been cut off;
you, along with the hosts of Maruts, have been defeated by Dadhīca in battle.
While you were scratching your head, how was it that you forgot that discus which is dear to you, O Cakrapāṇi, as you stride with valor?
From where did you come, and by whom was it done? You have even forgotten that;
all those worlds were seized by me, and you were cast into the ocean.
Overpowered by sleep, you lie there; how can you be one of sattva?
From the primordial pillar down to you, everything is the manifestation of Rudra’s power.
You are powerful on all sides, and you are indeed the fire; yet, both of you are deluded, for neither of you is capable of beholding the majesty of that [supreme] splendor.
For those who perceive that supreme abode of Viṣṇu as something gross—the heaven and earth, Indra, Agni, Yama, and Varuṇa—[they do not see it]. (LiP 1.96.55)
Having been born within the belly of darkness from the moon, you are the Supreme Lord;
you are Time, Mahākāla, the Great Lord who is the Death of Death.
Therefore, by means of your fierce power, you shall become the death of death;
you shall be the firm-bowed one, the destroyer, the hero, the hero surpassing all, the Lord.
Bearing a golden deer and birds in his hand, Bhīma is the fever [of destruction];
you are not the teacher of the entire world, nor indeed are you the four-faced Brahmā.
Having thus observed all this, withdraw yourself by means of the self;
otherwise, now [you will fall] before Krodha, who possesses the form of Mahābhairava.
"Death shall fall upon you like a thunderbolt from a pillar.
Sūta said:
Having been addressed thus by Vīrabhadra, Nṛsiṃha was overwhelmed with rage.
He roared with great force and proceeded to seize him;
in the meantime, there arose a most terrible sound that caused fear to his enemies.
That form of Vīrabhadra, which pervades the sky, is invincible, and arises from the splendor of Śiva,
was seen at that very moment.
That Maheśvara is not made of gold, nor is he lunar, nor born of fire; he is not like lightning or the moon—he is beyond all comparison.
Then all energies were absorbed into that Śārṅkara;
from him, the one of great splendor became manifest, and from that manifestation he was born.
Marked with the common signs of Rudra and possessing a transformed form,
the Supreme Lord is then clearly manifest in the aspect of withdrawal.
While all the gods were looking on amidst auspicious sounds such as shouts of victory,
he appeared with a thousand arms, matted hair, and the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
O twice-born ones, he had the body of a deer, with wings and a beak,
possessing exceedingly sharp great tusks and claws as weapons like thunderbolts.
Kāla, the mighty-armed, four-footed one born from fire,
possesses a deep and terrifying roar like the clouds raised at the end of a Yuga.
With his three eyes rolling due to the fire of his provoked wrath,
with prominent fangs and a quivering lower lip, Hara was accompanied by the sound "huṃ."
At the mere sight of him, Hari’s strength and prowess were destroyed;
bearing the luster of the thousand-rayed sun, it became like the flickering glow of a firefly beneath it. (LiP 1.96.70)
Then, having whirled about, he tore at his navel and feet with his two wings;
he bound his feet with his tail and his circle of arms with his two forelimbs.
Tearing at his chest with his two arms, Hara seized Hari;
thereupon, he ascended into the sky together with the gods and the great seers.
Suddenly, out of fear, like a bird toward a serpent, he repeatedly lifted up Viṣṇu,
seized him, and threw him down again and again.
Flying up again and again, the Blessed One seized Hari as he was carrying off the bull— the Lord of the Universe, that Supreme Sovereign— while Hari was bewildered by his wing-injury.
All the gods followed him and praised him with words of homage;
being led away against his will, he was dejected in countenance and joined his palms in reverence.
Hari praised that Supreme Lord with graceful words. Śrī Nṛsiṃha said:
Homage to Rudra, to Śarva, to the Great Devourer, and to Viṣṇu.
Salutation to the fierce one, to the terrifying one; salutation to wrath, to fury;
salutation to you who are Bhava, Śarva, Śaṅkara, and Śiva.
To Kālakāla, to Kāla, to Mahākāla, to Mṛtyu;
to Vīra, to Vīrabhadra, to Kṣayadvīra, to the wielder of the trident.
Salutation to Mahādeva, the great lord of animals;
salutation to the one, the blue-throated one, the illustrious-throated one, the wielder of the Pināka bow.
Homage to the infinite and subtle one; homage to you, the wrath of Death! Homage to you, the supreme lord, higher than the highest.
Salutations to you, the one higher than the highest, the universal one; salutations to you whose form is the universe.
Salutations to the consort of Viṣṇu, to the field of Viṣṇu, and to the Sun.
To the fisherman, to the hunter, to the great archer, to the eternal one;
to Bhairava, the refuge, who possesses the form of Mahābhairava.
Homage to the destroyer of Nṛsiṃha, the enemy of Kāma, Kāla, and Pura;
the destroyer of the great flood of bonds, the bringer of an end to Viṣṇu’s Māyā.
To the three-eyed one, to the one whose name consists of three syllables, to Śipiviṣṭa, to the bountiful giver,
to the conqueror of death, to Śarva, to the omniscient one, and to the consumer of sacrifices.
Salutations to you, the lord of sacrifice, the most excellent one, who takes the form of fire;
salutations to the great sense of smell, to the tongue, and to the one who sets in motion the prāṇa and apāna breaths.
To the one who possesses the three qualities, to the wielder of the trident, to the one who has transcended the qualities, to the yogin,
to the cycle of worldly existence, to the flowing current, and to the setter-in-motion of the great machine.
Salutations to the one who is the moon, fire, and sun; to the cause of the manifold variety of liberation;
to the bestower of boons, the incarnation, the cause of all causes.
To Kapālin, to Karāla, to the Lord, to the one of holy fame,
to Amogha, to Agninetra, to Lakulīśa, and to Śambhu.
Salutation to the best of physicians, to the shaven-headed one, to the bearer of the staff, to the one whose form is yoga,
to the god borne by clouds, to the lord of Pārvatī.
Salutation to the unmanifest, to the sorrowless, to the steadfast one who possesses a firm bow, to Sthāṇu, to the one clothed in animal skins, and to the cause of the five objects of sense.
Homage to the granter of boons, the one-footed one, whose crown is adorned with the crescent moon;
homage to you, the king of sacrifices; homage to the lord of birds.
Salutations to you, the Lord of Yogins, the eternal, the true, the supreme abode;
salutations to you, the soul of all, salutations to you, the Lord of all.
May there be salutation after salutation to you one, two, three, four, and five times;
and may there be salutation after salutation to you ten times and even a thousand times.

Having performed homage an immeasurable number of times, I offer salutation, salutation again and again; salutation, salutation, salutation repeatedly, and yet again and again, salutation, salutation.
Sūta said:
Having thus praised him with these one hundred and eight names consisting of nectar,
Nṛsiṃha again made a request to Śarabheśvara.
Whenever my ignorance, corrupted by excessive egoism, arises,
it must be removed by you alone, O Supreme Lord.
Addressing Śaṅkara in this manner, Narasiṃha was filled with joy;
"Surely you, O Viṣṇu, were powerless and have been defeated to the end of your life! (LiP 1.96.97).
Having reduced the entire body to nothing more than the remnants of its mouth,
Vīrabhadra then instantly shattered that limb into pieces as small as oyster shells.
The gods said:
"O Vīrabhadra, by your glance all of us, beginning with Brahmā,
have been restored to life, just as trees are revived by the rain-cloud."
Out of fear of whom fire burns and the sun itself rises,
and the wind blows— you are that Death who runs as the fifth.
O Blessed One, those who discourse on Brahman call You alone Bhava— the unmanifest, supreme ether, beyond all parts (kalās), and the eternally auspicious (Sadāśiva).
"Who among us is the supreme lord over the sensations of the elements?
You do not know the supreme abode in the description of form and beauty."
O Lord of the Gaṇas, protect us from all calamities;
O Blessed One, Hara exists as the elevenfold self, endowed with form.
O Śiva, having seen such numerous incarnations of yours, one might perhaps sometimes fall into darkness; yet we are not so, for our thoughts are ever absorbed in you.
Withdraw entirely all forms that extend as far as the slopes of Mount Guñjā;
you must not lead [anyone] to what is accessible to the highest and the lowest.
The Brahmins who know the Vedas understand that you, Rudra, have two forms:
one is terrible and the other is auspicious; each of these is manifold.
Protect us here, O Blessed One, you who possess eternal, unassailable, and great power;
for the entire world is pervaded by you with your own splendor.
O Maheśvara, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, Candra, and others, as well as ourselves and the foremost gods—
all gods and demons alike— have been born from you.
Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, Yama, and the others could not restrain the gods or the asuras;
therefore, having subdued Hari, they addressed Upacetas as "Siṃha."
Since you sustain the entire universe by dividing your body into eight parts,
therefore, O Blessed One, protect us gods with the boons we desire.
The God spoke to those gods and the ancient great seers:
"Just as water poured into water, milk into milk, or ghee into ghee [becomes one]."
At that time, Viṣṇu was indeed one, merged with Śiva and not otherwise;
he alone was the self of Nṛsiṃha, full of pride and possessed of great strength.
The Man-Lion, who has set out as the agent of the world’s destruction, is to be worshipped by those desiring the perfection of devotion to me; salutations to him!
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One Vīrabhadra, possessed of great strength,
vanished right there from the sight of all beings.
From that time forth, Śaṅkara, wearing the skin of Nṛsiṃha,
designated that head as the central one in his garland of skulls.
Then the gods, free from fear, their eyes wide with wonder as they recounted this story, all departed as they had come.
Whoever reads or even hears this supreme narrative, which is meritorious and endowed with the Vedas, shall have all suffering destroyed.
It brings fortune, renown, long life, health, and increases nourishment;
it pacifies all obstacles and destroys all diseases.
It pacifies untimely death, brings about great peace, and is auspicious;
it subdues the circle of enemies and destroys all calamities.
Then follows the pacification of bad dreams, the warding off of all malevolent spirits,
the destruction of poisons and planetary seizures, and the increase of sons, grandsons, and other progeny.
It perfectly bestows the perfection of yoga, illuminates the knowledge of Śiva,
serves as a staircase for the rest of the world, and is the sole means for accomplishing one's desired goals.
It dispels the illusion of Viṣṇu, bestows the supreme goal upon the deities,
grants the fulfillment of desires, and is the means for attaining supernatural powers, wisdom, and other virtues.
But this supreme form of the wielder of the Pināka bow, which has the appearance of a Śarabha,
should be revealed to devotees who have long been diligent in their efforts.
Those whose nature is auspicious (śiva) should themselves recite and listen to it during all festivals of Śiva, as well as on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days.
One should recite this at the times of consecration, for it causes the presence of Śiva;
it also brings an end to thieves, tigers, snakes, and lions, as well as to fears of kings.
In this regard, [one should avoid] other portents, earthquakes, forest fires, showers of dust,
the falling of meteors, great winds, and instances of drought or excessive rain.
Therefore, a wise man who is a devotee of Śiva and firm in his vows should recite it there;
whoever should read or even hear this hymn, which is unsurpassed in all respects.
Having attained the state of Rudra, he shall become an attendant of Rudra.
Thus ends the ninety-sixth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Śarabha," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
The sages said:
How did the Lord Hara, who wears matted locks on his head and who took away the eyes of Bhaga, slay Jalandhara, whose prowess was like that of Indra in ancient times?
"O Romaharṣaṇa of noble vows, you ought to tell us [this].
Sūta said:
"He who was born from the circle of waters is known as Jalandhara."
He was like the God of Death himself, having acquired prowess through ascetic penance;
by him, the gods, along with the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas, [were overcome].
All were utterly defeated in battle, including the unborn Lord Brahmā;
indeed, having conquered the host of gods, Jalandhara defeated even Brahmā.
He went to Viṣṇu, the Lord of the gods, the teacher who withdraws the universe;
between the two of them there occurred a battle that continued day and night without rest.
By him, the Lord of Jalandhara defeated Madhusūdana;
and Jalandhara, having conquered that Janārdana, the God of gods, [prevailed].
The one whose intellect was fixed on justice spoke thus to the sons of Diti, who were seeking to conquer the Lord:
"All have been conquered by me in battle; indeed, Śaṅkara alone remains unconquered in combat."
Having conquered that all-powerful one together with Nandin and the hosts of Gaṇas in an instant,
I myself shall become you, as well as the state of Brahmā and likewise the state of Viṣṇu.
"And I shall grant you the status of Vāsava, O foremost of Dānavas.
Having heard Jalandhara’s words, all those lowest of Dānavas [rejoiced].
The most wicked ones, intent on seeing death,
roared loudly along with these Daityas and others, mounted upon chariots, elephants, and horses.
Having armed himself along with those who were already armored, the powerful one went forth against Śarva;
and Bhava, seeing the lord of the Daityas standing there like a peak of Mount Meru, [prepared for battle].
Even after hearing that he was invulnerable,
the Lord, the protector of the worlds and the destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes, remained so while honoring the word of Brahmā.
Accompanied by Sāmba, Nandin, and his own retinue, he spoke as if laughing:
"O Lord of Asuras, what is the purpose of this battle at present?"
With all his limbs pierced by my arrows,
Jalandhara, having heard those words which tore at his ears, joyfully prepared for death.
The lord of the hosts of the enemies of the gods spoke thus to Sureśvara:
"Enough with these words, O mighty-armed one, O God of gods, whose banner bears the bull! (LiP 1.97.15)

"Come here to fight with weapons resembling the rays of the moon! Hearing these words of his, the wielder of the trident (Śiva) playfully used his big toe to instantly cast the great ocean upon the formidable weapon, the discus.
Having fashioned a white discus from the waters of the ocean and remembering the three worlds, the Blessed One struck the gods with it;
he who is the destroyer of Dakṣa, Andhaka, and the three cities, and the plunderer of the sacrifice, the bringer of end to the three worlds, laughed and then spoke: LiP_1,97.17 //
"O Daitya Jalandhara, if you are powerful enough to lift with your foot this [mountain] fashioned by Brahmā in the great ocean, then stay to fight; otherwise, do not."
Having heard those words of his, his eyes ablaze with anger,
as if burning the three worlds with his two eyes, he spoke while looking out upon them.
Jalandhara said: "O Śaṅkara, having raised my mace and struck down Nandin as well as you,
I shall destroy the worlds along with the gods, just as Garuḍa destroys the serpents."
"I am capable of destroying everything moving and unmoving, including Indra himself;
O Maheśvara, who in the three worlds cannot be pierced by my arrows?"
In his childhood, the Blessed One was completely conquered by asceticism alone;
Brahmā was powerful in his youth, and the sages were [conquered] by the foremost of the gods.
In an instant, the entire triple world, including all that is mobile and immobile, was consumed by you;
O Rudra, what [more] could be achieved by your asceticism, since even the Blessed Lord was conquered by you?
Indra, Agni, Yama, Kubera, Vāyu, Varuṇa,
and the others could not endure him, just as serpents cannot bear the scent of the Lord of Birds.
O Śaṅkara, O Lord of the Gaṇas, having reached all the mountains on earth and in heaven, my arms were not found and were rubbed away.
The glorious Mandara, lord of mountains, and the beautiful blue Meru,
having been rubbed by his staff-like arms for the sake of relieving his itching, fell down.
