On the Himavat mountain, for the sake of sport, I blocked the Gaṅgā with my two arms;
and by my servants, Vajra was bound by the women of the gods.
Having seized the mouth of the mare with his hand, he broke it;
at that very instant, all this became a single ocean.
The nāgas, beginning with Airāvata, were cast upon the waters of the ocean;
and the Blessed Lord Indra, along with his chariot, was hurled a hundred yojanas away.
Even Garuḍa was bound by me with the serpent-noose of Viṣṇu;
and women such as Urvaśī were led by me into the interior of prison.
"O Lord of Umā, Śakra has somehow obtained Śacī alone after bowing down to me;
you do not recognize me, O Lord of Daityas, as Jalandhara."
Sūta said:
Thus addressed, Mahādeva then indeed set his chariot ablaze,
agitating it with half of a half of a single sixteenth part of the fire from his eye.
By the horses and elephants of the Daityas, who possessed incomparable strength, the lords of the Daityas were destroyed at the mere glance of the enemy of Tripura;
and having suffered this slaughter by the serpents, the one of small intellect addressed these words to the Lord of the Gods.
What task remains for me in battle, O Lord, which you are capable of slaying in an instant—all these hosts of gods and daityas combined?
Since there is no fear here from them regarding combat, this desire of yours to fight is far greater; of this there is no doubt.

Therefore, O enemy of Madana, foe of Dakṣa, adversary of sacrifice, and destroyer of Tripura, if you indeed possess the strength here to fight with my heroes, with the lords of spirits, with the face of Hari, and with the hosts of gods, then stay!
Having spoken thus to Mahādeva, the son of the enemy of Mahādeva neither moved nor remembered his kinsmen slain in battle.
Intoxicated and of unsubdued self, he slapped his arms with the strength of his forearms and prepared to slay [him] with the discus named Sudarśana.
O best of the twice-born, although it was difficult even for him to do so, he placed the wheel upon his shoulder with great effort; yet, because of that very act, he indeed split in two.
O twice-born ones, just as a great mountain might be split in two by a thunderbolt,
so the powerful Daitya fell like a second Mount Añjana.
In an instant, it became completely filled with his fierce blood;
by the command of Rudra, that entire blood as well as the flesh [vanished].
Having reached Mahāraurava, alas, there was a pool of blood;
seeing Jalandhara slain, the attendants of the gods and Gandharvas were overcome.
Having let out a great lion’s roar, they cried out, "Excellent, O God!"—
those who would either recite or even hear this account of the subduing of Jalandhara.
Or, by reciting it according to the rule, one shall attain the state of Gaṇapati.
Thus ends the ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Slaying of Jalandhara," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
The sages said:
O Sūta, you ought to tell me how the god Viṣṇu indeed obtained from Maheśvara, the God of gods, that which is known as Sudarśana.
Sūta said:
A great and most terrible conflict arose between the gods and the lords of the asuras,
causing the destruction of all living beings.
Being pierced by those gods with spears, clubs, straight-jointed arrows,
and lances, they fled, overwhelmed by fear.
Then the defeated gods, their minds agitated by grief, bowed down to Hari, the Lord of the gods of gods and the Sovereign of the deities.
Then, having observed those gods who stood prostrate before him, Hari, the Blessed One, the Lord of the gods of gods, spoke these words:
"O children, why indeed have you gods come together so distressed, having lost your ornaments and prowess? O you of noble vows, you ought to tell me."
Having heard those words of his, the foremost gods, being in such a state,
bowed down and reported everything as it had happened to Viṣṇu, the god of gods.
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Viṣṇu, Jiṣṇu, Janārdana! We have all been oppressed by the Dānavas and have come to you for refuge.
O Lord of the gods of gods, O Supreme Person, you alone are our refuge;
for you indeed are the Supreme Self and the father of all the worlds.
O Janārdana, you alone are the sustainer, the destroyer, the enjoyer, and the giver;
therefore, O crusher of the Dānavas, you ought to slay these Dānavas.
And the Daityas were [struck] by the Vaiṣṇava, Brāhma, Raudra, Yāmya, and most terrible Kaubera mantras,
as well as by the Saumya, Nairṛtya, and firm Vāruṇa mantras.
And likewise with those belonging to Vāyu, Agni, Īśāna, and Varṣa; with the auspicious ones of Sūrya, as well as the fierce, terrifying, trembling, yawning, and firm ones.
O lotus-eyed one, by virtue of the boon you have received, all [beings] are invulnerable;
your discus, born from the solar orb, has been raised up.
O Preceptor of the World, because it was blunted by Dadhīca and Cyāvana,
the staff, the Śārṅga bow, and your weapon have been obtained by the Daityas through their favor.
"In former times, a sharp and terrible discus was fashioned by Tripurāri to slay Jalandhara; with that, you ought to kill them."
Therefore, he must be slain by him alone, and not by others even with hundreds of weapons.
Then, having heard those words of theirs, the lotus-eyed one [acted].
Hari himself, the wielder of the discus, spoke to those headed by Vācaspati;
Śrī Viṣṇu said:
"O gods, [go] with all the eternal deities to Mahādeva."
Having now obtained everything, I shall accomplish the purpose of the dwellers of heaven;
for Jalandhara has been created by the Enemy of Tripura (Śiva) in order to slay the gods.
Having obtained the discus from him and having slain the great asuras—
the six thousand eight hundred Daityas headed by Dhundhu— he [protected] the gods.
"I shall deliver you all, along with your kinsmen, in an instant.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus to the foremost of the gods, he meditated upon the Supreme God.
Then the best of gods, having duly installed the excellent Śaṅkara-liṅga upon the auspicious peak of Himavat, worshipped it according to the prescribed rites.
Janārdana was fashioned by Viśvakarman, resembling Mount Meru,
by the fierce Rudra known as Tvarita.

Having bathed and worshipped [the deity] with perfumes and other offerings, he then praised Rudra— who was beautiful and flame-like in form— after having fully honored him in the fire and prostrated before him.
And he worshipped Śiva with the Thousand Names of the Lord, beginning with "Bhava" and following the proper sequence, starting with the syllable Om (praṇava) and ending with "namas."
With the thousand names beginning with "Bhava," he worshipped the god Maheśvara, Śaṅkara, offering a lotus for each individual name.

And having offered oblations into the fire according to the rules, ten thousand times for each, to the Lord using the names beginning with "Bhava" and so forth, along with fuel-sticks and other materials, ending with the word "svāhā."
And Śrī Viṣṇu again praised Śambhu, the Lord of existence and so forth, with words beginning with "Bhava.
Śrī Viṣṇu said: "Bhava, Śiva, Hara, Rudra, Puruṣa, Padmalocana..."
One should always seek Maheśvara, who is auspiciousness itself in every way;
he is the Lord, the Immovable One, the Sovereign, the thousand-eyed, and the thousand-footed.
The most excellent, the giver of boons, the venerable Śaṅkara, the Supreme Lord,
the bearer of the Gaṅgā, the wielder of the trident, whose sole purpose is the welfare of others.
The omniscient one, whose bow is the mountain of all the gods and others, who wears matted locks,
who is adorned with the moon, the moon-crested one, the wise lord of all the immortals.
He is the essence of the Vedānta, the collection of its truths; he is Kapālī, the blue-and-red one (Nīlalohita);
he is to be discerned as the support for meditation; he is the husband of Gaurī and the Lord of the Gaṇas.
He who has eight forms and is the form of the universe; he who is the triple aggregate and the means to attain heaven;
he who is accessible through knowledge and possesses firm wisdom; the God of gods, the three-eyed one.
Vāmadeva, Mahādeva, Pāṇḍu, Paridṛḍha, Dṛḍha,
Viśvarūpa, Virūpākṣa, Vāgīśa, Śuci, and Antara.
He is the one who accords with all expressions of affection, the bull-bannered, the one whose vehicle is the bull, the Lord,
the wielder of the Pināka bow, the bearer of the skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), the one of variegated attire, and the eternal one.

The dispeller of darkness, the great yogin, the protector, the heart of the limbs of Brahmā, the one with matted hair, the death of Death, the one clad in animal skin, the fortunate one, whose essence is the syllable Om.
Unmattaveṣa, Cakṣuṣya, Durvāsas, Smaraśāsana,
Dṛḍhāyudha, Skandaguru, Parameṣṭhin, and Parāyaṇa.
He is without beginning, middle, or end; the Lord of the Mountain, the kinsman of the Mountain;
the friend of Kubera; the one whose throat is auspicious; the most excellent among the highest of all classes of beings in the world.
Sāmānyadeva, Kodaṇḍin, Nīlakaṇṭha, Paraśvadhin,
Viśālākṣa, Mṛgavyādha, Sureśa, and Sūryatāpana.
The Blessed One, who destroyed the eyes of Bhaga, is the field incapable of [ordinary] dharma-action;
he is Ugra, Paśupati, Tārkṣya, the lover of his devotees, and the one who speaks kindly.
The giver, the compassionate one, the skillful, the one with matted hair, the subduer of desire,
whose abode is the cremation ground, the subtle, who dwells in the cremation ground, the Great Lord (Maheśvara).
The creator of the world, the lord of beings, the great creator, the great medicinal herb, the supreme one, the lord of rays, the protector, accessible through knowledge, and the ancient one.
Nīti, Sunīti, Śuddhātman, Soma, Somarata, Sukhin, Somapa, Amṛtapa, Soma, Mahānīti, and Mahāmati.
Ajātaśatru, Āloka, Saṃbhāvya, Havyavāhana,
Lokakāra, Vedakāra, Sūtrakāra, and Sanātana.
The great seer Kapila Ācārya, the light of the universe, the three-eyed one,
who holds the Pināka bow in his hand, the god on earth, the bestower of well-being, and the eternal creator of auspiciousness.
He who has three abodes, the auspicious one, Śarva, the omniscient, whose range is everywhere;
he who upholds the Brahman, the creator of the universe, heaven itself, the Karṇikāra tree, the beloved, and the sage.
Śākha, Viśākha, Gośākha, Śiva, Aneka, Kratu, Sama,
Gaṅgāplavodaka, Bhāva, Sakala, Sthapati, and Sthira.
He is one who has conquered his self, whose self is disciplined, the charioteer of the vehicle of living beings,
accompanied by his retinue, the performer of the tasks of the Gaṇas, possessed of good fame, and one whose doubts have been severed.
Kāmadeva, Kāmapāla, whose body is smeared with ashes;
he who loves ashes, who sleeps upon ashes, the desirous one, the beloved, the author of the sacred scriptures.
Endowed with equanimity, his self withdrawn, united with Dharma, he is Sadāśiva;
four-faced and four-armed, he is difficult to dwell with and difficult to approach.
He is difficult to traverse, hard to attain, and impregnable; he is skilled in all weapons, the abode of the yoga of the inner self, the excellent thread, and the increaser of the thread.
He of auspicious limbs, the essence of the world, the Lord of the universe, the consumer of nectar;
he who purifies with ashes, Mount Meru, the vigorous one, whose form is pure.
He is the one whose essence is gold, the one who carries across, the radiant one, the abode of greatness,
the great lake, the great womb, and he who is worshipped by the hosts of Siddhas and Apsarases.
He who wears a tiger skin, the serpent, the great being, the great treasure,
whose limbs are nectar, whose body is nectar, the fivefold sacrifice, and the wind.

He who knows the twenty-five principles, the Pārijāta tree, the one who transcends both the high and the low, the easily attained, the one of excellent vows, the hero, the sole treasury of speech, and the treasure-store.
The teacher of the castes and stages of life, the student, the conqueror of enemies, the scorcher of foes;
the hermitage, the destroyer, the emaciated, the possessor of knowledge, the immovable among the moving.
He is the embodiment of valid authority, difficult to comprehend, the well-winged one whose vehicle is the wind;
he is the wielder of the bow, the science of archery, a mass of virtues, and a mine of excellence.
He is infinite vision, bliss, the staff, the subduer, and self-restraint;
he is the one to be saluted, the great teacher, the architect of the universe, and the fearless one.
Free from passion, self-disciplined, an ascetic, the creator of beings,
disguised in the garb of a madman, he was concealed, having conquered desire and overcome affection.
He is of auspicious nature, the Kalpa, the Lord of Progeny for all the worlds;
he is an ascetic, the deliverer, the wise one, the primordial Lord, and the imperishable.
The world-protector, whose self has vanished, who is the beginning of the eon, whose eyes are like lotuses,
who knows the true meaning of the Vedas and scriptures, who is the restraint itself and the refuge of restraint.

He is the moon, the sun, Saturn, and Ketu; he is the cessation [of worldly existence], possessing the luster of coral; he is accessible through devotion, the Supreme Brahman, the one who fixed the arrow upon the deer, and the sinless one.
The beloved one whose abode is the king of mountains, the Supreme Self, the Teacher of the World,
the immovable performer of all actions, the Creator, the Auspicious One surrounded by auspiciousness.
He is the one of great austerity, of long austerity, the most steadfast, the ancient, and the eternal;
he is the day, the year, the pervader, the measure, and the supreme asceticism.
He is the mantra that brings about the year, the means of realization, and the all-seeing one;
he is the unborn, the Lord of all, the affectionate, the one of great seed, and the one of great power.
The yogi is the worthy one, possessed of great semen, the perfected one, the source of all, the giver of fire;
he is the Vasu, the one of noble mind, the truth, the remover of all sins, and Hara.
He is immortal, eternal, and tranquil; he holds a bow in his hand and is full of majesty.
He carries a water-pot, wields a bow, is the embodiment of the Vedāṅgas, a knower of the Vedas, and a sage.
Radiant, the enjoyer of food, the leader of the world, the invincible;
beyond the senses, possessed of great illusion, the abode of all, and the crossroads.
He is the Yogi of Time, the Great Sound, the Great Zeal, and the Great Strength;
he is the Great Intelligence, the Great Heroism, the Wanderer among Beings, and the Destroyer of Cities.
He is a night-walker, a roamer among the spirits of the dead, possessed of great power and great splendor;
his form is indescribable, he is glorious, the destroyer of all, and his movement is beyond measure.

He is the one of great learning, composed of many forms, self-restrained, and the source of worldly existence; he is the creator of vigor, splendor, and radiance, the dancer, and the fulfiller of all desires.
He who is fond of dance, who dances the dance, whose nature is luminous, who causes heat;
he is the mantra of the Buddha consisting of clear syllables, the true honor, and the flood of the essence.
The creator of the beginning of the ages, the one who turns the ages, the profound, the one whose vehicle is the bull;
the beloved, the distinguished, the one desired by the learned, the Śarabha, the Śarabha, and the bow.
He is the ocean, the foundation, victory, and the knower of the time of triumph;
he is firmly established, the knower of valid means of knowledge, the one clad in golden armor, and the tawny-hued Lord.
Virocana, the host of gods, the Lord of Knowledge, the refuge of the wise;
he who takes the form of a child, the destroyer of strength, the transformation, the profound, and the Guru.
He is the instrument, the cause, and the agent; the liberator from all bonds;
the most wise, free from fear, the sustainer of the universe, and the maker of night.

He is resolve, he is steadfastness, the giver of station, and the source of the origin of the world; he is Dundubha, the playful one, the universe itself, the self of existence, established within the Self.
Vīreśvara, Vīrabhadra, Vīrahā, Vīrabhṛt, Virāṭ, Vīracūḍāmaṇi, Vettā, Tīvranāda, and Nadīdhara.
The bearer of the command, the trident-bearer, Śipiviṣṭa, the abode of Śiva,
the Vālakhilya, the wielder of the great bow, the one of fierce rays, the inexhaustible treasure.
He is the Delightful One, the Excellent Refuge, the Noble Brahmin, the Lord of Nectar;
He is Maghavan, Kauśika, the Possessor of Cows, the Rest, and the Teacher of All.
He has an eye on his forehead, possesses a universal body, is the essence, and sustains the wheel of worldly existence;
he wields an unfailing rod of punishment, stands as an impartial mediator, is golden-hued, and is endowed with the splendor of Brahman.
Paramārtha, Paramaya, Śambara, Vyāghraka, Anala, Ruci, Vararuci, Vandya, Vācaspati, and Aharpati.
Ravi, Virocana, Skandha, Śāstṛ, Vaivasvata, Jana, Yukti, Unnatakīrti, Śāntarāga, and Parājaya.
The enemy of the lord of Kailāsa, the progenitor with sun-like eyes,
the most learned, free from fear, and the destroyer of the universe was restrained.

He is eternal, of constant auspiciousness, whose hearing and chanting are meritorious; his fame is heard afar, he sustains the universe, he is the object of meditation, and he is the destroyer of evil dreams.
The deliverer, the remover of evil deeds, the invincible, the unassailable, the fearless;
the beginningless, the support of the earth, the prosperity of the worlds, the crowned one, the lord of the thirty gods.

The protector of the universe, the sustainer of the universe, the very steadfast one, he whose armlets are radiant; the progenitor, the source of the birth of all beings, the gracious one, the possessor of ethics, and the embodiment of right conduct.
The distinguished Kāśyapa, Bhānu, Bhīma of terrible prowess,
the sacred syllable Om (Praṇava), the one who moves in seven ways, the great-bodied, and the wielder of the great bow.
The lord of his birth was Mahādeva, who had reached the further shore of all the Āgamas;
whose nature was the discernment between reality and unreality, who was radiant, and adorned with sacred ashes.
The seer, the victor over the Brahmins, who has transcended birth, death, and old age;
he is the sacrifice, the lord of sacrifice, the sacrificer, the end of sacrifice, and one whose prowess is never in vain.
Mahendra, Durbhara, Senī, Yajñāṅga, Yajñavāhana,
Pañcabrahmasamutpatti, Viśveśa, and Vimalodaya.
He is self-born, without beginning or end, the sustainer of the twenty-six principles and the seven worlds;
he is the beloved of Gāyatrī, the lofty one, the abode of the universe, and the maker of light.

The child, the one who delights in the mountain, the sovereign, the one with a beautiful army, the slayer of the enemies of the gods, the unerring, the destroyer of misfortune, the deliverer from suffering, and the one free from fever.

He is self-luminous, with light as his companion, and has the Self as his light; he is unshakable, tawny-hued, with reddish-brown hair and beard, having the scriptures as his eyes and the three Vedas as his body.
He is the aggregate of knowledge, the possessor of great wisdom, non-arising, and free from affliction;
he is Bhaga, Vivasvat, Āditya, the teacher of yoga, and Bṛhaspati.
He is of noble renown, the industrious one, the true yogin, composed of both the existent and the non-existent;
he is garlanded with stars, the lord of the full moon, possessed of the supreme abode, and the refuge of the six.
With the sacrificial grass in hand, the enemy of evil, Maṇipūra, moving with the speed of thought,
seated within the lotus of the heart, white, peaceful, and Vṛṣākapi.
Viṣṇu, the lord of the planets, Kṛṣṇa, the capable one who destroys misfortune,
the enemy of unrighteousness, the imperishable, invoked by many, and praised by many.
The womb of Brahman, the vast womb, the cow of dharma, the source of wealth;
the one who desires the welfare of the world, the Sugata, the Youth, the arrival of virtue.
Golden-hued, radiant, the bearer of various beings, and sound;
free from disease, the overseer of discipline, Viśvāmitra, the best of the twice-born.
Bṛhajjyotis, Sudhāmā, Mahājyotis, Anuttama,
Mātāmaha, Mātariśvan, Nabhasvān, and Nāgahāradhṛk.
Pulastya, Pulaha, Agastya, Jātūkarṇya, Parāśara,
Viriñca— who knows the dharma free from all veils— and Viṣṭaraśravas.
Self-born, Aniruddha, the embodiment of the threefold knowledge, of great renown,
the crest-jewel of the world, the hero, possessing fierce and true valor.
Vyālakalpa, Mahākalpa, Mahāvṛkṣa, Kalādhara,
Alaṃkariṣṇu, Acala, Rociṣṇu, and Vikramottama.
He is the swift lord of sound, the impetuous one, the leaper, and he whose charioteer is fire;
he is the unattached guest, the powerful Śakra, the destroyer, and the annihilator of evil.
Vasuśravas, Kavyavāha, Pratapta, Viśvabhojana,
Jaryo, Jarādhiśamana, Lohita, and Tanūnapāt.
Pṛṣadaśva, Nabhoyoni, Supratīka, Tamisrahā,
Nidāgha, Tapana, Megha, Pakṣa, and Parapurañjaya.
The breath from his mouth was perfectly formed, fragrant, and cool in nature;
it was Vasantas, Mādhavas, Grīṣmas, Nabhasyas, and Bījavāhanas.
The sage Aṅgiras, Ātreya, Vimala, Viśvavāhana,
Pāvana, Purujit, Śakra, Trividyas, and Naravāhana.
Mind, intellect, ego, the knower of the field, the protector of the field,
the treasury of splendor, the treasury of knowledge, the ripening [of karma], and the creator of obstacles.
He is to be known as the lower and the unsurpassed, the eldest, and the abode of the highest good;
he is the mountain, the tree, the body, and the physical form; he is the enemy of the Dānavas and the subduer of foes.
He is of beautiful intellect, the progenitor, the one who removes the thorns of the world, the creator of the world's thorns;
he is the knower of the four Vedas, possessed of the four states of being, the skillful one, and the beloved of the clever.

He is the sacred tradition and the compendium of that tradition; he is the holy ford, the deity, and the temple of Śiva; he is of manifold forms, of great forms, and of all forms; he is both the moving and the unmoving.
He is the logic that establishes right reasoning, accessible through logic, and stainless;
he is the thousand-headed Lord of Gods, the shatterer of all weapons.
Shaven-headed, deformed, and disfigured, yet bearing a staff, self-controlled, and supreme in virtue;
with tawny eyes, or else with lion-like eyes, blue-necked, and free from all ailment.
He has a thousand arms, he is the Lord of all, the refuge, and the sustainer of all worlds;
he is seated upon the lotus, the supreme light, both the higher and the lower, and the ultimate fruit.
The one whose womb is the lotus, the great womb, the universal womb, the far-sighted;
the knower of the high and the low, the lord of the seed, the fair-faced, and the one of great sound.
The god who is the preceptor of gods and asuras, honored by gods and asuras;
the great minister of gods and asuras, the great refuge of gods and asuras.
The god of gods, the divine sage, the bestower of boons upon gods and asuras;
the lord of gods and asuras, the divine one, the great sovereign of gods and asuras.
He consists of all the gods, is inconceivable, the self of the deities, and self-born;
he is the one to be praised, the lordless one, the tiger among gods, the lion of the gods, and the maker of day.
The most excellent among the foremost of the wise, the highest of all the best of gods,
devoted to the knowledge of Śiva, glorious, and fond of Śikhiśrīparvata.
The pillar of victory, the supreme support, the one who strikes down Narasiṃha;
the celibate student, the wanderer of the world, the practitioner of dharma, and the lord of wealth.
Nandī, Nandīśvara, the naked one, the observer of the vow of nudity, the pure one;
the presiding lord of the liṅga, the presiding lord of the gods, the presiding lord of the ages, and the bringer of the ages.
He who is self-dependent and dependent on all; heaven itself; the primordial sound; whose voice consists of the essence of sound;
the overseer of the seed; the creator of the seed; the maker of wealth; and the increaser of dharma.
He is hypocrisy, non-hypocrisy, and great hypocrisy; the supreme lord of all beings;
whose abode is the cremation ground; the age of Kali; the bridge; and one of incomparable form.
He is the transcendent, clear light, the three-eyed one adorned with serpents;
the enemy of Andhaka, the hater of sacrifices, and the one who struck down the neck of Viṣṇu.
Free from defects and possessed of inexhaustible qualities, the subduer of Dakṣa, the remover of Pūṣan’s teeth;
the one with matted hair, the wielder of the broken axe, the manifest, the unmanifest, and the sinless.
The support, the support of all, white-hued, the benevolent one, the dancer;
the full, the fulfiller, the meritorious, the delicate, the one with beautiful eyes.
Sāmageya, Priyakara, Puṇyakīrti, Anāmaya,
Manojava, Tīrthakara, Jaṭila, and Jīviteśvara.
The ender of life, eternal, whose seed is wealth, who loves wealth,
the true goal, the honored one, the attached, the dark-throated, and the bearer of the arts.
The honorable Mahākāla, who is himself worthy of honor; the true prosperity, the ultimate refuge; the reviver of the moon, the teacher, the secret of the world, and the lord of the immortals.
The kinsman of the world, the lord of the world, grateful, the ornament of the wise,
the imperishable one who never departs, the beloved, and the best among those who uphold all the scriptures.
Consisting of splendor, possessing radiance, the illusion of the world, the foremost leader, subtle;
with a pure smile and a serene soul, he is difficult to conquer and impossible to transcend.
He is composed of light, formless, the Lord of the World, and the Master of the Waters;
he holds a gourd-lute, possesses a great body, is free from sorrow, and is the destroyer of grief.
The soul of the three worlds, the lord of the three worlds, the pure, the source of purity, born from the axle of the chariot;
he whose characteristics are unmanifest, yet manifest, both manifest and unmanifest, the lord of all beings.
He is of excellent character, of excellent form, pride itself, and rich in honor;
he is Maya, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Prajāpāla, the Swan, the one whose gait is like a swan’s, and Yama.
He is the piercer, the creator, the ordainer, the self, the destroyer, and the four-faced one;
he dwells upon the peak of Kailāsa, resides in all things, and is the refuge of the virtuous.
Hiraṇyagarbha, the golden-hued, the Puruṣa, the first-born, the Father;
the abode of beings, the Lord of beings, the bestower of existence, the Sovereign of the world.
He is the possessor of union, the knower of yoga, Brahman, the one devoted to Brahman, the lover of brahmins,
the beloved of the gods, the lord of the gods, the knower of the gods, and the contemplator of the gods.
He has uneven eyes, he is the presiding lord of the arts, he is marked by the bull, and he is the increaser of the bull;
he is free from passion, free from egoism, free from delusion, and free from affliction.
The destroyer of pride, yet proud himself; the haughty one; the transformer of all seasons;
the seven-tongued; the thousand-rayed; the gentle; and the naturally benevolent.
The Lord of the past, future, and present; the source of all; the destroyer of delusion;
the goal and the non-goal; the great treasury; and the one who is solely expert in the affairs of others.
Free from thorns, he has brought joy to all; he is guileless and the crusher of deceit.
Endowed with courage, he is of the nature of pure goodness (sāttvika); his fame for truthfulness is established by the scriptures.
Unshakable, a perceiver of virtues, not of a single nature, and not performing only one action;
well-pleased, pleasant-faced, subtle, easy to perform [rites for], dexterous, and insatiable.
The aggregate, the bearer of the aggregates, the leader, the manifest, the increaser of joy,
the unconquered, the all-enduring, the clever, and the vehicle of all.
Adhṛta, Svadhṛta, Sādhya, Pūrvamūrti,
Yaśodhara, Varāhaśṛṅgadhṛk, Vāyu, Balavān, and Ekanāyaka.
He is the illuminator of the Vedas, possessed of the Vedas, the sole kinsman, and the sustainer of many;
he is the beloved of Śrī, the source of Śiva, auspiciously tranquil, and perfectly consistent.
He dwells upon the earth, he is the creator of prosperity, he is prosperity itself; he is the ornament and has beings as his vehicle.
He is bodiless, yet resides within the bodies of his devotees; he knows time and possesses a body of artistic skill.
He is one whose vow is truth, a great renouncer, devoted to steadfastness and peace;
he acts for the sake of others, is a granter of boons, solitary, and an ocean of sacred learning.
He is free from despondency, a perceiver of virtues, marked by blemish yet the destroyer of blemish;
he is Rudra by nature, impartial, the slayer of enemies, and the annihilator of the middle.
He has a crest-lock, wears armor, carries a trident, is fierce, is shaven-headed, and wears earrings;
he wears a girdle, bears a breastplate, wields a sword, possesses illusory power, and is the charioteer of worldly existence.
He is deathless, all-seeing, a lion, a mass of splendor, and a great jewel;
he is incalculable, immeasurable in essence, heroic, and skilled in action.
He is the one to be known, the knower of the meaning of the Vedas, the protector, the lord of sages who embodies all proper conduct;
he is unsurpassed, invincible, sweet-natured, and pleasant to behold.
The Lord of the gods, the refuge of all, the Brahman that is sound, the goal of the virtuous;
the devourer of time, the maker of the mark [on the moon], who has made Vāsuki his armlet.
The great archer, the lord of the earth, the stainless one, the unshackled one;
the jewel of heaven, the sun, the blessed one, the bestower of perfection, and the means for achieving perfection.
He is withdrawn, restrained, skilled in the arts, broad-chested, and long-armed;
he is the singular light, free from affliction, a man beloved by Nārāyaṇa.
Untainted, his self free from conceptual proliferation, undisturbed, the destroyer of agitation;
he who is to be praised, who loves praise, the praiser himself, the embodiment of Vyāsa, and unperturbed.
He possesses the means to the faultless state, is a mass of knowledge, and is free from violence;
his intellect is tranquil, he is not mean-spirited, he destroys the base, and he is eternally beautiful.
The foremost among the steadfast, the Lord of the Earth, Śākalya, the Lord of the Night,
the Guru of the ultimate truth, Vision, the Teacher, and the one who is affectionate toward those who have taken refuge.
The essence, the knower of essence, the omniscient one, the support for all beings;
Sūta said:
With these thousand names, he thus praised the one whose banner is the bull.
The omnipresent Lord bathed him and honored him with lotuses; Maheśvara placed those lotuses used for the worship of Hari there for the purpose of testing him.
The Lord of the World concealed that one lotus;
there, having had his flower taken away, Hari reflected, "What is this?"
Having understood this, he plucked out his own eye as an offering for all sentient beings,
and with devotion, he worshipped the Teacher of the World by means of that very name.
Then, seeing Hari in such a state there,
the all-pervading Hara quickly descended from that circle of fire.
Resembling ten million suns, adorned with a crown of matted locks,
encircled by garlands of flames, divine, possessing sharp fangs, and terrifying.
Hara holds a trident, an axe, a mace, a discus, a spear, and a noose;
his hands grant boons and fearlessness, and he wears a tiger skin as an upper garment.
Seeing Bhava thus adorned with ashes at that time,
Janārdana was delighted and quickly paid homage to the God of gods.
The gods, led by Indra, ran around the three-eyed Lord;
the abode of Brahmā trembled and the earth shook.
The splendor of Śambhu burned for a hundred yojanas around its edge, both below and above, while cries of "Alas! Alas! were raised upon the earth.
Then Mahādeva Śaṅkara, as if smiling,
spoke after looking with affection at Viṣṇu, who stood there with his palms joined in reverence.
"O Janārdana, I have now understood this task of the gods;
and I give to you the beautiful discus named Sudarśana."
O you of noble vows, that form which was seen by you, which causes terror to all the worlds, was manifested through your effort for your own benefit and for your spiritual welfare.
O Viṣṇu, the battlefield has been pacified, which was a source of suffering for the gods;
let the weapon also be pacified, for one who is peaceful should remain tranquil—what fruit is there in a weapon that is pacified?
For those who have attained peace, the weapon in battle is peace itself; for ascetics, it is peace alone.
For a warrior, the destruction of the enemy's strength through peace brings about an increase in one's own power.
"O destroyer of the enemies of the gods, since you perceive my immutable form as being unappeased by the gods, what indeed is the use of weapons for fighting?"
O destroyer of the enemies of the gods, you must not practice forbearance in battle;
for it is improper to fight when one's own kin are either weak or already slain.
"O Vanquisher of Waters, regarding that which is not timely, unrighteousness,
and that which is harmful," having spoken thus, he gave [him] a discus possessing a radiance equal to ten thousand suns.
The eye of the Lord who leads the worlds was indeed like a lotus;
from that time forth, they called that observer of noble vows "Padmākṣa" (Lotus-eyed).
Having given this eye and the discus to Viṣṇu,
Nīlalohita indeed touched him with his two very beautiful hands and spoke.
"I am the giver of boons, O best of boon-granters; choose whatever boons you desire.
O Supreme Person, I have surely been brought under your control by your devotion."
Thus addressed by the God of gods, he bowed to that God of gods and said:
"O Mahādeva, may there be devotion toward you; be gracious and grant this supreme boon."
"O Lord, I desire nothing else for my devotees than that they may have no afflictions.
Having heard those words of his, Bhava became exceedingly compassionate.

And the moon-adorned Mahādeva touched him, bestowed faith upon him, and spoke thus to the imperishable Supreme Self: LiP_1,98.182: "He touched him and gave him faith; the moon-adorned Mahādeva spoke thus to the imperishable Supreme Self."
"O best of gods, by my grace you shall become devoted to me, and you shall be worthy of salutation and worship by both gods and asuras; of this there is no doubt."
When Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa and the fair-eyed one, having indeed censured her mother and her father Dakṣa, becomes the sovereign goddess of the gods.
O Viṣṇu of excellent vows, at that time you too were the divine Haimavatī;
[you were] Umā, the auspicious goddess, your sister Haimavatī.
"By the command of Brahmā, you shall give that virtuous woman to me alone;
and through this connection with me, you shall become worthy of worship among the worlds."
And from that time forward, you shall behold Śaṅkara with a divine disposition and a gracious mind, as if he were your own friend.
Having spoken thus, the Lord Rudra, who is blue-and-red (Nīlalohita), vanished;
and the Lord Janārdana also [vanished] in the presence of the gods.
Together with the sages, he entreated Mahādeva and Brahmā, saying:
"O Lotus-born One, I have recited this divine and most beautiful hymn of praise."
Whoever should read it, or listen to it, or cause the best of the twice-born to hear it,
shall obtain that fruit which corresponds to the weight of gold [given].
Indeed, the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices accrues to him who bathes Rudra with ghee and other substances using vessels and auspicious jars.
By means of these thousand names, with faith, he worshipped Śiva, the Lord;
and having obtained the fruit of a thousand sacrifices, he was honored by the lords of the asuras.
"He shall be worthy of worship by Rudra, and he shall indeed find his favor.
Thus did Janārdana speak "So be it" to the Lotus-born One.
Having prostrated before him, the God of gods and Teacher of the World, they departed;
therefore, O sinless twice-born ones, one should worship him with his thousand names.
And by reciting the thousand names, he attains the supreme goal.
Thus ends the ninety-eighth chapter, titled "The Attainment of Viṣṇu’s Discus through Worship with the Thousand Names," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
The sages said:
O Sūta of great intelligence, you have indicated the birth of the Goddess;
now describe it in detail, as well as her state of chastity, exactly as it occurred.
[How did] Menā obtain the status of Great Goddess, [and how occurred] the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice? And how was she given by Viṣṇu to Śambhu, the God of gods?
"How can you now speak what is auspicious for him?
Having heard those words of theirs, the Sūta, the best of those learned in the Purāṇas, [spoke].
Sūta said: He related the birth of those great-souled ones and of the Great Goddess;
that had previously been told by Brahmā to Daṇḍin in great detail.
Indeed, you [received it] from that wise Vyāsa for the sake of the prince;
having heard it from him, I shall now proclaim it in great detail.
"O highly fortunate ones, having bowed to me as well as to Bhava at my command, she who is called Bhaga—the supporter of the world—is the triple altar for the linga-form. (LiP 1.99.6)
O best of the twice-born, the Lord exists as the *liṅga*; from these two [principles] arises the creation of the world. Śiva, whose form is the *liṅga*, is light situated above darkness.
Through the union of the male organ and the altar, he became Ardhanārīśvara;
first, he created the god Brahmā, his four-faced son.
The omniscient Hara, the Lord who transcends the universe, the all-pervading Ardhanārīśvara, imparted his own knowledge to him.
The god beheld that Hiraṇyagarbha as he was being born;
he, in turn, beheld Rudra Mahādeva, Śaṅkara, who is Brahmā.
Seeing the Lord standing there as the deity Ardhanārīśvara,
the one born from the lotus praised the granter of boons with pleasing words.
"Divide yourself," [said] the unborn, all-pervading Lord of the Universe, the soul of the universe; and from his left side, he created a goddess as his wife, equal to himself.
For Faith was his auspicious and ancient wife;
by the command of the Lord, that goddess became the daughter of Dakṣa.
Then, having censured Dakṣa, that goddess Satī indeed took refuge in Rudra alone as her husband; however, in the course of time, she did not become Mainā again.
And Dakṣa, intoxicated by his own contempt, having thus reviled the God of gods, the Lord of Umā, was likewise cursed by Nārada himself.
Disregarding his actions and realizing he was no longer true to her, Satī, at that very moment,
reduced her own body to ashes by means of the path of yoga.
And because of the ascetic power of the Lord of the Mountain, the goddess Pārvatī came into being;
knowing this, the Lord Bharga, the Master, became enraged and consumed her with fire.
At the command of Cyavana, the wise son of Cyavana, renowned as Dadhīca, [destroyed] the vast sacrifice of Dakṣa.
Having conquered Viṣṇu in battle through the grace of Tryambaka,
the lord of sages cursed Viṣṇu and the guardians of the worlds as well.
By the fire born of Rudra's wrath alone,
the gods were indeed destroyed in an instant as an oblation, through the illusory power (māyā) of Śaṅkara.
Thus ends the ninety-ninth chapter, titled "The Birth of the Goddess," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
The sages said:
Having conquered [the demons] together with Viṣṇu, how did the Lord Parameśvara,
the Great Lord Maheśvara, act toward all of them according to the word of Dadhīca?
Sūta said: At Dakṣa’s vast sacrifice, the Blessed Lord Rudra consumed all the gods, headed by Viṣṇu, as well as all the hosts of sages.
O you of excellent vows, a host named Bhadra was sent by that Supreme Lord because of the truly unbearable separation from the Goddess.
And Vīrabhadra created auspicious lords of the Gaṇas born from his body hair;
then the powerful Bhadra, having mounted his chariot along with those lords of the Gaṇas, [set forth].
He whose charioteer was the unborn Lord Brahmā set his mind on departing;
and all those lords of the Gaṇas, with various weapons in their hands, [followed him].
Then the gods followed him in celestial chariots auspicious on all sides,
to the delightful and beautiful golden-peaked mountain of Himavat.
Likewise, O twice-born ones, his sacrificial enclosure was near Gaṅgādvāra; and in that region, there is the famous and auspicious place known as Kanakhala.
That Blessed One was indeed sent by the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin) to burn [the world];
then there occurred a portent foreboding fear for the worlds.
The mountains shattered, the earth trembled,
the winds whirled about, and the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters, was agitated.
The sacrificial fires did not blaze, nor did the sun shine;
the planets were not visible, nor were the gods or the dānavas.
Then, in an instant, Bhadra entered the sacrificial enclosure of the Great-souled One together with his sons born from his body-hair, like another fire of cosmic destruction.
The auspicious Lord spoke to Dakṣa of immeasurable splendor:
"O Dakṣa, today the sages and gods have been purified by their very contact with the wielder of the Pināka bow."
"I have been sent by you and the lords of sages to burn [the sacrifice]," said that leader of the Gaṇas, and having spoken thus, he set fire to that sacrificial hall.
And the furious lords of the Gaṇas uprooted the sacrificial posts and hurled them;
they even incinerated both the Prastotṛ and the Hotṛ with those very Gaṇa-lords.
Having seized all the leaders of the Gaṇas, they threw them into the current of the Gaṅgā;
the immensely powerful Vīrabhadra [seized] the hand of Śakra as he was about to strike.
The one of undaunted soul likewise paralyzed the other gods, and having plucked out the eyes of Bhaga with the tip of his fingernail as if in play; (LiP 1.100.16).
Having struck out Pūṣan’s teeth with his fist,
he likewise cast down the god Candramas with his big toe as if in play.
The powerful Lord Vīrabhadra crushed him,
and the Lord cut off the head of that sovereign Śakra.
Having effortlessly severed both hands of Vahni and torn out his tongue,
the exceedingly powerful Vīrabhadra struck him on the head with his foot.
The Blessed One, the Lord himself, cut asunder the staff of Yama;
he struck down the mighty god Īśāna with his trident.
Having thus effortlessly struck down the thirty-three gods,
as well as three hundred and three thousand of them, he did so with ease.
That god slew the three lords of the gods,
as well as the lords of the sages and all other deities who stood ready for battle.
The Lord Rudra struck him with arrows such as swords and clubs;
then Viṣṇu, endowed with great splendor, raised his discus while [Rudra] was unconscious.
The Blessed One Mādhava fought with that Rudra;
between them there occurred a most terrible battle that made the hair stand on end.
By the power of Viṣṇu’s yoga, they possessed divine bodies that were most formidable.
And innumerable beings were born with conchs, discs, and maces in their hands;
all of them possessed a splendor equal to that of the god Nārāyaṇa.
Having struck Viṣṇu with his mace, he then hit that god on the head and, as if in play, struck him on the chest on the field of battle.
Then Puruṣottama fell unconscious upon the ground;
rising again, that Lord raised his discus to slay him.
The glorious bull among men stood there with eyes red with rage;
and his was that fierce discus, possessing a radiance equal to the sun at the end of time.
The one of undaunted soul paralyzed him; he did not move from his hand, and being thus immobilized by him, he stood motionless like Mount Śṛṅgavat.
Then the Śārṅga bow, struck by the three [arrows], broke into three parts;
and indeed, from the contact with the tip of the Śārṅga, he severed the head of the Lord.
And his severed head fell into the netherworld (rasātala),
impelled by the wind generated from his own vital breaths by the wielder of the Pināka bow.
And at that very moment, he entered his sacrificial fire-chamber,
which had its water-pots shattered, its sacrificial posts broken, and its archways destroyed.
Seeing the great śāla tree set ablaze, Yajña also fled;
he then ran toward the sky in the form of a deer.
Vīrabhadra, having composed himself, then rendered him headless,
as well as Prajāpati, Dharma, and Kaśyapa, the teacher of the world.
The heroic and mighty one [worshipped] Ariṣṭanemi, Bahuputra, the lord of sages,
the sage Aṅgiras, and Kṛṣṇāśva.
O best of the twice-born, he struck the illustrious Dakṣa on the head with his foot,
severed his head, and burned it in the fire.
And the powerful Vīrabhadra, having severed the tip of the nose of Sarasvatī as well as that of the Mother of the Gods with the tips of his fingernails, [acted].
Surrounded by splendor, he stood in the midst of the place of the dead like Bhava himself;
at that very time, however, the Blessed One Padmasambhava [appeared].
The Lord of great splendor, bowing down and making a request, spoke kindly to Bhadra:
"Enough with this anger, Bhadra! The inhabitants of heaven have already perished."
"Be gracious; let everything be forgiven along with those born from your body hairs, O you of noble vows.
And Bhadra, too, by the power of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin, [was restored].
He gradually attained tranquility and remained there at his command;
likewise, the blessed Lord whose banner is the bull remained there in the atmosphere.
Accompanied by his retinue, Śarva, the giver of all, the Great Lord of all the worlds—
the blessed Bhava— was entreated by the divine Brahmā.
Then he restored the bodies of those who had been slain, as they were before,
as well as the head of Indra and that of the high-souled Viṣṇu.
Maheśvara likewise [touched] the tip of the nose of Dakṣa, the lord of sages, as well as those of others,
and also that of Vāgīśī and Devamātṛ.
The Lord, the Master, restored life to the ruined Dakṣa and granted him various boons, while Dakṣa bowed his head.
The Great Bhava indeed fashioned a face with ease;
and Dakṣa, having regained consciousness, rose up with palms joined in reverence.
He praised Śaṅkara, the Lord of the gods of gods, whose banner is the bull;
being thus lauded by him, the one of great splendor granted various boons.
He bestowed the leadership of the Gaṇas upon that Dakṣa of unwearied actions,
and all the gods praised the Supreme Lord, the God of gods.
And the blessed Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā, and all the sages, with palms joined in reverence, each separately praised the one born from the Egg.
They praised the Lord of the gods, the blue-throated one who has the bull as his emblem;
and having bestowed his grace upon those gods, Bhava likewise vanished from sight.
Thus ends the one hundredth chapter, titled "The Destruction of Dakṣa’s Sacrifice by Śiva," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
The sages said:
How did the auspicious Satī become the daughter of Himavat?
And how did she obtain as her husband the Lord Īśvara, the sovereign of the gods?
Sūta said:
O best of the twice-born, that excellent woman Menā, having assumed a body by her own will, was then born as Haimavatī through the power of her ascetic penance.
And the Lord of the Mountain performed all the rites, beginning with the birth-ceremony;
and when twelve years had then been completed, the auspicious daughter of Himavat [was born].
She performed austerities together with her younger sister of auspicious countenance,
as well as another queen, her younger sister, who was indeed honored by all the worlds.
And then all the sages, having surrounded the Goddess— the Great Sovereign of all the worlds— from every side, praised her through their ascetic power.
For Jyeṣṭhā was Aparṇā, and her younger sister was the fair-faced Ekaparṇā;
the third was Varārohā, and likewise Ekapāṭalā.
And by the ascetic power of the great goddess Pārvatī, the Supreme Lord,
Mahādeva Bhava, the master of all beings, was brought under her influence.
At that very time, however, there was a Dānava named Tāraka,
the son of Tārā, possessed of great splendor, and a descendant of Diti.
He had three sons as well: the great asura Tārakākṣa, the lordly Vidyunmālī, and the heroic Kamalākṣa.
Likewise, their grandfather was the very powerful one named Tāra,
who had acquired heroic vigor through ascetic penance by the grace of the Lord Brahmā.
That Tāra, possessed of great splendor, having previously conquered the three worlds including all that is mobile and immobile, also defeated Viṣṇu in battle.
Between the two of them there occurred a most terrible battle that made the hair stand on end;
it lasted for a thousand divine years, day and night, without ceasing.
Taking Viṣṇu along with his chariot, he hurled him a hundred yojanas away;
defeated in battle by Tāra, the one whose banner bears Garuḍa fled.
Having obtained from Tāraka a boon increased a hundredfold and a hundredfold strength,
the son of Diti acquired the entire world from Pitāmaha.
Having conquered the gods headed by Indra, the Lord of the lords of gods restrained those gods in all the worlds through his illusory power (māyā).
And the gods, together with Indra, being tormented by fear of Tāraka, did not find peace; though they were heroes, they were afflicted by terror and found no refuge.
Then the glorious lord of the immortals,
the divine master of the gods, having assembled together, spoke to Aṅgiras in the presence of the gods as well.
"O Blessed One, there is a supreme Dānava named Tāraka, born of Tārā;
by him the Vatsas have been struck down in battle, like cattle by their master."
Out of fear of that, O illustrious Bṛhaspati, these beings wander like birds in a cage, homeless in the great battle.
O best of the Angirasas, those weapons of ours which are never-failing become futile through the power of the enemy of the gods.
For twenty thousand years, O Bṛhaspati,
he fought with Viṣṇu in battle, yet even by him he was not slain.
How can one such as I stand before him in battle— he who was not conquered in combat by the all-powerful Viṣṇu?
Thus addressed by Śakra, Jīva, together with the lords of the gods and the thousand-eyed one, approached the Lord and spoke to Kuśadhvaja.
Having heard this from his mouth, the Grandfather (Brahmā), who removes the distress of those who bow in devotion, spoke to Jīva out of affection, along with all the gods including Indra.
I know of the distress of you, the lords of the gods; nevertheless, listen now:
the goddess Satī, born from the body of Rudra, having censured Dakṣa...
Umā, the daughter of Himavat, was born, she who is honored by all the worlds;
and by her very form, you gods, the best of deities, [are surpassed].
"Exert yourselves to attract the great mind of this Rudra;
through the union of those two, the lord Skanda, the wielder of the spear, shall be born. (LiP 1.101.27)
The six-faced one, twelve-armed, the commander of the army, the son of Agni, the lord,
the son of Svāhā, Kārttikeya, the son of Gaṅgā, and the one born in a reed-thicket.
The god Śākha, Viśākha, and the powerful Naigameśa—
the commander-in-chief known as Kumāra, who is honored by all the worlds.
Even as a child, Mahāsena, having slain the powerful Tārakāsura with mere ease, shall alone deliver the gods.
Thus addressed then by that Brahmā Parameṣṭhin,
Bṛhaspati, together with Indra and the gods, bowed down to that deity.
Having reached the peak of Mount Meru, the one of firm vows remembered Smara;
and by the remembrance of the God of gods, Smara too, along with his wife, [appeared].
O best of the twice-born, having come together with Rati and having paid homage with palms joined in reverence, that life-force of the world addressed Jīva in the presence of Śakra.
"O Jīva, since you have been remembered by me, I have arrived in your presence;
tell me what must be ordained for me," said he who is worshipped by the gods.
The Blessed Śakra, honoring Makaradhvaja, said to him:
"Today, unite Ambikā with Śaṅkara as you please."
Delight with her in that manner by which the Blessed One, whose banner is the bull, takes delight;
follow that path together with this wife, Rati.
But Mahādeva, being pleased, will grant him an auspicious state after he has been previously separated from her, once he has obtained that Umā, the daughter of the mountain.
Having been addressed thus, he paid homage to the God of gods, the Lord of Śacī,
and set his mind upon going to the hermitage of the God of gods together with her.
Then, having gone to the abode of Śambhu together with Rati, the mighty one,
with Vasanta as his companion, became intent on uniting with the God.
Then, beholding Madana, the three-eyed god smiled and looked at him with his third eye with a look of contempt.
Then the fire born from his eye instantly consumed Madana who was standing at his side; at that very moment, Rati lamented piteously.
Having heard the lamentation of Rati, the bull-bannered God of gods,
looking upon the wife of Kāma, spoke with supreme compassion.
"O auspicious lady, although he is formless, your husband will certainly perform every duty for you during the time of sexual union; of this there is no doubt."
When Viṣṇu, the highly illustrious and most radiant Vāsudeva,
shall come into being for the welfare of all the worlds due to the curse of Bhṛgu.
Then he whose son he was shall become your husband;
having bowed to Rudra at that time, she, the wife of Kāma, possessed of a radiant smile, [spoke].
Having obtained Madana, she departed accompanied by Vasanta.
Thus ends the one hundred and first chapter, titled "The Burning of Madana," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
And by the ascetic penance of the great goddess Pārvatī, O bull-bannered Lord,
the blessed Śarva was then pleased at the word of Brahmā.
For the welfare of the hermitages and for the sake of sport, the Blessed Lord Bhava then married the goddess Haimavatī according to the prescribed rites.
The lotus-born Brahmā himself went to the penance grove of the great goddess Pārvatī, accompanied by the great seers such as Marīci.
Having circumambulated that goddess, the source of the world, he asked:
"O daughter of the mountain, for what purpose do you torment the worlds with your asceticism?"
The entire world was created by you; O Mother, do not destroy it.
For you alone sustain all these worlds by your own splendor.
The glorious Bhava is the lord of all gods and the sovereign of all worlds;
indeed, we are but the servants of that God of gods.
That Supreme Lord himself will choose you as his bride,
O Giver of Boons, for he by whom you were created cannot exist without you, O Ambikā.
"There is no doubt that he shall become your husband";
having spoken thus to her, and having repeatedly gazed upon Pārvatī while offering salutations, [he departed].
When the grandfather had departed, the divine Lord Parameśvara went to the hermitage in the form of a brahmin to bestow his grace.
And she, seeing Mahādeva standing in the form of a brahmin,
recognized the Lord through her intuitive insight and other faculties, and bowed down to the bull-bannered god.
Having worshipped the boon-granting god who had arrived in the guise of a brahmin,
Pārvatī praised the Supreme Lord, the Great Sovereign.
Then, having favored the goddess, he spoke as if smiling,
while observing the family duty of the high-souled mountain.
And for the sake of sport among the virtuous, Bhava, the lord of all the gods,
[chose] the great goddess for you at your own-choice marriage ceremony, O most beautiful one.
"Assuming a gentle form, I shall come together with you";
having spoken thus and gazed upon her with his divine eye, the god [vanished].
Then she went to her beloved divine city and departed;
seeing the goddess, the Snowy Mountain was then delighted along with Menā.
Having embraced, smelled the head of, and honored his daughter— who was truly an ascetic—
the God of Gods did not realize that she had been consecrated with mantras.
Then he proclaimed the self-choice marriage of the goddess throughout all the worlds;
and then the blessed Brahmā and Viṣṇu himself, Janārdana, [arrived].
Śakra, the Blessed One Vahni, Bhāskara, and Bhaga; Tvaṣṭṛ, Aryaman, Vivasvat, Yama, and Varuṇa as well.
Vāyu, Soma, as well as Īśāna, the Rudras, and likewise the sages;
the two Aśvins, the twelve Ādityas, the Gandharvas, and Garuḍa as well.
The Yakṣas, Siddhas, as well as Sādhyas, Daityas, Kiṃpuruṣas, and Uragas; the oceans, rivers, Vedas, mantras, hymns and the like, and the moments (kṣaṇas).
All the Nāgas, the mountains, the sacrifices, the sun and other planets,
and the thirty-three gods as well as the three hundred and thirty [deities].
Three [times] three thousand, as well as many other gods,
went to the unsurpassed svayaṃvara of the daughter of the Lord of Mountains.
Then the goddess Śailasutā, having ascended a beautiful golden celestial chariot that was auspicious in every respect and adorned with all kinds of jewels, [departed].
Then the Daughter of the Mountain stood there while being praised by bards,
and she likewise held a white parasol mingled with the rays of jewels.
Mālinī was the daughter of the Mountain King; she was like the twilight with its full orb of the moon, and was surrounded by divine women holding chowries in their hands.
Taking a garland produced from the celestial tree, Jayā stood there;
taking a fan, Vijayā stood near the Goddess.
While the Goddess stood holding the garland in the assembly of the gods,
Mahādeva, whose banner is the bull, became a child for the sake of play.
The blessed Lord Bhava fell fast asleep on the surface of her lap;
then the gods, seeing the infant situated within her lap, [were struck with wonder].
"Who is this here? they consulted together, and having assembled, they were agitated;
the slayer of Vṛtra raised his arm and brought forth his thunderbolt against him.
That arm of his, which had been raised up, remained just as it was,
paralyzed by the God of gods through his effortless play, assuming the form of a child.
He was unable to hurl the vajra nor even to move his arm;
likewise, Agni remained there, unable to hurl his spear.
O best of sages, Yama [holds] the staff and the sword, Nirṛti [the sword],
Varuṇa the serpent-noose, and Samīraṇa the banner-staff.
Soma held a mace, and Dhaneśa, the best among wielders of the staff, held a staff;
likewise, Īśāna stood firm, having raised aloft his fierce trident.
The Rudras were paralyzed with their tridents, the Ādityas with their maces, and likewise the Vasus with their hammers; all those dwellers of heaven were swiftly rendered motionless by the god.
Thus the other dwellers of heaven were paralyzed by the God of gods;
Viṣṇu stood there, brandishing his discus and shaking his head.
The boy rendered even that head motionless;
he was unable to hurl the discus, nor could he move his arms.
Pūṣan, biting his teeth with his teeth, looked at the child in bewilderment;
yet his own teeth fell out as soon as he was seen by Śambhu.
The All-pervading Lord likewise paralyzed their strength, splendor, and yogic power;
and so it was even while those gods remained there, full of wrath.
Brahmā, deeply agitated, entered into meditation and perceived the god Śaṅkara, the Lord Īśāna, seated upon the lap of Umā.
Having recognized the Lord Īśāna, the Grandfather (Brahmā) rose up quickly in amazement;
he prostrated at the feet of Śambhu and offered him praise.
You are the Buddhahood of all the worlds; you are the ego-consciousness, O Lord.
You alone, O Master, are the impeller of the elements and the sense organs.
"I was created from your right hand in the past, O ancient one;
the Lord, the divine Nārāyaṇa, was created from your left hand, O mighty-armed one."
And this Goddess Prakṛti, who is always the cause of your creation,
has come as the cause of the world, assuming the form of a wife.
Salutations to you, O Mahādeva; salutations again and again to the Great Goddess.
By your grace, O Lord of Gods, and by your command, [I have created] the subjects.
These beings, beginning with the gods, have been created as deluded and now bewildered by your yoga;
show them favor so that they may become as they were before.
Sūta said:
Having thus addressed Maheśvara, the God of gods, Brahmā, the lotus-born Lord, was then paralyzed by him; thereupon, the Blessed One spoke.
All you gods are deluded; you do not perceive Śaṅkara, the god of gods, who is honored by all deities, as he approaches here.
"Go quickly for refuge, O gods led by Śakra, all together with Nārāyaṇa and the sages, to the Lord Śaṅkara!"
Together with me, [he approached] the Lord of Gods, the Supreme Self, the Sovereign,
that most excellent being, along with this Haimavatī and Prakṛti.
There, those best of gods were thus paralyzed by him;
together with Nārāyaṇa, they all bowed mentally to the Lord.
Then the three-eyed God of gods, being pleased with them,
the Lord, at the word of Brahmā, quickly restored them as they were before.
Then, once he was thus propitiated, the Lord of Gods assumed a divine body that was supreme and most wonderful, capable of warding off all the gods.
By his splendor, those gods— including Indra, the Moon, and the Sun,
along with Brahmā, the Sādhyas, and likewise Nārāyaṇa— [were overwhelmed].
The Sādhyas and the Rudras sought the All-pervasive One as their eye;
and from Him they received the supreme eye, which possesses the power for all vision.
Śarva, the husband of Ambā, gave [the eye] to Bhavānī and to Cala;
and having then regained their sight, the gods, led by Indra and Viṣṇu, [rejoiced].
Accompanied by Brahmā and Śakra, Brahmā and the others, as well as Bhavānī and the Lord of the Mountains, quickly approached and beheld that Maheśvara.
The sages, the lords of the Gaṇas approved by Śiva, and the Siddhas and Cāraṇas moving through the sky, showered a rain of flowers upon Mahādeva.
The divine drums resounded, the sages praised the Lord,
the chiefs of the Gandharvas sang, and the hosts of Apsaras danced.
All the leaders of the Gaṇas were bewildered, and Ambā Pārvatī rejoiced;
then the Goddess was delighted in the presence of the inhabitants of heaven.
He placed a divine, fragrant garland at his feet;
having exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent!", he was honored right there by that [garland].
Together with the Goddess, all the gods— including Brahmā, along with the yakṣas, uragas, and rākṣasas— paid homage with their heads resting upon the surface of the earth.
Thus ends the one hundred and second chapter, titled "The Self-Choice of Umā," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
Then Brahmā, having paid homage to Mahādeva with palms joined in reverence, said to Maheśvara, "O Lord, let the wedding be performed."
Having heard those words of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin,
the Lord and Master of Beings said to the Lord of the World, "As you wish."
O observers of noble vows, at that very moment, for the sake of Maheśa’s marriage,
Brahmā fashioned a divine, auspicious city made of jewels.
Then there were Aditi, Diti herself, Danu, Kadru, Sukālikā,
Pulomā, Surasā, Siṃhikā, and Vinatā.
She is Siddhi, Māyā, Kriyā, Durgā, the Goddess herself, Sudhā, Svadhā,
Sāvitrī, the Mother of the Vedas, Rajanī, Dakṣiṇā, and Dyuti.
Svāhā, Svāhāmatis, Buddhi, Ṛddhi, Vṛddhi, Sarasvatī,
Rākā, Kuhū, Sinīvālī, and likewise the goddess Anumati.
Dharaṇī, Dhāraṇī, Celā, Śacī, and likewise Nārāyaṇī—
these and other mothers and wives of the gods.
"The wedding of Śaṅkara has begun!"— thus all the serpents, Garuḍas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and Gaṇas departed, filled with joy.
The oceans, mountains, clouds, months, and likewise years;
the Vedas, mantras, as well as sacrifices, hymns, and all duties in their entirety.
The sound *huṃ* and the sacred syllable *oṃ*, as well as thousands of *pratihāra* chants,
and ten million divine apsarases along with their attendants.
And all those rivers that exist in every continent and in the worlds of the gods,
they all assumed female forms and approached him with joyful hearts.
And the highly fortunate Gaṇapas, who are honored by all the worlds,
arrived there filled with joy at the wedding of Śaṅkara.
And ten koṭis of Gaṇeśvaras, white as conch shells, approached;
likewise Keṅkarākṣa with ten, and Vidyut with eight.
Viśākha has sixty-four [hands], Pārayātrika nine,
and the illustrious Sarvāntaka as well as Vikṛtānana each have six.
Jvālākeśa, the preeminent leader of the Gaṇas, is accompanied by twelve crores;
the glorious Samada by seven, and Dundubha by eight.
Kapālīśa has five [attendants], the auspicious Saṃdāraka has six,
and both Gaṇḍaka and Kumbhaka have ten million times ten million here.
O twice-born ones, Viṣṭambha, the leader of the hosts and the most excellent of all beings, is accompanied by eight; Pippala by a thousand; and likewise Saṃnāda.
Āveṣṭana is likewise surrounded by eight [crores], Candratāpana by seven,
and Mahākeśa, the leader of the Gaṇas, is surrounded by a thousand crores.
The hero Kuṇḍī with twelve [attendants], as well as the auspicious Parvataka;
and Kāla, Kālaka, and Mahākāla indeed with a hundred.
Āgnika indeed [is worshipped] with a hundred crores, Koṭyagnimukha with one crore,
Ādityamūrdhā with one crore, and likewise Dhanāvaha with one crore.
Sannāma is with a hundred, Kumuda likewise with ten million, Amogha and Kokila each with ten billion, and Sumantraka with a hundred billion.
Another was Kākapāṭa; the lord Saṃtānaka had sixty sons, each group of sixty;
and there were Mahābala with nine sons, as well as Madhupiṅga and Piṅgala.
Nīla, the lord of gods, with ninety [crores], and likewise Pūrṇabhadra;
and Caturvaktra, of great strength, with seventy crores.
Surrounded by twenty hundred thousand times ten million [attendants],
all those gods likewise arrived there at Śaṅkara Bhava.
Pramatha was accompanied by a thousand bhūtas,
Vīrabhadra by thirty million, and the hair-born [attendants] by sixty-four million.
Karaṇa, Viṃśati, Navati, Kevala-śubha, Pañcākṣa, Śatamanyu, and likewise Meghamanyu.
Kāṣṭhakūṭa with sixty-four, as well as Sukeśa, Vṛṣabha,
the Lord Virūpākṣa, and Sanātana, each with sixty-four.
Tāluketu, Ṣaḍāsya, Pañcāsya, Sanātana, Saṃvartaka, Caitra, and Lakulīśa, the Lord himself.
Lokāntaka, Dīptāsya, and likewise the lord Daityāntaka;
Mṛtyuhṛt, Kālahā, Kāla, and likewise the one who brings about victory over death (Mṛtyuñjayakara).
Viṣāda, Viṣada, Vidyuta, Kāntaka, Prabhu, the god Bhṛṅgī, the illustrious Riṭi, and likewise Devadevapriya.
Aśani and Bhāsaka, with sixty-four thousand feet—
these and other lords of the hosts (gaṇapas) are innumerable and possess great strength.
All of them have a thousand arms, wear crests of matted hair,
are adorned with crescents of the moon, possess blue throats, and have three eyes.
Adorned with necklaces, earrings, armlets, crowns, and other ornaments,
they resemble Brahmā, Indra, and Viṣṇu, and are endowed with the supernatural powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest.
The lords of the Gaṇas, resembling ten million suns, arrived there—
those who roam the netherworld as well as those who dwell in all the worlds.
Tuṃbaru, Nārada, Hāhā, and Hūhū— the chanters of the Sāmaveda—
then arrived at that city, bringing jewels and musical instruments.
There, the sages whose wealth is asceticism, having been praised by the gods, with joyful hearts recited the holy marriage mantras in their entirety.
Then, while the assembly was thus proceeding from all sides,
he himself adorned that daughter of the mountain, who possessed a pure smile.
Keśava himself took [the Lord] and led him into the city; then the Unborn One addressed Hari, the Lord of Gods, Nārāyaṇa, as follows: LiP_1,103.38.
O Lord, you were born first along with Bhavānī and the gods from the left side of this Rudra, while I was born from his right side.
Indeed, the Lord of the Snowy Mountain, who is my own form, was created for the sake of the sacrifice;
this daughter of Himavat was born through the illusory power (*māyā*) of the Supreme Lord.
"He has come here for the purpose of performing rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, and for the sake of marriage;
therefore, he is the sustainer of the worlds, the creator of both you and me."
The world was fashioned by the forms of this god Rudra,
for Bhava is the self of earth, fire, ether, moon, sun, and wind.
Nevertheless, she must be given to him at my word;
for this goat—white, black, and red—is indeed Prakṛti, while you are Bhava.
Even this alliance with the king of mountains is for your own welfare;
for I was born from the navel-lotus in your Padma-kalpa.
"You are the preceptor of this mountain, which is a portion of me, and you are my own preceptor as well.
Sūta said:
"So be it," Janārdana, the God of gods, replied to the Unborn One (Aja).
Then all the gods, the sages, and Śaṅkara, the God of Gods,
as well as the wise Padmanābha, rose up and bowed down to her.
Having washed the feet of the God with both hands, the lotus-eyed one sprinkled the water upon his own head, as well as upon that of Brahmā and the Mountain.
"O Lord of Gods, this Menajā, my younger sister, is yours for the sake of marriage.
Having said this, he gave her, along with water, to the Lord of Gods.
Hari even offered himself along with water to the God;
then all the best of sages, who had reached the further shore of the meaning of all the Vedas, [did likewise].
The giver and the receiver said, "Considering the fruit and the substance, this is surely the god Hara; for by means of his māyā, he [creates] the world."
Having spoken thus, they bowed down to him with their skin bristling with joy;
the sky-dwellers, the Siddhas and Cāraṇas, released showers of flowers.
The celestial drums resounded and throngs of apsarases danced;
and the Vedas, manifest in embodied form, bowed down to that Maheśvara.
Together with Brahmā and the sages,
the god [Śiva] gazed upon the goddess Umā, the daughter of the Snowy Mountain, who was filled with modesty before the God of gods.
And she, whose limbs were faultless, was not satiated with the god who has the bull as his emblem;
he said to Hari, "I am the giver of boons," and Hari likewise spoke to Śaṅkara.
"May devotion to you be gracious," he said, and he bestowed upon him the name Brahmā;
thereafter, Brahmā spoke once more, addressing the Lord with a request.
Standing in the position of my preceptor, I offer the oblation into the fire;
for if you grant me your command, the rite that remains unperformed must indeed be carried out.
To him, Śaṅkara, the God of gods and Lord of the universe, said:
"O best of deities, do whatever you desire, just as you wish."
"I shall carry out every word [you have spoken], O God of gods, Grandfather.
Then, having bowed down with a joyful heart, Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds, [departed].
The Supreme Lord joined the hands of the god and the goddess;
and Agni himself stood there before them with palms joined in reverence.
Having offered oblations with these great Vedic mantras, which have appeared in embodied form, according to the prescribed rule, one should likewise offer parched grains (lājā) in due order.
Having honored the brahmins brought by Viṣṇu with various boons,
he caused him to circumambulate that god Agni three times.
Releasing the joining of their hands, together with all the deities,
the gods, and all human beings, they were filled with joy in their innermost hearts.
The Lord Brahmā bowed to the God of gods, the husband of Umā; then he offered water for the feet to both of them, as well as water for sipping to Śambhu.
Having offered the madhuparka and the cow, and having bowed again to Śiva,
the blessed Lord Brahmā stood there together with the gods led by Indra.
All the sages, beginning with Bhṛgu, having worshipped the Sun and the other deities with unbroken sesame seeds and rice grains, praised the Bull-bannered Lord.
Having completed what was commanded by the gods and having absorbed the fire into himself,
Rudra united with her for the welfare of all the worlds.

He who, with a pure smile, should read or hear this account of Bhava’s marriage, or should cause pure brahmins who have mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences to hear it; ||| LiP_1,103.67 |||
Having attained the status of a leader of the Gaṇas, he rejoices together with Bhava;
for as long as this [mantra] is recited by Brahmins, for that long does Bhava remain there.
Therefore, O twice-born ones, having worshipped according to the rules, one should recite [the names], and not otherwise;
likewise at the marriage of the best of the twice-born and of the Kṣatriyas, O most excellent of the twice-born.
All this, which brings about the crossing over of worldly existence, is most excellent and worthy of praise;
then the bull-bannered god, having performed the marriage with the goddess Haimavatī, [became so].
Accompanied by his retinue and together with Nandin, surrounded by all the hosts of gods,
the one of great splendor arrived at the divine city of Vārāṇasī.
Having bowed to the bull-bannered Lord who was seated comfortably in Avimukta,
Bhavānī, her face radiant with joy, asked about the greatness of that sacred field.
Then Ardhendutilaka spoke: "The supreme majesty of the sacred field, the majesty of Avimukta, cannot indeed be recounted in detail."
O Queen of the Gods, what can I describe to you, who are honored by the hosts of sages, for you, O Goddess, are the source of the fruit of liberation?
Wherein there shall be liberation for sinners from their sins in a single birth after death,
whereas elsewhere, a sin committed elsewhere is removed in Vārāṇasī.
A sin committed in Vārāṇasī brings about the state of a Piśāca and hell;
for men, it is better to undergo the condition of a Piśāca after committing thousands of sins.
But the state of being a thousand Śakras in heaven is not possible without the city of Kāśī,
where the god Triviṣṭapa resides and where the all-pervading Lord Viśveśvara dwells.
"Oṃkāreśa, clad in animal skins, there is no rebirth for those who die [there]," said the moon-crested Lord after briefly describing the majesty of the sacred field.
And having left the garden, he showed [them] the lords of the Gaṇas;
it was right there that the Blessed One, the elephant-faced Vināyaka, was born.
For the sake of creating obstacles for the Daityas and for the removal of obstacles for the gods,
all this, the supreme essence of all narratives, has been told to you.
Everything that I have heard from you all is most excellent, owing to my faith.
Thus ends the one hundred and third chapter, titled "The Description of Pārvatī’s Marriage," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
The sages said:
How did the Leader (Vināyaka) come to have the face of an elephant and become the Lord of the Gaṇas?
O Sūta, you ought to tell us here how his power is such as this.
Sūta said:
O twice-born ones, in the meantime, the gods, including Indra and Upendra, assembled together to create an obstacle to the dharma of the Daityas.
Asuras, Yātudhānas, and Rākṣasas who perform cruel deeds,
as well as others on earth who are characterized by tamas and likewise by rajas.
O Brahmins, having worshipped Maheśvara, Brahmā, and Hari with sacrifices, gifts, and other rites without obstacle, they obtained their desired boons.
Therefore, O best of gods, victory shall always be ours;
whereas for those [others], it will lead to obstacles, while for the dwellers of heaven it shall be without hindrance.
For the sake of obtaining sons for women, and for the successful accomplishment of the rites of men,
you ought to praise Gaṇapa, the Lord of Obstacles, the Creator Śaṅkara.
Having spoken thus, they praised the sinless Lord Śiva, saying:
"Obeisance to you, the soul of all, the omniscient wielder of the Pināka bow!"
To the sinless Viriñca, who grants the fulfillment of the Goddess’s purpose;
to the bodiless one who possesses a body of meaning, and who took away the body of Hari.
Homage to you, who abide in the mandala that is the support of the nectar residing within the body;
homage to you, Kālavega, whose time is divided into the [Yugas] beginning with Kṛta.
Salutations to you who possess the form of Kālāgnirudra, whose eight feet are Dharma and the other [virtues],
whose body is purified by Kālī, and who are the cause of Kālikā.
Salutations to you, the black-throated one, the foremost, the excellent vehicle,
the lord of Ambikā, and the lord of gold.
And salutations indeed to Hiraṇyaretas, and to Śarva, the wielder of the trident,
who bears the skull-bowl, the staff, the noose, the sword, the shield, and the goad.
Salutations to you, the lord of Haimavatī, who are white as gold;
salutations to the one with black trails, who is yellow-white for the sake of protecting the gods.
Salutations to you, who bestow the fruit of the five great sacrifices,
who wear a five-headed serpent as a necklace, and who consist of the five syllables.
Salutations to you, who possess fivefold forms worshipped by the gods of the five states of isolation,
who perceive the five syllables, and who are higher than the highest.
Homage to you, whose faces are the limbs of the sixteen vowels and vajras, who possess an imperishable form, who have the five *ka*-letters in your hands, and who have the *ca*-letters in your hands.
Salutation to Rudra, whose feet begin with the letter *ṭa*, and salutation to you, whose feet begin with the letter *ta*;
salutation to him whose feet are his phallus, who bears the seven constituent elements (*dhātu*) of the body.
Salutations to you, whose form is directly the tranquil Self, who is the destroyer of the Destroyer;
salutations to you, whose body consists of the letters *la*, *ra*, and *ha*, and yet who is without limbs.
Salutations to You, whose eyes are the sun, the moon, and fire; who are the very nature of the Supreme Self; who abide beyond the three qualities; and whose feet are the source of all sacred waters.
Salutations again and again to you, the essence of the truths of the sacred fords, who are even beyond that, the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, and the syllable Oṃ.
To the one who dwells above, having assumed a threefold form within the syllable Oṃ—
to the yellow, the black-colored, and the red one of exceeding splendor.
To you who are established in the five abodes outside the five eggs in sequence—
to Brahmā, to Viṣṇu, and to you, Kumāra, salutations again and again!
Salutations to you, the Supreme Lord of Ambā, who transcends all; salutations to you whose nature is both subtle and fundamental, and who are both gross and subtle.
Salutations again and again to You who are void of all conceptual constructions, who protect from everything, who are void of beginning, middle, and end, and who abide as pure consciousness.
Salutations to you, who are eternally worshipped in every direction by Yama, Agni, Vāyu, Rudra, Varuṇa, Soma, Śakra, and the night-stalkers, together with their hosts.
Salutations to you, who are worshipped by all at all times on every path; to you,
Rudra, the blue-hued Rudra, the one who dispels evil,
the wise one, to Maheśvara, the steadfast, salutations to you, Śiva himself.

"Now listen, O Blessed One, to that which was told under the guise of praise by the lords of the gods and asuras, headed by Indra; forgive the various deeds [of yours] such as the destruction of the sacrifice, of Madana, of Yama, of Agni, and of Dakṣa’s sacrifice. Sūta said:
