The wise man who recites this hymn with devotion, or causes it to be heard, has it proclaimed by the gods headed by Śakra and Agni; he goes to the supreme goal.
Thus ends the one hundred and fourth chapter, titled "The Praise of the Deity," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
When the lords of the gods stood there having thus bowed to the Lord,
then Bhava, the husband of Ambikā, the wielder of the Pināka bow, Maheśvara—
In an instant, Bhava cast his gaze upon those best of gods;
the gods, their eyes moist with joy, bowed with reverence to Hara.
Then Maheśvara, gazing upon the lords of the gods with glances resembling nectar and ambrosia, said: "May it be well with you."
"O Lord, these gods have come to your abode seeking a boon.
Having observed his master, the fearless Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati) bowed and spoke.
For you have always been entreated without hindrance by Suretara and others who act for the harm of the gods, so that all their undertakings may succeed.
Therefore, may you be gracious; this very [obstacle] which causes such great impediments is our boon here for those who have done harm to the gods.
Then, having heard that, Śiva, the wielder of the Pināka bow and lord of the gods,
assumed the form of the lord of the Gaṇas, the lord of the gods.
And the lords of the Gaṇas and the lords of the gods praised Maheśvara,
the auspicious source of all worlds and the remover of the suffering of existence.
Then Ambikā [beheld] Gajānana, who is seated upon the elephant-faced one, the bestower of boons, bearing a trident and a noose, and the source of all the worlds.
Then the Siddhas, the lords of sages, the sky-dwellers, and the hosts of gods rained down a shower of flowers;
and at that time, the lords of the gods, free from weariness, praised the One-Tusked One and bowed to Gaṇeśa, the Great Lord.
Then, having emerged from those two, that most terrifying boy, the personified abode of all auspiciousness, stood there and danced.
Adorned with various garments and ornaments, Gajānana,
the son of Maheśvara, paid homage to his father and Ambikā.
Upon seeing his son as soon as he was born, the Blessed Lord Bhava himself, the sovereign of all, performed for Gajānana all the rites that were to be done.
And Bhava himself, the Great God and Teacher of the World, taking him with his two very pleasant hands, embraced him and smelled the crown of his head.
O my son, your descent is for the destruction of the Daityas and for the benefit of the gods and the twice-born who discourse on Brahman.
And for that man on the surface of the earth by whom a sacrifice has been performed devoid of sacrificial fees,
create an obstacle to his merit while you remain on the path to heaven.
Teaching, studying, exposition, and ritual action—
always seize the life-breaths of whoever performs these in this world unjustly.
O bull among men, O Lord, take away the lives of those women and men who have fallen from their caste and who are devoid of their own dharma.
O Vināyaka, you ought to grant equality with yourself to those women and men who always worship you at all times.
O Lord of the Host of Children, being worshipped here and in the hereafter, protect all your devotees with every effort— whether they be youths, those in their prime, or the elderly.
Indeed, throughout all three worlds here, you shall undoubtedly become the Lord of the hosts of obstacles (Vighneśvara), worthy of worship and salutation.
O son, you shall become worthy of worship even before me, Nārāyaṇa, and Brahmā as well; indeed, the Brahmins shall worship you with sacrifices.
If one performs an auspicious rite— whether prescribed by the Vedas (śrauta), the Smṛtis (smārta), or worldly custom (laukika)— without first worshipping you,
that auspicious act will turn into an inauspicious one for him.

O Gajānana, having been worshipped by Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras alike with auspicious foods such as snacks and meals for the sake of attaining all perfections (siddhis), [one should proceed].
Without first worshipping you with perfumes, flowers, incense, and other offerings, there is nothing whatsoever to be obtained anywhere in the three worlds, even by the gods or others.
Those people who worship Vināyaka shall undoubtedly become worthy of worship even by Śakra and the other gods.
Whether it be Aja, Hari, me, Śakra, or even other gods—
if those seeking rewards do not worship you, you shall afflict them with obstacles.
Then the Lord Gaṇapati created a host of obstacles;
having prostrated along with his attendants, he stood before him.
From that time forward, people in this world have worshipped Gaṇeśvara;
furthermore, that Gaṇeśvara created obstacles to the dharma of the Daityas.
All this has been told to you concerning the origin of Skanda’s elder brother;
whoever reads it, hears it, or causes it to be heard shall become happy.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifth chapter, titled "The Origin of Vināyaka," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
The sages said:
O Śambhu, you ought to tell us exactly how and for what purpose the commencement of the dance occurred; we have already heard of the birth of Skanda’s elder brother.
Sūta said:
Dāruka, born of an asura and having acquired prowess through ascetic penance,
began to slaughter the gods and the best of the twice-born like the fire of cosmic destruction.
Then Dāruka struck the gods, afflicting them severely—
namely Brahmā, Īśāna, Kumāra, and Viṣṇu as well.
Having approached Yama and Indra, the Asura was told by Brahmā and the other gods— who stood ready for battle, assuming female forms and offering praise— that he was to be slain by a woman.
Having been defeated by him, all those twice-born ones approached Brahmā; having informed him of everything, they went with him to the Lord of Umā.
Having arrived, all of them, led by the Grandfather (Brahmā), offered praise;
and Brahmā, having reached the Lord of Gods, bowed down many times with deep humility.
The Lord is Dāruṇa; formerly, the Dāru demons were conquered by him.
Having slain the Daitya Dāruka, who is to be slain by a woman, you ought to protect us.
Having heard the request of Brahmā, the Blessed One, the Lord of Gods who destroyed the eyes of Bhaga,
spoke to the Goddess Girijā as if smiling.
"O auspicious one, O fair-faced lady, I entreat you today for the welfare of the worlds, for the sake of slaying this Dāruka, who is to be killed by a woman."
Then, having heard his words, she— the source of the world,
the mistress of the gods, and intent upon taking birth— entered the body of the god.
Having entered the Lord of Gods, the best of deities, with one part,
Brahmā and the gods led by Indra did not perceive it at that time.
Seeing the auspicious Girijā standing by Śambhu’s side as before,
even the four-faced one, though omniscient, was deluded by her illusory power (māyā).
Having entered the body of that God of gods, Pārvatī then made her own body one with his by means of the poison located in his throat.
And having perceived her to be such with his third eye,
the Enemy of Kama indeed created Kali— she who has a dark throat and wears her hair in a matted lock.
When she was born with a dark throat, then a vast glory of victory arose;
for the gods were invincible due to her lack of success, yet there was satisfaction for Bhavānī and the Supreme Lord.

Then, seeing her born like a blazing fire, adorned with black ornaments and a dark throat, the hosts of gods and siddhas fled in fear; even those led by Upendra, Padmodbhava, and Śakra were struck with terror.
In the same way, an eye appeared on his forehead, a brilliant crescent moon upon his head,
a formidable and sharp trident at his throat, and fierce ornaments upon his hand.
Together with the goddesses, clad in divine garments and adorned with all ornaments,
the lords of the Siddhas, the Siddhas, and likewise the Piśācas were born once again.
At the command of that Pārvatī, the Supreme Goddess caused the Dānava— who was slaughtering the lords of the gods— to be destroyed by means of Dāruka.
O best of Brahmins, due to her excessive intensity of agitation, this entire world then became distressed by the fire of her wrath.
Lord Bhava, in order to drink the fire of her wrath through his illusory power, wept in the form of a child in a cremation ground crowded with hungry ghosts.
O brahmins, seeing that young lord, she was deluded by his illusory power; having raised him up and smelled his head, she gave him her breast to suck.
Then he drank her breast-born milk along with her anger;
indeed, by means of this wrath, the child became the protector of the fields.
And there were eight forms of that wise Kṣetrapāla as well;
thus indeed was she made by that boy, who was overcome with rage.
At twilight, the trident-bearing God of gods, being pleased, performed the *tāṇḍava* dance for the sake of her grace, together with all the lords of beings and the *pretas*.
Having drunk the nectar of Śambhu’s dance to the very brim, that supreme goddess and the yoginīs danced at ease in the abode of the spirits.
There, the gods, including Brahmā, Indra, and Upendra, bowed down from all sides and praised Kālī and the goddess Pārvatī once again.
Thus has the *tāṇḍava* of the Lord who wields the trident been briefly described;
others say that the *tāṇḍava* of the Lord was performed by Yogānanda as well.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventh chapter, titled "The Narration of Śiva’s Tāṇḍava Dance," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
The sages said:
O Sūta, you ought to tell me now how Upamanyu obtained the status of a leader of Gaṇas from Maheśvara and how he attained the Ocean of Milk.
Sūta said:
When the three-eyed Lord had thus rebuked Kālī and departed,
Upamanyu, having worshipped him, obtained the fruit through his ascetic penance.
O best of the twice-born, there was a sage known as Upamanyu,
who, radiant like Kumāra, was playing at his own will.
Once, while he was drinking a small amount of milk in his maternal uncle’s hermitage,
the son of the maternal uncle drank the finest milk out of envy.
Having drunk as much as he desired and remaining there, he saw his mother and said to her:
"O Mother, O Mother, O highly fortunate one, O ascetic woman, give [it] to me!"
"I bow to the cow's milk, which is exceedingly sweet, not meager, and warm.
Sūta said:
Having been thus cherished by her son, she affectionately embraced her son.
Distressed and afflicted, she lamented, remembering her own poverty;

and remembering again and again, O twice-born ones, the highly effulgent Upamanyu, weeping, said to her, "Give me milk! Give me milk!"* LiP 1.107.7 *The original text contains the Sanskrit term *dehi*.
Then, having herself ground the seeds obtained through the practice of gleaning, she,
speaking with the sweet voice of a young elephant, mixed that ground seed with water.
Then, saying "Come, come, my son! with gentle words, she embraced her son, and overcome with grief, she gave him artificial milk to drink.
And having drunk the artificial milk given by his mother, O best of the twice-born,
he became extremely distressed and said to his mother, "This is not milk."
Then, filled with sorrow, she spoke after gazing at him, smelling his head,
and wiping her son’s lotus-like eyes with both hands.
Those rivers filled with jewels, which range through the realms of heaven and the netherworld,
are not seen by those devoid of fortune and those devoid of devotion to Śiva.
They do not obtain kingdom, heaven, liberation, or food produced from milk—things they hold dear; yet Bhava is never satisfied with them.
Everything arises from grace toward Bhava, not from grace toward other deities;
those devoted to other gods wander about, afflicted by suffering.
"O son, how could we have milk there? For in a previous birth, Mahādeva was not worshipped by us; indeed, having raised up Śiva, [the merit] was given away."
"Only that is obtainable, and nothing else, even by lifting up the Lord Viṣṇu himself.
Having heard these words of his mother, the highly effulgent Upamanyu—
Even the boy, having prostrated before his ascetic mother, said:
"O illustrious lady, abandon your grief if Mahādeva exists anywhere."
"Whether it takes a long time or even a short time, I shall accomplish the churning of the Ocean of Milk.
Sūta said:
Having bowed to her and spoken thus, he proceeded to perform penance.
His mother said to her son, "Perform what is most auspicious.
Having been granted permission by her, he performed there a very difficult penance.
Having reached the Himavat mountain, he subsisted on air alone with a concentrated mind;
by the ascetic power of that brahmin, the entire world was purified.
Having bowed down, all those best of gods spoke to Hari;
then, having heard their words, the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, [replied].
Thinking, "What is this? and having understood its cause, he went quickly to Mount Mandara out of a desire to see Maheśvara.
Having seen the god and bowed down, he spoke thus with palms joined in reverence:
"O Blessed One, there is a certain brahmin known as Upamanyu."
"Restrain him by means of ascetic penance so that he does not consume everything for the sake of milk.
In the meantime, the god Pinākin, the Supreme Lord,
then resolved to go there, assuming the form of Śakra.
Then Sadāśiva himself, having assumed the body of the King of the Immortals, went to the ascetic grove of the sage on a magnificent white elephant,
accompanied by gods, asuras, siddhas, and great serpents.
Having mounted that elephant together with Vivasvat, who held a yak-tail fan,
and holding with one hand the lord of the gods accompanied by Śacī on his left, and with the other hand a white parasol,
the blessed Soma, in the form of Śakra, shone as Sadāśiva.
Like Mount Mandara with its white parasol, which resembles the orb of the moon.
Having thus assumed the very form of Śakra, the Supreme Lord went to the hermitage of Upamanyu in order to bestow his grace upon him.
Having seen that Supreme Lord Śiva assuming the form of Śakra,
the sage himself bowed his head and spoke, O best of sages.
This hermitage of mine has been purified by the Lord of Gods himself;
Śakra, the Lord of the World, the Blessed One, the powerful Sun, has arrived.
Seeing the twice-born man standing thus with his palms joined in reverence after he had spoken,
Hara, assuming the form of Śakra, spoke in a deep voice.
"I am pleased with you; choose a boon, O observer of noble vows, on account of this asceticism.
O eldest brother of Dhaumya, O high-minded one, I shall grant you all that you desire."
Thus addressed by Śakra at that time, the best of sages, with palms joined in reverence, said: "I choose devotion to Śiva."

Then, having heard the words of the sage, the Lord himself, assuming the form of Śakra, spoke with agitation as if enraged: LiP_1,107.34: "Then, having heard the words of the sage, the Lord himself, assuming the form of Śakra, spoke with agitation as if enraged."
"O divine sage, you do not know me— Śakra, the king of the gods, the lord, the sovereign of the three worlds, who is saluted by all the gods."
"O brahmin-sage, become my devotee; worship me alone at all times.
I shall grant you everything; may it be well with you; abandon Rudra, who is devoid of qualities."
Then, having heard Śakra’s words which were ear-tearing,
Upamanyu spoke this while chanting the auspicious five-syllabled mantra.
I believe that some lowest of Daityas has surely come here in person in the form of Śakra, for no other reason than to create an obstacle to dharma.

Everything was indeed told by you yourself, who were intent on censuring the Lord, concerning the state of being devoid of qualities (nirguṇatva) of the Great-Souled God of gods, as it arose in the course of conversation.
What is the use of saying much more here? Today I have inferred a great evil committed in another life, for you have heard a censure of Śiva.
Having heard this censure of worldly existence, he should then renounce it at that very moment;
having swiftly slain his own body, he goes to the world of Śiva.
But he who would pluck out the tongue of one devoted to reviling Śiva,
having delivered twenty-one generations of his family, goes to the world of Śiva.
"Let alone my desire for the milk of this lowest of gods;
having slain you with the Śiva-weapon, I shall cast off this body."
"Long ago it was told by my mother that this is indeed the truth, without a doubt:
'In a previous birth, the Lord was not worshipped by us.'"
Having spoken thus to that god, Upamanyu,
the knower of mantras, fearlessly set his mind on killing Śakra with the Atharva weapon.
Then the one of great splendor, taking a handful of ashes from the receptacle of ashes,
discharged the Atharva weapon at him and let out a roar.
Then, having meditated upon the fire-element concentration (dhāraṇā) in order to burn his own body,
he of great splendor stood there, imperishable like dry fuel.
When the brahmin had thus resolved, the Blessed One, the destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes,
restrained that yogin’s concentration with gentleness.
Then, by the command of Nandin, that Atharva weapon of his, which resembled the fire of cosmic destruction, was withdrawn by Candraka.
Assuming his own true form, the Supreme Lord, the Blessed One,
revealed himself to the brahmin, adorned with the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
(Śchlaraffenland) A thousand streams of milk and the ocean of milk itself,
as well as the ocean of curds and so forth, and the ocean of clarified butter; LiP_1,107.51 //
And for the child, there were oceans of fruit as well as oceans of various kinds of food,
and mountains of cakes likewise stood on all sides.
The compassionate Lord, seeing Girijā smiling and looking upon Upamanyu with compassion, spoke with a smile to him who was surrounded by his kinsmen.
"Enjoy pleasures as you desire, and behold your kinsmen, my child;
O illustrious Upamanyu, for this Pārvatī is indeed your mother.
Today I have made you my son, and likewise, the Ocean of Milk has been granted to you."
And there was an ocean of honey, and likewise an ocean of curd.
There was an ocean of clarified butter and boiled rice, as well as an ocean of fruits and syrups;
there were mountains of cakes, and furthermore, an ocean of various kinds of foods and edibles.
O sage, Mahādeva is indeed your father and the father of the worlds;
your mother is the illustrious Mother of the World—of this there is no doubt.
"Immortality has been granted by me, as well as the eternal status of a leader of the Gaṇas (Gāṇapatya). Choose boons; I shall grant them—there is no need for hesitation in this matter."
Having spoken thus, the omnipresent Great God Bhava took him by both hands, smelled his head, and then presented him to the Goddess.
O best of the twice-born, having beheld her son, the daughter of the mountain king, being then pleased, bestowed upon him the power of yoga and the knowledge of Brahman.
Having obtained that boon from her and eternal youth as well,
he too praised Mahādeva with a voice faltering with joy.
Then, having joined his palms in reverence and prostrating again and again, he chose the excellent one with dustless eyes as his boon.
Be gracious, O Lord of the gods; may there be unwavering faith in you, O Mahādeva, and may your presence be with me at all times.
Thus addressed by him, Śaṅkara, as if smiling,
granted the desired boon to the brahmin and vanished right there.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventh chapter, titled "The Account of Upamanyu," in the first part of the glorious *Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa*.
The sages said:
He was seen by Vāsudeva Kṛṣṇa, whose actions are effortless;
thereafter, the elder brother of Dhaumya obtained the divine Pāśupata vow.
O Sūta, you ought to relate that sin-destroying narrative: how was that knowledge then obtained by the wise Kṛṣṇa?
Sūta said:
Although the eternal Vāsudeva had descended by his own will,
he performed the purification of his body while indeed disparaging human nature.
For the sake of obtaining a son, the Blessed One went there to perform austerities,
and he beheld that sage in the hermitage of Upamanyu.
O brahmins, having seen that elder brother of Dhaumya,
Kṛṣṇa paid homage to him with great reverence, performing the circumambulation three times.
By the mere sight of that wise sage Kṛṣṇa,
all impurity— both that born of the body and likewise that born of action— was utterly destroyed.
Having performed the smearing with ashes, Upamanyu, of great luster, [worshipped] him,
O best of Brahmins, with the mantras beginning with "Agni" and "Vāyu" in due order.
With a delighted mind, he bestowed the divine Pāśupata knowledge;
O twice-born ones, that venerable Kṛṣṇa [attained it] through the grace of the sage in the Pāśupata tradition.
But at the end of one year, through his ascetic penance, having beheld the god Maheśvara together with Ambā and his attendants, he undisturbedly obtained a son of his own.
From that time forward, all those divine sages of firm vows, devoted to the Pāśupata path, remained constantly surrounding that Kṛṣṇa.
And I shall further describe another method for the constant liberation of living beings:
having fashioned a golden girdle, one should hold it as a support while carrying a staff.
A golden pedestal, a fan, and a handle—these may be made by men or women; likewise, an ink-pot and a pen [should be provided].
Razors, scissors,
and even a vessel should be given to the Pāśupata, whose body is smeared with ashes.
A wise person should offer a vessel made of gold, silver, or even copper, and worship the yogin according to his own means and wealth.
All of them, liberated from sin along with their entire families, go to the divine abode of Rudra; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
Therefore, by this gift, a householder is liberated from worldly existence;
through the bestowing of gifts upon yogins, Śiva quickly becomes propitious.
If one desires supreme liberation, one should give away the kingdom, a son, wealth, a noble horse, a vehicle, or even one's entire possession.
With this unstable body, one should strive to accomplish that which is stable—
the eternal Pāśupata state, which is auspicious and delivers one from the ocean of saṃsāra.
All this has been told to you in brief, and there is no doubt about it;
whoever reads or even hears this goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the one hundred and eighth chapter in the Pūrvabhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
